| Outcome exists         | Is the label recorded, unambiguously?        | Count labelled rows per month        |
| Sufficient history     | Enough events, covering enough seasons?      | Events per period, minority count    |
| Grain matches          | Does the data's unit match the decision's?   | Compare keys to the framing doc      |
| Available at inference | Is each feature known before scoring?        | Timeline test per feature            |
| Legal and ethical      | May it be used for this purpose?             | Review with legal and privacy        |
| Signal plausible       | Any relationship at all in a quick check?    | Simple model on a sample             |
| Decision ready         | Is someone waiting to act on the output?     | Name the owner and the campaign date |

```python
# A one-day feasibility spike. If this fails, do not start the project.

# 1. Label volume: rare outcomes need far more rows than people expect.
labels = df.groupby(df["event_month"])["churned"].agg(["size", "sum"])
print(labels.tail(12))
# Rule of thumb: fewer than a few hundred minority events total means the
# project is a data-collection problem before it is a modelling problem.

# 2. Timeline test: every feature must predate the scoring moment.
for col, populated_at in FEATURE_TIMESTAMPS.items():
    if (populated_at > SCORING_MOMENT).any():
        print(f"LEAK RISK: {col} is sometimes populated after scoring")

# 3. Signal check: a quick model on a sample. Not to be accurate, but to
# distinguish "no signal" from "needs work".
quick = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_iter=60).fit(X_s, y_s)
print(f"sample AUC = {roc_auc_score(y_hold, quick.predict_proba(X_hold)[:,1]):.3f}")
# ~0.50 after honest feature work suggests the predictors are unrelated
# to the label as defined -- revisit the framing, not the algorithm.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A feasibility spike costs days and routinely prevents quarters of wasted
>   work.
> - Check availability at prediction time, not just presence in the
>   warehouse; the difference is a leak.
> - Rare outcomes turn modelling problems into data-collection problems.
> - Organizational readiness is a feasibility criterion: without a waiting
>   decision and a named owner, the output will not be used.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Run the timeline test on five features from a project you know and flag
>    any that could not be computed at scoring time.
> 2. Write a feasibility checklist for predicting equipment failure in a
>    factory with two years of sensor data and nine recorded failures.
> 3. Interview: A stakeholder wants to predict which employees will be high
>    performers before hiring. Assess feasibility. (Hint: consider what the
>    label really measures and who is missing from the training data.)

<a id="2-mathematical-foundations"></a>
## 2. Mathematical Foundations

This chapter covers the mathematics that every later technique quietly
depends on: linear algebra for representing and transforming data, calculus
and optimization for fitting models, probability for reasoning about
uncertainty, and information theory for measuring how much a signal tells
you. You do not need to derive these results from scratch, but you do need to
recognize them, because almost every modelling failure later in the book is a
violation of an assumption stated here.

<a id="21-linear-algebra"></a>
### 2.1 Linear Algebra

Linear algebra is the language of data representation: a dataset is a matrix,
a model is often a transformation, and most efficient algorithms are matrix
operations in disguise.

#### Vectors and Vector Spaces

A dataset row is a list of numbers: age 34, income 52000, tenure 19. Treating
that list as a point in space, rather than three unrelated facts, is the move
that makes the whole subject useful. Once rows are points, "similar
customers" becomes "nearby points", "a trend" becomes "a direction", and
"redundant features" becomes "points that lie on a lower-dimensional sheet".

A *vector* is an ordered list of numbers. Geometrically it is an arrow from
the origin to a point, which gives it two readings: a location, and a
direction with a magnitude. Both readings are used constantly. A data row is
a location. A gradient is a direction.

A *vector space* is the set of all vectors you can build from a starting set
using two operations: adding vectors, and scaling them by a number. Being
closed under these operations is what makes the space well-behaved. The
*span* of a set of vectors is everything reachable this way.

Two related ideas matter for data work. Vectors are *linearly independent* if
none of them can be built from the others; if one can, it adds no new
direction and is redundant. A *basis* is a minimal set that spans the space,
and its size is the *dimension*.

An analogy: a basis is a set of ingredients. Flour, water, and salt span a
range of doughs. Adding "flour again, but pre-measured" adds no new dough you
could not already make, which is exactly what linear dependence means.

```text
  VECTORS AS ARROWS AND AS DATA ROWS

        y
        ^
      4 |          * b = (3, 4)
        |         /|
      3 |        / |
        |       /  |          a + b = (5, 5)
      2 |      /   |            . - - - - - *
        |     /    |          /
      1 |    /     |  * a = (2, 1)
        |   /   ___/__/
      0 +--/---/-------------------> x
        0  1  2   3   4   5

  Same object, two readings:
    location  -> "a customer with 2 years tenure and 1 support ticket"
    direction -> "move 2 right and 1 up"

  SPAN of {a} is the infinite line through a.
  SPAN of {a, b} is the whole plane, because a and b are independent.
  SPAN of {a, 2a} is still just the line: 2a adds nothing.
```

```python
import numpy as np

a = np.array([2, 1])
b = np.array([3, 4])

print(a + b)        # [5 5]  -- tip-to-tail addition
print(3 * a)        # [6 3]  -- scaling changes magnitude, not direction
print(a @ b)        # 10     -- dot product: 2*3 + 1*4

# Independence check: stack as rows and ask for the rank.
# rank = number of genuinely distinct directions present.
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(np.vstack([a, b])))      # 2 -> independent
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(np.vstack([a, 2 * a])))  # 1 -> dependent

# Why this matters on real data: a redundant feature is a dependent column.
X = np.array([
    [1.0, 2.0, 3.0],     # feature 3 = feature 1 + feature 2, exactly
    [2.0, 1.0, 3.0],
    [4.0, 5.0, 9.0],
])
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(X))   # 2, not 3 -- one column is redundant
# Linear regression on this X has no unique solution. The redundancy is
# not a nuisance to clean up later; it breaks the model outright.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Treating rows as points in space turns similarity, trend, and redundancy
>   into geometric questions.
> - A vector reads both as a location (a data row) and as a direction (a
>   gradient or a trend).
> - Linear dependence means a vector adds no new direction, which on a data
>   matrix means a redundant feature.
> - The dimension of a space is the size of its basis, and matrix rank counts
>   the distinct directions actually present.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. By hand, determine whether `(1, 2)`, `(2, 4)`, and `(0, 1)` span the
>    plane. Verify with `matrix_rank`.
> 2. Construct a 4-by-4 data matrix whose rank is 3, and say which column is
>    redundant and why.
> 3. Interview: A colleague one-hot encodes a three-category feature into
>    three columns and adds an intercept, and the regression fails. What
>    happened? (Hint: sum the three dummy columns and compare to the
>    intercept column.)

#### Matrix Operations

A matrix is a grid of numbers, but that description hides why it matters. A
matrix does two jobs in data science, and keeping them separate prevents most
confusion. First, it *stores* a dataset: rows are observations, columns are
features. Second, it *acts* as a transformation: multiplying a vector by a
matrix rotates, scales, projects, or otherwise moves it.

Matrix multiplication is the operation that makes the second reading work.
The product `AB` is defined so that applying `AB` to a vector is the same as
applying `B` first and then `A`. The mechanical rule follows from that: the
entry at row `i`, column `j` of `AB` is the dot product of row `i` of `A`
with column `j` of `B`. Inner dimensions must match, which is the single most
common source of runtime errors in numerical code.

Two properties surprise newcomers. Multiplication is *not commutative*: `AB`
and `BA` are usually different and may not both exist. It *is* associative,
which is what allows the optimization of reordering a chain of products.

An analogy: matrices are verbs, not nouns. "Rotate then stretch" is a
different instruction from "stretch then rotate", which is exactly why order
matters.

```text
  SHAPE ALGEBRA -- the rule that prevents most errors

     A          B          AB
  (m x n) @ (n x p)  =  (m x p)
        \      /
         must match

  Example: predictions = X @ w
     X: (1000 x 5)   1000 rows, 5 features
     w: (5 x 1)      one weight per feature
     ->  (1000 x 1)  one prediction per row

  A MATRIX AS A TRANSFORMATION

   unit square        after A = [[2, 1],      sheared and
                                 [0, 1]]      stretched
   (0,1) +----+ (1,1)             (1,1) +------+ (3,1)
         |    |          --->           /      /
         |    |                        /      /
   (0,0) +----+ (1,0)           (0,0) +------+ (2,0)

  The columns of A are where the basis vectors land:
  column 1 = (2,0) is the image of (1,0); column 2 = (1,1) is the image
  of (0,1). Reading a matrix by its columns tells you what it does.
```

```python
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[2, 1],
              [0, 1]])
B = np.array([[1, 0],
              [3, 1]])

print(A @ B)        # [[5 1]  matrix product: apply B, then A
                    #  [3 1]]
print(B @ A)        # [[2 1]  DIFFERENT: order changes the result
                    #  [6 4]]
print(A * B)        # [[2 0]  element-wise, NOT matrix multiplication
                    #  [0 1]]  -- a frequent and silent bug

# The three multiplications above are all legal and all mean different
# things. Only `@` composes transformations.

X = np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=(1000, 5))
w = np.array([0.5, -1.2, 0.0, 2.0, 0.3])

preds = X @ w                     # (1000,5) @ (5,) -> (1000,)
print(preds.shape)                # (1000,)

# Associativity is a real performance lever, not a curiosity:
# (X @ W1) @ W2  vs  X @ (W1 @ W2) give identical results at very
# different costs when the inner matrices are small.
W1 = np.random.default_rng(1).normal(size=(5, 5))
W2 = np.random.default_rng(2).normal(size=(5, 5))
np.allclose((X @ W1) @ W2, X @ (W1 @ W2))   # True -- but time them
```

| Operation        | Notation      | Shape rule                  | Meaning                     |
| ---------------- | ------------- | --------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| Addition         | `A + B`       | identical shapes            | Element-wise sum            |
| Scalar multiple  | `c * A`       | any                         | Scale every entry           |
| Element-wise     | `A * B`       | identical (or broadcastable)| Hadamard product            |
| Matrix product   | `A @ B`       | `(m,n) @ (n,p)`             | Compose transformations     |
| Transpose        | `A.T`         | `(m,n)` becomes `(n,m)`     | Swap rows and columns       |
| Matrix-vector    | `A @ v`       | `(m,n) @ (n,)`              | Transform a vector          |

> Key Takeaways
> - A matrix both stores a dataset and acts as a transformation; keep the two
>   readings distinct.
> - Matrix multiplication composes transformations, so it is associative but
>   not commutative.
> - The columns of a matrix are the images of the basis vectors, which is the
>   fastest way to read what it does.
> - `A * B` and `A @ B` are both legal and mean different things, which makes
>   the confusion silent rather than loud.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Multiply a `(3,4)` by a `(4,2)` matrix by hand for one entry, then check
>    the whole product with NumPy.
> 2. Find a 2-by-2 matrix that rotates the plane 90 degrees, by deciding where
>    `(1,0)` and `(0,1)` must land.
> 3. Interview: You must compute `A @ B @ C` where shapes are `(1000,2)`,
>    `(2,1000)`, and `(1000,2)`. Which grouping do you choose and why? (Hint:
>    count the multiplications each order performs.)

#### Matrix Inverse and Rank

Solving a linear system means undoing a transformation: given `Ax = b`, find
the `x` that `A` turned into `b`. The *inverse* `A^-1` is the transformation
that undoes `A`, so that `A^-1 A x = x`. When it exists, the solution is
`x = A^-1 b`.

The catch is that most matrices have no inverse, and understanding when is
more useful than knowing the formula. A transformation can be undone only if
it loses no information. If `A` squashes two distinct inputs onto the same
output, there is no way to recover which one you started from. Such a matrix
is *singular*.

*Rank* is what measures this. The rank of a matrix is the number of linearly
independent columns, which is the dimension of the space its outputs live in.
A square `n`-by-`n` matrix is invertible exactly when its rank is `n`, called
*full rank*. Lower rank means the transformation collapsed the space.

The practically important case is the near-singular matrix: technically
invertible but numerically hopeless. The *condition number* measures this. A
high condition number means tiny changes in `b` cause huge changes in `x`, so
the solution is meaningless in floating point.

```text
  RANK AS INFORMATION LOSS

  Full rank (rank 2)              Rank deficient (rank 1)
  A = [[2, 0],                    A = [[2, 4],
       [0, 3]]                         [1, 2]]

    plane -> plane                   plane -> line
                                      \
   +----+      +------+                \  every input lands on
   |    |  ->  |      |                 \ one line; infinitely many
   +----+      +------+                  \ inputs share an output
                                          \
  invertible: each output              singular: cannot invert,
  came from exactly one input          information was destroyed

  IN DATA TERMS
  rank deficiency in X'X means two features are (nearly) redundant,
  so the regression cannot decide how to split the credit between them.
```

```python
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[2.0, 0.0],
              [0.0, 3.0]])
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(A))      # 2 -> full rank, invertible
print(np.linalg.inv(A))              # [[0.5, 0], [0, 0.333]]

S = np.array([[2.0, 4.0],
              [1.0, 2.0]])           # column 2 = 2 * column 1
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(S))      # 1 -> singular
# np.linalg.inv(S)  -> LinAlgError: Singular matrix

# The dangerous case is NEARLY singular, which raises no error at all.
N = np.array([[1.0, 1.0],
              [1.0, 1.0000001]])
print(f"condition number = {np.linalg.cond(N):.3e}")   # ~4e+07
b = np.array([2.0, 2.0])
x1 = np.linalg.solve(N, b)
x2 = np.linalg.solve(N, b + np.array([0.0, 1e-6]))     # tiny perturbation
print(x1, x2)     # wildly different answers from nearly identical inputs

# Practical rule: never invert to solve a system. `solve` is faster and
# numerically better than forming the inverse and multiplying.
x = np.linalg.solve(A, b)            # preferred
x_bad = np.linalg.inv(A) @ b         # works, but slower and less stable

# For rank-deficient or ill-conditioned systems, use the pseudo-inverse,
# which returns the minimum-norm least-squares solution instead of failing.
print(np.linalg.pinv(S) @ b)
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A matrix is invertible exactly when it destroys no information, which is
>   equivalent to having full rank.
> - Rank counts independent columns and therefore the true dimensionality of
>   the transformation's output.
> - Near-singular matrices raise no error but produce meaningless solutions;
>   check the condition number.
> - Use `solve` rather than forming an explicit inverse, and `pinv` when the
>   system is rank deficient.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a 3-by-3 matrix of rank 2 and confirm that `inv` fails while
>    `pinv` returns an answer.
> 2. Compute the condition number of a matrix whose two columns are nearly
>    parallel, then increase the angle and watch it fall.
> 3. Interview: A regression on 40 features and 30 rows returns wildly large
>    coefficients. What is going on structurally? (Hint: compare the number of
>    rows to the number of columns and ask what the rank can possibly be.)

#### Norms and Distance Metrics

Almost every data science method needs to answer "how far apart are these two
things?" Clustering groups nearby points, nearest-neighbour methods retrieve
them, regularization penalizes large coefficients, and loss functions measure
the distance between prediction and truth. All of these need a definition of
size and distance, and crucially, the definition is a *choice*.

A *norm* measures the size of a single vector. A *distance metric* measures
separation between two, and the most common ones are just the norm of the
difference.

The main family is the p-norms. The L2 (Euclidean) norm is straight-line
distance and is the default almost everywhere. The L1 (Manhattan) norm sums
absolute values and behaves as if you must travel along a grid. The
L-infinity norm takes the largest single component.

The choice has real consequences. L2 penalizes one large error far more than
several small ones, because it squares. L1 treats them proportionally, which
makes it robust to outliers and, when used as a regularizer, drives
coefficients to exactly zero.

An analogy: L2 is the distance a bird flies, L1 is the distance a taxi
drives, and L-infinity is the number of moves a chess king needs.

```text
  UNIT BALLS: the set of points at distance 1 from the origin

     L1 (Manhattan)        L2 (Euclidean)       L-infinity (max)
                                    
         /\                    _--_                +------+
        /  \                  /    \               |      |
       <    >                |      |              |      |
        \  /                  \ _ _/               |      |
         \/                                        +------+

   diamond: corners on       circle: no            square: corners
   the axes                  preferred direction   on the diagonals

  WHY L1 PRODUCES SPARSITY
  The diamond's corners lie ON the axes. When a loss contour first
  touches the L1 ball, it very often touches at a corner, where one
  coordinate is exactly zero. The circle has no corners, so L2 shrinks
  coefficients toward zero without ever setting them to zero.
```

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.spatial import distance

v = np.array([3.0, -4.0])

print(np.linalg.norm(v, ord=1))        # 7.0   = |3| + |-4|
print(np.linalg.norm(v, ord=2))        # 5.0   = sqrt(9 + 16)
print(np.linalg.norm(v, ord=np.inf))   # 4.0   = max(|3|, |-4|)

# Different norms rank the same errors differently.
errors_spread   = np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0])   # four small errors
errors_spiked   = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 2.0])   # one larger error
for name, p in [("L1", 1), ("L2", 2)]:
    s, k = np.linalg.norm(errors_spread, p), np.linalg.norm(errors_spiked, p)
    print(f"{name}: spread={s:.2f} spiked={k:.2f} -> "
          f"{'spread' if s > k else 'spiked'} is penalized more")
# L1: spread=4.00 spiked=2.00 -> spread is penalized more
# L2: spread=2.00 spiked=2.00 -> a tie; push the spike higher and L2 loses

# Cosine distance ignores magnitude entirely, which is why it dominates
# text and embedding retrieval where document length should not matter.
short_doc = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 1.0])
long_doc  = np.array([10.0, 20.0, 10.0])      # same topic mix, 10x longer
print(np.linalg.norm(short_doc - long_doc))   # 22.05 -- "very different"
print(distance.cosine(short_doc, long_doc))   # 0.0  -- "identical direction"
```

| Metric        | Formula sketch              | Robust to outliers | Typical use                   |
| ------------- | --------------------------- | ------------------ | ----------------------------- |
| L1 / Manhattan| sum of `abs(xi - yi)`       | Yes                | Lasso, robust loss, grids     |
| L2 / Euclidean| sqrt of sum of squares      | No                 | Default distance, ridge, MSE  |
| L-infinity    | max of `abs(xi - yi)`       | No (max-driven)    | Worst-case bounds             |
| Cosine        | 1 minus normalized dot      | Magnitude-blind    | Text, embeddings, retrieval   |
| Hamming       | count of differing positions| N/A                | Categorical, binary strings   |
| Mahalanobis   | L2 after decorrelating      | No                 | Correlated features, outliers |

> Key Takeaways
> - Distance is a modelling choice, not a fixed fact, and it changes which
>   points count as similar.
> - L2 squares errors and so punishes single large errors; L1 is
>   proportional and therefore robust.
> - The L1 ball's corners lie on the axes, which is the geometric reason
>   Lasso produces exact zeros.
> - Cosine distance discards magnitude, which is desirable for text and
>   embeddings and wrong for physical quantities.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compute L1, L2, and cosine distance between two feature vectors and
>    explain why the rankings differ.
> 2. Show empirically that scaling one feature by 100 changes k-nearest
>    neighbours under L2 but not under cosine.
> 3. Interview: You cluster customers by spend and visit count and every
>    cluster is driven by spend alone. Why, and what do you change? (Hint:
>    compare the numeric ranges of the two features.)

#### Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors

Most vectors, when hit with a matrix, change direction. A few special ones do
not: they come out pointing the same way, merely stretched or shrunk. Those
are the *eigenvectors*, and the factor by which each is scaled is its
*eigenvalue*. The defining equation is `A v = lambda v`.

Why care? Because eigenvectors reveal the intrinsic axes of a transformation.
Instead of describing what a matrix does to every possible input, you can
describe what it does along a handful of special directions, and everything
else follows. This is the engine behind principal component analysis,
spectral clustering, PageRank, and stability analysis.

For a *covariance* matrix specifically, the eigenvectors are the directions
of greatest variance in the data, and the eigenvalues are how much variance
lies along each. That is precisely the statement that PCA rests on.

An analogy: spinning a slightly lopsided object, most ways you spin it, it
wobbles. There are a few axes about which it spins cleanly. Those axes are
the eigenvectors, intrinsic to the object rather than to how you happened to
set up coordinates.

```text
  A v = lambda v  -- direction preserved, length scaled

   generic vector u                eigenvector v
   +                               +
   | u                             | v
   |                               |
   +------->            A          +------->
                       ===>
   A u points somewhere else       A v = 2v, same line, twice as long
   +                               +
   |        \  Au                  |
   |         \                     |          Av
   +          v                    +------------------->

  EIGENVECTORS OF A COVARIANCE MATRIX = PRINCIPAL COMPONENTS

        x2
         ^        . ' .  . '
         |    . ' . '. ' .        <- first eigenvector: direction of
         |  ' . ' . ' .              maximum variance (long axis)
         | . ' . '
         +--------------------> x1
                                  <- second eigenvector: perpendicular,
                                     the remaining variance (short axis)

  eigenvalue 1 >> eigenvalue 2 means the cloud is nearly one-dimensional,
  so one component captures almost everything.
```

```python
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[2.0, 1.0],
              [1.0, 2.0]])

values, vectors = np.linalg.eig(A)
print(values)          # [3. 1.]
print(vectors)         # columns are the eigenvectors, unit length
# column 0 ~ [0.707, 0.707]  -> the (1,1) direction, scaled by 3
# column 1 ~ [-0.707, 0.707] -> the (-1,1) direction, scaled by 1

v = vectors[:, 0]
print(np.allclose(A @ v, values[0] * v))    # True -- the defining property

# PCA in five lines, to show the connection is not metaphorical.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
data = rng.normal(size=(500, 2)) @ np.array([[3.0, 1.0],
                                             [0.0, 0.5]])   # correlated
centered = data - data.mean(axis=0)          # eigen-analysis assumes centred
cov = np.cov(centered, rowvar=False)         # (2,2) covariance matrix
vals, vecs = np.linalg.eigh(cov)             # eigh: symmetric, sorted, stable
order = np.argsort(vals)[::-1]               # largest variance first
vals, vecs = vals[order], vecs[:, order]

print(f"variance explained: {vals / vals.sum()}")   # e.g. [0.93 0.07]
# 93% of the spread lies along one direction, so the second axis is
# nearly discardable. That sentence IS dimensionality reduction.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Eigenvectors are the directions a transformation leaves pointing the same
>   way, scaled by their eigenvalues.
> - They expose a matrix's intrinsic axes, which is why so many methods
>   reduce to an eigen-decomposition.
> - For a covariance matrix, eigenvectors are directions of variance and
>   eigenvalues are the amount along each.
> - Use `eigh` for symmetric matrices such as covariance; it is faster and
>   numerically better than `eig`.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors of `[[4,0],[0,1]]` by hand and
>    explain geometrically what the matrix does.
> 2. Generate correlated 2-D data, find the covariance eigenvectors, and plot
>    them over the scatter to confirm they follow the cloud's axes.
> 3. Interview: A covariance matrix has one eigenvalue near zero. What does
>    that say about the features? (Hint: near-zero variance along a direction
>    means the data barely moves that way.)

#### Singular Value Decomposition

Eigen-decomposition has a serious limitation: it requires a square matrix,
and works cleanly only for some of those. Data matrices are almost never
square. The *singular value decomposition* is the generalization that always
exists, for any matrix of any shape, real or complex.

SVD factors any matrix `A` into three pieces: `A = U S V'`. Here `V'`
describes a rotation in the input space, `S` is a diagonal matrix of
non-negative *singular values* that stretch along each axis, and `U` is a
rotation in the output space. The claim is remarkable and true: every linear
transformation, however complicated, is a rotation, then a scaling, then
another rotation.

The singular values are ordered from largest to smallest, and they measure
how much of the matrix's action happens along each direction. This ordering
is what makes SVD the workhorse of compression and noise reduction: keep the
largest few, discard the rest, and you have the best possible low-rank
approximation of the original.

An analogy: SVD is a spectral analysis for matrices. Just as a chord
decomposes into notes ranked by loudness, a matrix decomposes into rank-one
pieces ranked by importance. Dropping the quietest notes is barely audible.

```text
  A  =  U  @  S  @  V'
 (m,n)  (m,m) (m,n) (n,n)        full SVD

  ANY TRANSFORMATION = ROTATE, SCALE, ROTATE

   input circle      V' rotates      S scales         U rotates
       _--_             _--_          _------_          /\
      /    \    ->     /    \   ->   |        |   ->   |  |
      \ _ _/           \ _ _/         \______/          \/

  TRUNCATION = COMPRESSION

  A  ~=  U[:, :k] @ S[:k, :k] @ V'[:k, :]
         \_____________________________/
          best rank-k approximation of A (Eckart-Young theorem)

  storage: m*n   ->   k*(m + n + 1)
  for a 1000x1000 image at k=50: 1,000,000 -> 100,050 numbers
```

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
A = rng.normal(size=(200, 50))

U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A, full_matrices=False)   # economy SVD
print(U.shape, s.shape, Vt.shape)    # (200,50) (50,) (50,50)
print(np.allclose(A, U @ np.diag(s) @ Vt))         # True -- exact

# s is a 1-D array of singular values, already sorted descending.
print(s[:5].round(2))

# Low-rank approximation: keep the k largest singular values.
def truncate(U, s, Vt, k):
    return U[:, :k] @ np.diag(s[:k]) @ Vt[:k, :]

for k in (1, 5, 20, 50):
    approx = truncate(U, s, Vt, k)
    # Relative error in the Frobenius norm, i.e. total squared difference.
    err = np.linalg.norm(A - approx) / np.linalg.norm(A)
    kept = s[:k].sum() / s.sum()
    print(f"k={k:2d}  relative error={err:.3f}  singular mass kept={kept:.3f}")

# Energy captured is often the criterion for choosing k:
energy = np.cumsum(s**2) / np.sum(s**2)
k90 = int(np.searchsorted(energy, 0.90) + 1)
print(f"rank needed for 90% of squared variation: {k90}")

# Connection to PCA: on centred data, the right singular vectors (rows of
# Vt) ARE the principal components, and s**2/(n-1) are the eigenvalues
# of the covariance matrix. PCA is usually computed via SVD for stability.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - SVD exists for every matrix, unlike eigen-decomposition, which needs a
>   square and well-behaved one.
> - Every linear map is a rotation, then an axis-aligned scaling, then
>   another rotation.
> - Truncating to the largest `k` singular values gives the provably best
>   rank-`k` approximation.
> - PCA is normally computed through SVD of the centred data rather than by
>   eigen-decomposing the covariance matrix.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Run SVD on a grayscale image and view reconstructions at `k` = 5, 20,
>    and 100. Note where quality stops improving visibly.
> 2. Plot the cumulative energy curve for a dataset and choose `k` for 95%.
> 3. Interview: Why is PCA usually implemented with SVD rather than by
>    eigen-decomposing `X'X`? (Hint: think about what squaring does to the
>    condition number.)

#### Matrix Factorization Basics

The recurring idea behind the previous two topics deserves naming on its own.
*Matrix factorization* means writing one matrix as a product of simpler ones.
This is not an aesthetic preference. Factorizations expose structure, make
computation cheaper, and let you fill in missing entries.

The last use is the one that built the recommender systems industry. Consider
a matrix of users by items where the entry is a rating. It is almost entirely
missing, since no user rates most items. Factorizing it as `R ~= P Q'`, with
`P` a small matrix of user factors and `Q` a small matrix of item factors,
forces every rating to be explained by a handful of latent traits. Once
fitted, the product gives a value for every cell, including the ones that
were never observed. Those are the predictions.

An analogy: factoring 143 into 11 times 13 does not change the number but
reveals structure invisible in the original. Matrix factorization does the
same for data, except the factors have interpretable meaning: latent genres,
topics, or customer archetypes.

```text
  RATINGS MATRIX             USER FACTORS      ITEM FACTORS
  (mostly missing)

        i1  i2  i3  i4              f1   f2         i1   i2   i3   i4
   u1 [ 5   ?   3   ? ]        u1 [ 1.2 -0.3 ]  f1 [ 2.1  0.4  1.8  0.2 ]
   u2 [ ?   4   ?   1 ]   ~=   u2 [ 0.1  1.5 ] @ f2 [ 0.3  2.2  0.1  0.9 ]
   u3 [ 4   ?   4   ? ]        u3 [ 1.1  0.0 ]
   u4 [ ?   5   ?   2 ]        u4 [-0.2  1.7 ]

     (4 x 4), 8 known            (4 x 2)            (2 x 4)
     8 unknown                   \________ 16 parameters ________/

  The product fills EVERY cell. Cell (u1, i2) becomes a prediction.
  The low rank is the point: it forces generalization instead of
  memorization, exactly as a small model does.

  COMMON FACTORIZATIONS
   LU    A = LU        solving systems, determinants
   QR    A = QR        least squares, stable regression
   SVD   A = U S V'    compression, PCA, pseudo-inverse
   NMF   A ~= W H      parts-based, non-negative, topics
   Chol  A = L L'      symmetric positive definite, sampling, speed
```

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import NMF, TruncatedSVD

# NMF constrains both factors to be non-negative, which makes the
# factors additive parts rather than signed mixtures -- much easier
# to interpret as "topics" or "genres".
counts = np.array([                 # documents x words
    [3, 0, 1, 0, 0],
    [2, 0, 2, 0, 1],
    [0, 4, 0, 3, 0],
    [0, 3, 0, 4, 1],
], dtype=float)

nmf = NMF(n_components=2, init="nndsvd", random_state=0, max_iter=500)
W = nmf.fit_transform(counts)       # documents x topics
H = nmf.components_                 # topics x words

print("document-topic weights:\n", W.round(2))
print("topic-word weights:\n", H.round(2))
print("reconstruction:\n", (W @ H).round(2))
# Docs 1-2 load on one topic, docs 3-4 on the other, and H shows which
# words define each. No labels were supplied; the structure was latent.

# Truncated SVD does the same job without the non-negativity constraint,
# and handles sparse matrices, which is why it is standard for text.
svd = TruncatedSVD(n_components=2, random_state=0)
embedded = svd.fit_transform(counts)
print("explained variance:", svd.explained_variance_ratio_.round(3))
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Factorization rewrites a matrix as a product of simpler matrices,
>   exposing structure and reducing cost.
> - Low rank forces generalization, which is what lets a factorization
>   predict entries it never observed.
> - Different factorizations serve different goals: QR for least squares, SVD
>   for compression, NMF for interpretable parts.
> - Non-negativity constraints make factors readable as additive components
>   rather than signed mixtures.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a small ratings matrix with missing entries and use NMF to predict
>    two held-out ratings.
> 2. Compare NMF and truncated SVD factors on the same document-term matrix
>    and describe which is easier to interpret.
> 3. Interview: In a recommender, what does increasing the number of latent
>    factors do to training error and to test error? (Hint: the rank is a
>    capacity parameter like any other.)

<a id="22-calculus-and-optimization"></a>
### 2.2 Calculus and Optimization

Fitting a model means searching for parameters that minimize a loss, and
calculus provides both the compass that says which way to move and the
guarantees that say when moving will work.

#### Derivatives and Partial Derivatives

Training a model is a search problem: adjust the parameters until the error
is as small as possible. To search efficiently you need to know, from where
you currently stand, whether nudging a parameter up or down makes the error
better or worse. That is exactly what a derivative reports.

A *derivative* measures the instantaneous rate of change of a function. If
`f(x)` is the error and `x` is a weight, then `f'(x)` tells you how fast the
error changes per unit change in the weight, right here. Its sign says which
direction is uphill; its magnitude says how steep.

Real models have many parameters, so the function has many inputs. A *partial
derivative* is the derivative with respect to one input while holding all
others fixed. Written `df/dx`, it answers: if I change only this weight and
touch nothing else, how does the loss respond?

An analogy: standing on a hillside, the derivative in the east-west direction
is how steeply the ground rises if you step east. The north-south partial is
a different number. Neither alone tells you the steepest way up; together
they do, which is the next topic.

```text
  DERIVATIVE = SLOPE OF THE TANGENT

   f(x)
    ^                        .
    |                      .'
    |                    .'  <- steep: large derivative, big step helps
    |                 ..'
    |            ...''
    |      ..''''            <- flat: derivative near 0, you are near
    |  .''                      a minimum (or a plateau)
    +-------------------------> x
         x0        x1

  PARTIAL DERIVATIVES ON A SURFACE

   loss(w1, w2), a bowl seen from above as contour lines

        w2
         ^   ____
         |  /    \        df/dw1 : slope moving purely right
         | |  .   |       df/dw2 : slope moving purely up
         |  \____/        At the centre both are 0 -> minimum
         +-----------> w1
```

```python
import numpy as np

# Mean squared error for a one-parameter model: f(w) = mean((w*x - y)^2)
x = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0])
y = np.array([2.0, 4.0, 6.0, 8.0])        # true relationship: y = 2x

def loss(w):
    return np.mean((w * x - y) ** 2)

def dloss(w):
    # d/dw mean((wx - y)^2) = mean(2x(wx - y))  -- chain rule applied
    return np.mean(2 * x * (w * x - y))

for w in [0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0]:
    print(f"w={w}: loss={loss(w):6.2f}  derivative={dloss(w):7.2f}")
# w=0.0: loss= 30.00  derivative= -30.00   <- negative: increase w
# w=1.0: loss=  7.50  derivative= -15.00   <- still increase, less urgently
# w=2.0: loss=  0.00  derivative=   0.00   <- zero: this is the minimum
# w=3.0: loss=  7.50  derivative=  15.00   <- positive: decrease w

# Numerical check by finite differences. Useful for verifying hand-derived
# gradients, which is where most training bugs actually live.
def numeric_derivative(f, w, h=1e-6):
    return (f(w + h) - f(w - h)) / (2 * h)      # central difference

print(np.isclose(dloss(1.5), numeric_derivative(loss, 1.5)))   # True
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A derivative gives the local rate of change: its sign is the direction
>   and its magnitude is the steepness.
> - A partial derivative varies one parameter while holding the rest fixed.
> - A derivative of zero marks a flat point, which is a candidate minimum,
>   maximum, or saddle.
> - Verify analytic derivatives against finite differences; mismatched
>   gradients are a leading cause of silent training failure.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Differentiate `f(w) = (w - 3)^2 + 5` by hand, find where the derivative
>    is zero, and confirm it is the minimum.
> 2. Write a gradient-check function and use it to catch a deliberately
>    wrong analytic gradient.
> 3. Interview: Your loss stops decreasing and the gradient is near zero, but
>    the loss is still high. What are two possible explanations? (Hint: zero
>    gradient does not by itself mean a good minimum.)

#### Gradients and the Jacobian

One partial derivative tells you about one direction. With a hundred
parameters you have a hundred partials, and you need them assembled into
something you can act on. That assembly is the gradient.

The *gradient*, written `grad f`, is the vector of all partial derivatives of
a scalar-valued function. Its crucial property is geometric: it points in the
direction of steepest increase, and its length is how steep that is. This
single fact is the basis of essentially all model training. To decrease the
loss, step in the direction of the negative gradient.

When the output is a vector rather than a scalar, the generalization is the
*Jacobian*: a matrix whose row `i` is the gradient of output `i`. Neural
network layers are vector-to-vector functions, so their local behaviour is
described by Jacobians, and backpropagation is a sequence of Jacobian
products arranged to avoid ever forming them explicitly.

An analogy: on a hillside in fog, the gradient is what a marble tells you.
Set it down and it rolls along the negative gradient, the steepest way down,
without needing a map of the whole terrain.

```text
  THE GRADIENT POINTS STEEPEST UPHILL

   contour map of loss(w1, w2)

     w2 ^
        |    .-''''''-.
        |   /   .--.   \        grad f  ->  perpendicular to the contour,
        |  |   / .. \   |                   pointing toward higher loss
        |  |  | (  ) |  |
        |  |   \ '' /   |       -grad f ->  the descent direction we take
        |   \   '--'   /
        |    '-......-'
        +------------------> w1

  Key property: the gradient is always perpendicular to the contour line
  it sits on. Moving along a contour changes nothing; moving across it
  changes the loss fastest.

  SHAPES

   scalar output:  f: R^n -> R      grad is (n,)        one gradient
   vector output:  f: R^n -> R^m    Jacobian is (m, n)  m gradients stacked
```

```python
import numpy as np

# f(w1, w2) = w1^2 + 3*w2^2  -- an elongated bowl
def f(w):
    return w[0]**2 + 3 * w[1]**2

def grad_f(w):
    # partials: df/dw1 = 2*w1,  df/dw2 = 6*w2
    return np.array([2 * w[0], 6 * w[1]])

w = np.array([3.0, 1.0])
g = grad_f(w)
print(g)                         # [6. 6.] -- equal partials here
print(np.linalg.norm(g))         # 8.49 -- steepness at this point

# The descent step goes AGAINST the gradient.
step = 0.1
print(f(w), f(w - step * g))     # 12.0 -> 6.24, the loss fell

# Jacobian for a vector-valued function g: R^2 -> R^3
def vec_fn(w):
    return np.array([w[0] * w[1], w[0]**2, np.sin(w[1])])

def jacobian(w):
    # row i = gradient of output i  -> shape (3, 2)
    return np.array([
        [w[1],        w[0]      ],   # d(w1*w2)/dw1, d(w1*w2)/dw2
        [2 * w[0],    0.0       ],   # d(w1^2)/dw1,  d(w1^2)/dw2
        [0.0,         np.cos(w[1])], # d(sin w2)/dw1, d(sin w2)/dw2
    ])

print(jacobian(np.array([2.0, 0.5])).shape)   # (3, 2)

# Note the anisotropy in f: the w2 direction is 3x steeper than w1.
# A single shared learning rate must be small enough for the steep
# direction, so it crawls along the shallow one. That mismatch is the
# reason adaptive optimizers such as Adam exist.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - The gradient collects all partial derivatives and points in the direction
>   of steepest increase.
> - Training descends by stepping along the negative gradient.
> - The gradient is perpendicular to the contour line through the current
>   point.
> - The Jacobian generalizes the gradient to vector-valued functions and
>   underlies backpropagation.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compute the gradient of `f(w1,w2) = w1^2 + w1*w2 + w2^2` at `(1, 2)` by
>    hand and verify numerically.
> 2. Write the Jacobian of the softmax function for a 3-element input and
>    check its shape.
> 3. Interview: Why does a loss surface with very different curvature along
>    two axes slow down plain gradient descent? (Hint: one learning rate must
>    serve both directions.)

#### Chain Rule

Models are compositions. A neural network applies a linear map, then an
activation, then another linear map, then a loss. To train it you need the
derivative of the final loss with respect to a weight buried several layers
back. The chain rule is what makes that computable, and it is the single most
important calculus result in machine learning.

The rule states that if `y = f(g(x))`, then `dy/dx = f'(g(x)) * g'(x)`.
Derivatives of composed functions multiply. Sensitivity propagates: if a
small change in `x` moves `g` a lot, and a small change in `g` moves `f` a
lot, then `x` moves `f` by the product.

*Backpropagation* is the chain rule applied to a computation graph, evaluated
from the output backwards. Going backwards is not arbitrary: with one scalar
loss and many parameters, the reverse direction reuses shared work and costs
roughly the same as one forward pass, while the forward direction would cost
one pass per parameter.

An analogy: a chain of gears. If gear A turns gear B three times as fast, and
B turns C twice as fast, then A turns C six times as fast. Ratios multiply
along the chain.

```text
  FORWARD PASS: values flow right

   x ---[ g ]---> h ---[ f ]---> y ---[ loss ]---> L

  BACKWARD PASS: derivatives flow left, multiplying as they go

   dL/dx  <--- dL/dh <--- dL/dy <--- dL/dL = 1
    |          |           |
    |          |           +-- local derivative of loss w.r.t. y
    |          +-- multiply by f'(h)
    +-- multiply by g'(x)

   dL/dx = dL/dy * dy/dh * dh/dx
           \_______ a product of local derivatives _______/

  WHY BACKWARD IS CHEAPER
   forward mode:  cost proportional to NUMBER OF INPUTS
   reverse mode:  cost proportional to NUMBER OF OUTPUTS
   deep learning: millions of inputs (weights), one output (loss)
   => reverse mode wins by a factor of millions
```

```python
import numpy as np

# A two-layer chain: z = w2 * tanh(w1 * x), loss = (z - target)^2
x, target = 2.0, 1.0
w1, w2 = 0.5, 1.5

# ---- forward pass: save intermediate values, they are needed later ----
a = w1 * x                 # pre-activation
h = np.tanh(a)             # hidden activation
z = w2 * h                 # output
L = (z - target) ** 2      # loss
print(f"forward: a={a:.4f} h={h:.4f} z={z:.4f} L={L:.4f}")

# ---- backward pass: multiply local derivatives, right to left ----
dL_dz = 2 * (z - target)          # d/dz (z - t)^2
dL_dw2 = dL_dz * h                # z = w2*h, so dz/dw2 = h
dL_dh = dL_dz * w2                # dz/dh = w2
dL_da = dL_dh * (1 - h ** 2)      # d/da tanh(a) = 1 - tanh(a)^2
dL_dw1 = dL_da * x                # a = w1*x, so da/dw1 = x

print(f"dL/dw1 = {dL_dw1:.6f}   dL/dw2 = {dL_dw2:.6f}")

# Verify against finite differences -- always do this when hand-deriving.
def loss_at(w1_, w2_):
    return (w2_ * np.tanh(w1_ * x) - target) ** 2

eps = 1e-6
num_w1 = (loss_at(w1 + eps, w2) - loss_at(w1 - eps, w2)) / (2 * eps)
print(f"numeric dL/dw1 = {num_w1:.6f}")     # matches to ~6 decimals

# Note dL_da multiplies by (1 - h^2), which is at most 1 and near 0 when
# |h| is close to 1. Stack fifty such layers and the product collapses.
# That is the vanishing gradient problem, and it is pure chain rule.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Derivatives of composed functions multiply, which is what makes deep
>   models trainable.
> - Backpropagation is the chain rule evaluated backwards over a computation
>   graph.
> - Reverse mode costs scale with the number of outputs, so one scalar loss
>   with millions of weights is the ideal case.
> - Repeated multiplication by small local derivatives causes vanishing
>   gradients, and by large ones, exploding gradients.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Differentiate `f(x) = sin(3x^2 + 1)` by hand, naming each local
>    derivative in the chain.
> 2. Extend the code above to three layers and verify every gradient
>    numerically.
> 3. Interview: Why do sigmoid activations cause vanishing gradients in deep
>    networks? (Hint: find the maximum value of the sigmoid's derivative and
>    raise it to the power of the depth.)

#### Convexity

Gradient descent follows the slope downhill. Whether that strategy actually
finds the best answer, or merely a locally acceptable one, depends on the
shape of the loss surface. Convexity is the property that makes the
difference, and knowing whether your problem has it tells you how much to
trust your optimizer.

A function is *convex* if the line segment joining any two points on its
graph lies on or above the graph. Visually, it is bowl-shaped with no dents.
The consequence is decisive: a convex function has no local minima other than
the global one. Any downhill path reaches the best answer.

Non-convex functions have multiple valleys, plateaus, and saddle points.
Gradient descent can settle in a poor valley, and the result depends on where
you started. Neural network losses are thoroughly non-convex, which is why
random initialization and restarts matter there and not in linear regression.

A practical test in one dimension: a twice-differentiable function is convex
when its second derivative is non-negative everywhere. In many dimensions,
the equivalent condition is that the Hessian matrix is positive
semi-definite, meaning all its eigenvalues are non-negative.

```text
  CONVEX                          NON-CONVEX

   \                    /          \      /\        /
    \                  /            \    /  \      /
     \                /              \  /    \    /
      \              /                \/      \  /
       \____________/                          \/
                                   local min   global min
   any chord lies ABOVE           a chord can cut BELOW the curve
   one minimum, always found      where you start decides where you end

  THE CHORD TEST

   f(x)                             f(x)
    |    .                           |   .        .
    |   . \___  chord above          |  . \  .-'/   chord dips below
    |  .      '-.                    | .   \/  /    the curve here
    | .          '.                  |.    /\ /
    +----------------                +----------------
```

| Property                 | Convex problem          | Non-convex problem            |
| ------------------------ | ----------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Local minima             | All are global          | Can be far from global        |
| Effect of initialization | None on final answer    | Decides which basin you reach |
| Stopping guarantee       | Zero gradient is optimal| Zero gradient means little     |
| Typical models           | Linear, logistic, SVM, Lasso | Neural nets, k-means, GMM |
| Practical tactic         | Just run the optimizer  | Restarts, schedules, momentum |

```python
import numpy as np

# Second-derivative test in one dimension.
def is_convex_1d(second_derivative, grid):
    return np.all(second_derivative(grid) >= -1e-12)   # tolerance for float

grid = np.linspace(-5, 5, 1001)
print(is_convex_1d(lambda x: np.full_like(x, 2.0), grid))        # x^2  -> True
print(is_convex_1d(lambda x: 12 * x**2 - 12, grid))              # x^4-6x^2 -> False

# Multivariate test: all Hessian eigenvalues non-negative.
def hessian_convex(H):
    return np.all(np.linalg.eigvalsh(H) >= -1e-12)

print(hessian_convex(np.array([[2.0, 0.0], [0.0, 6.0]])))    # bowl -> True
print(hessian_convex(np.array([[2.0, 0.0], [0.0, -6.0]])))   # saddle -> False

# Why it matters in practice: the same optimizer, two problems.
def descend(grad, start, lr=0.05, steps=300):
    x = float(start)
    for _ in range(steps):
        x -= lr * grad(x)
    return x

convex_grad     = lambda x: 2 * x                     # from x^2
nonconvex_grad  = lambda x: 4 * x**3 - 12 * x         # from x^4 - 6x^2

print([round(descend(convex_grad, s), 4) for s in (-4, 0.5, 7)])
# [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]        -- same answer from every start
print([round(descend(nonconvex_grad, s), 4) for s in (-4, 0.5, 7)])
# [-1.7321, 1.7321, 1.7321]  -- the starting point decided the outcome
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A convex function is bowl-shaped, so every local minimum is the global
>   minimum.
> - On convex problems the starting point is irrelevant; on non-convex ones
>   it decides the basin you land in.
> - Convexity is checked by a non-negative second derivative, or a positive
>   semi-definite Hessian in higher dimensions.
> - Linear and logistic regression are convex; neural networks and k-means
>   are not, which is why the latter need restarts.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Show that `f(x) = x^4 - 3x^2` is non-convex and find both local minima.
> 2. Verify that the logistic regression loss is convex in the weights for a
>    small dataset by checking the Hessian numerically.
> 3. Interview: k-means gives different clusters on different runs. Is that a
>    bug? (Hint: consider the shape of the objective it minimizes.)

#### Gradient Descent

With a gradient available and convexity understood, the algorithm follows
directly: to reduce the loss, repeatedly step in the direction of the
negative gradient. Gradient descent is the most important optimization
algorithm in machine learning, not because it is the best, but because it is
the only one that scales to millions of parameters.

The update rule is `w := w - lr * grad(w)`, where `lr` is the *learning
rate*. That one hyperparameter controls everything about whether training
works. Too small and progress is glacial. Too large and steps overshoot the
valley, bouncing up the far wall and diverging. There is a critical value
above which divergence is guaranteed, determined by the curvature.

Why not solve for the minimum directly? For linear regression you can, via
the normal equations. But that requires inverting a matrix whose size is the
number of features, costing roughly cubic time, and it does not exist for
most models. Gradient descent needs only the ability to compute a gradient,
which is why it generalizes to everything.

An analogy: descending a mountain in fog by always stepping downhill.
Learning rate is stride length. Tiny steps take forever; huge steps step over
the valley and land higher up the opposite slope.

```text
  THE LEARNING RATE DECIDES EVERYTHING

  lr too small          lr well chosen        lr too large
   \        /            \        /            \        /
    \  ....            .  \      /              \  1   /
     \ ....           2 \  \    /                \ / \/ 3
      \...           .   \1 \  /                  X   X
       \..          3 \   \  \/                  / \ / \
        \_/            \___\_/                  /   V   2
                                               /    4    \
  crawls, may stop      converges              diverges: each step
  before converging     in a few steps         overshoots further

  CONVERGENCE CRITERION
   stop when any of:
     - gradient norm < tolerance          (flat: likely a minimum)
     - loss change between steps < tol    (no progress)
     - max iterations reached             (give up, investigate)
```

```python
import numpy as np

# Linear regression by gradient descent, with the closed form for comparison.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = np.c_[np.ones(200), rng.normal(size=(200, 2))]      # bias column + 2 feats
true_w = np.array([1.0, 2.0, -3.0])
y = X @ true_w + rng.normal(scale=0.5, size=200)

def mse_grad(w):
    residual = X @ w - y
    # d/dw mean(residual^2) = (2/n) X' residual
    return (2 / len(y)) * X.T @ residual

def gradient_descent(lr, steps=500, tol=1e-8):
    w = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    history = []
    for i in range(steps):
        g = mse_grad(w)
        w = w - lr * g                       # THE update rule
        history.append(np.mean((X @ w - y) ** 2))
        if np.linalg.norm(g) < tol:          # converged: gradient is flat
            break
    return w, history

for lr in (0.001, 0.1, 1.05):
    w, hist = gradient_descent(lr)
    status = "diverged" if not np.isfinite(hist[-1]) or hist[-1] > 1e3 else "ok"
    print(f"lr={lr:<6} final loss={hist[-1]:>12.4f}  {status}")
# lr=0.001  loss still falling   ok        (far too slow, not converged)
# lr=0.1    loss near the noise floor of 0.25  ok   (converged)
# lr=1.05   loss overflows to inf  diverged  (overshoots every step)
#
# The divergence threshold is not arbitrary: gradient descent on a
# quadratic diverges once lr exceeds 2 / (largest Hessian eigenvalue).
# Here the Hessian is (2/n) X'X, whose largest eigenvalue is near 2,
# so the critical learning rate is near 1.0.

# Closed form, available for linear regression only:
w_exact = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y)   # normal equations
print("exact:   ", w_exact.round(3))
print("descent: ", gradient_descent(0.1, 5000)[0].round(3))   # same answer

# Feature scaling is not optional. Unscaled features create elongated
# contours, and the largest safe learning rate is set by the steepest
# direction, so the shallow ones barely move.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - The update `w := w - lr * grad(w)` is the core of nearly all model
>   training.
> - The learning rate is the decisive hyperparameter: too small stalls, too
>   large diverges.
> - Gradient descent needs only a gradient, which is why it works where
>   closed-form solutions do not exist.
> - Unscaled features distort the loss surface and force a smaller usable
>   learning rate.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement gradient descent for `f(w) = (w - 4)^2` and plot the loss for
>    three learning rates including one that diverges.
> 2. Fit a linear regression by gradient descent and confirm it matches the
>    normal equations to three decimals.
> 3. Interview: Your loss decreases then suddenly becomes NaN. What are the
>    likely causes? (Hint: think about the step size and the magnitude of the
>    inputs.)

#### Stochastic and Mini-Batch Gradient Descent

Plain gradient descent computes the gradient over the entire dataset before
taking a single step. With ten million rows, that is ten million evaluations
to move once. Training would take days to perform a few hundred updates. The
fix is to accept a noisy estimate of the gradient in exchange for taking far
more steps.

*Stochastic gradient descent* uses one randomly chosen example per update.
The gradient from one example is a poor estimate of the true gradient, but it
is unbiased, and cheap enough that you can take thousands of steps in the
time full-batch takes one. *Mini-batch* gradient descent is the compromise
used in practice: estimate the gradient on a small batch, typically 32 to 512
examples, which reduces noise and maps efficiently onto hardware that
performs matrix operations in parallel.

The noise turns out to be a feature, not just a tolerated cost. On non-convex
surfaces, the jitter helps escape shallow local minima and saddle points that
would trap a deterministic optimizer.

An analogy: full-batch is surveying the whole mountain before each step.
Stochastic is glancing at the ground and stepping immediately. You wobble,
but you cover far more ground per hour, and the wobble sometimes shakes you
out of a ditch.

```text
  PATHS TO THE MINIMUM

   FULL BATCH              MINI-BATCH            STOCHASTIC
    smooth, few steps       slight wobble         very noisy

      \                       \                     \  ,
       \                       \.                    '\ '
        \                       \'                   ,\'
         \                       \.                 '  \,
          *                       *                    '*

   1 step per epoch        ~n/B steps per epoch   n steps per epoch
   exact gradient          low-variance estimate  high-variance estimate
   slow on big data        the practical default  rarely used alone

  COST PER EPOCH IS ROUGHLY EQUAL; NUMBER OF UPDATES IS NOT.
   n = 1,000,000 rows, batch size B = 256
   full batch:  1 update per epoch
   mini-batch:  3,906 updates per epoch
```

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 10_000
X = np.c_[np.ones(n), rng.normal(size=(n, 3))]
true_w = np.array([0.5, 2.0, -1.0, 3.0])
y = X @ true_w + rng.normal(scale=0.5, size=n)

def batch_grad(w, Xb, yb):
    return (2 / len(yb)) * Xb.T @ (Xb @ w - yb)

def train(batch_size, epochs=10, lr=0.05, seed=0):
    rng_local = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    w = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    updates = 0
    for _ in range(epochs):
        order = rng_local.permutation(n)        # reshuffle every epoch:
        for start in range(0, n, batch_size):   # without it, batch order
            idx = order[start:start + batch_size]   # becomes a fixed bias
            w -= lr * batch_grad(w, X[idx], y[idx])
            updates += 1
    return w, updates

for bs in (n, 256, 1):
    w, updates = train(bs)
    label = {n: "full batch", 256: "mini-batch", 1: "stochastic"}[bs]
    err = np.linalg.norm(w - true_w)
    print(f"{label:<12} batch={bs:<6} updates={updates:<6} |w-w*|={err:.4f}")
# full batch   batch=10000  updates=10     |w-w*|~1.3     barely moved
# mini-batch   batch=256    updates=400    |w-w*|~0.01    converged
# stochastic   batch=1      updates=100000 |w-w*|~0.02    converged, noisy
#
# Full batch is not worse per update; it simply took 10 updates while
# mini-batch took 400 for the same number of passes over the data.
```

| Variant     | Batch size | Updates per epoch | Gradient quality | Notes                      |
| ----------- | ---------- | ----------------- | ---------------- | -------------------------- |
| Full batch  | All rows   | 1                 | Exact            | Smooth, impractical at scale |
| Mini-batch  | 32 to 512  | n / B             | Low variance     | The practical default      |
| Stochastic  | 1          | n                 | High variance    | Noisy, poor hardware use   |

> Key Takeaways
> - Mini-batching trades gradient accuracy for far more updates in the same
>   compute budget.
> - The batch gradient is an unbiased estimate of the full gradient, so the
>   noise averages out over steps.
> - Gradient noise helps escape saddle points and shallow minima on
>   non-convex surfaces.
> - Reshuffle the data each epoch, or the fixed batch composition becomes a
>   systematic bias.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Train the same model at batch sizes 1, 32, and full, and plot loss
>    against wall-clock time rather than epochs.
> 2. Remove the per-epoch shuffle and describe how the loss curve changes.
> 3. Interview: Doubling the batch size, how should you change the learning
>    rate and why? (Hint: consider what happens to the variance of the
>    gradient estimate.)

#### Constrained Optimization and Lagrange Multipliers

So far the search has been unconstrained: any parameter values are allowed.
Real problems often forbid that. Portfolio weights must sum to one.
Probabilities must be non-negative. A regularized model must keep its
coefficients within a budget. These are *constraints*, and they change the
answer, because the best point overall may be outside the permitted region.

The key insight is geometric. At a constrained optimum, you cannot improve
the objective without leaving the feasible set. For an equality constraint
`g(x) = 0`, that happens exactly when the objective's gradient is parallel to
the constraint's gradient: every direction that keeps you on the constraint
surface is perpendicular to the objective's gradient, so no legal move
improves anything.

Writing "parallel" as "equal up to a scalar" gives `grad f = lambda grad g`.
That scalar is the *Lagrange multiplier*, and it has a useful interpretation
of its own: it is the rate at which the optimal objective value would improve
if the constraint were relaxed by one unit, which economists call the shadow
price.

This is not an abstraction in data science. Ridge and Lasso regression are
literally constrained least squares: minimize error subject to a budget on
coefficient size. The regularization strength people tune is a Lagrange
multiplier.

```text
  TANGENCY AT THE CONSTRAINED OPTIMUM

        contours of f (objective)
             ___
           /     \            * unconstrained minimum (infeasible)
          | . ' . |
          |'  *  '|
           \ ___ /
        ______________  g(x) = 0   (the feasible line)
              @
              ^
              constrained optimum: the LOWEST contour that still
              touches the line. At that point the contour is TANGENT
              to the constraint, so their gradients are parallel:
                   grad f = lambda * grad g

  REGULARIZATION IS THIS PICTURE

   minimize ||y - Xw||^2   subject to   ||w||^2 <= t     (ridge)
   minimize ||y - Xw||^2   subject to   ||w||_1 <= t     (lasso)

   The L1 ball is a diamond with corners on the axes, so tangency
   commonly occurs AT a corner, where a coefficient is exactly zero.
   That is why Lasso selects features and Ridge does not.
```

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize

# Minimize f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2 subject to x + y = 1.
# By symmetry the answer should be (0.5, 0.5).

f = lambda v: v[0]**2 + v[1]**2
constraint = {"type": "eq", "fun": lambda v: v[0] + v[1] - 1}   # g(v) = 0

result = minimize(f, x0=[2.0, 0.0], constraints=[constraint])
print(result.x.round(4))       # [0.5 0.5]
print(result.fun.round(4))     # 0.5

# Analytic solution via the Lagrangian:
#   L(x,y,lam) = x^2 + y^2 - lam*(x + y - 1)
#   dL/dx = 2x - lam = 0   -> x = lam/2
#   dL/dy = 2y - lam = 0   -> y = lam/2
#   dL/dlam = x + y - 1 = 0 -> lam = 1, so x = y = 0.5
# The multiplier lam = 1 says: relaxing the constraint to x+y = 1.01
# would change the optimal objective by about 0.01 * 1.

# Ridge regression as constrained least squares, two equivalent views.
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge, Lasso
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.normal(size=(100, 8))
y = X @ np.array([3.0, -2.0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1.5]) + rng.normal(scale=.5, size=100)

ridge = Ridge(alpha=5.0).fit(X, y)     # alpha IS the Lagrange multiplier
lasso = Lasso(alpha=0.2).fit(X, y)
print("ridge:", ridge.coef_.round(2))  # all shrunk, none exactly zero
print("lasso:", lasso.coef_.round(2))  # several are exactly 0.0
# The difference is entirely the shape of the constraint region.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - At a constrained optimum the objective's gradient is parallel to the
>   constraint's gradient, which is the Lagrange condition.
> - The multiplier is a shadow price: the improvement gained per unit of
>   constraint relaxation.
> - Ridge and Lasso are constrained least squares, and their regularization
>   strength is a Lagrange multiplier.
> - The geometry of the constraint region decides the behaviour, which is why
>   L1 zeroes coefficients and L2 only shrinks them.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Minimize `x^2 + 4y^2` subject to `x + y = 3` by hand using a Lagrangian,
>    then verify with `scipy.optimize.minimize`.
> 2. Fit Ridge and Lasso across a range of alpha values and plot how each
>    coefficient path behaves.
> 3. Interview: Why does Lasso produce exactly zero coefficients while Ridge
>    does not? (Hint: draw both constraint regions and ask where a contour
>    first touches each.)

<a id="23-probability-theory"></a>
### 2.3 Probability Theory

Probability is the mathematics of uncertainty, and since every dataset is a
sample rather than the whole truth, it is the language in which every honest
data science conclusion is stated.

#### Sample Spaces and Events

Before computing any probability you must be precise about what could happen.
Vagueness here produces paradoxes that look profound and are merely sloppy.
The formal setup exists to force that precision.

The *sample space*, written `S` or `Omega`, is the set of all possible
outcomes of an experiment, where outcomes are mutually exclusive and
collectively exhaustive. Exactly one occurs. An *event* is any subset of the
sample space: a collection of outcomes you care about. "The die shows an even
number" is the event `{2, 4, 6}`.

Because events are sets, set operations have probabilistic meaning. Union is
"A or B", intersection is "A and B", complement is "not A". Three axioms,
due to Kolmogorov, generate everything else: probabilities are non-negative,
the whole sample space has probability 1, and probabilities of mutually
exclusive events add.

The one rule worth memorizing is inclusion-exclusion, because forgetting it
is the most common arithmetic error in the subject. `P(A or B)` is not
`P(A) + P(B)` unless the events cannot co-occur; otherwise the overlap is
counted twice and must be subtracted.

```text
  SAMPLE SPACE AND EVENTS AS SETS

   S = all outcomes
   +-----------------------------------+
   |                                   |
   |    +---------+                    |
   |    |    A    |                    |     A          = event A
   |    |     +---+-----+              |     A and B    = overlap
   |    |     |///|     |              |     A or B     = both regions
   |    +-----+---+     |              |     not A      = everything else
   |          |    B    |              |
   |          +---------+              |
   |                                   |
   +-----------------------------------+

  P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B)
                              ^
                              the shaded overlap, otherwise double-counted

  MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE means the overlap is empty:
   +-------+   +-------+     P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B), no correction
   |   A   |   |   B   |
   +-------+   +-------+
```

```python
from itertools import product

# Sample space for two fair dice: 36 equally likely outcomes.
S = list(product(range(1, 7), repeat=2))
print(len(S))                                  # 36

def prob(event):
    """Probability of an event given as a predicate over outcomes."""
    return sum(1 for outcome in S if event(outcome)) / len(S)

A = lambda o: sum(o) == 7           # the sum is seven
B = lambda o: o[0] == 6             # the first die shows six

print(f"P(A)        = {prob(A):.4f}")                  # 0.1667 = 6/36
print(f"P(B)        = {prob(B):.4f}")                  # 0.1667 = 6/36
print(f"P(A and B)  = {prob(lambda o: A(o) and B(o)):.4f}")   # 0.0278 = 1/36

# The naive sum double-counts the (6,1) outcome that satisfies both.
naive = prob(A) + prob(B)
correct = prob(lambda o: A(o) or B(o))
print(f"naive       = {naive:.4f}")     # 0.3333  WRONG
print(f"correct     = {correct:.4f}")   # 0.3056  = 11/36
print(f"difference  = {naive - correct:.4f}")   # 0.0278, exactly the overlap
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A sample space lists mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive
>   outcomes, and exactly one occurs.
> - Events are subsets, so set operations translate directly into "and",
>   "or", and "not".
> - `P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B)`; dropping the overlap term is the
>   most common error.
> - Most probability paradoxes dissolve once the sample space is written
>   down explicitly.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write the sample space for three coin flips and compute the probability
>    of at least two heads.
> 2. Verify inclusion-exclusion empirically for two overlapping events by
>    enumerating a sample space in code.
> 3. Interview: A family has two children and at least one is a girl. What is
>    the probability both are girls? (Hint: enumerate the sample space and
>    remove only the outcomes the information excludes.)

#### Conditional Probability

Probabilities are not fixed properties of events; they depend on what you
know. Learning that a patient is a smoker changes the probability of lung
disease. Conditional probability is the machinery for updating in light of
information, and it is the foundation of every predictive model, since a
prediction is a conditional probability given features.

The definition is `P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B)`, read as "the probability of
A given B". The intuition is that learning B occurred shrinks the sample
space to B alone. You then ask what fraction of that reduced world also has
A. The division by `P(B)` renormalizes so probabilities in the new world
still sum to one.

Rearranging gives the *multiplication rule*, `P(A and B) = P(A | B) P(B)`,
which is how joint probabilities are built up.

Two events are *independent* when conditioning changes nothing:
`P(A | B) = P(A)`, equivalently `P(A and B) = P(A) P(B)`. Independence is an
assumption that must be justified, not a default. Assuming it wrongly is one
of the most consequential errors in applied statistics, because it makes
compound risks look far smaller than they are.

```text
  CONDITIONING SHRINKS THE WORLD

  BEFORE: full sample space S      AFTER learning B: only B remains
  +---------------------------+       +-------------+
  |          +--------+       |       |    +----+   |
  |   +------+--------+---+   |       |    |////|   |   the new universe
  |   |  A   |////////| B |   |  -->  |    |////|   |   is B; P(A|B) is
  |   +------+--------+---+   |       |    +----+   |   the shaded share
  |          +--------+       |       +-------------+
  +---------------------------+
                                      P(A|B) = shaded / total(B)
                                             = P(A and B) / P(B)

  INDEPENDENCE
   P(A|B) = P(A)  -- knowing B tells you nothing about A
   Careful: independent is NOT the same as mutually exclusive.
   Mutually exclusive events are maximally DEPENDENT: if one happens,
   the other definitely did not.
```

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 10_000
smoker = rng.random(n) < 0.20
# Disease risk depends on smoking: 15% for smokers, 2% otherwise.
disease = rng.random(n) < np.where(smoker, 0.15, 0.02)
df = pd.DataFrame({"smoker": smoker, "disease": disease})

p_disease = df["disease"].mean()
p_smoker = df["smoker"].mean()
p_both = (df["smoker"] & df["disease"]).mean()

print(f"P(disease)            = {p_disease:.4f}")           # ~0.0458
print(f"P(disease | smoker)   = {p_both / p_smoker:.4f}")   # ~0.1500
print(f"P(disease | nonsmoker)= "
      f"{df.loc[~df['smoker'], 'disease'].mean():.4f}")     # ~0.0200

# Independence test: does P(A and B) equal P(A)*P(B)?
print(f"P(A and B)   = {p_both:.4f}")
print(f"P(A)*P(B)    = {p_disease * p_smoker:.4f}")
# 0.0300 vs 0.0092 -- far apart, so the events are strongly dependent.

# Why assuming independence is dangerous. Suppose three subsystems each
# fail with probability 0.01 and share a power supply.
print(f"if independent: {0.01 ** 3:.8f}")       # 1 in a million
# If a power failure takes out all three at once, the true joint failure
# rate is closer to the probability of THAT single common cause, perhaps
# 0.005 -- five thousand times larger than the independent estimate.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Conditioning restricts the sample space and renormalizes within it.
> - Every predictive model outputs a conditional probability given the
>   features.
> - Independence means conditioning changes nothing, and it must be argued
>   for rather than assumed.
> - Mutually exclusive events are strongly dependent, not independent; the
>   two terms are frequently confused.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. From a contingency table of 100 customers, compute `P(churn | premium)`
>    and `P(premium | churn)` and explain why they differ.
> 2. Simulate two independent and two dependent binary variables and verify
>    the multiplication rule for each pair.
> 3. Interview: An insurer prices flood policies assuming each house floods
>    independently. What goes wrong? (Hint: ask what causes floods and
>    whether neighbouring houses share that cause.)

#### Bayes' Theorem

Often you know the probability of evidence given a cause, but you need the
probability of the cause given the evidence. A test's manufacturer reports
`P(positive | disease)`, while the patient wants `P(disease | positive)`.
These are different numbers and confusing them is called the base rate
fallacy. Bayes' theorem is the conversion.

The theorem follows immediately from the definition of conditional
probability written two ways:

```text
                P(E | H) * P(H)
  P(H | E)  =  -----------------
                     P(E)

  posterior  =  likelihood * prior / evidence

  P(H)     prior       what you believed before seeing evidence
  P(E|H)   likelihood  how well the hypothesis explains the evidence
  P(E)     evidence    total probability of the evidence, a normalizer
  P(H|E)   posterior   the updated belief
```

The decisive term is the prior. When a condition is rare, even an accurate
test produces mostly false positives, because there are so many more healthy
people to generate them. This is not a flaw in the test. It is arithmetic,
and it is counterintuitive to nearly everyone on first encounter.

An analogy: a car alarm that is 99% accurate still mostly signals wind,
because thefts are rare and wind is not. The alarm is not broken; the base
rate is doing the work.

```python
def bayes(prior, sensitivity, specificity):
    """P(disease | positive test).

    sensitivity = P(positive | disease)      -- true positive rate
    specificity = P(negative | no disease)   -- true negative rate
    """
    true_pos = sensitivity * prior
    false_pos = (1 - specificity) * (1 - prior)
    return true_pos / (true_pos + false_pos)     # the denominator is P(E)

# A very good test: 99% sensitive, 99% specific.
for prevalence in (0.5, 0.01, 0.001):
    p = bayes(prevalence, 0.99, 0.99)
    print(f"prevalence {prevalence:<6} -> P(disease | positive) = {p:.4f}")
# prevalence 0.5    -> 0.9900   as intuition expects
# prevalence 0.01   -> 0.5000   a coin flip, despite a 99% accurate test
# prevalence 0.001  -> 0.0902   nine out of ten positives are FALSE

# Why: count the people out of 100,000 at 0.1% prevalence.
#   100 have the disease  -> 99 test positive
#   99,900 are healthy    -> 999 test positive (1% of them)
#   total positives = 1,098, of which only 99 are real => 9%.

# Sequential updating: today's posterior is tomorrow's prior.
posterior = bayes(0.001, 0.99, 0.99)         # 0.0902 after one test
posterior_2 = bayes(posterior, 0.99, 0.99)   # retest, using the update
print(f"after a second independent positive: {posterior_2:.4f}")   # 0.9075
# Two independent positives move the belief decisively; one does not.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Bayes' theorem converts `P(evidence | hypothesis)` into
>   `P(hypothesis | evidence)`, which is usually what you actually want.
> - When the base rate is low, most positives from an accurate test are
>   false; this is arithmetic, not a defect.
> - The posterior of one update becomes the prior of the next, which is how
>   evidence accumulates.
> - Reporting a classifier's precision without stating the class prevalence
>   is close to meaningless.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. A test is 95% sensitive and 90% specific for a condition affecting 2% of
>    people. Compute the probability of disease given a positive result.
> 2. Plot posterior probability against prevalence for a fixed test and find
>    where it crosses 50%.
> 3. Interview: Your fraud model has 90% precision in testing but flags
>    mostly legitimate transactions in production. What changed? (Hint:
>    compare the fraud rate in your test set with the live rate.)

#### Random Variables

Sample spaces of raw outcomes are awkward to compute with. A *random
variable* is a function that assigns a number to each outcome, which turns
questions about events into questions about numbers, where arithmetic works.

Rolling two dice has a 36-outcome sample space, but you usually care about
the sum. Define `X` = sum of the dice, and you now have a numeric quantity
with a distribution, an average, and a spread.

Random variables come in two kinds. *Discrete* variables take countably many
values and are described by a *probability mass function*, `P(X = x)`, which
gives the probability of each exact value. *Continuous* variables take values
in a range and are described by a *probability density function*, where
`P(X = x)` is zero for every single point and only intervals carry
probability. Density is probability per unit length, not probability.

Both are summarized by the *cumulative distribution function*,
`F(x) = P(X <= x)`, which is defined the same way for either kind and is
what quantiles and p-values are computed from.

```text
  DISCRETE: mass at points          CONTINUOUS: density over a range

   P(X=x)                             f(x)
    |                                  |      ____
    |      |                           |    .'    '.
    |    | | |                         |   /        \
    |  | | | | |                       |  /          \
    |  | | | | | |                     | /            \
    +--+-+-+-+-+-+--> x                +----------------> x
       2 3 4 5 6 7                        a        b

   heights ARE probabilities          AREA is probability
   sum of all heights = 1             total area under curve = 1
   P(X = 4) is meaningful             P(X = 4) = 0 exactly
                                      P(a < X < b) = shaded area

  CDF (both kinds): F(x) = P(X <= x), non-decreasing from 0 to 1

    1 |          .----------
      |        .'
      |      .'
      |   .-'
    0 +-'------------------> x
```

```python
import numpy as np
from itertools import product
from scipy import stats

# Discrete: X = sum of two dice, derived from the raw sample space.
outcomes = list(product(range(1, 7), repeat=2))
sums = [a + b for a, b in outcomes]
pmf = {s: sums.count(s) / len(sums) for s in sorted(set(sums))}
print({k: round(v, 4) for k, v in pmf.items()})
# {2: 0.0278, 3: 0.0556, ..., 7: 0.1667, ..., 12: 0.0278}
```
