```python
print(f"total mass = {sum(pmf.values()):.4f}")        # 1.0000

# The CDF answers range questions directly.
cdf = {s: sum(p for k, p in pmf.items() if k <= s) for s in pmf}
print(f"P(X <= 5) = {cdf[5]:.4f}")                    # 0.2778

# Continuous: density is NOT probability. It can exceed 1.
narrow = stats.norm(loc=0, scale=0.1)
print(f"density at 0 = {narrow.pdf(0):.4f}")          # 3.9894, above 1
print(f"P(X = 0)     = 0 exactly")
print(f"P(-0.1<X<0.1)= {narrow.cdf(0.1) - narrow.cdf(-0.1):.4f}")  # 0.6827

# Only intervals have probability, and they come from the CDF.
# This is why a probability density plot's y-axis is not interpretable
# as a probability, a routine misreading of histograms with density=True.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A random variable maps outcomes to numbers so probability questions
>   become arithmetic.
> - Discrete variables have a mass function where heights are probabilities;
>   continuous ones have a density where areas are.
> - For a continuous variable the probability of any exact value is zero, and
>   density can exceed one.
> - The cumulative distribution function works for both kinds and is what
>   quantiles and p-values come from.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build the probability mass function for the maximum of two dice and
>    confirm it sums to one.
> 2. Show numerically that a normal density with small scale exceeds 1 at its
>    peak, and explain why that is not a contradiction.
> 3. Interview: What does the y-axis mean on a density histogram, and why can
>    it exceed 1? (Hint: check what has to integrate to one.)

#### Expectation, Variance, Covariance

A distribution can be complicated, so we summarize it with a few numbers.
The three that matter most describe where it sits, how spread out it is, and
how two variables move together.

*Expectation*, `E[X]`, is the probability-weighted average: the long-run mean
over many repetitions. It is the balance point of the distribution, not
necessarily a value the variable can take. The expected value of a die roll
is 3.5.

*Variance*, `Var(X) = E[(X - E[X])^2]`, is the expected squared deviation
from the mean. Squaring makes deviations positive and penalizes large ones
disproportionately. Its square root, the *standard deviation*, returns to the
original units and is what you should usually report.

*Covariance* measures joint variation: positive when the two tend to exceed
their means together, negative when one rises as the other falls. Its size is
uninterpretable because it carries the product of both units, which is why
*correlation*, covariance divided by both standard deviations, exists. It is
bounded in `[-1, 1]` and is unitless.

The critical limitation: correlation measures *linear* association only. A
perfect deterministic relationship can have zero correlation.

```text
  EXPECTATION IS A BALANCE POINT       VARIANCE IS SPREAD

    |  |                                 low variance    high variance
    |  |  |                                  ||            |  |  |
   _|__|__|__|___                          __||||__      __|__|__|__
       ^                                     ^               ^
     E[X]                                 same mean, different spread

  CORRELATION IS LINEAR ASSOCIATION ONLY

   r = +0.9        r = -0.9        r = 0.0         r = 0.0 (!)
     .  .'           '.  .            . . .          .  .  .
    . .'              '. .           . . . .        .       .
   . .'                '. .           . . .        .         .
  ..'                    '..         . . . .        '.     .'
                                                       '''''
   strong linear   strong inverse   no pattern     PERFECT parabola,
                                                   zero correlation

  Always plot. Correlation collapses a scatter into one number and
  discards exactly the structure that would have warned you.
```

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# Expectation of a die: a value the die can never show.
faces = np.arange(1, 7)
print(f"E[X] = {(faces * (1/6)).sum():.2f}")          # 3.50

x = rng.normal(loc=10, scale=3, size=100_000)
print(f"mean={x.mean():.3f} var={x.var(ddof=1):.3f} sd={x.std(ddof=1):.3f}")
# ddof=1 gives the unbiased sample variance; ddof=0 (the NumPy default)
# divides by n and underestimates the population variance.

# Covariance and correlation on correlated data.
a = rng.normal(size=1000)
b = 2 * a + rng.normal(scale=0.5, size=1000)
cov = np.cov(a, b)[0, 1]
corr = np.corrcoef(a, b)[0, 1]
print(f"cov={cov:.3f}  corr={corr:.3f}")              # cov=2.01 corr=0.970

# Scaling changes covariance but not correlation -- which is the point.
print(f"cov after scaling b by 100: {np.cov(a, 100 * b)[0,1]:.1f}")  # 201.0
print(f"corr after scaling:         {np.corrcoef(a, 100*b)[0,1]:.3f}")  # 0.970

# The trap: perfect dependence, zero correlation.
u = rng.uniform(-3, 3, size=10_000)
v = u ** 2                                   # v is fully determined by u
print(f"corr(u, u^2) = {np.corrcoef(u, v)[0,1]:.4f}")   # ~0.0
# Reporting "no correlation, therefore no relationship" here would be
# exactly wrong. The relationship is perfect; it is just not linear.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Expectation is the probability-weighted mean and need not be an
>   attainable value.
> - Variance squares deviations, so it punishes large ones and is reported in
>   squared units; prefer the standard deviation.
> - Correlation is covariance rescaled to `[-1, 1]` and is unitless, which
>   makes it comparable across variables.
> - Zero correlation rules out a linear relationship only, so always plot the
>   scatter as well.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compute expectation and variance for a biased coin paying 10 on heads
>    and -5 on tails with `P(heads) = 0.3`.
> 2. Generate data with correlation near zero but obvious visual structure,
>    and plot it.
> 3. Interview: Two stocks each have 8% expected return. One has twice the
>    variance. Why might an investor still prefer it? (Hint: variance
>    penalizes upside and downside identically.)

#### Discrete Distributions

Rather than deriving a distribution for every new problem, it pays to
recognize the handful of standard shapes that recur. Each arises from a
specific generative story, and identifying the story tells you which
distribution applies and what its parameters mean.

The *Bernoulli* distribution models a single trial with two outcomes and
probability `p` of success. The *binomial* counts successes in `n`
independent Bernoulli trials with the same `p`. The *Poisson* counts events
in a fixed interval when they occur independently at a constant average rate
`lambda`; it is the limit of the binomial when `n` is huge and `p` is tiny.
The *geometric* counts trials until the first success. The *multinomial*
generalizes the binomial to more than two categories.

The commonest modelling error is applying a Poisson to overdispersed count
data. Poisson assumes variance equals the mean. Real counts, such as website
visits or insurance claims, are usually more variable than that, and the
negative binomial exists precisely for those.

| Distribution   | Generative story                            | Parameters   | Mean       | Variance        |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------- | ------------ | ---------- | --------------- |
| Bernoulli      | One trial, success or failure               | `p`          | `p`        | `p(1-p)`        |
| Binomial       | Successes in `n` independent trials         | `n`, `p`     | `np`       | `np(1-p)`       |
| Poisson        | Events per interval at constant rate        | `lambda`     | `lambda`   | `lambda`        |
| Geometric      | Trials until the first success              | `p`          | `1/p`      | `(1-p)/p^2`     |
| Negative binom.| Overdispersed counts                        | `r`, `p`     | varies     | exceeds mean    |
| Multinomial    | Counts across `k` categories in `n` trials  | `n`, `p_k`   | `n*p_k`    | `n*p_k(1-p_k)`  |

```text
  BINOMIAL n=20, p=0.3             POISSON lambda=3

   P(X=k)                            P(X=k)
    |     ||                          |  ||
    |    ||||                         |  |||
    |   ||||||                        | ||||
    |  ||||||||                       | |||||
    +--+-+-+-+-+-+---> k              +-+-+-+-+-+-+---> k
       2 4 6 8 10                      0 2 4 6 8

   bounded above by n                 unbounded, right-skewed
   "how many of 20 converted?"        "how many arrive per hour?"
```

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# Binomial: 20 visitors, each converts with probability 0.3.
binom = stats.binom(n=20, p=0.3)
print(f"P(exactly 6)   = {binom.pmf(6):.4f}")          # 0.1916
print(f"P(at least 10) = {1 - binom.cdf(9):.4f}")      # 0.0480
print(f"mean={binom.mean():.2f} var={binom.var():.2f}")  # 6.00, 4.20

# Poisson: support tickets arriving at 3 per hour.
pois = stats.poisson(mu=3)
print(f"P(zero tickets) = {pois.pmf(0):.4f}")          # 0.0498
print(f"P(more than 6)  = {1 - pois.cdf(6):.4f}")      # 0.0335

# The Poisson assumption, stated and testable: variance == mean.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
real_counts = np.r_[rng.poisson(1, 800), rng.poisson(20, 200)]  # mixed rates
mean, var = real_counts.mean(), real_counts.var(ddof=1)
print(f"mean={mean:.2f} variance={var:.2f} ratio={var/mean:.2f}")
# mean=4.80 variance=53.84 ratio=11.22 -- massively overdispersed.
# A Poisson model here will produce far too narrow prediction intervals
# and will look badly calibrated. Use a negative binomial instead.

# Binomial converges to Poisson when n is large and p is small.
print(stats.binom(n=10_000, p=0.0003).pmf(3).round(6))   # 0.224042
print(stats.poisson(mu=3).pmf(3).round(6))               # 0.224042
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Each standard distribution encodes a generative story; identify the story
>   and the distribution follows.
> - Binomial counts successes in a fixed number of trials; Poisson counts
>   events in an interval with no fixed maximum.
> - Poisson assumes variance equals the mean, which real count data
>   frequently violates.
> - Overdispersed counts need a negative binomial, or prediction intervals
>   will be far too narrow.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. A page converts at 4%. Using the binomial, find the probability of at
>    least 10 conversions from 150 visitors.
> 2. Test whether a count column in a real dataset is overdispersed by
>    comparing its variance to its mean.
> 3. Interview: When is a Poisson model inappropriate for daily website
>    visits? (Hint: consider weekends, marketing campaigns, and whether the
>    rate is really constant.)

#### Continuous Distributions

Continuous distributions describe quantities measured on a scale rather than
counted: durations, revenues, measurement errors, latencies. As with discrete
distributions, a handful of shapes cover most situations, and recognizing
them saves work.

The *normal* (Gaussian) distribution is the default for quantities formed by
adding many small independent effects, which the central limit theorem
explains. It is symmetric, and fully described by its mean and standard
deviation.

The *uniform* distribution assigns equal density across a range and encodes
complete ignorance within bounds. The *exponential* models waiting times
between Poisson events and is memoryless. The *log-normal* applies when a
quantity is the product of many small effects rather than their sum, giving
the right-skewed shape typical of incomes, file sizes, and session lengths.
The *beta* distribution lives on `[0, 1]` and is the natural choice for
modelling a probability or a rate.

The most consequential mistake is assuming normality for skewed data. Revenue
per customer, request latency, and time on site are almost never normal, and
treating them as such produces confidence intervals that are wrong in both
directions.

```text
  NORMAL              LOG-NORMAL            EXPONENTIAL
     _--_                |                  |
    /    \               |\                 |\
   /      \              | \___              \
  /        \             |     ----__         \___
 -----------          ---+-----------       ------------
  symmetric           right-skewed,          decays from 0,
  mean = median       mean > median          memoryless

  UNIFORM              BETA(2,5)             BETA(5,5)
  +---------+            _-_                    _--_
  |         |           /   \_                 /    \
  |         |          /      ---_            /      \
 -+---------+---     -+----------+--        -+--------+--
  0         1         0          1           0        1
  ignorance           rate near 0.25         rate near 0.5

  WHY LOG-NORMAL MATTERS: mean != median for skewed data.
  Reporting "average revenue per user" on a log-normal spend
  distribution describes almost nobody in the dataset.
```

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# Normal: the 68-95-99.7 rule, worth knowing by heart.
z = stats.norm()
for k in (1, 2, 3):
    print(f"within {k} sd: {z.cdf(k) - z.cdf(-k):.4f}")
# 0.6827, 0.9545, 0.9973

# Log-normal revenue: the shape almost all spend data actually has.
revenue = rng.lognormal(mean=3.0, sigma=1.0, size=100_000)
print(f"mean   = {revenue.mean():.2f}")       # 33.13
print(f"median = {np.median(revenue):.2f}")   # 20.07
print(f"90th   = {np.percentile(revenue, 90):.2f}")   # 72.29
# The mean sits at roughly the 65th percentile. "Average revenue" is
# above what two thirds of customers actually spend.

# Test normality before assuming it.
stat, p = stats.shapiro(revenue[:5000])       # Shapiro-Wilk, capped sample
print(f"shapiro p = {p:.2e}")                 # ~0 -> reject normality
log_rev = np.log(revenue)
print(f"after log, p = {stats.shapiro(log_rev[:5000])[1]:.3f}")  # ~0.5

# Exponential is memoryless: having waited does not change the future.
exp = stats.expon(scale=10)                   # mean wait 10 minutes
p_gt_5 = 1 - exp.cdf(5)
p_gt_15_given_10 = (1 - exp.cdf(15)) / (1 - exp.cdf(10))
print(f"{p_gt_5:.4f} vs {p_gt_15_given_10:.4f}")   # identical: 0.6065
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Normal arises from sums of small effects; log-normal from products, which
>   is why skewed positive quantities are usually log-normal.
> - For skewed data the mean and median differ substantially, and the mean
>   describes almost no individual.
> - The exponential distribution is memoryless: elapsed waiting time carries
>   no information about remaining wait.
> - Test the normality assumption rather than inheriting it, and consider a
>   log transform when it fails.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Generate log-normal data, compare mean and median, and show how a log
>    transform makes it approximately normal.
> 2. Model support wait times as exponential and compute the probability of
>    waiting more than twice the mean.
> 3. Interview: Why is reporting average revenue per user often misleading?
>    (Hint: sketch the distribution and mark where the mean falls.)

#### Joint and Marginal Distributions

Single-variable distributions are insufficient because data has multiple
columns that interact. Joint distributions describe several random variables
at once, and the operations of marginalizing and conditioning let you move
between the full picture and any slice of it.

The *joint distribution* `P(X, Y)` gives the probability of each combination.
The *marginal* distribution of `X` is obtained by summing or integrating the
joint over all values of `Y`, which discards information about `Y`
entirely. The name comes from the practice of writing these sums in the
margins of a table.

*Conditioning* fixes `Y` at a value and renormalizes the remaining row or
column, giving `P(X | Y = y)`.

The essential warning is that marginal and conditional relationships can
point in opposite directions. Simpson's paradox is the name for this, and it
is not an exotic curiosity. It appears routinely in real analyses whenever a
lurking variable differs across groups, and it is the reason a result that
holds overall can reverse in every subgroup.

```text
  JOINT, MARGINAL, CONDITIONAL IN ONE TABLE

                 Y = rainy   Y = dry   |  MARGINAL P(X)
   X = commute      0.15      0.25     |     0.40
   X = wfh          0.10      0.50     |     0.60
   ---------------------------------- +
   MARGINAL P(Y)    0.25      0.75     |     1.00
                     ^
                sum down the column -> marginal of Y
                sum across the row  -> marginal of X

   CONDITIONAL: fix Y = rainy, then renormalize that column by 0.25
     P(commute | rainy) = 0.15 / 0.25 = 0.60
     P(wfh     | rainy) = 0.10 / 0.25 = 0.40   (sums to 1, as required)
```

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# Simpson's paradox: admissions across two departments.
# Department A admits generously; department B admits almost nobody.
applicants = pd.DataFrame({
    "dept":     ["A", "A", "B", "B"],
    "gender":   ["M", "F", "M", "F"],
    "applied":  [800, 100, 200, 900],
    "admitted": [496,  82,  12,  63],
})
applicants["rate"] = applicants["admitted"] / applicants["applied"]

# Within EVERY department, women are admitted at a higher rate.
print(applicants.pivot(index="dept", columns="gender", values="rate").round(3))
#        F      M
# A  0.820  0.620
# B  0.070  0.060

# Marginalizing over department REVERSES the conclusion.
overall = applicants.groupby("gender")[["applied", "admitted"]].sum()
overall["rate"] = overall["admitted"] / overall["applied"]
print(overall["rate"].round(3))
# F  0.145     <- lower overall
# M  0.508     <- higher overall

# The lurking variable: women applied overwhelmingly to department B,
# which admits almost nobody regardless of gender. Marginalizing threw
# away the department, and with it the explanation.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Marginalizing sums the joint over a variable and discards its
>   information entirely.
> - Conditioning fixes a variable and renormalizes the remaining slice.
> - Simpson's paradox means a marginal relationship can reverse within every
>   subgroup, and it occurs routinely in practice.
> - Before trusting an aggregate comparison, check whether the groups differ
>   in composition on some third variable.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a two-way joint probability table and compute both marginals and
>    both sets of conditionals.
> 2. Construct your own Simpson's paradox example with two groups and verify
>    the reversal numerically.
> 3. Interview: Treatment A beats B overall, but B wins for both mild and
>    severe cases. Which do you recommend? (Hint: ask how patients were
>    assigned to each treatment.)

#### Law of Large Numbers

Why should a sample tell you anything about a population? The law of large
numbers is the guarantee, and it is the reason statistics works at all.

The law states that as the sample size grows, the sample mean converges to
the true expected value. Averaging many independent observations cancels
their random deviations, because they are equally likely to fall above and
below the mean.

Two points are routinely misunderstood. First, convergence is slow: the
error shrinks in proportion to one over the square root of `n`, so
quadrupling the sample halves the error. Getting one more decimal place of
precision costs a hundred times more data.

Second, the law says nothing about short runs. The *gambler's fallacy* is the
belief that a run of heads makes tails "due", as though the process
compensates. It does not. Convergence happens because later observations
*dilute* the early deviation, not because they offset it.

```text
  CONVERGENCE OF A RUNNING MEAN (fair coin, true value 0.5)

  1.0 |*
      | *
      |  **                                  error shrinks like 1/sqrt(n):
  0.5 |----**---*--**----*---------------     n=100   -> about 0.05
      |      *    *    **     ***========     n=10000 -> about 0.005
      |                                       100x the data for 10x
  0.0 +------------------------------------>     the precision
      1    10    100   1000   10000   n

  The early wild swings are never "corrected". They are DILUTED:
  after 10,000 flips, an excess of 5 heads moves the mean by 0.0005.
```

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
flips = rng.integers(0, 2, size=100_000)
running = np.cumsum(flips) / np.arange(1, len(flips) + 1)

for n in (10, 100, 1_000, 10_000, 100_000):
    print(f"n={n:>7}: mean={running[n-1]:.5f}  error={abs(running[n-1]-0.5):.5f}")
# n=     10: mean=0.30000  error=0.20000
# n=    100: mean=0.47000  error=0.03000
# n=   1000: mean=0.49300  error=0.00700
# n=  10000: mean=0.50130  error=0.00130
# n= 100000: mean=0.49934  error=0.00066

# The 1/sqrt(n) rate, made explicit.
for n in (100, 400, 1600):
    errors = [abs(rng.integers(0, 2, n).mean() - 0.5) for _ in range(2000)]
    print(f"n={n:>5}: average error = {np.mean(errors):.4f}")
# n=  100: 0.0397     quadrupling n
# n=  400: 0.0200     roughly halves the error
# n= 1600: 0.0100

# Gambler's fallacy, tested directly.
after_three_heads = [flips[i+3] for i in range(len(flips)-3)
                     if flips[i] == flips[i+1] == flips[i+2] == 1]
print(f"P(heads | three heads) = {np.mean(after_three_heads):.4f}")   # ~0.50
# Exactly the base rate. The coin has no memory of the run.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - The sample mean converges to the population mean as the sample grows,
>   which is why sampling works.
> - Error shrinks like one over the square root of `n`, so precision is
>   expensive.
> - Deviations are diluted by later data, never corrected by it.
> - The law describes long-run behaviour and says nothing useful about any
>   short sequence.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Simulate a running mean for a fair die and plot the error against `n` on
>    log axes to see the rate.
> 2. Determine empirically how many samples are needed to estimate a
>    proportion within 1 percentage point.
> 3. Interview: An A/B test shows a 30% lift after 40 users. Do you ship?
>    (Hint: estimate the error you would expect at that sample size.)

#### Central Limit Theorem

The law of large numbers says the sample mean converges. The central limit
theorem says something much stronger and far more useful: it tells you the
*shape* of the distribution of that sample mean, and the shape barely depends
on the population it came from.

The theorem states that the sample mean of `n` independent observations is
approximately normally distributed for large `n`, centred at the true mean,
with standard deviation equal to the population standard deviation divided by
the square root of `n`. That last quantity is the *standard error*.

The remarkable part is the universality. The underlying data can be skewed,
bimodal, or discrete; the distribution of its mean still approaches a normal.
This is why confidence intervals and t-tests work on data that is visibly
non-normal, a point that confuses many beginners into over-testing for
normality of the raw data.

The caveats matter. Convergence needs a finite variance, so heavy-tailed
distributions can fail. Convergence is slower for more skewed populations,
and the theorem describes the *sample mean*, not the raw data, which stays
exactly as skewed as it ever was.

```text
  POPULATION (heavily skewed)      DISTRIBUTION OF ITS SAMPLE MEAN

   |\                               n = 2      n = 30
   | \____                            /\         _-_
   |      -----___                   /  \_      /   \
   +---------------                 /     \_   /     \
                                  -+--------  -+-------+-
   nothing like a normal           still skew  nearly normal

  STANDARD ERROR SHRINKS WITH SAMPLE SIZE

   SE = sigma / sqrt(n)

   n:      10      40     160     640
   SE:  0.316   0.158   0.079   0.040       (for sigma = 1)
        \_____/  \_____/ \_____/
         4x the n halves the SE each time

  This single formula is why sample size planning is possible at all.
```

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# A deliberately non-normal population: exponential, heavily right-skewed.
population = rng.exponential(scale=10, size=1_000_000)
print(f"population skew = {stats.skew(population):.3f}")     # ~2.0

# Take many samples of size n and look at the distribution of their means.
for n in (2, 5, 30, 100):
    means = population[rng.integers(0, len(population), size=(5000, n))].mean(axis=1)
    observed_se = means.std(ddof=1)
    predicted_se = population.std() / np.sqrt(n)      # sigma / sqrt(n)
    print(f"n={n:>3}: skew of means={stats.skew(means):>6.3f}  "
          f"SE observed={observed_se:.3f} predicted={predicted_se:.3f}")
# n=  2: skew of means= 1.410  SE observed=7.072 predicted=7.070
# n=  5: skew of means= 0.895  SE observed=4.475 predicted=4.472
# n= 30: skew of means= 0.365  SE observed=1.826 predicted=1.826
# n=100: skew of means= 0.199  SE observed=1.001 predicted=1.000
# The skew of the means falls toward zero; the SE formula is exact.

# This is what licenses a confidence interval on skewed data.
sample = rng.choice(population, size=200, replace=False)
se = sample.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(sample))
ci = (sample.mean() - 1.96 * se, sample.mean() + 1.96 * se)
print(f"95% CI for the mean: ({ci[0]:.2f}, {ci[1]:.2f}), truth = "
      f"{population.mean():.2f}")
# The raw data is wildly non-normal; the interval is still valid, because
# the theorem applies to the MEAN, not to the observations.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - The sample mean is approximately normal for large `n` regardless of the
>   population's shape, given finite variance.
> - The standard error is the population standard deviation divided by the
>   square root of the sample size.
> - This universality is what makes confidence intervals and t-tests valid on
>   non-normal data.
> - The theorem applies to the mean, not to the raw observations, and
>   converges more slowly for more skewed populations.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Simulate sample means from a uniform, an exponential, and a bimodal
>    population and plot each at `n` = 2, 10, and 50.
> 2. Verify the standard error formula empirically for three sample sizes.
> 3. Interview: Your revenue data is heavily skewed. Can you still build a
>    confidence interval for the mean? (Hint: ask which quantity the theorem
>    actually describes.)

<a id="24-discrete-mathematics-and-information-theory"></a>
### 2.4 Discrete Mathematics and Information Theory

Counting and set reasoning underpin probability itself, while information
theory supplies the measures of surprise and shared signal that decide how
decision trees split, how classifiers are trained, and how features are
selected.

#### Combinatorics and Counting

Probability on equally likely outcomes reduces to counting: how many outcomes
satisfy the event, divided by how many exist. Doing that reliably requires
knowing which counting rule applies, and the choice hinges on two questions.
Does order matter, and can items repeat?

The *product rule* is the foundation: if one choice has `m` options and an
independent second choice has `n`, the pair has `m * n` possibilities.
Everything else follows from it.

A *permutation* counts arrangements where order matters. The number of ways
to order `k` items chosen from `n` is `n! / (n-k)!`. A *combination* counts
selections where order does not matter, written `C(n, k)` and equal to
`n! / (k! (n-k)!)`. The division by `k!` removes the orderings you just
decided to ignore.

Combinatorics matters in practice for computing the size of a search space.
Before launching a grid search, count its points. The reason hyperparameter
grids explode is multiplicative growth, and the reason random search often
beats grid search is that the grid spends its budget on redundant
combinations along dimensions that do not matter.

```text
  THE DECISION TREE FOR COUNTING

   Does order matter?
        |
        +-- YES --> Can items repeat?
        |            +-- YES --> n^k           (passwords, sequences)
        |            +-- NO  --> n!/(n-k)!     (rankings, podium places)
        |
        +-- NO  --> Can items repeat?
                     +-- YES --> C(n+k-1, k)   (multiset selections)
                     +-- NO  --> C(n, k)       (committees, hands, subsets)

  CHOOSING 3 FROM {A, B, C, D}

   PERMUTATIONS (order matters): 4!/(4-3)! = 24
     ABC ABD ACB ACD ADB ADC BAC BAD ... (all 24 arrangements)

   COMBINATIONS (order ignored): C(4,3) = 4
     ABC  ABD  ACD  BCD
     each corresponds to 3! = 6 permutations, hence 24/6 = 4
```

```python
from math import comb, perm, factorial
from itertools import combinations, product

print(perm(4, 3))      # 24  -- ordered selections
print(comb(4, 3))      # 4   -- unordered selections
print(comb(52, 5))     # 2,598,960 -- distinct five-card poker hands

# Probability of a flush, computed purely by counting.
flushes = 4 * comb(13, 5)          # pick a suit, then 5 of its 13 ranks
print(f"P(flush) = {flushes / comb(52, 5):.6f}")     # 0.001981

# Where this bites in practice: grid search size is a product.
grid = {
    "n_estimators":   [100, 300, 500],
    "max_depth":      [3, 5, 7, 10],
    "learning_rate":  [0.01, 0.05, 0.1],
    "subsample":      [0.7, 0.85, 1.0],
    "min_child_wt":   [1, 5, 10],
}
sizes = [len(v) for v in grid.values()]
total = 1
for s in sizes:
    total *= s                      # the product rule, literally
print(f"grid points = {total}")     # 324
print(f"with 5-fold CV: {total * 5} model fits")   # 1620

# Adding ONE more three-valued parameter triples the cost.
print(f"one more parameter: {total * 3 * 5} fits")  # 4860
# This multiplicative blowup is why random search over the same budget
# usually wins: it samples distinct values along every axis, whereas the
# grid repeats each value many times over the irrelevant dimensions.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Choose a counting rule by asking whether order matters and whether items
>   may repeat.
> - Combinations divide permutations by `k!` to remove orderings you have
>   decided to ignore.
> - Search spaces grow multiplicatively, so each added hyperparameter
>   multiplies rather than adds cost.
> - Random search beats grid search at equal budget partly because the grid
>   wastes evaluations repeating values along unimportant axes.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compute the probability of being dealt a full house using counting
>    arguments only.
> 2. Count the total fits implied by a grid you have used, including
>    cross-validation folds.
> 3. Interview: Why does random search often outperform grid search at the
>    same budget? (Hint: consider how many distinct values of the single most
>    important hyperparameter each method actually tries.)

#### Set Theory Basics

Sets are the substrate underneath probability, database joins, and feature
engineering. A *set* is an unordered collection of distinct elements, and
the distinctness is what makes it useful: it models membership without
duplication.

The operations have direct data-work meanings. *Union* combines, giving
everything in either set. *Intersection* keeps only shared elements.
*Difference* removes one set's elements from another. *Symmetric difference*
keeps what is in exactly one. The *cardinality* is the count of elements.

Two results are worth remembering. *De Morgan's laws* state that the
complement of a union is the intersection of complements, and vice versa,
which is how a filter condition is correctly negated. The *inclusion-
exclusion principle* gives the size of a union without double-counting, and
is the counting version of the probability rule from earlier.

The immediate practical payoff is that set operations are how you reason
about joins and about overlaps between cohorts, and they are dramatically
faster than looping when implemented as hash sets.

```text
  SET OPERATIONS AND THEIR SQL-JOIN COUNTERPARTS

   A union B          A intersect B       A minus B
   +-----+-----+      +-----+-----+       +-----+-----+
   |#####|#####|      |     |     |       |#####|     |
   |##+--+--+##|      |  +--+--+  |       |##+--+--+  |
   |##|#####|##|      |  |#####|  |       |##|  |  |  |
   +--+--+--+--+      +--+--+--+--+       +--+--+--+--+
      |     |            |     |             |     |
      +-----+            +-----+             +-----+
   FULL OUTER JOIN    INNER JOIN          LEFT ANTI JOIN

  DE MORGAN'S LAWS
   not (A or B)  ==  (not A) and (not B)
   not (A and B) ==  (not A) or  (not B)

   Applied to a filter: the opposite of
     "premium AND active"
   is NOT "not premium AND not active", it is
     "not premium OR not active".
   Getting this wrong silently drops rows from a cohort.

  INCLUSION-EXCLUSION FOR THREE SETS
   |A u B u C| = |A|+|B|+|C| - |AnB| - |AnC| - |BnC| + |AnBnC|
                              \___ remove doubles ___/  \_ add back _/
```

```python
mobile = {"u1", "u2", "u3", "u4", "u7"}
web    = {"u3", "u4", "u5", "u6"}
email  = {"u1", "u4", "u6", "u8"}

print(mobile | web)            # union: any channel
print(mobile & web)            # intersection: both channels
print(mobile - web)            # difference: mobile only
print(mobile ^ web)            # symmetric difference: exactly one

# Inclusion-exclusion, verified against the direct count.
formula = (len(mobile) + len(web) + len(email)
           - len(mobile & web) - len(mobile & email) - len(web & email)
           + len(mobile & web & email))
print(formula, len(mobile | web | email))       # 8 8 -- they agree

# De Morgan in practice: negating a compound filter.
all_users = mobile | web | email
premium = {"u1", "u3", "u6"}
active  = {"u1", "u2", "u3", "u4"}

target = premium & active                       # "premium AND active"
wrong  = (all_users - premium) & (all_users - active)   # NOT the complement
right  = (all_users - premium) | (all_users - active)   # correct complement

print(sorted(target))                            # ['u1', 'u3']
print(sorted(wrong))                             # ['u5', 'u7', 'u8']  too few
print(sorted(right))                             # everything except u1, u3
print(target | right == all_users)               # True -- a valid partition

# Membership testing is O(1) in a set and O(n) in a list. On a million
# ids this is the difference between milliseconds and minutes.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Set operations map directly onto join types and cohort overlap
>   questions.
> - De Morgan's laws govern how compound filters negate, and getting them
>   wrong silently drops rows.
> - Inclusion-exclusion counts a union without double-counting the overlaps.
> - Hash-set membership is constant time, so replacing list scans with sets
>   is often the single biggest easy speedup.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Given three campaign audiences, compute how many users saw at least one
>    and how many saw all three.
> 2. Write the correct negation of "active AND (premium OR trial)" and verify
>    it on a small set.
> 3. Interview: An anti-join returns more rows than the left table. What went
>    wrong? (Hint: check whether the join key is unique on the right side.)

#### Entropy

How much uncertainty is in a random variable? "A lot" is not actionable.
Entropy makes it a number, and that number turns out to govern decision tree
splits, compression limits, and the loss functions used to train
classifiers.

The starting intuition is *surprise*. An outcome that was almost certain
carries little information when it occurs. A rare outcome carries a lot.
Defining surprise as `-log2(p)` captures this: it is zero for a certain
event and grows without bound as the probability shrinks. Using base 2 makes
the unit the *bit*.

*Entropy* is the expected surprise: `H(X) = -sum p(x) * log2(p(x))`. It
measures the average uncertainty per observation, and equivalently, the
minimum average number of bits needed to encode outcomes from the
distribution.

Entropy is maximized by the uniform distribution, where every outcome is
equally likely and you learn the most from an observation. It is zero when
one outcome has probability 1, since there is nothing left to learn. This is
exactly the property decision trees exploit: a split is good when it reduces
the entropy of the label within the resulting groups.

An analogy: entropy is the average number of yes-or-no questions needed to
pin down the outcome, when you ask optimally. Guessing a fair coin needs
one. Guessing one of eight equally likely items needs three.

```text
  ENTROPY OF A BINARY VARIABLE

   H(p)
  1.0 |          _.-''-._
      |        .'        '.            maximum at p = 0.5:
      |      .'            '.          maximum uncertainty
  0.5 |    .'                '.
      |  .'                    '.
  0.0 +-'------------------------'--> p
      0        0.25  0.5  0.75      1
      ^                             ^
   certain (H=0)               certain (H=0)

  ENTROPY AS OPTIMAL ENCODING LENGTH

   Four symbols, UNIFORM: p = 1/4 each
     H = 4 * (1/4 * log2 4) = 2 bits    -> encode as 00, 01, 10, 11

   Four symbols, SKEWED: 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8
     H = 1.75 bits    -> encode as 0, 10, 110, 111
     the frequent symbol gets the short code, so the AVERAGE
     message is shorter than 2 bits. That is compression.
```

```python
import numpy as np

def entropy(probs, base=2):
    p = np.asarray([x for x in probs if x > 0])     # 0 * log 0 is taken as 0
    return float(-(p * np.log(p) / np.log(base)).sum())

print(entropy([0.5, 0.5]))                  # 1.0    fair coin, one bit
print(entropy([0.9, 0.1]))                  # 0.469  biased, less uncertain
print(entropy([1.0]))                       # 0.0    certain, no information
print(entropy([0.25] * 4))                  # 2.0    four equally likely
print(entropy([0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.125]))   # 1.75   skewed, compressible

# Decision trees pick the split that reduces entropy the most.
def information_gain(parent_labels, left_labels, right_labels):
    def h(labels):
        _, counts = np.unique(labels, return_counts=True)
        return entropy(counts / counts.sum())
    n = len(parent_labels)
    weighted_child = (len(left_labels) / n * h(left_labels)
                      + len(right_labels) / n * h(right_labels))
    return h(parent_labels) - weighted_child      # the gain from splitting

parent = np.array([0]*50 + [1]*50)            # perfectly mixed: H = 1.0
clean_left, clean_right = np.zeros(50), np.ones(50)     # a perfect split

print(f"perfect split gain = "
      f"{information_gain(parent, clean_left, clean_right):.4f}")   # 1.0000
useless_l = np.array([0]*25 + [1]*25)
useless_r = np.array([0]*25 + [1]*25)
print(f"useless split gain = "
      f"{information_gain(parent, useless_l, useless_r):.4f}")      # 0.0000
# A split that leaves both children as mixed as the parent gains nothing,
# and the tree will not choose it. That comparison IS the algorithm.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Surprise is `-log2(p)`, and entropy is its expected value, measured in
>   bits.
> - Entropy peaks at the uniform distribution and is zero when an outcome is
>   certain.
> - Entropy equals the minimum average code length, which is why skewed
>   distributions compress.
> - Decision trees choose splits by maximizing the entropy reduction, called
>   information gain.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compute the entropy of a fair six-sided die and of a die loaded to show
>    six half the time.
> 2. Implement information gain and use it to pick the best split on a small
>    labelled dataset.
> 3. Interview: Why does a decision tree prefer a split producing pure child
>    nodes? (Hint: express purity in terms of the entropy of each child.)

#### Cross-Entropy and KL Divergence

Entropy measures the uncertainty in one distribution. Training a classifier
requires comparing two: the true labels and the model's predicted
probabilities. Cross-entropy and Kullback-Leibler divergence are the tools
for that, and cross-entropy is the loss function behind essentially every
classifier and language model in use.

*Cross-entropy* `H(p, q)` is the average number of bits needed to encode
outcomes from the true distribution `p` using a code optimized for the
predicted distribution `q`. If the prediction is perfect, cross-entropy
equals the entropy of `p` and is as small as it can be. If the prediction is
wrong, you pay extra bits.

*KL divergence* is exactly that penalty: `KL(p || q) = H(p, q) - H(p)`. It is
the excess cost of using the wrong distribution, is always non-negative, and
is zero only when the two distributions match.

KL divergence is *not* a distance, because it is asymmetric:
`KL(p || q)` differs from `KL(q || p)`. The asymmetry has real consequences
in variational inference, where the choice of direction determines whether an
approximation covers all the modes or concentrates on one.

The practical property that matters most: cross-entropy punishes confident
wrong predictions brutally, because the loss involves the log of the
predicted probability, and the log of a small number is a large negative.

```text
  THE THREE QUANTITIES

   H(p)      = cost of encoding p with the BEST possible code
   H(p, q)   = cost of encoding p with a code built for q
   KL(p||q)  = H(p,q) - H(p)  = the WASTE from using the wrong code

         |<------------- H(p, q) ------------->|
         |<------ H(p) ------>|<-- KL(p||q) -->|
         |   irreducible      |   your model's |
         |   uncertainty      |   error        |

  CROSS-ENTROPY LOSS PER PREDICTION (true label = 1)

   predicted p:  0.99   0.9    0.7    0.5    0.1    0.01   0.001
   loss -ln(p):  0.01   0.11   0.36   0.69   2.30   4.61   6.91
                                                     ^
                          confident and wrong is catastrophically costly,
                          which is exactly the incentive you want
```

```python
import numpy as np

def cross_entropy(p, q, eps=1e-12):
    p, q = np.asarray(p, float), np.clip(np.asarray(q, float), eps, 1)
    return float(-(p * np.log(q)).sum())        # natural log -> nats

def kl_divergence(p, q, eps=1e-12):
    p = np.clip(np.asarray(p, float), eps, 1)
    q = np.clip(np.asarray(q, float), eps, 1)
    return float((p * np.log(p / q)).sum())

p = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0])          # true label: class 0 (one-hot)

for q in ([0.9, 0.05, 0.05], [0.5, 0.3, 0.2], [0.05, 0.9, 0.05]):
    print(f"pred={q}  CE={cross_entropy(p, q):.4f}")
# pred=[0.9, 0.05, 0.05]   CE=0.1054   confident and right: cheap
# pred=[0.5, 0.3, 0.2]     CE=0.6931   uncertain: moderate
# pred=[0.05, 0.9, 0.05]   CE=2.9957   confident and WRONG: expensive

# When p is one-hot, H(p) = 0, so cross-entropy and KL coincide. This is
# why classifier training can minimize either and call it the same thing.
print(kl_divergence(p, [0.9, 0.05, 0.05]))     # 0.1054, identical

# Asymmetry: KL is not a distance.
a = np.array([0.7, 0.2, 0.1])
b = np.array([0.3, 0.4, 0.3])
print(f"KL(a||b) = {kl_divergence(a, b):.4f}")   # 0.3446
print(f"KL(b||a) = {kl_divergence(b, a):.4f}")   # 0.3527
# Different numbers. If you need symmetry, use Jensen-Shannon divergence,
# which averages both directions and is bounded.

# Why clipping matters: an unclipped log(0) is -inf and poisons the loss.
# Every production implementation clips, and this is the reason.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Cross-entropy is the cost of encoding the truth with the model's
>   distribution, and it is the standard classification loss.
> - KL divergence is the excess cost over the irreducible entropy, always
>   non-negative and zero only for a perfect match.
> - KL is asymmetric and therefore not a distance; use Jensen-Shannon when
>   symmetry is needed.
> - Cross-entropy punishes confident wrong predictions severely, which is why
>   implementations clip probabilities away from zero.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compute cross-entropy loss for three predicted distributions against a
>    one-hot label and rank them.
> 2. Show numerically that `KL(p||q)` and `KL(q||p)` differ for two
>    distributions of your choice.
> 3. Interview: Why is cross-entropy preferred over mean squared error for
>    classification? (Hint: compare the gradient each supplies when the model
>    is confidently wrong.)

#### Mutual Information

Correlation detects linear association and misses everything else. Mutual
information detects *any* statistical dependence, linear or not, which makes
it a far more general tool for deciding whether a feature carries signal
about a target.

*Mutual information* `I(X; Y)` measures how much knowing one variable reduces
uncertainty about the other. Formally it is the entropy of `X` minus the
entropy of `X` given `Y`: the uncertainty you started with, minus what
remains after learning `Y`. Equivalently, it is the KL divergence between
the joint distribution and the product of the marginals, which is the precise
statement of how far the variables are from independent.

Its key properties: it is symmetric, it is zero exactly when the variables
are independent, and it is never negative. Unlike correlation, a zero value
genuinely means no relationship of any kind.

The costs are real. Mutual information requires estimating a joint
distribution, which means binning continuous variables, and the result is
sensitive to how you bin. It is also measured in bits rather than on a fixed
scale, so values are not comparable across variable pairs without
normalization.

```text
  MUTUAL INFORMATION AS OVERLAPPING UNCERTAINTY

     H(X)                      H(Y)
   .-------------------.  .-------------------.
   |                   |  |                   |
   |     H(X|Y)     .--+--+--.     H(Y|X)     |
   |                |  I(X;Y) |                |
   |                '--+--+--'                |
   '-------------------'  '-------------------'

   I(X;Y) = H(X) - H(X|Y) = H(Y) - H(Y|X)
          = the shared information, the overlap

   independent variables -> no overlap -> I = 0
   Y fully determined by X -> H(Y|X) = 0 -> I = H(Y), maximal

  WHERE IT BEATS CORRELATION

    y = x^2 relationship          correlation:        ~0.00
      .        .                  mutual info:        HIGH
       .      .
        .    .                    Correlation reports "no relationship"
         .  .                     and is wrong. MI reports the dependence
          ..                      that is plainly visible in the plot.
```

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.feature_selection import mutual_info_regression
from sklearn.metrics import mutual_info_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.uniform(-3, 3, size=5000)

relationships = {
    "linear":     2 * x + rng.normal(scale=0.3, size=5000),
    "quadratic":  x**2 + rng.normal(scale=0.3, size=5000),
    "sinusoidal": np.sin(3 * x) + rng.normal(scale=0.3, size=5000),
    "noise":      rng.normal(size=5000),
}

for name, y in relationships.items():
    corr = abs(np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1])
    mi = mutual_info_regression(x.reshape(-1, 1), y, random_state=0)[0]
    print(f"{name:<11} |correlation|={corr:.3f}   mutual info={mi:.3f}")
# linear      |correlation|~0.99    mutual info HIGH
# quadratic   |correlation|~0.01    mutual info HIGH    <- corr blind, MI sees it
# sinusoidal  |correlation|~0.05    mutual info HIGH    <- same story
# noise       |correlation|~0.01    mutual info ~0      <- both agree: nothing
# Exact MI values depend on the estimator's neighbourhood parameter, so
# read the ranking rather than the magnitudes.

# For discrete variables, MI is computed directly from the joint counts.
a = rng.integers(0, 3, size=5000)
b = (a + rng.integers(0, 2, size=5000)) % 3       # dependent on a
c = rng.integers(0, 3, size=5000)                 # independent of a
print(f"I(a;b) = {mutual_info_score(a, b):.4f}")  # ~0.41 nats, dependent
print(f"I(a;c) = {mutual_info_score(a, c):.4f}")  # ~0.000, independent
# The 0.41 is not arbitrary: knowing `a` narrows `b` from three equally
# likely values to two, so I = ln(3) - ln(2) = 0.4055 nats.

# Caveat: MI on continuous data depends on the binning or the estimator's
# neighbourhood size. Compare MI values computed the same way, and treat
# the absolute number as far less trustworthy than the ranking.
```

| Measure           | Detects              | Range      | Symmetric | Needs binning |
| ----------------- | -------------------- | ---------- | --------- | ------------- |
| Pearson correlation | Linear only        | `[-1, 1]`  | Yes       | No            |
| Spearman correlation| Monotonic          | `[-1, 1]`  | Yes       | No            |
| Mutual information| Any dependence       | `[0, inf)` | Yes       | Yes, usually  |
| KL divergence     | Distribution mismatch| `[0, inf)` | No        | Yes, usually  |

> Key Takeaways
> - Mutual information measures how much one variable reduces uncertainty
>   about another, capturing non-linear dependence.
> - It is zero exactly when variables are independent, unlike correlation,
>   whose zero is much weaker evidence.
> - It is symmetric and non-negative, and equals the KL divergence between
>   the joint and the product of marginals.
> - Estimates depend on binning, so trust the ranking of features more than
>   the absolute values.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Generate a quadratic relationship and show that correlation is near zero
>    while mutual information is clearly positive.
> 2. Rank the features of a dataset by mutual information with the target and
>    compare the ordering to a correlation ranking.
> 3. Interview: When would you prefer correlation over mutual information for
>    feature screening? (Hint: consider interpretability, sample size, and
>    what binning does to a small dataset.)

<a id="3-statistical-foundations"></a>
## 3. Statistical Foundations

This chapter covers how to summarize data honestly, how to reason from a
sample to the population it came from, and how to decide whether an observed
difference is real or noise. It ends with causal inference, which addresses
the question every stakeholder actually asks and that correlation alone
cannot answer. Chapter 2 gave the probability machinery; this chapter is
where it meets data you actually have.

<a id="31-descriptive-statistics"></a>
### 3.1 Descriptive Statistics

Descriptive statistics compress a dataset into a few numbers, and the whole
skill lies in knowing what each number hides as well as what it reveals.

#### Measures of Central Tendency

Faced with a thousand values, the first question is always "what is the
typical one?" Three answers compete, and picking the wrong one is the most
common way a summary misleads without technically lying.

The *mean* is the arithmetic average: the balance point of the data. It uses
every value, which is its strength and its weakness. A single extreme value
drags it arbitrarily far.

The *median* is the middle value when sorted, with half the data on each
side. It ignores magnitude entirely and responds only to rank, which makes it
immune to outliers. Formally, its *breakdown point* is 50%: you must corrupt
half the data before you can move it arbitrarily.

The *mode* is the most frequent value. It is the only one of the three that
works on nominal categories, and it is the right answer to "what is the most
common plan?"

The practical rule: for symmetric data the three roughly coincide and the
mean is most efficient. For skewed data they diverge, and the median usually
describes a typical case better. Since Chapter 2 established that revenue,
latency, and session length are typically log-normal, this is not an edge
case but the default situation in data science.

```text
  SYMMETRIC                        RIGHT-SKEWED (typical of money, time)

        _--_                         |\
       /    \                        | \___
      /      \                       |     -----____
     ---------                      -+-----------------
         ^                           ^   ^        ^
     all three                    mode median   mean
     coincide                                    ^
                                     the mean is dragged toward the tail
                                     by a few very large values

  RULE OF THUMB FOR SKEW DIRECTION
   mean > median  ->  right-skewed (a long tail of large values)
   mean < median  ->  left-skewed
   mean = median  ->  symmetric (or symmetric-ish)

  BREAKDOWN POINT: how much corruption before the statistic is garbage
   mean:   1/n  (one bad value is enough)
   median: 50%  (you must corrupt half the data)
```

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

salaries = np.array([42, 45, 47, 48, 50, 52, 55, 58, 61, 850])  # thousands
                                                    # one founder included

print(f"mean   = {salaries.mean():.1f}")            # 130.8
print(f"median = {np.median(salaries):.1f}")        # 51.0
print(f"mode   = {stats.mode(salaries, keepdims=False).mode}")   # 42

# The mean describes nobody here: nine of ten people earn far less.
print(f"share below the mean = {(salaries < salaries.mean()).mean():.0%}")  # 90%

# Remove the outlier and the mean collapses toward the median.
print(f"mean without founder = {salaries[:-1].mean():.1f}")     # 50.9

# A trimmed mean is the middle ground: drop a percentage from each end,
# keeping some efficiency of the mean with much of the median's robustness.
print(f"10% trimmed mean = {stats.trim_mean(salaries, 0.1):.1f}")   # 52.0

# For categorical data only the mode is defined.
plans = np.array(["free", "pro", "free", "premium", "free", "pro"])
print(stats.mode(plans, keepdims=False).mode)       # 'free'
# np.mean(plans) would be a TypeError, which is the correct outcome.
```

| Measure | Uses all data | Outlier-robust | Works on categories | Best when            |
| ------- | ------------- | -------------- | ------------------- | -------------------- |
| Mean    | Yes           | No             | No                  | Symmetric, no outliers |
| Median  | No (rank only)| Yes            | Ordinal only        | Skewed or contaminated |
| Mode    | No            | Yes            | Yes                 | Categorical, multimodal |

> Key Takeaways
> - The mean uses every value and so moves arbitrarily far with a single
>   outlier; the median needs half the data corrupted.
> - For skewed data the mean and median diverge, and the median usually
>   describes a typical case better.
> - Comparing mean to median is a fast skew diagnostic requiring no plot.
> - Only the mode is defined for nominal categories.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compute all three measures for a small salary dataset, then add one
>    extreme value and recompute. Note which moved.
> 2. Generate log-normal data and report the percentage of observations
>    falling below the mean.
> 3. Interview: A company reports average employee salary of 95,000 and the
>    union reports 62,000. Can both be honest? (Hint: ask which statistic
>    each side chose and what the distribution looks like.)

#### Measures of Dispersion

Two datasets can share a mean and be nothing alike. One might cluster tightly
and the other sprawl. Dispersion measures the spread, and it is frequently
more decision-relevant than the centre: a delivery service averaging 30
minutes with a 5-minute spread is a different business from one averaging 30
minutes with a 40-minute spread.

The *range* is maximum minus minimum. It is trivially computed and nearly
useless, since it depends entirely on the two most extreme points.

*Variance* is the mean squared deviation from the mean, and *standard
deviation* is its square root, returning to the original units. Chapter 2
defined these for a distribution; here the concern is estimating them from a
sample. The subtlety is the divisor. Dividing by `n` underestimates the
population variance, because deviations are measured from the sample mean,
which is itself pulled toward the data. Dividing by `n - 1` corrects this and
is called Bessel's correction.

The *interquartile range* is the spread of the middle 50%, robust in the same
way the median is. The *median absolute deviation* is more robust still.

The *coefficient of variation*, standard deviation divided by mean, is
unitless and lets you compare variability across quantities on different
scales.

```text
  SAME MEAN, DIFFERENT SPREAD

   A:        ||||||||              sd = 1.2   "reliable"
   B:  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |      sd = 4.8   "unpredictable"
       +---------+---------+
                mean

  WHY n-1 AND NOT n

   The sample mean sits, by construction, at the centre of YOUR sample,
   not at the true population mean. Deviations measured from it are
   therefore systematically too small.

      population mean  *
                        \
      sample:      o  o  o  o          deviations from the SAMPLE mean
                      ^                are smaller than from the TRUE mean
                 sample mean

   Dividing by n-1 inflates the estimate just enough to remove the bias.
   The effect vanishes as n grows: at n=1000 it is a 0.1% correction.
```

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

a = np.array([48, 49, 50, 51, 52])
b = np.array([20, 35, 50, 65, 80])

for name, x in [("A", a), ("B", b)]:
    print(f"{name}: mean={x.mean():.1f} sd={x.std(ddof=1):.2f} "
          f"IQR={stats.iqr(x):.1f} range={x.ptp()}")
# A: mean=50.0 sd=1.58 IQR=2.0  range=4
# B: mean=50.0 sd=23.72 IQR=30.0 range=60

# ddof matters. NumPy defaults to ddof=0 (population); pandas defaults
# to ddof=1 (sample). The same column can give two different answers
# depending on which library computed it.
print(f"ddof=0: {b.std(ddof=0):.3f}   ddof=1: {b.std(ddof=1):.3f}")
# 21.213 vs 23.717 -- a 12% difference at n=5

# Demonstrate the bias that n-1 corrects.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
true_var = 9.0                                    # population variance
biased, unbiased = [], []
for _ in range(20_000):
    s = rng.normal(0, 3, size=5)                  # small samples exaggerate it
    biased.append(s.var(ddof=0))
    unbiased.append(s.var(ddof=1))
print(f"E[var, ddof=0] = {np.mean(biased):.3f}  (true {true_var})")   # ~7.2
print(f"E[var, ddof=1] = {np.mean(unbiased):.3f}  (true {true_var})") # ~9.0
# ddof=0 underestimates by a factor of (n-1)/n = 4/5 = 0.8, exactly.

# Robust alternatives, for data with outliers.
contaminated = np.append(a, 500)
print(f"sd  = {contaminated.std(ddof=1):.1f}")                  # 183.7
print(f"IQR = {stats.iqr(contaminated):.1f}")                   # 2.5
print(f"MAD = {stats.median_abs_deviation(contaminated):.1f}")  # 1.5
# One bad value destroyed the standard deviation and left IQR untouched.

# Coefficient of variation compares spread across different scales.
revenue = np.array([1000, 1200, 950, 1100])       # dollars
latency = np.array([45, 52, 41, 48])              # milliseconds
for name, x in [("revenue", revenue), ("latency", latency)]:
    print(f"{name}: CV = {x.std(ddof=1) / x.mean():.3f}")
# revenue: 0.104   latency: 0.100
# Nearly identical relative variability, even though one is measured in
# dollars around 1000 and the other in milliseconds around 46.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Spread is often more decision-relevant than the centre, especially for
>   service-level promises.
> - Use `ddof=1` for a sample variance; NumPy defaults to 0 and pandas to 1,
>   which silently produces different numbers.
> - Standard deviation is destroyed by a single outlier, while the
>   interquartile range and median absolute deviation are not.
> - The coefficient of variation is unitless and enables comparison across
>   quantities measured on different scales.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compute variance with both `ddof=0` and `ddof=1` on a sample of five and
>    explain the gap.
> 2. Show empirically that the interquartile range is unaffected by adding an
>    extreme value that doubles the standard deviation.
> 3. Interview: Two delivery services both average 30 minutes. What single
>    additional number would you ask for, and why? (Hint: think about what a
>    customer actually experiences on a bad day.)

#### Skewness and Kurtosis

Mean and standard deviation describe location and spread, but two
distributions sharing both can still look completely different. The third
and fourth standardized moments capture shape: whether the distribution
leans, and how heavy its tails are.

*Skewness* measures asymmetry. Positive (right) skew means a long tail of
large values, which is the signature of money, durations, and counts.
Negative (left) skew means a long tail of small values, seen in exam scores
near a ceiling or in time-to-deadline data. Zero skew means symmetric.

*Kurtosis* measures tail heaviness relative to a normal distribution. The
commonly reported *excess kurtosis* subtracts 3 so that a normal scores zero.
Positive excess kurtosis means heavier tails and more extreme outliers than
normal; negative means lighter tails.

Kurtosis matters more than its obscurity suggests. Financial returns and
latency distributions are leptokurtic, meaning extreme events happen far more
often than a normal model predicts. Risk models that assume normality
systematically underestimate the frequency of disasters, which is not an
academic point.

The practical use of both is as a diagnostic before choosing a method. High
skew suggests a transformation or a robust statistic. High kurtosis warns
that outlier-sensitive methods will behave badly.

```text
  SKEWNESS                           KURTOSIS (excess)

   negative      zero      positive    heavy tails (>0)   light tails (<0)
     __/|        _--_      |\__             /\                 ____
    /   |       /    \     |   \           /  \               /    \
   /    |      /      \    |    \_        /    \             /      \
  -------     ---------   --------      _/      \_          /        \
  tail left   symmetric   tail right    sharp peak,         flat, bounded
                                        fat tails           (e.g. uniform)

  ROUGH INTERPRETATION GUIDE

   |skew| < 0.5     approximately symmetric
   0.5 to 1.0       moderately skewed
   > 1.0            highly skewed -- consider a transform

   excess kurtosis > 0   more outliers than a normal would produce
   excess kurtosis < 0   fewer outliers, flatter than normal
```

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

samples = {
    "normal":      rng.normal(0, 1, 100_000),
    "log-normal":  rng.lognormal(0, 1, 100_000),
    "uniform":     rng.uniform(-2, 2, 100_000),
    "exponential": rng.exponential(1, 100_000),
    "t (df=3)":    rng.standard_t(3, 100_000),
}

for name, x in samples.items():
    # bias=False applies the small-sample correction; fisher=True (default)
    # returns EXCESS kurtosis, so a normal scores ~0 rather than ~3.
    print(f"{name:<12} skew={stats.skew(x, bias=False):>7.3f}  "
          f"excess kurtosis={stats.kurtosis(x, bias=False):>8.3f}")
# normal        skew~ 0.00   excess kurtosis~  0.00
# log-normal    skew~ 6.2    excess kurtosis~ 90+     highly skewed, fat tail
# uniform       skew~ 0.00   excess kurtosis~ -1.20   flat, light tails
# exponential   skew~ 2.00   excess kurtosis~  6.00   theoretical values
# t (df=3)      skew~ 0.00   excess kurtosis~ large   symmetric but fat-tailed

# Why kurtosis matters for risk: count the 4-sigma events.
for name in ("normal", "t (df=3)"):
    x = samples[name]
    z = (x - x.mean()) / x.std(ddof=1)
    print(f"{name}: |z| > 4 occurs {(np.abs(z) > 4).mean() * 100:.3f}% of the time")
# normal:   ~0.006%  -- matches the theoretical 0.0063%
# t (df=3): ~0.3%    -- roughly fifty times more often
# A model assuming normality would call each of those a once-in-a-decade
# event while they arrive monthly.

# Skew as a decision trigger: does a log transform fix it?
rev = samples["log-normal"]
print(f"skew before log = {stats.skew(rev, bias=False):.3f}")     # ~6.2
print(f"skew after log  = {stats.skew(np.log(rev), bias=False):.3f}")  # ~0.0
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Skewness measures asymmetry and kurtosis measures tail heaviness, both
>   invisible in the mean and standard deviation.
> - Positive excess kurtosis means extreme events are far more frequent than
>   a normal distribution predicts.
> - Absolute skew above 1 is a signal to consider a transformation or a
>   robust statistic.
> - Assuming normality for fat-tailed data systematically understates the
>   frequency of extreme outcomes.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compute skewness and excess kurtosis for a normal, a uniform, and an
>    exponential sample and match them to the shapes.
> 2. Take a right-skewed column, apply a log transform, and report skewness
>    before and after.
> 3. Interview: Why do financial risk models that assume normality fail
>    during crises? (Hint: compare the predicted and observed frequency of
>    five-sigma moves.)

#### Percentiles and Quantiles

A single centre-and-spread summary assumes the distribution has a simple
shape. Quantiles make no such assumption: they describe the distribution by
reporting where it sits at each point along its range, which is why they
dominate in performance engineering and in any setting where the tail is the
point.

A *percentile* is the value below which a given percentage of observations
fall. The 90th percentile of latency is the time that 90% of requests beat.
*Quantiles* are the same idea on a 0-to-1 scale, and *quartiles* are the
special case splitting data into four parts.

The reason this matters: averages hide tails, and users experience tails. If
mean latency is 100ms but the 99th percentile is 4 seconds, then one request
in a hundred is unbearable. For a page making 50 backend calls, most page
loads will contain at least one such call. Reporting the mean would describe
a system nobody is using.

A wrinkle that trips people up: there is no single definition of a
percentile. When the desired position falls between two data points, methods
differ in how they interpolate. NumPy offers nine. The differences are
negligible on large samples and can be material on small ones.

```text
  THE BOX PLOT IS A QUANTILE SUMMARY

        Q1     median    Q3
         |       |        |
    |----[=======|========]----|        o     o
    |    |                |    |
   min  25%      50%      75%  max      outliers beyond the whiskers
        |<------ IQR ---->|
        |<-1.5*IQR->|          |<-1.5*IQR->|
        whisker limits: the furthest data point still inside the fence

  WHY THE TAIL IS THE PRODUCT

   latency distribution
    |####
    |#######
    |##########
    |#############_
    |                ----____________________
    +-----------------------------------------> ms
     50   100                            4000
      ^                                    ^
    mean = 100ms                     p99 = 4000ms
    "the system is fast"          "1 in 100 users waits 4 seconds"

   With 50 backend calls per page, P(at least one slow call)
     = 1 - 0.99^50 = 39.5% of page loads.
```

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
# Realistic latency: mostly fast, with a slow tail.
latency = np.concatenate([
    rng.lognormal(mean=3.5, sigma=0.4, size=9800),    # the healthy majority
    rng.lognormal(mean=7.0, sigma=0.8, size=200),     # the slow 2%
])

for q in (50, 90, 95, 99, 99.9):
    print(f"p{q:<5} = {np.percentile(latency, q):8.1f} ms")
print(f"mean  = {latency.mean():8.1f} ms")
# p50   ~    33 ms
# p90   ~    58 ms
# p95   ~    70 ms
# p99   ~  1100 ms     <- more than thirty times the median
# p99.9 ~  4000 ms
# mean  ~    65 ms     <- describes neither the typical nor the bad case

# The compounding problem, computed rather than asserted.
p_slow = 0.01
for calls in (1, 10, 50):
    print(f"{calls:>2} calls -> P(at least one p99 hit) = "
          f"{1 - (1 - p_slow) ** calls:.1%}")
#  1 calls ->  1.0%
# 10 calls ->  9.6%
# 50 calls -> 39.5%    tail latency is a page-level problem, not a rare one

# Interpolation method matters on small samples.
small = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
for method in ("linear", "lower", "higher", "midpoint", "nearest"):
    print(f"{method:<9} p75 = {np.percentile(small, 75, method=method)}")
# linear 3.25 | lower 3 | higher 4 | midpoint 3.5 | nearest 3
# All are defensible. Fix one method and use it consistently, especially
# when comparing numbers computed by different tools.

# A critical operational point: percentiles do NOT average.
shard_p99 = [1400, 1350, 1500]
print(f"mean of shard p99s = {np.mean(shard_p99):.0f} ms")   # 1417 -- WRONG
# The true global p99 requires the pooled distribution, or a mergeable
# sketch such as t-digest or HDR histogram. Averaging percentiles across
# shards, hosts, or time buckets is one of the most common metric bugs.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Quantiles describe a distribution without assuming its shape, which is
>   why tail-sensitive systems are specified with them.
> - Users experience tail latency, and averages conceal it entirely.
> - Tail events compound: a 1% slow call rate makes a 50-call page slow 40%
>   of the time.
> - Percentiles cannot be averaged across shards or time windows; pool the
>   data or use a mergeable sketch.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Generate a skewed latency sample and report p50, p95, p99 alongside the
>    mean. Describe what each tells an on-call engineer.
> 2. Compute p75 of a four-element array under three interpolation methods
>    and explain the differences.
> 3. Interview: A dashboard averages hourly p99 latency into a daily number.
>    What is wrong with it? (Hint: ask what the average of two percentiles is
>    a percentile of.)

#### Correlation Coefficients

Chapter 2 introduced correlation as rescaled covariance. Here the concern is
practical: which coefficient to use, and what each one can and cannot detect.
Choosing the wrong one produces confident conclusions about relationships
that are not there, or misses relationships that are.

*Pearson's r* measures linear association. It assumes both variables are
roughly interval-scaled and is sensitive to outliers, since it is built from
means and standard deviations. A single extreme point can create or destroy
it.

*Spearman's rho* is Pearson's correlation computed on ranks instead of
values. Because ranks discard magnitude, it detects any *monotonic*
relationship, linear or not, and is robust to outliers. It is the right
default for ordinal data.

*Kendall's tau* counts concordant and discordant pairs. It is more
interpretable as a probability statement, more robust with small samples, and
slower to compute.

For categorical associations, *Cramer's V* generalizes the chi-square
statistic to a 0-to-1 measure, and the *point-biserial* correlation handles
one binary against one continuous variable.

The universal caution remains: correlation is not causation, and a
coefficient collapses a scatter plot into one number that cannot distinguish
a clean linear trend from a plot with entirely different structure.

```text
  ANSCOMBE'S QUARTET: four datasets, identical statistics

   I            II           III          IV
    .  '         . . .          .           |
   . '         .       .       .            |
  . '         .         .     .             |
 . '          .         .    .              .
 -------      ---------      ------      ---------
 clean        curved        outlier      one point
 linear       (parabola)    drives it    drives everything

 ALL FOUR: mean x = 9, mean y = 7.5, Pearson r = 0.816, same
 regression line. Only one of them should be modelled with a line.

  WHAT EACH COEFFICIENT SEES

   relationship        Pearson    Spearman    Kendall
   perfectly linear      1.00       1.00       1.00
   monotonic curve       ~0.9       1.00       1.00     <- rank-based win
   U-shaped              ~0.0       ~0.0       ~0.0     <- all blind; plot it
   linear + 1 outlier    ~0.0       ~0.9       ~0.9     <- robustness wins
```

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = np.arange(1, 21, dtype=float)

cases = {
    "linear":          2 * x + rng.normal(0, 1, 20),
    "monotonic curve": np.exp(x / 4),            # increasing but very curved
    "u-shaped":        (x - 10.5) ** 2,
}

for name, y in cases.items():
    r = stats.pearsonr(x, y)
    rho = stats.spearmanr(x, y)
    tau = stats.kendalltau(x, y)
    print(f"{name:<16} pearson={r.statistic:>6.3f}  "
          f"spearman={rho.statistic:>6.3f}  kendall={tau.statistic:>6.3f}")
# linear           pearson~ 0.998  spearman~ 0.998  kendall~ 0.98
# monotonic curve  pearson~ 0.83   spearman= 1.000  kendall= 1.000
# u-shaped         pearson= 0.000  spearman= 0.000  kendall= 0.000
#                  ^ the curve is PERFECTLY monotonic; only rank methods say so
#                  ^ the U is a perfect deterministic relation; none detect it

# Outlier sensitivity, demonstrated.
a = np.arange(20, dtype=float)
b = a + rng.normal(0, 0.5, 20)
print(f"clean:   pearson={stats.pearsonr(a, b).statistic:.3f}  "
      f"spearman={stats.spearmanr(a, b).statistic:.3f}")
a2, b2 = np.append(a, 100.0), np.append(b, 0.0)      # one wild point
print(f"+outlier: pearson={stats.pearsonr(a2, b2).statistic:.3f}  "
      f"spearman={stats.spearmanr(a2, b2).statistic:.3f}")
# clean:    pearson=0.996  spearman=0.995
# +outlier: pearson~0.0    spearman~0.86
# One point destroyed Pearson and barely dented Spearman.

# Categorical association: Cramer's V from a contingency table.
def cramers_v(table):
    chi2 = stats.chi2_contingency(table, correction=False).statistic
    n = table.sum()
    return np.sqrt(chi2 / (n * (min(table.shape) - 1)))

table = np.array([[30, 10],
                  [ 5, 55]])
print(f"Cramer's V = {cramers_v(table):.3f}")        # strong association
```

| Coefficient      | Detects            | Robust to outliers | Data type              |
| ---------------- | ------------------ | ------------------ | ---------------------- |
| Pearson r        | Linear             | No                 | Two continuous         |
| Spearman rho     | Monotonic          | Yes                | Continuous or ordinal  |
| Kendall tau      | Monotonic          | Yes                | Continuous or ordinal  |
| Point-biserial   | Linear             | No                 | One binary, one continuous |
| Cramer's V       | Any association    | N/A                | Two categorical        |

> Key Takeaways
> - Pearson detects linear association only and is destroyed by a single
>   outlier; Spearman and Kendall work on ranks and are robust.
> - A perfectly monotonic curve gives Spearman 1.0 and Pearson noticeably
>   less, which is a useful diagnostic pair.
> - No correlation coefficient detects a symmetric non-monotonic
>   relationship such as a parabola.
> - Anscombe's quartet shows that identical coefficients can describe
>   completely different data, so always plot.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compute Pearson and Spearman on an exponential relationship and explain
>    why they differ.
> 2. Reproduce Anscombe's quartet and verify the four datasets share
>    summary statistics.
> 3. Interview: Ice cream sales correlate with drownings at r = 0.9. What do
>    you conclude? (Hint: look for a variable that drives both.)

#### Contingency Tables

When both variables are categorical, scatter plots and correlation
coefficients do not apply. A contingency table, also called a cross-tab, is
the right summary: a grid of counts for every combination of categories. It
is the categorical analogue of the joint distribution from Chapter 2, filled
with observed counts rather than probabilities.

The table itself is just bookkeeping. What makes it powerful is the
comparison between what you observed and what you would expect if the two
variables were independent. Under independence, the expected count in a cell
is the row total times the column total divided by the grand total. Large
gaps between observed and expected are evidence of association, and the
chi-square test formalizes that comparison.

Reading a cross-tab correctly requires choosing the right percentages. Row
percentages, column percentages, and percentages of the total answer
different questions, and confusing them reverses conclusions. This is the
same trap as confusing `P(A | B)` with `P(B | A)`.

The final caution is Simpson's paradox from Chapter 2: a two-way table can
mislead whenever a third variable differs across the groups. Always ask what
is being collapsed.

```text
  A CONTINGENCY TABLE AND ITS THREE PERCENTAGE VIEWS

   OBSERVED COUNTS
                churned  retained | total
      free          120      380  |   500
      pro            40      460  |   500
      ----------------------------+------
      total         160      840  |  1000

   EXPECTED IF INDEPENDENT  (row total * col total / grand total)
      free: 500*160/1000 = 80     500*840/1000 = 420
      pro:  500*160/1000 = 80     500*840/1000 = 420

   Observed 120 vs expected 80 for free churn -> far more than chance.

   ROW %      "of free users, what share churned?"     120/500 = 24%
   COLUMN %   "of churners, what share were free?"     120/160 = 75%
   TOTAL %    "what share of all users are free and churned?"  12%

   These are three different numbers answering three different
   questions. Quoting the wrong one is the base rate fallacy again.
```

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "plan":   ["free"] * 500 + ["pro"] * 500,
    "churned": [1] * 120 + [0] * 380 + [1] * 40 + [0] * 460,
})

table = pd.crosstab(df["plan"], df["churned"])
print(table)
#  churned    0    1
#  plan
#  free     380  120
#  pro      460   40

# The three percentage views, each answering a different question.
print(pd.crosstab(df["plan"], df["churned"], normalize="index").round(3))
#   of each PLAN, what fraction churned?     free 0.24, pro 0.08
print(pd.crosstab(df["plan"], df["churned"], normalize="columns").round(3))
#   of each OUTCOME, what fraction was each plan?   churners: 75% free
print(pd.crosstab(df["plan"], df["churned"], normalize="all").round(3))
#   share of the whole dataset in each cell

# Is the association real, or could it be chance?
result = stats.chi2_contingency(table)
print(f"chi2 = {result.statistic:.1f}, p = {result.pvalue:.2e}")
print("expected counts under independence:\n", result.expected_freq.round(1))
# expected: [[420, 80], [420, 80]] against observed [[380,120],[460,40]]
# chi2 is large and p is tiny: the plans genuinely differ in churn.

# Effect size, because with enough rows everything is "significant".
n = table.values.sum()
cramers_v = np.sqrt(result.statistic / (n * (min(table.shape) - 1)))
print(f"Cramer's V = {cramers_v:.3f}")        # ~0.22, a moderate association

# Always add margins when presenting: readers need the denominators.
print(pd.crosstab(df["plan"], df["churned"], margins=True))
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A contingency table cross-tabulates counts and is the right summary for
>   two categorical variables.
> - Association is judged by comparing observed counts to those expected
>   under independence.
> - Row, column, and total percentages answer different questions, and
>   quoting the wrong one inverts the conclusion.
> - Report an effect size such as Cramer's V alongside a chi-square p-value,
>   since large samples make trivial associations significant.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a cross-tab of two categorical columns and produce all three
>    percentage views, stating the question each answers.
> 2. Compute the expected counts under independence by hand for a 2-by-2
>    table and compare them to the observed values.
> 3. Interview: A cross-tab shows a treatment works overall, but you learn
>    patients chose their own treatment. What now? (Hint: ask what else
>    differs between the two groups.)

<a id="32-sampling-and-estimation"></a>
### 3.2 Sampling and Estimation
