```python
print(f"means:   A={a.mean():.1f}  B={b.mean():.1f}")
print(f"medians: A={np.median(a):.1f}  B={np.median(b):.1f}")
print(f"Welch t p = {t_res.pvalue:.4f}")
print(f"Mann-Whitney p = {u_res.pvalue:.4f}")
# The means are dominated by four extreme sessions and the t-test is
# swamped. Mann-Whitney sees the consistent rank shift and detects it.

# Paired version: Wilcoxon signed-rank on before/after measurements.
before = rng.exponential(100, 30)
after = before * rng.uniform(0.6, 0.95, 30)        # a consistent improvement
print(f"\npaired t p    = {stats.ttest_rel(before, after).pvalue:.5f}")
print(f"Wilcoxon p    = {stats.wilcoxon(before, after).pvalue:.5f}")

# Several groups without normality: Kruskal-Wallis.
gs = [rng.exponential(scale, 40) for scale in (20, 22, 35)]
print(f"\nANOVA p        = {stats.f_oneway(*gs).pvalue:.4f}")
print(f"Kruskal p      = {stats.kruskal(*gs).pvalue:.4f}")

# The cost of robustness, measured. When normality DOES hold, how much
# power does Mann-Whitney give up against the t-test?
t_wins = u_wins = 0
for _ in range(5_000):
    x = rng.normal(0, 1, 30)
    y = rng.normal(0.6, 1, 30)                     # a real effect
    t_wins += stats.ttest_ind(x, y).pvalue < 0.05
    u_wins += stats.mannwhitneyu(x, y).pvalue < 0.05
print(f"\npower on clean normal data -- t: {t_wins/5000:.3f}  "
      f"Mann-Whitney: {u_wins/5000:.3f}")
# The rank test retains roughly 95% of the t-test's power. Cheap
# insurance against assumptions you cannot verify.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Non-parametric tests replace values with ranks, which removes both
>   distributional assumptions and outlier sensitivity.
> - Each parametric test has a standard rank-based counterpart worth
>   memorizing.
> - They compare distributions generally, and compare medians only when the
>   distributions share a shape.
> - On genuinely normal data they retain about 95% of the parametric test's
>   power, making them cheap insurance.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compare a t-test and Mann-Whitney on skewed data with outliers and
>    explain the divergence.
> 2. Run Wilcoxon signed-rank on paired measurements and compare to the
>    paired t-test.
> 3. Interview: When would you choose Mann-Whitney over a t-test? (Hint:
>    consider what you can verify about the distribution at n = 15.)

#### Multiple Comparisons Correction

If you run one test at alpha = 0.05, you accept a 5% false positive rate. If
you run 100 tests on data with no real effects, you should expect about five
significant results. Nothing has malfunctioned. This is the advertised rate,
and it is why testing many hypotheses without adjustment produces confident
nonsense.

The problem appears everywhere in data science, usually without anyone
labelling it: testing a treatment across 20 user segments, screening 10,000
genes, comparing every pair of groups, checking an A/B test daily for a
month, or trying many features until one looks predictive.

Two families of correction exist, and they control different things. The
*family-wise error rate* is the probability of *any* false positive.
Bonferroni controls it by dividing alpha by the number of tests, which is
simple and extremely conservative. Holm's method achieves the same guarantee
with more power and should generally be preferred to plain Bonferroni.

The *false discovery rate* controls the expected *proportion* of false
positives among the results you call significant. Benjamini-Hochberg is the
standard method. This is usually the better choice in exploratory data
science, where tolerating a known fraction of false leads is sensible and
demanding zero is paralyzing.

```text
  THE PROBLEM, QUANTIFIED

   P(at least one false positive) = 1 - (1 - alpha)^m

   tests m:    1      5      10     20     100
   P(error): 5.0%  22.6%  40.1%  64.2%   99.4%

   At 100 tests you are essentially GUARANTEED a false positive.

  TWO DIFFERENT GUARANTEES

   FAMILY-WISE ERROR RATE (FWER)
     "P(any false positive among all tests) <= 0.05"
     strict; use when a single false claim is costly
     methods: Bonferroni (simple), Holm (uniformly better)

   FALSE DISCOVERY RATE (FDR)
     "expected share of false positives AMONG REJECTIONS <= 0.05"
     permissive; use for screening and exploration
     method: Benjamini-Hochberg

   Of 100 rejections, FDR at 0.05 expects about 5 to be wrong.
   FWER at 0.05 expects a 5% chance that even ONE is wrong.

  BENJAMINI-HOCHBERG PROCEDURE
   1. sort the m p-values ascending
   2. find the largest k with  p(k) <= (k / m) * alpha
   3. reject hypotheses 1 through k
```

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
from statsmodels.stats.multitest import multipletests

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# Test a treatment across 20 segments where it does NOTHING anywhere.
p_values = []
for _ in range(20):
    a = rng.normal(0, 1, 100)
    b = rng.normal(0, 1, 100)            # no effect, by construction
    p_values.append(stats.ttest_ind(a, b).pvalue)
p_values = np.array(p_values)

print(f"raw significant at 0.05: {(p_values < 0.05).sum()} of 20")
# Typically 1 or 2 "discoveries", all of them false.

for method, label in [("bonferroni", "Bonferroni"),
                      ("holm", "Holm"),
                      ("fdr_bh", "Benjamini-Hochberg")]:
    reject, adjusted, _, _ = multipletests(p_values, alpha=0.05, method=method)
    print(f"{label:<20} significant: {reject.sum()}")
# All three correctly report 0 discoveries.

# Now a realistic mix: 100 tests, 10 with a genuine effect.
p_mixed = []
truth = []
for i in range(100):
    effect = 0.8 if i < 10 else 0.0           # first ten are real
    a = rng.normal(0, 1, 50)
    b = rng.normal(effect, 1, 50)
    p_mixed.append(stats.ttest_ind(a, b).pvalue)
    truth.append(effect > 0)
p_mixed, truth = np.array(p_mixed), np.array(truth)

print(f"\n{'method':<22}{'found':>7}{'true':>7}{'false':>7}")
for method, label in [("none", "no correction"),
                      ("bonferroni", "Bonferroni"),
                      ("holm", "Holm"),
                      ("fdr_bh", "Benjamini-Hochberg")]:
    if method == "none":
        reject = p_mixed < 0.05
    else:
        reject, _, _, _ = multipletests(p_mixed, alpha=0.05, method=method)
    tp = (reject & truth).sum()
    fp = (reject & ~truth).sum()
    print(f"{label:<22}{reject.sum():>7}{tp:>7}{fp:>7}")
# no correction      ~14     ~10      ~5    many false leads
# Bonferroni          ~7      ~7       0    strict, misses real effects
# Holm                ~7      ~7       0    same guarantee, more power
# Benjamini-Hochberg ~10      ~9      ~1    best balance for screening

# Bonferroni by hand, to show there is no magic in it.
print(f"\nBonferroni threshold = {0.05 / 100:.5f}")
print(f"tests below it: {(p_mixed < 0.05 / 100).sum()}")
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Running `m` tests at alpha = 0.05 makes at least one false positive
>   nearly certain once `m` reaches about 100.
> - Family-wise methods control the chance of any false positive; Holm
>   dominates plain Bonferroni and should replace it.
> - False discovery rate control bounds the proportion of false positives
>   among rejections and suits exploratory screening.
> - Checking an experiment repeatedly over time is a multiple comparisons
>   problem, even though it looks like one test.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Run 50 tests on pure noise and count significant results before and
>    after Benjamini-Hochberg correction.
> 2. Implement the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure by hand and verify it against
>    `multipletests`.
> 3. Interview: An analyst tested 30 segments and reports the two that came
>    back significant. What do you ask? (Hint: work out how many significant
>    results 30 null tests would produce on their own.)

<a id="34-bayesian-statistics"></a>
### 3.4 Bayesian Statistics

Bayesian statistics treats parameters as uncertain quantities with
distributions rather than fixed unknowns, which lets you state directly what
everyone wants to know: how probable each possible value is, given the data.

#### Priors, Likelihoods, Posteriors

The frequentist machinery of the previous section answers a slightly awkward
question. A confidence interval tells you about the long-run behaviour of a
procedure, when what you wanted was a probability statement about the
parameter. Bayesian inference provides that directly, at the cost of
requiring you to state your beliefs before seeing the data.

The framework has three components, connected by Bayes' theorem from Chapter
2. The *prior* is your belief about the parameter before observing data,
expressed as a probability distribution. The *likelihood* is how probable the
observed data would be under each possible parameter value. The *posterior*
is the updated belief after combining them.

The mechanism is simple to describe: the posterior is proportional to the
likelihood times the prior. Parameter values that both fit the data well and
were plausible beforehand come out with high posterior probability.

The prior is the controversial part, and the objection is that it injects
subjectivity. Two responses matter in practice. First, with enough data the
likelihood dominates and the prior's influence vanishes, so reasonable people
with different priors converge. Second, a prior is an explicit, auditable
assumption, whereas frequentist analyses carry implicit assumptions that are
harder to inspect.

An analogy: a doctor seeing a patient with a cough does not start from
scratch. Prior knowledge of what is circulating this season plus the specific
symptoms yields a diagnosis. Ignoring the prior would mean treating a common
cold and a rare tropical disease as equally likely.

```text
  POSTERIOR = LIKELIHOOD x PRIOR  (then normalized)

   PRIOR                LIKELIHOOD            POSTERIOR
   (belief before)      (what data says)      (updated belief)

      _--_                     /\                  /\
    .'    '.                  /  \                /  \
   /        \        x       /    \      =       /    \
  ----------------         --------------      -------------
   broad, uncertain         data is             narrower, and
                            informative         pulled toward
                                                the data

  THE PRIOR'S INFLUENCE FADES WITH DATA

   n = 5            n = 50           n = 500
    _--_              /\               |
  .'    '.           /  \              |
 /        \         /    \            /|\
 ----------        --------          --+--
 prior still       data taking       prior irrelevant;
 dominates         over              likelihood wins

  Two analysts with different priors converge as evidence accumulates.
  If they do not, the disagreement is about the data, not the prior.
```

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# Estimating a conversion rate. The Beta distribution is the natural
# prior for a probability, since it lives on [0, 1].

# Three analysts with different starting beliefs.
priors = {
    "uninformative": (1, 1),        # Beta(1,1) is uniform: anything goes
    "optimistic":    (8, 2),        # believes the rate is around 80%
    "skeptical":     (2, 18),       # believes the rate is around 10%
}

observed_successes, observed_trials = 30, 100      # 30% observed

print(f"{'prior':<15}{'prior mean':>12}{'posterior mean':>16}{'95% CI':>22}")
for name, (a, b) in priors.items():
    # Beta is CONJUGATE to the binomial: the posterior is just
    # Beta(a + successes, b + failures). No integration required.
    post_a = a + observed_successes
    post_b = b + (observed_trials - observed_successes)
    post = stats.beta(post_a, post_b)
    lo, hi = post.interval(0.95)
    print(f"{name:<15}{a/(a+b):>12.3f}{post.mean():>16.3f}"
          f"{f'({lo:.3f}, {hi:.3f})':>22}")
# uninformative   0.500          0.304        (0.221, 0.394)
# optimistic      0.800          0.345        (0.257, 0.438)
# skeptical       0.100          0.267        (0.187, 0.354)
# The priors disagreed wildly (0.10 vs 0.80) and the posteriors are
# already close after only 100 observations.

# With more data they converge completely.
print()
for n in (10, 100, 1000, 10_000):
    s = int(0.30 * n)                              # same 30% rate throughout
    means = []
    for name, (a, b) in priors.items():
        means.append(stats.beta(a + s, b + n - s).mean())
    print(f"n={n:>6}: posterior means = "
          f"{[round(m, 3) for m in means]}  spread={max(means)-min(means):.3f}")
# n=    10: spread ~0.38   the prior is doing most of the work
# n=   100: spread ~0.08
# n=  1000: spread ~0.008
# n= 10000: spread ~0.001  the prior is now irrelevant

# The posterior answers the question people actually ask.
post = stats.beta(1 + 30, 1 + 70)
print(f"\nP(rate > 0.25 | data) = {1 - post.cdf(0.25):.3f}")     # ~0.88
print(f"P(rate > 0.35 | data) = {1 - post.cdf(0.35):.3f}")       # ~0.15
# These are direct probability statements about the parameter, which a
# frequentist p-value cannot provide.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - The posterior is proportional to the likelihood times the prior,
>   combining prior belief with observed evidence.
> - Priors are explicit and auditable assumptions rather than hidden ones.
> - With sufficient data the likelihood dominates and different reasonable
>   priors converge to the same posterior.
> - The posterior supports direct probability statements about parameters,
>   which frequentist methods cannot provide.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Update a Beta(1,1) prior with 8 successes in 20 trials and report the
>    posterior mean and interval.
> 2. Show how three different priors converge as the sample grows from 10 to
>    10,000 observations.
> 3. Interview: A colleague objects that priors are subjective. How do you
>    respond? (Hint: consider what assumptions a frequentist analysis makes
>    and whether they are stated anywhere.)

#### Conjugate Priors

Bayes' theorem requires dividing by the probability of the data, which is an
integral over all parameter values. For most models that integral has no
closed form, which is why Bayesian methods were impractical for most of their
history. Conjugate priors are the special cases where the mathematics works
out exactly.

A prior is *conjugate* to a likelihood when the resulting posterior belongs
to the same distribution family as the prior. Updating then reduces to
arithmetic on the parameters instead of integration. Beta is conjugate to the
binomial, so a Beta prior updated with binomial data yields a Beta posterior
whose parameters are simply the prior's plus the observed counts.

This produces an unusually clear interpretation: the prior parameters act as
*pseudo-counts*, observations you are pretending to have seen already. A
Beta(8, 2) prior behaves exactly like having previously observed 8 successes
and 2 failures. That makes the prior's strength concrete and easy to justify
or challenge.

Conjugate updates are also what make streaming Bayesian inference trivial.
Since the posterior has the same form as the prior, it becomes the prior for
the next batch, and the update is a few additions.

| Likelihood        | Conjugate prior | Posterior parameters                    |
| ----------------- | --------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Binomial          | Beta(a, b)      | Beta(a + successes, b + failures)       |
| Poisson           | Gamma(a, b)     | Gamma(a + sum of counts, b + n)         |
| Normal, known var | Normal          | Precision-weighted blend of both means  |
| Multinomial       | Dirichlet       | Dirichlet(alpha + category counts)      |
| Exponential       | Gamma           | Gamma(a + n, b + sum of observations)   |

```text
  PRIOR PARAMETERS AS PSEUDO-COUNTS

   Beta(a, b)  behaves exactly like having already seen
               a - 1 successes and b - 1 failures

   Beta(1, 1)    = 0 pseudo-observations   -> uniform, no information
   Beta(3, 7)    = weak belief near 0.3    -> 8 pseudo-observations
   Beta(30, 70)  = strong belief near 0.3  -> 98 pseudo-observations

   The SAME mean, very different strength:

     Beta(3,7)                    Beta(30,70)
        _---_                          /\
      .'     '.                       /  \
     /         \                     /    \
    ------------                   ---------
    wide: easily moved             narrow: needs a lot of data to shift

  STREAMING UPDATES ARE FREE

   day 1: Beta(1,1)   + (12 conv, 88 no)  -> Beta(13, 89)
   day 2: Beta(13,89) + (15 conv, 85 no)  -> Beta(28, 174)
   day 3: Beta(28,174)+ (11 conv, 89 no)  -> Beta(39, 263)

   No refitting, no stored history. Just addition.
```

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# Pseudo-count interpretation, demonstrated.
for a, b in [(1, 1), (3, 7), (30, 70)]:
    prior = stats.beta(a, b)
    # Observe a run of data that disagrees with the prior: 70% success.
    post = stats.beta(a + 70, b + 30)
    print(f"Beta({a:>2},{b:>2}): prior mean={prior.mean():.3f} "
          f"sd={prior.std():.3f} -> posterior mean={post.mean():.3f}")
# Beta( 1, 1): prior mean=0.500 sd=0.289 -> posterior mean=0.696
# Beta( 3, 7): prior mean=0.300 sd=0.138 -> posterior mean=0.664
# Beta(30,70): prior mean=0.300 sd=0.046 -> posterior mean=0.500
# The strong prior resists the data: 100 observations at 70% only move
# it halfway, because it already carries 98 pseudo-observations.

# Streaming: the posterior becomes the next prior, at no cost.
a, b = 1.0, 1.0
daily = [(12, 88), (15, 85), (11, 89), (18, 82)]
for day, (conv, no_conv) in enumerate(daily, start=1):
    a, b = a + conv, b + no_conv
    post = stats.beta(a, b)
    lo, hi = post.interval(0.95)
    print(f"day {day}: Beta({a:.0f}, {b:.0f}) mean={post.mean():.4f} "
          f"95% CI=({lo:.4f}, {hi:.4f})")
# The interval tightens each day and no past data needs to be retained.

# Poisson-Gamma: estimating a support ticket arrival rate.
observed_counts = np.array([3, 5, 2, 7, 4, 6])     # tickets per hour
prior_a, prior_b = 2.0, 1.0                        # weak belief near 2/hour
post_a = prior_a + observed_counts.sum()
post_b = prior_b + len(observed_counts)
rate_post = stats.gamma(a=post_a, scale=1 / post_b)
print(f"\nrate posterior mean = {rate_post.mean():.3f} per hour")
print(f"95% credible interval = "
      f"({rate_post.ppf(0.025):.2f}, {rate_post.ppf(0.975):.2f})")

# Verify conjugacy numerically against a brute-force grid posterior.
grid = np.linspace(0.01, 15, 20_000)
log_post = (stats.gamma.logpdf(grid, a=prior_a, scale=1 / prior_b)
            + np.array([stats.poisson.logpmf(observed_counts, g).sum()
                        for g in grid]))
dens = np.exp(log_post - log_post.max())
dens /= np.trapezoid(dens, grid)
grid_mean = np.trapezoid(grid * dens, grid)
print(f"grid-computed mean  = {grid_mean:.3f}")    # matches the closed form
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A conjugate prior makes the posterior fall in the same family, reducing
>   Bayesian updating to arithmetic.
> - Prior parameters act as pseudo-counts, which makes the prior's strength
>   explicit and easy to justify.
> - A strong prior resists new data in proportion to the pseudo-observations
>   it encodes.
> - Conjugacy makes streaming updates free, since the posterior becomes the
>   next prior with no stored history.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Show that a Beta(2,2) prior with 10 successes in 15 trials gives a
>    Beta(12,7) posterior, and report its mean.
> 2. Implement a streaming Beta-binomial update over a week of daily data.
> 3. Interview: How would you choose between Beta(1,1) and Beta(30,70) as a
>    prior for a new feature's conversion rate? (Hint: ask how many
>    comparable features you have already launched.)

#### Bayesian Inference vs Frequentist Inference

The two schools answer different questions, and most confusion comes from
expecting one to answer the other's. Neither is universally correct; they
make different trade-offs about what probability means and what you are
allowed to say.

The *frequentist* view treats probability as long-run frequency. A parameter
is a fixed unknown constant, not a random variable, so it cannot have a
distribution. Randomness lives in the data, and therefore in the procedure's
behaviour across hypothetical repetitions. That is why confidence attaches to
the interval-producing method rather than to any particular interval.

The *Bayesian* view treats probability as a degree of belief. A parameter can
have a distribution because your knowledge about it is uncertain, even though
its true value is fixed. That permits direct statements like "there is a 94%
probability the rate exceeds 10%".

The practical differences matter most in three places. Bayesian methods
incorporate prior information, which is valuable with small samples and
awkward when priors are contested. Bayesian methods permit continuous
monitoring, since the posterior is valid whenever you look, whereas repeated
frequentist testing inflates the false positive rate. Frequentist methods
have guarantees that do not depend on a prior being reasonable, and they are
computationally cheaper.

| Aspect               | Frequentist                        | Bayesian                          |
| -------------------- | ---------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Probability means    | Long-run frequency                 | Degree of belief                  |
| Parameter is         | Fixed unknown constant             | Random variable with a distribution |
| Prior information    | Not used                           | Required and explicit             |
| Interval             | Confidence: covers 95% of the time | Credible: 95% probability inside  |
| Answers              | `P(data given H)`                  | `P(H given data)`                 |
| Peeking at data      | Inflates the error rate            | Valid at any time                 |
| Computation          | Usually cheap                      | Often expensive                   |
| Small samples        | Weak                               | Strong, if the prior is good      |

```text
  THE SAME EXPERIMENT, TWO ANSWERS

   data: 30 conversions in 100 trials

   FREQUENTIST (Wilson interval)
     point estimate   0.300
     95% CI           (0.219, 0.396)
     statement        "if I repeated this study many times, 95% of
                       intervals built this way would cover the truth"
     cannot say       "there is a 95% chance the rate is in here"

   BAYESIAN (uniform prior)
     posterior        Beta(31, 71)
     posterior mean   0.304
     95% credible     (0.221, 0.394)
     statement        "given the data and my prior, there is a 95%
                       probability the rate lies in here"
     can also say     "P(rate > 0.25) = 0.87"

   The numbers are nearly identical. The INTERPRETATIONS differ
   completely, and only one of them matches how people speak.
```

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

successes, trials = 30, 100

# Frequentist: Wilson interval, which behaves better than the normal
# approximation for proportions near 0 or 1.
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_confint
lo_f, hi_f = proportion_confint(successes, trials, alpha=0.05, method="wilson")
print(f"frequentist 95% CI       = ({lo_f:.3f}, {hi_f:.3f})")

# Bayesian with a uniform prior.
post = stats.beta(1 + successes, 1 + trials - successes)
lo_b, hi_b = post.interval(0.95)
print(f"Bayesian 95% credible    = ({lo_b:.3f}, {hi_b:.3f})")
# Very close numerically, but they mean different things.

# The peeking problem: where the two genuinely diverge in practice.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

def frequentist_peeking(trials=2000, checks=20):
    """Check significance repeatedly under a TRUE null."""
    false_positives = 0
    for _ in range(trials):
        a, b = [], []
        for _ in range(checks):
            a.extend(rng.binomial(1, 0.12, 100))   # identical rates
            b.extend(rng.binomial(1, 0.12, 100))
            table = [[sum(a), len(a) - sum(a)], [sum(b), len(b) - sum(b)]]
            if stats.chi2_contingency(table).pvalue < 0.05:
                false_positives += 1
                break                               # stop at first "win"
    return false_positives / trials

print(f"\nfrequentist false positive rate with 20 peeks: "
      f"{frequentist_peeking():.1%}")
# ~25-30%, far above the nominal 5%. Each look is another chance to
# cross the threshold by luck, and stopping when you win locks it in.
#
# A Bayesian posterior does not have this problem: it is a summary of
# the evidence you currently hold, and looking at it does not change
# what it says. But note the honest caveat -- if you STOP collecting
# data when the posterior looks good, your decision rule still has
# frequentist properties worth checking.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Frequentists treat the parameter as fixed and the data as random;
>   Bayesians treat the parameter as uncertain and the data as given.
> - A confidence interval describes the procedure; a credible interval
>   describes the parameter.
> - Repeated frequentist testing inflates the false positive rate sharply,
>   while a posterior is valid whenever you inspect it.
> - Neither framework is universally correct; they trade prior information
>   against assumption-free guarantees.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compute a frequentist confidence interval and a Bayesian credible
>    interval for the same proportion and state each interpretation
>    precisely.
> 2. Simulate the peeking problem and measure how the false positive rate
>    grows with the number of checks.
> 3. Interview: When would you strongly prefer a Bayesian approach? (Hint:
>    consider a launch with 40 users and ten comparable past launches.)

#### Credible Intervals

A credible interval is the Bayesian answer to "where is the parameter likely
to be?" and it says exactly what most people incorrectly believe a confidence
interval says.

A 95% *credible interval* is a range containing 95% of the posterior
probability mass. Given the data and the prior, there is a 95% probability
the parameter lies inside it. No reference to hypothetical repeated
experiments is needed.

There are two common constructions. The *equal-tailed interval* cuts 2.5%
from each end of the posterior, which is simple and the usual default. The
*highest density interval* is the shortest interval containing 95% of the
mass, which guarantees every point inside is more probable than every point
outside. For a symmetric posterior they coincide. For a skewed one they
differ, and the highest density interval is preferable because the
equal-tailed version can include less probable values while excluding more
probable ones.

The practical advantage over confidence intervals is that credible intervals
compose naturally. You can ask directly for the probability that a parameter
exceeds a threshold, or that one variant beats another, by integrating the
posterior. These are the quantities decisions actually need.

```text
  EQUAL-TAILED vs HIGHEST DENSITY on a SKEWED posterior

        posterior density
         |     _
         |    / \
         |   /   \__
         |  /       \___
         | /            \______
         +----------------------------
           |   |              |     |
          HDI_lo             HDI_hi |
             |                      |
            ET_lo                 ET_hi

   EQUAL-TAILED: 2.5% cut from each side. Simple, but on a skewed
                 posterior it excludes high-density values on the left
                 while including low-density values on the right.

   HIGHEST DENSITY: the SHORTEST interval holding 95%. Every point
                 inside is more probable than every point outside.

  WHAT A CREDIBLE INTERVAL LETS YOU SAY

   "P(conversion rate > 0.25) = 0.87"
   "P(variant B beats variant A) = 0.96"
   "P(lift is between 1% and 3%) = 0.62"

   All are integrals of the posterior. None has a frequentist analogue
   that means the same thing.
```

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# A skewed posterior, where the two interval types visibly differ.
post = stats.beta(2, 20)          # low rate, right-skewed

# Equal-tailed: 2.5% from each end.
et_lo, et_hi = post.ppf(0.025), post.ppf(0.975)
print(f"equal-tailed  95%: ({et_lo:.4f}, {et_hi:.4f})  "
      f"width={et_hi - et_lo:.4f}")

def highest_density_interval(dist, mass=0.95, grid_size=200_000):
    """Shortest interval containing `mass` of the probability."""
    lows = np.linspace(0, 1 - mass, grid_size)          # candidate left tails
    los = dist.ppf(lows)
    his = dist.ppf(lows + mass)
    widths = his - los
    k = int(np.argmin(widths))                          # the narrowest one
    return los[k], his[k]

hdi_lo, hdi_hi = highest_density_interval(post)
print(f"highest density 95%: ({hdi_lo:.4f}, {hdi_hi:.4f})  "
      f"width={hdi_hi - hdi_lo:.4f}")
# The HDI is narrower and shifted left, because the posterior's mass
# piles up near zero. The equal-tailed version wastes width on a long
# thin right tail while cutting off denser values on the left.

# Direct decision probabilities, which is the real payoff.
posterior_a = stats.beta(1 + 120, 1 + 880)      # variant A: 120/1000
posterior_b = stats.beta(1 + 150, 1 + 850)      # variant B: 150/1000

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
samples_a = posterior_a.rvs(200_000, random_state=rng)
samples_b = posterior_b.rvs(200_000, random_state=rng)

print(f"\nP(B > A)              = {(samples_b > samples_a).mean():.4f}")
print(f"P(B beats A by >2pp)  = {((samples_b - samples_a) > 0.02).mean():.4f}")
lift = samples_b - samples_a
print(f"expected lift         = {lift.mean():.4f}")
print(f"95% credible on lift  = "
      f"({np.percentile(lift, 2.5):.4f}, {np.percentile(lift, 97.5):.4f})")
# P(B > A) is near 0.98, and the expected lift is about 3pp. The
# business can act on these numbers directly. A p-value would only
# have said "the difference is unlikely under the null".

# Expected loss from choosing wrongly -- the quantity that should
# actually drive a ship / no-ship decision.
loss_if_ship_b = np.maximum(samples_a - samples_b, 0).mean()
loss_if_keep_a = np.maximum(samples_b - samples_a, 0).mean()
print(f"\nexpected loss shipping B = {loss_if_ship_b:.5f}")
print(f"expected loss keeping  A = {loss_if_keep_a:.5f}")
# Ship whichever has the smaller expected loss. This is a decision rule,
# not a significance threshold.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A credible interval contains a stated probability of the parameter,
>   which is what people wrongly assume a confidence interval means.
> - Equal-tailed intervals are the simple default; highest density intervals
>   are shorter and preferable on skewed posteriors.
> - Posteriors compose, so you can compute the probability one variant beats
>   another directly.
> - Expected loss derived from the posterior is a better ship decision rule
>   than a significance threshold.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compute both interval types for a Beta(2,20) posterior and explain why
>    they differ.
> 2. Given two Beta posteriors, estimate the probability that one exceeds
>    the other by sampling.
> 3. Interview: Your posterior says P(B beats A) = 0.91. Do you ship?
>    (Hint: ask what shipping costs if you are in the other 9%.)

#### Markov Chain Monte Carlo

Conjugate priors cover a small set of tidy models. For anything realistic,
with several parameters, hierarchical structure, or a non-standard
likelihood, the posterior has no closed form and the normalizing integral is
intractable. Markov chain Monte Carlo is the method that made Bayesian
inference practical for real models.

The key realization is that you rarely need the posterior's formula. You need
to compute means, intervals, and probabilities from it, and all of those can
be estimated from *samples*. MCMC generates samples from the posterior
without ever computing the normalizing constant.

It works by constructing a random walk through parameter space whose
long-run visiting frequency matches the posterior. Steps toward
higher-probability regions are always accepted; steps toward lower
probability are accepted with a probability equal to the density ratio. That
ratio cancels the unknown normalizing constant, which is the entire trick.

Because samples arrive as a correlated chain, diagnostics are mandatory. You
must discard an initial *burn-in* period before the chain reaches the
posterior, run multiple chains from different starting points, and check
convergence. The *R-hat* statistic compares within-chain to between-chain
variance and should sit below about 1.01. *Effective sample size* reports how
many independent samples your correlated draws are worth.

```text
  THE CHAIN EXPLORES THE POSTERIOR

   parameter
      ^
      |   burn-in        stationary sampling
      |  /\  /                                     the chain forgets
      | /  \/  ,-,_,-'-,_,'-,_,-'-,_,-'-,_,'       its starting point
      |/        (samples from here are usable)     and then wanders
      +-----|----------------------------------->  the posterior in
      0   discard              iteration           proportion to density

  METROPOLIS-HASTINGS ACCEPTANCE

   propose theta'  from  theta
   ratio = p(theta' | data) / p(theta | data)
         = [ L(theta') prior(theta') ] / [ L(theta) prior(theta) ]
                                           the normalizing constant
                                           CANCELS -- this is the trick
   if ratio >= 1  -> always accept  (uphill)
   else           -> accept with probability = ratio  (sometimes downhill,
                                                       which is what makes
                                                       it explore, not just
                                                       climb)

  DIAGNOSTICS THAT ARE NOT OPTIONAL
   R-hat < 1.01          chains agree with each other
   ESS > ~400 per chain  enough effective independent draws
   trace plot            should look like a fuzzy caterpillar, not a trend
```

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# Data: normal with unknown mean and unknown standard deviation.
true_mu, true_sigma = 5.0, 2.0
data = rng.normal(true_mu, true_sigma, size=200)

def log_posterior(mu, log_sigma):
    """Unnormalized log posterior. The constant is never needed."""
    sigma = np.exp(log_sigma)                  # sample log sigma to keep it >0
    log_prior = (stats.norm.logpdf(mu, 0, 10)          # weak prior on mu
                 + stats.norm.logpdf(log_sigma, 0, 2)) # weak prior on log sd
    log_like = stats.norm.logpdf(data, mu, sigma).sum()
    return log_prior + log_like

def metropolis(n_steps=40_000, step=0.15, seed=0):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    mu, log_sigma = 0.0, 0.0                   # deliberately poor start
    current = log_posterior(mu, log_sigma)
    chain, accepted = np.empty((n_steps, 2)), 0
    for i in range(n_steps):
        prop_mu = mu + r.normal(0, step)
        prop_ls = log_sigma + r.normal(0, step)
        proposed = log_posterior(prop_mu, prop_ls)
        # Compare in LOG space: log(ratio) = proposed - current.
        if np.log(r.random()) < proposed - current:
            mu, log_sigma, current = prop_mu, prop_ls, proposed
            accepted += 1
        chain[i] = (mu, np.exp(log_sigma))
    return chain, accepted / n_steps

chain, acceptance = metropolis()
print(f"acceptance rate = {acceptance:.3f}")    # aim for roughly 0.2 to 0.5

burn = 10_000                                   # discard the approach phase
samples = chain[burn:]
print(f"mu:    mean={samples[:,0].mean():.3f}  "
      f"95% CI=({np.percentile(samples[:,0], 2.5):.3f}, "
      f"{np.percentile(samples[:,0], 97.5):.3f})   true={true_mu}")
print(f"sigma: mean={samples[:,1].mean():.3f}  "
      f"95% CI=({np.percentile(samples[:,1], 2.5):.3f}, "
      f"{np.percentile(samples[:,1], 97.5):.3f})   true={true_sigma}")

# R-hat: run several chains from different seeds and compare variances.
chains = [metropolis(seed=s)[0][burn:, 0] for s in range(4)]
chains = np.array(chains)
m, n = chains.shape
W = chains.var(axis=1, ddof=1).mean()                    # within-chain
B = n * chains.mean(axis=1).var(ddof=1)                  # between-chain
var_est = ((n - 1) / n) * W + B / n
r_hat = np.sqrt(var_est / W)
print(f"\nR-hat for mu = {r_hat:.4f}")          # want < 1.01
# If R-hat is well above 1.01, the chains have not mixed and every
# posterior summary computed from them is untrustworthy.

# In practice use a probabilistic programming library (PyMC, Stan,
# NumPyro). They implement Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, which explores far
# more efficiently, and compute these diagnostics automatically.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - MCMC estimates posterior quantities from samples, avoiding the
>   intractable normalizing integral.
> - The Metropolis acceptance ratio cancels the unknown constant, which is
>   what makes the method possible.
> - Samples are correlated, so burn-in must be discarded and convergence
>   must be checked.
> - Check R-hat below about 1.01 and adequate effective sample size before
>   trusting any posterior summary.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement Metropolis-Hastings for a single-parameter model and compare
>    the result to the conjugate answer.
> 2. Run four chains from different starting points and compute R-hat.
> 3. Interview: Your MCMC trace plot shows a slow upward drift. What is
>    wrong? (Hint: ask whether the chain has reached its stationary
>    distribution yet.)

#### Probabilistic Programming Basics

Writing your own sampler, as above, is instructive once and impractical
thereafter. Probabilistic programming languages let you declare a model as a
generative story and leave inference to a well-tested engine.

The shift is from *how* to *what*. You specify which parameters exist, what
priors they have, and how the data is generated from them. The library
handles gradients, sampling, adaptation, and diagnostics. Modern engines use
Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and the No-U-Turn Sampler, which use the posterior's
gradient to propose distant, high-quality moves rather than random small
steps, exploring far more efficiently than plain Metropolis.

The capability that makes this genuinely valuable is *hierarchical models*.
When you have many related groups, such as conversion rates across 50 
landing pages, you can model each group's parameter as drawn from a shared
population distribution. Groups with little data are then pulled toward the
overall mean, an effect called *partial pooling* or shrinkage. This is
automatic regularization with a principled justification, and it outperforms
both analysing each group separately and lumping them all together.

```text
  THREE WAYS TO HANDLE MANY GROUPS

   NO POOLING            COMPLETE POOLING       PARTIAL POOLING
   each group alone      one rate for all       hierarchical

   p1  p2  p3 ... p50         p                    mu, tau
    |   |   |      |          |                  /  |  |  \
   y1  y2  y3 ... y50      y1..y50             p1  p2 p3 .. p50
                                                |   |  |      |
                                               y1  y2 y3 .. y50

   overfits small         ignores real          small groups borrow
   groups; a page         differences           strength from the
   with 3 visits and                            population; large
   1 conversion gets                            groups keep their own
   an estimate of 33%                           estimate

  SHRINKAGE IN ACTION

   raw rate    n      partially pooled estimate
     0.33      3   ->   0.14    pulled hard toward the mean
     0.30     50   ->   0.22    pulled moderately
     0.28    900   ->   0.277   barely moved; it has its own evidence

   The amount of shrinkage is learned from the data, not chosen.
```

```python
# Sketch in PyMC. The model reads as the generative story itself.
import pymc as pm
import numpy as np

# 50 landing pages with very unequal traffic.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n_pages = 50
visits = rng.integers(3, 1000, n_pages)
true_rates = rng.beta(2, 18, n_pages)               # true rate near 0.10
conversions = rng.binomial(visits, true_rates)

with pm.Model() as hierarchical:
    # POPULATION level: what rates look like across pages in general.
    mu = pm.Beta("mu", alpha=2, beta=20)            # typical rate
    kappa = pm.HalfNormal("kappa", sigma=50)        # how tightly grouped

    # GROUP level: each page's rate is drawn from that population.
    rates = pm.Beta("rates",
                    alpha=mu * kappa,
                    beta=(1 - mu) * kappa,
                    shape=n_pages)

    # OBSERVED data, linking parameters to the counts we actually saw.
    pm.Binomial("obs", n=visits, p=rates, observed=conversions)

    # NUTS runs automatically; diagnostics are computed for you.
    trace = pm.sample(2000, tune=1000, chains=4, target_accept=0.9,
                      random_seed=0, progressbar=False)

import arviz as az
summary = az.summary(trace, var_names=["mu", "kappa"])
print(summary[["mean", "hdi_3%", "hdi_97%", "r_hat", "ess_bulk"]])
# Always read r_hat (want < 1.01) and ess_bulk (want > 400) before
# interpreting anything else in the table.

# Shrinkage, made visible.
posterior_rates = trace.posterior["rates"].mean(dim=["chain", "draw"]).values
raw_rates = conversions / visits
for i in np.argsort(visits)[[0, 1, -2, -1]]:       # two smallest, two largest
    print(f"visits={visits[i]:>4}  raw={raw_rates[i]:.3f}  "
          f"pooled={posterior_rates[i]:.3f}  true={true_rates[i]:.3f}")
# Low-traffic pages are pulled sharply toward the population mean and
# end up CLOSER to their true rate than the raw estimate was.
# High-traffic pages barely move, because their own data dominates.
```

| Library  | Language | Sampler      | Notable for                        |
| -------- | -------- | ------------ | ---------------------------------- |
| PyMC     | Python   | NUTS         | Readable models, strong ecosystem  |
| Stan     | Own DSL  | NUTS         | Reference implementation, fast     |
| NumPyro  | Python   | NUTS on JAX  | GPU acceleration, very fast        |
| Turing   | Julia    | Several      | Composable with Julia code         |

> Key Takeaways
> - Probabilistic programming lets you declare the generative model and
>   delegates inference to a tested engine.
> - Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and NUTS use posterior gradients and explore far
>   more efficiently than plain Metropolis.
> - Hierarchical models let groups borrow strength, shrinking small-sample
>   estimates toward the population mean.
> - The degree of shrinkage is learned from the data rather than chosen,
>   which makes it principled regularization.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Fit a hierarchical Beta-binomial model over several groups and compare
>    pooled estimates to raw rates.
> 2. Show that groups with the fewest observations are shrunk the most.
> 3. Interview: Why does partial pooling usually beat fitting each group
>    separately? (Hint: consider a group with three observations and what
>    its unpooled estimate looks like.)
