> 3. Interview: Why does the tidyverse discourage row names? (Hint: what
>    can a row name hold that a column cannot, and what breaks when rows are
>    filtered?)

#### The tidyverse Workflow

The tidyverse is a collection of packages sharing a design philosophy, and
the philosophy is what makes it worth learning rather than any individual
function.

The organising idea is **tidy data**: each variable is a column, each
observation is a row, each type of observational unit is a table. This is
the same long format that pandas reshaping targets, stated as a principle
rather than a technique. Once data is tidy, every tidyverse verb applies
without special cases.

The second idea is that a small set of **verbs** covers most manipulation,
and they compose. `filter` selects rows, `select` selects columns, `mutate`
adds columns, `arrange` orders, `summarise` aggregates, and `group_by`
changes the scope of the others. Each takes a data frame first and returns a
data frame, which is what makes them chainable.

The **pipe** is what turns the verbs into a workflow. `x |> f()` is `f(x)`,
so a sequence of transformations reads top to bottom in the order it
happens, rather than inside out. R now has a native pipe `|>` alongside the
magrittr `%>%`, and they are interchangeable for typical use.

The feature with no clean Python equivalent is **non-standard evaluation**.
Verbs accept bare column names without quotes because they capture the
expression and evaluate it inside the data frame. This makes interactive
code much cleaner and makes writing *functions* over columns harder, which
is what the embrace operator `{{ }}` exists to solve.

```r
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

sales <- tibble(
  region  = c("eu", "us", "eu", "ap", "us", "eu"),
  product = c("a", "a", "b", "b", "b", "a"),
  revenue = c(100, 250, 175, 320, 90, 210),
  units   = c(4, 9, 6, 11, 3, 8)
)

# THE SIX CORE VERBS, composed with a pipe.
result <- sales |>
  filter(revenue > 90) |>                        # rows
  mutate(unit_price = revenue / units) |>        # new columns
  group_by(region) |>                            # change the scope
  summarise(
    total   = sum(revenue),
    avg     = mean(unit_price),
    n       = n(),
    .groups = "drop"                             # always state this
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(total))                           # order
print(result)

# .groups = "drop" matters: without it the result stays grouped and the
# NEXT verb silently operates per group. This is the most common
# tidyverse surprise, and it is why summarise warns about it.

# mutate WITH group_by broadcasts, like pandas transform.
sales |>
  group_by(region) |>
  mutate(
    region_total = sum(revenue),
    share        = revenue / region_total,
    rank         = min_rank(desc(revenue))
  ) |>
  ungroup()

# ACROSS applies one operation to many columns.
sales |>
  group_by(region) |>
  summarise(across(c(revenue, units), list(sum = sum, mean = mean)),
            .groups = "drop")

sales |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ .x / max(.x)))
# ~ .x is a lambda shorthand: .x is the column being operated on.

# TIDYR: reshaping, the direct analogue of melt and pivot.
wide <- tibble(store = c("s1", "s2"), jan = c(100, 150), feb = c(110, 140))

long <- wide |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -store, names_to = "month", values_to = "sales")
print(long)

long |> pivot_wider(names_from = month, values_from = sales)

# SEPARATE and UNITE for composite fields.
tibble(code = c("eu-a-2024", "us-b-2023")) |>
  separate_wider_delim(code, delim = "-",
                       names = c("region", "product", "year"))

# MISSING VALUES, with explicit verbs.
gaps <- tibble(g = c("a", "a", "b"), v = c(1, NA, 3))
gaps |> drop_na(v)
gaps |> replace_na(list(v = 0))
gaps |> group_by(g) |> fill(v, .direction = "down") |> ungroup()

# complete MAKES IMPLICIT MISSINGNESS EXPLICIT, which matters before
# any time series or panel operation.
partial <- tibble(store = c("s1", "s1", "s2"),
                  month = c("jan", "feb", "jan"),
                  sales = c(10, 20, 30))
partial |> complete(store, month, fill = list(sales = 0))
# s2/feb did not exist as a row; now it does, with an explicit zero.

# JOINS mirror SQL, with the same names.
targets <- tibble(region = c("eu", "us"), target = c(400, 300))
sales |> left_join(targets, by = "region")
sales |> inner_join(targets, by = "region")
sales |> anti_join(targets, by = "region")     # rows with NO match: ap
# anti_join has no direct pandas equivalent and is the cleanest way to
# answer "which keys are missing from the lookup table".

# NON-STANDARD EVALUATION: why bare column names work, and how to write
# functions over them.
summarise_by <- function(data, group_col, value_col) {
  data |>
    group_by({{ group_col }}) |>                  # embrace to pass through
    summarise(total = sum({{ value_col }}), .groups = "drop")
}
summarise_by(sales, region, revenue)

# With a column name held in a STRING variable, use .data instead.
col <- "revenue"
sales |> summarise(total = sum(.data[[col]]))
```

```text
  THE TIDY DATA RULE

  UNTIDY (wide)                    TIDY (long)
  store  jan  feb                  store  month  sales
  s1     100  110                  s1     jan    100
  s2     150  140                  s1     feb    110
                                   s2     jan    150
  "month" is spread across          s2     feb    140
  column NAMES, so it cannot
  be filtered or grouped on         every variable is a column,
                                    every observation a row

  THE PIPE, and why it reads better

  arrange(summarise(group_by(filter(sales, revenue > 90), region),
                    total = sum(revenue)), desc(total))

  sales |>                      read inside out, right to left
    filter(revenue > 90) |>
    group_by(region) |>         versus top to bottom, in order
    summarise(total = sum(revenue)) |>
    arrange(desc(total))
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Tidy data puts one variable per column and one observation per row,
>   which is the precondition for every tidyverse verb applying uniformly.
> - Six verbs cover most manipulation, and each takes and returns a data
>   frame, which is what makes them compose.
> - Always set `.groups` in `summarise`, because a silently retained
>   grouping changes what the next verb does.
> - `across` applies an operation to several columns, and `complete` turns
>   implicit missing combinations into explicit rows.
> - Non-standard evaluation allows bare column names; use `{{ }}` to pass
>   them into your own functions and `.data[[ ]]` for strings.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write one pipeline that filters, adds a derived column, groups,
>    summarises, and sorts, then compare it line by line with the pandas
>    equivalent.
> 2. Use `complete` to fill missing store-month combinations with zero, and
>    explain why doing this before a time series step matters.
> 3. Interview: What does the embrace operator solve, and why is it needed
>    at all? (Hint: what happens to a bare column name passed as a function
>    argument?)

#### ggplot2 Grammar of Graphics

ggplot2 is the strongest argument for learning R. It implements a *grammar*
of graphics, meaning plots are composed from independent components rather
than selected from a catalogue of chart types.

The grammar has five parts. **Data** is the tidy table. **Aesthetics** map
columns to visual properties: position, colour, size, shape. **Geometries**
are the marks drawn: points, lines, bars. **Scales** control how data values
become visual values. **Facets** split one plot into a grid of small
multiples.

The consequence is compositional. There is no "grouped bar chart with a
trend line" function; you add a bar geometry and a smooth geometry to the
same aesthetic mapping. Any combination that makes sense can be expressed,
which is not true of libraries built around named chart types.

The distinction people get wrong is **inside versus outside `aes()`**.
Inside, a property is *mapped* to a column, so it varies by row and gets a
legend. Outside, it is *set* to a constant. Writing `colour = "blue"` inside
`aes()` creates a single-category legend labelled "blue" and colours the
points red, which is confusing exactly once.

Faceting deserves emphasis because it is underused. Splitting a cluttered
plot into small multiples by a categorical variable is usually more
informative than adding a third colour dimension, and it costs one line.

```r
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

set.seed(42)
d <- tibble(
  x       = rnorm(300),
  y       = NA_real_,
  region  = sample(c("eu", "us", "ap"), 300, replace = TRUE),
  segment = sample(c("smb", "ent"), 300, replace = TRUE),
  size    = runif(300, 1, 5)
) |> mutate(y = 2 * x + rnorm(300, 0, 1.5) + ifelse(region == "eu", 2, 0))

# THE MINIMUM: data, aesthetic mapping, geometry.
ggplot(d, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point()

# MAPPING versus SETTING: the distinction that matters.
ggplot(d, aes(x = x, y = y, colour = region)) +   # MAPPED: varies, legend
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 2)               # SET: constant, no legend

# The classic error:
# geom_point(aes(colour = "blue"))  -> maps every row to the literal
# string "blue", producing one red series with a legend entry "blue".

# LAYERS ACCUMULATE, each optionally with its own data or mapping.
ggplot(d, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = region), alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, colour = "black") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  labs(
    title    = "Revenue response is steeper in EU",
    subtitle = "Linear fit with 95% confidence band",
    x        = "Standardised spend",
    y        = "Revenue lift",
    colour   = "Region",
    caption  = "n = 300, simulated"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

# A title that states the FINDING rather than naming the variables does
# most of the communication work. See chapter 7 for why.

# FACETING: small multiples instead of a third colour dimension.
ggplot(d, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ region)                      # one panel per region

ggplot(d, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  facet_grid(segment ~ region)              # rows x columns

# free scales when panels have very different ranges; fixed scales when
# comparing magnitudes across panels is the point.
ggplot(d, aes(x = y)) + geom_histogram(bins = 20) +
  facet_wrap(~ region, scales = "free_y")

# GEOMETRIES for the common cases.
ggplot(d, aes(x = region, y = y)) + geom_boxplot()
ggplot(d, aes(x = region, y = y)) + geom_violin() + geom_jitter(width = 0.15,
                                                                alpha = 0.3)
ggplot(d, aes(x = y)) + geom_density(aes(fill = region), alpha = 0.4)
ggplot(d, aes(x = region, fill = segment)) + geom_bar(position = "dodge")
ggplot(d, aes(x = region, fill = segment)) + geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent)

# SCALES control the data-to-visual mapping.
ggplot(d, aes(x = x, y = y, colour = size)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_viridis_c() +                       # perceptually uniform
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-3, 3), breaks = seq(-3, 3, 1))

# LIMITS VERSUS ZOOM: a real correctness difference.
# scale_*_continuous(limits = ...)  DROPS points outside the range, which
#   changes any statistic computed by a later layer, such as a smooth.
# coord_cartesian(xlim = ...)       ZOOMS without dropping data.
ggplot(d, aes(x, y)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-1, 1))                 # the safe one

# SAVING: specify dimensions, never screenshot.
# ggsave("plot.png", width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)

# The grammar composes: any sensible combination is expressible, which
# is why ggplot2 handles plots that a chart-type library cannot.
```

```text
  THE GRAMMAR AS LAYERS

  ggplot(data, aes(...))      the data and the variable mapping
    + geom_point()            a layer of marks
    + geom_smooth()           another layer, same mapping
    + scale_colour_viridis_c()how values become colours
    + facet_wrap(~ group)     split into small multiples
    + labs(...)               text
    + theme_minimal()         non-data ink

  MAPPED vs SET

  aes(colour = region)              colour VARIES by the region column,
                                    and a legend appears
  geom_point(colour = "blue")       colour is CONSTANT, no legend
  geom_point(aes(colour = "blue"))  WRONG: maps every row to the literal
                                    string, one series, misleading legend
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Plots are composed from data, aesthetic mappings, geometries, scales,
>   and facets rather than chosen from a list of chart types.
> - Properties inside `aes()` are mapped to columns and produce a legend;
>   properties outside are set to constants.
> - Layers accumulate and can each carry their own data and mapping, which
>   is what makes arbitrary combinations expressible.
> - Faceting into small multiples usually communicates better than encoding
>   a third variable as colour.
> - Setting scale limits drops data and changes computed layers; use
>   `coord_cartesian` to zoom safely.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a scatter plot with points coloured by one variable, a linear
>    fit per group, and facets by a second variable, all in one expression.
> 2. Demonstrate the difference between `scale_x_continuous(limits=)` and
>    `coord_cartesian(xlim=)` on a plot containing a smoother.
> 3. Interview: Someone writes `geom_point(aes(colour = "red"))` and gets
>    red-free output with an odd legend. Explain. (Hint: what does `aes`
>    treat its arguments as?)

#### Statistical Modeling in R

This is where R's origins pay off most directly. Fitting a model, getting
correct standard errors, and running diagnostics take three lines, because
the language was built by people who needed exactly that.

The **formula interface** is the core abstraction. `y ~ x1 + x2` declares a
model specification declaratively, and every modelling function in R accepts
it. The notation is compact and expressive: `:` is an interaction, `*` is
main effects plus interaction, `poly(x, 2)` is an orthogonal polynomial, and
`.` means all remaining columns.

Factors are handled automatically. A character or factor predictor is
expanded into dummy variables with a reference level, and the coefficients
are labelled with the level names. There is no manual encoding step, and no
opportunity to leak the encoding across a train-test split.

The output objects are rich. `summary()` gives coefficients, standard
errors, t-statistics, p-values, R-squared, and an F-test. `confint()` gives
intervals, `anova()` compares nested models, and `plot()` produces four
standard diagnostic plots. Compare this with the several libraries and
manual assembly the Python equivalent requires.

The `broom` package converts model output into tidy data frames, which is
what makes comparing many models practical: fit them, tidy them, bind the
rows, and plot.

```r
library(broom)
library(dplyr)

data(mtcars)

# THE FORMULA INTERFACE.
m1 <- lm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars)
summary(m1)
# Coefficients, standard errors, t values, p values, R-squared, and the
# overall F test, all from one call.

# FORMULA NOTATION.
# y ~ x1 + x2          main effects
# y ~ x1:x2            the interaction only
# y ~ x1 * x2          main effects AND the interaction
# y ~ . - x3           every other column except x3
# y ~ poly(x, 2)       orthogonal polynomial, safer than I(x^2)
# y ~ log(x)           transformations inline
# y ~ x + (1 | group)  a random intercept, with lme4

m2 <- lm(mpg ~ wt * factor(cyl), data = mtcars)
coef(m2)      # levels are labelled: factor(cyl)6, factor(cyl)8, ...

# FACTORS EXPAND AUTOMATICALLY, with a reference level.
mtcars$cyl_f <- factor(mtcars$cyl)
levels(mtcars$cyl_f)                       # "4" "6" "8": 4 is the reference
m3 <- lm(mpg ~ wt + cyl_f, data = mtcars)
# Coefficients read as differences FROM the reference level.
mtcars$cyl_f <- relevel(mtcars$cyl_f, ref = "8")    # change the baseline

# EXTRACTORS, uniform across model types.
coef(m1); confint(m1); fitted(m1)[1:3]; resid(m1)[1:3]
AIC(m1); BIC(m1); logLik(m1); nobs(m1)
predict(m1, newdata = data.frame(wt = 3, hp = 150), interval = "prediction")
# interval = "confidence" for the MEAN response, "prediction" for a NEW
# observation. The second is wider, and confusing them understates risk.

# DIAGNOSTICS, in one call.
# par(mfrow = c(2, 2)); plot(m1)
# Residuals vs fitted (linearity), Q-Q (normality),
# scale-location (homoscedasticity), residuals vs leverage (influence).

# MODEL COMPARISON.
m_small <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)
anova(m_small, m1)                         # nested F test
AIC(m_small, m1)

# GENERALIZED LINEAR MODELS, the same interface.
mtcars$efficient <- as.integer(mtcars$mpg > 20)
g1 <- glm(efficient ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars, family = binomial)
summary(g1)
exp(coef(g1))                              # odds ratios
predict(g1, type = "response")[1:3]        # probabilities, not log-odds

# Poisson for counts, with an offset for exposure.
# glm(events ~ x + offset(log(person_years)), family = poisson)

# BROOM turns model output into tidy tables.
tidy(m1, conf.int = TRUE)                  # one row per coefficient
glance(m1)                                 # one row per MODEL
augment(m1) |> select(mpg, .fitted, .resid, .cooksd) |> head(3)
# .cooksd flags influential points, which is the diagnostic most often
# skipped and most often responsible for a surprising coefficient.

# COMPARING MANY MODELS becomes a data frame operation.
specs <- list(
  simple      = mpg ~ wt,
  with_hp     = mpg ~ wt + hp,
  interaction = mpg ~ wt * hp
)
comparison <- purrr::imap_dfr(specs, function(f, name) {
  glance(lm(f, data = mtcars)) |> mutate(model = name, .before = 1)
})
print(comparison |> select(model, r.squared, adj.r.squared, AIC))

# MIXED EFFECTS, where R is clearly ahead of Python.
# library(lme4)
# lmer(score ~ treatment + (1 | school), data = d)
# A random intercept per school, correctly accounting for the fact that
# pupils within a school are not independent observations.

# SURVIVAL ANALYSIS, likewise.
# library(survival)
# coxph(Surv(time, event) ~ treatment + age, data = d)
```

> Key Takeaways
> - The formula interface declares model structure compactly and is
>   accepted by essentially every modelling function in R.
> - Factor predictors expand into dummy variables automatically with
>   labelled, reference-relative coefficients.
> - One `summary` call gives coefficients, standard errors, p-values, and
>   fit statistics, and `plot` gives four standard diagnostics.
> - Confidence intervals cover the mean response while prediction intervals
>   cover a new observation and are wider.
> - `broom` converts models into tidy tables, making many-model comparison
>   an ordinary data frame operation.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Fit three nested models, compare them with `anova` and AIC, and state
>    which you would report and why.
> 2. Fit a logistic regression, convert the coefficients to odds ratios,
>    and produce predicted probabilities for three hypothetical rows.
> 3. Interview: A regression coefficient flips sign when one observation is
>    removed. Which diagnostic would have warned you? (Hint: it appears in
>    `augment` output.)

#### R Markdown Reporting

A result that lives in a console is not a deliverable. R Markdown, and its
successor Quarto, let you write a document in which the code, its output,
and the prose live in one file, so the report is regenerated from source
every time.

The mechanism is *literate programming*. A plain-text file contains
Markdown prose and fenced code chunks. Rendering executes every chunk in a
fresh session and weaves the results into the output document. Because the
session is fresh, a document that renders is reproducible by construction:
every object it uses is created by code in the file.

That property is the real argument. The alternative workflow, running
analysis and pasting numbers into a document, breaks silently whenever the
data updates. With a rendered document, updating means re-rendering, and
there is no version where the text and the numbers disagree.

**Chunk options** control what appears. `echo` shows or hides the code,
`eval` runs it or not, `message` and `warning` control noise, and `cache`
stores results of expensive chunks. A report for stakeholders typically
hides all code; a technical appendix shows it.

**Inline code** embeds a computed value in a sentence, so a number in your
prose is generated rather than typed. This is a small feature with a large
effect, because typed numbers are exactly what goes stale.

**Parameterized reports** take variables from the render call, letting one
template produce a document per region, per month, or per customer.

````markdown
---
title: "Regional Revenue Review"
author: "Analytics"
date: "`r Sys.Date()`"
params:
  region: "eu"
  min_date: "2024-01-01"
output:
  html_document:
    toc: true
    code_folding: hide      # readers can reveal code if they want it
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# include=FALSE runs the chunk but shows neither code nor output.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo    = FALSE,     # hide code by default in a stakeholder report
  message = FALSE,     # suppress library loading chatter
  warning = FALSE,
  fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 150
)
library(dplyr); library(ggplot2)
```

```{r load, cache=TRUE}
# cache=TRUE stores the result; the chunk re-runs only when its code
# changes. Useful for slow queries, and a trap when the DATA changes
# without the code changing. Set cache.extra = file.mtime(path) to fix.
sales <- readr::read_csv("data/sales.csv") |>
  filter(region == params$region, date >= as.Date(params$min_date))
```

## Summary

Revenue for **`r params$region`** totalled
`r scales::dollar(sum(sales$revenue))` across
`r nrow(sales)` orders, a
`r scales::percent(sum(sales$revenue) / sum(sales$prior_revenue) - 1)`
change on the prior period.

Every number in that paragraph is computed at render time. None of them
can go stale, because none of them was typed.

```{r trend, fig.cap="Daily revenue with a 7-day trailing mean"}
sales |>
  arrange(date) |>
  mutate(ma7 = zoo::rollmean(revenue, 7, fill = NA, align = "right")) |>
  ggplot(aes(date)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = revenue), colour = "grey70") +
  geom_line(aes(y = ma7), linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Revenue") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r table}
sales |>
  group_by(product) |>
  summarise(revenue = sum(revenue), orders = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(revenue)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 0, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

## Appendix

```{r session, echo=TRUE}
sessionInfo()   # record package versions so the run is reproducible
```
````

```r
# RENDERING, including one document per region from one template.
# rmarkdown::render("report.Rmd", params = list(region = "us"))

for (r in c("eu", "us", "ap")) {
  # rmarkdown::render(
  #   "report.Rmd",
  #   params      = list(region = r),
  #   output_file = paste0("review_", r, ".html")
  # )
}

# QUARTO is the successor, with the same model and multi-language support.
# quarto render report.qmd -P region:us
# The same document can contain R, Python, and Julia chunks sharing state.

# OUTPUT FORMATS from one source: html_document, pdf_document (LaTeX),
# word_document, powerpoint_presentation, and dashboards via flexdashboard.

# THE REPRODUCIBILITY POINT, stated as a test:
#   delete every object in the environment, restart R, render.
#   If it fails, the document depended on hidden state and was never
#   reproducible. This is worth doing before sending anything.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Literate programming keeps code, output, and prose in one file, so the
>   report regenerates rather than being assembled by hand.
> - Rendering runs in a fresh session, which makes a document that renders
>   reproducible by construction.
> - Chunk options control visibility and caching; stakeholder reports
>   usually hide code while appendices show it.
> - Inline code embeds computed values in sentences, eliminating typed
>   numbers that go stale.
> - Parameterized reports produce one document per segment from a single
>   template.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a short report with one plot, one table, and at least two inline
>    computed values, then change the input data and re-render.
> 2. Parameterize the report by region and generate three outputs from one
>    template in a loop.
> 3. Interview: Why is "it renders from a clean session" a stronger
>    reproducibility claim than "the script runs"? (Hint: what can a script
>    quietly rely on that a fresh render cannot?)

<a id="43-sql-and-query-languages"></a>
### 4.3 SQL and Query Languages

SQL is where most analytical data actually lives, and pushing work into the
database rather than pulling rows into Python is usually the difference
between a query that returns in seconds and one that never finishes; this
section covers the language from selection through window functions and the
optimization habits that keep queries fast.

#### SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY

SQL is *declarative*: you describe the result you want, and the database
decides how to produce it. This is the opposite of pandas, where you
specify each transformation step. The consequence is that two queries
expressing the same result can run identically even when written very
differently, and that you cannot debug by stepping through operations.

The single most useful thing to know is the **logical evaluation order**,
which differs from the written order. The database conceptually evaluates
`FROM`, then `WHERE`, then `GROUP BY`, then `HAVING`, then `SELECT`, then
`ORDER BY`, then `LIMIT`.

That order explains two persistent confusions. A column alias defined in
`SELECT` cannot be used in `WHERE`, because `WHERE` runs first. But it *can*
be used in `ORDER BY`, because that runs after. Knowing the order turns both
from arbitrary rules into consequences.

The other fundamental is **three-valued logic**. SQL has `TRUE`, `FALSE`,
and `UNKNOWN`, and any comparison with `NULL` yields `UNKNOWN`. A `WHERE`
clause keeps only rows where the condition is `TRUE`, so rows where it is
`UNKNOWN` are dropped. This means `WHERE status != 'active'` silently
excludes rows where status is `NULL`, which is almost never intended.

`NULL` is not a value; it is the absence of one. `= NULL` is never true, not
even for a null. You must write `IS NULL`.

```sql
-- LOGICAL EVALUATION ORDER, which is not the written order:
--   FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT

SELECT
    order_id,
    customer_id,
    amount,
    amount * 0.2                         AS estimated_tax,   -- an alias
    UPPER(region)                        AS region_code
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= DATE '2024-01-01'
  AND amount > 100
  -- AND estimated_tax > 20             -- ERROR: WHERE runs before SELECT
ORDER BY estimated_tax DESC              -- fine: ORDER BY runs after SELECT
LIMIT 20;

-- THREE-VALUED LOGIC: the most common silent bug in SQL.
-- Suppose 1000 rows, 100 with status = 'active', 50 with status NULL.
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE status = 'active';      --  100
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE status != 'active';     --  850, not 900
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE status IS NULL;         --   50
-- The 50 NULL rows appear in NEITHER of the first two counts, because
-- NULL != 'active' evaluates to UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only TRUE.

-- The correct form when NULLs should be included:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders
WHERE status IS DISTINCT FROM 'active';                   --  900
-- or, portably:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders
WHERE status != 'active' OR status IS NULL;

-- NULL COMPARISON never works with =.
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE region = NULL;      -- always zero rows
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE region IS NULL;     -- correct

-- NULL HANDLING functions.
SELECT
    COALESCE(region, 'unknown')      AS region,   -- first non-null argument
    NULLIF(amount, 0)                AS amount,   -- NULL when it equals 0
    COALESCE(discount, 0) + amount   AS total     -- avoid NULL arithmetic
FROM orders;
-- Any arithmetic involving NULL yields NULL, so one missing discount
-- makes the whole total NULL rather than leaving it unchanged.

-- FILTERING vocabulary.
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE amount BETWEEN 100 AND 500               -- inclusive on both ends
  AND region IN ('eu', 'us')
  AND customer_name LIKE 'A%'                  -- prefix match
  AND customer_email ILIKE '%@example.com'     -- case-insensitive, Postgres
  AND order_date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days';

-- CASE: conditional logic, usable anywhere an expression is allowed.
SELECT
    order_id,
    amount,
    CASE
        WHEN amount >= 1000 THEN 'large'
        WHEN amount >=  200 THEN 'medium'
        ELSE 'small'                            -- without ELSE, NULL
    END AS size_band
FROM orders;
-- Branches are evaluated in order and the first match wins, so put the
-- most specific condition first.

-- DISTINCT removes duplicate ROWS, considering every selected column.
SELECT DISTINCT region FROM orders;
SELECT DISTINCT region, status FROM orders;    -- distinct PAIRS

-- ORDER BY: direction and NULL placement are separate choices.
SELECT * FROM orders
ORDER BY region ASC, amount DESC NULLS LAST;
-- Databases disagree on where NULLs sort by default. State it.

-- LIMIT WITHOUT ORDER BY IS NON-DETERMINISTIC. The database may return
-- any 10 rows, and a different 10 on the next run.
SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY order_id LIMIT 10;      -- reproducible
SELECT * FROM orders LIMIT 10;                        -- arbitrary

-- Deterministic paging needs a unique tiebreaker in the sort.
SELECT * FROM orders
ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC                -- unique overall
LIMIT 50 OFFSET 100;
```

```text
  WRITTEN ORDER vs LOGICAL ORDER

  written:              logical:
    SELECT      5         FROM        1   pick the tables
    FROM        1         WHERE       2   filter ROWS
    WHERE       2         GROUP BY    3   form groups
    GROUP BY    3         HAVING      4   filter GROUPS
    HAVING      4         SELECT      5   compute output columns
    ORDER BY    6         ORDER BY    6   sort
    LIMIT       7         LIMIT       7   truncate

  Consequences you can now derive rather than memorise:
    - a SELECT alias is unusable in WHERE   (2 runs before 5)
    - a SELECT alias IS usable in ORDER BY  (6 runs after 5)
    - WHERE filters rows, HAVING filters groups
    - LIMIT without ORDER BY is arbitrary

  THREE-VALUED LOGIC

     x = 5      when x is 5      -> TRUE      kept
                when x is 7      -> FALSE     dropped
                when x is NULL   -> UNKNOWN   dropped

  So a filter and its negation together return FEWER rows than the table.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - SQL is declarative, and its logical evaluation order differs from the
>   written order, which explains where aliases can and cannot be used.
> - Comparisons with NULL yield UNKNOWN, and `WHERE` keeps only TRUE, so a
>   filter and its negation both exclude null rows.
> - `NULL` requires `IS NULL` rather than `= NULL`, and any arithmetic
>   involving it propagates.
> - `COALESCE` supplies a default and `NULLIF` creates a null, which
>   together handle most null-safety needs.
> - `LIMIT` without `ORDER BY` returns arbitrary rows, and stable paging
>   needs a unique tiebreaker in the sort.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a query that counts rows matching a condition, rows failing it,
>    and rows where the column is null, then show the three sum to the
>    table total only when nulls are handled explicitly.
> 2. Write a query using a computed alias in `ORDER BY` and explain why the
>    same alias fails in `WHERE`.
> 3. Interview: A report of "non-active customers" undercounts. What is the
>    first thing you check? (Hint: what does a comparison against a null
>    column return?)

#### Joins and Set Operations

Joins combine rows from several tables, and the mental model that makes
them predictable is that a join produces every pair of rows satisfying the
condition, then the join type decides what happens to unmatched rows.

`INNER` keeps only matched pairs. `LEFT` keeps all left rows, padding with
nulls where no match exists. `RIGHT` is the mirror. `FULL OUTER` keeps
everything. `CROSS` produces every combination with no condition at all.

The behaviour that surprises people is **row multiplication**. If a key
appears twice on the left and three times on the right, the join emits six
rows for that key. A `SUM` over the result is then wrong by a factor
nobody notices, because the total is plausible. Checking key uniqueness
before joining is the only reliable defence.

The subtlety with `LEFT JOIN` is the difference between a condition in the
`ON` clause and one in `WHERE`. A condition in `ON` restricts what counts
as a match, preserving unmatched left rows. The same condition in `WHERE`
filters after the join, and since unmatched rows have nulls there, it
removes them, silently converting the left join into an inner join.

**Set operations** combine query results vertically instead of horizontally.
`UNION` removes duplicates and `UNION ALL` does not, which makes `UNION ALL`
substantially faster and the right default when you know the inputs are
disjoint.

```sql
-- SETUP: customers 1-4, orders referencing 1, 1, 2, and 99.

-- INNER: matched pairs only.
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, o.order_id, o.amount
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
-- Customers with no orders vanish; order 99 vanishes.

-- LEFT: every customer, with nulls where there is no order.
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, o.order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;

-- FINDING NON-MATCHES: the anti-join pattern.
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;               -- customers who never ordered

-- The same thing with NOT EXISTS, usually clearer and often faster.
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
);
-- Prefer NOT EXISTS over NOT IN: if the subquery returns any NULL,
-- NOT IN returns no rows at all, which is a notorious silent failure.

-- ON versus WHERE with a LEFT JOIN: not interchangeable.
SELECT c.name, o.order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
       ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
      AND o.amount > 100;               -- restricts what MATCHES
-- Customers with only small orders still appear, with NULL order_id.

SELECT c.name, o.order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.amount > 100;                   -- filters AFTER the join
-- Unmatched rows have NULL amount, NULL > 100 is UNKNOWN, so they are
-- dropped. This is now an INNER JOIN written misleadingly.

-- ROW MULTIPLICATION: the bug that inflates every downstream total.
-- orders has 2 rows for customer 1; if a shipments table also has 2
-- rows for each of those orders, the join emits 4 rows and SUM(amount)
-- double counts.
SELECT o.customer_id, SUM(o.amount) AS inflated
FROM orders o
JOIN shipments s ON s.order_id = o.order_id
GROUP BY o.customer_id;

-- The fix: aggregate the many side FIRST, then join one-to-one.
SELECT o.customer_id, SUM(o.amount) AS correct_total
FROM orders o
JOIN (
    SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) AS shipment_count
    FROM shipments
    GROUP BY order_id
) s ON s.order_id = o.order_id
GROUP BY o.customer_id;

-- CHECK CARDINALITY BEFORE JOINING. One query, and it settles it.
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows, COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS distinct_keys
FROM orders;                            -- equal means unique

-- MULTI-TABLE joins chain left to right.
SELECT c.name, o.order_id, p.product_name, oi.quantity
FROM customers  c
JOIN orders     o  ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id   = o.order_id
JOIN products   p  ON p.product_id  = oi.product_id
WHERE o.order_date >= DATE '2024-01-01';

-- SELF JOIN: a table against itself, for hierarchies and comparisons.
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.employee_id;

-- CROSS JOIN: every combination. Useful for building a complete grid
-- of dates and entities before a left join, so gaps become explicit.
SELECT d.date, s.store_id, COALESCE(f.sales, 0) AS sales
FROM dates d
CROSS JOIN stores s
LEFT JOIN facts f ON f.date = d.date AND f.store_id = s.store_id;

-- SET OPERATIONS combine vertically; column count and types must match.
SELECT customer_id FROM orders_2023
UNION ALL                                -- keeps duplicates: fast
SELECT customer_id FROM orders_2024;

SELECT customer_id FROM orders_2023
UNION                                    -- deduplicates: needs a sort
SELECT customer_id FROM orders_2024;

SELECT customer_id FROM orders_2023
INTERSECT
SELECT customer_id FROM orders_2024;     -- retained customers

SELECT customer_id FROM orders_2023
EXCEPT                                   -- MINUS in Oracle
SELECT customer_id FROM orders_2024;     -- churned customers
```

```text
  JOIN TYPES, WITH THE SAME TWO TABLES

  customers          orders
  1 Alice            10 -> 1
  2 Bob              11 -> 1
  3 Carla            12 -> 2
                     13 -> 99

  INNER      3 rows   (10,11 for Alice; 12 for Bob)
  LEFT       4 rows   (+ Carla with NULL order)
  RIGHT      4 rows   (+ order 13 with NULL customer)
  FULL       5 rows   (both extras)
  CROSS      12 rows  (3 x 4, no condition)

  ON vs WHERE ON A LEFT JOIN

  LEFT JOIN o ON c.id = o.cid AND o.amount > 100
     -> Carla still appears, with NULLs.        LEFT JOIN preserved.

  LEFT JOIN o ON c.id = o.cid WHERE o.amount > 100
     -> Carla's amount is NULL, NULL > 100 is UNKNOWN, row dropped.
     -> silently an INNER JOIN.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A join emits every matching pair, so duplicate keys multiply rows and
>   inflate any downstream aggregate.
> - Check that the join key is unique on at least one side before joining,
>   and aggregate the many side first when it is not.
> - A condition in `ON` restricts matching while the same condition in
>   `WHERE` filters after the join and converts a left join to an inner one.
> - Prefer `NOT EXISTS` over `NOT IN`, because a single null in the
>   subquery makes `NOT IN` return nothing.
> - `UNION ALL` skips deduplication and is markedly faster than `UNION`
>   when inputs are known to be disjoint.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write the same filtered left join twice, once with the condition in
>    `ON` and once in `WHERE`, and explain the different row counts.
> 2. Construct a case where joining two tables inflates a revenue sum, then
>    fix it by pre-aggregating.
> 3. Interview: A `NOT IN` subquery returns zero rows although you can see
>    non-matching records. What is the cause? (Hint: what does the
>    comparison return when the subquery contains a null?)

#### Aggregations and GROUP BY

Aggregation in SQL is the same split-apply-combine idea as pandas
`groupby`, expressed declaratively. The rules are few and strict, and the
strictness is what makes the results unambiguous.

The core rule: every column in `SELECT` must either appear in `GROUP BY` or
be wrapped in an aggregate function. If a column is neither, the database
cannot know which of the group's values to return, so standards-compliant
databases raise an error. MySQL historically returned an arbitrary value,
which is why that rule is worth stating explicitly.

`WHERE` and `HAVING` both filter, at different times. `WHERE` filters rows
before grouping; `HAVING` filters groups after aggregating. Putting a
condition in the right one matters for both correctness and speed: filtering
early means fewer rows to aggregate.

The counting functions differ in ways that matter. `COUNT(*)` counts rows.
`COUNT(col)` counts non-null values in that column. `COUNT(DISTINCT col)`
counts distinct non-null values. Using the wrong one is a routine source of
mismatched metrics between teams.

Aggregates other than `COUNT(*)` **ignore nulls**, which is usually helpful
and occasionally wrong. `AVG(col)` divides by the count of non-null values,
not by the row count. If nulls should count as zero, say so with `COALESCE`.

```sql
-- THE BASIC FORM.
SELECT
    region,
    COUNT(*)                      AS order_count,
    SUM(amount)                   AS total_revenue,
    AVG(amount)                   AS avg_order,
    MIN(amount)                   AS smallest,
    MAX(amount)                   AS largest,
    COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)   AS unique_customers
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= DATE '2024-01-01'     -- filters ROWS, before grouping
GROUP BY region
HAVING SUM(amount) > 10000                -- filters GROUPS, after
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;

-- THE THREE COUNTS, which are not interchangeable.
SELECT
    COUNT(*)                   AS all_rows,          -- includes NULL rows
    COUNT(discount)            AS rows_with_discount,-- excludes NULLs
    COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)AS distinct_customers
FROM orders;

-- AGGREGATES IGNORE NULLS, which changes the denominator of an average.
SELECT
    AVG(discount)                  AS avg_of_present,  -- n = non-null count
    SUM(discount) / COUNT(*)       AS avg_over_all,    -- n = row count
    AVG(COALESCE(discount, 0))     AS avg_treating_null_as_zero
FROM orders;
-- These three differ, and each answers a different question. Decide
-- which one the stakeholder means before reporting a number.

-- WHERE vs HAVING: both filter, at different stages.
SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'completed'         -- discard rows first: cheaper
GROUP BY region
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 10;             -- then discard small groups

-- Putting a row condition in HAVING works but scans more data:
-- HAVING can only reference grouped columns and aggregates anyway.

-- MULTI-COLUMN GROUPING produces one row per combination present.
SELECT region, product, SUM(amount) AS total, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM orders
GROUP BY region, product
ORDER BY region, total DESC;

-- CONDITIONAL AGGREGATION: the pivot idiom, and one of the most useful
-- patterns in analytical SQL.
SELECT
    region,
    COUNT(*)                                              AS total_orders,
    COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'completed')          AS completed,
    COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'cancelled')          AS cancelled,
    SUM(amount) FILTER (WHERE order_date >= DATE '2024-06-01') AS h2_revenue,
    AVG(CASE WHEN is_new_customer THEN amount END)        AS avg_new_customer
FROM orders
GROUP BY region;
-- FILTER is the standard form; CASE inside the aggregate is the portable
-- one, and works because aggregates skip the NULLs that CASE produces.

-- ROLLUP and CUBE add subtotal rows in one pass.
SELECT
    COALESCE(region, 'ALL')  AS region,
    COALESCE(product, 'ALL') AS product,
    SUM(amount)              AS total
FROM orders
GROUP BY ROLLUP (region, product)
ORDER BY region, product;
-- Produces: each region-product pair, a subtotal per region, and one
-- grand total. GROUPING SETS gives arbitrary combinations; CUBE gives all.

-- GROUPING() distinguishes a real NULL from a subtotal marker.
SELECT
    region,
    GROUPING(region) AS is_subtotal,
    SUM(amount)
FROM orders
GROUP BY ROLLUP (region);

-- STATISTICAL aggregates, available without leaving the database.
SELECT
    region,
    STDDEV_SAMP(amount)                                  AS sd,
    VAR_SAMP(amount)                                     AS variance,
    PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY amount)  AS median,
    PERCENTILE_CONT(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY amount) AS p95,
    CORR(amount, discount)                               AS correlation
FROM orders
GROUP BY region;
-- The median is an ORDERED-SET aggregate and needs the WITHIN GROUP
-- syntax, because it depends on the order of values rather than a
-- running accumulation.

-- STRING and ARRAY aggregation collapse a group into one value.
SELECT
    customer_id,
    STRING_AGG(product_name, ', ' ORDER BY product_name) AS products,
    ARRAY_AGG(DISTINCT region)                           AS regions
FROM order_items
GROUP BY customer_id;

-- GROUPING BY AN EXPRESSION, such as a time bucket.
SELECT
    DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS month,
    SUM(amount)                     AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)      -- repeat it, or GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY month;
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Every selected column must be grouped or aggregated, because otherwise
>   the database cannot choose which value to return.
> - `WHERE` filters rows before grouping and `HAVING` filters groups after,
>   so filter as early as the logic allows.
> - `COUNT(*)`, `COUNT(col)`, and `COUNT(DISTINCT col)` answer different
>   questions and are a common source of metric disagreement.
> - Aggregates ignore nulls, so an average's denominator is the non-null
>   count unless you wrap the column in `COALESCE`.
> - Conditional aggregation with `FILTER` or `CASE` pivots categories into
>   columns in a single pass.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write one query returning, per region, the total order count plus
>    separate counts of completed and cancelled orders as columns.
> 2. Show three different averages of a column containing nulls and explain
>    which stakeholder question each answers.
> 3. Interview: Two teams report different "active customer" counts from
>    the same table. Name three definitional differences that could cause
>    it. (Hint: consider the counting function and the null handling.)

#### Subqueries and CTEs

As queries grow, the question becomes how to structure them. SQL offers
subqueries and common table expressions, and the choice affects readability
far more than performance in modern databases.

A **subquery** is a query nested inside another. It can appear in `SELECT`
as a scalar, in `FROM` as a derived table, or in `WHERE` as a filter. The
important distinction is between *uncorrelated* subqueries, which are
evaluated once, and *correlated* ones, which reference the outer query and
are conceptually evaluated per outer row.

Correlated subqueries are the performance hazard. A correlated subquery in
`SELECT` over a million-row outer query may execute a million times. Modern
optimizers often rewrite them as joins, but not always, and a query that
performs fine on test data can fall over in production.

A **CTE**, written with `WITH`, names a query and makes it available to the
statement that follows. The benefit is structural: a pipeline of named steps
reads top to bottom, each step can be inspected independently, and a CTE can
be referenced several times without repeating its text.

The historical warning about CTEs being "optimization fences" applied to
older PostgreSQL. Since version 12 they are inlined by default unless
materialization is requested. Treat CTEs as the default structuring tool and
measure if you suspect a problem.

**Recursive CTEs** handle hierarchies and sequences, which plain SQL cannot
express. They are the tool for organizational trees, bill-of-materials
explosions, and generating a complete date series.

```sql
-- SCALAR SUBQUERY in SELECT: must return exactly one row and column.
SELECT
    order_id,
    amount,
    amount - (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders) AS diff_from_overall_avg
FROM orders;
-- Uncorrelated, so the inner query runs ONCE.

-- CORRELATED subquery: references the outer row, runs per row.
SELECT
    o.order_id,
    o.amount,
    (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders o2
      WHERE o2.region = o.region) AS region_avg      -- depends on o.region
FROM orders o;
-- Conceptually one execution per outer row. A window function does the
-- same thing in a single pass and is almost always preferable:
SELECT order_id, amount, AVG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY region) AS region_avg
FROM orders;

-- DERIVED TABLE in FROM: a subquery used as a table.
SELECT region, avg_amount
FROM (
    SELECT region, AVG(amount) AS avg_amount
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY region
) AS region_stats
WHERE avg_amount > 200;

-- IN, EXISTS, and NOT EXISTS in WHERE.
SELECT * FROM customers
WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE amount > 1000);

SELECT * FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM orders o                     -- SELECT 1: the value is
    WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id        -- irrelevant, existence is
      AND o.amount > 1000                      -- all that matters
);
-- EXISTS can stop at the first match, so it is often faster than IN,
-- and it is null-safe where NOT IN is not.

-- CTEs: the same pipeline, readable top to bottom.
WITH monthly_revenue AS (
    SELECT
        customer_id,
        DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS month,
        SUM(amount)                     AS revenue
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY customer_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)
),
customer_totals AS (
    SELECT
        customer_id,
        SUM(revenue)   AS lifetime_revenue,
        COUNT(*)       AS active_months,
        AVG(revenue)   AS avg_monthly
    FROM monthly_revenue                       -- references the CTE above
    GROUP BY customer_id
),
segmented AS (
    SELECT
        *,
        CASE
            WHEN lifetime_revenue >= 10000 THEN 'platinum'
            WHEN lifetime_revenue >=  2000 THEN 'gold'
            ELSE 'standard'
        END AS segment
    FROM customer_totals
)
SELECT segment, COUNT(*) AS customers, ROUND(AVG(lifetime_revenue)) AS avg_ltv
FROM segmented
GROUP BY segment
ORDER BY avg_ltv DESC;
-- Each step is independently inspectable: replace the final SELECT with
-- "SELECT * FROM monthly_revenue LIMIT 10" to debug the first stage.

-- A CTE REFERENCED TWICE, which a derived table cannot do without repeating.
WITH base AS (
    SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY region
)
SELECT
    b.region,
    b.total,
    ROUND(100.0 * b.total / (SELECT SUM(total) FROM base), 1) AS pct_of_all
FROM base b
ORDER BY b.total DESC;

-- RECURSIVE CTE: an organizational hierarchy.
WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
    -- anchor: the starting rows
    SELECT employee_id, name, manager_id, 1 AS level, name::text AS path
    FROM employees
    WHERE manager_id IS NULL

    UNION ALL

    -- recursive term: joins back to the CTE itself
    SELECT e.employee_id, e.name, e.manager_id, o.level + 1,
           o.path || ' > ' || e.name
    FROM employees e
    JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.employee_id
    WHERE o.level < 10                 -- ALWAYS bound the recursion
)
SELECT level, name, path FROM org ORDER BY path;
-- Without the depth bound, a cycle in the data loops forever.

-- RECURSIVE date generation, for filling gaps in a time series.
WITH RECURSIVE dates AS (
    SELECT DATE '2024-01-01' AS d
    UNION ALL
    SELECT d + 1 FROM dates WHERE d < DATE '2024-01-31'
)
SELECT d.d, COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0) AS revenue
FROM dates d
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.order_date = d.d
GROUP BY d.d
ORDER BY d.d;
-- Days with no orders now appear as zero rather than being absent,
-- which any subsequent moving average requires.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Uncorrelated subqueries run once while correlated ones conceptually run
>   per outer row, which is the main performance risk.
> - A correlated subquery computing a group statistic is nearly always
>   better expressed as a window function.
> - CTEs name pipeline steps so a long query reads top to bottom and each
>   stage can be inspected in isolation.
> - A CTE can be referenced several times, which a derived table cannot
>   without repeating its text.
> - Recursive CTEs handle hierarchies and generated sequences, and always
>   need an explicit depth bound.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Rewrite a correlated subquery that computes a per-region average as a
>    window function, and compare the execution plans.
> 2. Build a three-stage CTE pipeline that aggregates, segments, and
>    summarizes, then debug it by selecting from an intermediate stage.
> 3. Interview: When would you choose `EXISTS` over `IN`? (Hint: consider
>    both early termination and what happens when the subquery yields a
>    null.)

#### Window Functions

Window functions are the most important analytical feature in SQL and the
one most often missing from a self-taught repertoire. They compute a value
for each row using a set of related rows, without collapsing the result.

That is the whole distinction. `GROUP BY` reduces many rows to one per
group. A window function keeps every row and attaches a group-derived value
to it. Running totals, rankings, period-over-period changes, and
percent-of-total all need this, and none can be expressed with `GROUP BY`
alone.

The syntax has three parts inside `OVER`. `PARTITION BY` defines the group,
analogous to `GROUP BY`. `ORDER BY` defines the ordering within it, which
ranking and cumulative functions require. The **frame** clause defines which
rows around the current one are included.

The frame default is the trap. When you supply `ORDER BY` without a frame,
the default is `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`, which
gives a running total. Without `ORDER BY` the frame is the whole partition.
Also, `RANGE` includes all *peer* rows with the same sort value while `ROWS`
counts physical rows, so a moving average over data with tied timestamps
differs between them.

The three ranking functions differ only in tie handling, and the difference
matters: `ROW_NUMBER` is arbitrary among ties, `RANK` leaves gaps, and
`DENSE_RANK` does not.

```sql
-- THE CONTRAST: GROUP BY collapses, OVER does not.
SELECT region, SUM(amount) FROM orders GROUP BY region;      -- 3 rows

SELECT order_id, region, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY region) AS region_total
FROM orders;                                                  -- all rows

-- RANKING, and how each handles ties.
SELECT
    product,
    revenue,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS row_num,   -- 1,2,3,4
    RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS rnk,       -- 1,2,2,4
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS dense,     -- 1,2,2,3
    PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS pct_rank,
    NTILE(4)     OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS quartile
FROM product_revenue;
-- ROW_NUMBER among ties is nondeterministic unless the ORDER BY is
-- unique. Add a tiebreaker column when the result must be stable.

-- TOP N PER GROUP: the canonical window-function problem.
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT
        region, product, revenue,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS rn
    FROM product_revenue
)
SELECT region, product, revenue
FROM ranked
WHERE rn <= 3;
-- Window functions cannot appear in WHERE, because WHERE runs before
-- SELECT. Wrapping in a CTE is the standard workaround.

-- OFFSET FUNCTIONS: comparing a row to its neighbours.
SELECT
    order_date,
    revenue,
    LAG(revenue, 1)  OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS prev_day,
    LEAD(revenue, 1) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS next_day,
    revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS day_change,
    ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue, 7) OVER (ORDER BY order_date))
          / NULLIF(LAG(revenue, 7) OVER (ORDER BY order_date), 0), 1)
        AS wow_pct,
    FIRST_VALUE(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS first_day,
    LAST_VALUE(revenue)  OVER (
        ORDER BY order_date
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
    ) AS last_day
FROM daily_revenue;
-- LAST_VALUE needs an explicit frame: with the default frame ending at
-- the current row, "last" means "current", which is a classic surprise.
-- NULLIF guards the division when the prior value is zero.

-- FRAMES: running totals and moving averages.
SELECT
    order_date,
    revenue,
    SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS running_total,
    -- the default frame above is UNBOUNDED PRECEDING to CURRENT ROW

    AVG(revenue) OVER (
        ORDER BY order_date
        ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW      -- 7 rows, trailing
    ) AS ma7,

    AVG(revenue) OVER (
        ORDER BY order_date
        ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND 3 FOLLOWING      -- centred: LEAKAGE
    ) AS ma7_centred,

    SUM(revenue) OVER () AS grand_total               -- no ORDER BY: all rows
FROM daily_revenue;
-- The centred window uses future rows. Fine for a chart, wrong as a
-- feature for a model that must predict before those rows exist.

-- ROWS vs RANGE, which differ whenever the sort key has ties.
SELECT
    order_date, amount,
    SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date
                      ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)  AS by_rows,
    SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date
                      RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '1 day' PRECEDING
                                AND CURRENT ROW)                 AS by_range
FROM orders;
-- ROWS counts physical rows; RANGE covers a value span and includes
-- every peer sharing the current sort value. With several orders per
-- day these produce very different numbers.

-- PERCENT OF TOTAL, at two levels at once.
SELECT
    region, product, revenue,
    ROUND(100.0 * revenue / SUM(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY region), 1)
        AS pct_of_region,
    ROUND(100.0 * revenue / SUM(revenue) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_company
FROM product_revenue;

-- NAMED WINDOWS remove repetition when several columns share a frame.
SELECT
    order_date,
    SUM(revenue) OVER w  AS running_total,
    AVG(revenue) OVER w  AS running_avg,
    COUNT(*)     OVER w  AS running_count
FROM daily_revenue
WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY order_date ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING);

-- DEDUPLICATION, one of the most reused window patterns.
WITH numbered AS (
    SELECT *,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id, order_date
                              ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn
    FROM orders_raw
)
SELECT * FROM numbered WHERE rn = 1;      -- keep the latest per key

-- GAP AND ISLANDS: finding consecutive runs, such as login streaks.
WITH marked AS (
    SELECT
        user_id, activity_date,
        activity_date - (ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id
                                            ORDER BY activity_date))::int
            AS streak_group      -- constant within a consecutive run
    FROM user_activity
)
SELECT user_id, MIN(activity_date) AS streak_start,
       MAX(activity_date) AS streak_end, COUNT(*) AS streak_length
FROM marked
GROUP BY user_id, streak_group
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
ORDER BY streak_length DESC;
```

```text
  GROUP BY VERSUS OVER

  input                GROUP BY region        OVER (PARTITION BY region)

  eu  100              eu  485                eu  100  485
  us  250      --->    us  340        --->    us  250  340
  eu  175              ap  320                eu  175  485
  ap  320                                     ap  320  320
  eu  210              3 rows                 eu  210  485
  us   90                                     us   90  340

                                              6 rows: nothing collapsed

  FRAME DEFAULTS, the source of most surprises

  OVER (ORDER BY d)
     -> RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
     -> a RUNNING total, not the partition total

  OVER ()
     -> the whole partition
     -> the GRAND total

  OVER (ORDER BY d ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
     -> a 7-row TRAILING window, safe as a model feature
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Window functions attach a group-derived value to every row instead of
>   collapsing rows, which `GROUP BY` cannot do.
> - `ROW_NUMBER`, `RANK`, and `DENSE_RANK` differ only in tie handling, and
>   `ROW_NUMBER` needs a unique sort to be deterministic.
> - Supplying `ORDER BY` without a frame gives a running total by default,
>   not the partition total.
> - `ROWS` counts physical rows while `RANGE` includes all peers sharing
>   the sort value, which differ whenever ties exist.
> - Window functions cannot appear in `WHERE`, so top-N-per-group requires
>   wrapping the ranking in a CTE.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a query returning the top three products by revenue within each
>    region, using a ranking function and a CTE.
> 2. Compute a seven-day trailing average and a seven-day centred average
>    in one query, and explain which is safe as a model feature.
> 3. Interview: `LAST_VALUE` returns the current row's value instead of the
>    partition's last. Why, and what is the fix? (Hint: what frame applies
>    when you supply `ORDER BY`?)

#### Query Optimization Basics

A query that works on ten thousand rows and fails on ten million usually
has one of a small number of problems. Recognising them is a more
productive skill than memorising database internals.

The first habit is to **read the execution plan**. `EXPLAIN` shows what the
optimizer intends to do; `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` actually runs it and reports
real timings and row counts. The single most valuable signal is a large
discrepancy between estimated and actual rows, because the optimizer chose
its strategy from the estimate, and a bad estimate means a bad plan.

The second is understanding **indexes**. An index is a sorted structure that
turns a full scan into a targeted lookup, the same trade as a book's index.
It costs storage and slows writes, so indexes are added deliberately, on
columns used in `WHERE`, `JOIN`, and `ORDER BY`.

The rule that catches people is that **wrapping an indexed column in a
function disables the index**. `WHERE YEAR(order_date) = 2024` cannot use
an index on `order_date`, because the index stores dates, not years.
Rewriting as a range comparison restores it. The same applies to leading
wildcards in `LIKE` and to implicit type casts.

For composite indexes, the *leftmost prefix* rule governs use. An index on
`(a, b, c)` serves queries filtering on `a`, on `a` and `b`, or on all
three, but not on `b` alone. The order of columns in the index is a design
decision, not an arbitrary one.

Beyond indexing, the principle is to **reduce data early**. Filter before
joining, select only needed columns, and aggregate before joining when the
join would multiply rows.

```sql
-- READ THE PLAN FIRST. Never optimize from intuition.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT c.name, SUM(o.amount)
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.order_date >= DATE '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY c.name;

-- What to look for, in priority order:
--  1. Seq Scan on a large table where a filter should have used an index
--  2. estimated rows vs actual rows differing by 10x or more
--  3. Nested Loop over a large outer input
--  4. Sort or Hash spilling to disk ("external merge Disk: 240MB")
--  5. the node with the largest actual time, which is where to work

-- INDEXES: the basic kinds.
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_date     ON orders (order_date);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust     ON orders (customer_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust_date ON orders (customer_id, order_date);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_customers_email ON customers (email);

-- THE LEFTMOST PREFIX RULE for composite indexes.
-- With an index on (customer_id, order_date):
--   WHERE customer_id = 5                          uses it
--   WHERE customer_id = 5 AND order_date > '...'   uses it fully
--   WHERE order_date > '...'                       CANNOT use it
-- Put the equality-filtered column first, the range-filtered one second.

-- SARGABILITY: a predicate the index can use.
-- NOT sargable: the column is wrapped in a function.
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) = 2024;
-- Sargable: the same condition as a range.
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= DATE '2024-01-01'
  AND order_date <  DATE '2025-01-01';

-- NOT sargable: a leading wildcard forces a full scan.
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE '%smith';
-- Sargable: a prefix match can seek into the sorted index.
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE 'smith%';

-- NOT sargable: arithmetic on the column.
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE amount * 1.2 > 100;
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE amount > 100 / 1.2;          -- sargable

-- An EXPRESSION INDEX when the function genuinely must stay.
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_year ON orders (EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date));

-- IMPLICIT CASTS silently disable indexes too.
-- If customer_id is a bigint:
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '12345';   -- may cast per row
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345;     -- correct type

-- REDUCE DATA EARLY.
-- Slower: join everything, then filter.
SELECT c.name, o.amount
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.order_date >= DATE '2024-06-01' AND c.region = 'eu';

-- Often faster: filter each side before joining.
WITH recent AS (
    SELECT customer_id, amount FROM orders
    WHERE order_date >= DATE '2024-06-01'
),
eu AS (
    SELECT customer_id, name FROM customers WHERE region = 'eu'
)
SELECT e.name, r.amount FROM eu e JOIN recent r USING (customer_id);
-- A good optimizer does this itself. Many do not, especially across
-- views and federated sources.

-- SELECT ONLY WHAT YOU NEED. SELECT * prevents index-only scans and
-- moves columns you never read across the network.
SELECT customer_id, amount FROM orders WHERE order_date > DATE '2024-01-01';

-- A COVERING INDEX lets the database answer without touching the table.
CREATE INDEX idx_cover ON orders (order_date) INCLUDE (customer_id, amount);

-- AGGREGATE BEFORE JOINING when the join would multiply rows.
SELECT c.name, o.total
FROM customers c
JOIN (
    SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total
    FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id          -- now one row per customer
) o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;

-- EXISTS instead of COUNT when you only need "any".
-- Slow: counts every matching row.
SELECT * FROM customers c
WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id) > 0;
-- Fast: stops at the first match.
SELECT * FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id);

-- UNION ALL when duplicates are impossible: skips a deduplicating sort.

-- KEEP STATISTICS CURRENT. Stale statistics cause bad estimates, which
-- cause bad plans, which is the most common cause of a query that was
-- fast last month and is slow today with no code change.
ANALYZE orders;

-- PARTITIONING for very large tables: the planner skips whole partitions.
-- CREATE TABLE orders (...) PARTITION BY RANGE (order_date);
-- A query filtered to one month then reads one partition, not the table.
```

| Symptom in the plan | Likely cause | Remedy |
|---------------------|--------------|--------|
| Seq Scan on a big table | no usable index | add one, or make the predicate sargable |
| estimate far from actual | stale statistics | `ANALYZE` |
| Nested Loop, large outer | bad join order | fix estimates, or pre-filter |
| Sort spilling to disk | insufficient work memory | reduce rows earlier, or raise the limit |
| Index exists but unused | function or cast on the column | rewrite as a range |

> Key Takeaways
> - Start from `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, and treat a large gap between estimated
>   and actual rows as the primary signal of a bad plan.
> - Indexes speed reads and slow writes, so add them deliberately on
>   columns used in filters, joins, and sorts.
> - Wrapping an indexed column in a function, a leading wildcard, or an
>   implicit cast all disable the index.
> - Composite indexes serve only leftmost prefixes, so column order is a
>   design decision.
> - Reduce rows and columns as early as possible, and aggregate before a
>   join that would otherwise multiply rows.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on a query filtering by year with a function,
>    rewrite it as a date range, and compare the plans.
> 2. Create a composite index and demonstrate a query that uses it and one
>    that cannot, explaining why.
> 3. Interview: A nightly query that ran in 30 seconds now takes 20 minutes
>    with no code change. What are your first three checks? (Hint: consider
>    data volume, statistics, and index health.)

#### Analytical SQL Patterns

Certain analytical questions recur across every organization, and each has
a standard SQL form. Learning the patterns is more valuable than learning
more syntax, because the syntax is already covered.

The patterns below share a structure: a CTE pipeline that prepares a clean
base, a window function that computes the per-row analytic, and a final
aggregation. Recognising which pattern a question maps to turns a vague
request into a query you can write directly.

Two cautions apply throughout. First, **define the metric before writing
the query**. "Active user" and "churn" have several defensible definitions,
and the SQL is the definition, so it belongs in code review alongside the
logic. Second, **generate a complete date spine** before any time series
calculation, because absent rows are silently treated as gaps rather than
zeros and a moving average over sparse data is wrong.

Cohort retention, funnel conversion, running totals, period comparison,
sessionization, and top-N-per-group cover the large majority of analytical
requests. Each appears below in a form you can adapt.

```sql
-- 1. COHORT RETENTION: do users acquired in month M still return later?
WITH first_purchase AS (
    SELECT customer_id,
           DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(order_date)) AS cohort_month
    FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id
),
activity AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT
           o.customer_id,
           f.cohort_month,
           DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date) AS active_month
    FROM orders o
    JOIN first_purchase f USING (customer_id)
),
sized AS (
    SELECT cohort_month,
           active_month,
           COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS active_customers,
           (EXTRACT(YEAR  FROM active_month) - EXTRACT(YEAR  FROM cohort_month)) * 12
         + (EXTRACT(MONTH FROM active_month) - EXTRACT(MONTH FROM cohort_month))
             AS months_since
    FROM activity
    GROUP BY cohort_month, active_month
)
SELECT
    cohort_month,
    months_since,
    active_customers,
    ROUND(100.0 * active_customers
          / FIRST_VALUE(active_customers) OVER (
                PARTITION BY cohort_month ORDER BY months_since), 1)
        AS retention_pct
FROM sized
ORDER BY cohort_month, months_since;

-- 2. FUNNEL CONVERSION: how many users reach each step, in order?
WITH steps AS (
    SELECT
        user_id,
        MIN(CASE WHEN event = 'view'     THEN event_time END) AS t_view,
        MIN(CASE WHEN event = 'add_cart' THEN event_time END) AS t_cart,
        MIN(CASE WHEN event = 'checkout' THEN event_time END) AS t_checkout,
        MIN(CASE WHEN event = 'purchase' THEN event_time END) AS t_purchase
    FROM events
    GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT
    COUNT(*)                                                    AS viewed,
    COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE t_cart     > t_view)                 AS carted,
    COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE t_checkout > t_cart)                 AS checked_out,
    COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE t_purchase > t_checkout)             AS purchased,
    ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE t_purchase > t_checkout)
          / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0), 2)                             AS overall_pct
FROM steps
WHERE t_view IS NOT NULL;
-- Comparing timestamps rather than mere presence enforces ORDER, so a
-- user who purchased before viewing is not counted as converted.

-- 3. THE DATE SPINE: generate every date, then left join the facts.
WITH spine AS (
    SELECT generate_series(DATE '2024-01-01', DATE '2024-03-31',
                           INTERVAL '1 day')::date AS d
),
daily AS (
    SELECT s.d, COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0) AS revenue
    FROM spine s
    LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.order_date = s.d
    GROUP BY s.d
)
SELECT
    d,
    revenue,
    SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY d) AS running_total,
    ROUND(AVG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY d ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING
                                            AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS ma7
FROM daily
ORDER BY d;
-- Without the spine, a zero-revenue day is an ABSENT row, so the 7-row
-- window spans more than 7 calendar days and the average is wrong.

-- 4. PERIOD-OVER-PERIOD comparison.
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS month, SUM(amount) AS revenue
    FROM orders GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT
    month,
    revenue,
    LAG(revenue)     OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_month,
    ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month))
          / NULLIF(LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 0), 1) AS mom_pct,
    LAG(revenue, 12) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS same_month_last_year,
    ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue, 12) OVER (ORDER BY month))
          / NULLIF(LAG(revenue, 12) OVER (ORDER BY month), 0), 1) AS yoy_pct
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;
-- Year-over-year comparison controls for seasonality that
-- month-over-month cannot.

-- 5. SESSIONIZATION: group events into sessions with a 30-minute gap.
WITH gaps AS (
    SELECT
        user_id, event_time,
        CASE WHEN event_time - LAG(event_time) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id
                                                     ORDER BY event_time)
                  > INTERVAL '30 minutes'
             OR LAG(event_time) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id
                                      ORDER BY event_time) IS NULL
             THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_new_session
    FROM events
),
sessions AS (
    SELECT user_id, event_time,
           SUM(is_new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id
                                     ORDER BY event_time) AS session_id
    FROM gaps                        -- a running sum of the new-session flag
)                                    -- assigns a stable id per session
SELECT
    user_id, session_id,
    MIN(event_time) AS started,
    MAX(event_time) AS ended,
    COUNT(*)        AS events,
    MAX(event_time) - MIN(event_time) AS duration
FROM sessions
GROUP BY user_id, session_id
ORDER BY user_id, started;

-- 6. RFM SEGMENTATION: recency, frequency, monetary value.
WITH rfm AS (
    SELECT
        customer_id,
        CURRENT_DATE - MAX(order_date) AS recency_days,
        COUNT(*)                       AS frequency,
        SUM(amount)                    AS monetary
    FROM orders
    WHERE order_date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '365 days'
    GROUP BY customer_id
),
scored AS (
    SELECT *,
        NTILE(5) OVER (ORDER BY recency_days DESC) AS r_score,  -- recent = 5
        NTILE(5) OVER (ORDER BY frequency)         AS f_score,
        NTILE(5) OVER (ORDER BY monetary)          AS m_score
    FROM rfm
)
SELECT
    customer_id, recency_days, frequency, monetary,
    r_score, f_score, m_score,
    CASE
        WHEN r_score >= 4 AND f_score >= 4 THEN 'champion'
        WHEN r_score >= 4                  THEN 'promising'
        WHEN r_score <= 2 AND f_score >= 4 THEN 'at risk'
        ELSE 'standard'
    END AS segment
FROM scored
ORDER BY monetary DESC;

-- 7. TOP N PER GROUP with a deterministic tiebreaker.
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT region, product, revenue,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY region
                              ORDER BY revenue DESC, product ASC) AS rn
    FROM product_revenue
)
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn <= 3 ORDER BY region, rn;
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Most analytical requests map to a small set of patterns built from a
>   CTE pipeline, a window function, and a final aggregation.
> - Define the metric in writing before coding it, since the query becomes
>   the operative definition.
> - Generate a complete date spine before any time series calculation, or
>   absent rows will distort moving averages and running totals.
> - Funnels should compare timestamps rather than mere presence, so that
>   step order is actually enforced.
> - Sessionization uses a running sum over a new-session flag, which is the
>   same gaps-and-islands technique that finds streaks.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a cohort retention query and present the output as a triangle
>    with cohort months as rows and months-since as columns.
> 2. Build a sessionization query with a configurable inactivity gap, then
>    report median session length per user segment.
> 3. Interview: A seven-day moving average of daily signups looks wrong on
>    low-traffic days. What is the most likely structural cause? (Hint:
>    what happens to a day with zero signups in the source table?)

<a id="44-development-environment-and-practices"></a>
### 4.4 Development Environment and Practices

Analytical code is still code, and the practices that keep software
maintainable apply with one addition: data changes underneath you, so
reproducibility requires pinning the environment and the data as well as
the logic; this section covers notebooks, version control, project
structure, testing, and containers.

#### Jupyter Notebooks and Notebook Hygiene

Notebooks are the dominant interface for exploratory data work, for good
reasons and at a real cost. Understanding both determines whether they help
or quietly undermine your results.

The strength is the tight feedback loop. Load an expensive dataset once,
then iterate on transformations against the live object with plots and
tables inline. For exploration, nothing else comes close.

The weakness is **hidden state**. A notebook's output reflects the order
cells were *executed*, not the order they appear. Deleting a cell does not
remove the variables it created. Editing a cell and not re-running it
leaves output that no longer matches the code. A notebook can display a
result that no execution of its current code could reproduce.

The execution counter is the tell. Cells numbered `[1] [5] [2] [12]` mean
the visible order is not the run order, and any conclusion drawn from that
state is unverified. The habit that fixes this is *restart and run all*
before trusting or sharing anything.

The second problem is version control. A notebook is JSON containing
outputs, execution counts, and base64-encoded images, so a trivial change
produces an unreadable diff and merges conflict constantly. Stripping
outputs before commit solves most of it.

The mature workflow is a division of labour: explore in the notebook, and
once logic stabilises, move it into an importable module that the notebook
then calls. The notebook stays a thin narrative; the logic becomes testable.

```python
# THE HIDDEN STATE PROBLEM, made concrete.
# Cell [1]:  df = load_data()
# Cell [2]:  df = df[df.amount > 0]
# Cell [3]:  print(len(df))          -> 950
#
# You now edit cell [2] to df[df.amount > 100] but re-run only cell [3].
# It still prints 950, because df in memory reflects the OLD filter.
# The notebook now shows code that does not produce the output beside it.

# DIAGNOSTIC: list variables and check the execution counter.
# %whos                       shows every variable in memory
# %reset -f                   clears everything, forcing a clean rerun

# THE DISCIPLINE, in order of value:
#  1. Restart and Run All before trusting, sharing, or committing.
#  2. Keep imports and configuration in the FIRST cell.
#  3. Never define a function in one cell and edit it in another.
#  4. Write cells to be idempotent: running twice gives the same result.

# NOT IDEMPOTENT: each run mutates the same object further.
df["amount"] = df["amount"] * 1.1          # run twice, compounded twice

# IDEMPOTENT: derived from a source that does not change.
df["amount_adjusted"] = df["amount_raw"] * 1.1

# AUTORELOAD lets you edit a module and see changes without restarting,
# which is what makes the notebook-plus-module workflow practical.
# %load_ext autoreload
# %autoreload 2
from src.features import build_features      # your own module
# Edit src/features.py, re-run the cell, and the new code is used.

# USEFUL MAGICS.
```
