```python
print(f"\ntrue  sd(hours)={complete['hours'].std():.2f}"
      f"  corr(age,hours)={complete['age'].corr(complete['hours']):+.3f}")

mean_filled = X.fillna(X.mean())
print(f"mean  sd(hours)={mean_filled['hours'].std():.2f}"
      f"  corr(age,hours)={mean_filled['age'].corr(mean_filled['hours']):+.3f}")

# Conditional median by age band keeps far more of the structure.
band = pd.cut(X["age"], bins=[19, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70])
cond = X.copy()
cond["hours"] = cond["hours"].fillna(cond.groupby(band, observed=True)["hours"]
                                     .transform("median"))
print(f"cond  sd(hours)={cond['hours'].std():.2f}"
      f"  corr(age,hours)={cond['age'].corr(cond['hours']):+.3f}")

# --- The leakage trap, shown concretely. ---
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)

# WRONG: statistic computed over train AND test before splitting.
leaky_median = X["hours"].median()          # <- uses test rows
# RIGHT: statistic computed on train only, then applied to test.
clean_median = Xtr["hours"].median()
print(f"\nmedian from all data {leaky_median:.2f} vs train only {clean_median:.2f}")

# A Pipeline makes the right thing the default: fit() sees only train.
def build(imputer, add_flag: bool) -> Pipeline:
    return Pipeline([
        ("impute", ColumnTransformer([
            ("num", SimpleImputer(strategy="median", add_indicator=add_flag)
                    if isinstance(imputer, str) else imputer,
             ["age", "hours"]),
        ])),
        ("model", Ridge(alpha=1.0)),
    ])

candidates = {
    "median":            build("median", add_flag=False),
    "median + flag":     build("median", add_flag=True),
    "knn (k=5)":         build(KNNImputer(n_neighbors=5, add_indicator=True), True),
    "iterative (MICE)":  build(IterativeImputer(max_iter=10, random_state=0,
                                                add_indicator=True), True),
}
for name, pipe in candidates.items():
    pipe.fit(Xtr, ytr)                       # imputer fitted on TRAIN only
    err = mean_absolute_error(yte, pipe.predict(Xte))
    print(f"{name:18s} MAE {err:9,.0f}")

# --- Time series: ordering changes the right default. ---
ts = pd.Series(
    [10.0, np.nan, np.nan, 13.0, 14.0, np.nan, 16.0],
    index=pd.date_range("2024-01-01", periods=7, freq="D"), name="temp_c",
)
print("\n", pd.DataFrame({
    "raw": ts,
    "ffill": ts.ffill(),                        # a state that persists
    "interpolate": ts.interpolate("time"),      # a quantity that moves
    "mean": ts.fillna(ts.mean()),               # wrong: ignores order
}).to_string())

# LIMIT the reach of a forward fill, or one gap propagates indefinitely.
print("\nbounded ffill:\n", ts.ffill(limit=1).to_string())
```

```text
  WHAT EACH IMPUTER PRESERVES

  method               mean   variance   correlations   cost      leak risk
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  drop rows            ~      yes        yes            loses n   none
  constant (0, -1)     NO     NO         NO             trivial   none
  mean / median        yes    NO         NO             trivial   if fit on all
  mode (categorical)   ~      NO         NO             trivial   if fit on all
  conditional median   yes    partly     partly         low       if fit on all
  KNN                  yes    mostly     mostly         O(n^2)    if fit on all
  iterative / MICE     yes    mostly     yes            high      if fit on all
  multiple imputation  yes    yes        yes            highest   if fit on all

  THE VARIANCE COLLAPSE, DRAWN

    original          after mean imputation
      .  . .            .  .  |  .
    . . . . . .        . . . .|| . . .      <- spike at the mean
   .............      .........||.........
   low   mean  high   low    mean    high

  RULE: fit on train, transform everywhere; and always keep the indicator.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Imputation trades a visible gap for an invisible assumption, and single
>   imputation always understates uncertainty.
> - Mean and median filling preserve the centre while shrinking variance and
>   flattening correlations.
> - Conditional and model-based imputation respect MAR by using the columns
>   that explain the missingness.
> - Time series call for forward fill or interpolation, chosen by whether
>   the quantity persists or moves; bound the fill so one gap cannot spread.
> - Fit every imputer inside a pipeline on training data only, and add a
>   missing indicator so the model can use the gap itself.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Take a numeric column, remove 25% of it at random, impute with the mean,
>    and report the change in standard deviation and in its correlation with
>    another column.
> 2. Build two scikit-learn pipelines for the same data, one imputing with
>    the median fitted on the full dataset and one fitted inside the
>    pipeline, and compare their cross-validated scores.
> 3. For a daily time series with a five-day gap, produce forward-filled and
>    time-interpolated versions and state which you would defend for a price
>    series and which for a temperature series.
> 4. Interview: Your median imputation improves cross-validated accuracy but
>    the model performs worse in production. What is the most likely cause?
>    (Hint: what did the imputer learn from, and what does production look
>    like that your validation split did not?)

#### Outlier Detection and Treatment

An outlier is a value far from the rest of the data. That definition is
descriptive and useless on its own, because it says nothing about what you
should do. The useful question is different: **is this value wrong, or is it
rare?** Those two cases have opposite correct responses, and no statistical
test can tell them apart.

A temperature reading of 450 degrees Celsius in a room is wrong. The same
value in a kiln is the measurement you cared about. A transaction of ten
million is an error in a coffee shop's ledger and the single most important
row in a fraud dataset. Deleting outliers without establishing which case
you are in is how people remove the signal and keep the noise.

So the workflow is: **detect, then diagnose, then decide.** Detection is
mechanical. Diagnosis needs domain knowledge. Only the decision is a
technique.

For detection, the methods differ in what they assume.

**Z-score** measures distance from the mean in standard deviations. Its flaw
is that the mean and standard deviation are themselves dragged by the
outliers you are trying to find, an effect called masking. With one extreme
value in a small sample, no z-score can exceed a bound set by the sample
size, so the test can structurally fail to flag anything.

**The IQR rule** uses quartiles, which extreme values cannot move, and flags
anything beyond 1.5 times the interquartile range from the nearest quartile.
It is robust and it is the sensible default for one column at a time. Its
weakness is that on a skewed distribution it flags a large fraction of the
long tail, which is not an error, it is the shape of the data.

**Modified z-score** uses the median and the median absolute deviation
instead of the mean and standard deviation, giving a robust score you can
threshold. The conventional cutoff is 3.5.

All three are **univariate**, and this is their shared blind spot. A person
who is 1.5 metres tall is unremarkable. A person who weighs 120 kilograms is
unremarkable. A person who is 1.5 metres tall *and* weighs 120 kilograms is
a multivariate outlier that no single-column method can see. For that you
need **Mahalanobis distance**, which measures distance in units of the
data's own covariance, or a model such as **isolation forest** or **local
outlier factor**, which learn what "typical" looks like jointly.

For treatment, the options in increasing aggression:

- **Investigate and fix.** The best outcome. A unit error, a misplaced
  decimal, a sentinel value: all repairable once identified.
- **Leave it.** Correct whenever the value is real and your method tolerates
  it. Tree-based models barely care about outliers in features.
- **Winsorize or clip.** Cap values at a percentile. Keeps the row, bounds
  the influence, distorts the tail.
- **Transform.** A log transform compresses a right tail so that extreme
  values stop dominating without being altered relative to each other.
- **Use a robust method.** Median instead of mean, quantile regression
  instead of least squares, Huber loss instead of squared loss. Often this
  is better than touching the data at all.
- **Drop the row.** Last resort, and only for values you have established
  are impossible. Always record how many you dropped.

One more thing that deserves emphasis: **clip bounds are parameters fitted
on training data**, exactly like an imputation median. Computing the 1st and
99th percentile over your whole dataset before splitting leaks.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
clean = rng.normal(50, 5, 200)
x = pd.Series(np.concatenate([clean, [140.0, 145.0, -20.0]]), name="value")

# --- Z-SCORE MASKING: the outliers inflate the denominator. ---
z = (x - x.mean()) / x.std(ddof=0)
print(f"mean {x.mean():.1f}  sd {x.std():.1f}")
print(f"z-score flags (|z|>3): {(z.abs() > 3).sum()}")

# --- ROBUST ALTERNATIVES: quartiles and MAD cannot be dragged. ---
q1, q3 = x.quantile([0.25, 0.75])
iqr = q3 - q1
lo, hi = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr
print(f"\nIQR fence [{lo:.1f}, {hi:.1f}] flags {((x < lo) | (x > hi)).sum()}")

med = x.median()
mad = (x - med).abs().median()
# 0.6745 rescales MAD so the score is comparable to a normal z-score.
mod_z = 0.6745 * (x - med) / mad
print(f"modified z (>3.5) flags {(mod_z.abs() > 3.5).sum()}")
print("\ncomparison of flagged values:")
print(pd.DataFrame({"value": x, "z": z.round(2), "mod_z": mod_z.round(2)})
      .loc[mod_z.abs() > 3.5].to_string())

# --- MULTIVARIATE: neither column is extreme, the PAIR is. ---
h = rng.normal(1.70, 0.08, 300)
w = 25 * h ** 2 + rng.normal(0, 4, 300)        # weight tracks height
people = pd.DataFrame({"height_m": h.round(2), "weight_kg": w.round(1)})
people.loc[len(people)] = [1.50, 120.0]        # plausible alone, not together

for col in people.columns:                      # univariate sees nothing
    c1, c3 = people[col].quantile([0.25, 0.75])
    f = 1.5 * (c3 - c1)
    flagged = ((people[col] < c1 - f) | (people[col] > c3 + f)).sum()
    print(f"\nunivariate IQR on {col}: {flagged} flagged")

cov_inv = np.linalg.pinv(np.cov(people.values, rowvar=False))
centred = people.values - people.values.mean(axis=0)
# Mahalanobis: distance measured in units of the data's own covariance,
# so it accounts for the height/weight relationship the columns share.
md = np.sqrt(np.einsum("ij,jk,ik->i", centred, cov_inv, centred))
people["mahalanobis"] = md.round(2)
print("\ntop 3 by Mahalanobis distance:")
print(people.nlargest(3, "mahalanobis").to_string())

# --- Model-based, for many columns at once. ---
from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest
iso = IsolationForest(contamination=0.01, random_state=0)
people["iso_outlier"] = iso.fit_predict(people[["height_m", "weight_kg"]]) == -1
print(f"\nisolation forest flagged {people['iso_outlier'].sum()} row(s)")

# --- TREATMENT: four responses, same column, different consequences. ---
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
tr, te = train_test_split(x, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)

p01, p99 = tr.quantile([0.01, 0.99])            # bounds from TRAIN only
treated = pd.DataFrame({
    "raw": te,
    "clipped": te.clip(p01, p99),               # winsorize: keep row, cap value
    "log1p": np.log1p(te.clip(lower=0)),        # compress the tail
})
print("\nmean / sd under each treatment:")
print(treated.agg(["mean", "std"]).round(2).to_string())

# Robust statistics: change the estimator, not the data.
print(f"\nmean {x.mean():.2f}  vs  median {x.median():.2f}"
      f"  vs  10% trimmed mean {x.sort_values().iloc[20:-20].mean():.2f}")

# ALWAYS LOG WHAT YOU REMOVED. An undocumented drop is unreproducible.
mask_impossible = x < 0                          # a negative measurement here
print(f"\ndropping {mask_impossible.sum()} impossible value(s): "
      f"{x[mask_impossible].tolist()}")
```

```text
  DETECTION METHOD SELECTION

  method            assumes        robust?   dimensions   flags on skew
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------
  z-score > 3       normality      NO        one          moderate
  IQR fence 1.5x    nothing        yes       one          MANY (false)
  modified z > 3.5  nothing        yes       one          moderate
  Mahalanobis       elliptical     no        many         n/a
  isolation forest  nothing        yes       many         n/a
  local outlier f.  nothing        yes       many         n/a

  THE MASKING EFFECT

    without outlier:   mean=50  sd=5    a value of 70 sits at z = 4.0  FLAGGED
    with two at 140:   mean=51  sd=13   the same 70 sits at z = 1.5    MISSED

  DECIDE BEFORE YOU TREAT

    is the value physically possible?
        no  -> it is an error. fix it, or drop it and log the count.
        yes -> does your method's conclusion depend on it?
                 no  -> leave it alone.
                 yes -> transform, or clip, or switch to a robust estimator.
                        Removing it means answering a different question.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - "Wrong" and "rare" look identical statistically and demand opposite
>   treatments, so diagnosis must come between detection and action.
> - Z-scores are dragged by the very values they should flag; prefer the IQR
>   fence or a modified z-score built on the median and MAD.
> - Univariate methods cannot see a combination that is only jointly
>   implausible, which is what Mahalanobis distance and isolation forests
>   are for.
> - Prefer a robust estimator or a transform over editing data; drop rows
>   only for values established as impossible, and log the count.
> - Clip and winsorize bounds are fitted parameters, so compute them on
>   training data only.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add two extreme values to a normal sample and show that the z-score
>    rule flags fewer points than the modified z-score rule does.
> 2. Build a two-column dataset in which a row is flagged by Mahalanobis
>    distance while passing the IQR test on both columns individually.
> 3. Fit the same linear regression on data that is raw, winsorized at the
>    1st and 99th percentile, and log-transformed, then compare the
>    coefficients and explain which question each one answers.
> 4. Interview: A stakeholder asks you to remove outliers before reporting
>    average order value. What do you ask them first? (Hint: what decision
>    will the number be used for, and are the large orders real?)

#### Deduplication and Record Linkage

Duplicates are two kinds of problem wearing the same name, and conflating
them wastes a lot of time. **Exact duplicates** are the same row recorded
twice, usually from a pipeline retry or a double-submitted form. **Fuzzy
duplicates** are two records describing the same real-world entity with
different text: "Robert Smith" and "Bob Smith Jr.", or "Acme Inc." and "ACME
Incorporated". The first is a data-integrity bug you fix with a key. The
second is an inference problem called **record linkage** or **entity
resolution**, and it never has a provably correct answer.

For exact duplicates the essential move is to **define the grain** of your
table: the set of columns that should uniquely identify a row. An orders
table might be one row per `order_id`. An events table might be one row per
`(user_id, event_type, timestamp)`. Once the grain is written down,
duplicates are just violations of it, and you can assert the grain in the
pipeline so violations fail loudly instead of quietly doubling your revenue
figure.

Deduplicating is not only about which rows to remove but **which to keep**.
If two rows share a key but differ in other columns, dropping "the
duplicate" silently picks one. Usually you want the most recent, or the most
complete, and you should say which. Sorting before dropping makes the choice
explicit and reproducible.

Fuzzy matching is harder because comparing every record to every other
record is quadratic. Ten thousand records is fifty million comparisons; a
million records is five hundred billion. The standard solution is
**blocking**: only compare records that agree on some cheap key, such as the
first letter of the surname plus the postcode. Blocking trades recall for
tractability, which is why you often block on several different keys and
take the union.

Within a block you compute **similarity** on each field. The main string
metrics:

| Metric | Measures | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| Levenshtein | edit operations | typos, short strings |
| Jaro-Winkler | transpositions, prefix match | names |
| Jaccard on tokens | shared word sets | addresses, company names |
| Soundex / Metaphone | pronunciation | names captured by ear |
| Cosine on n-grams | shared character chunks | long messy strings, scalable |

Then you combine field similarities into a decision. A weighted sum with a
threshold is the simple version. The classical probabilistic version is the
**Fellegi-Sunter** model, which weights each field by how informative
agreement on it is: two people sharing a surname is weak evidence, two
people sharing a phone number is strong evidence. Modern tooling trains a
classifier on labelled pairs.

Finally, matches are **transitive but your scores are not**. If A matches B
and B matches C, you have implicitly claimed A matches C even if their score
was below threshold. Resolving this means treating matches as edges in a
graph and taking connected components, which is also how you get an
entity-level identifier to join on.

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from itertools import combinations

# --- EXACT DUPLICATES: define the grain, then assert it. ---
orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4],
    "user_id":  [10, 11, 11, 12, 13, 13],
    "amount":   [50.0, 20.0, 20.0, 75.0, 30.0, 35.0],   # note: 4 differs
    "updated":  pd.to_datetime(["2024-01-01", "2024-01-02", "2024-01-02",
                                "2024-01-03", "2024-01-04", "2024-01-05"]),
})

def assert_grain(df: pd.DataFrame, keys: list[str]) -> None:
    """Fail loudly if the table is not one row per `keys`."""
    dup = df.duplicated(subset=keys, keep=False)
    if dup.any():
        raise ValueError(
            f"grain violated on {keys}: {dup.sum()} rows in "
            f"{df.loc[dup, keys].drop_duplicates().shape[0]} groups")

try:
    assert_grain(orders, ["order_id"])
except ValueError as e:
    print("caught:", e)

# FULL-ROW duplicates are safe to drop: no information is lost.
print("\nidentical rows:", orders.duplicated().sum())

# KEY duplicates that DIFFER need a rule. Make the rule visible.
print("\nconflicting on key:")
print(orders[orders.duplicated("order_id", keep=False)].to_string(index=False))

# Sort first so `keep="last"` means something specific and reproducible.
latest = (orders.sort_values(["order_id", "updated"])
                .drop_duplicates("order_id", keep="last"))
print("\nkeep most recent:\n", latest.to_string(index=False))

# Alternative rule: keep the most complete row.
orders["completeness"] = orders.notna().sum(axis=1)
most_complete = (orders.sort_values(["order_id", "completeness"])
                       .drop_duplicates("order_id", keep="last"))

# Or aggregate instead of choosing, when both rows are real events.
collapsed = orders.groupby("order_id", as_index=False).agg(
    user_id=("user_id", "first"),
    amount=("amount", "sum"),          # <- a DIFFERENT claim about the data
    last_seen=("updated", "max"),
)
print("\naggregated (treats both rows as real):\n", collapsed.to_string(index=False))

# --- FUZZY DUPLICATES: normalise, block, score, resolve. ---
people = pd.DataFrame({
    "rid":   [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6],
    "name":  ["Robert Smith", "Bob Smith", "Roberta Smythe",
              "Acme Inc.", "ACME Incorporated", "Zenith Ltd"],
    "email": ["r.smith@x.com", "rsmith@x.com", "rsmythe@y.com",
              "info@acme.com", "info@acme.com", "hi@zenith.com"],
    "zip":   ["10001", "10001", "10001", "94107", "94107", "60601"],
})

def normalise(s: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    """Cheap canonical form: the single highest-value step in linkage."""
    return (s.str.lower()
             .str.replace(r"[^a-z0-9\s]", "", regex=True)   # drop punctuation
             .str.replace(r"\b(inc|incorporated|ltd|llc|jr|sr)\b", "", regex=True)
             .str.replace(r"\s+", " ", regex=True)
             .str.strip())

people["key"] = normalise(people["name"])
print("\nnormalised:\n", people[["rid", "name", "key"]].to_string(index=False))

# BLOCKING: compare only within a cheap shared key, here the postcode.
# Without it, n records cost n*(n-1)/2 comparisons.
def jaccard(a: str, b: str) -> float:
    ta, tb = set(a.split()), set(b.split())
    return len(ta & tb) / len(ta | tb) if ta | tb else 0.0

def bigrams(s: str) -> set[str]:
    s = s.replace(" ", "")
    return {s[i:i + 2] for i in range(len(s) - 1)}

def bigram_sim(a: str, b: str) -> float:
    ba, bb = bigrams(a), bigrams(b)
    return len(ba & bb) / len(ba | bb) if ba | bb else 0.0

pairs = []
for _, block in people.groupby("zip"):
    for (_, a), (_, b) in combinations(block.iterrows(), 2):
        # Weighted evidence: an exact email match is far stronger than a
        # name resemblance, so it gets the larger weight.
        name_s = (0.5 * jaccard(a["key"], b["key"])
                  + 0.5 * bigram_sim(a["key"], b["key"]))
        email_s = float(a["email"] == b["email"])
        score = 0.45 * name_s + 0.55 * email_s
        pairs.append((a["rid"], b["rid"], round(name_s, 2), email_s, round(score, 2)))

scored = pd.DataFrame(pairs, columns=["a", "b", "name_sim", "email_eq", "score"])
print("\ncandidate pairs within blocks:\n", scored.to_string(index=False))

n_all = len(people) * (len(people) - 1) // 2
print(f"\nblocking compared {len(scored)} pairs instead of {n_all}")

# --- TRANSITIVE CLOSURE: matches form a graph, entities are components. ---
THRESHOLD = 0.55
parent = {r: r for r in people["rid"]}

def find(x):
    while parent[x] != x:
        parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]        # path compression
        x = parent[x]
    return x

def union(x, y):
    rx, ry = find(x), find(y)
    if rx != ry:
        parent[max(rx, ry)] = min(rx, ry)    # smallest rid becomes entity id

for _, row in scored[scored["score"] >= THRESHOLD].iterrows():
    union(int(row["a"]), int(row["b"]))

people["entity_id"] = [find(r) for r in people["rid"]]
print("\nresolved entities:\n",
      people[["rid", "name", "entity_id"]].to_string(index=False))
# Now join on entity_id, not on name. The cluster, not the pair, is the unit.
```

```text
  TWO DIFFERENT PROBLEMS

  exact duplicates                    fuzzy duplicates
  ----------------------------------  ----------------------------------
  cause: retry, double submit, bad    cause: free-text entry, multiple
         join fan-out                        source systems, name changes
  detect: duplicated(subset=grain)    detect: similarity above a threshold
  fix:    drop, or aggregate          fix:    cluster into entities
  correct answer exists               correct answer is a judgement call
  assert it in the pipeline           measure precision AND recall

  THE COST OF SKIPPING BLOCKING

      records      all pairs        blocked by postcode (avg 50/block)
      10,000       50 million       ~2.5 million
      100,000      5 billion        ~25 million
      1,000,000    500 billion      ~250 million

  THRESHOLD TRADE-OFF

      low threshold  -> over-merges: two real customers become one
      high threshold -> under-merges: one customer counted twice
      Both inflate or deflate every per-customer metric you report.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Write down the grain of every table and assert it in the pipeline, so
>   duplicate keys fail loudly rather than doubling your totals.
> - When duplicate keys carry different values, "which row to keep" is a
>   business rule; sort explicitly rather than letting the drop choose.
> - Normalising text before matching removes more duplicates than any
>   similarity metric does.
> - Blocking is what makes fuzzy matching tractable, and it trades recall
>   for a feasible number of comparisons.
> - Matches are transitive, so resolve them as connected components and join
>   on the resulting entity identifier.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write an `assert_grain` function and add it to a load routine, then
>    demonstrate it catching an injected duplicate key.
> 2. Given a table with duplicate keys whose rows differ, produce three
>    deduplicated versions using "keep latest", "keep most complete", and
>    "aggregate", and explain which is right for an orders table.
> 3. Implement blocking on the first three characters of a normalised name,
>    then report how many candidate pairs it produces versus the full
>    cross-product on a thousand records.
> 4. Interview: Your customer count fell 12% after a deduplication release
>    and marketing says the number is wrong. How do you determine whether
>    the new number or the old one is correct? (Hint: what would you sample,
>    and what does each error type look like in that sample?)

#### Type Conversion and Parsing

Data arrives as text far more often than people expect, and the conversion
from text to typed values is where silent corruption concentrates. The
reason is that parsers are built to be helpful: given something ambiguous,
they guess, and a guess produces a plausible value rather than an error. A
failed parse is a good day. A successful wrong parse is the expensive case.

The recurring pattern is that **type inference is a heuristic applied to a
sample**. Pandas reads the first chunk of a CSV, decides a column is an
integer, and then meets a row where it is not, which is why columns
mysteriously become `object` or why integers become floats the moment a
single null appears. The fix is always the same: declare the types you
expect rather than accepting the ones you are given.

Four conversions deserve specific attention.

**Numbers.** Thousands separators, currency symbols, parentheses for
negatives in accounting exports, European decimal commas, and percentage
signs all defeat a naive conversion. Strip deliberately, then convert with
`errors="coerce"` so that failures become nulls you can count rather than
exceptions that stop the load. Then *check the count*, because coercion
turns a loud failure into a quiet one.

**Dates.** The worst offender, because `03/04/2024` is a valid date under two
different conventions and nothing in the file says which. Always pass an
explicit format when you know it. When a column mixes formats, parse in
passes: try each known format, and only fall back to inference for what
remains. Also decide about time zones once, at the boundary: store UTC,
convert for display, and never mix naive and aware timestamps in the same
column.

**Booleans.** `"true"`, `"TRUE"`, `"T"`, `"1"`, `"yes"`, `"Y"` all mean true
somewhere. The trap is that `bool("false")` is `True` in Python, because any
non-empty string is truthy. Map explicitly from a dictionary and leave
anything unrecognised as null instead of guessing.

**Integers with nulls.** NumPy's integer types cannot hold a missing value,
so pandas historically promoted such columns to float. That turns an ID into
`1.0002e+15` and loses precision above 2^53. Pandas' nullable `Int64` dtype
solves this, and it is worth using by default for any integer that can be
missing.

Underneath all of this sits **encoding**. Text is bytes plus an assumption,
and if the assumption is wrong you get mojibake or a decode error. UTF-8 is
the correct default; detect rather than guess when a source is unknown; and
remember that a byte-order mark at the start of a file will otherwise become
part of your first column's name.

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import io

messy = pd.DataFrame({
    "amount":  ["1,234.56", "$99.00", "(45.00)", "1.234,56", "12%", "N/A"],
    "count":   ["10", "20", None, "40", "50", "60"],
    "flag":    ["true", "FALSE", "Y", "0", "yes", "maybe"],
    "when":    ["2024-01-05", "05/03/2024", "2024-03-05T10:00:00Z",
                "March 7, 2024", "20240308", "not a date"],
    "zip":     ["01234", "02345", "03456", "04567", "05678", "06789"],
})

# --- NUMBERS: strip deliberately, then coerce, then COUNT the failures. ---
def parse_money(s: pd.Series, decimal_comma: bool = False) -> pd.Series:
    t = s.astype("string").str.strip()
    neg = t.str.match(r"^\(.*\)$").fillna(False)       # accounting negatives
    t = t.str.replace(r"^\((.*)\)$", r"\1", regex=True)
    t = t.str.replace(r"[^\d.,\-]", "", regex=True)    # drop $, %, spaces
    if decimal_comma:
        t = t.str.replace(".", "", regex=False).str.replace(",", ".", regex=False)
    else:
        t = t.str.replace(",", "", regex=False)        # thousands separator
    out = pd.to_numeric(t, errors="coerce")
    return out.where(~neg, -out)

amt = parse_money(messy["amount"])
print(pd.DataFrame({"raw": messy["amount"], "parsed": amt}).to_string(index=False))
failed = amt.isna() & messy["amount"].notna()
print(f"\nunparseable: {failed.sum()} -> {messy.loc[failed, 'amount'].tolist()}")
# NOTE: "12%" became 12.0, not 0.12, and "1.234,56" became 1.23456 under the
# comma-as-thousands assumption. Coercion did not fail; it was WRONG.
# This is why you inspect parsed values against raw, not just the null count.

# --- INTEGERS WITH NULLS: float promotion destroys identifiers. ---
naive = pd.to_numeric(messy["count"])                 # -> float64
nullable = messy["count"].astype("Int64")             # -> nullable integer
print(f"\nnaive dtype {naive.dtype}, values {naive.tolist()}")
print(f"Int64 dtype {nullable.dtype}, values {nullable.tolist()}")

big = pd.Series(["9007199254740993", "9007199254740994"])
print("\nfloat64 loses precision above 2^53:",
      pd.to_numeric(big).astype("int64").tolist())
print("Int64 preserves it:            ", big.astype("Int64").tolist())

# --- IDENTIFIERS ARE NOT NUMBERS. Keep them as strings. ---
print(f"\nzip as string: {messy['zip'].tolist()[:2]}")
print(f"zip as number: {pd.to_numeric(messy['zip']).tolist()[:2]}   <- zeros gone")

# --- DATES: parse in passes with explicit formats, infer only as fallback. ---
KNOWN_FORMATS = ["%Y-%m-%d", "%d/%m/%Y", "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z",
                 "%B %d, %Y", "%Y%m%d"]

def parse_dates(s: pd.Series, formats: list[str]) -> tuple[pd.Series, pd.Series]:
    """Return parsed timestamps plus the format that matched each row."""
    out = pd.Series(pd.NaT, index=s.index, dtype="datetime64[ns, UTC]")
    which = pd.Series(pd.NA, index=s.index, dtype="string")
    for fmt in formats:
        pending = out.isna() & s.notna()
        if not pending.any():
            break
        try:
            got = pd.to_datetime(s[pending], format=fmt, errors="coerce", utc=True)
        except ValueError:
            continue
        out[pending] = got
        which[pending & got.notna().reindex(s.index, fill_value=False)] = fmt
    return out, which

parsed, fmt_used = parse_dates(messy["when"], KNOWN_FORMATS)
print("\n", pd.DataFrame({"raw": messy["when"], "parsed": parsed,
                          "format": fmt_used}).to_string(index=False))
# The `format` column is the audit trail: if one format suddenly matches
# 90% of rows when it used to match 10%, the upstream source changed.

# --- THE AMBIGUITY THAT NO ERROR REPORTS ---
for dayfirst in (True, False):
    got = pd.to_datetime("03/04/2024", dayfirst=dayfirst)
    print(f"dayfirst={dayfirst!s:5s} -> {got.date()}")

# --- TIME ZONES: decide once, at the boundary. ---
naive_ts = pd.to_datetime(["2024-03-10 02:30", "2024-07-01 12:00"])
ny = naive_ts.tz_localize("America/New_York", nonexistent="shift_forward")
print("\nlocalised then to UTC:", ny.tz_convert("UTC").tolist())
# nonexistent="shift_forward" handles the hour that does not exist on a
# spring-forward date. Without it, localisation raises.

# --- BOOLEANS: map explicitly; never rely on truthiness. ---
print(f"\nthe trap: bool('false') is {bool('false')}")
TRUE_SET = {"true", "t", "yes", "y", "1"}
FALSE_SET = {"false", "f", "no", "n", "0"}

def parse_bool(s: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    t = s.astype("string").str.strip().str.lower()
    return pd.Series(
        np.select([t.isin(TRUE_SET), t.isin(FALSE_SET)], [True, False], default=None),
        index=s.index, dtype="boolean",     # nullable: unknown stays unknown
    )

flags = parse_bool(messy["flag"])
print(pd.DataFrame({"raw": messy["flag"], "parsed": flags}).to_string(index=False))

# --- PUT IT TOGETHER: a declared schema is the whole defence. ---
SCHEMA = {"zip": "string", "count": "Int64"}
csv = "zip,count,when\n01234,10,2024-01-05\n02345,,2024-01-06\n"
loaded = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(csv), dtype=SCHEMA,
                     parse_dates=["when"], date_format="%Y-%m-%d",
                     na_values=["", "NA", "N/A", "null", "NULL", "-"])
print("\n", loaded.dtypes.to_dict())

# CATEGORY dtype: large memory win on repeated strings, plus it makes an
# unexpected new value visible instead of silently accepted.
country = pd.Series(["US"] * 5000 + ["CA"] * 5000)
print(f"\nobject {country.memory_usage(deep=True)/1e3:.0f} kB -> "
      f"category {country.astype('category').memory_usage(deep=True)/1e3:.0f} kB")
```

```text
  FAILURE MODES, RANKED BY HOW LONG THEY GO UNNOTICED

  1. ambiguous date convention      never noticed; months are simply wrong
  2. decimal comma vs thousands     values off by 1000x in some rows only
  3. leading zeros stripped from ID joins miss, silently, for a subset
  4. int -> float promotion         precision loss above 2^53 on large IDs
  5. truthy string booleans         every row becomes True
  6. wrong encoding                 visible mojibake, or a loud decode error

  THE SAFE CONVERSION LOOP

    read as string
         |
         v
    strip known decorations ($, %, commas, parentheses)
         |
         v
    convert with errors="coerce"
         |
         v
    count new nulls  ------> non-zero? inspect the raw values, fix the rule
         |
         v
    spot-check PARSED against RAW  <- catches the wrong-but-successful parse
         |
         v
    assert dtype and range
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Type inference is a guess made from a sample, so declare dtypes, date
>   formats, and null tokens rather than accepting the defaults.
> - A successful but wrong parse costs far more than a failed one; compare
>   parsed values against raw, not only the null count.
> - Identifiers are strings, not numbers, or leading zeros and precision
>   above 2^53 disappear.
> - Use pandas' nullable `Int64` and `boolean` dtypes so a missing value
>   stays missing instead of promoting the column or becoming `True`.
> - Normalise time zones to UTC at the ingestion boundary and keep a record
>   of which date format matched each row.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a `parse_money` function handling thousands separators, currency
>    symbols, and accounting parentheses, and prove it on a column
>    containing all three.
> 2. Build a date column that mixes three formats, parse it in passes, and
>    output a table of which format matched how many rows.
> 3. Show that reading a zero-padded identifier without a declared dtype
>    breaks a join, then fix it with a schema.
> 4. Interview: A nightly load has produced correct row counts for months,
>    but a monthly report is suddenly wrong for 3% of customers. Where do
>    you look first? (Hint: which conversions fail for only a subset of
>    values rather than for all of them?)

#### Standardizing Text and Categories

Two strings that a human reads as identical are different values to a
computer, and every such difference splits a group, breaks a join, or
invents a category. `"United States"`, `"united states"`, `"USA"`, `"U.S."`,
and `" US "` are five categories where there should be one. Standardizing
means collapsing surface variation so that equal things compare equal.

The work divides into three layers, and doing them in order matters.

**Unicode normalization** comes first, because it is invisible. The
character `é` can be stored as one code point or as `e` followed by a
combining accent. The two look the same and are not equal. Normalizing to
NFC makes them equal. Similarly, non-breaking spaces, zero-width characters,
and typographic quotes all masquerade as ordinary characters. Normalize
before you compare anything, or your comparisons are unreliable in ways that
are extremely hard to debug from a printed table.

**Mechanical cleaning** comes second: trim whitespace, collapse internal
runs of whitespace, and case-fold. Use `casefold` rather than `lower` if you
handle non-English text, because it handles cases like the German sharp s
that `lower` does not. Decide whether to strip punctuation and accents based
on the domain: removing accents merges `"Muller"` and `"Müller"`, which is
right for fuzzy matching and wrong for a mailing label.

**Semantic mapping** comes third and is the only layer that requires
knowledge. This is where `"USA"` becomes `"US"`. The right structure is an
explicit dictionary, version-controlled, applied deterministically, with
anything unmatched routed to a review list rather than silently dropped or
bucketed as "Other". Wherever a standard exists, use it: ISO 3166 for
countries, ISO 4217 for currencies, ISO 639 for languages. A canonical
external standard is a mapping you do not have to maintain or defend.

For the messy remainder, fuzzy grouping helps. Computing string similarity
within a column and clustering near-identical values surfaces the
`"Acme Inc"` / `"Acme Inc."` pairs quickly. Treat its output as a *proposal
for a human to approve*, not an automatic merge, because the same technique
that merges typos will happily merge `"Springfield, IL"` and
`"Springfield, MA"`.

Finally, once a column is standardized, **pin the allowed values**. Convert
to a categorical dtype with an explicit list of categories, so that a new
value arriving next month appears as a null or an error rather than
enlarging your category set without notice. That turns a silent data drift
into a failing check.

```python
import pandas as pd
import unicodedata
import re
from difflib import SequenceMatcher

raw = pd.Series([
    "United States", "united states", "USA", "U.S.", " US ",
    "  Canada", "CANADA", "canada\u00a0", "Deutschland", "Germany",
    "Café", "Cafe\u0301", "", None, "acme inc", "Acme Inc.",
], name="value")

# --- LAYER 1: Unicode normalization, the invisible problem. ---
a, b = "Café", "Cafe\u0301"                   # composed vs decomposed
print(f"look identical: {a == b}   lengths: {len(a)} vs {len(b)}")
nfc = unicodedata.normalize
print(f"after NFC:      {nfc('NFC', a) == nfc('NFC', b)}")

INVISIBLES = {
    "\u00a0": " ",    # non-breaking space
    "\u200b": "",     # zero-width space
    "\ufeff": "",     # byte-order mark
    "\u2019": "'",    # right single quote
    "\u2014": "-",    # em dash
}

def normalise_text(s: pd.Series, strip_accents: bool = False) -> pd.Series:
    t = s.astype("string")
    t = t.map(lambda v: unicodedata.normalize("NFC", v) if pd.notna(v) else v)
    for bad, good in INVISIBLES.items():
        t = t.str.replace(bad, good, regex=False)
    if strip_accents:
        # NFKD splits a letter from its accent, then we drop the accents.
        t = t.map(lambda v: "".join(
            c for c in unicodedata.normalize("NFKD", v)
            if not unicodedata.combining(c)) if pd.notna(v) else v)
    # LAYER 2: mechanical cleaning. casefold beats lower on non-English text.
    t = t.str.strip().str.replace(r"\s+", " ", regex=True).str.casefold()
    return t.replace("", pd.NA)               # empty string is a null

key = normalise_text(raw, strip_accents=True)
print("\n", pd.DataFrame({"raw": raw, "key": key}).to_string())
print(f"\ndistinct before {raw.nunique()} -> after {key.nunique()}")

# --- LAYER 3: semantic mapping against a standard. ---
# Version-control this dictionary. It is business logic, not a constant.
COUNTRY_MAP = {
    "united states": "US", "usa": "US", "us": "US", "united states of america": "US",
    "canada": "CA", "ca": "CA",
    "germany": "DE", "deutschland": "DE", "de": "DE",
}

mapped = key.map(COUNTRY_MAP)
unmatched = key[mapped.isna() & key.notna()]
print("\nmapped:\n", pd.DataFrame({"key": key, "iso": mapped}).dropna().to_string())
print("\nTO REVIEW (never silently bucket these):", unmatched.unique().tolist())
# Routing the remainder to a review queue is the difference between a
# mapping you can trust and an "Other" bucket that grows forever.

# --- FUZZY GROUPING: propose merges, do not apply them. ---
def propose_merges(values: pd.Series, threshold: float = 0.88) -> pd.DataFrame:
    uniq = sorted(values.dropna().unique())
    out = []
    for i, a in enumerate(uniq):
        for b in uniq[i + 1:]:
            r = SequenceMatcher(None, a, b).ratio()
            if r >= threshold:
                out.append({"a": a, "b": b, "ratio": round(r, 3)})
    return pd.DataFrame(out).sort_values("ratio", ascending=False)

companies = normalise_text(pd.Series(
    ["Acme Inc", "Acme Inc.", "ACME INC", "Acme Corp",
     "Springfield IL", "Springfield MA", "Zenith Ltd"]))
print("\nproposed merges for human review:")
print(propose_merges(companies).to_string(index=False))
# Note the Springfield pair: high similarity, and merging them would be a
# factual error. This is exactly why the output is a proposal.

# --- PIN THE ALLOWED VALUES so drift fails a check instead of passing. ---
ALLOWED = ["US", "CA", "DE", "GB", "FR"]
col = pd.Series(["US", "CA", "DE", "MX"]).astype(
    pd.CategoricalDtype(categories=ALLOWED))
print("\npinned categories:\n", col.to_string())
print(f"unexpected values became null: {col.isna().sum()}")

def assert_allowed(s: pd.Series, allowed: list[str], name: str) -> None:
    unexpected = set(s.dropna().unique()) - set(allowed)
    if unexpected:
        raise ValueError(f"{name}: unexpected categories {sorted(unexpected)}")

try:
    assert_allowed(pd.Series(["US", "CA", "MX"]), ALLOWED, "country")
except ValueError as e:
    print("caught:", e)

# --- RARE-CATEGORY COLLAPSING: a threshold, applied from TRAIN counts. ---
cats = pd.Series(["a"] * 500 + ["b"] * 300 + ["c"] * 8 + ["d"] * 3 + ["e"] * 1)
freq = cats.value_counts(normalize=True)
keep = freq[freq >= 0.01].index                  # 1% floor, fitted on train
collapsed = cats.where(cats.isin(keep), "__rare__")
print("\nbefore:", cats.nunique(), "after:", collapsed.nunique())
print(collapsed.value_counts().to_string())
# Store `keep` as a fitted parameter. Recomputing it on test data leaks.
```

```text
  THE THREE LAYERS, IN ORDER

  1. UNICODE           NFC normalize, strip invisibles      no knowledge needed
     "Cafe\u0301" -> "Café",  "US\u00a0" -> "US "

  2. MECHANICAL        trim, collapse spaces, casefold      no knowledge needed
     " United States " -> "united states"

  3. SEMANTIC          map to a canonical value             DOMAIN KNOWLEDGE
     "united states" -> "US"  (ISO 3166)

  Skipping layer 1 makes layers 2 and 3 unreliable in ways a printed
  table cannot show you.

  WHERE TO GET CANONICAL VALUES

    countries   ISO 3166-1 alpha-2      currencies  ISO 4217
    languages   ISO 639-1               time zones  IANA tz database
    industries  NAICS / SIC             units       UCUM

  Using a standard means the mapping is someone else's job to maintain.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Normalize Unicode first, because composed and decomposed characters look
>   identical while comparing unequal.
> - Separate mechanical cleaning, which needs no knowledge, from semantic
>   mapping, which needs domain expertise and belongs in a version-
>   controlled dictionary.
> - Map to an external standard such as ISO 3166 whenever one exists.
> - Fuzzy grouping proposes merges for review; applied automatically it will
>   merge genuinely distinct values.
> - Pin allowed categories so a new value fails a check instead of quietly
>   expanding the category set, and fit rare-category thresholds on training
>   data.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a series containing a composed and a decomposed version of the
>    same accented word, show they are unequal, and fix it with NFC
>    normalization.
> 2. Write a standardization function with all three layers and report the
>    distinct-value count after each layer on a real categorical column.
> 3. Implement a rare-category collapse at a 1% threshold as a fitted
>    transform, then apply it to a held-out set without recomputing counts.
> 4. Interview: A dashboard's country breakdown shows both "US" and "USA"
>    with separate totals. Where in the pipeline would you fix it, and what
>    do you do about the historical rows? (Hint: fixing forward and fixing
>    backward are different projects with different risks.)

<a id="62-data-transformation"></a>
### 6.2 Data Transformation

Transformation is the vocabulary of data manipulation: a small set of
operations that compose into any reshaping you need, and whose failure modes
are mostly about accidentally changing the grain of a table without
realising it.

#### Filtering, Sorting, Slicing

These three operations are the ones everybody learns first and the ones that
produce the most subtle bugs, precisely because they look too simple to get
wrong. The bugs come from three places: nulls do not behave like values in
comparisons, sorting is not stable unless you ask, and selecting by position
and selecting by label are different operations that sometimes give the same
answer.

**Filtering** is selecting rows by a condition. The critical fact is that a
comparison against a null is neither true nor false, and so a filter silently
drops null rows *from both sides*. `df[df.age > 30]` excludes nulls, and so
does `df[df.age <= 30]`. Their row counts do not add up to the total, and
whoever is reading your output will not know why. If you want the nulls, you
must say so.

The second filtering trap is chained comparisons. In Python, `a < x < b` on a
Series does not work as written because the ampersand and pipe operators bind
more tightly than comparison, so every compound condition needs parentheses.
`between` avoids the issue entirely and is clearer, but be aware that it is
inclusive on both ends by default.

**Sorting** matters more than it seems because downstream operations depend
on order: forward fills, rolling windows, `drop_duplicates(keep="first")`,
and `head`. The trap is ties. Two rows with the same sort key can come out in
either order, and the order can change between library versions or when the
data changes upstream. That makes results non-reproducible in a way that is
maddening to debug. The fix is to always sort by enough columns to break
every tie, and to use a stable sort algorithm when you cannot.

Null placement in sorts is also a choice, not a default worth trusting. Say
where you want them.

**Slicing** distinguishes label-based and position-based access. `loc` takes
labels and includes the endpoint; `iloc` takes positions and excludes it.
When your index happens to be `0..n-1` they coincide, which is exactly how
the bug hides until the index is a date or has been filtered.

Finally, a practical point about **copies and views**. Filtering usually
returns a new object, but assigning into the result of a chained selection
may write into a temporary and vanish, or may raise a warning about setting
on a copy. Assign through a single `loc` call, or call `copy()` explicitly
when you intend an independent frame.

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "user":   ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f"],
    "age":    [25, 34, np.nan, 41, 34, 19],
    "plan":   ["free", "pro", "pro", "free", "pro", None],
    "spend":  [0.0, 120.0, 80.0, 15.0, 120.0, 5.0],
    "joined": pd.to_datetime(["2024-01-05", "2024-02-11", "2024-02-11",
                              "2024-03-02", "2024-03-02", "2024-04-19"]),
})

# --- NULLS VANISH FROM BOTH SIDES OF A FILTER ---
over = df[df["age"] > 30]
under = df[df["age"] <= 30]
print(f"total {len(df)}, over30 {len(over)}, under30 {len(under)},"
      f" sum {len(over) + len(under)}   <- does not add up")
print("the missing row:\n", df[df["age"].isna()].to_string(index=False))

# Be explicit about which side the nulls belong on.
over_or_unknown = df[(df["age"] > 30) | df["age"].isna()]
print(f"\nover30 including unknown age: {len(over_or_unknown)}")

# --- COMPOUND CONDITIONS NEED PARENTHESES ---
# WRONG: `df["age"] > 20 & df["age"] < 40` binds as `20 & df["age"]`.
mask = (df["age"] > 20) & (df["age"] < 40)
print(f"\nparenthesised mask selects {mask.sum()} rows")
print(f"between(20, 40) selects {df['age'].between(20, 40).sum()} rows"
      f"   <- inclusive on BOTH ends")
print(f"between exclusive: {df['age'].between(20, 40, inclusive='neither').sum()}")

# `isin` for set membership; `~` to negate. Note nulls are never `isin`.
print(f"\npro or free: {df['plan'].isin(['pro', 'free']).sum()} of {len(df)}")
print("query() reads well for long conditions:\n",
      df.query("age > 20 and spend < 100").to_string(index=False))

# --- SORTING: TIES ARE NON-DETERMINISTIC UNLESS YOU BREAK THEM ---
ambiguous = df.sort_values("age")                  # rows b and e tie at 34
deterministic = df.sort_values(["age", "user"], kind="mergesort")  # stable
print("\nambiguous tie order:", ambiguous["user"].tolist())
print("deterministic order: ", deterministic["user"].tolist())
# kind="mergesort" is stable: equal keys keep their original relative order.
# The default quicksort is not, so the same code can reorder on new data.

# Null placement is a decision.
print("\nnulls last: ", df.sort_values("age", na_position="last")["user"].tolist())
print("nulls first:", df.sort_values("age", na_position="first")["user"].tolist())

# Multi-key with mixed direction: newest first, then cheapest.
print("\n", df.sort_values(["joined", "spend"], ascending=[False, True])
        [["user", "joined", "spend"]].to_string(index=False))

# WHY ORDER MATTERS DOWNSTREAM: the same dedupe, two answers.
for direction in (True, False):
    kept = (df.sort_values("joined", ascending=direction)
              .drop_duplicates("plan", keep="first")["user"].tolist())
    print(f"dedupe after ascending={direction}: kept {kept}")

# --- LOC VS ILOC: labels include the endpoint, positions do not ---
indexed = df.set_index("user")
print("\nloc 'b':'d' (inclusive):", indexed.loc["b":"d"].index.tolist())
print("iloc 1:3   (exclusive):  ", indexed.iloc[1:3].index.tolist())

filtered = df[df["spend"] > 10]                   # index is now 1,2,3,4
print("\nindex after filtering:", filtered.index.tolist())
print("iloc[0] ->", filtered.iloc[0]["user"], " (position)")
print("loc[1]  ->", filtered.loc[1]["user"], " (label)")
# reset_index(drop=True) after filtering, or these two keep diverging.

# --- BOOLEAN MASKS ARE COMPOSABLE AND SELF-DOCUMENTING ---
is_paying = df["spend"] > 0
is_recent = df["joined"] >= "2024-03-01"
print(f"\npaying {is_paying.sum()}, recent {is_recent.sum()},"
      f" both {(is_paying & is_recent).sum()}")
# Naming masks turns an unreadable one-liner into a readable filter.

# --- ASSIGNMENT: one loc call, not a chained selection ---
safe = df.copy()
safe.loc[safe["plan"].isna(), "plan"] = "unknown"   # single indexing operation
print("\n", safe[["user", "plan"]].to_string(index=False))
```

```text
  FILTER TRUTH TABLE WITH NULLS

    value    x > 30    x <= 30    x.isna()
    41       True      False      False
    19       False     True       False
    NaN      False     False      True        <- excluded by BOTH comparisons

    Any partition built from comparisons alone loses the null rows.
    Row counts that do not sum to the total are the symptom.

  LOC VS ILOC

    index:   'a'  'b'  'c'  'd'  'e'
    position  0    1    2    3    4

    loc['b':'d']  -> b, c, d      (labels, endpoint INCLUDED)
    iloc[1:3]     -> b, c         (positions, endpoint EXCLUDED)
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A comparison against a null is false, so filters silently drop null rows
>   from both sides of a partition; decide explicitly where they belong.
> - Parenthesise every compound mask, and remember `between` is inclusive by
>   default.
> - Break every sort tie with an additional key, and use a stable sort, or
>   results change when the data does.
> - `loc` is label-based and endpoint-inclusive; `iloc` is position-based and
>   endpoint-exclusive, and they coincide only on a default index.
> - Name boolean masks as variables; it documents intent and makes
>   composition readable.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a column with nulls and show that the counts of `x > k` and
>    `x <= k` do not sum to the row count, then write a partition that does.
> 2. Create a table with tied sort keys and demonstrate two different
>    `drop_duplicates` outcomes depending on sort direction.
> 3. Filter a frame, then show that `iloc[0]` and `loc[0]` return different
>    rows, and explain when this bites in production code.
> 4. Interview: A colleague reports that a filtered report's totals do not
>    match the unfiltered table's total. What are the two most likely
>    causes? (Hint: one involves nulls, the other involves the grain.)

#### Grouping and Aggregation

Grouping is the single most useful operation in analysis, and it works by a
pattern worth naming explicitly: **split, apply, combine**. Split the rows
into groups by some key, apply a function to each group, and combine the
results into one output. Once you see the pattern, SQL's `GROUP BY`, pandas'
`groupby`, and Spark's aggregations are all the same thing with different
syntax.

The thing that turns grouping from a formula into a tool is understanding the
three shapes the "apply" step can produce, because choosing the wrong one is
the most common source of confusion.

**Aggregate** reduces each group to a single row. Ten thousand orders become
fifty rows, one per country. This changes the grain of the table, which is
the point.

**Transform** returns a value for *every original row*, broadcast from its
group. The group mean attached to each row, so you can compute a deviation
from the group's own average. The grain is unchanged, which is what makes
this composable with the original frame.

**Filter** keeps or discards whole groups based on a group-level condition.
Keep only countries with more than a hundred orders. Rows survive or not
together.

The analogy: aggregate is writing one summary line per class on a report.
Transform is writing each student's class average next to their own mark.
Filter is deciding which classes appear in the report at all.

Beyond the shapes, several practical points separate reliable aggregation
from misleading aggregation.

**Nulls are skipped by default**, which means `mean` divides by the count of
non-null values, not by the group size. That is usually what you want and
occasionally a serious misrepresentation, so report the count alongside any
mean. Similarly `count` counts non-nulls while `size` counts rows, and the
difference between them is exactly the null count.

**Empty groups disappear.** If a category has no rows in this period, it
simply does not appear in the output, and a chart built from that output
shows no gap. Reindexing against the full set of expected keys turns a
missing row into an explicit zero.

**Averages of averages are wrong.** The mean of per-country conversion rates
is not the overall conversion rate unless every country has the same number
of users. Aggregate the numerator and denominator separately, then divide.
This mistake, sometimes met as Simpson's paradox when it reverses a
conclusion, appears constantly in real reporting.

Finally, **named aggregation** is the syntax worth defaulting to. It states
the output column name, the input column, and the function on one line, which
means the result has readable flat column names instead of a multi-level
index you then have to flatten.

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "country": rng.choice(["US", "CA", "DE"], 400, p=[0.6, 0.3, 0.1]),
    "plan":    rng.choice(["free", "pro"], 400),
    "amount":  rng.gamma(2, 40, 400).round(2),
    "items":   rng.integers(1, 6, 400),
})
orders.loc[rng.random(400) < 0.08, "amount"] = np.nan     # some missing values

# --- AGGREGATE: one row per group. Named aggregation gives flat names. ---
summary = orders.groupby("country", as_index=False).agg(
    n_rows=("amount", "size"),          # ALL rows in the group
    n_amounts=("amount", "count"),      # NON-NULL rows only
    revenue=("amount", "sum"),
    avg_amount=("amount", "mean"),
    p90_amount=("amount", lambda s: s.quantile(0.90)),
    distinct_plans=("plan", "nunique"),
)
summary["n_missing"] = summary["n_rows"] - summary["n_amounts"]
print(summary.round(2).to_string(index=False))
# size - count IS the null count. Reporting a mean without the count that
# produced it hides how much data the mean rests on.

# --- TRANSFORM: same shape as the input, broadcast from the group. ---
orders["country_avg"] = orders.groupby("country")["amount"].transform("mean")
orders["vs_country"] = (orders["amount"] - orders["country_avg"]).round(2)
# Group-relative z-score: a standard feature-engineering move.
orders["z_in_country"] = orders.groupby("country")["amount"].transform(
    lambda s: (s - s.mean()) / s.std(ddof=0)).round(2)
print("\n", orders.head(5)[
    ["country", "amount", "country_avg", "vs_country", "z_in_country"]
].round(2).to_string(index=False))

# Rank within group, another transform that is hard to write any other way.
orders["rank_in_country"] = orders.groupby("country")["amount"].rank(
    method="dense", ascending=False)

# --- FILTER: keep or drop entire groups. ---
big = orders.groupby("country").filter(lambda g: len(g) >= 50)
print(f"\nkept {big['country'].nunique()} of {orders['country'].nunique()}"
      f" countries, {len(big)} of {len(orders)} rows")

# --- THE AVERAGE-OF-AVERAGES ERROR ---
per_country = orders.groupby("country").agg(
    rev=("amount", "sum"), n=("amount", "count"))
per_country["avg"] = per_country["rev"] / per_country["n"]

wrong = per_country["avg"].mean()                       # unweighted
right = per_country["rev"].sum() / per_country["n"].sum()  # pooled
print(f"\nmean of group means {wrong:.2f}  vs  overall mean {right:.2f}")
print("weighted by group size:",
      round(np.average(per_country["avg"], weights=per_country["n"]), 2))
# RULE: aggregate the numerator and the denominator, THEN divide.

# --- EMPTY GROUPS DISAPPEAR unless you reindex. ---
EXPECTED = ["US", "CA", "DE", "FR", "JP"]
counts = orders.groupby("country").size()
print("\nas produced:\n", counts.to_string())
print("\nreindexed against the expected set:\n",
      counts.reindex(EXPECTED, fill_value=0).to_string())
# The second version shows FR and JP as zero. The first shows nothing, and
# a chart built on it silently omits them.

# Same issue with two keys: observed=False materialises absent combinations
# for categorical keys.
cat = orders.assign(
    country=orders["country"].astype("category"),
    plan=orders["plan"].astype("category"))
full_grid = cat.groupby(["country", "plan"], observed=False).size()
present = len(cat.groupby(["country", "plan"], observed=True).size())
print(f"\ncombinations present {present}"
      f", full grid {len(full_grid)}")

# --- MULTI-KEY GROUPING and flattening a MultiIndex result. ---
multi = orders.groupby(["country", "plan"]).agg({"amount": ["sum", "mean"],
                                                 "items": "sum"})
multi.columns = ["_".join(c) for c in multi.columns]     # flatten
print("\n", multi.round(2).to_string())

# --- SIMPSON'S PARADOX: the aggregate reverses the subgroups. ---
trial = pd.DataFrame({
    "group":    ["A"] * 2 + ["B"] * 2,
    "severity": ["mild", "severe"] * 2,
    "treated":  [100, 900, 900, 100],
    "cured":    [90, 270, 800, 25],
})
trial["rate"] = trial["cured"] / trial["treated"]
print("\nby severity:\n", trial.to_string(index=False))
overall = trial.groupby("group").apply(
    lambda g: g["cured"].sum() / g["treated"].sum(), include_groups=False)
print("\noverall rate:\n", overall.round(3).to_string())
# A beats B in BOTH severity strata and loses overall, because the groups
# have different severity mixes. Never aggregate across a confounded split.
```

```text
  THE THREE SHAPES OF SPLIT-APPLY-COMBINE

  input: 6 rows, 2 groups                   AGGREGATE (grain changes)
  +-----+--------+                          +-----+-------+
  | grp | value  |                          | grp | mean  |
  +-----+--------+   groupby("grp")         +-----+-------+
  |  A  |   10   | ------------------>      |  A  |  20   |
  |  A  |   30   |     .agg("mean")         |  B  |  50   |
  |  A  |   20   |                          +-----+-------+
  |  B  |   40   |
  |  B  |   60   |   .transform("mean")     TRANSFORM (grain preserved)
  |  B  |   50   | ------------------>      +-----+-------+------+
  +-----+--------+                          | grp | value | mean |
                                            |  A  |  10   |  20  |
                     .filter(len >= 4)      |  A  |  30   |  20  |
                   ------------------>      |  ...       |      |
                     FILTER: both groups    +-----+-------+------+
                     have 3 rows, so the
                     output is EMPTY

  COUNT VS SIZE

    size()  = rows in the group          (nulls included)
    count() = non-null values            (nulls excluded)
    size - count = the null count, and the gap your mean ignored
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Aggregate changes the grain, transform preserves it, and filter keeps or
>   drops whole groups; picking the wrong one is the usual confusion.
> - Aggregations skip nulls, so report `size` alongside any mean to show how
>   much data it rests on.
> - Averaging group averages is wrong unless group sizes are equal; sum the
>   numerator and denominator, then divide.
> - Groups with no rows vanish from the output, so reindex against the full
>   expected key set to make zeros explicit.
> - Prefer named aggregation for flat, readable output columns.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. For a grouped table, compute the mean of group means and the pooled
>    mean, and construct group sizes that make them differ by more than 20%.
> 2. Add a column holding each row's deviation from its group's median using
>    `transform`, then use it to find the most unusual row per group.
> 3. Produce a monthly count by category that includes zero rows for
>    categories absent in a given month.
> 4. Interview: A weekly report shows conversion rate rising in every
>    channel while the overall rate falls. Explain how that is possible and
>    what you would present instead. (Hint: what changed about the mix?)

#### Joins and Merges

A join combines two tables by matching rows on a key. It is the operation
that makes relational data useful and the operation most likely to silently
change your row count, which is why the single most valuable habit in this
whole chapter is: **check the row count before and after every join, and know
what you expected it to be.**

The join types differ in which non-matching rows survive.

| Join | Keeps | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| inner | rows matching in both | you need both sides populated |
| left | all left rows | enriching a table you must not shrink |
| right | all right rows | rarely; write it as a left join instead |
| outer (full) | all rows from both | reconciling two sources |
| cross | every pair | building a complete grid deliberately |
| anti | left rows with no match | finding what is missing |

Join *type* is only half the story. The other half is **cardinality**, the
relationship between key multiplicities, and this is where the damage
happens.

A **one-to-one** join leaves row counts alone. A **many-to-one** join, the
normal case of looking up an attribute, also leaves the left row count alone,
because each left row finds exactly one match. A **many-to-many** join
multiplies: three rows on the left sharing a key and four on the right
produce twelve rows. If you expected an enrichment you now have duplicated
revenue, and because every row looks individually plausible, nothing alerts
you except the total.

Pandas will tell you if you ask. The `validate` parameter asserts the
cardinality and raises if the data violates it. Using it converts a silent
fan-out into a stack trace, which is precisely the trade you want.

Several more traps are worth internalising.

**Key type mismatches** produce zero matches with no error. An integer `101`
does not equal the string `"101"`, and a key with trailing whitespace does not
equal one without. A join returning suspiciously few rows is almost always
this.

**Nulls do not match nulls.** Two rows with a null key are not joined
together, which is correct behaviour and surprising the first time.

**Indicator columns** are the diagnostic tool. Merging with
`indicator=True` adds a column saying whether each row came from the left,
the right, or both, and the counts of those three values tell you immediately
what your join did.

For time series there is a distinct operation: **as-of joins**, which match
each left row to the most recent right row at or before its timestamp. This
is how you attach a price to a trade or a configuration to an event, and
doing it with a regular join plus a filter is both slower and easier to get
wrong. Crucially, an as-of join with the direction reversed is a leakage bug:
matching to the *next* value attaches future information.

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5],
    "user_id":  [10, 11, 12, 11, 99],
    "amount":   [50.0, 20.0, 75.0, 30.0, 10.0],
})
users = pd.DataFrame({
    "user_id": [10, 11, 12, 13],
    "country": ["US", "CA", "DE", "FR"],
})

# --- THE HABIT: assert what you expect, every time. ---
def safe_merge(left, right, expect_rows=None, **kw):
    out = left.merge(right, indicator=True, **kw)
    counts = out["_merge"].value_counts().to_dict()
    print(f"  {len(left)} x {len(right)} -> {len(out)} rows   {counts}")
    if expect_rows is not None and len(out) != expect_rows:
        raise AssertionError(f"expected {expect_rows} rows, got {len(out)}")
    return out.drop(columns="_merge")

print("inner:")
inner = safe_merge(orders, users, on="user_id", how="inner")
print("left:")
left = safe_merge(orders, users, on="user_id", how="left", expect_rows=len(orders))
print("outer:")
outer = safe_merge(orders, users, on="user_id", how="outer")

# ANTI-JOIN: what is on the left and missing on the right. This is the
# question "which orders reference a user we do not have?" and it is the
# check that finds broken referential integrity.
merged = orders.merge(users, on="user_id", how="left", indicator=True)
orphans = merged[merged["_merge"] == "left_only"]
print("\norphan orders:\n", orphans[["order_id", "user_id"]].to_string(index=False))

# --- THE FAN-OUT: many-to-many silently multiplies rows and money. ---
addresses = pd.DataFrame({          # a user can have several addresses
    "user_id": [10, 10, 11, 11, 11],
    "kind":    ["home", "work", "home", "work", "billing"],
})
fanned = orders.merge(addresses, on="user_id", how="left")
print(f"\nrows {len(orders)} -> {len(fanned)}")
print(f"revenue {orders['amount'].sum():.2f} -> {fanned['amount'].sum():.2f}"
      f"   <- INFLATED, and every row looks fine")

# The fix is to decide the grain BEFORE joining: collapse the right side.
one_per_user = (addresses[addresses["kind"] == "home"]
                .drop_duplicates("user_id"))
fixed = orders.merge(one_per_user, on="user_id", how="left")
print(f"after collapsing right side: {len(fixed)} rows,"
      f" revenue {fixed['amount'].sum():.2f}")

# `validate` turns the silent fan-out into an exception.
try:
    orders.merge(addresses, on="user_id", how="left", validate="many_to_one")
except Exception as e:
    print("\nvalidate caught it:", type(e).__name__, "-", str(e)[:60])

# --- KEY TYPE MISMATCH: zero matches, no error. ---
a = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 3], "x": ["a", "b", "c"]})
b = pd.DataFrame({"id": ["1", "2", "3"], "y": ["p", "q", "r"]})
print(f"\nint vs string key -> {len(a.merge(b, on='id'))} matches")
print(f"after aligning dtypes -> "
      f"{len(a.assign(id=a['id'].astype(str)).merge(b, on='id'))} matches")

# Whitespace is the same class of bug and even less visible.
c = pd.DataFrame({"k": ["us ", "ca"], "v": [1, 2]})
d = pd.DataFrame({"k": ["us", "ca"], "w": [3, 4]})
print(f"with whitespace -> {len(c.merge(d, on='k'))} matches")
print(f"after strip     -> "
      f"{len(c.assign(k=c['k'].str.strip()).merge(d, on='k'))} matches")

# --- NULL KEYS DO NOT MATCH EACH OTHER ---
e = pd.DataFrame({"k": [1, None], "v": ["x", "y"]})
f = pd.DataFrame({"k": [1, None], "w": ["p", "q"]})
print(f"\nnull key matches: {len(e.merge(f, on='k'))} (not 2)")

# --- COLUMN NAME COLLISIONS: always name the suffixes. ---
g = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1], "value": [10], "updated": ["2024-01-01"]})
h = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1], "value": [99], "updated": ["2024-02-01"]})
collided = g.merge(h, on="id", suffixes=("_order", "_invoice"))
print("\n", collided.to_string(index=False))

# --- AS-OF JOIN: the correct tool for "the latest value at that time". ---
trades = pd.DataFrame({
    "time":  pd.to_datetime(["2024-01-01 09:31", "2024-01-01 09:35",
                             "2024-01-01 09:47"]),
    "shares": [100, 250, 75],
}).sort_values("time")
prices = pd.DataFrame({
    "time":  pd.to_datetime(["2024-01-01 09:30", "2024-01-01 09:34",
                             "2024-01-01 09:40", "2024-01-01 09:50"]),
    "price": [10.0, 10.5, 11.0, 12.0],
}).sort_values("time")

# direction="backward" is the only safe default: it can only use the past.
asof = pd.merge_asof(trades, prices, on="time", direction="backward")
print("\nas-of backward (safe):\n", asof.to_string(index=False))

leaky = pd.merge_asof(trades, prices, on="time", direction="forward")
print("\nas-of forward (LEAKS the future):\n", leaky.to_string(index=False))

# tolerance bounds how stale a match may be; beyond it, the value is null,
# which is more honest than silently using an hour-old price.
bounded = pd.merge_asof(trades, prices, on="time", direction="backward",
                        tolerance=pd.Timedelta("2min"))
print("\nwith a 2-minute tolerance:\n", bounded.to_string(index=False))
```

```text
  CARDINALITY DECIDES THE ROW COUNT, NOT THE JOIN TYPE

  left keys    right keys    result            validate=
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  unique       unique        len(left) rows    "one_to_one"
  repeated     unique        len(left) rows    "many_to_one"   <- lookups
  unique       repeated      MORE than left    "one_to_many"
  repeated     repeated      product per key   (no safe option)

  THE FAN-OUT, DRAWN

    left                right                 result
    k=A amount=50       k=A kind=home         k=A 50 home
                        k=A kind=work         k=A 50 work     <- 50 counted twice
    sum(amount)=50                            sum(amount)=100

  DIAGNOSING A JOIN WITH indicator=True

    both        matched as intended
    left_only   right side is missing keys -> referential integrity gap
    right_only  left side is missing keys  -> filtered upstream? wrong grain?

  ZERO MATCHES CHECKLIST
    dtype mismatch (int vs str) | whitespace | case | leading zeros stripped
    | null keys | key is actually two columns
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Check row counts before and after every join against an expectation you
>   stated in advance.
> - The join type decides which non-matches survive; cardinality decides the
>   row count, and many-to-many fan-out inflates every sum.
> - Use `validate` to turn an unexpected fan-out into an exception.
> - Zero matches almost always means a key dtype, whitespace, or case
>   mismatch rather than genuinely absent data.
> - Use an as-of join for "latest value at that time", always backward, and
>   set a tolerance so stale matches become null.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build two frames whose join fans out, show that the sum of a numeric
>    column inflates, then fix it by collapsing the right side first.
> 2. Merge with `indicator=True` on data with orphan keys on both sides and
>    interpret all three indicator counts.
> 3. Use `merge_asof` to attach the most recent price to each trade, then
>    repeat with `direction="forward"` and explain why the second version
>    would inflate a backtest.
> 4. Interview: A join that should enrich 1 million orders returns 1.4
>    million rows. Walk through your diagnosis. (Hint: which side has
>    duplicate keys, and what is the intended grain of the output?)

#### Reshaping: Wide and Long Formats

The same data can be laid out in two fundamentally different ways, and moving
between them is one of the most common operations in practice. In **wide**
format, each variable has its own column: one row per entity, with `jan`,
`feb`, `mar` as separate columns. In **long** format, one column holds the
variable name and another holds the value: one row per entity-month pair.

Neither is correct in general. They serve different purposes.

Wide format is for **reading and reporting**. A human comparing months
scans across a row. A spreadsheet pivot table is wide. Correlation matrices
and many statistical routines expect wide input.

Long format is for **computing and storing**. Adding a new month means adding
rows, not altering a schema. Grouping, filtering, and plotting libraries all
prefer it, because "the variable" is a value you can filter on rather than a
column name you have to enumerate. Databases store long for the same reason.

The mental model: wide is a printed table, long is a list of facts. A fact is
`(entity, variable, value)`, and any wide table is just a pivoted view of the
underlying facts.

The operations, by name:

- **melt** or **unpivot** goes wide to long. You name the columns that stay
  fixed, the identifiers, and the rest collapse into a name column and a
  value column.
- **pivot** goes long to wide. It requires that the combination of index and
  column keys be unique, and it raises if it is not, which is a useful
  safety check.
- **pivot_table** goes long to wide *with aggregation*, so duplicates are
  summarised rather than rejected. Useful, but be aware that it silently
  aggregates where `pivot` would have warned you about unexpected
  duplicates.
- **stack** and **unstack** move levels between the index and the columns,
  which is the same reshape expressed on a MultiIndex.

Two practical hazards. First, pivoting produces columns whose names come from
*data*, which means a new value upstream changes your schema. Code that
indexes those columns by name breaks in production, so either pin the expected
set or work in long format until the last step. Second, pivoting creates
nulls for combinations that do not exist, and those nulls mean "no
observation", not "zero". Filling them with zero is a claim, sometimes right
and sometimes badly wrong.

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

wide = pd.DataFrame({
    "store": ["A", "B", "C"],
    "region": ["north", "north", "south"],
    "jan": [100, 150, 90],
    "feb": [110, 140, 95],
    "mar": [120, 160, np.nan],
})
print("WIDE (good for reading):\n", wide.to_string(index=False))

# --- WIDE -> LONG with melt ---
long = wide.melt(
    id_vars=["store", "region"],      # columns that stay as identifiers
    value_vars=["jan", "feb", "mar"],  # columns to collapse
    var_name="month",
    value_name="sales",
)
print("\nLONG (good for computing):\n", long.to_string(index=False))

# Why long is easier to compute on: one expression, no column enumeration.
print("\ngrouped in long form:\n",
      long.groupby("month", as_index=False)["sales"].agg(["sum", "count"])
      .to_string(index=False))
# In wide form the same result needs the month columns listed by name, and
# adding April means editing the code.

# --- LONG -> WIDE with pivot; it REJECTS duplicate index/column pairs. ---
back = long.pivot(index=["store", "region"], columns="month",
                  values="sales").reset_index()
back.columns.name = None
print("\npivoted back:\n", back.to_string(index=False))

dupes = pd.concat([long, long.iloc[[0]]])       # inject a duplicate fact
try:
    dupes.pivot(index="store", columns="month", values="sales")
except ValueError as e:
    print("\npivot refuses duplicates:", str(e)[:58])

# pivot_table AGGREGATES instead of refusing. Convenient, and it hides the
# duplicate you might have wanted to know about.
pt = dupes.pivot_table(index="store", columns="month", values="sales",
                       aggfunc="sum", margins=True, margins_name="total")
print("\npivot_table with margins:\n", pt.to_string())

# --- NULLS FROM PIVOTING MEAN "NO ROW", NOT "ZERO" ---
sparse = pd.DataFrame({
    "store": ["A", "A", "B"],
    "month": ["jan", "feb", "jan"],
    "sales": [100, 110, 150],
})
grid = sparse.pivot(index="store", columns="month", values="sales")
print("\nsparse pivot:\n", grid.to_string())
print("\nfilled with 0 (a CLAIM that B sold nothing in feb):\n",
      grid.fillna(0).to_string())
# If the store did not exist in February, 0 is wrong and NaN is right.
# If it existed and sold nothing, 0 is right. The data cannot tell you.

# --- STACK / UNSTACK: the same reshape on a MultiIndex ---
mi = long.dropna().set_index(["store", "month"])["sales"]
print("\nunstack moves an index level to columns:\n",
      mi.unstack("month").to_string())
print("\nstack moves it back:\n", mi.unstack("month").stack().head().to_string())

# --- WIDE COLUMN NAMES THAT ENCODE TWO VARIABLES ---
messy = pd.DataFrame({
    "id": [1, 2],
    "sales_2023": [10, 20], "sales_2024": [11, 21],
    "cost_2023": [5, 9],    "cost_2024": [6, 10],
})
# wide_to_long splits a stub name from a suffix in one call.
tidy = pd.wide_to_long(messy, stubnames=["sales", "cost"], i="id",
                       j="year", sep="_").reset_index()
print("\nwide_to_long:\n", tidy.to_string(index=False))

# The general version: melt, then split the name column.
melted = messy.melt(id_vars="id", var_name="metric_year", value_name="value")
melted[["metric", "year"]] = melted["metric_year"].str.rsplit("_", n=1, expand=True)
print("\nmelt + split:\n",
      melted.drop(columns="metric_year").to_string(index=False))

# --- SCHEMA STABILITY: pin expected columns after any pivot. ---
EXPECTED_MONTHS = ["jan", "feb", "mar", "apr"]
stable = grid.reindex(columns=EXPECTED_MONTHS)
print("\npinned columns (apr present and null, not absent):\n",
      stable.to_string())
# Now downstream code that reads `apr` works whether or not April had data.
```

```text
  THE SAME FOUR FACTS, TWO LAYOUTS

  WIDE                             LONG
  store  jan  feb                  store  month  sales
  A      100  110                  A      jan    100
  B      150  140                  A      feb    110
                                   B      jan    150
                                   B      feb    140

  adding March:  ALTER the schema   adding March:  INSERT rows
  human reading: easy               human reading: harder
  grouping:      enumerate columns  grouping:      one expression
  storage:       sparse -> nulls    storage:       dense, no nulls

  THE ROUND TRIP

       melt / unpivot / stack
   WIDE -------------------------> LONG
```
