```text
  7     contextual/sentence  word sense, context high     no

  Start at 4. Climb only when a measurement says to.

  WHAT PREPROCESSING COSTS

  step             merges                     destroys
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  lowercase        Apple / apple              proper nouns, acronyms
  remove stop wd   shrinks vocabulary         negation ("not good")
  stemming         run/running/ran            readability of features
  lemmatisation    run/running/ran (properly) nothing, costs compute
  strip punctuation                           "!!!", emoticons, URLs

  TF-IDF INTUITION

    tf(t,d)  = how often t occurs in d          -> local importance
    idf(t)   = log(N / documents containing t)  -> global rarity
    "the" is in every document -> idf ~ 0 -> weight ~ 0, automatically.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Manual surface features are unreasonably strong for tasks where form
>   rather than meaning carries the signal.
> - Bag of words discards order; n-grams restore the local order that matters,
>   such as negation.
> - TF-IDF downweights terms that appear everywhere and is the baseline any
>   more expensive method has to beat.
> - Every preprocessing step is deliberate information loss, and removing stop
>   words destroys negation.
> - Fit the vectorizer inside the pipeline, or the test set's vocabulary and
>   document frequencies leak into training.

>    binary label on any labelled text you have.
> 2. Show that a unigram vectorizer maps two sentences differing only in "not"
>    to nearly identical vectors, and that adding bigrams separates them.
> 3. Compare word-token and character n-gram similarity for a misspelled pair

#### Target and Frequency Encoding

One-hot encoding a variable with ten thousand categories gives you ten
thousand columns, most of which are almost always zero. That is unusable, so
you need an encoding whose width does not grow with cardinality. The two main
options both replace a category with a statistic about it.

**Frequency encoding** replaces each category with how often it occurs. It is
unsupervised, so it cannot leak the target, and it is surprisingly useful:
rarity is often predictive in its own right, since rare merchant codes, rare
user agents, and rare error messages all tend to behave differently from
common ones. Its weakness is that two categories with the same count become
indistinguishable.

**Target encoding**, also called mean encoding or likelihood encoding,
replaces each category with the mean of the target within that category. A
postcode becomes its historical default rate. This is enormously powerful
because it compresses all the information the category carries about the
target into one number, and it is enormously dangerous for exactly the same
reason: you have put the answer into the feature.

Two things go wrong, and both have standard fixes.

**Overfitting on rare categories.** A category with one row gets that row's
target as its encoded value, which is a perfect predictor of that row and pure
noise for any other. The fix is **smoothing**: blend the category mean toward
the global mean, weighted by how many rows the category has. With many rows,
trust the category; with few, fall back to the prior. The weight is usually
`n / (n + m)` for a smoothing constant `m`, which is a simple form of
empirical Bayes shrinkage.

**Leakage through the row's own target.** If a row's encoded value was computed
using that row's own label, the feature contains the answer. Cross-validated
or out-of-fold encoding fixes this: compute each row's encoding from the
*other* folds only, so no row ever sees its own target. The version of this
used by CatBoost goes further, computing each row's encoding from rows that
precede it in a random permutation, which removes the leakage almost entirely.

The failure mode to recognise is distinctive: a target-encoded model shows an
excellent validation score and a much worse test score, and the gap grows with
the cardinality of the encoded variable. If you see that, suspect the
encoding before anything else.

There are variants worth knowing. **Count-and-sum encoding** keeps the
numerator and denominator as separate features, letting the model combine them
itself. **Weight-of-evidence encoding** is the credit-scoring standard, using a
log-odds ratio and inheriting the same smoothing needs. For multiclass
problems you need one encoded column per class, which starts to cost width
again.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold, cross_val_score, train_test_split
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingClassifier

rng = np.random.default_rng(9)
n = 4000
# 300 categories with very uneven support: the long tail is where it breaks.
cats = rng.choice([f"z{i:03d}" for i in range(300)], n,
                  p=(w := rng.dirichlet(np.full(300, 0.3))))
true_rate = dict(zip([f"z{i:03d}" for i in range(300)],
                     rng.beta(2, 5, 300)))
y = pd.Series((rng.random(n) < np.array([true_rate[c] for c in cats])).astype(int))
X = pd.DataFrame({"cat": cats})
print(f"{X['cat'].nunique()} categories, "
      f"{(X['cat'].value_counts() <= 3).sum()} of them with 3 rows or fewer")

# --- FREQUENCY ENCODING: unsupervised, so it cannot leak. ---
freq = X["cat"].value_counts(normalize=True)
X["cat_freq"] = X["cat"].map(freq)
X["cat_count"] = X["cat"].map(X["cat"].value_counts())
print(f"\nfrequency encoding: 1 column, correlation with y "
      f"{X['cat_freq'].corr(y):+.3f}")

# --- NAIVE TARGET ENCODING: the leak, demonstrated. ---
naive_map = y.groupby(X["cat"]).mean()
X["te_naive"] = X["cat"].map(naive_map)
print(f"\nnaive target encoding correlation with y: {X['te_naive'].corr(y):+.3f}")

singles = X["cat"].map(X["cat"].value_counts()) == 1
print(f"rows in singleton categories: {singles.sum()}")
print("for those rows the encoded value EQUALS their own label:",
      bool((X.loc[singles, 'te_naive'] == y[singles]).all()))
# The feature contains the answer for exactly the rows where it helps least.

# --- SMOOTHING: shrink small categories toward the global mean. ---
def smooth_target_encode(keys: pd.Series, target: pd.Series, m: float = 20.0):
    """Empirical-Bayes shrinkage: weight n/(n+m) on the category mean."""
    prior = target.mean()
    stats = target.groupby(keys).agg(["sum", "count"])
    smoothed = (stats["sum"] + m * prior) / (stats["count"] + m)
    return smoothed, prior

mapping, prior = smooth_target_encode(X["cat"], y, m=20.0)
X["te_smooth"] = X["cat"].map(mapping).fillna(prior)

show = pd.DataFrame({
    "count": y.groupby(X["cat"]).count(),
    "raw_mean": y.groupby(X["cat"]).mean().round(3),
    "smoothed": mapping.round(3),
}).sort_values("count")
print(f"\nglobal prior {prior:.3f}")
print("\nsmallest categories are pulled hard toward the prior:")
print(show.head(4).to_string())
print("\nlargest categories keep their own mean:")
print(show.tail(3).to_string())

# --- OUT-OF-FOLD ENCODING: no row sees its own target. ---
def oof_target_encode(keys: pd.Series, target: pd.Series,
                      n_splits: int = 5, m: float = 20.0, seed: int = 0):
    out = pd.Series(np.nan, index=keys.index, dtype=float)
    kf = KFold(n_splits=n_splits, shuffle=True, random_state=seed)
    for fit_idx, apply_idx in kf.split(keys):
        mp, pr = smooth_target_encode(keys.iloc[fit_idx], target.iloc[fit_idx], m)
        out.iloc[apply_idx] = keys.iloc[apply_idx].map(mp).fillna(pr).values
    return out

X["te_oof"] = oof_target_encode(X["cat"], y)
print("\ncorrelation with the target:")
print(pd.Series({
    "frequency (safe)": X["cat_freq"].corr(y),
    "naive TE (leaks)": X["te_naive"].corr(y),
    "smoothed TE (leaks less)": X["te_smooth"].corr(y),
    "out-of-fold TE (safe)": X["te_oof"].corr(y),
}).round(3).to_string())
# The naive correlation is inflated by construction. The out-of-fold value
# is the honest estimate of how much the category actually tells you.

# --- THE VALIDATION GAP, MEASURED ---
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X[["cat"]], y, test_size=0.3, random_state=1)

# WRONG: encode with a map fitted on everything, then split.
bad_map = y.groupby(X["cat"]).mean()
bad_tr = Xtr["cat"].map(bad_map).to_frame("te")
bad_te = Xte["cat"].map(bad_map).fillna(y.mean()).to_frame("te")

# RIGHT: out-of-fold on train, and a train-only map applied to test.
good_tr = oof_target_encode(Xtr["cat"], ytr).to_frame("te")
mp, pr = smooth_target_encode(Xtr["cat"], ytr, m=20.0)
good_te = Xte["cat"].map(mp).fillna(pr).to_frame("te")

clf = GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0)
for label, (a, b) in {"leaky encoding": (bad_tr, bad_te),
                      "out-of-fold encoding": (good_tr, good_te)}.items():
    clf.fit(a, ytr)
    print(f"\n{label}")
    print(f"  train-fit score {clf.score(a, ytr):.3f}"
          f"   held-out score {clf.score(b, yte):.3f}")
# The leaky version shows a wide train/test gap. The honest version's
# numbers are lower and are the ones that will hold in production.

# --- UNSEEN CATEGORIES fall back to the prior, always. ---
unseen = pd.Series(["brand_new_code"])
print(f"\nunseen category encodes to the prior: "
      f"{unseen.map(mp).fillna(pr).iloc[0]:.3f}")

# --- COUNT-AND-SUM: give the model the parts, let it combine them. ---
parts = y.groupby(X["cat"]).agg(["sum", "count"])
X["cat_pos"] = X["cat"].map(parts["sum"])
X["cat_n"] = X["cat"].map(parts["count"])
print("\ncount-and-sum keeps the sample size visible to the model, so it can")
print("distrust a 1.0 rate that rests on two rows.")
```

```text
  SHRINKAGE: HOW MUCH TO TRUST A CATEGORY

  encoded = (sum_of_target + m * prior) / (count + m)

    count    weight on the category mean (m=20)
    1        0.05      almost entirely the prior
    5        0.20
    20       0.50      half and half
    100      0.83
    1000     0.98      almost entirely its own mean

  larger m = more conservative. Tune it; it is a real hyperparameter.

  THE THREE WAYS TARGET ENCODING LEAKS

  1. own row      the encoding used this row's label      -> out-of-fold
  2. whole set    the map was fitted before the split     -> fit on train only
  3. time         the map used rows after the prediction  -> fit on past only

  ALL THREE must be closed. Closing one is not enough.

  SYMPTOM TO RECOGNISE

    validation AUC 0.94, test AUC 0.71, and the gap widens with cardinality
    -> suspect the target encoding before the model.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Frequency encoding is unsupervised and cannot leak, and rarity is often
>   predictive on its own.
> - Target encoding compresses a high-cardinality category into one strong
>   feature and puts the answer into the input if done carelessly.
> - Smooth toward the global mean with weight `n / (n + m)` so rare categories
>   do not memorise their own rows.
> - Compute encodings out of fold so no row ever sees its own target, and fit
>   the final map on training rows only.
> - A wide validation-to-test gap that grows with cardinality is the signature
>   of leaky target encoding.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Target-encode a high-cardinality column naively and show that singleton
>    categories receive their own row's label as the feature value.
> 2. Implement smoothed encoding and plot or tabulate the shrinkage weight
>    against category size for two values of the smoothing constant.
> 3. Compare held-out scores for a model trained on a leaky encoding and one
>    trained on out-of-fold encoding.

>    AUC. What do you predict happens in production, and how do you show them
>    without a deployment? (Hint: which rows contributed to their own
>    feature's value?)

#### Feature Selection Methods

More features are not better. Past a point they cost accuracy, not just
compute, and the reasons are worth understanding rather than taking on faith.

Irrelevant features add variance: the model fits noise in them, and the noise
does not repeat. Redundant features destabilise coefficients, since two
near-identical columns can trade arbitrarily large opposite weights and the
model has no basis to choose. Sheer dimensionality thins the data: in high
dimensions every point is far from every other, distances become
uninformative, and the volume the model must cover grows exponentially. This
last effect is the **curse of dimensionality**, and it is why a
distance-based method degrades sharply as you add columns.

There are also operational costs. Every feature is a pipeline dependency, a
potential source of drift, and something that can be null in production for a
reason nobody anticipated. Fewer features is less to monitor.

Selection methods fall into three families.

**Filter methods** score each feature against the target independently of any
model. Correlation, mutual information, chi-squared, ANOVA F-statistic. They
are fast, they scale to very wide data, and they share a blind spot: they
evaluate features one at a time, so they keep two redundant features that both
score well and discard a feature that is useless alone and essential in
combination. The XOR pattern is the standard counterexample, where each input
has zero marginal association with the target and the pair determines it
completely.

**Wrapper methods** train the model repeatedly on different feature subsets
and keep what improves the score. Forward selection adds features one at a
time; backward elimination removes them; recursive feature elimination drops
the weakest feature and refits, repeatedly. These account for interactions
because the model does, and they are expensive, and they overfit the selection
criterion if the score you optimise is the same one you report.

**Embedded methods** select as part of fitting. Lasso's L1 penalty drives
coefficients to exactly zero, which is selection. Tree ensembles produce
importances. These are the best value in practice: one fit, interactions
accounted for, and the selection is consistent with the model you will ship.

Two warnings about importances specifically. **Impurity-based importance is
biased** toward high-cardinality and continuous features, because they offer
more places to split, and it can rank a pure-noise column with many distinct
values above a genuinely useful binary one. **Permutation importance** is
measured on held-out data by shuffling one column and observing the drop in
score, which is model-agnostic and far more trustworthy, though it splits
credit oddly between correlated features, since shuffling one leaves the other
to compensate.

The overriding procedural rule: **selection is part of the model, so it must
happen inside cross-validation.** Selecting features using the whole dataset
and then cross-validating the reduced set is leakage, and it produces
impressively wrong scores. The demonstration below shows it selecting pure
noise and reporting high accuracy.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.feature_selection import (SelectKBest, f_classif,
                                       mutual_info_classif, RFECV)
from sklearn.linear_model import LassoCV, LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

Xa, ya = make_classification(n_samples=1200, n_features=30, n_informative=5,
                            n_redundant=5, n_repeated=0, shuffle=False,
                            random_state=0)
X = pd.DataFrame(Xa, columns=[f"f{i:02d}" for i in range(30)])
y = pd.Series(ya)
# By construction f00-f04 are informative, f05-f09 are redundant copies,
# and f10-f29 are noise.

# --- FILTER: fast, univariate, blind to interactions. ---
f_scores = pd.Series(f_classif(X, y)[0], index=X.columns)
mi = pd.Series(mutual_info_classif(X, y, random_state=0), index=X.columns)
print("top 8 by ANOVA F:", f_scores.nlargest(8).index.tolist())
print("top 8 by mutual information:", mi.nlargest(8).index.tolist())

# THE BLIND SPOT: XOR. Each feature alone is uninformative.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
a, b = rng.integers(0, 2, 2000), rng.integers(0, 2, 2000)
xor = pd.DataFrame({"a": a, "b": b})
yx = pd.Series(a ^ b)
print("\nXOR: univariate mutual information per feature:",
      np.round(mutual_info_classif(xor, yx, random_state=0), 4).tolist())
print("accuracy of a model using both:",
      round(cross_val_score(RandomForestClassifier(random_state=0),
                            xor, yx, cv=5).mean(), 3))
# Both scores are ~0 and the pair predicts perfectly. Any filter method
# would discard both features.

# --- EMBEDDED: L1 drives coefficients to exactly zero. ---
lasso = Pipeline([("s", StandardScaler()),
                  ("m", LassoCV(cv=5, random_state=0, max_iter=5000))]).fit(X, y)
coefs = pd.Series(lasso.named_steps["m"].coef_, index=X.columns)
print(f"\nlasso kept {(coefs != 0).sum()} of {len(coefs)} features:"
      f" {coefs[coefs != 0].index.tolist()[:8]}")

# --- IMPURITY IMPORTANCE IS BIASED toward many-valued features. ---
Xb = X.copy()
Xb["noise_continuous"] = rng.normal(size=len(Xb))    # pure noise, many values
Xb["noise_binary"] = rng.integers(0, 2, len(Xb))     # pure noise, two values
rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=250, random_state=0).fit(Xb, y)
imp = pd.Series(rf.feature_importances_,
                index=Xb.columns).sort_values(ascending=False)
rank = {c: i + 1 for i, c in enumerate(imp.index)}
print(f"\nimpurity rank of noise_continuous: {rank['noise_continuous']}/{len(imp)}")
print(f"impurity rank of noise_binary:     {rank['noise_binary']}/{len(imp)}")
print("the continuous noise column outranks the binary one purely because")
print("it offers more candidate split points.")

# --- PERMUTATION IMPORTANCE: measured on held-out data. ---
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Xb, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)
rf2 = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=0).fit(Xtr, ytr)
perm = permutation_importance(rf2, Xte, yte, n_repeats=10, random_state=0)
pi = pd.Series(perm.importances_mean, index=Xb.columns).sort_values(ascending=False)
print("\ntop 6 by permutation importance:", pi.head(6).round(4).to_dict())
print(f"noise_continuous permutation importance: "
      f"{pi['noise_continuous']:+.4f}  <- at or below zero, correctly")

# --- WRAPPER: RFE with cross-validation picks the subset size. ---
rfecv = RFECV(LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000), step=2, cv=5,
              scoring="accuracy", min_features_to_select=2)
rfecv.fit(StandardScaler().fit_transform(X), y)
print(f"\nRFECV chose {rfecv.n_features_} features")

# --- THE LEAKAGE, DEMONSTRATED ON PURE NOISE ---
noise = pd.DataFrame(rng.normal(size=(200, 2000)))    # NOTHING is predictive
rand_y = pd.Series(rng.integers(0, 2, 200))

# WRONG: select on all the data, then cross-validate the survivors.
best = SelectKBest(f_classif, k=10).fit(noise, rand_y).get_support(indices=True)
leaky = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000),
                        noise.iloc[:, best], rand_y, cv=5).mean()

# RIGHT: selection inside the pipeline, re-run on every training fold.
honest = cross_val_score(
    Pipeline([("sel", SelectKBest(f_classif, k=10)),
              ("m", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))]),
    noise, rand_y, cv=5).mean()

print(f"\nPURE NOISE, true accuracy must be ~0.50")
print(f"  select-then-validate: {leaky:.3f}   <- leakage")
print(f"  selection in pipeline: {honest:.3f}  <- honest")
# With 2000 noise columns, 10 of them correlate with the label by chance in
# THIS sample. Selecting them using the labels you then score against is
# how a pipeline reports skill it does not have.

# --- REDUNDANCY: drop one of a near-duplicate pair. ---
corr = X.corr().abs()
upper = corr.where(np.triu(np.ones(corr.shape), k=1).astype(bool))
drop = [c for c in upper.columns if (upper[c] > 0.95).any()]
print(f"\nfeatures above 0.95 correlation with an earlier one: {drop}")
```

```text
  THE THREE FAMILIES

  family     how                    cost    interactions   ships with model
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  filter     score each feature     O(p)    NO             no
  wrapper    refit on subsets       O(p^2)  yes            no
  embedded   penalty or importance  O(1)    yes            YES

  WHY FILTERS MISS XOR

    a  b  y=a^b       marginal association of a with y: zero
    0  0  0           marginal association of b with y: zero
    0  1  1           joint: perfectly determined
    1  0  1
    1  1  0

  THE SELECTION LEAKAGE LOOP

    WRONG                                RIGHT
    select on all data                   for each fold:
        |                                    select on THIS fold's train
    split into folds                         fit on THIS fold's train
        |                                    score on THIS fold's test
    cross-validate                       average

    The wrong version lets the test labels choose the features, and
    reports ~0.70 accuracy on data with no signal whatsoever.

  IMPORTANCE: WHICH TO TRUST

    impurity      fast, biased to high-cardinality, computed on TRAIN
    permutation   slower, honest, computed on HELD-OUT data
    SHAP          per-row attributions, consistent, slowest
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Extra features cost accuracy through variance, instability, and the curse
>   of dimensionality, and they cost operationally through drift and
>   monitoring.
> - Filter methods are fast and evaluate features one at a time, so they
>   discard features that only matter jointly.
> - Embedded methods such as L1 penalties and tree importances are the best
>   default because selection is consistent with the model being fitted.
> - Impurity importance favours high-cardinality features; prefer permutation
>   importance measured on held-out data.
> - Selection is part of the model and must run inside cross-validation, or
>   you can report high accuracy on pure noise.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build an XOR dataset, show that mutual information for each feature is
>    near zero, and that a model using both predicts almost perfectly.
> 2. Add a pure-noise continuous column to a dataset and compare its impurity
>    importance rank with its permutation importance.
> 3. Reproduce the noise experiment: select the ten best of two thousand
>    random columns before and inside cross-validation, and report both
>    accuracies.
> 4. Interview: A stakeholder asks you to cut a 400-feature model to 20
>    without losing accuracy. What is your plan and what do you measure?
>    (Hint: which family of methods gives you both a ranking and a stopping
>    rule in one fit?)

#### Handling High-Cardinality Features

High cardinality means a categorical variable with very many distinct values:
postcodes, product SKUs, user IDs, IP addresses, merchant codes, URLs. They are
common, they often carry real signal, and every standard encoding handles them
badly. One-hot gives you an unusable number of columns. Ordinal invents an
order over ten thousand levels. Target encoding works and leaks if you are
careless.

The first question is diagnostic and frequently decides everything:
**is the identifier itself predictive, or is it a proxy for attributes you
could use directly?** A postcode predicts default risk because it proxies
income, density, and local economy. If you can obtain those attributes, use
them: they generalise to postcodes you have never seen, they are stable, and
they are explainable. The identifier only earns its place when the
entity-specific effect is real and irreducible.

The second question is about the **tail**. Cardinality distributions are
almost always extremely skewed: a few values cover most rows and thousands
appear once or twice. Those singletons cannot support an estimate of anything.
The standard moves:

- **Collapse the tail.** Keep values covering, say, 95% of rows or appearing at
  least `k` times, and map the rest to a single "rare" bucket. One threshold,
  fitted on training data, and most of the problem goes away.
- **Group semantically.** A postcode's first two characters are a region. A URL
  has a domain. A SKU has a category prefix. Hierarchical structure is usually
  present in the identifier itself and is far more stable than the leaf.
- **Encode with a statistic.** Frequency and smoothed out-of-fold target
  encoding, as covered above.
- **Hash.** Fixed width, no vocabulary, accepts collisions. The right choice
  when new values arrive continuously and you cannot refit a vocabulary.
- **Learn an embedding.** A dense vector per level, learned jointly with the
  model. This is what neural networks do with entity embeddings and it works
  well given enough rows per level. It is also how recommender systems handle
  millions of item IDs.
- **Use a model with native support.** LightGBM and CatBoost handle
  categorical columns internally, with CatBoost's ordered target statistics
  designed specifically for this problem.

The operational trap to plan for: **the category set changes**. Tomorrow
brings a new SKU. Your encoder must have a defined behaviour for it, the
fallback value must be sensible, and you should monitor the rate of unseen
values, because a spike in that rate is an early warning of upstream change
that no accuracy metric will show you until much later.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.feature_extraction import FeatureHasher
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier

rng = np.random.default_rng(13)
n = 6000
# A realistic skewed identifier: 3000 levels, most of them nearly unused.
weights = rng.dirichlet(np.full(3000, 0.25))
sku = rng.choice([f"SKU-{c:02d}-{i:04d}" for c in range(8)
                  for i in range(375)], n, p=weights)
df = pd.DataFrame({"sku": sku})
df["category"] = df["sku"].str.slice(4, 6)          # the hierarchy is IN the id
y = pd.Series((rng.random(n) < df["category"].map(
    dict(zip([f"{i:02d}" for i in range(8)], rng.beta(2, 6, 8))))).astype(int))

vc = df["sku"].value_counts()
print(f"{len(vc)} distinct SKUs in {n} rows")
print(f"rows covered by the top 100 SKUs: {vc.head(100).sum() / n:.1%}")
print(f"SKUs appearing once: {(vc == 1).sum()} "
      f"({(vc == 1).sum() / len(vc):.0%} of levels, "
      f"{vc[vc == 1].sum() / n:.1%} of rows)")

# --- THE ONE-HOT COST ---
print(f"\none-hot would produce {len(vc)} columns for {n} rows:"
      f" {len(vc) / n:.2f} columns per row")

# --- MOVE 1: COLLAPSE THE TAIL. One fitted threshold. ---
def fit_tail_collapse(s: pd.Series, min_count: int = 20):
    keep = set(s.value_counts()[lambda v: v >= min_count].index)
    return keep

def apply_tail_collapse(s: pd.Series, keep: set, other: str = "__other__"):
    return s.where(s.isin(keep), other)

tr_idx, te_idx = train_test_split(df.index, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)
keep = fit_tail_collapse(df.loc[tr_idx, "sku"], min_count=20)
df["sku_collapsed"] = apply_tail_collapse(df["sku"], keep)
other_share = (df["sku_collapsed"] == "__other__").mean()
print(f"\ncollapsed to {df['sku_collapsed'].nunique()} levels;"
      f" '__other__' covers {other_share:.1%} of rows")
# `keep` is a fitted parameter. Recomputing it on test data leaks and also
# makes train and test disagree about which levels exist.

# --- MOVE 2: SEMANTIC GROUPING. The identifier contains a hierarchy. ---
print(f"\nhierarchy from the id: {df['category'].nunique()} categories")
grouped_rate = y.groupby(df["category"]).agg(["mean", "size"])
print(grouped_rate.round(3).to_string())
print("this generalises to SKUs never seen, because the category is known")

# --- MOVE 3: STATISTICS. Frequency plus out-of-fold target encoding. ---
df["sku_freq"] = df["sku"].map(df["sku"].value_counts(normalize=True))

from sklearn.model_selection import KFold
def oof_te(keys, target, m=30.0, splits=5):
    out = pd.Series(np.nan, index=keys.index, dtype=float)
    for fit_i, app_i in KFold(splits, shuffle=True, random_state=0).split(keys):
        t, k = target.iloc[fit_i], keys.iloc[fit_i]
        prior = t.mean()
        st = t.groupby(k).agg(["sum", "count"])
        mp = (st["sum"] + m * prior) / (st["count"] + m)
        out.iloc[app_i] = keys.iloc[app_i].map(mp).fillna(prior).values
    return out

df["sku_te"] = oof_te(df["sku"], y)
print(f"\nout-of-fold target encoding: 1 column,"
      f" correlation {df['sku_te'].corr(y):+.3f}")

# --- MOVE 4: HASHING. Fixed width, no vocabulary, tolerates new values. ---
for width in (64, 256, 1024):
    H = FeatureHasher(n_features=width, input_type="string").transform(
        [[v] for v in df["sku"]])
    distinct = len(np.unique(H.toarray(), axis=0))
    print(f"hash to {width:5d} cols -> {distinct:5d} distinct patterns"
          f" of {len(vc)} levels ({1 - distinct/len(vc):.0%} collided)")
# Collisions merge unrelated levels. Wider is safer and costs more.

# --- MOVE 5: NATIVE CATEGORICAL SUPPORT ---
native = df[["sku_collapsed", "category"]].astype("category")
model = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(categorical_features="from_dtype",
                                       random_state=0, max_iter=120)
print("\nnative categorical handling, CV accuracy:",
      round(cross_val_score(model, native, y, cv=5).mean(), 3))

# --- COMPARE THE REPRESENTATIONS HONESTLY ---
import warnings; warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
options = {
    "category only (8 levels)": pd.get_dummies(df["category"]),
    "frequency only": df[["sku_freq"]],
    "collapsed one-hot": pd.get_dummies(df["sku_collapsed"]),
    "category + frequency": pd.concat(
        [pd.get_dummies(df["category"]), df[["sku_freq"]]], axis=1),
}
print("\nCV accuracy and width:")
for name, rep in options.items():
    s = cross_val_score(HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0, max_iter=80),
                        rep, y, cv=5).mean()
    print(f"  {name:26s} {rep.shape[1]:5d} cols   {s:.3f}")
# The 8-level hierarchy does most of the work. That is the common outcome:
# the identifier was a proxy, and the attribute it proxied is better.

# --- OPERATIONAL: monitor the unseen rate. ---
train_levels = set(df.loc[tr_idx, "sku"])
unseen_rate = (~df.loc[te_idx, "sku"].isin(train_levels)).mean()
print(f"\nunseen SKU rate on held-out data: {unseen_rate:.1%}")
print("track this in production; a jump means the upstream catalogue changed")
print("and it will move before any accuracy metric does.")
```

```text
  THE SKEW YOU WILL ALWAYS FIND

  rows
   |#
   |#
   |##
   |###
   |#####___________________________________________
   +--------------------------------------------------> levels, sorted
    top 100 levels: ~60% of rows     |  thousands of singletons: ~10% of rows
    estimable                        |  not estimable, ever

  STRATEGY BY SITUATION

  situation                              approach
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  the id proxies known attributes        use the attributes, drop the id
  the id has structure (prefix, domain)  extract the hierarchy
  moderate cardinality, enough rows      collapse tail + one-hot
  high cardinality, enough rows/level    out-of-fold target encoding
  new levels arrive constantly           hashing
  very many levels, deep model, big n    learned embedding
  gradient boosting available            native categorical support

  WIDTH COMPARISON, 10,000 LEVELS

    one-hot       10,000 columns
    hashing(512)      512 columns, with collisions
    binary             14 columns, uninterpretable
    frequency           1 column
    target              1 column, needs out-of-fold discipline
    embedding(16)      16 columns, learned

  ALWAYS: a defined fallback for unseen levels, and a monitor on their rate.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Ask first whether the identifier is predictive in itself or a proxy for
>   attributes you could use directly, because the attributes generalise to
>   unseen levels.
> - Cardinality distributions are heavily skewed, so collapsing the tail at a
>   fitted count threshold removes most of the problem.
> - Identifiers usually contain a hierarchy such as a region, domain, or
>   category prefix, and the coarser level is far more stable.
> - Hashing gives fixed width with no vocabulary and is the right answer when
>   new levels arrive continuously.
> - Define the fallback for unseen levels explicitly and monitor the unseen
>   rate, because it moves before accuracy does.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. For a high-cardinality column, report how many rows the top hundred
>    levels cover and what share of levels appear only once.
> 2. Collapse the tail at a threshold fitted on training data, then apply it
>    to a test split and confirm no new level appears.
> 3. Compare cross-validated accuracy for the raw identifier, an extracted
>    hierarchy, and a frequency encoding, with the column count for each.
> 4. Interview: A fraud model keys on merchant ID and performs well offline.
>    What is your main concern about deploying it? (Hint: what fraction of
>    tomorrow's merchants existed in your training window?)

#### Leakage Prevention

Data leakage is when information reaches the model that will not be available
at prediction time. It is the most damaging error in applied machine learning,
because its symptom is *success*. The model scores wonderfully, everyone is
pleased, it ships, and production performance is a fraction of what was
promised. Nothing about a leaked model looks wrong until it is live.

Leakage takes three forms, and it is worth being able to name them.

**Target leakage** happens when a feature contains the answer, often
indirectly. A hospital readmission model that uses "discharge medication
count" is fine; one that uses "days in the follow-up program" is not, because
enrolment happens after readmission. The classic tell is a feature that is
implausibly predictive on its own. If one column gets you 0.99 AUC, you have
not found a great feature, you have found the label.

**Train-test contamination** happens when the preprocessing that produced the
features saw the test rows. Every fitted transform is a channel: imputation
medians, scaler means, bin edges, target encodings, PCA components,
vectorizer vocabularies, feature selection. Fitting any of them on the full
dataset before splitting moves information across the boundary. This is by far
the most common form, and the fix is entirely mechanical: put every transform
in a pipeline and let cross-validation refit it per fold.

**Temporal leakage** happens when training data includes information from
after the prediction moment. A random split of time-ordered data lets the model
learn from a future it will not have. Aggregates computed over the full history
do the same thing more subtly. The fix is a time-based split plus a stated
as-of timestamp for every feature.

There is a fourth, easy to miss: **group leakage**. If one patient contributes
several visits, or one user several sessions, a random split puts the same
entity in both training and test. The model recognises the entity rather than
learning the pattern, and the score measures memorisation. Split by group.

A practical defence checklist, in the order that catches the most:

1. Split first. Do everything else after.
2. Wrap every fitted transform in a pipeline.
3. For each feature, write the timestamp at which its value is known. If you
   cannot, that is your answer.
4. Split by time for temporal problems and by group for repeated entities.
5. Be suspicious of any single feature with implausible standalone power.
6. Check feature-target correlations and investigate anything extreme.
7. Compare a model's validation score against a plausible ceiling. If a
   fraud model is at 0.999 AUC, something is wrong.
8. Keep a final holdout used once, at the end, to confirm the story.

The reason to internalise this list rather than trusting your instincts is
that leakage feels like competence while it is happening.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, f_classif
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import (cross_val_score, train_test_split,
                                     GroupKFold, TimeSeriesSplit)
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(21)
n = 1500

# --- FORM 1: TARGET LEAKAGE. A column that exists because of the label. ---
churned = rng.random(n) < 0.25
data = pd.DataFrame({
    "tenure": rng.integers(1, 60, n),
    "monthly_spend": rng.gamma(3, 20, n).round(2),
    # This field is populated by the retention team AFTER churn is known.
    "retention_call_made": np.where(churned, rng.random(n) < 0.9,
                                    rng.random(n) < 0.02).astype(int),
})
y = pd.Series(churned.astype(int))

honest_cols = ["tenure", "monthly_spend"]
print("AUC with an honest feature set:",
      round(cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000),
                            data[honest_cols], y, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean(), 3))
print("AUC including the post-outcome field:",
      round(cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000),
                            data, y, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean(), 3))

# THE DETECTOR: score each feature alone. An implausible single-feature AUC
# is the signature of a label in disguise.
print("\nsingle-feature AUC:")
for col in data.columns:
    print(f"  {col:22s} {roc_auc_score(y, data[col]):.3f}")
print("  anything above ~0.90 alone deserves an explanation, not celebration")

# --- FORM 2: TRAIN-TEST CONTAMINATION via a fitted transform. ---
noise = pd.DataFrame(rng.normal(size=(300, 3000)))
rand_y = pd.Series(rng.integers(0, 2, 300))

sel = SelectKBest(f_classif, k=15).fit(noise, rand_y)       # sees all labels
leaky = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000),
                        noise.iloc[:, sel.get_support(indices=True)],
                        rand_y, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean()
honest = cross_val_score(
    Pipeline([("sel", SelectKBest(f_classif, k=15)),
              ("m", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))]),
    noise, rand_y, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean()
print(f"\nPURE NOISE (true AUC = 0.500)")
print(f"  selection before CV: {leaky:.3f}")
print(f"  selection inside CV: {honest:.3f}")

# THE FIX IS STRUCTURAL: one pipeline holding every fitted step.
num = ["tenure", "monthly_spend"]
safe_pipeline = Pipeline([
    ("prep", ColumnTransformer([
        ("num", Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
                          ("sc", StandardScaler())]), num),
    ])),
    ("select", SelectKBest(f_classif, k=2)),
    ("model", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)),
])
print("\npipelined AUC on honest features:",
      round(cross_val_score(safe_pipeline, data[num], y, cv=5,
                            scoring="roc_auc").mean(), 3))
print("every fitted step above is refitted per fold, automatically")

# --- FORM 3: TEMPORAL LEAKAGE. A random split on ordered data. ---
dates = pd.date_range("2023-01-01", periods=n, freq="6h")
drift = np.linspace(0, 2.5, n)                     # the relationship changes
ts = pd.DataFrame({"x": rng.normal(size=n) + drift, "date": dates})
ts_y = pd.Series((rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(ts["x"] - drift)))).astype(int))

random_cv = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000), ts[["x"]],
                            ts_y, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean()
time_cv = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000), ts[["x"]], ts_y,
                          cv=TimeSeriesSplit(5), scoring="roc_auc").mean()
print(f"\nrandom 5-fold CV     {random_cv:.3f}   <- optimistic")
print(f"time-series split CV {time_cv:.3f}   <- what production looks like")
print("every random fold contains rows from after its own test rows")

# --- FORM 4: GROUP LEAKAGE. The same entity on both sides. ---
groups = rng.integers(0, 120, n)                  # 120 users, many rows each
user_effect = rng.normal(0, 2, 120)[groups]       # a strong per-user effect
gX = pd.DataFrame({"x": rng.normal(size=n) + user_effect})
gy = pd.Series((rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-user_effect))).astype(int))

naive = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000), gX, gy, cv=5,
                        scoring="roc_auc").mean()
grouped = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000), gX, gy,
                          cv=GroupKFold(5), groups=groups,
                          scoring="roc_auc").mean()
print(f"\nrandom CV  {naive:.3f}   grouped CV {grouped:.3f}")
print("the gap is memorised users, not learned behaviour")

# --- THE AS-OF AUDIT: write the availability time of every feature. ---
FEATURE_TIMING = pd.DataFrame([
    ("tenure",              "signup date",        "before prediction", "safe"),
    ("monthly_spend",       "billing, prior mo.",  "before prediction", "safe"),
    ("retention_call_made", "retention workflow",  "AFTER outcome",     "LEAK"),
    ("support_tickets_30d", "ticket system",       "before prediction", "safe"),
    ("cancellation_reason", "cancellation form",   "AFTER outcome",     "LEAK"),
], columns=["feature", "source", "available", "verdict"])
print("\n", FEATURE_TIMING.to_string(index=False))
# Producing this table is the single highest-value hour in any project.
# Every row you cannot fill in confidently is a row to investigate.

def audit_leakage(X: pd.DataFrame, y: pd.Series, auc_alarm: float = 0.90):
    """Flag any single feature whose standalone power is implausible."""
    flags = []
    for col in X.select_dtypes("number").columns:
        try:
            auc = roc_auc_score(y, X[col])
        except ValueError:
            continue
        auc = max(auc, 1 - auc)                    # direction does not matter
        if auc >= auc_alarm:
            flags.append((col, round(auc, 3)))
    return flags

print("\nautomated flag:", audit_leakage(data, y))
```

```text
  THE FOUR FORMS

  form              information crossing            fix
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  target            a feature caused by the label   audit feature provenance
  contamination     a transform fitted on all data  Pipeline + CV
  temporal          rows from after the prediction  TimeSeriesSplit, as-of
  group             same entity on both sides       GroupKFold

  EVERY FITTED TRANSFORM IS A CHANNEL

    imputation median      scaler mean/sd        bin edges
    target encoding map    PCA components        vectorizer vocabulary
    feature selection      outlier clip bounds   resampling (SMOTE)

    If it has a .fit(), it must be inside the pipeline.

  THE CORRECT ORDER

    raw data
       |
    SPLIT  <----------------- first, always
       |
       +-- train ---> fit transforms ---> fit model
       |                   |                  |
       +-- test  ----> apply the SAME --> score
                          fitted objects

  SMELL TEST

    one feature alone gives AUC > 0.95        -> it is the label
    validation >> test, gap grows with        -> leaky target encoding
      cardinality
    great offline, poor live, no code change  -> temporal or group leakage
    accuracy above the known human ceiling    -> stop and investigate
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Leakage's symptom is an excellent score, which is why it survives review
>   and fails in production.
> - Any object with a fit step is a leakage channel; putting every one inside
>   a pipeline closes the whole class mechanically.
> - Split by time for temporal problems and by group for repeated entities,
>   because a random split breaks both.
> - Write down when each feature's value becomes available relative to the
>   prediction moment; a feature you cannot place is a suspect.
> - Treat an implausibly strong single feature or a score above the known
>   ceiling as evidence of leakage rather than of success.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Construct a dataset with a feature populated after the outcome, then show
>    the cross-validated AUC with and without it.
> 2. Reproduce the noise experiment for feature selection and report both
>    scores, then explain to a non-specialist why the higher one is wrong.
> 3. Build panel data with a strong per-entity effect and compare random
>    k-fold against grouped k-fold scores.
> 4. Write the feature-availability audit table for a model you have built or
>    read about, marking each feature safe or leaking.
> 5. Interview: A colleague's model reaches 0.99 AUC on fraud detection.
>    Which three questions do you ask first? (Hint: when was each feature
>    written, how was the data split, and what did the preprocessing see?)

<a id="64-handling-imbalanced-and-skewed-data"></a>
### 6.4 Handling Imbalanced and Skewed Data

Real target variables are rarely balanced and real numeric variables are
rarely symmetric; this section covers how to diagnose both conditions, the
techniques that genuinely help, and the much larger set of techniques that
only appear to.

#### Class Imbalance Diagnosis

Fraud is 0.2% of transactions. Rare disease is 1% of patients. Click-through
is 3% of impressions. Imbalance is the normal state of any interesting binary
problem, and the first thing to understand is that imbalance itself is not
automatically a problem. Diagnosing whether it is a problem, and what kind,
comes before reaching for any technique.

The headline failure is that **accuracy stops meaning anything**. A classifier
that predicts "not fraud" for every transaction is 99.8% accurate and worth
nothing. This is easy to state and easy to fall for, because 99.8% reads as
excellent to anyone not looking closely.

The metrics that survive imbalance:

**Precision** is, of the cases you flagged, how many were real. It answers
"how much of my review team's time is wasted?" **Recall** is, of the real
cases, how many you caught. It answers "how much fraud got through?" These
trade off against each other and you cannot maximise both.

**F1** is their harmonic mean, useful as a single number and opaque about
which side it came from. Report precision and recall alongside it.

**ROC AUC** measures ranking quality across all thresholds. Its known weakness
under heavy imbalance is that the false positive rate has a huge denominator,
so thousands of false positives barely move it. A model can look strong by ROC
AUC and be unusable in practice.

**PR AUC**, the area under the precision-recall curve, uses precision instead
and therefore reflects the cost that actually hurts. Under heavy imbalance it
is the more informative summary, and note that its baseline is the positive
rate rather than 0.5.

The second insight is that **the real problem is often not the ratio but the
absolute count**. A thousand positives in a hundred thousand rows is a 1%
imbalance and enough data to learn from. Twenty positives in two thousand rows
is the same ratio and hopeless, because twenty examples cannot define a
decision boundary in any interesting feature space. Before resampling
anything, count the minority class in absolute terms. If it is small, you have
a data collection problem, and no technique will substitute.

The third insight is about **thresholds**. Most classifiers produce a
probability, and the 0.5 cutoff is a default, not a decision. Changing it
moves you along the precision-recall curve at no training cost. A great deal
of what people attempt with resampling is better achieved by picking a
threshold from the costs of the two error types, which is a business input, not
a modelling one.

Finally, decide whether you need **calibration**. If a downstream process uses
the probability itself, for example to compute expected loss, the probabilities
must mean what they say. Resampling deliberately breaks calibration by
changing the base rate, which is one of its least-discussed costs.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import (accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score,
                             f1_score, roc_auc_score, average_precision_score,
                             confusion_matrix, precision_recall_curve)

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=20000, n_features=20, n_informative=6,
                           weights=[0.995, 0.005], flip_y=0.01, random_state=0)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0,
                                      stratify=y)   # stratify, always
print(f"positives: {y.sum()} of {len(y)} ({y.mean():.3%})")
print(f"test set positives: {yte.sum()}")

# --- ACCURACY IS USELESS HERE ---
dummy = DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent").fit(Xtr, ytr)
print(f"\n'always negative' accuracy: {accuracy_score(yte, dummy.predict(Xte)):.4f}")
print(f"'always negative' recall:   {recall_score(yte, dummy.predict(Xte)):.4f}")

model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(Xtr, ytr)
proba = model.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]
pred = (proba >= 0.5).astype(int)

cm = confusion_matrix(yte, pred)
print("\nconfusion matrix at threshold 0.5:")
print(pd.DataFrame(cm, index=["actual neg", "actual pos"],
                   columns=["pred neg", "pred pos"]).to_string())

print("\nmetrics at 0.5:")
print(f"  accuracy   {accuracy_score(yte, pred):.4f}   <- looks great, means little")
print(f"  precision  {precision_score(yte, pred, zero_division=0):.4f}")
print(f"  recall     {recall_score(yte, pred, zero_division=0):.4f}")
print(f"  F1         {f1_score(yte, pred, zero_division=0):.4f}")
print(f"  ROC AUC    {roc_auc_score(yte, proba):.4f}   <- threshold-free ranking")
print(f"  PR AUC     {average_precision_score(yte, proba):.4f}"
      f"   <- baseline is {yte.mean():.4f}, not 0.5")

# --- WHY ROC AUC FLATTERS: the FPR denominator is enormous. ---
tn, fp, fn, tp = cm.ravel()
print(f"\n{fp} false positives out of {tn + fp} negatives"
      f" -> FPR {fp / (tn + fp):.4f}")
print("a reviewer sees those false positives; the ROC curve barely notices them")

# --- RATIO VS ABSOLUTE COUNT: the same imbalance, different problems. ---
print("\nsame 1% imbalance, different feasibility:")
for total in (2_000, 20_000, 200_000):
    print(f"  {total:>7,} rows -> {int(total * 0.01):>5,} positives"
          f"   {'too few to learn a boundary' if total * 0.01 < 100 else 'workable'}")

# --- THRESHOLD SELECTION: free movement along the curve. ---
prec, rec, thr = precision_recall_curve(yte, proba)
print("\nthreshold sweep:")
for t in (0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.30, 0.50):
    p = (proba >= t).astype(int)
    print(f"  t={t:<5} precision {precision_score(yte, p, zero_division=0):.3f}"
          f"  recall {recall_score(yte, p, zero_division=0):.3f}"
          f"  flagged {p.sum():>5}")
# No retraining happened. The whole curve was already available.

# --- COST-OPTIMAL THRESHOLD: a business input, not a default. ---
COST_FN, COST_FP = 500.0, 10.0       # missed fraud vs a wasted review
grid = np.linspace(0.001, 0.6, 300)
costs = [(t, COST_FN * ((yte == 1) & (proba < t)).sum()
             + COST_FP * ((yte == 0) & (proba >= t)).sum()) for t in grid]
best_t, best_c = min(costs, key=lambda kv: kv[1])
cost_at_half = dict(costs).get(min(grid, key=lambda t: abs(t - 0.5)))
print(f"\ncost-minimising threshold {best_t:.3f} at cost {best_c:,.0f}")
print(f"cost at the default 0.5:  {cost_at_half:,.0f}")
print("the ratio of the two error costs sets the threshold, nothing else")

# --- F-BETA when one error matters more, without full cost numbers. ---
from sklearn.metrics import fbeta_score
for beta, meaning in [(0.5, "precision matters more"), (2.0, "recall matters more")]:
    scores = [(t, fbeta_score(yte, (proba >= t).astype(int), beta=beta,
                              zero_division=0)) for t in grid]
    t_best = max(scores, key=lambda kv: kv[1])[0]
    print(f"F{beta} ({meaning:24s}) peaks at threshold {t_best:.3f}")

# --- STRATIFY EVERY SPLIT, or folds may contain no positives at all. ---
skf = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
counts = [ytr[te_i].sum() for _, te_i in skf.split(Xtr, ytr)]
print(f"\npositives per stratified fold: {counts}")
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold
plain = [ytr[te_i].sum() for _, te_i in KFold(5, shuffle=True,
                                              random_state=3).split(Xtr)]
print(f"positives per unstratified fold: {plain}  <- unstable, sometimes zero")

# --- CALIBRATION: does the probability mean what it says? ---
from sklearn.calibration import calibration_curve
frac_pos, mean_pred = calibration_curve(yte, proba, n_bins=5, strategy="quantile")
print("\ncalibration (predicted vs observed):")
for mp, fp_ in zip(mean_pred, frac_pos):
    print(f"  predicted {mp:.4f}  observed {fp_:.4f}")
# If a downstream process multiplies this probability by a loss amount, these
# two columns must agree. Resampling will make them disagree.
```

```text
  WHY ACCURACY FAILS

  20,000 rows, 100 positives (0.5%)

  always-negative classifier
                pred neg   pred pos
  actual neg    19,900     0            accuracy  = 19,900/20,000 = 99.5%
  actual pos       100     0            recall    = 0
                                        precision = undefined
  A model with zero value scores 99.5%.

  ROC AUC VS PR AUC UNDER IMBALANCE

    FPR = FP / (FP + TN)     denominator ~ 19,900   -> 200 FPs move it by 0.01
    precision = TP / (TP+FP) denominator ~ flagged  -> 200 FPs halve it

    ROC AUC answers "does it rank well?"
    PR AUC answers  "is the flagged list usable?"

  DIAGNOSE BEFORE TREATING

    minority count < ~100          -> data collection problem, not a modelling one
    metric is accuracy             -> change the metric, not the data
    threshold is still 0.5         -> tune the threshold first, it is free
    probabilities feed a decision  -> preserve calibration, avoid resampling
    ranking is all you need        -> imbalance may not need any treatment
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Accuracy is meaningless under imbalance; use precision, recall, and the
>   area under the precision-recall curve, whose baseline is the positive rate.
> - ROC AUC flatters imbalanced models because the false positive rate has an
>   enormous denominator.
> - The absolute count of minority examples matters more than the ratio; too
>   few positives is a data problem no technique solves.
> - Threshold tuning moves you along the precision-recall curve for free and
>   often replaces the need for resampling.
> - Stratify every split, and remember that resampling breaks calibration if a
>   downstream process uses the probabilities.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a dataset with a 1% positive rate, fit a majority-class classifier,
>    and report its accuracy, precision, and recall.
> 2. Sweep the decision threshold and tabulate precision, recall, and the
>    number of flagged cases at five thresholds.
> 3. Given a cost of 500 for a false negative and 10 for a false positive,
>    compute the cost-minimising threshold and compare its cost with the
>    default.
> 4. Interview: A model reports 0.93 ROC AUC on a 0.3% positive rate and the
>    review team says the alerts are useless. Reconcile the two.
>    (Hint: compute precision at the operating threshold and count the false
>    positives a reviewer actually sees.)

#### Resampling Techniques

Resampling changes the class ratio in the training data, either by discarding
majority examples or by duplicating minority ones. It is the first thing most
people try and it is less often the right answer than its popularity suggests,
so it is worth being precise about what it does and does not fix.

**Random undersampling** discards majority rows until the ratio improves. It
is fast, it shrinks the dataset so training gets cheaper, and it throws away
real data. With a large majority class that redundancy may be genuinely
wasteful and undersampling costs little; with a small dataset it discards
information you cannot afford to lose.

**Random oversampling** duplicates minority rows. No information is lost and no
information is gained. Exact duplicates give the model repeated identical
points, which invites memorising them, and for a model that can fit arbitrarily
complex boundaries this is a direct route to overfitting.

**Informed undersampling** is more interesting than the random kind. Tomek
links remove majority points that form a nearest-neighbour pair with a minority
point, cleaning the boundary. Edited nearest neighbours removes majority points
whose neighbours disagree with them. Cluster centroids replaces the majority
class with a smaller set of cluster centres, keeping coverage of the feature
space while reducing count. These aim to remove the *least useful* majority
points rather than arbitrary ones.

**Combined approaches** oversample the minority and then clean the boundary,
which is where SMOTE plus Tomek links or SMOTE plus edited nearest neighbours
come from.

Three rules govern correct use, and violating any of them invalidates your
evaluation.

**Resample only the training data.** The test set must keep the real class
distribution, because that is the distribution production has. Resampling
before splitting puts duplicated or synthesised minority points on both sides
and produces a meaningless score. This is the most common mistake.

**Resample inside the cross-validation loop.** The resampler is a fitted step,
so each fold must resample only its own training portion. Use a pipeline that
understands resampling, such as `imblearn`'s, because a plain scikit-learn
pipeline applies its steps to the test fold as well.

**Expect probabilities to become miscalibrated.** By changing the base rate you
have changed what the model's output means. If you need calibrated
probabilities, either recalibrate on unresampled data afterwards or prefer
class weighting, which leaves the data alone.

A last point that deserves more attention than it gets: **before resampling,
try class weights and threshold tuning.** They are cheaper, they do not distort
the data, they preserve calibration better, and in a great many cases they
perform as well or better. Resampling is worth reaching for when the minority
class is genuinely tiny, when the model has no class-weight option, or when an
experiment shows it wins.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from collections import Counter
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, StratifiedKFold, cross_validate
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score, roc_auc_score, brier_score_loss
from imblearn.under_sampling import (RandomUnderSampler, TomekLinks,
                                     EditedNearestNeighbours, ClusterCentroids)
from imblearn.over_sampling import RandomOverSampler
from imblearn.pipeline import Pipeline as ImbPipeline

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=6000, n_features=15, n_informative=5,
                           weights=[0.97, 0.03], flip_y=0.02, random_state=0)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0,
                                      stratify=y)
print("train distribution:", Counter(ytr), " test distribution:", Counter(yte))

# --- WHAT EACH RESAMPLER DOES TO THE TRAINING SET ---
samplers = {
    "random under": RandomUnderSampler(random_state=0),
    "random over": RandomOverSampler(random_state=0),
    "Tomek links": TomekLinks(),
    "edited NN": EditedNearestNeighbours(),
    "cluster centroids": ClusterCentroids(random_state=0),
}
rows = []
for name, s in samplers.items():
    Xr, yr = s.fit_resample(Xtr, ytr)
    c = Counter(yr)
    rows.append({"sampler": name, "rows": len(yr), "negatives": c[0],
                 "positives": c[1], "ratio": round(c[1] / c[0], 3)})
print("\n", pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))
# Note random under discards thousands of real rows; random over adds no new
# information; Tomek and ENN barely change the ratio and clean the boundary.

# Random oversampling creates exact duplicates, which is its whole problem.
Xo, yo = RandomOverSampler(random_state=0).fit_resample(Xtr, ytr)
minority = Xo[yo == 1]
uniq = len(np.unique(minority, axis=0))
print(f"\noversampled minority: {len(minority)} rows, {uniq} distinct"
      f" -> each real point repeated ~{len(minority)/uniq:.1f} times")

# --- THE FATAL MISTAKE: resampling before the split. ---
Xall, yall = RandomOverSampler(random_state=0).fit_resample(X, y)
Xa_tr, Xa_te, ya_tr, ya_te = train_test_split(Xall, yall, test_size=0.3,
                                              random_state=0, stratify=yall)
wrong = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=120, random_state=0).fit(Xa_tr, ya_tr)
print(f"\nresample-then-split PR AUC: "
      f"{average_precision_score(ya_te, wrong.predict_proba(Xa_te)[:, 1]):.3f}"
      "   <- meaningless")

right = ImbPipeline([("res", RandomOverSampler(random_state=0)),
                     ("m", RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=120, random_state=0))
                     ]).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print(f"split-then-resample PR AUC: "
      f"{average_precision_score(yte, right.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]):.3f}"
      "   <- honest")
print("the first number is inflated because duplicated minority rows appear")
print("in BOTH the training and the test halves.")

# --- RESAMPLE INSIDE THE CV LOOP, never outside it. ---
cv = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
configs = {
    "baseline (nothing)": ImbPipeline([
        ("m", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000))]),
    "class_weight balanced": ImbPipeline([
        ("m", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, class_weight="balanced"))]),
    "random undersample": ImbPipeline([
        ("res", RandomUnderSampler(random_state=0)),
        ("m", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000))]),
    "random oversample": ImbPipeline([
        ("res", RandomOverSampler(random_state=0)),
        ("m", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000))]),
    "Tomek cleaning": ImbPipeline([
        ("res", TomekLinks()),
        ("m", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000))]),
}
print("\ncross-validated on the TRAINING set (test distribution untouched):")
for name, pipe in configs.items():
    res = cross_validate(pipe, Xtr, ytr, cv=cv,
                         scoring=["average_precision", "roc_auc"])
    print(f"  {name:24s} PR AUC {res['test_average_precision'].mean():.3f}"
          f"   ROC AUC {res['test_roc_auc'].mean():.3f}")
# The baseline is often competitive. Measure before assuming resampling helps.

# --- CALIBRATION COST: resampling changes what the output means. ---
plain = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(Xtr, ytr)
over = ImbPipeline([("res", RandomOverSampler(random_state=0)),
                    ("m", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000))]).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print(f"\ntrue positive rate in test: {yte.mean():.4f}")
for name, m in [("no resampling", plain), ("oversampled", over)]:
    p = m.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]
    print(f"  {name:15s} mean predicted {p.mean():.4f}"
          f"   Brier {brier_score_loss(yte, p):.5f}")
# The oversampled model's mean prediction tracks the RESAMPLED base rate,
# not the real one. Any expected-value calculation using it is wrong.

# Recalibrating on unresampled data repairs it, at the cost of a holdout.
from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV
recal = CalibratedClassifierCV(over, method="isotonic", cv=3).fit(Xtr, ytr)
pr = recal.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]
print(f"  recalibrated    mean predicted {pr.mean():.4f}"
      f"   Brier {brier_score_loss(yte, pr):.5f}")

# --- UNDERSAMPLING WITH AN ENSEMBLE: keep the data, not the imbalance. ---
from imblearn.ensemble import BalancedBaggingClassifier
bag = BalancedBaggingClassifier(
    estimator=RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=30, random_state=0),
    n_estimators=8, sampling_strategy="auto", random_state=0).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print(f"\nbalanced bagging PR AUC: "
      f"{average_precision_score(yte, bag.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]):.3f}")
print("each base learner sees a different balanced subsample, so across the")
print("ensemble no majority row is permanently discarded.")
```

```text
  WHAT RESAMPLING ACTUALLY DOES

  original          undersampled         oversampled
  N N N N N N N N   N N N               N N N N N N N N
  N N N N N N N N   N N                 N N N N N N N N
  P                 P                   P P P P P P P P     <- P duplicated
                                        P P P P P P P P

  information lost: none | majority rows | none
  information gained:      none          | NONE
  overfitting risk:        lower (less data) | HIGHER (repeated points)
  calibration:             preserved      broken (base rate changed)

  THE ORDER THAT MATTERS

    WRONG                              RIGHT
    resample                           split
       |                                  |
    split  <- duplicates land on both   resample TRAIN only
       |       sides of the split          |
    score (inflated)                   score on untouched test

  TRY IN THIS ORDER

    1. change the metric        (free, and often the whole problem)
    2. tune the threshold       (free, no retraining)
    3. class weights            (one parameter, keeps all data)
    4. resample                 (distorts data, breaks calibration)
    5. collect more positives   (best, slowest)
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Undersampling discards real data and oversampling adds no information, so
>   neither creates signal that was not there.
> - Resample only the training portion, inside the cross-validation loop, using
>   a pipeline that leaves test folds untouched.
> - Resampling before splitting puts duplicated minority rows on both sides and
>   produces a meaningless score.
> - Informed undersampling such as Tomek links or edited nearest neighbours
>   cleans the boundary instead of discarding rows arbitrarily.
> - Try metric choice, threshold tuning, and class weights before resampling,
>   and expect to recalibrate if you resample anyway.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Resample an imbalanced dataset before and after splitting, and report the
>    gap between the two held-out precision-recall scores.
> 2. Compare cross-validated PR AUC for a baseline, class weighting, random
>    undersampling, and random oversampling on the same data.
> 3. Show that oversampling shifts the mean predicted probability away from the
>    true positive rate, then repair it with calibration.
> 4. Interview: Your teammate reports that oversampling lifted accuracy from
>    0.97 to 0.99. What do you check? (Hint: where in the workflow did the
>    resampling happen, and which metric would have revealed nothing?)

#### SMOTE and Synthetic Data

Random oversampling duplicates existing minority points, which gives a model
the same information repeated. **SMOTE**, the Synthetic Minority
Over-sampling Technique, tries to do better by manufacturing new points
instead. The idea is simple and geometric: take a minority point, pick one of
its k nearest minority neighbours, and place a new point at a random position
on the line segment between them.

The intuition is that the space between two examples of the same class is
probably also that class, so filling it in gives the model a denser region to
learn a boundary around rather than a handful of isolated points to memorise.

That intuition is also exactly where SMOTE fails, and the failure modes are
worth knowing precisely because SMOTE is applied reflexively.

**It interpolates across gaps.** If the minority class forms two separate
clusters, the segment between a point in one cluster and a point in the other
passes through majority territory, and SMOTE will happily put synthetic
minority points there. The model then learns a boundary around a region that
contains no real minority examples at all.

**It amplifies noise.** A mislabelled minority point deep inside the majority
region becomes the seed for a line of synthetic points reaching further into
that region. One bad label becomes many.

**It struggles with categorical features.** The midpoint of "red" and "blue" is
not a colour. SMOTE-NC handles this by interpolating numeric features and
taking the most common category among neighbours, which is a workable
compromise rather than a solution.

**It degrades in high dimensions.** Nearest neighbours become unreliable as
dimensionality grows, so "the line between a point and its neighbour" becomes a
less meaningful place to sample from. In very sparse high-dimensional spaces,
such as text features, SMOTE is usually not appropriate.

The variants address specific weaknesses. **Borderline-SMOTE** only synthesises
from minority points near the boundary, where the extra density is most useful.
**ADASYN** generates more points for minority examples in harder
neighbourhoods. **SMOTE-Tomek** and **SMOTE-ENN** synthesise and then clean up
the resulting boundary. **SVM-SMOTE** uses support vectors to choose seeds.

The honest empirical picture is that SMOTE helps sometimes, does nothing
sometimes, and hurts sometimes, and which of those happens is not reliably
predictable from the dataset's description. Several careful studies have found
that on tabular problems with strong modern classifiers, SMOTE rarely beats
simple class weighting. So the guidance is: treat it as one candidate among
several, evaluate it honestly on a test set with the real class distribution,
and do not assume it because the class ratio is skewed.

Beyond SMOTE there is a broader category of **synthetic data generation**:
generative adversarial networks, variational autoencoders, and copula or
Bayesian-network models that learn the joint distribution and sample from it.
These matter more for privacy-preserving data sharing than for imbalance, and
they carry the same fundamental caveat, in a stronger form. A generator can
only reproduce structure it learned from real data. It cannot add information,
and it can leak the training examples it memorised.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from collections import Counter
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, StratifiedKFold, cross_validate
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score
from imblearn.over_sampling import SMOTE, BorderlineSMOTE, ADASYN, SMOTENC
from imblearn.combine import SMOTETomek, SMOTEENN
from imblearn.pipeline import Pipeline as ImbPipeline

# --- SMOTE FROM SCRATCH: the whole algorithm is five lines. ---
def smote_manual(Xmin: np.ndarray, n_new: int, k: int = 5, seed: int = 0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    nn = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=min(k + 1, len(Xmin))).fit(Xmin)
    _, idx = nn.kneighbors(Xmin)
    out = np.empty((n_new, Xmin.shape[1]))
    for i in range(n_new):
        a = rng.integers(len(Xmin))                    # a real minority point
        b = idx[a][rng.integers(1, idx.shape[1])]      # one of its neighbours
        lam = rng.random()                             # position on the segment
        out[i] = Xmin[a] + lam * (Xmin[b] - Xmin[a])
    return out

real = np.array([[1.0, 1.0], [1.0, 2.0], [2.0, 1.5], [8.0, 8.0]])
fake = smote_manual(real, 6, k=3)
print("real minority points:\n", real)
print("\nsynthesised points:\n", np.round(fake, 2))
print("\nsome lie on the segment toward the isolated point at (8, 8),")
print("which may be majority territory or a mislabelled row.")

# --- FAILURE MODE 1: interpolating across a gap between clusters. ---
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
cluster_a = rng.normal([0, 0], 0.4, (20, 2))
cluster_b = rng.normal([10, 10], 0.4, (20, 2))
two_clusters = np.vstack([cluster_a, cluster_b])
synth = smote_manual(two_clusters, 300, k=5, seed=1)
midzone = ((synth[:, 0] > 3) & (synth[:, 0] < 7)).sum()
print(f"\nsynthetic points landing in the empty corridor between clusters:"
      f" {midzone} of 300 ({midzone/300:.0%})")
print("no real minority example lives there, and the majority class does")

# --- FAILURE MODE 2: one mislabelled point becomes a line of them. ---
mostly_tight = np.vstack([rng.normal([0, 0], 0.3, (30, 2)), [[9.0, 9.0]]])
noisy = smote_manual(mostly_tight, 400, k=5, seed=2)
far = (np.linalg.norm(noisy, axis=1) > 3).sum()
print(f"\nwith ONE mislabelled point, {far} of 400 synthetic points"
      f" ({far/400:.0%}) reach toward it")

# --- FAILURE MODE 3: categorical features have no midpoint. ---
mixed = pd.DataFrame({"age": [25.0, 60.0], "colour_code": [0.0, 2.0]})
print("\nnaive interpolation of a categorical code:")
print(f"  midpoint of red(0) and blue(2) is {mixed['colour_code'].mean():.1f}"
      " = green, a category neither point had")
# SMOTENC interpolates the numeric columns and votes on the categorical ones.

# --- COMPARE THE VARIANTS HONESTLY, on real class distributions. ---
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=5000, n_features=18, n_informative=6,
                           n_clusters_per_class=3, weights=[0.96, 0.04],
                           flip_y=0.03, random_state=1)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0,
                                      stratify=y)
print(f"\ntrain {Counter(ytr)}   test {Counter(yte)} (untouched)")

candidates = {
    "baseline": None,
    "class_weight balanced": "weight",
    "SMOTE": SMOTE(random_state=0, k_neighbors=5),
    "Borderline-SMOTE": BorderlineSMOTE(random_state=0),
    "ADASYN": ADASYN(random_state=0),
    "SMOTE + Tomek": SMOTETomek(random_state=0),
    "SMOTE + ENN": SMOTEENN(random_state=0),
}
cv = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
print("\ncross-validated PR AUC (resampling inside each fold):")
for name, sampler in candidates.items():
    if sampler == "weight":
        pipe = ImbPipeline([("m", RandomForestClassifier(
            n_estimators=150, class_weight="balanced_subsample", random_state=0))])
    elif sampler is None:
        pipe = ImbPipeline([("m", RandomForestClassifier(
            n_estimators=150, random_state=0))])
    else:
        pipe = ImbPipeline([("res", sampler),
                            ("m", RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=150,
                                                         random_state=0))])
    s = cross_validate(pipe, Xtr, ytr, cv=cv, scoring="average_precision")
    print(f"  {name:24s} {s['test_average_precision'].mean():.3f}"
          f"  +/- {s['test_average_precision'].std():.3f}")
# Read the standard deviations. Differences smaller than the spread are not
# results. Class weighting frequently matches or beats every SMOTE variant.

# --- MIXED TYPES: SMOTENC ---
Xm = pd.DataFrame(X[:, :4], columns=["n1", "n2", "n3", "n4"])
Xm["cat"] = pd.Series(np.where(X[:, 4] > 0, "A", "B"))
nc = SMOTENC(categorical_features=[4], random_state=0)
Xr, yr = nc.fit_resample(Xm, y)
print(f"\nSMOTENC output categories: {sorted(Xr['cat'].unique())}"
      "  <- no invented category")

# --- THE PIPELINE POSITION IS NOT OPTIONAL ---
print("\nWRONG: SMOTE(...).fit_resample(X, y) then train_test_split")
print("RIGHT: ImbPipeline([('res', SMOTE()), ('m', model)]) inside CV")
wrong_X, wrong_y = SMOTE(random_state=0).fit_resample(X, y)
a, b, c, d = train_test_split(wrong_X, wrong_y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0,
                              stratify=wrong_y)
m = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=120, random_state=0).fit(a, c)
print(f"  resample-then-split PR AUC "
      f"{average_precision_score(d, m.predict_proba(b)[:, 1]):.3f} (inflated)")
# Synthetic points derived from a training row can land in the test half,
# which is a near-duplicate of something the model has already seen.
```

```text
  HOW SMOTE PLACES A POINT

    minority point a ----------o--------- neighbour b
                          new point at a + lam*(b-a), lam ~ U(0,1)

  WHEN THAT IS SENSIBLE           WHEN IT IS NOT

    P P P                          P P                    P P
    P P P   dense cluster,         P P   <-- corridor --> P P
    P P P   interior is            N N N N N N N N N N N N
            plausibly P            the segment crosses majority territory

  NOISE AMPLIFICATION

    before:  P P P P               N N N [P] N N N     one mislabelled P
    after:   P P P P  p p p p p p p p p [P] N N N      a bridge of synthetic
                                                       points into the N region

  VARIANT SELECTION

  variant            seeds from                     use when
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------
  SMOTE              all minority points            default attempt
  Borderline-SMOTE   minority points near the edge   boundary is the problem
  ADASYN             harder neighbourhoods           density varies a lot
  SVM-SMOTE          support vectors                 SVM-shaped problems
  SMOTE-Tomek/ENN    synthesise, then clean          noisy labels
  SMOTENC            mixed numeric + categorical     any real tabular data

  THE BOTTOM LINE
    SMOTE cannot create information. It redistributes the information in the
    minority points you already have. Compare it against class weighting and
    let the held-out score decide.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - SMOTE interpolates between a minority point and one of its neighbours,
>   which densifies the minority region instead of duplicating points.
> - When the minority class has separate clusters, interpolation places
>   synthetic points in majority territory.
> - A single mislabelled minority point seeds a whole line of synthetic points
>   reaching into the majority region.
> - Categorical features have no midpoint and high dimensions make nearest
>   neighbours unreliable, so SMOTE-NC and caution are required.
> - SMOTE creates no new information and frequently fails to beat class
>   weighting, so benchmark it rather than assuming it.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement SMOTE in under ten lines and use it on a minority class made of
>    two well-separated clusters, then count how many synthetic points fall in
>    the empty corridor.
> 2. Add one mislabelled minority point deep in majority territory and measure
>    how many synthetic points reach toward it.
> 3. Benchmark baseline, class weighting, SMOTE, and Borderline-SMOTE with
>    cross-validated PR AUC, reporting standard deviations, and state whether
>    any difference exceeds the noise.
> 4. Interview: When would you actively avoid SMOTE? (Hint: think about the
>    feature types, the dimensionality, and whether anything downstream
>    consumes the predicted probability.)

#### Class Weighting

Class weighting attacks imbalance from the loss function rather than the data.
Instead of changing how many minority examples exist, you change how much each
one costs to get wrong. Misclassifying a minority example incurs a larger
penalty, so the optimiser stops finding it acceptable to ignore the whole
class.

This is usually the right first thing to try, and the reasons are worth
listing because they are all practical rather than theoretical. You keep every
row of data. You add no duplicated or synthesised points, so nothing is
invented. Training time does not increase. Calibration is distorted less than
by resampling. And it is one parameter, which means it is trivial to include in
a hyperparameter search alongside everything else.

The mechanics are straightforward. The loss for each example is multiplied by
