that slicing enough ways will always produce an extreme slice, which is the
multiple comparisons problem from the previous topic.

**Cohort analysis** groups users by *when they started* and follows each group
over time. It answers "is the product getting better?", and it is the tool that
separates two things an aggregate metric confuses: changes in behaviour, and
changes in the mix of users.

That distinction is the whole reason cohort analysis exists, and it is worth
spelling out. Suppose total retention is flat month over month. Two very
different worlds produce that number. In one, every cohort retains identically,
and nothing is changing. In the other, newer cohorts retain much better while
the shrinking older cohorts retain worse, and the two effects cancel. The
aggregate is identical; the businesses are not. Only a cohort view distinguishes
them.

The analogy is a school's average test score. If it is flat year over year, you
cannot tell whether teaching is unchanged, or whether teaching improved while
the intake got weaker. Following each entering class separately answers it.

The standard construction is a **cohort table**: rows are the cohort, usually
the signup month, columns are the periods since signup, and cells hold the
retained fraction. Reading it has two directions and both matter. Reading
**across a row** shows how one cohort decays, and the shape of that decay is a
property of the product. Reading **down a column** compares cohorts at the same
age, which is the only fair comparison and the one that shows whether things are
improving.

Three practical cautions.

**The triangle is not missing data.** Recent cohorts have not existed long
enough to have a period-12 number. The empty cells are unmeasured, not zero, and
averaging down a column while ignoring that the cell counts differ produces a
number that drifts for purely structural reasons.

**Small cohorts are noisy.** A cohort of forty users produces retention
percentages that jump around by several points for no reason. Show the counts
next to the rates, or your reader will interpret noise as trend.

**Define the event precisely.** Retention depends entirely on what counts as
active, and whether periods are calendar months or rolling 30-day windows from
each user's own signup date. Those two choices produce materially different
tables, and mixing them across analyses is a common source of numbers that do
not reconcile.

Beyond retention, the same structure supports revenue cohorts, which reveal
whether newer customers are worth more, and **survival analysis**, which handles
the censoring properly when you care about time-to-event rather than a fixed
checkpoint.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)

# --- BUILD A SYNTHETIC EVENT LOG WITH IMPROVING COHORTS ---
signup_months = pd.period_range("2024-01", "2024-08", freq="M")
records = []
for i, m in enumerate(signup_months):
    n_users = [500, 520, 600, 640, 700, 900, 1100, 1200][i]
    # Later cohorts retain better: the product is genuinely improving.
    base_retention = 0.55 + 0.025 * i
    for u in range(n_users):
        uid = f"{m}-{u}"
        records.append({"user": uid, "cohort": m, "period": 0})
        alive = True
        for p in range(1, 9):
            if m + p > signup_months[-1]:       # the future has not happened
                break
            # Monthly survival decays with age, improves with cohort.
            p_survive = base_retention * np.exp(-0.12 * (p - 1))
            alive = alive and (rng.random() < p_survive)
            if alive:
                records.append({"user": uid, "cohort": m, "period": p})
log = pd.DataFrame(records)

# --- THE COHORT TABLE ---
sizes = log[log["period"] == 0].groupby("cohort")["user"].nunique()
counts = log.pivot_table(index="cohort", columns="period",
                         values="user", aggfunc="nunique")
rates = counts.div(sizes, axis=0) * 100

print("cohort sizes:\n", sizes.to_string())
print("\nretention %, rows = cohort, columns = months since signup:")
print(rates.round(1).to_string())
print("\nNaN cells are UNMEASURED, not zero: those months have not happened.")

# --- READ IT TWO WAYS ---
print("\nACROSS a row (cohort 2024-01 decaying over its own lifetime):")
print(rates.loc[signup_months[0]].dropna().round(1).to_string())

print("\nDOWN column 3 (every cohort at the same age -- the FAIR comparison):")
col = pd.DataFrame({"retention_m3": rates[3].round(1), "cohort_size": sizes})
print(col.dropna().to_string())
print("month-3 retention is rising across cohorts: the product is improving.")

# --- WHY THE AGGREGATE HIDES THIS ---
# The blended 'active users / total users' number mixes cohorts of every age.
active_by_month = {}
for m in signup_months:
    total = alive = 0
    for c in signup_months:
        if c > m:
            continue
        age = (m - c).n
        if age in counts.columns and not pd.isna(counts.loc[c, age]):
            alive += counts.loc[c, age]
            total += sizes[c]
    active_by_month[str(m)] = 100 * alive / total
blended = pd.Series(active_by_month).round(1)
print("\nblended retention across all cohorts:\n", blended.to_string())
print("\nThis single series moves for two reasons at once: real changes in")
print("behaviour, and a changing mix of cohort ages. It cannot separate them.")

# --- THE CANCELLATION CASE: flat aggregate, two opposite trends. ---
demo = pd.DataFrame({
    "cohort": ["old"] * 3 + ["new"] * 3,
    "period": [1, 2, 3] * 2,
    "retention": [60, 50, 42, 75, 66, 58],       # new cohorts clearly better
    "users": [8000, 8000, 8000, 1000, 1000, 1000],  # but old dominates volume
})
weighted = (demo.assign(w=demo["retention"] * demo["users"])
                .groupby("period").apply(
                    lambda g: g["w"].sum() / g["users"].sum(),
                    include_groups=False))
print("\nper-cohort retention:\n",
      demo.pivot(index="cohort", columns="period",
                 values="retention").to_string())
print("\nsize-weighted blend:\n", weighted.round(1).to_string())
print("The blend tracks the large old cohort and understates the improvement.")

# --- SEGMENTATION: where does a problem live, and is the slice trustworthy? ---
users = pd.DataFrame({
    "plan": rng.choice(["free", "pro", "enterprise"], 3000, p=[.7, .25, .05]),
    "device": rng.choice(["ios", "android", "web"], 3000),
})
p_churn = {"free": .30, "pro": .12, "enterprise": .05}
users["churned"] = [rng.random() < p_churn[p] for p in users["plan"]]

def segment_report(df, dim, outcome, min_n=100):
    g = df.groupby(dim)[outcome].agg(n="size", rate="mean")
    overall = df[outcome].mean()
    g["rate"] = (g["rate"] * 100).round(1)
    g["lift_vs_overall"] = (g["rate"] - overall * 100).round(1)
    # A standard error on a proportion, so the reader sees the noise floor.
    g["std_err_pts"] = (100 * np.sqrt(
        (g["rate"]/100) * (1 - g["rate"]/100) / g["n"])).round(2)
    g["trustworthy"] = g["n"] >= min_n
    return g.sort_values("rate", ascending=False)

print("\nchurn by plan:\n", segment_report(users, "plan", "churned").to_string())
print("\nchurn by device (no real effect -- note the gaps sit within ~2 SE):")
print(segment_report(users, "device", "churned").to_string())
# Printing the standard error next to the rate is what stops a reader from
# reading a 1.5-point noise gap as a finding.

# --- CROSS-SEGMENT: where slicing gets dangerous. ---
cross = (users.groupby(["plan", "device"])["churned"]
              .agg(n="size", rate="mean"))
cross["rate"] = (cross["rate"] * 100).round(1)
print(f"\n{len(cross)} cells from two dimensions;"
      f" {(cross['n'] < 100).sum()} of them have n < 100")
print(cross.to_string())
print("\nThe most extreme cell in a grid of small cells is almost always")
print("noise. Require a minimum n before reporting a cell at all.")
```

```text
  THE COHORT TABLE AND ITS TWO READINGS

                   months since signup
  cohort    n     0     1     2     3     4     5
  2024-01  500  100   55.2  48.1  42.0  37.4  33.1   --> READ ACROSS:
  2024-02  520  100   57.9  50.4  44.6  39.8   .          one cohort's decay
  2024-03  600  100   60.1  53.0  47.2   .     .          (a product property)
  2024-04  640  100   62.8  55.6   .    .     .
  2024-05  700  100   65.0   .    .     .     .
  2024-06  900  100    .     .    .     .     .
                       |
                       v
                  READ DOWN: every cohort at the SAME age.
                  The only fair comparison, and the one that
                  answers "are we getting better?"

  The empty triangle is UNMEASURED time, not churn and not zero.

  WHAT THE BLENDED NUMBER CANNOT TELL YOU

  aggregate retention: 52%, 52%, 52%   <- flat, three months running

  world A                          world B
  every cohort retains 52%         new cohorts 75%, old cohorts 40%,
  nothing is changing              and the mix shifts to cancel out
                                   the product is improving fast
  Identical aggregate. Only the cohort table separates them.

  SEGMENT VS COHORT

             segmentation                cohort analysis
  splits by  an attribute (plan, geo)    a start date
  answers    where is the problem now?   are we improving over time?
  risk       multiple comparisons        misreading the empty triangle
  guardrail  minimum n + standard error  show cohort sizes beside rates
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Segmentation finds where a problem lives right now; cohort analysis shows
>   whether the product is improving over time.
> - A flat aggregate metric is consistent with both "nothing is changing" and
>   "behaviour improved while the mix shifted", and only a cohort view
>   separates them.
> - Read a cohort table across a row for one cohort's decay and down a column
>   to compare cohorts at the same age, which is the only fair comparison.
> - The empty triangle is unmeasured time rather than zero, so never average a
>   column without accounting for which cohorts are present.
> - Show cohort sizes and a standard error beside every rate, because the most
>   extreme small segment is almost always noise.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a cohort retention table from an event log with signup dates, and
>    print the cohort sizes next to it.
> 2. Construct a case where per-cohort retention improves every month while
>    the size-weighted blended metric stays flat or falls.
> 3. Write a segment report that outputs the rate, the row count, and the
>    standard error per level, and use it to argue that one apparent gap is
>    noise.
> 4. Cross two segmentation dimensions and count how many resulting cells fall
>    below a minimum sample size you consider reportable.
> 5. Interview: Monthly active users are flat for six months and leadership
>    concludes the product has stalled. Which two views would you build first,
>    and what could each reveal? (Hint: one separates new from returning
>    users, the other follows each signup month separately.)

<a id="72-visualization-principles"></a>
### 7.2 Visualization Principles

A chart is a claim about data that the reader will believe, which makes chart
design a correctness concern rather than a matter of taste; this section covers
the grammar that generates charts, the rules for choosing among them, and the
specific constructions that mislead.

#### Grammar of Graphics

Most people learn charts as a catalogue: here is a bar chart, here is a scatter
plot, here is a pie chart, pick one. That model breaks down as soon as you need
something the catalogue does not contain, and it gives you no way to reason
about why one chart works and another does not.

The **grammar of graphics** replaces the catalogue with a small set of
components that combine. Leland Wilkinson formalised it in 1999 and Hadley
Wickham's ggplot2 made it the dominant mental model; Vega-Lite, plotnine, and
Altair all implement it. The insight is that a chart is not a type, it is a
**mapping from data columns to visual properties**, plus a choice of geometry.

The components:

**Data** is the tidy table you start from, one row per observation. The grammar
assumes tidy input, which is why chapter 6's tidy-data discipline pays off here.

**Aesthetic mappings** connect columns to visual properties: x position, y
position, colour, size, shape, opacity. This is the heart of the grammar. You do
not "colour the bars blue", you map the `region` column to the colour channel,
and the library derives the legend, the scale, and the assignment.

**Geometries** are the marks that represent each row: point, line, bar, area,
text, tile. Changing only the geometry turns a scatter plot into a line chart,
which reveals that these are not different kinds of chart so much as different
marks over the same mapping.

**Statistical transformations** are computations the chart performs before
drawing: binning for a histogram, counting for a bar chart of frequencies,
smoothing for a trend line, computing quartiles for a box plot. Recognising that
a histogram is "bar geometry plus a binning stat" is what makes the grammar
generative.

**Scales** control how data values become visual values: the axis range, whether
it is linear or logarithmic, which colours a categorical variable receives.

**Coordinate systems** position the marks. Cartesian is the default; flipping it
gives horizontal bars; polar coordinates turn a stacked bar into a pie chart,
which is a genuinely useful thing to understand, because it explains why pie
charts are hard to read: they encode with angle instead of length.

**Facets** split the data into panels by a variable, producing small multiples.

The payoff is composability. A histogram, a density plot, a box plot, and a
violin plot are all the same data with different stats and geometries. Once you
think this way you stop looking for the right chart type in a list and start
asking which channels your variables should map to.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")                     # headless: render to file, not screen
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "month": pd.date_range("2024-01-01", periods=24, freq="MS").tolist() * 2,
    "region": ["north"] * 24 + ["south"] * 24,
})
df["revenue"] = (100 + np.arange(48) % 24 * 4
                 + np.where(df["region"] == "north", 30, 0)
                 + rng.normal(0, 8, 48)).round(1)

# --- THE SAME MAPPING, THREE GEOMETRIES ---
# Only the mark changes. The data, the aesthetics, and the scales are fixed.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 3.2), sharey=True)
north = df[df["region"] == "north"]
for ax, geom in zip(axes, ["point", "line", "bar"]):
    if geom == "point":
        ax.scatter(north["month"], north["revenue"], s=18, color="#2a78d6")
    elif geom == "line":
        ax.plot(north["month"], north["revenue"], lw=2, color="#2a78d6")
    else:
        ax.bar(north["month"], north["revenue"], width=20, color="#2a78d6")
    ax.set_title(f"geom = {geom}", loc="left", fontsize=10)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
fig.savefig("/tmp/claude-0/geoms.png", dpi=110, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)

# --- AESTHETIC MAPPING: colour is a MAPPING, not a decoration. ---
# Wrong mental model: "make the north line blue".
# Right mental model: map `region` -> colour; the legend follows automatically.
PALETTE = {"north": "#2a78d6", "south": "#eb6834"}    # fixed, per entity

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.4))
for region, g in df.groupby("region"):
    ax.plot(g["month"], g["revenue"], lw=2, color=PALETTE[region], label=region)
    # Direct-label the endpoint so identity is not colour-alone.
    last = g.iloc[-1]
    ax.annotate(region, (last["month"], last["revenue"]),
                xytext=(6, 0), textcoords="offset points",
                color=PALETTE[region], fontsize=9, va="center")
ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper left", fontsize=9)
ax.set_ylabel("revenue")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(axis="y", lw=0.5, color="#e6e6e4")            # hairline, solid, recessive
ax.set_axisbelow(True)
fig.savefig("/tmp/claude-0/mapping.png", dpi=110, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)

# --- STATISTICAL TRANSFORMATIONS: four charts, one column. ---
# Each is "a stat + a geom". This is what makes the grammar generative.
values = rng.lognormal(3.2, 0.5, 900)
recipes = {
    "histogram":   "stat=bin,      geom=bar",
    "density":     "stat=kde,      geom=area",
    "box plot":    "stat=quantile, geom=box",
    "violin":      "stat=kde,      geom=violin (mirrored)",
    "ECDF":        "stat=ecdf,     geom=step",
}
for name, recipe in recipes.items():
    print(f"  {name:11s} = {recipe}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(13, 3))
axes[0].hist(values, bins=30, color="#2a78d6")
axes[0].set_title("bin + bar", loc="left", fontsize=10)
from scipy.stats import gaussian_kde
grid = np.linspace(values.min(), values.max(), 200)
axes[1].fill_between(grid, gaussian_kde(values)(grid), color="#2a78d6", alpha=0.25)
axes[1].plot(grid, gaussian_kde(values)(grid), color="#2a78d6", lw=2)
axes[1].set_title("kde + area", loc="left", fontsize=10)
axes[2].boxplot(values, vert=True, widths=0.4)
axes[2].set_title("quantile + box", loc="left", fontsize=10)
xs = np.sort(values)
axes[3].step(xs, np.arange(1, len(xs) + 1) / len(xs), color="#2a78d6", lw=2)
axes[3].set_title("ecdf + step", loc="left", fontsize=10)
for ax in axes:
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
fig.savefig("/tmp/claude-0/stats.png", dpi=110, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)

# --- COORDINATE SYSTEMS: a pie chart IS a stacked bar in polar coordinates. ---
parts = pd.Series({"a": 40, "b": 30, "c": 18, "d": 12})
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.2))
left = 0
for i, (k, v) in enumerate(parts.items()):
    axes[0].barh([0], [v], left=left, height=0.4,
                 color=["#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a", "#eda100"][i],
                 edgecolor="white", linewidth=2)   # 2px surface gap, not a border
    left += v
axes[0].set_title("cartesian: stacked bar (length)", loc="left", fontsize=10)
axes[0].set_yticks([])
axes[1].pie(parts.values, labels=parts.index,
            colors=["#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a", "#eda100"],
            wedgeprops={"edgecolor": "white", "linewidth": 2})
axes[1].set_title("polar: the same bar (angle)", loc="left", fontsize=10)
fig.savefig("/tmp/claude-0/coords.png", dpi=110, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)
print("\nSame data, same stat, same geom -- only the coordinate system differs.")
print("The pie encodes with ANGLE, which people judge far worse than LENGTH,")
print("which is the whole reason to prefer the bar.")

# --- FACETS: split into panels by a variable. ---
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3), sharey=True)
for ax, (region, g) in zip(axes, df.groupby("region")):
    ax.plot(g["month"], g["revenue"], lw=2, color=PALETTE[region])
    ax.set_title(region, loc="left", fontsize=10)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
fig.savefig("/tmp/claude-0/facets.png", dpi=110, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)

# --- THE SAME CHART, DECLARED GRAMMATICALLY (plotnine / ggplot2 syntax) ---
print("""
  ggplot2 / plotnine, where the grammar is explicit:

    (ggplot(df, aes(x="month", y="revenue", color="region"))
     + geom_line(size=1)
     + geom_smooth(method="lm", se=False)    # a second layer, same mapping
     + scale_y_continuous(limits=(0, None))  # a bar-safe zero baseline
     + facet_wrap("~region")                 # small multiples
     + labs(title="Revenue by region", y="Revenue (USD)"))

  Read it as: data + mapping + geometry + scale + facet. Adding a layer or
  swapping a geom is a one-line change, because nothing about the mapping
  was baked into the chart type.
""")
```

```text
  THE SEVEN COMPONENTS

    DATA           a tidy table, one row per observation
      |
    AESTHETICS     column -> channel   (x, y, colour, size, shape, alpha)
      |
    STATISTICS     a computation before drawing (bin, count, smooth, quantile)
      |
    GEOMETRY       the mark (point, line, bar, area, tile, text)
      |
    SCALES         data value -> visual value (range, log, palette)
      |
    COORDINATES    cartesian, flipped, polar
      |
    FACETS         split into panels by a variable
      |
      v
    the chart

  ONE COLUMN, FIVE CHARTS -- ONLY stat AND geom CHANGE

    stat=bin      + geom=bar     -> histogram
    stat=kde      + geom=area    -> density plot
    stat=quantile + geom=box     -> box plot
    stat=kde      + geom=violin  -> violin plot
    stat=ecdf     + geom=step    -> ECDF

  WHY THE PIE CHART IS HARD TO READ

    stacked bar  = stat=identity, geom=bar, coord=cartesian  -> LENGTH
    pie chart    = stat=identity, geom=bar, coord=POLAR      -> ANGLE

    Same numbers. Length is judged accurately; angle is not.
    The grammar makes the pie's weakness a property of one component.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A chart is a mapping from columns to visual channels plus a geometry, not
>   an entry in a catalogue of chart types.
> - Aesthetic mappings mean you map a column to colour rather than colouring a
>   mark, which is what makes legends and scales derive automatically.
> - A histogram, density plot, box plot, and violin plot are the same column
>   under different statistical transformations and geometries.
> - A pie chart is a stacked bar in polar coordinates, which is exactly why it
>   encodes with angle and reads worse than a bar.
> - The grammar assumes tidy input, so the reshaping discipline from the
>   previous chapter is a prerequisite.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Take one numeric column and produce a histogram, a density plot, a box
>    plot, and an ECDF, labelling each with its stat and geom.
> 2. Build the same line chart twice, once by hard-coding colours per series
>    and once by mapping a column to colour, and describe what the second
>    version gives you for free.
> 3. Render the same part-to-whole data as a stacked bar and as a pie, then ask
>    someone to rank the segments from each and compare their accuracy.
> 4. Interview: A stakeholder asks for "a chart showing revenue by region over
>    time, split by product line". Decompose the request into grammar
>    components. (Hint: four variables, and you have x, y, colour, and facet
>    available.)

#### Choosing the Right Chart Type

The most common charting mistake is not an ugly chart, it is a chart that
answers a different question than the reader has. Choosing well starts from one
question: **what does the reader need to do with this data?** The job determines
the form, and the form determines the encoding.

Before picking a chart, ask whether you need one at all. A single current value
is a **stat tile**, a number with a label and maybe a delta, and a one-bar bar
chart is a worse version of it. A handful of headline numbers is a row of stat
tiles. The number a report leads with is a **hero figure**, set large. More than
about seven meaningful classes is usually a **table**, possibly beside a chart,
because past that point adjacent colours blur and the chart stops functioning.

When a chart is right, map the job to the form:

| The reader must | Default form | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Compare magnitudes | bar or column | length from a shared baseline is read precisely |
| See a trend over time | line | connection implies ordered continuity |
| See a distribution | histogram, ECDF, violin | shape is the subject |
| Compare distributions | box or violin per group | compact, sortable |
| See a relationship | scatter, hexbin if dense | two positions at once |
| See part of a whole | stacked bar | length, not angle |
| See an ordered share | diverging stacked bar | centred on the neutral point |
| Compare before and after | dumbbell or slope chart | two points, one connection |
| See a value on a grid | heatmap | many cells, sequential colour |
| See a value on a map | choropleth or symbol map | geography is the question |
| Notice one series | emphasis: highlight one, gray the rest | the story is one line |

A few rules behind the table are worth stating, because they resolve most real
decisions.

**Bars need a zero baseline; lines do not.** A bar encodes value as length from
the axis, so truncating the axis lies about the ratio between bars. A line
encodes change through slope, so a truncated axis is legitimate and often
necessary to see the variation at all. This is the single most useful asymmetry
in charting.

**Never use a dual axis.** Two y-scales on one plot invent a relationship,
because the alignment of the two scales is arbitrary: slide one and the series
appear to cross wherever you like. The honest alternatives are two charts
stacked, small multiples, or indexing both series to 100 at a common starting
point so they share one axis.

**Emphasis is the most underused form.** When the story is "this one segment
moved", colouring eight series in eight hues buries it. One series in an accent
colour with the rest in gray is usually the honest answer to "make this chart
clearer".

**Horizontal bars for long labels and many categories.** Rotated text is hard
to read and there is more vertical room on a page than horizontal. Sort bars by
value unless the categories have an inherent order such as time or size tiers.

**Pie charts are acceptable only for part-to-whole at a glance with few
segments.** For comparing close values, use a bar or just print the numbers.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

BLUE, ORANGE, GRAY, INK = "#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#c9c9c5", "#0b0b0b"

# --- IS IT EVEN A CHART? A single value is a stat tile, not a bar. ---
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 2.6))
axes[0].bar(["conversion"], [3.4], width=0.3, color=BLUE)
axes[0].set_title("one-bar bar chart (wrong)", loc="left", fontsize=10)
axes[0].set_ylim(0, 5)
axes[1].axis("off")
axes[1].text(0, .62, "3.4%", fontsize=38, color=INK, va="center")   # hero figure
axes[1].text(0, .28, "Conversion rate", fontsize=10, color="#52514e")
axes[1].text(0, .10, "+0.5 pts vs last month", fontsize=9, color="#008300")
axes[1].set_title("stat tile (right)", loc="left", fontsize=10)
fig.savefig("/tmp/claude-0/stat_tile.png", dpi=110, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)

# --- THE BASELINE ASYMMETRY: bars must start at zero, lines need not. ---
cats = ["A", "B", "C", "D"]
vals = [102, 105, 100, 108]
months = pd.date_range("2024-01-01", periods=12, freq="MS")
series = 100 + np.cumsum(np.random.default_rng(1).normal(0.4, 1.2, 12))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(14, 3))
axes[0].bar(cats, vals, color=BLUE, width=0.55)
axes[0].set_ylim(0, 120)
axes[0].set_title("bar, zero baseline: HONEST", loc="left", fontsize=9)

axes[1].bar(cats, vals, color=ORANGE, width=0.55)
axes[1].set_ylim(98, 110)          # D now looks ~4x B. It is 3% larger.
axes[1].set_title("bar, truncated: LIES", loc="left", fontsize=9)

axes[2].plot(months, series, lw=2, color=BLUE)
axes[2].set_ylim(0, series.max() * 1.1)
axes[2].set_title("line, zero baseline: hides the trend", loc="left", fontsize=9)

axes[3].plot(months, series, lw=2, color=BLUE)
axes[3].set_title("line, fitted range: FINE", loc="left", fontsize=9)
for ax in axes:
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
fig.savefig("/tmp/claude-0/baseline.png", dpi=110, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)

print("bar D is 8% above bar C, and the truncated panel makes it look 4x.")
print("A bar encodes LENGTH from the axis; a line encodes SLOPE. Hence the")
print("asymmetry: zero is mandatory for bars and optional for lines.")

# --- NEVER A DUAL AXIS. Index to a common base instead. ---
users = np.array([12, 14, 15, 18, 21, 24, 26, 29, 31, 34, 36, 39]) * 1000
sessions = np.array([190, 250, 230, 300, 360, 420,
                     390, 470, 520, 560, 600, 640]) * 1000

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 3.2))
ax1 = axes[0]
ax2 = ax1.twinx()                                  # the anti-pattern
ax1.plot(months, users, color=BLUE, lw=2)
ax2.plot(months, sessions, color=ORANGE, lw=2)
ax1.set_title("dual axis: WRONG", loc="left", fontsize=9)
# Slide the right-hand scale and the crossing point moves anywhere you want.
ax2.set_ylim(0, sessions.max() * 2.4)

axes[1].plot(months, users / users[0] * 100, color=BLUE, lw=2, label="users")
axes[1].plot(months, sessions / sessions[0] * 100, color=ORANGE, lw=2,
             label="sessions")
axes[1].axhline(100, lw=0.8, color="#c9c9c5")
axes[1].set_title("indexed to 100: one axis, honest", loc="left", fontsize=9)
axes[1].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9)

axes[2].plot(months, sessions / users, color=BLUE, lw=2)
axes[2].set_title("the ratio, if that IS the question", loc="left", fontsize=9)
for ax in axes:
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
fig.savefig("/tmp/claude-0/dual_axis.png", dpi=110, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)

# --- EMPHASIS BEATS EIGHT HUES WHEN THE STORY IS ONE SERIES ---
rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
many = pd.DataFrame(
    {f"region_{i}": 100 + np.cumsum(rng.normal(0.2, 1.1, 12)) for i in range(7)},
    index=months)
many["region_hero"] = 100 + np.cumsum(rng.normal(1.6, 1.1, 12))   # the story

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.4), sharey=True)
for i, col in enumerate(many.columns):
    axes[0].plot(many.index, many[col], lw=2, label=col)
axes[0].set_title("8 categorical hues: the story is buried", loc="left", fontsize=9)
axes[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=6, ncol=2)

for col in many.columns:
    is_hero = col == "region_hero"
    axes[1].plot(many.index, many[col], lw=2 if is_hero else 1.4,
                 color=BLUE if is_hero else GRAY, zorder=3 if is_hero else 1)
axes[1].annotate("region_hero", (many.index[-1], many["region_hero"].iloc[-1]),
                 xytext=(-78, 6), textcoords="offset points",
                 color=BLUE, fontsize=9, fontweight="bold")
axes[1].set_title("emphasis: one accent, rest gray", loc="left", fontsize=9)
for ax in axes:
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
fig.savefig("/tmp/claude-0/emphasis.png", dpi=110, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)

# --- HORIZONTAL AND SORTED for long labels and many categories ---
labels = ["Enterprise self-serve", "Mid-market direct", "SMB partner channel",
          "Consumer mobile app", "Education licensing", "Government contracts"]
amounts = [412, 388, 265, 190, 96, 74]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.4))
axes[0].bar(labels, amounts, color=BLUE, width=0.6)
axes[0].tick_params(axis="x", rotation=45, labelsize=7)
axes[0].set_title("vertical, rotated labels: hard to read", loc="left", fontsize=9)
order = np.argsort(amounts)                            # ascending -> biggest on top
axes[1].barh([labels[i] for i in order], [amounts[i] for i in order],
             color=BLUE, height=0.6)
axes[1].tick_params(labelsize=8)
axes[1].set_title("horizontal and sorted: readable", loc="left", fontsize=9)
for ax in axes:
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
fig.savefig("/tmp/claude-0/horizontal.png", dpi=110, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)

# --- A DECISION FUNCTION, to make the reasoning explicit ---
def suggest_form(n_values: int, x_type: str, n_series: int,
                 story: str = "compare") -> str:
    if n_values == 1:
        return "stat tile or hero figure (never a one-bar chart)"
    if story == "one_series_moved":
        return "emphasis: accent the one series, gray the rest"
    if x_type == "time":
        extra = " (or small multiples above 5 series)" if n_series > 5 else ""
        return "line" + extra
    if x_type == "numeric":
        dense = " -> hexbin or 2-D histogram if dense" if n_values > 5000 else ""
        return "scatter" + dense
    if x_type == "categorical":
        if n_series > 1:
            return "grouped bar (few series) or stacked bar (part-to-whole)"
        if n_values > 12:
            return "horizontal bar, sorted by value"
        return "bar, sorted by value, zero baseline"
    return "table"

for case in [(1, "none", 1, "compare"), (48, "time", 8, "one_series_moved"),
             (40000, "numeric", 1, "compare"), (25, "categorical", 1, "compare"),
             (12, "time", 3, "compare")]:
    print(f"  {str(case):32s} -> {suggest_form(*case)}")
```

```text
  THE JOB DECIDES THE FORM

  job                        form                     encoding channel
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  one current value          stat tile / hero number  text
  a few headline numbers     KPI row of stat tiles    text
  compare magnitudes         bar (horizontal if long) length from baseline
  trend over time            line                     position + slope
  one series is the point    emphasis (1 hue + gray)  position + salience
  distribution shape         histogram / ECDF         position + area
  compare distributions      box / violin per group   position
  relationship               scatter (hexbin if dense) two positions
  part-to-whole              stacked bar              length
  ordered share (Likert)     diverging stacked bar    length from centre
  value on a grid            heatmap                  sequential colour
  more than ~7 classes       a table                  text

  THE BASELINE RULE

  BAR: encodes LENGTH            LINE: encodes SLOPE
   108|    #  <- looks 4x B       truncating is FINE, and often required
   105| #  #                      to see the variation at all
   102|#   #
      +------- truncated at 98    zero-baselining a line chart flattens
      A B C D                     the trend into a useless straight line
  Truncating a bar axis lies about the RATIO. Zero is mandatory.

  DUAL AXIS: WHY IT IS ALWAYS WRONG

    users     0 -> 40k   on the left
    sessions  0 -> 800k  on the right
    The crossing point is set by YOUR choice of the two ranges, not by the
    data. Slide one scale and the story reverses. Fixes: two charts, small
    multiples, or index both to 100 at t0 on ONE axis.

  SERIES-COUNT LADDER (categorical colour)

    1-3    colour alone is comfortable; direct-label
    4      direct labels become mandatory
    5-6    soft cap: legend or small multiples
    7-8    ceiling; past it fold the tail into "Other" or facet
    9+     never generate another hue -- it is indistinguishable under CVD
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Ask what the reader must do with the data, and whether a stat tile, hero
>   number, or table serves better than any chart.
> - Bars encode length so they require a zero baseline; lines encode slope so a
>   truncated axis is legitimate.
> - Dual-axis charts invent a relationship because the alignment of the two
>   scales is arbitrary; index both series to a common base instead.
> - When one series is the story, emphasis with a single accent and gray
>   context beats eight categorical hues.
> - Use horizontal sorted bars for long labels and many categories, and stop
>   adding hues past about eight series.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Render the same four-category data as a zero-baselined bar chart and a
>    truncated one, and state the ratio a reader would infer from each.
> 2. Take two series of very different scale, build the dual-axis version, then
>    rebuild it indexed to 100 and explain what the first version implied.
> 3. Convert an eight-series line chart into an emphasis chart and note how
>    many colours you needed.
> 4. Write a function mapping value count, x-axis type, series count, and story
>    to a recommended chart form, and test it on five real requests.
> 5. Interview: A manager asks you to "make the difference clearer" in a bar
>    chart where the bars are 102 and 108. What do you do? (Hint: what is the
>    honest way to show a 6% difference, and what would truncating the axis
>    imply?)

#### Encoding Data with Visual Channels

A chart works by converting numbers into visual properties, and human vision
reads some of those properties far more accurately than others. That ranking is
not a style preference, it is a measured perceptual fact, and knowing it turns
chart design into an ordering problem: put your most important variable on your
most accurate channel.

The foundational work is Cleveland and McGill's 1984 experiments, which asked
people to judge magnitudes from different encodings and measured the errors. The
resulting ranking, from most to least accurate for quantitative data:

1. **Position along a common scale.** Two bars on the same axis, two points in
   the same scatter. This is by a wide margin the most accurate channel.
2. **Position along identical non-aligned scales.** The same variable in two
   panels of a small-multiple grid.
3. **Length.** A bar not sharing a baseline with the one you compare it to, such
   as segments inside different stacked bars.
4. **Angle and slope.** Pie wedges, line steepness.
5. **Area.** Bubble sizes, treemap rectangles.
6. **Volume.** Three-dimensional representations.
7. **Colour saturation and lightness.** Heatmap intensity, choropleth shading.
8. **Colour hue.** Which category something is.

Two consequences follow directly.

**Use position for what matters most.** If the reader's main question is "which
is bigger", put that variable on an axis. This is why bars beat pies: the pie
moves the comparison from position and length down to angle.

**Area is judged poorly, and the error is systematic.** People underestimate
area differences. A circle with twice the radius has four times the area and is
usually read as roughly twice as large. This means bubble charts communicate
only coarse differences, and it means any chart sizing marks by value must scale
by **area, not radius**, or it exaggerates by the square.

The channels also differ in type suitability, which is a separate question from
accuracy. Hue is poor for magnitude and excellent for identity, because hues
have no natural order: nobody thinks green is more than purple. Lightness has a
natural order, which is exactly why sequential colour scales vary lightness
rather than hue. Shape carries identity for a handful of categories and no
magnitude at all.

A final rule that removes a surprising amount of clutter: **do not encode the
same variable twice.** Colouring bars darker where they are taller adds no
information, because bar length already showed it, and it spends the colour
channel, which was the one channel still free to carry something else. Reserve
each channel for one variable.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

BLUE, ORANGE, GRAY = "#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#c9c9c5"
values = np.array([28.0, 34.0, 31.0, 40.0, 36.0])
labels = list("ABCDE")

# --- THE SAME FIVE NUMBERS ON FIVE CHANNELS, best to worst ---
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(15, 2.9))

axes[0].bar(labels, values, color=BLUE, width=0.6)     # POSITION + LENGTH
axes[0].set_ylim(0, 45)
axes[0].set_title("1. position, common scale", loc="left", fontsize=9)

# LENGTH without a shared baseline: segments inside separate stacks.
offsets = np.array([0, 12, 5, 18, 9])
axes[1].bar(labels, values, bottom=offsets, color=BLUE, width=0.6)
axes[1].set_title("3. length, no shared baseline", loc="left", fontsize=9)

axes[2].pie(values, labels=labels, wedgeprops={"edgecolor": "white",
                                               "linewidth": 2})
axes[2].set_title("4. angle", loc="left", fontsize=9)

# AREA: the sizes must be proportional to VALUE, so radius ~ sqrt(value).
axes[3].scatter(range(5), [0] * 5, s=values * 40, color=BLUE)  # s IS area
axes[3].set_xticks(range(5), labels)
axes[3].set_yticks([])
axes[3].set_title("5. area", loc="left", fontsize=9)

axes[4].imshow(values.reshape(1, -1), cmap="Blues", aspect="auto")
axes[4].set_xticks(range(5), labels)
axes[4].set_yticks([])
axes[4].set_title("7. colour lightness", loc="left", fontsize=9)

for ax in axes[:2]:
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
fig.savefig("/tmp/claude-0/channels.png", dpi=110, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)
print("Rank A..E from each panel. Accuracy falls sharply left to right,")
print("and the underlying numbers never changed.")

# --- THE AREA TRAP: scaling radius by value exaggerates by the square. ---
a, b = 10.0, 20.0                       # b is exactly twice a
r_wrong = np.array([a, b])              # radius proportional to value
r_right = np.sqrt(np.array([a, b]))     # AREA proportional to value
print(f"\nvalue ratio                     {b/a:.1f}x")
print(f"area ratio, radius ~ value     {(r_wrong[1]/r_wrong[0])**2:.1f}x"
      "   <- looks 4x bigger")
print(f"area ratio, radius ~ sqrt(value) {(r_right[1]/r_right[0])**2:.1f}x"
      "   <- correct")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 2.8))
for ax, radii, title in [(axes[0], r_wrong, "radius ~ value (WRONG)"),
                         (axes[1], r_right * 4.5, "area ~ value (right)")]:
    ax.scatter([0, 1], [0, 0], s=(radii * 30) ** 2 / 30, color=BLUE)
    ax.set_title(title, loc="left", fontsize=9)
    ax.set_xlim(-.6, 1.8); ax.set_ylim(-1, 1); ax.axis("off")
fig.savefig("/tmp/claude-0/area_trap.png", dpi=110, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)
print("\nmatplotlib's `s` parameter is already an AREA in points squared,")
print("which is why passing the raw value is correct there and passing a")
print("radius is the bug. Check the convention in whatever library you use.")

# --- CHANNEL SUITABILITY BY DATA TYPE ---
suitability = pd.DataFrame([
    ("position",   "excellent", "excellent", "excellent", "unlimited"),
    ("length",     "excellent", "good",      "poor",      "unlimited"),
    ("angle",      "fair",      "fair",      "poor",      "unlimited"),
    ("area",       "fair",      "fair",      "poor",      "unlimited"),
    ("lightness",  "good",      "excellent", "poor",      "~7 bins"),
    ("hue",        "poor",      "poor",      "excellent", "5-8 levels"),
    ("shape",      "none",      "none",      "good",      "4-5 levels"),
    ("texture",    "none",      "fair",      "good",      "3-4 levels"),
], columns=["channel", "quantitative", "ordinal", "nominal", "capacity"])
print("\n", suitability.to_string(index=False))

# --- DO NOT DOUBLE-ENCODE: one variable, one channel. ---
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3))
import matplotlib.cm as cm
norm = plt.Normalize(values.min(), values.max())
axes[0].bar(labels, values, color=cm.Blues(norm(values)), width=0.6)
axes[0].set_title("value on BOTH length and colour (wasteful)",
                  loc="left", fontsize=9)
axes[0].set_ylim(0, 45)

# The colour channel is now free to carry a SECOND variable.
is_new = [False, True, False, True, False]
axes[1].bar(labels, values, width=0.6,
            color=[ORANGE if n else BLUE for n in is_new])
axes[1].set_title("length = value, colour = launched this year",
                  loc="left", fontsize=9)
axes[1].set_ylim(0, 45)
handles = [plt.Rectangle((0, 0), 1, 1, color=c) for c in (BLUE, ORANGE)]
axes[1].legend(handles, ["existing", "new"], frameon=False, fontsize=8)
for ax in axes:
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
fig.savefig("/tmp/claude-0/double_encode.png", dpi=110, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)

# --- CHANNEL BUDGET: how many variables can one chart carry honestly? ---
print("""
  A SCATTER PLOT'S CHANNEL BUDGET

    x            variable 1   continuous, precise
    y            variable 2   continuous, precise
    colour hue   variable 3   nominal, <= 5-7 levels
    size (area)  variable 4   continuous, COARSE differences only
    shape        variable 5   nominal, <= 4-5 levels
    facet        variable 6   nominal, 10-20 panels

  Six is the theoretical ceiling and four is the practical one. Past that,
  facet: position comparison across panels beats a fifth channel inside one.
""")
```

```text
  THE ACCURACY RANKING (Cleveland & McGill, 1984)

  most accurate
    1  position, common scale     |###  #####  ####   two bars, one axis
    2  position, identical scales  small multiples
    3  length                      stacked-bar segments
    4  angle / slope               pie wedges, line steepness
    5  area                        bubble size, treemap
    6  volume                      3-D anything
    7  colour saturation/lightness heatmap intensity
    8  colour hue                  which category
  least accurate

  Put the variable the reader cares about most on channel 1.

  THE AREA TRAP

    value doubles: 10 -> 20

    radius ~ value              area ~ value
      o        (  )               o       ( )
      r=10     r=20               r=3.2   r=4.5
      area 1x  area 4x            area 1x area 2x
      READS AS 4x                 READS AS ~2x (correct)

    Scale by sqrt(value) when you control the radius. Check your library:
    matplotlib's `s` is already an area.

  ONE VARIABLE, ONE CHANNEL

    BAD                          GOOD
    length = revenue             length = revenue
    colour = revenue             colour = is_new_product
    (colour says nothing new)    (colour carries a second variable)
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Human accuracy at reading channels is ranked and measured, so put the most
>   important variable on position along a common scale.
> - Area is judged poorly and systematically underestimated, so bubble charts
>   convey only coarse differences.
> - Scale marks by area rather than radius, or a doubling looks like a
>   quadrupling.
> - Hue carries identity and not magnitude; lightness carries magnitude, which
>   is why sequential scales vary lightness.
> - Never encode one variable on two channels, because it spends a channel that
>   could have carried something new.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Render the same five values as bars, pie wedges, bubbles, and heatmap
>    cells, then ask someone to rank the values from each and record the
>    errors.
> 2. Draw two circles whose radii are proportional to values of 10 and 20, then
>    redraw with area proportional, and state the perceived ratio in each.
> 3. Take a chart that colours bars by their own height and rework it so colour
>    carries a second variable.
> 4. Interview: You need to show revenue, growth rate, region, and customer
>    segment in one view. How do you allocate the channels? (Hint: which two
>    variables deserve the axes, and what do you do with the fourth?)

#### Color Theory and Accessibility

Colour is the channel people reach for first and reason about least. It is also
the one with a hard accessibility constraint: roughly 8% of men and 0.5% of
women have some form of colour vision deficiency, most commonly difficulty
distinguishing red from green. A chart that encodes meaning in hue alone is
unreadable to a meaningful share of any audience.

The discipline that fixes most colour problems is to ask what **job** the colour
is doing. There are only four, and each has one correct structure.

**Categorical** colour encodes identity: which series is which. The structure is
a fixed set of distinguishable hues, assigned in a fixed order. The two rules
that matter: assign hues in a fixed sequence so the same entity always gets the
same colour, and never generate a ninth hue, because at that point adjacent
colours are indistinguishable under colour vision deficiency.

**Sequential** colour encodes magnitude: how much. The structure is one hue
varying from light to dark. Lightness carries the order, which is why a
single-hue ramp is readable in greyscale and by every viewer. Never use a
rainbow for magnitude: hues have no perceptual order, so a rainbow scale
introduces boundaries where the data is smooth and hides differences where it is
not. The classic offender is the old `jet` colormap.

**Diverging** colour encodes polarity: which side of a meaningful midpoint. The
structure is two hues that read as opposites, separated by a neutral grey
midpoint. Two requirements: the midpoint must be neutral, because a hue there
implies a category that does not exist, and the two poles must be genuinely
opposite, so blue against orange or blue against red works while blue against
teal does not, both being cool. Diverging scales must also be centred on the
real midpoint. Centring a profit-and-loss scale anywhere but zero misstates who
is profitable.

**Status** colour encodes state: good, warning, serious, critical. These
meanings are reserved, so a status colour must never double as "series four",
and status must always ship with an icon or a label, never colour alone.

Three practices make colour reliable rather than hopeful.

**Use perceptually uniform colormaps.** Viridis, magma, and cividis are
constructed so equal steps in data are equal steps in perceived lightness. The
older rainbow maps are not, which means they create visual features that are not
in the data.

**Never encode by colour alone.** Colour should be redundant with something
else: a direct label, a shape, a position, a texture, or a line style. This is
the single most effective accessibility practice, and it also helps when a chart
is printed in greyscale or photocopied.

**Check colour choices with a simulator rather than by eye.** Colour vision
deficiency simulation is a computation, not an aesthetic judgement, and tools
exist for it in every language. The test is whether every pair of colours that
can appear side by side remains distinguishable under simulated protanopia and
deuteranopia. Anything you can compute, you should compute rather than guess.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.colors import to_rgb

# --- A VALIDATED CATEGORICAL PALETTE, in fixed slot order. ---
# Fixed order is the colour-vision-deficiency safety mechanism: the sequence
# is chosen so that ADJACENT slots stay separable. Never shuffle it, and
# never append a 9th hue.
CATEGORICAL = ["#2a78d6",  # 1 blue
               "#eb6834",  # 2 orange
               "#1baf7a",  # 3 aqua
               "#eda100",  # 4 yellow
               "#e87ba4",  # 5 magenta
               "#008300",  # 6 green
               "#4a3aa7",  # 7 violet
               "#e34948"]  # 8 red

# --- SIMULATE COLOUR VISION DEFICIENCY: compute it, do not eyeball it. ---
# Machado, Oliveira & Fernandes (2009) linear transforms at severity 1.0.
CVD = {
    "protanopia": np.array([[0.1522, 0.1178, -0.028],
                            [0.1052, 0.8933,  0.0018],
                            [-0.0038, -0.0291, 1.0329]]),
    "deuteranopia": np.array([[0.3674, 0.8607, -0.2281],
                              [0.2801, 0.6725,  0.0474],
                              [-0.0118, 0.0428, 0.9690]]),
}

def srgb_to_linear(c):
    c = np.asarray(c, dtype=float)
    return np.where(c <= 0.04045, c / 12.92, ((c + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4)

def linear_to_srgb(c):
    c = np.clip(c, 0, 1)
    return np.where(c <= 0.0031308, c * 12.92, 1.055 * c ** (1/2.4) - 0.055)

def simulate(hex_color: str, kind: str) -> tuple:
    lin = srgb_to_linear(to_rgb(hex_color))
    return tuple(linear_to_srgb(CVD[kind] @ lin))

def oklab(hex_color: str) -> np.ndarray:
    """OKLab is roughly perceptually uniform, so Euclidean distance in it
    approximates perceived difference."""
    r, g, b = srgb_to_linear(to_rgb(hex_color))
    l = 0.4122214708*r + 0.5363325363*g + 0.0514459929*b
    m = 0.2119034982*r + 0.6806995451*g + 0.1073969566*b
    s = 0.0883024619*r + 0.2817188376*g + 0.6299787005*b
    l_, m_, s_ = np.cbrt([l, m, s])
    return np.array([
        0.2104542553*l_ + 0.7936177850*m_ - 0.0040720468*s_,
        1.9779984951*l_ - 2.4285922050*m_ + 0.4505937099*s_,
        0.0259040371*l_ + 0.7827717662*m_ - 0.8086757660*s_,
    ])

def delta_e(c1, c2) -> float:
    """Perceptual distance, OKLab scaled by 100. Target >= 8 for adjacent
    series; below ~6 the pair is effectively the same colour."""
    return float(np.linalg.norm(oklab(c1) - oklab(c2)) * 100)

# Check adjacent slot pairs, simulated. This is the test that matters for
# stacked bars and multi-line charts, where only neighbours touch.
print("adjacent slot separation under simulated CVD (target >= 8):")
worst = 1e9
for i in range(len(CATEGORICAL) - 1):
    a, b = CATEGORICAL[i], CATEGORICAL[i+1]
    row = {"pair": f"{i+1}-{i+2}", "normal": round(delta_e(a, b), 1)}
    for kind in CVD:
        sa = "#%02x%02x%02x" % tuple(int(v*255) for v in simulate(a, kind))
        sb = "#%02x%02x%02x" % tuple(int(v*255) for v in simulate(b, kind))
        row[kind[:5]] = round(delta_e(sa, sb), 1)
        worst = min(worst, row[kind[:5]])
    print(f"  {row}")
print(f"worst adjacent pair under CVD: {worst:.1f}")

# A NAIVE palette that looks fine and collapses under simulation.
naive = ["#d62728", "#2ca02c"]            # the classic red/green pair
print(f"\nred vs green, normal vision:  {delta_e(*naive):.1f}")
for kind in CVD:
    sa = "#%02x%02x%02x" % tuple(int(v*255) for v in simulate(naive[0], kind))
    sb = "#%02x%02x%02x" % tuple(int(v*255) for v in simulate(naive[1], kind))
    print(f"red vs green, {kind:12s}: {delta_e(sa, sb):.1f}"
          f"  {'FAILS' if delta_e(sa, sb) < 8 else 'ok'}")

# --- SEQUENTIAL: lightness must increase monotonically. ---
def lightness(hex_color: str) -> float:
    return oklab(hex_color)[0]

print("\nis the ramp monotone in lightness?")
for cmap_name in ("viridis", "Blues", "jet"):
    cmap = plt.get_cmap(cmap_name)
    hexes = ["#%02x%02x%02x" % tuple(int(v*255) for v in cmap(t)[:3])
             for t in np.linspace(0, 1, 9)]
    ls = [lightness(h) for h in hexes]
    diffs = np.diff(ls)
    mono = bool(np.all(diffs > 0) or np.all(diffs < 0))
    print(f"  {cmap_name:8s} monotone: {str(mono):5s}"
          f"  lightness range {min(ls):.2f}-{max(ls):.2f}"
          f"  {'' if mono else '<- creates bands the data does not have'}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 2, figsize=(10, 4.2))
grid = np.linspace(0, 1, 256).reshape(1, -1)
for row, name in enumerate(["viridis", "Blues", "jet"]):
    axes[row][0].imshow(grid, cmap=name, aspect="auto")
    axes[row][0].set_title(f"{name}", loc="left", fontsize=9)
    cmap = plt.get_cmap(name)
    ls = [lightness("#%02x%02x%02x" % tuple(int(v*255) for v in cmap(t)[:3]))
          for t in np.linspace(0, 1, 60)]
    axes[row][1].plot(ls, color="#0b0b0b", lw=2)
    axes[row][1].set_title("perceived lightness along the ramp",
                           loc="left", fontsize=8)
    for ax in axes[row]:
        ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
fig.savefig("/tmp/claude-0/ramps.png", dpi=110, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)

# --- DIVERGING: neutral midpoint, and CENTRED ON THE REAL MIDPOINT. ---
profit = np.array([-42.0, -18.0, -3.0, 5.0, 12.0, 30.0])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 2.8))
from matplotlib.colors import TwoSlopeNorm
axes[0].bar(range(6), profit,
            color=plt.get_cmap("RdBu")(
                plt.Normalize(profit.min(), profit.max())(profit)))
axes[0].axhline(0, color="#0b0b0b", lw=0.8)
axes[0].set_title("diverging NOT centred at 0: WRONG", loc="left", fontsize=9)

norm = TwoSlopeNorm(vmin=profit.min(), vcenter=0.0, vmax=profit.max())
axes[1].bar(range(6), profit, color=plt.get_cmap("RdBu")(norm(profit)))
axes[1].axhline(0, color="#0b0b0b", lw=0.8)
axes[1].set_title("centred at 0: colour agrees with sign", loc="left", fontsize=9)
for ax in axes:
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
fig.savefig("/tmp/claude-0/diverging.png", dpi=110, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)
print("\nuncentred, a small LOSS can be shaded the same as a small PROFIT.")
print("Diverging scales must be centred on the value that means 'neither'.")

# --- REDUNDANT ENCODING: never colour alone. ---
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
x = np.arange(12)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.2), sharey=True)
styles = [("-", "o"), ("--", "s"), (":", "^")]
for i, name in enumerate(["alpha", "beta", "gamma"]):
    y = 10 + i * 3 + np.cumsum(rng.normal(0, .8, 12))
    axes[0].plot(x, y, color=CATEGORICAL[i], lw=2)          # colour only
    ls, mk = styles[i]
    axes[1].plot(x, y, color=CATEGORICAL[i], lw=2, linestyle=ls,
                 marker=mk, markersize=5, label=name)       # colour + style
    axes[1].annotate(name, (x[-1], y[-1]), xytext=(5, 0),
                     textcoords="offset points", fontsize=8,
                     color=CATEGORICAL[i], va="center")
axes[0].set_title("colour alone: unreadable in greyscale or with CVD",
                  loc="left", fontsize=9)
axes[1].set_title("colour + line style + marker + direct label",
                  loc="left", fontsize=9)
axes[1].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
for ax in axes:
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
fig.savefig("/tmp/claude-0/redundant.png", dpi=110, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)

# --- CONTRAST: marks need >= 3:1 against the surface; text 4.5:1. ---
def rel_luminance(hex_color: str) -> float:
    r, g, b = srgb_to_linear(to_rgb(hex_color))
    return 0.2126 * r + 0.7152 * g + 0.0722 * b

def contrast(a: str, b: str) -> float:
    la, lb = rel_luminance(a), rel_luminance(b)
    hi, lo = max(la, lb), min(la, lb)
    return (hi + 0.05) / (lo + 0.05)

SURFACE = "#fcfcfb"
print(f"\ncontrast against the light surface (marks need >= 3:1):")
for i, c in enumerate(CATEGORICAL, 1):
    ratio = contrast(c, SURFACE)
    print(f"  slot {i} {c}  {ratio:5.2f}:1"
          f"  {'ok' if ratio >= 3 else 'needs a visible label or table view'}")
```

```text
  THE FOUR JOBS OF COLOUR

  job          encodes            structure                    capacity
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  categorical  identity           fixed distinct hues, in a     5-8 levels
                                  fixed assignment order
  ordinal      position in order  ONE hue, monotone lightness   ~7 steps
  sequential   magnitude          ONE hue, light -> dark        continuous
  diverging    polarity           two opposite hues + NEUTRAL   continuous
                                  grey midpoint
  status       state              reserved scale + icon/label   4 states

  WHY A RAINBOW FAILS FOR MAGNITUDE

  jet:      blue cyan green yellow red
  lightness  .3   .8    .6    .95  .4     <- NOT monotone
                  ^           ^
            bright bands the data does not contain, and dark regions where
            real differences disappear.

  viridis:  dark purple -> teal -> yellow
  lightness  .15  .35  .55  .75  .95      <- monotone, so equal data steps
                                             look like equal steps

  DIVERGING MUST BE CENTRED ON THE REAL MIDPOINT

    values: -42 ... +30, scale centred on the data's mean (-2.7)
      -3 (a LOSS) shades nearly the same as +5 (a PROFIT)   WRONG

    scale centred on 0
      every negative is one hue, every positive the other    RIGHT

  THE ACCESSIBILITY RULES, IN PRIORITY ORDER

    1. never encode by colour ALONE (add label, shape, style, or position)
    2. simulate protanopia and deuteranopia; compute, do not eyeball
    3. one-hue ramps for magnitude, so greyscale printing still works
    4. marks >= 3:1 contrast on the surface, text >= 4.5:1
    5. a legend for 2+ series, and direct labels for <= 4
    6. a table view exists for every chart
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Decide what job the colour is doing: identity, order, magnitude, polarity,
>   or status, and each has one correct structure.
> - Categorical hues are assigned in a fixed order so an entity keeps its
>   colour, and a ninth generated hue is indistinguishable under colour
>   vision deficiency.
> - Sequential scales vary lightness within one hue; rainbow scales are not
>   monotone in lightness and invent bands the data does not have.
> - Diverging scales need a neutral midpoint, two genuinely opposite hues, and
>   centring on the value that means "neither".
> - Never encode by colour alone, and verify palettes with a simulation rather
>   than by eye, because it is a computation.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement a colour vision deficiency simulation and report the perceptual
>    distance between red and green under normal vision and under
>    deuteranopia.
> 2. Plot perceived lightness along the viridis, Blues, and jet ramps and
>    identify which are monotone.
> 3. Render a profit-and-loss bar chart with a diverging scale centred on the
>    data mean and again centred on zero, and describe the misreading the first
>    invites.
> 4. Take a three-series line chart encoded by colour alone and add two
>    redundant channels, then convert it to greyscale to confirm it still
>    reads.
> 5. Interview: A stakeholder wants your dashboard to use the company's red and
>    green brand colours for "bad" and "good". How do you respond? (Hint: what
>    share of viewers is affected, and what can carry the meaning alongside
>    hue?)

#### Scales, Axes, and Annotation

Scales and axes are the chart's units. They tell the reader what the marks mean,
and almost every misleading chart is misleading through its axes rather than
through its data. Annotation is what converts a chart from a display of numbers
into a statement someone can act on.

**Scale type** is the first decision. A **linear** scale puts equal data
differences at equal distances and is the default. A **logarithmic** scale puts
equal *ratios* at equal distances, which is correct in three situations: the
data spans several orders of magnitude, the meaningful comparison is
proportional rather than absolute, or the growth is exponential and you want it
to appear straight. A log scale must always be labelled, because a reader who
misses it will read growth completely wrong. Note that log scales cannot show
zero or negative values, which is a hard constraint rather than an
inconvenience.

**Axis range** carries the asymmetry from the earlier topic: zero is mandatory
for bars because they encode length, and optional for lines because they encode
slope. Two more range rules. When comparing panels in a small-multiple grid,
share the axis range, or the comparison the layout invites is invalid. And when
a range is truncated deliberately, say so.

**Tick marks and labels** should be few and readable. Four to seven ticks is
usually right; more becomes visual noise. Use round numbers, format them for
humans with thousands separators or abbreviations, and put units in the axis
label rather than repeating them on every tick.

**Gridlines** should be hairline, solid, and one step off the background. They
exist to support reading a value, not to be seen. Dashed gridlines add noise and
falsely suggest a threshold or a projection.

Then **annotation**, which is the highest-value and most neglected part of a
chart. A chart without a written conclusion makes the reader do the
interpretation, and they may not do it the way you would.

The elements worth including:

- **A title that states the finding**, not the contents. "Checkout conversion
  fell 1.8 points after the March release" beats "Conversion over time". The
  title is the one piece of text everyone reads.
- **Direct labels on the marks that matter.** A label on the endpoint, the
  extreme, or the one series being discussed. Never a number on every point,
  which is chaos and goes unread.
- **Reference lines** for a target, a baseline, an average, or a threshold, so
  the reader can see whether a value is acceptable rather than just what it is.
- **Event markers** for a release, a campaign, an outage, or a definition
  change. A step in a metric with no annotation invites the reader to invent an
  explanation.
- **A source and an as-of timestamp.** Which table, which filters, and when it
  was computed. This is what makes a chart auditable and reconcilable.
- **Honest treatment of gaps and incomplete periods.** A partial final period
  looks like a collapse. Either exclude it or mark it explicitly.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.ticker import FuncFormatter

BLUE, GRAY, INK, MUTED = "#2a78d6", "#c9c9c5", "#0b0b0b", "#52514e"

# --- LINEAR VS LOG: the same data, two different readings. ---
months = pd.date_range("2022-01-01", periods=36, freq="MS")
users = 1000 * 1.14 ** np.arange(36)          # steady 14% monthly growth

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.2))
axes[0].plot(months, users, lw=2, color=BLUE)
axes[0].set_title("linear: growth looks like it began in year 3",
                  loc="left", fontsize=9)
axes[1].plot(months, users, lw=2, color=BLUE)
axes[1].set_yscale("log")
axes[1].set_title("log: a straight line = CONSTANT growth rate",
                  loc="left", fontsize=9)
axes[1].set_ylabel("users (log scale)")        # ALWAYS label a log axis
for ax in axes:
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
    ax.grid(axis="y", lw=0.5, color="#e6e6e4", linestyle="-")  # solid hairline
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)
fig.savefig("/tmp/claude-0/log_scale.png", dpi=110, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)

growth = pd.Series(users).pct_change().dropna()
print(f"actual monthly growth: min {growth.min():.1%},"
      f" max {growth.max():.1%} -- perfectly constant")
print("The linear panel implies acceleration that does not exist. On a log")
print("axis a constant growth RATE is a straight line, which is the point.")

# --- LOG CANNOT SHOW ZERO OR NEGATIVES ---
with_zero = np.array([0.0, 5.0, 50.0, 500.0])
safe = np.where(with_zero > 0, with_zero, np.nan)
print(f"\nlog10 of the series: {np.log10(safe)}")
print("the zero becomes NaN and silently vanishes from the plot.")
print("Use a symlog scale, or plot the zeros separately and say so.")

# --- SHARED AXES IN SMALL MULTIPLES, or the comparison is invalid. ---
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
panels = {"north": 100 + np.cumsum(rng.normal(1.0, 2, 24)),
          "south": 40 + np.cumsum(rng.normal(0.3, 1, 24)),
          "east":  180 + np.cumsum(rng.normal(-0.4, 3, 24))}
idx = pd.date_range("2024-01-01", periods=24, freq="MS")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(12, 4.6))
for col, (name, vals) in enumerate(panels.items()):
    axes[0][col].plot(idx, vals, lw=2, color=BLUE)        # independent scales
    axes[0][col].set_title(f"{name} (own scale)", loc="left", fontsize=8)
    axes[1][col].plot(idx, vals, lw=2, color=BLUE)
    axes[1][col].set_ylim(0, 260)                         # SHARED scale
    axes[1][col].set_title(f"{name} (shared scale)", loc="left", fontsize=8)
for ax in axes.ravel():
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
fig.savefig("/tmp/claude-0/shared_axes.png", dpi=110, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)
print("\nTop row: all three look similar in size. Bottom row: south is a")
print("quarter of east. Independent scales make a grid layout lie.")

# --- TICK FORMATTING: humans, not machines ---
def human(v, _=None):
    for lim, suf in ((1e9, "B"), (1e6, "M"), (1e3, "k")):
        if abs(v) >= lim:
            return f"{v/lim:,.1f}{suf}".replace(".0", "")
    return f"{v:,.0f}"

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 2.9))
big = np.array([1_240_000, 3_800_000, 2_150_000, 5_600_000])
for ax, fmt in zip(axes, [None, human]):
    ax.bar(list("ABCD"), big, color=BLUE, width=0.55)
    if fmt:
        ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(FuncFormatter(fmt))
        ax.set_yticks(np.linspace(0, 6e6, 4))       # 4 ticks, round numbers
        ax.set_title("4 round ticks, abbreviated", loc="left", fontsize=9)
    else:
        ax.set_title("default: too many ticks, raw digits",
                     loc="left", fontsize=9)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
fig.savefig("/tmp/claude-0/ticks.png", dpi=110, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)

# --- ANNOTATION: turn a chart into a statement. ---
conv = np.concatenate([
    np.random.default_rng(9).normal(4.2, .12, 14),     # before the release
    np.random.default_rng(9).normal(2.4, .12, 10),     # after
])
days = pd.date_range("2024-03-01", periods=24, freq="D")
RELEASE = days[14]
TARGET = 4.0

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.8))
ax.plot(days, conv, lw=2, color=BLUE, zorder=3)

# 1. A reference line for the target, labelled in place.
ax.axhline(TARGET, lw=1, color=GRAY, zorder=1)
ax.annotate(f"target {TARGET}%", (days[0], TARGET), xytext=(2, 4),
            textcoords="offset points", fontsize=8, color=MUTED)

# 2. An event marker, so the reader does not invent an explanation.
ax.axvline(RELEASE, lw=1, color="#eb6834", zorder=2)
ax.annotate("v2.4 checkout release", (RELEASE, ax.get_ylim()[1]),
            xytext=(4, -10), textcoords="offset points",
            fontsize=8, color="#eb6834")

# 3. Selective direct labels: the endpoint and the extreme, not every point.
last = conv[-1]
ax.annotate(f"{last:.1f}%", (days[-1], last), xytext=(6, 0),
            textcoords="offset points", fontsize=9, fontweight="bold",
            color=BLUE, va="center")

# 4. A title that states the FINDING, with a subtitle for the mechanism.
ax.set_title("Checkout conversion fell 1.8 points after the v2.4 release",
             loc="left", fontsize=12, color=INK, pad=16)
ax.text(0, 1.04, "Daily conversion, all traffic. The drop begins the day of "
        "the release and has not recovered.",
        transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=8.5, color=MUTED)

# 5. Source and as-of stamp: what makes the chart auditable.
ax.text(0, -0.22, "Source: analytics.fct_checkout_sessions  |  "
        "filters: bots excluded, web only  |  as of 2024-03-25 06:00 UTC",
        transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=7, color=MUTED)

ax.set_ylabel("conversion rate (%)")
ax.set_ylim(0, 5.5)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(axis="y", lw=0.5, color="#e6e6e4")
ax.set_axisbelow(True)
fig.savefig("/tmp/claude-0/annotated.png", dpi=110, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)

# --- THE PARTIAL-PERIOD TRAP ---
full = pd.Series([980, 1010, 1040, 1080, 1120],
                 index=pd.period_range("2024-01", periods=5, freq="M"))
partial = full.copy()
partial.iloc[-1] = 380           # month 5 is only 10 days in
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 2.9))
axes[0].bar([str(p) for p in partial.index], partial.values, color=BLUE, width=.55)
axes[0].set_title("partial final month: looks like a collapse",
                  loc="left", fontsize=9)
axes[1].bar([str(p) for p in partial.index[:-1]], partial.values[:-1],
            color=BLUE, width=.55)
axes[1].bar([str(partial.index[-1])], [partial.values[-1]], width=.55,
            color=BLUE, alpha=0.35, hatch="//")
axes[1].annotate("partial\n(10 of 31 days)", (4, 420), fontsize=7,
                 ha="center", color=MUTED)
axes[1].set_title("marked as incomplete", loc="left", fontsize=9)
for ax in axes:
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
fig.savefig("/tmp/claude-0/partial.png", dpi=110, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)
print("\nAn unmarked partial period is the most common accidental lie in")
print("routine reporting. Exclude it or hatch it, every time.")
```

```text
  WHEN TO USE A LOG SCALE

  use it when                          do NOT when
  --------------------------------     ------------------------------------
  data spans >= 2 orders of magnitude   values include 0 or negatives
  ratios are the meaningful comparison  the audience will not notice the axis
  growth is exponential                 differences, not ratios, are the point
  Always label the axis "(log scale)".

  CONSTANT GROWTH, TWO AXES

  linear                          log
        |                  /            |        ____----
        |                 /             |  __----
        |               /               |--
        |         _____/                |
        |___-----                       |
        +------------------             +------------------
    "growth started in year 3"     "growth rate never changed"
    Both are the same 14%/month. Only one reads correctly.

  SHARED SCALES IN A GRID

  own scales                      shared scale
  north  south  east              north  south  east
   /\     /\     /\                /\
   ||     ||     ||                ||           /\
   ||     ||     ||                ||    __     ||
  all "the same size"             south is 1/4 of east
  A grid invites comparison, so unshared scales make the layout lie.

  THE ANNOTATION CHECKLIST

    [ ] title states the FINDING, not the contents
    [ ] subtitle gives the population, filter, and mechanism
    [ ] units in the axis label, not on every tick
    [ ] 4-7 round ticks, human-formatted (1.2M, not 1240000)
    [ ] reference line for target / baseline / threshold
    [ ] event markers for releases, campaigns, outages, definition changes
    [ ] direct labels on the endpoint and the extreme only
    [ ] gridlines hairline and SOLID, one step off the surface
    [ ] partial periods excluded or visibly marked
    [ ] source table, filters, and an as-of timestamp
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A log scale makes equal ratios equal distances, so constant exponential
>   growth becomes a straight line; always label it, and remember it cannot
>   show zero.
> - Zero baselines are mandatory for bars and optional for lines, and panels in
>   a grid must share an axis range or the comparison is invalid.
> - Use four to seven round, human-formatted ticks, and keep gridlines hairline
>   and solid so they support reading without being seen.
> - A title should state the finding rather than the contents, because it is
>   the one piece of text every reader reads.
> - Mark events, targets, and partial periods explicitly, and stamp every chart
>   with its source and as-of time.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Plot a series growing at a constant percentage on linear and log axes and
>    describe what a reader would conclude from each.
> 2. Build a three-panel small-multiple grid with independent axes, then with a
>    shared axis, and state which comparison each supports.
> 3. Take an unannotated line chart and add a finding-based title, a target
>    reference line, an event marker, one direct label, and a source stamp.
> 4. Render a bar chart whose final period is incomplete, then mark it as
>    partial, and describe the wrong conclusion the first version invites.
> 5. Interview: A chart shows a metric dropping sharply on one date and a
>    stakeholder asks what caused it. You do not know yet. What do you add to
>    the chart before sending it? (Hint: what would stop the reader from
>    inventing a cause, and what would let someone else reproduce the number?)

#### Avoiding Misleading Visuals

A chart can be factually accurate and still cause the reader to believe
something false. That gap between accurate and honest is where most misleading
visuals live, and almost none of them involve fabricated data. They involve a
defensible-sounding choice that changes the conclusion.

This matters for a practical reason beyond ethics: you will make most of these
mistakes accidentally, because every one of them is a default in some tool or a
natural-seeming response to a stakeholder request. Knowing the catalogue is the
only reliable defence.

**Truncated bar axes** are the most common. Bars encode value as length, so
starting the axis at 98 instead of 0 makes a 6% difference look like a
fourfold one. The chart is accurate and the reader's takeaway is wrong.

**Dual axes** invent correlations. Because the alignment of two independent
scales is arbitrary, you can make two series appear to move together, diverge,
or cross wherever you choose. There is no honest version of this chart.

**Inconsistent bin widths or intervals** distort. A histogram with uneven bins
must plot density rather than count, or the wide bins look artificially tall. A
time axis with uneven spacing, treated as evenly spaced categories, compresses
and stretches the trend arbitrarily.

**Cherry-picked ranges** are the subtlest, because nothing about the chart is
wrong. Choose a start date at a local minimum and any series shows growth.
Always ask whether the window was chosen before or after seeing the result.

**Area and volume exaggeration** multiplies. Scaling an icon's width and height
by a value squares the perceived difference; a three-dimensional shape cubes it.
Scale by area, and avoid three-dimensional charts entirely, since perspective
also makes near items look larger than far ones of the same value.

**Reversed or inverted axes** invert the message. The notorious example is a
chart of firearm deaths with an inverted y-axis, which made a sharp rise look
like a decline to anyone reading the shape rather than the numbers.

**Aggregation that hides the distribution.** A bar of group means conceals
whether the groups overlap almost completely. Show the distribution, or the
interval, or the sample size.

**Missing uncertainty** is arguably the biggest one in routine work. A point
estimate drawn as a solid line implies precision it does not have. Two bars
whose confidence intervals overlap heavily should not be described as different,
and a chart without intervals gives the reader no way to know.

**Unequal denominators.** Comparing raw counts across groups of different sizes
is the classic error: a region with more crimes may simply have more people.
Rates, not counts, unless the count itself is the question.

The defence is a checklist, applied to your own charts before sending them,
because the question is never whether you meant to mislead.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

BLUE, ORANGE, GRAY, MUTED = "#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#c9c9c5", "#52514e"
rng = np.random.default_rng(8)

# --- 1. TRUNCATED BAR AXIS: same data, two conclusions. ---
vals = np.array([102.0, 108.0])
print("TRUNCATION MATH")
ratio = vals[1] / vals[0]
print(f"  true ratio: {ratio:.2f}x  ({(ratio-1)*100:.0f}% larger)")
for floor in (0, 98, 101):
    drawn = (vals - floor) / (vals[0] - floor) if vals[0] > floor else vals
    print(f"  axis starting at {floor:>3}: bar B looks {drawn[1]:.1f}x bar A")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11, 2.9))
for ax, floor in zip(axes, (0, 98, 101)):
    ax.bar(["A", "B"], vals, color=BLUE if floor == 0 else ORANGE, width=.5)
    ax.set_ylim(floor, 110)
    ax.set_title(f"axis from {floor}", loc="left", fontsize=9)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
fig.savefig("/tmp/claude-0/truncate.png", dpi=110, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)

# --- 2. CHERRY-PICKED RANGE: one series, four honest-looking stories. ---
full = pd.Series(100 + np.cumsum(rng.normal(0.05, 2.2, 240)),
                 index=pd.date_range("2023-01-01", periods=240, freq="D"))
windows = {"full series": (0, 240), "growth story": None,
           "decline story": None, "flat story": (100, 160)}
# Find the windows that produce each story, which is exactly what a motivated
# analyst does without ever falsifying a number.
best_up = max(((i, j) for i in range(0, 180, 10) for j in range(i+40, 240, 10)),
              key=lambda ij: full.iloc[ij[1]-1] - full.iloc[ij[0]])
best_dn = min(((i, j) for i in range(0, 180, 10) for j in range(i+40, 240, 10)),
              key=lambda ij: full.iloc[ij[1]-1] - full.iloc[ij[0]])
windows["growth story"], windows["decline story"] = best_up, best_dn

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(14, 2.8))
for ax, (name, (i, j)) in zip(axes, windows.items()):
    seg = full.iloc[i:j]
    ax.plot(seg.index, seg.values, lw=2, color=BLUE)
    change = (seg.iloc[-1] / seg.iloc[0] - 1) * 100
    ax.set_title(f"{name}: {change:+.0f}%", loc="left", fontsize=9)
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=6)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
fig.savefig("/tmp/claude-0/cherry_pick.png", dpi=110, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)
print(f"\nCHERRY-PICKING: one random-walk series yields "
      f"{(full.iloc[best_up[1]-1]/full.iloc[best_up[0]]-1)*100:+.0f}% and "
```
