```python
          "alpine": 12, "coastal": 180, "delta": 55, "plateau": 8}
rows = []
for region, scale in scales.items():
    trend = -1.6 if region == "coastal" else rng.uniform(0.2, 0.9)  # the story
    series = scale + np.cumsum(rng.normal(trend, scale * 0.04, 18))
    rows += [{"region": region, "month": m, "revenue": round(v, 1)}
             for m, v in zip(months, series)]
df = pd.DataFrame(rows)

# --- OVERLAY VS FACET: the same nine series, two treatments. ---
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(14, 4))
ax = fig.add_subplot(1, 2, 1)
for region, g in df.groupby("region"):
    ax.plot(g["month"], g["revenue"], lw=1.6, label=region)
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=6, ncol=3)
ax.set_title("9 series overlaid: 9 hues, crossings, nothing stands out",
             loc="left", fontsize=9)
ax.set_ylabel("revenue")
fig.savefig("/tmp/claude-0/overlay.png", dpi=110, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)

# --- RULE 1: SHARED SCALES. Compare the two versions directly. ---
order = (df.groupby("region")["revenue"].mean()
           .sort_values(ascending=False).index)      # RULE 2: meaningful order

for shared, tag in [(False, "independent"), (True, "shared")]:
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 3, figsize=(10, 6.4),
                             sharex=True, sharey=shared)
    for ax, region in zip(axes.ravel(), order):
        g = df[df["region"] == region]
        ax.plot(g["month"], g["revenue"], lw=1.8, color=BLUE)
        ax.set_title(region, loc="left", fontsize=8, color=INK)
        ax.tick_params(labelsize=6)
        ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
    fig.suptitle(f"{tag} y scales", x=.02, ha="left", fontsize=10)
    fig.savefig(f"/tmp/claude-0/facet_{tag}.png", dpi=110, bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.close(fig)

span = df.groupby("region")["revenue"].agg(["min", "max"])
print("panel ranges (why independent scales lie):")
print(span.round(0).sort_values("max", ascending=False).to_string())
print(f"\nlargest panel max {span['max'].max():.0f},"
      f" smallest {span['max'].min():.0f}"
      f" -> a {span['max'].max()/span['max'].min():.0f}x difference that")
print("independent scales render as nine identically sized charts.")

# --- RULE 4: CONTEXT IN EVERY PANEL. The highest-value addition. ---
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 3, figsize=(10.5, 6.6), sharex=True, sharey=True)
overall = df.groupby("month")["revenue"].mean()
for ax, region in zip(axes.ravel(), order):
    # All other series, faint: the reader sees the specific AND the general.
    for other, g2 in df.groupby("region"):
        if other != region:
            ax.plot(g2["month"], g2["revenue"], lw=.9, color="#e4e4e1", zorder=1)
    g = df[df["region"] == region]
    is_story = region == "coastal"
    ax.plot(g["month"], g["revenue"], lw=2,
            color="#e34948" if is_story else BLUE, zorder=3)
    # Direct-label the endpoint of the panel's own series only.
    ax.annotate(f"{g['revenue'].iloc[-1]:.0f}",
                (g["month"].iloc[-1], g["revenue"].iloc[-1]),
                xytext=(3, 0), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=6.5,
                color="#e34948" if is_story else MUTED, va="center")
    change = g["revenue"].iloc[-1] / g["revenue"].iloc[0] - 1
    ax.set_title(f"{region}   {change:+.0%}", loc="left", fontsize=8,
                 color="#e34948" if is_story else INK,
                 fontweight="bold" if is_story else "normal")
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=6)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
fig.suptitle("Coastal is the only region declining", x=.02, ha="left",
             fontsize=11, fontweight="bold")
fig.text(.02, .935, "Monthly revenue by region, shared scale. Other regions "
         "shown faint for context.", fontsize=8, color=MUTED)
fig.savefig("/tmp/claude-0/facet_context.png", dpi=110, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)
print("\nThe declining region is now findable in under a second, because the")
print("grid encodes on POSITION and the one exception is coloured.")

# --- FACET GRID: two variables, rows and columns, showing interaction. ---
n = 2400
panel = pd.DataFrame({
    "segment": rng.choice(["smb", "mid", "enterprise"], n),
    "channel": rng.choice(["direct", "partner"], n),
    "seats": rng.integers(1, 250, n),
})
# The seats-to-revenue slope differs BY CELL: that interaction is the point.
slope = {("smb", "direct"): 9, ("smb", "partner"): 5,
         ("mid", "direct"): 14, ("mid", "partner"): 13,
         ("enterprise", "direct"): 26, ("enterprise", "partner"): 11}
panel["revenue"] = [
    slope[(s, c)] * k + rng.normal(0, 260)
    for s, c, k in zip(panel["segment"], panel["channel"], panel["seats"])]

g = sns.FacetGrid(panel, row="channel", col="segment", height=2.3,
                  aspect=1.25, margin_titles=True,
                  col_order=["smb", "mid", "enterprise"])   # meaningful order
g.map_dataframe(sns.regplot, x="seats", y="revenue",
                scatter_kws={"s": 6, "alpha": .35, "color": BLUE},
                line_kws={"color": "#eb6834", "lw": 2})
g.set_titles(col_template="{col_name}", row_template="{row_name}")
g.figure.suptitle("Revenue per seat rises with segment, but only via direct",
                  x=.02, ha="left", fontsize=11)
g.figure.subplots_adjust(top=.86)
g.figure.savefig("/tmp/claude-0/facet_grid.png", dpi=110, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(g.figure)

fitted = (panel.groupby(["channel", "segment"])
          .apply(lambda d: np.polyfit(d["seats"], d["revenue"], 1)[0],
                 include_groups=False)
          .unstack().round(1))
print("\nfitted revenue per seat by cell (the interaction the grid shows):")
print(fitted.to_string())

# --- THE PANEL-COUNT LIMIT, and the heatmap as the compressed limit. ---
print("""
  PANEL COUNT

    1-4      large panels, full detail, axis labels on each
    5-12     the sweet spot; shared axes, outer labels only
    13-25    small panels; titles only, no tick labels inside
    25-60    too small to read -> aggregate the tail, or use a heatmap
    60+      heatmap, or select the subset that matters
""")

# A heatmap IS a small-multiple grid with colour replacing position.
wide = df.pivot(index="region", columns="month", values="revenue")
indexed = wide.div(wide.iloc[:, 0], axis=0) * 100      # index to 100 at t0
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3.4))
sns.heatmap(indexed.loc[order], cmap="RdBu_r", center=100, ax=ax,
            cbar_kws={"label": "indexed to 100 at Jan 2024"},
            xticklabels=[m.strftime("%b") for m in wide.columns],
            linewidths=2, linecolor="white")           # 2px surface gap
ax.set_title("the same nine series as a heatmap: 60+ panels would fit here",
             loc="left", fontsize=9)
ax.set_ylabel("")
fig.savefig("/tmp/claude-0/heatmap_limit.png", dpi=110, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)
print("Indexing each row to 100 at t0 is what makes a heatmap of series at")
print("different scales comparable; the diverging scale is centred on 100.")
```

```text
  OVERLAY VS SMALL MULTIPLES, 9 SERIES

  OVERLAY                          SMALL MULTIPLES
   ___/\__/\___                    +------+------+------+
   /\_/  \/  \/                    | /\   | __/  | \__  |
  _/\/\__/\_/\_                    +------+------+------+
   needs 9 hues                    | _/\  | /\/  | \/\  |
   lines cross and occlude         +------+------+------+
   legend lookup per series        | /~\  | \    | ___  |
   the one decline is invisible    +------+------+------+
                                   1 hue, no occlusion, titles in place,
                                   and the odd shape is found by scanning

  Overlay wins ONLY when the comparison is between series at the same x.

  WHY SHARED SCALES ARE NOT OPTIONAL

  INDEPENDENT                       SHARED
  north  south  alpine             north  south  alpine
   /\     /\     /\                 /\     /\
   ||     ||     ||                 ||           .
   ||     ||     ||                 ||    __      (alpine is 12 vs south 420)
  all look the same size           the 35x difference is visible

  A grid invites comparison. Independent scales make the LAYOUT lie.

  THE FOUR RULES

    1. SHARE the scales                  (or the grid misleads)
    2. ORDER panels by value/time/size   (never alphabetically)
    3. MINIMISE chrome                   (outer axis labels only)
    4. ADD context to each panel         (faint others, or the average)

  THE COMPRESSION LADDER

    one panel per series       -> small multiples   position, high precision
    one ROW per series         -> heatmap           colour, low precision
                                                    but 60+ series fit
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Small multiples compare using position, the most accurately read channel,
>   while overlays force the reader onto colour and cope with occlusion.
> - Shared scales are mandatory, because a grid invites comparison and
>   independent axes make the layout itself misleading.
> - Order panels by value, magnitude, time, or geography, since readers infer
>   meaning from the sequence regardless of your intent.
> - Add a faint copy of the other series or the overall average to each panel so
>   the specific and the general read together.
> - Past roughly twenty panels, aggregate the tail or move to a heatmap, which
>   is the same grid with colour replacing position.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Take nine series at widely different scales, render them overlaid and as a
>    faceted grid, and time how long it takes someone to find the one that
>    declines.
> 2. Build the same grid twice, with independent and shared y axes, and state
>    the wrong conclusion the first invites.
> 3. Add faint context series and an endpoint label to each panel of a grid, and
>    sort the panels by their mean value.
> 4. Construct a two-variable facet grid where the relationship differs by cell,
>    then print the fitted slope per cell.
> 5. Interview: You need to show a metric's trend for 80 stores to a regional
>    manager. What do you build? (Hint: 80 panels is unreadable, so what does
>    the manager actually need to identify, and which form fits 80 rows?)

<a id="74-dashboards-and-reporting"></a>
### 7.4 Dashboards and Reporting

A chart that nobody acts on has no value, so the last step is delivery: the
layouts, definitions, tooling, automation, and narrative structure that carry a
finding from your notebook to a decision.

#### Dashboard Design Patterns

A dashboard is not a collection of charts, it is an interface built for a
recurring question. That distinction explains most dashboard failure: teams
build a place to put charts, the collection grows, nobody can say what any of
it is for, and eventually everyone goes back to asking an analyst.

Start by classifying what you are building, because the three kinds have
different designs and mixing them produces something that serves none of them.

**Operational dashboards** answer "is anything wrong right now?" They are
watched frequently, refresh often, and are dominated by current state against
thresholds. The reader wants to spend zero seconds on them when things are
fine, so the design goal is that normal looks obviously normal.

**Analytical dashboards** answer "why did this change?" They are used
occasionally, in longer sessions, and need breakdowns, comparisons, and enough
interaction to follow a question down a level.

**Strategic dashboards** answer "are we on track?" They are reviewed on a
cadence, show a few metrics against targets over long horizons, and should be
the sparsest of the three.

The layout patterns that work follow from how people read a screen. Attention
goes to the **top left first**, so the most important number belongs there, and
importance should decrease down and to the right. The standard structure is an
**inverted pyramid**: a row of headline numbers at the top, the main trend chart
below, breakdowns below that, and detail tables last. A reader who stops after
the first row should still have the answer.

Five rules carry most of the value.

**One filter row, above everything it scopes.** All charts re-render against the
same slice, so the numbers always agree. Per-chart filters are how a dashboard
starts contradicting itself, and a chart with its own date range belongs on a
different page.

**Every number needs a comparison.** "Revenue: 1.2M" is not information. Against
last month, against target, or against the same period last year, it becomes
information. A number with no reference point cannot be acted on.

**Show uncertainty and sample size.** A conversion rate of 8% from 25 sessions
should not look like one from 25,000. Cells built on small samples need their
counts visible or they will be read as signal.

**Define everything in reach.** Every metric needs a definition available from
the dashboard itself, ideally on hover or behind a single click. Ambiguity about
what a number means is the leading cause of dashboards being distrusted and
abandoned.

**Handle empty, loading, and error states deliberately.** A chart that renders
blank when a filter matches nothing looks broken. Say "no data for this
selection". While refreshing, hold the previous render at reduced opacity rather
than flashing a skeleton, so the layout does not jump.

The anti-patterns are worth naming because each is common. The **wall of
charts** with no hierarchy makes the reader find the story. **Vanity metrics**
such as cumulative totals only ever go up and cannot indicate a problem.
**Overloading** one view with every possible breakdown serves nobody. And a
dashboard with **no owner** rots: definitions drift, a data source changes,
and nobody notices until someone makes a bad decision from it.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(12)

# --- A METRIC WITH ITS COMPARISONS: what makes a number actionable. ---
days = pd.date_range("2024-04-01", periods=90, freq="D")
sessions = (9000 + 600 * np.sin(np.arange(90) / 7 * 2 * np.pi)
            + np.arange(90) * 18 + rng.normal(0, 350, 90)).round(0)
conv = np.clip(0.041 + rng.normal(0, .002, 90) - (np.arange(90) > 70) * .006,
               0, 1)
daily = pd.DataFrame({"date": days, "sessions": sessions,
                      "conversions": (sessions * conv).round(0)})
daily["conv_rate"] = daily["conversions"] / daily["sessions"]

def stat_tile(df: pd.DataFrame, value_col: str, target: float | None = None,
              window: int = 7) -> dict:
    """A headline number is never shipped alone. Attach the comparisons."""
    cur = df[value_col].tail(window).mean()
    prev = df[value_col].tail(window * 2).head(window).mean()
    yoy_proxy = df[value_col].head(window).mean()      # earliest window
    # A standard error, so a small-sample tile does not read as certain.
    n = df["sessions"].tail(window).sum()
    se = np.sqrt(cur * (1 - cur) / n) if 0 < cur < 1 else np.nan
    out = {
        "value": round(cur, 4),
        "vs_prev_period": round((cur / prev - 1) * 100, 1),
        "vs_period_start": round((cur / yoy_proxy - 1) * 100, 1),
        "sample_n": int(n),
        "std_err": round(se, 5) if se == se else None,
    }
    if target is not None:
        out["vs_target_pts"] = round((cur - target) * 100, 2)
        out["status"] = ("good" if cur >= target
                         else "warning" if cur >= target * .9 else "critical")
    return out

tile = stat_tile(daily, "conv_rate", target=0.040)
print("HEADLINE TILE")
for k, v in tile.items():
    print(f"  {k:16s} {v}")
print("\n'4.1%' alone is not information. Against last week, against the")
print("target, and with the sample size, it supports a decision.")

# --- THE INVERTED PYRAMID, as an explicit layout spec. ---
LAYOUT = [
    {"tier": 1, "row": "KPI row",      "height": "small",
     "content": "4-6 stat tiles: value, delta, sparkline, status"},
    {"tier": 2, "row": "primary trend", "height": "large",
     "content": "the one metric that defines success, over time, vs target"},
    {"tier": 3, "row": "breakdowns",    "height": "medium",
     "content": "2-3 charts: the same metric split by the key dimensions"},
    {"tier": 4, "row": "detail table",  "height": "medium",
     "content": "sortable rows, the accessible twin of every chart above"},
]
print("\n", pd.DataFrame(LAYOUT).to_string(index=False))
print("\nA reader who stops after tier 1 must still have the answer.")

# --- SMALL SAMPLES: the cell that will be misread. ---
segments = pd.DataFrame({
    "segment": ["organic", "paid", "email", "partner", "affiliate"],
    "sessions": [42_000, 18_500, 6_200, 410, 38],
    "conversions": [1_780, 690, 300, 24, 4],
})
segments["rate"] = segments["conversions"] / segments["sessions"]
# Wilson interval: behaves correctly at small n, unlike the normal approximation.
def wilson(k, n, z=1.96):
    if n == 0:
        return (np.nan, np.nan)
    p = k / n
    denom = 1 + z**2 / n
    centre = (p + z**2 / (2*n)) / denom
    half = z * np.sqrt(p*(1-p)/n + z**2/(4*n**2)) / denom
    return (centre - half, centre + half)

ci = segments.apply(lambda r: wilson(r["conversions"], r["sessions"]), axis=1)
segments["ci_lo"] = [c[0] for c in ci]
segments["ci_hi"] = [c[1] for c in ci]
segments["ci_width_pts"] = ((segments["ci_hi"] - segments["ci_lo"]) * 100).round(2)
segments["reportable"] = segments["sessions"] >= 1000
print("\n", segments.assign(rate=(segments["rate"]*100).round(2))
        [["segment", "sessions", "rate", "ci_width_pts", "reportable"]]
        .to_string(index=False))
print("\nAffiliate shows the highest rate and its interval spans ~40 points.")
print("Without the count or the interval, a reader reallocates budget to it.")

# --- ONE FILTER ROW: why per-chart filters break a dashboard. ---
print("""
  FILTER SCOPE

  RIGHT                              WRONG
  +-------------------------------+   +------------------+ +---------------+
  | date range | region | segment |   | chart A [last 7d]| | chart B [MTD] |
  +-------------------------------+   +------------------+ +---------------+
  | every chart below uses THIS   |   two charts, two ranges, and the
  | slice, so totals reconcile    |   totals never add up. Readers lose
  +-------------------------------+   trust in the whole page.

  If one chart genuinely needs its own range, it belongs on another page.
""")

# --- STATE HANDLING: empty, loading, error, stale. ---
def render_state(rows: int, loading: bool, error: str | None,
                 as_of: pd.Timestamp, now: pd.Timestamp) -> str:
    if error:
        return f"ERROR: {error} -- last good data {as_of:%Y-%m-%d %H:%M} UTC"
    if loading:
        return "REFRESHING: hold previous render at 60% opacity, no layout jump"
    if rows == 0:
        return "EMPTY: 'No data for this selection' + a clear-filters button"
    staleness = (now - as_of).total_seconds() / 3600
    if staleness > 24:
        return f"STALE: data is {staleness:.0f}h old -- show a warning banner"
    return f"OK: {rows:,} rows, as of {as_of:%H:%M} UTC"

now = pd.Timestamp("2024-06-30 12:00")
for case in [
        {"rows": 4210, "loading": False, "error": None,
         "as_of": now - pd.Timedelta("2h")},
        {"rows": 0, "loading": False, "error": None,
         "as_of": now - pd.Timedelta("1h")},
        {"rows": 900, "loading": True, "error": None,
         "as_of": now - pd.Timedelta("1h")},
        {"rows": 4210, "loading": False, "error": None,
         "as_of": now - pd.Timedelta("40h")},
        {"rows": 0, "loading": False, "error": "upstream table missing",
         "as_of": now - pd.Timedelta("26h")}]:
    print(f"  {render_state(now=now, **case)}")

# --- VANITY VS ACTIONABLE METRICS ---
comparison = pd.DataFrame([
    ("cumulative signups",   "vanity",     "only ever rises; cannot signal a problem",
     "weekly new signups"),
    ("total page views",     "vanity",     "no link to any decision",
     "conversion rate by landing page"),
    ("registered users",     "vanity",     "includes everyone who ever signed up",
     "weekly active users"),
    ("average revenue",      "misleading", "one whale moves it",
     "median revenue + the distribution"),
    ("uptime this quarter",  "lagging",    "too coarse to act on",
     "error rate per minute vs threshold"),
], columns=["metric", "problem", "why", "use instead"])
print("\n", comparison.to_string(index=False))

# --- A DASHBOARD SPEC AUDIT ---
def audit_dashboard(spec: dict) -> list[str]:
    issues = []
    if spec.get("kind") not in {"operational", "analytical", "strategic"}:
        issues.append("no declared kind: it will drift into serving none well")
    if spec.get("per_chart_filters"):
        issues.append("per-chart filters: totals will stop reconciling")
    if not spec.get("comparisons_on_every_metric"):
        issues.append("bare numbers with no baseline, target, or prior period")
    if not spec.get("shows_sample_size"):
        issues.append("no sample size or interval: small cells read as signal")
    if not spec.get("definitions_reachable"):
        issues.append("metric definitions not reachable from the dashboard")
    if not spec.get("empty_state"):
        issues.append("no empty state: a matched-nothing filter looks broken")
    if not spec.get("owner"):
        issues.append("no named owner: definitions will drift unnoticed")
    if not spec.get("as_of_stamp"):
        issues.append("no as-of timestamp: staleness is invisible")
    if spec.get("n_charts", 0) > 9:
        issues.append(f"{spec['n_charts']} charts: no hierarchy, reader must hunt")
    if spec.get("kind") == "operational" and not spec.get("thresholds"):
        issues.append("operational view without thresholds: 'normal' is not obvious")
    return issues

print("\naudit of a typical grown-organically dashboard:")
for i in audit_dashboard({"n_charts": 17, "per_chart_filters": True}):
    print("  -", i)
print("\naudit of a designed one:",
      audit_dashboard({
          "kind": "operational", "n_charts": 6, "thresholds": True,
          "comparisons_on_every_metric": True, "shows_sample_size": True,
          "definitions_reachable": True, "empty_state": True,
          "owner": "growth-analytics", "as_of_stamp": True}) or "no issues")
```

```text
  THE THREE KINDS

  kind         question              cadence      design goal
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  operational  anything wrong NOW?   continuous   normal looks OBVIOUSLY normal
  analytical   why did this change?  occasional   breakdowns + drill-down
  strategic    are we on track?      weekly/mo.   few metrics, long horizon,
                                                  against target
  Mixing them produces a page that serves none of them.

  THE INVERTED PYRAMID

  +---------------------------------------------------------------+
  | date range | region | segment            <- ONE filter row    |
  +---------------------------------------------------------------+
  | [ 4.1% ]  [ 9,240 ]  [ $1.2M ]  [ 2.3d ]  <- tier 1: KPIs     |
  |  +0.2pt    -3.1%      +8.4%      flat        value + delta     |
  +---------------------------------------------------------------+
  |                                                               |
  |     tier 2: the ONE trend that defines success, vs target     |
  |                                                               |
  +----------------------------+----------------------------------+
  |  tier 3: by channel        |  tier 3: by segment              |
  +----------------------------+----------------------------------+
  |  tier 4: detail table (the accessible twin of the charts)     |
  +---------------------------------------------------------------+
   Attention flows top-left -> down-right. A reader who stops after
   tier 1 still has the answer.

  EVERY NUMBER NEEDS A COMPARISON

    "Revenue: $1.2M"                          not information
    "Revenue: $1.2M, +8% vs last month,       information: a reader can
     3% below the $1.24M target, n=18,402"    act on this

  STATE HANDLING

    OK          rows + as-of timestamp
    EMPTY       "No data for this selection" + clear-filters (never blank)
    REFRESHING  hold the old render at reduced opacity (never a skeleton flash)
    STALE       a banner naming the age of the data
    ERROR       what broke + when the last good data was
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Classify the dashboard as operational, analytical, or strategic, because the
>   three have different designs and mixing them serves nobody.
> - Lay it out as an inverted pyramid so a reader who stops after the top row
>   still has the answer.
> - One filter row scoping everything keeps the numbers reconciling; per-chart
>   filters are how a dashboard contradicts itself.
> - Every number needs a comparison against a target, a prior period, or a
>   baseline, plus a visible sample size.
> - Design the empty, loading, stale, and error states, and give the dashboard a
>   named owner or its definitions will drift unnoticed.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a stat tile function returning a value alongside its change versus
>    the prior period, its gap to target, and its sample size.
> 2. Compute Wilson confidence intervals for conversion rates across segments
>    of very different sizes and identify which are not reportable.
> 3. Take a dashboard you use and classify it as operational, analytical, or
>    strategic, then list the charts that do not fit that classification.
> 4. Implement a dashboard audit function and run it against two real
>    dashboards.
> 5. Interview: A dashboard has 22 charts and the team says it is not useful.
>    Where do you start? (Hint: what single question should it answer, and
>    what would you delete to make that question answerable in five seconds?)

#### Metric and KPI Definition

Most disagreements about numbers are not disagreements about data, they are
disagreements about definitions. Two teams report different revenue because one
counts refunds and the other does not. Both are right and the meeting is lost to
reconciliation. Defining metrics precisely is unglamorous and it prevents more
wasted time than any other practice in analytics.

A metric definition needs five things, and a definition missing any of them will
eventually produce two numbers.

**The precise event or entity.** Not "active users" but "distinct user IDs
with at least one recorded session of 10 seconds or more". Every vague word is
a place two implementations will diverge.

**The time basis.** Calendar month or rolling 30 days? Event timestamp or
ingestion timestamp? In which time zone? A daily metric computed in UTC and one
computed in local time disagree for a predictable fraction of users, forever.

**The population and its exclusions.** Internal accounts, bots, test users,
churned accounts, refunded orders. Exclusions are where definitions quietly
differ most.

**The aggregation.** Sum, mean, median, or percentile; and critically, whether a
ratio is computed per unit and then averaged, or as a total over a total. The
average of per-country conversion rates is not the overall conversion rate, as
covered in chapter 6, and this single distinction accounts for a large share of
reconciliation disputes.

**The grain.** One row per what? A metric whose grain is unstated cannot be
joined to anything safely.

Beyond individual definitions, three structural ideas make a metric set work.

**Distinguish leading from lagging indicators.** Revenue is lagging: it tells
you what happened and it is too late to act on. Trial-to-paid conversion is
leading: it moves first and predicts revenue. A dashboard of only lagging
metrics is a history lesson.

**Choose input metrics you can actually move.** Output metrics such as revenue
are the goal; input metrics such as page load time, activation rate, or support
response time are what a team can act on directly. Teams should be measured on
outputs and given inputs to work with.

**Pair every primary metric with a guardrail.** Optimising one number in
isolation reliably damages something else. Session count paired with session
quality. Speed of shipping paired with incident rate. Conversion paired with
refund rate. This is the practical answer to Goodhart's law, that a measure used
as a target stops being a good measure, and the mechanism is always the same:
someone finds a way to move the number without producing the underlying value.

The engineering practice that makes all of this stick is a **metrics layer**: a
single place where each metric is defined once, in code, and every dashboard and
query derives from it. The alternative, each dashboard implementing its own SQL,
guarantees drift.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

rng = np.random.default_rng(15)

# --- HOW MANY NUMBERS CAN "ACTIVE USERS" PRODUCE? ---
n = 6000
events = pd.DataFrame({
    "user": rng.integers(1, 1200, n),
    "ts_utc": pd.Timestamp("2024-06-01") + pd.to_timedelta(
        rng.integers(0, 30 * 24 * 60, n), "m"),
    "duration_s": rng.gamma(2, 20, n).round(0),
    "is_internal": rng.random(n) < 0.04,
    "is_bot": rng.random(n) < 0.07,
})
events["tz_offset_h"] = rng.choice([-8, -5, 0, 1, 9], n)
events["ts_local"] = events["ts_utc"] + pd.to_timedelta(
    events["tz_offset_h"], "h")

definitions = {
    "any event, UTC month":
        lambda d: d[d.ts_utc.dt.month == 6]["user"].nunique(),
    "+ exclude internal":
        lambda d: d[(d.ts_utc.dt.month == 6) & ~d.is_internal]["user"].nunique(),
    "+ exclude bots":
        lambda d: d[(d.ts_utc.dt.month == 6) & ~d.is_internal
                    & ~d.is_bot]["user"].nunique(),
    "+ session >= 10s":
        lambda d: d[(d.ts_utc.dt.month == 6) & ~d.is_internal & ~d.is_bot
                    & (d.duration_s >= 10)]["user"].nunique(),
    "same, but LOCAL month":
        lambda d: d[(d.ts_local.dt.month == 6) & ~d.is_internal & ~d.is_bot
                    & (d.duration_s >= 10)]["user"].nunique(),
    "rolling 30d to Jun 30":
        lambda d: d[(d.ts_utc > pd.Timestamp("2024-05-31")) & ~d.is_internal
                    & ~d.is_bot & (d.duration_s >= 10)]["user"].nunique(),
}
print("ONE PHRASE, SIX NUMBERS:")
results = {k: f(events) for k, f in definitions.items()}
for k, v in results.items():
    print(f"  {v:>5}   {k}")
spread = max(results.values()) - min(results.values())
print(f"\nspread: {spread} users ({spread/max(results.values()):.0%})."
      " Every one of these is a defensible reading of 'active users'.")

# --- RATIO OF SUMS VS MEAN OF RATIOS: the classic reconciliation dispute. ---
by_country = pd.DataFrame({
    "country": ["US", "CA", "DE", "JP"],
    "sessions": [80_000, 9_000, 6_000, 500],
    "conversions": [3_200, 450, 240, 45],
})
by_country["rate"] = by_country["conversions"] / by_country["sessions"]
mean_of_ratios = by_country["rate"].mean()
ratio_of_sums = by_country["conversions"].sum() / by_country["sessions"].sum()
print(f"\nmean of per-country rates : {mean_of_ratios:.4%}")
print(f"total conv / total sessions: {ratio_of_sums:.4%}")
print(f"difference: {(mean_of_ratios - ratio_of_sums)*100:.2f} points."
      " Both are computable; only one is 'the conversion rate'.")
print("Specify which in the definition, or two dashboards will disagree.")

# --- A METRIC DEFINITION AS CODE, not as a sentence in a wiki. ---
@dataclass
class MetricDefinition:
    name: str
    description: str
    entity: str                       # one row per WHAT
    event_filter: str                 # the precise event
    time_basis: str                   # calendar/rolling, which timestamp, which tz
    exclusions: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    aggregation: str = "count_distinct"
    ratio_rule: str | None = None     # ratio-of-sums or mean-of-ratios
    owner: str = "unowned"
    guardrails: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    source_table: str = ""

    def validate(self) -> list[str]:
        problems = []
        for word in ("active", "engaged", "successful", "valid", "recent"):
            described = word in self.description.lower()
            if described and word not in self.event_filter.lower():
                problems.append(f"'{word}' used in the description but not defined"
                                " in the filter")
        if "tz" not in self.time_basis and "UTC" not in self.time_basis:
            problems.append("time basis does not state a time zone")
        if self.aggregation.startswith("ratio") and not self.ratio_rule:
            problems.append("ratio metric without a ratio_rule: ambiguous")
        if not self.exclusions:
            problems.append("no exclusions listed: are bots and internal in?")
        if self.owner == "unowned":
            problems.append("no owner: this definition will drift")
        if not self.guardrails:
            problems.append("no guardrail metric: Goodhart's law applies")
        return problems

wau = MetricDefinition(
    name="weekly_active_users",
    description="Distinct users with a qualifying session in the trailing 7 days",
    entity="one row per (week_start, user_id)",
    event_filter="session_duration_s >= 10 AND event_name = 'session_start'",
    time_basis="rolling 7 days ending Sunday 23:59, event timestamp, tz=UTC",
    exclusions=["is_internal = true", "is_bot = true", "account_state = 'test'"],
    aggregation="count_distinct(user_id)",
    owner="growth-analytics",
    guardrails=["session_quality_score", "support_ticket_rate"],
    source_table="analytics.fct_sessions",
)
print(f"\n{wau.name}: {wau.validate() or 'definition complete'}")

vague = MetricDefinition(
    name="engagement",
    description="How engaged our active users are",
    entity="user",
    event_filter="event_name IS NOT NULL",
    time_basis="monthly",
    aggregation="ratio",
)
print(f"\n{vague.name} problems:")
for p in vague.validate():
    print("  -", p)

# --- LEADING VS LAGGING, AND INPUT VS OUTPUT ---
metrics = pd.DataFrame([
    ("monthly revenue",        "lagging", "output", "cannot be moved directly"),
    ("trial-to-paid rate",     "leading", "output", "predicts revenue ~1 mo ahead"),
    ("activation within 7d",   "leading", "input",  "a team can change onboarding"),
    ("page load p95",          "leading", "input",  "an engineer can fix this today"),
    ("net revenue retention",  "lagging", "output", "the quarterly scoreboard"),
    ("support first-response", "leading", "input",  "staffing and tooling move it"),
], columns=["metric", "timing", "type", "note"])
print("\n", metrics.to_string(index=False))
print("\nA dashboard of only lagging outputs is a history lesson. Pair each")
print("output with the inputs a team can actually act on.")

# --- GUARDRAILS: what optimising one number breaks. ---
print("""
  GOODHART PAIRS

  primary metric              guardrail                  what goes wrong alone
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  sessions per user           session quality / depth    autoplay, notification
                                                         spam
  conversion rate             refund + chargeback rate   dark patterns
  tickets closed per agent    reopen rate + CSAT         closing without fixing
  deploy frequency            change-failure rate        shipping breakage
  model accuracy              per-segment accuracy       ignoring a minority
                                                         group
  ad revenue per session      churn rate                 ad load that drives
                                                         people away

  Every primary metric ships with the guardrail that catches its cheat.
""")

# --- A METRICS LAYER: define once, derive everywhere. ---
print("""
  WITHOUT A METRICS LAYER          WITH ONE

  dashboard A: its own SQL          metrics.yml / semantic layer
  dashboard B: its own SQL   ---->    weekly_active_users:
  notebook C:  its own SQL              filter, exclusions, tz, grain
  the board deck: a spreadsheet             |
                                    +-------+--------+--------+
  four numbers, all called          dashboard   notebook   deck
  "active users"                    one definition, four consumers

  Implementations: dbt metrics, Cube, LookML, MetricFlow, or simply one
  SQL view per metric that everything else selects from. The tool matters
  far less than the rule: a metric is defined exactly once.
""")
```

```text
  FIVE PARTS OF A DEFINITION

    1. EVENT/ENTITY   "distinct user_id with a session >= 10s"
                      not "active user"
    2. TIME BASIS     "rolling 7d, event timestamp, UTC"
                      not "weekly"
    3. POPULATION     "excluding internal, bots, test accounts"
                      the most common source of divergence
    4. AGGREGATION    "count_distinct", and for ratios:
                      ratio-of-sums, NOT mean-of-ratios
    5. GRAIN          "one row per (week_start, user_id)"

  ONE PHRASE, SIX ANSWERS

    "active users in June"
      1,043   any event, UTC calendar month
        998   excluding internal accounts
        933   also excluding bots
        871   also requiring a session >= 10s
        864   the same, but on the user's LOCAL month
        879   rolling 30 days to 30 June
    A 17% spread, and every one is defensible.

  RATIO OF SUMS VS MEAN OF RATIOS

    country  sessions  conv   rate
    US        80,000   3,200  4.00%
    CA         9,000     450  5.00%
    DE         6,000     240  4.00%
    JP           500      45  9.00%

    mean of rates          5.50%   <- JP's 500 sessions count as much as
                                      the US's 80,000
    total conv / total     4.02%   <- "the conversion rate"

  LEADING VS LAGGING, INPUT VS OUTPUT

                  INPUT (a team can move it)   OUTPUT (the goal)
    LEADING       page load p95                trial-to-paid rate
                  activation within 7d
    LAGGING       -                            monthly revenue
                                               net revenue retention

    Measure teams on outputs; give them inputs to work with.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A metric definition needs the precise event, the time basis with a time
>   zone, the exclusions, the aggregation, and the grain, or two
>   implementations will diverge.
> - One vague phrase such as "active users" yields numbers that differ by tens
>   of percent, every one of them defensible.
> - For ratios, specify ratio-of-sums rather than mean-of-ratios, since the
>   difference drives a large share of reconciliation disputes.
> - Lagging output metrics are a history lesson; pair them with leading input
>   metrics that a team can actually move.
> - Give every primary metric a guardrail, because a measure used as a target
>   invites moving the number without producing the value.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compute "monthly active users" six ways by varying exclusions, the time
>    zone, and calendar versus rolling windows, and report the spread.
> 2. For a segmented conversion table, compute the mean of rates and the ratio
>    of sums, and construct segment sizes that make them differ by two points.
> 3. Write a metric definition dataclass with a validator that rejects
>    undefined adjectives, a missing time zone, and a ratio without a rule.
> 4. Pick three metrics your team reports and name the guardrail each needs.
> 5. Interview: Finance and product report different monthly revenue and both
>    insist they are right. How do you resolve it? (Hint: which of the five
>    definition parts is most likely to differ, and what artefact ends the
>    argument permanently?)

#### Self-Service BI Tools

Business intelligence tools exist because the bottleneck in most organisations
is not analysis, it is the analyst. Every routine question that requires a
person consumes hours and adds delay, and most of those questions are
variations on ones already answered. Self-service tooling aims to let people
answer their own variations.

The category divides along one axis that matters more than any feature list:
**who defines the metrics?**

In a **semantic-layer tool**, an analytics engineer defines dimensions,
measures, and joins centrally, and business users explore within that model.
Looker's LookML is the reference example. The benefit is that everyone's
numbers agree, because there is one definition. The cost is that every new
dimension requires a modelling change, which makes the tool feel slow to users
who want something now.

In a **direct-query tool**, users connect to tables and build their own logic.
Tableau, Power BI, and most notebook-based approaches work this way. The benefit
is speed and flexibility. The cost is that definitions multiply, and within a
year several dashboards report different values for the same metric name.

Neither is correct in general. The practical resolution most organisations reach
is a **layered model**: certified, governed metrics for the numbers that matter,
such as anything reported to leadership or used in compensation, and free
exploration for everything else, clearly marked as uncertified.

The landscape in brief:

| Tool | Model | Strength | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Looker | semantic layer, LookML | governed consistency | modelling effort, cost |
| Tableau | direct query, visual | visualisation depth | definition sprawl |
| Power BI | direct query, DAX | Microsoft integration, price | DAX learning curve |
| Metabase | light semantic layer | easy setup, open source | limited modelling |
| Superset | SQL-first, open source | free, extensible | self-hosted operations |
| Mode, Hex | notebook plus BI | analyst-friendly, SQL first | less end-user-friendly |
| dbt plus a semantic layer | definitions in the warehouse | version-controlled metrics | still needs a front end |

Whatever the tool, four practices determine whether self-service works.

**Model the data for the audience.** Business users cannot navigate a normalised
schema with forty tables. Build wide, denormalised, well-named tables where the
joins are already done and the columns mean what they say. Most self-service
failures are data-modelling failures wearing a tool's name.

**Certify a small set of dashboards and mark the rest.** A visible distinction
between "this is the official number" and "someone built this for themselves"
prevents the most damaging outcome, which is an ad-hoc chart being presented to
an executive as fact.

**Manage the sprawl actively.** Dashboards accumulate. Track usage, archive what
nobody opens, and require an owner for anything certified. An unmaintained
dashboard is worse than no dashboard because it looks authoritative.

**Control query cost.** Self-service against a cloud warehouse means users can
run expensive queries by accident. Aggregate tables, result caching, partition
limits, and per-user budgets are not optional at scale.

The honest trade-off to state plainly: self-service reduces analyst load on
routine questions and increases governance work. The total effort does not
vanish, it moves from answering questions to maintaining a model. That is
usually a good trade, and it is a trade rather than a saving.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(20)

# --- WHY MODELLING MATTERS MORE THAN THE TOOL ---
# A normalised schema: correct, efficient, and unusable by a business user.
orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": range(1, 9),
    "cust_id": [101, 102, 101, 103, 104, 102, 105, 103],
    "prod_id": [7, 8, 9, 7, 8, 7, 9, 8],
    "chan_id": [1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 1, 3, 2],
    "amt_cents": [4999, 12900, 899, 4999, 12900, 4999, 899, 12900],
    "st": ["C", "C", "R", "C", "P", "C", "C", "R"],   # what is "R"? "P"?
})
customers = pd.DataFrame({"cust_id": [101, 102, 103, 104, 105],
                          "seg_cd": ["E", "S", "M", "S", "E"],
                          "ctry": ["US", "CA", "US", "DE", "US"]})
products = pd.DataFrame({"prod_id": [7, 8, 9],
                         "nm": ["Basic", "Pro", "Addon"],
                         "cat": ["plan", "plan", "addon"]})
channels = pd.DataFrame({"chan_id": [1, 2, 3],
                         "chan": ["direct", "partner", "organic"]})

print("NORMALISED: a user must know 4 tables, 3 joins, and 5 code mappings")
print(orders.head(3).to_string(index=False))

# The same data, modelled FOR the audience: one wide table, decoded, named.
STATUS = {"C": "completed", "R": "refunded", "P": "pending"}
SEGMENT = {"E": "enterprise", "S": "smb", "M": "mid-market"}

wide = (orders
        .merge(customers, on="cust_id")
        .merge(products, on="prod_id")
        .merge(channels, on="chan_id")
        .assign(
            order_status=lambda d: d["st"].map(STATUS),
            customer_segment=lambda d: d["seg_cd"].map(SEGMENT),
            revenue_usd=lambda d: (d["amt_cents"] / 100).round(2),
            # Pre-compute the flag every definition argument is about.
            is_net_revenue=lambda d: d["st"] == "C",
        )
        .rename(columns={"ctry": "customer_country", "nm": "product_name",
                         "cat": "product_category", "chan": "acquisition_channel"})
        [["order_id", "order_status", "customer_segment", "customer_country",
          "product_name", "product_category", "acquisition_channel",
          "revenue_usd", "is_net_revenue"]])
print("\nMODELLED FOR THE AUDIENCE: one table, decoded, self-describing")
print(wide.head(4).to_string(index=False))

# A business user can now answer their own question with no joins.
print("\na user's own question, answered without an analyst:")
print(wide[wide["is_net_revenue"]]
      .groupby(["customer_segment", "acquisition_channel"])["revenue_usd"]
      .sum().round(2).to_string())

# --- THE SEMANTIC LAYER: define once, in version control. ---
SEMANTIC_MODEL = {
    "model": "orders",
    "source": "analytics.fct_orders_wide",
    "dimensions": {
        "customer_segment": {"type": "string", "label": "Customer segment"},
        "acquisition_channel": {"type": "string", "label": "Channel"},
        "order_month": {"type": "time", "grain": "month", "tz": "UTC"},
    },
    "measures": {
        "net_revenue": {
            "sql": "SUM(CASE WHEN is_net_revenue THEN revenue_usd ELSE 0 END)",
            "label": "Net revenue (USD)",
            "description": "Completed orders only; refunds and pending excluded",
            "owner": "finance-analytics", "certified": True,
        },
        "gross_revenue": {
            "sql": "SUM(revenue_usd)",
            "label": "Gross revenue (USD)",
            "description": "All orders regardless of status",
            "owner": "finance-analytics", "certified": True,
        },
        "conversion_rate": {
            "sql": "SUM(conversions) / NULLIF(SUM(sessions), 0)",
            "label": "Conversion rate",
            # State the rule explicitly: this is a ratio of sums.
            "description": "Ratio of sums, never the mean of per-group rates",
            "owner": "growth-analytics", "certified": True,
        },
    },
}
print(f"\nsemantic model exposes {len(SEMANTIC_MODEL['measures'])} certified"
      f" measures over {len(SEMANTIC_MODEL['dimensions'])} dimensions")
print("Both revenue definitions exist, are NAMED differently, and are")
print("documented. The dispute is resolved by naming, not by argument.")

# --- CERTIFICATION: the visible distinction that prevents the worst outcome. ---
catalogue = pd.DataFrame([
    ("Exec weekly review",   "certified",   "finance-analytics", 412, 2),
    ("Growth funnel",        "certified",   "growth-analytics",  260, 5),
    ("Support SLA",          "certified",   "support-ops",       118, 9),
    ("my churn exploration", "uncertified", "a.patel",             3, 240),
    ("Q2 campaign v3 FINAL", "uncertified", "unowned",             1, 310),
    ("Copy of Copy of KPIs", "uncertified", "unowned",             0, 380),
], columns=["dashboard", "status", "owner", "views_30d", "days_since_edit"])

catalogue["action"] = np.select(
    [(catalogue["status"] == "certified") & (catalogue["days_since_edit"] > 90),
     (catalogue["views_30d"] == 0) & (catalogue["days_since_edit"] > 180),
     (catalogue["views_30d"] < 5) & (catalogue["owner"] == "unowned"),
     catalogue["status"] == "certified"],
    ["REVIEW: certified but stale", "ARCHIVE: unused and abandoned",
     "ARCHIVE: orphaned", "keep"],
    default="keep as personal")
print("\nDASHBOARD LIFECYCLE AUDIT")
print(catalogue.to_string(index=False))

# --- QUERY COST: self-service means users can spend money by accident. ---
queries = pd.DataFrame({
    "dashboard": ["Exec weekly", "Growth funnel", "Ad-hoc explore",
                  "Support SLA", "Ad-hoc explore"],
    "gb_scanned": [0.4, 2.1, 840.0, 0.9, 1_250.0],
    "runs_per_day": [30, 120, 8, 200, 4],
})
COST_PER_TB = 6.25
queries["daily_usd"] = (queries["gb_scanned"] / 1024 * COST_PER_TB
                        * queries["runs_per_day"]).round(2)
queries["monthly_usd"] = (queries["daily_usd"] * 30).round(0)
print("\nQUERY COST BY DASHBOARD")
print(queries.sort_values("monthly_usd", ascending=False).to_string(index=False))
total = queries["monthly_usd"].sum()
adhoc = queries[queries["dashboard"] == "Ad-hoc explore"]["monthly_usd"].sum()
print(f"\ntotal ${total:,.0f}/mo, of which ad-hoc exploration is "
      f"${adhoc:,.0f} ({adhoc/total:.0%})")
print("Two unpartitioned exploratory queries cost more than every governed")
print("dashboard combined. Aggregate tables and partition limits, not policy.")

# --- THE TRADE-OFF, STATED HONESTLY ---
print("""
  WHAT SELF-SERVICE ACTUALLY TRADES

  decreases                          increases
  ---------------------------------  ---------------------------------------
  analyst time on routine questions  data-modelling and maintenance work
  turnaround time for the requester  governance: certification, definitions
  the analyst as a bottleneck        query cost exposure
                                     risk of conflicting numbers in circulation

  The effort does not vanish; it moves from ANSWERING to MODELLING. That is
  usually a good trade, and it is a trade, not a saving.

  THE LAYERED RESOLUTION

    certified   leadership reporting, compensation, board numbers
                -> semantic layer, named owner, change review
    exploratory everything else
                -> direct query, clearly marked uncertified, no SLA
""")
```

```text
  THE AXIS THAT MATTERS: WHO DEFINES THE METRICS?

  SEMANTIC LAYER                     DIRECT QUERY
  analytics engineer defines         users define their own
  dimensions + measures centrally    logic per dashboard
        |                                  |
        v                                  v
  everyone's numbers AGREE           fast and flexible
  new dimension = a modelling task   definitions MULTIPLY
  feels slow to users                4 dashboards, 4 "revenues"

  Resolution: layer them. Certified metrics for what matters, free
  exploration for everything else, and mark which is which.

  MODEL FOR THE AUDIENCE

  NORMALISED (correct, unusable)     WIDE (usable)
  orders    + customers              fct_orders_wide
  + products + channels              order_status   "completed"
  st = "C", seg_cd = "E"             customer_segment "enterprise"
  4 tables, 3 joins, 5 code maps     0 joins, 0 lookups
                                     is_net_revenue  true

  Most "the BI tool is bad" complaints are data-modelling complaints.

  THE FOUR PRACTICES

    1. MODEL for the audience     wide, denormalised, decoded, well named
    2. CERTIFY a small set        and visibly mark everything else
    3. MANAGE sprawl              track usage, archive the unused, require
                                  an owner
    4. CONTROL cost               aggregates, caching, partition limits,
                                  budgets
```

> Key Takeaways
> - The defining question for a business intelligence tool is who defines the
>   metrics, centrally in a semantic layer or per dashboard by users.
> - Most self-service failures are data-modelling failures: business users need
>   wide, denormalised, decoded tables with the joins already done.
> - Certify a small governed set and visibly mark everything else, so an ad-hoc
>   chart is never presented as the official number.
> - Dashboards accumulate, so track usage, require owners, and archive
>   actively, because an unmaintained dashboard still looks authoritative.
> - Self-service moves effort from answering questions to maintaining a model
>   and controlling query cost, which is a trade rather than a saving.

> 3. Build a dashboard lifecycle audit that flags certified-but-stale, unused,
>    and orphaned dashboards from usage and edit dates.
> 4. Estimate the monthly warehouse cost of five queries from their bytes
>    scanned and run frequency, and identify which one to fix first.
> 5. Interview: Leadership asks you to "let the business self-serve so analysts
>    can focus on deeper work". What do you tell them it will require? (Hint:
>    what work appears that did not exist before, and what happens to the
>    numbers without it?)

#### Automated Reporting Pipelines

Any report you produce more than twice should be automated. The reason is not
only the time saved, it is that a manual report is unreproducible and
inconsistent: someone forgets a filter, runs it a day early, or copies last
week's chart by accident. Automation makes the report a deterministic function
of the data plus a date.

The pieces of an automated report pipeline:

**A parameterised source.** One script or notebook taking a date range and any
filters as parameters, with no hard-coded values and no manual steps. If it
has a cell you have to edit, it is not automated.

**Scheduled execution** with retries and a timeout. Cron is the simplest form;
an orchestrator such as Airflow, Dagster, or Prefect adds dependency
management, backfills, and alerting, which you need as soon as a report
depends on an upstream job.

**Dependency awareness** is the piece people skip and regret. A report that runs
at a fixed time regardless of whether its source tables loaded will eventually
publish a report built on yesterday's data or on a half-loaded table. The report
should depend on the data being ready, not on the clock.

**Validation before publication.** This is the most important element and the
one most often missing. Check row counts against expectations, check that key
metrics fall in plausible ranges, check for nulls in required fields, and
check that the period is complete. A pipeline that publishes a wrong report on
schedule is worse than one that fails, because a failure gets noticed and a
wrong number gets believed and acted on.

**Rendering and delivery.** Produce the output format your audience actually
uses, and deliver it where they already are. A report emailed to people who
work in Slack does not get read. Include a link back to the source dashboard
so anyone can go deeper.

**Observability of the pipeline itself.** Log every run, alert on failures to a
person rather than a mailbox nobody watches, and make the last successful run
time visible in the report. A silently broken report is the standard failure
mode, and the usual way it manifests is that nobody notices for a month.

Two design principles worth adopting.

**Idempotency.** Running the report for the same date twice produces the same
output, and re-running never duplicates or corrupts anything. This makes retries
and backfills safe, which is what makes the pipeline operable.

**Alert on exceptions, not on schedule.** A report that arrives every morning
whether or not anything changed trains its recipients to ignore it. The
higher-value pattern for operational metrics is to send something only when a
threshold is crossed or an anomaly appears, with the routine numbers available
on a dashboard for anyone who wants them.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timezone

rng = np.random.default_rng(30)

# --- 1. PARAMETERISED, not hard-coded. Everything is an argument. ---
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ReportParams:
    as_of: pd.Timestamp                  # the run date, never datetime.now()
    lookback_days: int = 28
    region: str | None = None
    min_rows_expected: int = 1000

    @property
    def start(self) -> pd.Timestamp:
        return self.as_of - pd.Timedelta(days=self.lookback_days)

def extract(params: ReportParams) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Stand-in for a warehouse query. Note: bounded by params, not by now()."""
    days = pd.date_range(params.start, params.as_of - pd.Timedelta("1d"), freq="D")
    rows = []
    for d in days:
        for region in ["north", "south", "east"]:
            if params.region and region != params.region:
                continue
            base = {"north": 1400, "south": 900, "east": 480}[region]
            rows.append({"date": d, "region": region,
                         "sessions": int(base + rng.normal(0, base * .07)),
                         "orders": int(base * .042 + rng.normal(0, 6))})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

# --- 2. VALIDATION GATES: fail loudly rather than publish quietly wrong. ---
@dataclass
class Check:
    name: str
    passed: bool
    detail: str
    severity: str = "error"          # "error" blocks publication, "warn" notes it

def validate(df: pd.DataFrame, params: ReportParams) -> list[Check]:
    checks = []

    checks.append(Check("row_volume", len(df) >= params.min_rows_expected // 10,
                        f"{len(df)} rows"))

    # Completeness: every expected date present, and the period is finished.
    expected_days = params.lookback_days
    actual_days = df["date"].nunique()
    checks.append(Check("date_completeness", actual_days == expected_days,
                        f"{actual_days} of {expected_days} days present"))

    latest = df["date"].max()
    checks.append(Check("no_partial_period",
                        latest < params.as_of.normalize(),
                        f"latest date {latest:%Y-%m-%d}, as_of "
                        f"{params.as_of:%Y-%m-%d}"))

    # Required fields must not be null.
    nulls = df[["sessions", "orders"]].isna().sum().sum()
    checks.append(Check("no_nulls", nulls == 0, f"{nulls} nulls in key fields"))

    # Plausibility: a metric outside a sane band means something broke upstream.
    rate = df["orders"].sum() / max(df["sessions"].sum(), 1)
    checks.append(Check("rate_plausible", 0.005 <= rate <= 0.20,
                        f"conversion rate {rate:.3%}"))

    # Continuity: a sudden level shift is usually a pipeline change, not news.
    daily = df.groupby("date")["sessions"].sum()
    if len(daily) > 7:
        recent, prior = daily.tail(7).mean(), daily.head(len(daily) - 7).mean()
        shift = abs(recent / prior - 1)
        checks.append(Check("no_level_shift", shift < 0.35,
                            f"recent 7d differ from prior by {shift:.1%}",
                            severity="warn"))
    return checks

def gate(checks: list[Check]) -> bool:
    """Publication is blocked by any failing error-severity check."""
    for c in checks:
        mark = "PASS" if c.passed else ("FAIL" if c.severity == "error" else "WARN")
        print(f"  [{mark:4s}] {c.name:20s} {c.detail}")
    return all(c.passed for c in checks if c.severity == "error")

params = ReportParams(as_of=pd.Timestamp("2024-07-01"), lookback_days=28)
data = extract(params)
print("VALIDATION")
ok = gate(validate(data, params))
print(f"\npublish? {ok}")

# A broken extract must be BLOCKED, not published.
print("\nVALIDATION against a truncated, partly-null extract:")
broken = data.head(30).copy()
broken.loc[broken.index[:4], "orders"] = np.nan
blocked = gate(validate(broken, params))
print(f"\npublish? {blocked}   <- the gate did its job")

# --- 3. IDEMPOTENCY: same inputs, same output, safe to re-run. ---
def transform(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    out = (df.groupby("region")
             .agg(sessions=("sessions", "sum"), orders=("orders", "sum"))
             .assign(conv_rate=lambda d: (d["orders"] / d["sessions"]).round(5))
             .sort_values("orders", ascending=False))
    return out

a, b = transform(data), transform(data)
print(f"\nidempotent transform: {a.equals(b)}")

import hashlib
def content_hash(df: pd.DataFrame) -> str:
    return hashlib.sha256(
        pd.util.hash_pandas_object(df, index=True).values.tobytes()).hexdigest()[:12]
print(f"content hash: {content_hash(a)}  (same params -> same hash -> skip resend)")

# --- 4. DEPENDENCY ON DATA READINESS, not on the clock. ---
UPSTREAM = {
    "analytics.fct_sessions": pd.Timestamp("2024-07-01 04:12", tz="UTC"),
    "analytics.fct_orders":   pd.Timestamp("2024-07-01 04:31", tz="UTC"),
    "analytics.dim_region":   pd.Timestamp("2024-06-29 04:05", tz="UTC"),  # stale
}
def upstream_ready(freshness: dict, as_of: pd.Timestamp,
                   max_age_h: float = 26) -> list[str]:
    stale = []
    for table, loaded in freshness.items():
        age_h = (as_of - loaded).total_seconds() / 3600
        if age_h > max_age_h:
            stale.append(f"{table} is {age_h:.0f}h old")
    return stale

run_at = pd.Timestamp("2024-07-01 06:00", tz="UTC")
stale = upstream_ready(UPSTREAM, run_at)
print(f"\nupstream freshness check: {stale or 'all fresh'}")
print("A clock-triggered report would have published on a 2-day-old dimension")
print("table. Depend on data readiness, not on 06:00.")

# --- 5. EXCEPTION-BASED ALERTING beats a daily digest nobody reads. ---
daily_totals = data.groupby("date")["sessions"].sum()
THRESHOLDS = {"sessions_min": 2200, "z_score_max": 3.0}

def find_exceptions(series: pd.Series, thresholds: dict) -> list[str]:
    alerts = []
    latest_val = series.iloc[-1]
    if latest_val < thresholds["sessions_min"]:
        alerts.append(f"sessions {latest_val:,.0f} below floor "
                      f"{thresholds['sessions_min']:,}")
    # Robust z-score: median and MAD are not dragged by the anomaly itself.
    med = series.iloc[:-1].median()
    mad = (series.iloc[:-1] - med).abs().median()
    if mad > 0:
        z = 0.6745 * (latest_val - med) / mad
        if abs(z) > thresholds["z_score_max"]:
            alerts.append(f"sessions {latest_val:,.0f} is {z:+.1f} robust SDs "
                          f"from the {med:,.0f} median")
    return alerts

print(f"\nexceptions today: {find_exceptions(daily_totals, THRESHOLDS) or 'none'}")
shocked = daily_totals.copy()
shocked.iloc[-1] = shocked.iloc[-1] * 0.45          # simulate an incident
print(f"after a 55% drop:  {find_exceptions(shocked, THRESHOLDS)}")

# --- 6. RENDER with provenance baked in. ---
def render_summary(table: pd.DataFrame, params: ReportParams,
                   checks: list[Check], run_at: pd.Timestamp) -> str:
    warns = [c.name for c in checks if not c.passed and c.severity == "warn"]
    lines = [
        f"Weekly performance summary -- {params.start:%d %b} to "
        f"{params.as_of - pd.Timedelta('1d'):%d %b %Y}",
        "",
        f"Overall conversion: {table['orders'].sum()/table['sessions'].sum():.2%}"
        f" on {table['sessions'].sum():,} sessions",
        "",
        table.assign(conv_rate=lambda d: (d["conv_rate"]*100).round(2))
             .to_string(),
        "",
        f"Window: {params.lookback_days} days ending "
        f"{params.as_of - pd.Timedelta('1d'):%Y-%m-%d} (UTC)",
        f"Region filter: {params.region or 'all'}",
        f"Generated: {run_at:%Y-%m-%d %H:%M} UTC | "
        f"content hash: {content_hash(table)}",
        f"Source: analytics.fct_sessions, analytics.fct_orders",
        f"Checks: {sum(c.passed for c in checks)}/{len(checks)} passed"
        + (f" | warnings: {', '.join(warns)}" if warns else ""),
        "Full dashboard: https://bi.internal/d/weekly-performance",
    ]
    return "\n".join(lines)

if ok:
    print("\n" + "=" * 62)
    print(render_summary(a, params, validate(data, params), run_at))
    print("=" * 62)

# --- 7. RUN LOG: how you find out a report has been silently broken. ---
run_log = pd.DataFrame([
    ("2024-06-28", "success", 84, 6, 0, 12.4),
    ("2024-06-29", "success", 84, 6, 0, 11.8),
    ("2024-06-30", "failed",   0, 0, 1, 2.1),
    ("2024-07-01", "success", 84, 6, 1, 13.0),
], columns=["run_date", "status", "rows", "checks_passed", "warnings", "seconds"])
print("\nRUN LOG (surface this, or a broken report goes unnoticed for weeks)")
print(run_log.to_string(index=False))
streak = (run_log["status"] == "success").iloc[::-1].cumprod().sum()
print(f"\nconsecutive successful runs: {streak}")
print("Alert a PERSON on failure. A mailbox nobody reads is not monitoring.")
```

```text
  THE PIPELINE

    parameters (as_of, filters)
         |
    upstream freshness check  ----fail----> ALERT, do not run
         |
    extract (bounded by params, never by now())
         |
    validate: volume, completeness, nulls, plausibility, continuity
         |         |
         |         +----fail----> ALERT + BLOCK PUBLICATION
         v
    transform (idempotent: same params -> same content hash)
         |
    render (with provenance: window, filters, source, run time, hash)
         |
    deliver where the audience already works + link to the dashboard
         |
    log the run; alert a PERSON on failure

  WHY VALIDATION IS THE MOST IMPORTANT STEP

    a pipeline that FAILS        gets noticed and fixed
    a pipeline that publishes    gets BELIEVED and acted on
      a wrong number on time

    Failing loudly is a feature.

  SCHEDULE-TRIGGERED VS DEPENDENCY-TRIGGERED

    cron at 06:00               "when fct_orders for date D has loaded"
    runs whether or not the      runs when the data is actually ready
    data arrived
    -> eventually publishes      -> late rather than wrong
       yesterday's numbers

  DIGEST VS EXCEPTION ALERTING

    daily digest                 exception alert
    arrives every morning        arrives when a threshold is crossed
    read for two weeks, then     read every time, because it MEANS something
    filtered to a folder
    -> routine numbers belong on a dashboard; alerts belong in the inbox
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Anything produced more than twice should be parameterised and scheduled, so
>   the report becomes a deterministic function of the data and a date.
> - Validate before publishing, because a pipeline that publishes a wrong number
>   on time is worse than one that fails visibly.
> - Trigger on upstream data readiness rather than on the clock, or the report
>   eventually renders stale or half-loaded tables.
> - Make runs idempotent so retries and backfills are safe, and bound every
>   query by a parameter rather than by the current time.
> - Alert on exceptions rather than sending a digest nobody reads, and surface
>   the last successful run so silent breakage becomes visible.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a parameterised report function whose window comes from an `as_of`
>    argument rather than the current time, and run it for two historical dates.
> 2. Implement validation checks for row volume, date completeness, nulls, and
>    metric plausibility, then show them blocking a deliberately broken extract.
> 3. Add a content hash to a report so a re-run with identical inputs can be
>    detected and skipped.
> 4. Write a robust anomaly check using the median and median absolute deviation
>    and confirm it fires on an injected 50% drop.
> 5. Interview: A weekly report has been arriving on time for two months and you
>    discover it has been using stale data for three weeks. What went wrong and
>    what do you add? (Hint: what did the pipeline check before publishing, and
