<a id="9-machine-learning-fundamentals"></a>
## 9. Machine Learning Fundamentals

Machine learning is the practice of fitting a function to data so that it
works on data you have not seen, and almost everything difficult about it
follows from that last clause. This chapter covers the vocabulary and problem
types, the generalization theory that explains why models fail on new data,
the metrics that reveal whether a model is actually any good, and the
procedures for choosing among models without fooling yourself. Chapter 2
supplied the optimization machinery and chapter 6 the feature engineering;
this chapter is about what you are optimizing and how you know it worked.

<a id="91-core-concepts"></a>
### 9.1 Core Concepts

The core vocabulary of machine learning encodes a set of design decisions, and
knowing what each term commits you to is what makes the rest of the field
navigable; this section covers the problem types, the objects they operate on,
and the assumptions every model carries.

#### Supervised, Unsupervised, Reinforcement Learning

Machine learning divides into families by **what kind of feedback the learner
receives**, and that single distinction determines what problems each family can
solve, what data it needs, and how you evaluate it.

**Supervised learning** learns from labelled examples. You supply inputs paired
with correct outputs, and the model learns a mapping from one to the other. The
feedback is direct and complete: for every training example, you know the right
answer. This is the best-understood and most widely deployed family, and if your
problem can be framed as supervised learning with labels you can actually
obtain, it usually should be.

It splits by the type of output. **Classification** predicts a category, such
as spam or not spam, and **regression** predicts a continuous quantity, such
as a price. The distinction matters because it changes the loss function, the
metrics, and often the algorithm.

**Unsupervised learning** learns from inputs with no labels at all. There is
no right answer to compare against, so the model finds structure instead:
clusters of similar records, a lower-dimensional representation, association
patterns, or anomalies. The absence of labels has a consequence people
underestimate: **evaluation is genuinely hard**, because there is no ground
truth to score against. A clustering can be measured for internal cohesion,
but whether the clusters *mean* anything requires domain judgement.

**Reinforcement learning** learns from consequences. An agent takes actions in
an environment and receives rewards, and must discover which actions lead to
reward over time. The feedback is neither complete nor immediate: you learn
that a sequence of moves led to a loss without being told which move was the
mistake. This is the **credit assignment problem**, and it is why
reinforcement learning is harder and more sample-hungry than supervised
learning.

The analogy that holds up: supervised learning is studying with an answer key.
Unsupervised learning is sorting a box of unlabelled photographs into piles that
seem to belong together. Reinforcement learning is learning to cook by tasting
the result, with no recipe and no indication of which step went wrong.

Several families sit between these and are worth knowing because they solve the
labelling problem that dominates real projects.

**Semi-supervised learning** uses a small labelled set plus a large unlabelled
one, which matches the common situation where data is abundant and labels are
expensive. **Self-supervised learning** manufactures labels from the data's
own structure, such as predicting a masked word from its context, and is the
foundation of modern language and vision models. **Active learning** chooses
which examples to label next, targeting the ones the model is most uncertain
about, which can cut labelling cost dramatically.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# --- SUPERVISED: inputs paired with known outputs. ---
n = 600
X = pd.DataFrame({"sqft": rng.integers(600, 3200, n).astype(float),
                  "bedrooms": rng.integers(1, 6, n)})
price = 50_000 + 145 * X["sqft"] + 8_000 * X["bedrooms"] + rng.normal(0, 25_000, n)
is_luxury = (price > price.quantile(0.80)).astype(int)

from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, LogisticRegression
# REGRESSION: the target is a continuous quantity.
reg = LinearRegression().fit(X, price)
print(f"regression   predicts a NUMBER: ${reg.predict(X.iloc[[0]])[0]:,.0f}")
# CLASSIFICATION: the target is a category.
clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(X, is_luxury)
print(f"classification predicts a CLASS: {clf.predict(X.iloc[[0]])[0]}"
      f"  with P(luxury) = {clf.predict_proba(X.iloc[[0]])[0,1]:.3f}")
print("Same features, same rows. The TARGET TYPE changed everything downstream.")

# --- UNSUPERVISED: no target column exists at all. ---
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score, adjusted_rand_score

Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
km = KMeans(n_clusters=3, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(Xs)
print(f"\nclustering found {len(np.unique(km.labels_))} groups"
      f" of sizes {np.bincount(km.labels_)}")
# There is no accuracy to report. Only internal structure can be measured.
print(f"  silhouette (internal cohesion, -1 to 1): "
      f"{silhouette_score(Xs, km.labels_):.3f}")
print(f"  agreement with the luxury label: "
      f"{adjusted_rand_score(is_luxury, km.labels_):.3f}")
print("  The second number is only computable because we happen to HAVE a")
print("  label. In a real unsupervised problem you do not, which is why")
print("  evaluating clusters is a judgement call, not a metric.")

# --- REINFORCEMENT LEARNING: delayed, partial feedback. ---
# A two-state task: the reward arrives only at the END of a sequence, so the
# learner must work out which earlier action deserves the credit.
ACTIONS = ["left", "right"]
def episode_reward(seq):
    """Reward depends on the WHOLE sequence, not on any single action."""
    return 1.0 if seq == ["right", "right", "left"] else 0.0

# Monte Carlo credit assignment: distribute the final reward over the actions
# that produced it, and let repetition sort out which ones mattered.
value = {(t, a): 0.0 for t in range(3) for a in ACTIONS}
counts = {(t, a): 0 for t in range(3) for a in ACTIONS}
for ep in range(4000):
    eps = max(0.05, 1.0 - ep / 2000)              # explore, then exploit
    seq = []
    for t in range(3):
        if rng.random() < eps:
            seq.append(ACTIONS[rng.integers(2)])
        else:
            seq.append(max(ACTIONS, key=lambda a: value[(t, a)]))
    r = episode_reward(seq)
    for t, a in enumerate(seq):                   # the same r credited to all
        counts[(t, a)] += 1
        value[(t, a)] += (r - value[(t, a)]) / counts[(t, a)]

learned = [max(ACTIONS, key=lambda a: value[(t, a)]) for t in range(3)]
print(f"\nlearned policy: {learned}   (optimal: ['right', 'right', 'left'])")
print("Nothing told the agent which step was wrong. It inferred that from")
print("thousands of episodes, which is why RL needs so much more data.")

# --- THE LABELLING PROBLEM, and active learning as a response. ---
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
big_X = pd.DataFrame(rng.normal(size=(4000, 8)))
big_y = (big_X[0] + big_X[1] * 0.8 + rng.normal(0, 0.5, 4000) > 0).astype(int)
pool_X, test_X, pool_y, test_y = train_test_split(big_X, big_y, test_size=0.3,
                                                  random_state=0)

def learn_with_budget(strategy: str, budget: int = 120, seed: int = 0) -> float:
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    labelled = list(r.choice(len(pool_X), 20, replace=False))   # a seed set
    while len(labelled) < budget:
        m = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(
            pool_X.iloc[labelled], pool_y.iloc[labelled])
        remaining = [i for i in range(len(pool_X)) if i not in set(labelled)]
        if strategy == "random":
            pick = list(r.choice(remaining, 10, replace=False))
        else:
            # ACTIVE: label the points the model is least certain about,
            # i.e. those whose predicted probability sits nearest 0.5.
            p = m.predict_proba(pool_X.iloc[remaining])[:, 1]
            pick = [remaining[j] for j in np.argsort(np.abs(p - 0.5))[:10]]
        labelled += pick
    final = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(
        pool_X.iloc[labelled], pool_y.iloc[labelled])
    return final.score(test_X, test_y)

for strat in ("random", "active"):
    scores = [learn_with_budget(strat, seed=s) for s in range(5)]
    print(f"\n{strat:7s} sampling, 120 labels: accuracy {np.mean(scores):.4f}")
print("Active learning reaches higher accuracy from the same label budget by")
print("spending it near the decision boundary instead of uniformly.")

# --- FRAMING THE SAME BUSINESS PROBLEM THREE WAYS ---
framings = pd.DataFrame([
    ("Which customers will churn next month?", "supervised, classification",
     "historical churn labels", "AUC, precision at k"),
    ("What are our natural customer groups?", "unsupervised, clustering",
     "no labels needed", "silhouette + domain review"),
    ("What discount should we offer each user?", "reinforcement / bandit",
     "reward signal per action", "cumulative reward, regret"),
    ("Which customers should we call, given 50 calls?",
     "supervised + ranking + a budget", "churn labels + call outcomes",
     "precision at 50, uplift"),
], columns=["question", "framing", "data required", "how you evaluate"])
print("\n", framings.to_string(index=False))
print("\nThe framing is a choice, not a property of the data. It determines")
print("what you must collect and how you will know if it worked.")
```

```text
  THE THREE FAMILIES, BY FEEDBACK

  family          feedback per example        knows the right answer?
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  supervised      a label for every input     YES, completely
  unsupervised    none                        NO, there is no answer
  reinforcement   a delayed, aggregate        PARTIALLY: only the outcome
                  reward                      of a whole sequence

  SUPERVISED SPLITS BY OUTPUT TYPE

    classification  -> a category   spam / not spam, which of 10 digits
    regression      -> a quantity   price, duration, temperature

  THE CREDIT ASSIGNMENT PROBLEM

    supervised            reinforcement
    input -> label        action, action, action -> one reward
      |        |            ?       ?       ?        |
      +--------+            +-------+-------+--------+
      error known           WHICH action earned it?
      per example

    That gap is why RL needs orders of magnitude more interaction.

  THE LABEL-SCARCITY FAMILIES

  family             uses                        when to reach for it
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  semi-supervised    few labels + many unlabelled labels are expensive
  self-supervised    labels derived from the      you have raw text/images
                     data's own structure         at scale
  active learning    the model picks what to      you control the labelling
                     label next                   queue
  transfer learning  a model trained elsewhere    your dataset is small

  CHOOSING A FRAMING (the same business problem)

    "who will churn?"          -> supervised classification, needs labels
    "what groups exist?"       -> unsupervised, needs domain review
    "what offer for whom?"     -> bandit / RL, needs a reward signal
    "who do we call, top 50?"  -> supervised + ranking under a budget
```

> Key Takeaways
> - The families differ by the feedback available: complete labels, no labels,
>   or a delayed aggregate reward.
> - Supervised learning splits into classification and regression, and the
>   target type determines the loss, the metrics, and often the algorithm.
> - Unsupervised learning has no ground truth, so evaluation requires domain
>   judgement rather than a single metric.
> - Reinforcement learning faces the credit assignment problem, which is why
>   it needs far more interaction than supervised learning.
> - The framing is a choice you make, and it determines what data you must
>   collect and how you will know the model worked.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Take one dataset and fit both a regression and a classification model on
>    it by transforming the target, then list what changed in the evaluation.
> 2. Cluster a dataset that happens to have labels, and compare an internal
>    metric against agreement with the true labels.
> 3. Implement random and uncertainty-based sampling under a fixed label
>    budget and compare final accuracy.
> 4. Interview: A stakeholder asks you to "use machine learning to understand
>    our customers better". What do you ask before choosing an approach?
>    (Hint: what determines whether this is supervised at all, and what would
>    you evaluate against?)

#### Features, Labels, and Targets

The vocabulary here is simple and the decisions it encodes are not. A
**feature** is an input variable, a **label** or **target** is what you are
predicting, and an **example** or **instance** is one row pairing them. The
standard notation is `X` for the feature matrix, one row per example and one
column per feature, and `y` for the target vector.

Beyond the definitions, four decisions determine whether a supervised problem is
well-posed at all.

**What is one row?** This is the **grain**, introduced in chapter 6, and it is
the first thing to pin down. One row per customer, per customer-month, per
transaction, or per customer-product pair are four different problems with
different row counts, different independence properties, and different
interpretations. A model whose grain is unstated cannot be evaluated
correctly, because you do not know what the unit of prediction is.

**What exactly is the label?** "Churn" is not a label until you say that it
means no purchase within 60 days of the last one, measured as of a specific
date. Label definition is where most supervised projects are quietly decided,
because a label that is easy to compute is often not the thing you care about.
If you define churn as account deletion, you will build a model of a rare
administrative action rather than of customers drifting away.

**When is the label known relative to the prediction?** Every feature must be
available at prediction time, and the label must be observable afterwards.
This is the **as-of** discipline from chapter 6, and violating it produces
leakage, which chapter 6 covers in detail. The practical version is a table
with one row per feature and one column for the timestamp at which its value
becomes known.

**How long must you wait to observe the label?** This is the **label latency**
or maturation period, and it sets an unavoidable floor on how fast you can
iterate. If churn is defined over 90 days, your freshest usable training label
is 90 days old, and a model trained today has never seen the last quarter.

Two further distinctions worth having.

**Hard versus soft labels.** A hard label is a single class; a soft label is a
distribution, such as the fraction of annotators who chose each class. Soft
labels carry information about ambiguity that hard labels discard, and
training on them often improves calibration.

**Label noise.** Real labels are wrong sometimes, because annotators disagree,
definitions drift, or the recorded outcome is a proxy. Label noise caps
achievable accuracy at a level below 100%, and knowing roughly where that
ceiling sits stops you chasing performance the data cannot support. Measuring
inter-annotator agreement is how you estimate it.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)

# --- THE SAME RAW DATA, FOUR GRAINS, FOUR PROBLEMS ---
events = pd.DataFrame({
    "customer": rng.integers(1, 200, 5000),
    "product": rng.choice(list("ABCD"), 5000),
    "month": rng.choice(pd.period_range("2024-01", periods=8, freq="M"), 5000),
    "amount": rng.gamma(2, 40, 5000).round(2),
})
grains = {
    "one row per customer":
        events.groupby("customer").size(),
    "one row per customer-month":
        events.groupby(["customer", "month"]).size(),
    "one row per customer-product":
        events.groupby(["customer", "product"]).size(),
    "one row per transaction":
        events.groupby(events.index).size(),
}
print("THE GRAIN DECIDES THE PROBLEM")
for name, g in grains.items():
    print(f"  {name:32s} {len(g):>6,} rows")
print("\nThese are four different supervised problems with four different")
print("independence structures. Panel grains violate row independence, which")
print("matters for cross-validation (see 9.3) and for standard errors.")

# --- LABEL DEFINITION: one word, five labels, five different models. ---
AS_OF = pd.Timestamp("2024-06-01")
purchases = pd.DataFrame({
    "customer": rng.integers(1, 400, 3000),
    "ts": pd.Timestamp("2024-01-01") + pd.to_timedelta(
        rng.integers(0, 210, 3000), "D"),
})
last = purchases.groupby("customer")["ts"].max()
counts = purchases.groupby("customer").size()

definitions = {
    "no purchase in 30 days": (AS_OF - last).dt.days > 30,
    "no purchase in 60 days": (AS_OF - last).dt.days > 60,
    "no purchase in 90 days": (AS_OF - last).dt.days > 90,
    "only ever bought once": counts == 1,
    "never returned after first": (counts == 1) & ((AS_OF - last).dt.days > 60),
}
print("\n'CHURN' UNDER FIVE DEFINITIONS")
for name, mask in definitions.items():
    print(f"  {name:30s} positive rate {mask.mean():.3f}"
          f"  ({int(mask.sum()):>4} of {len(mask)})")
spread = max(m.mean() for m in definitions.values()) - \
         min(m.mean() for m in definitions.values())
print(f"\npositive rate spans {spread:.0%} across definitions. Each one trains")
print("a model of a different phenomenon. Write the definition down first.")

# --- LABEL LATENCY: how stale your freshest label must be. ---
print("\nLABEL LATENCY: the freshest usable training data")
today = pd.Timestamp("2024-09-01")
for horizon in (7, 30, 90, 365):
    newest_label = today - pd.Timedelta(days=horizon)
    print(f"  {horizon:>3}-day label horizon -> freshest complete label is"
          f" from {newest_label:%Y-%m-%d}"
          f" ({horizon} days of recent behaviour unusable)")
print("\nA 90-day label means a model trained today has never seen the last")
print("quarter. That is a hard constraint on how fast you can respond to")
print("a change in user behaviour, and no algorithm fixes it.")

# --- THE FEATURE AVAILABILITY TABLE (the leakage audit from chapter 6) ---
schema = pd.DataFrame([
    ("tenure_days", "feature", "signup date", "before prediction", "safe"),
    ("purchases_30d", "feature", "order log, trailing window",
     "before prediction", "safe"),
    ("support_tickets_7d", "feature", "ticket system", "before prediction", "safe"),
    ("avg_basket_value", "feature", "order log, trailing", "before prediction",
     "safe"),
    ("days_to_churn", "LABEL-DERIVED", "computed from the outcome",
     "AFTER the outcome", "LEAK"),
    ("cancellation_reason", "LABEL-DERIVED", "cancellation form",
     "AFTER the outcome", "LEAK"),
    ("churned_60d", "label", "order log, forward window",
     "60 days AFTER prediction", "the target"),
], columns=["column", "role", "source", "known when", "verdict"])
print("\nFEATURE AVAILABILITY AUDIT")
print(schema.to_string(index=False))

# --- HARD VS SOFT LABELS: annotator disagreement carries information. ---
n_items, n_annotators = 400, 5
true_difficulty = rng.beta(2, 2, n_items)     # how ambiguous each item is
votes = np.array([[rng.random() < (0.5 + 0.45 * (2*d - 1) * (1 if i % 2 else -1))
                   for i in range(n_annotators)] for d in true_difficulty])
soft = votes.mean(axis=1)
hard = (soft > 0.5).astype(int)
print(f"\nHARD VS SOFT LABELS ({n_annotators} annotators, {n_items} items)")
print(f"  unanimous items: {np.mean((soft == 0) | (soft == 1)):.1%}")
print(f"  split 3-2 or 2-3: {np.mean(np.isin(soft, [0.4, 0.6])):.1%}")
print("  soft label distribution:")
for v in sorted(np.unique(soft)):
    print(f"    {v:.1f} -> {np.mean(soft == v):.1%} of items")
print("\nHardening a 3-2 vote to a confident class discards the information")
print("that the item was genuinely ambiguous. Soft labels usually improve")
print("calibration (see 9.3).")

# --- LABEL NOISE SETS A CEILING ON ACHIEVABLE ACCURACY ---
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

m = 6000
Xc = pd.DataFrame(rng.normal(size=(m, 6)))
clean_y = (Xc[0] + 0.7 * Xc[1] - 0.4 * Xc[2] > 0).astype(int)
print("\nLABEL NOISE CEILING")
for noise in (0.00, 0.05, 0.15, 0.30):
    flip = rng.random(m) < noise
    noisy_y = np.where(flip, 1 - clean_y, clean_y)
    Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Xc, noisy_y, test_size=0.3,
                                          random_state=0)
    model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(Xtr, ytr)
    # Score against the NOISY labels (what you would observe) and the CLEAN
    # ones (the truth you cannot see).
    obs = model.score(Xte, yte)
    _, _, _, yte_clean = train_test_split(Xc, clean_y, test_size=0.3,
                                          random_state=0)
    true_acc = model.score(Xte, yte_clean)
    print(f"  {noise:.0%} label noise -> measured accuracy {obs:.3f},"
          f" true accuracy {true_acc:.3f}, ceiling ~{1-noise:.2f}")
print("\nAt 15% label noise, 0.85 measured accuracy is a PERFECT model.")
print("Estimate your ceiling from inter-annotator agreement before setting")
print("a performance target nobody can reach.")

# Cohen's kappa: agreement corrected for what chance alone would produce.
def cohens_kappa(a, b):
    observed = np.mean(a == b)
    pa, pb = np.mean(a), np.mean(b)
    expected = pa * pb + (1 - pa) * (1 - pb)
    return (observed - expected) / (1 - expected)

ann1, ann2 = votes[:, 0].astype(int), votes[:, 1].astype(int)
print(f"\ninter-annotator agreement: raw {np.mean(ann1 == ann2):.3f},"
      f" Cohen's kappa {cohens_kappa(ann1, ann2):.3f}")
print("Kappa corrects for chance agreement. Below ~0.6 the label definition")
print("itself needs work before any modelling is worthwhile.")
```

```text
  THE OBJECTS

    X  feature matrix    n rows (examples) x p columns (features)
    y  target vector     n entries, one per row
    one row = one EXAMPLE = one unit of prediction

      X                                    y
    +----------+----------+---------+     +--------+
    | tenure   | spend_30 | tickets |     | churn  |
    +----------+----------+---------+     +--------+
    | 412      | 88.50    | 0       |     | 0      |   <- one example
    | 37       | 12.00    | 3       |     | 1      |
    +----------+----------+---------+     +--------+

  FOUR DECISIONS THAT MAKE A PROBLEM WELL-POSED

    1. GRAIN       one row per WHAT? customer, customer-month, transaction?
    2. DEFINITION  what exactly does the label mean, in executable terms?
    3. TIMING      is every feature known BEFORE the prediction moment?
    4. LATENCY     how long until the label is observable?

  THE SAME WORD, FIVE LABELS

    "churn" positive rate under each definition:
      no purchase in 30 days      0.52
      no purchase in 60 days      0.31
      no purchase in 90 days      0.14
      only ever bought once       0.22
      never returned after first  0.09

    A 43-point spread. Each trains a model of a different phenomenon.

  LABEL LATENCY IS A HARD CONSTRAINT

    today = 2024-09-01

    horizon    freshest complete label   recent data unusable
    7 days     2024-08-25                1 week
    30 days    2024-08-02                1 month
    90 days    2024-06-03                1 QUARTER
    365 days   2023-09-02                1 YEAR

    With a 90-day label, today's model has never seen the last quarter.

  LABEL NOISE CAPS ACCURACY

    noise   measured accuracy   true accuracy   ceiling
    0%      0.938               0.938           1.00
    5%      0.893               0.936           0.95
    15%     0.806               0.933           0.85
    30%     0.667               0.931           0.70

    The model barely degrades; the MEASUREMENT does. At 15% noise, 0.85 is
    a perfect score. Estimate the ceiling from annotator agreement first.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Pin down the grain first, because one row per customer and one row per
>   customer-month are different problems with different independence
>   structures.
> - A label is not defined until it is executable, and the positive rate can
>   vary enormously across defensible definitions of the same word.
> - Every feature must be known before the prediction moment, and the label
>   observable after it, which is the leakage audit from chapter 6.
> - Label latency sets a hard floor on data freshness that no algorithm can
>   remove.
> - Label noise caps achievable accuracy, so estimate it from inter-annotator
>   agreement before setting a performance target.

#### Training, Validation, Test Splits

The entire point of a model is performance on data it has not seen, and the
only way to estimate that is to hold some data back. That idea is simple; the
discipline around it is where projects go wrong, and the failure is always the
same shape: the held-out data influenced the model, so the estimate is
optimistic.

The standard three-way split assigns each part a distinct job, and the jobs are
what matter.

**The training set** fits the model parameters. This is the only data the
fitting procedure sees directly.

**The validation set** chooses between models and tunes hyperparameters. Every
time you look at validation performance and change something, you use a little
of its independence. After a hundred such decisions, validation performance is
optimistic about the same way a training score is, because you have
effectively fitted your choices to it.

**The test set** estimates final performance. It must be used **once**, at the
end, after everything is decided. A test set consulted repeatedly is a
validation set, and you no longer have an unbiased estimate of anything.

That third rule sounds excessive until you see the mechanism. Each time you
pick the better of two options based on test performance, you select for
whichever one got luckier on that particular sample. With enough selections,
you can produce impressive test performance on pure noise, exactly as the
segment-fishing demonstration in chapter 8 does.

The split proportions depend on data volume rather than convention. With a few
thousand rows, 60/20/20 is reasonable and the validation estimate is noisy. With
ten million rows, 98/1/1 leaves a hundred thousand rows in each held-out set,
which is plenty, and gives the model far more to learn from.

The harder question is **how** to split, and the right answer depends on the
structure of the data. This connects to the temporal and panel material in
chapter 1.3.

**Random splitting** is correct only when rows are independent and identically
distributed and the deployment setting matches the sampled one.

**Temporal splitting** is required whenever you will predict the future from
the past. A random split lets the model learn from data that postdates its
test rows, which inflates performance and does not survive deployment.

**Group splitting** is required whenever rows share an entity. If one patient
contributes several visits, a random split puts the same patient in train and
test, and the model is scored on its ability to recognise a patient it has
already seen.

**Stratified splitting** preserves class proportions, which matters for
imbalanced targets and small samples.

Real problems often need several of these at once: split by time *and* by
entity, for instance, when you must generalise to new users in future periods.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import (train_test_split, StratifiedShuffleSplit,
                                     GroupShuffleSplit, TimeSeriesSplit)
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)

# --- SPLIT SIZES SCALE WITH VOLUME, not with convention. ---
print("held-out rows under different split ratios:")
for n in (2_000, 50_000, 10_000_000):
    for ratio in [(0.60, 0.20, 0.20), (0.80, 0.10, 0.10), (0.98, 0.01, 0.01)]:
        tr, va, te = (int(n*r) for r in ratio)
        # Standard error of an accuracy estimate near 0.9 on the test set.
        se = np.sqrt(0.9 * 0.1 / max(te, 1))
        print(f"  n={n:>10,}  {ratio}  train {tr:>9,}  val {va:>7,}"
              f"  test {te:>7,}  accuracy se +/-{1.96*se:.4f}")
    print()
print("With 10M rows a 1% test set gives a +/-0.002 interval, so spending")
print("20% on holdout is wasted training data.")

# --- THE TEST SET DEGRADES WITH EVERY LOOK ---
# 200 useless model variants on data with NO signal at all.
n, p = 400, 30
X = pd.DataFrame(rng.normal(size=(n, p)))
y = rng.integers(0, 2, n)                      # pure noise target
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.4, random_state=0)

best_score, best_k, trace = 0.0, None, []
for k in range(1, 201):
    r = np.random.default_rng(k)
    cols = list(r.choice(p, 4, replace=False))
    m = LogisticRegression(max_iter=500).fit(Xtr[cols], ytr)
    s = m.score(Xte[cols], yte)                # LOOKING AT TEST each time
    if s > best_score:
        best_score, best_k = s, k
    trace.append(best_score)
print(f"\nTEST-SET EROSION on a target with NO signal (true accuracy 0.50):")
for looks in (1, 5, 20, 50, 200):
    print(f"  best of {looks:>3} variants: test accuracy {trace[looks-1]:.3f}")
print("\nSelecting on test performance manufactures skill from noise. That is")
print("why the test set is used ONCE, after all decisions are final.")

# --- TEMPORAL SPLIT: a random split lets the model see its own future. ---
m = 4_000
dates = pd.date_range("2023-01-01", periods=m, freq="3h")
drift = np.linspace(0, 2.5, m)                 # the relationship CHANGES
Xt = pd.DataFrame({"x1": rng.normal(size=m), "x2": rng.normal(size=m)})
logit = Xt["x1"] * (1 + drift) - Xt["x2"] * 0.5 - drift
yt = (rng.random(m) < 1/(1+np.exp(-logit))).astype(int)
panel = Xt.assign(date=dates, y=yt)

# WRONG: random split on time-ordered data with drift.
a, b, ya, yb = train_test_split(Xt, yt, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)
random_auc = roc_auc_score(yb, LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)
                           .fit(a, ya).predict_proba(b)[:, 1])
# RIGHT: train on the past, test on the future.
cut = int(m * 0.7)
temporal_auc = roc_auc_score(
    yt[cut:], LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)
    .fit(Xt[:cut], yt[:cut]).predict_proba(Xt[cut:])[:, 1])
print(f"\nrandom split AUC   {random_auc:.4f}   <- optimistic")
print(f"temporal split AUC {temporal_auc:.4f}   <- what production sees")
print(f"gap {random_auc - temporal_auc:+.4f}: every random training fold")
print("contains rows that postdate its own test rows.")

# --- GROUP SPLIT: the same entity must not appear on both sides. ---
k = 3_000
group = rng.integers(0, 150, k)                 # 150 users, ~20 rows each
user_effect = rng.normal(0, 2.2, 150)[group]    # a strong per-user signal
Xg = pd.DataFrame({"x": rng.normal(size=k) * 0.4 + user_effect * 0.1})
yg = (rng.random(k) < 1/(1+np.exp(-user_effect))).astype(int)

ga, gb, yga, ygb = train_test_split(Xg, yg, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)
naive_auc = roc_auc_score(ygb, LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)
                          .fit(ga, yga).predict_proba(gb)[:, 1])
gss = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)
tr_i, te_i = next(gss.split(Xg, yg, groups=group))
grouped_auc = roc_auc_score(
    yg[te_i], LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)
    .fit(Xg.iloc[tr_i], yg[tr_i]).predict_proba(Xg.iloc[te_i])[:, 1])
overlap = len(set(group[np.setdiff1d(np.arange(k), tr_i)]) & set(group[tr_i]))
print(f"\nrandom split AUC  {naive_auc:.4f}  <- users appear on BOTH sides")
print(f"group split AUC   {grouped_auc:.4f}  <- users appear on one side only")
print(f"users shared between the grouped train and test sets: {overlap}")
print("The gap is memorised users, not learned behaviour.")

# --- STRATIFIED: preserve class balance, which matters when positives are few. ---
imb_y = (rng.random(1500) < 0.03).astype(int)
imb_X = pd.DataFrame(rng.normal(size=(1500, 3)))
print(f"\noverall positive rate {imb_y.mean():.4f} ({imb_y.sum()} positives)")
for label, strat in [("unstratified", None), ("stratified", imb_y)]:
    rates = []
    for seed in range(20):
        _, _, _, yy = train_test_split(imb_X, imb_y, test_size=0.2,
                                       random_state=seed, stratify=strat)
        rates.append(yy.mean())
    print(f"  {label:12s} test positive rate: min {min(rates):.4f},"
          f" max {max(rates):.4f}, zero-positive splits:"
          f" {sum(1 for r in rates if r == 0)}")
print("An unstratified split can hand you a test set with no positives at all,")
print("which makes several metrics undefined.")

# --- A SPLITTER THAT RESPECTS BOTH TIME AND GROUPS ---
def time_group_split(df, date_col, group_col, test_frac=0.2, val_frac=0.2):
    """Chronological split with no entity crossing a boundary: needed when
    you must generalise to NEW entities in FUTURE periods."""
    d = df.sort_values(date_col).reset_index(drop=True)
    n = len(d)
    cut_val = int(n * (1 - test_frac - val_frac))
    cut_test = int(n * (1 - test_frac))
    train_groups = set(d.loc[:cut_val, group_col])
    # Drop later rows whose group already appeared in training.
    val = d.loc[cut_val:cut_test]
    test = d.loc[cut_test:]
    return (d.loc[:cut_val],
            val[~val[group_col].isin(train_groups)],
            test[~test[group_col].isin(train_groups)])

demo = pd.DataFrame({"date": dates[:2000],
                     "user": rng.integers(0, 400, 2000),
                     "y": rng.integers(0, 2, 2000)})
tr_d, va_d, te_d = time_group_split(demo, "date", "user")
print(f"\ntime+group split: train {len(tr_d):,}  val {len(va_d):,}"
      f"  test {len(te_d):,}")
print(f"  users in both train and test: "
      f"{len(set(tr_d['user']) & set(te_d['user']))}")
print(f"  train ends {tr_d['date'].max():%Y-%m-%d},"
      f" test starts {te_d['date'].min():%Y-%m-%d}")
print("Rows are dropped to enforce both constraints, which is the cost of")
print("measuring what you actually need to measure.")
```

```text
  THREE SETS, THREE JOBS

    TRAIN        fits parameters                  seen constantly
    VALIDATION   selects models, tunes            seen many times
    TEST         estimates final performance      seen ONCE, at the end

    Each look at the test set spends a little of its independence.

  TEST-SET EROSION (target is pure noise, true accuracy 0.50)

    variants tried    best test accuracy
    1                 0.519
    5                 0.563
    20                0.600
    50                0.625
    200               0.663

    None of these models learned anything. Selection on test performance
    manufactured 0.66 out of noise.

  SPLIT SIZE SCALES WITH VOLUME

    n            ratio          test rows   accuracy interval
    2,000        60/20/20       400         +/-0.029
    50,000       80/10/10       5,000       +/-0.008
    10,000,000   98/1/1         100,000     +/-0.002

    Past a certain size, a bigger holdout buys precision you do not need
    and costs training data you do.

  HOW TO SPLIT, BY DATA STRUCTURE

  structure              splitter              what breaks otherwise
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  independent rows       random                nothing
  time-ordered           chronological         model learns from its future
  repeated entities      by group              model memorises entities
  imbalanced target      stratified            a fold with zero positives
  new entities, future   time AND group        both of the above
  periods

  THE TWO GAPS, MEASURED

    random split on drifting time series:  AUC 0.842
    temporal split:                        AUC 0.761   gap -0.081

    random split on panel data:            AUC 0.889
    grouped split:                         AUC 0.648   gap -0.241

    The second gap is larger because entity memorisation is a stronger
    shortcut than temporal leakage.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Training fits parameters, validation selects among options, and the test
>   set is used once at the very end.
> - Every decision made by looking at a held-out score spends its
>   independence, and enough selections manufacture skill from pure noise.
> - Split proportions should scale with data volume, since a 1% test set on
>   ten million rows is already precise.
> - Split by time when predicting the future, by group when entities repeat,
>   and stratify when the target is imbalanced.
> - Real problems often need several constraints at once, and enforcing them
>   costs rows, which is the price of a usable estimate.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Generate a target with no signal, try 200 model variants selecting on
>    test accuracy, and report how high the best test score climbs.
> 2. Build a drifting time series and compare the area under the curve from a
>    random split against a chronological one.
> 3. Construct panel data with a strong per-entity effect and compare random

> 4. Write a splitter enforcing both a chronological boundary and no entity

#### Loss Functions and Objectives

A model learns by minimising something, and that something is the loss function.
It is the most consequential choice in the entire modelling process, because it
defines what "good" means. Every property you want the model to have must be
expressed in the loss, or the optimiser will happily trade it away.

The gap worth naming immediately is between the **loss** you optimise and the
**metric** you care about. Many metrics are unusable as losses because they
are not differentiable or are piecewise constant: accuracy does not change at
all for small parameter adjustments, so it provides no gradient to follow. So
you optimise a differentiable surrogate, such as log loss, and evaluate on the
metric you actually want. Keeping this distinction clear explains a lot of
otherwise confusing behaviour, including why a model with better log loss can
have worse accuracy.

**For regression**, the choice is mostly about how to treat large errors.

**Squared error** penalises the square of the residual, so a single large miss
dominates. It is differentiable everywhere, it is the maximum likelihood
estimator under Gaussian noise, and its minimiser is the conditional **mean**.
Use it when large errors are genuinely disproportionately bad and the data has
no severe outliers.

**Absolute error** penalises linearly, so outliers have bounded influence. Its
minimiser is the conditional **median**, which is a substantively different
prediction on skewed data. Use it when you want robustness.

**Huber loss** is quadratic near zero and linear in the tails, combining the
gradient behaviour of squared error near the optimum with the robustness of
absolute error far from it.

**Quantile loss** is the asymmetric generalisation: weight over- and
under-predictions differently and the minimiser is the corresponding quantile.
This is how you produce prediction intervals and how you handle genuinely
asymmetric costs, such as inventory where a stockout costs more than overstock.

**Log-transformed targets or a Poisson/Tweedie loss** are the right answers when
the target is a count or is multiplicative, because squared error on raw counts
assumes constant variance that count data does not have.

**For classification**, the dominant choice is **log loss**, also called
binary cross-entropy. It is the negative log likelihood under a Bernoulli
model, and its defining property is that it is a **proper scoring rule**: it
is minimised only by reporting the true probability, so it rewards calibration
rather than just correct ranking. It punishes confident mistakes severely,
which is usually what you want.

**Hinge loss** underlies support vector machines and cares only about the
margin, producing no calibrated probability. **Focal loss** downweights easy
examples to concentrate learning on hard ones, which helps under extreme
imbalance.

Two additions apply across both.

**Class or sample weights** encode asymmetric costs directly in the objective,
as covered in chapter 6.4. If a false negative costs fifty times a false
positive, put that in the loss rather than correcting for it afterwards.

**Regularisation terms** added to the loss express a preference for simpler
models, which the next section covers.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)

# --- REGRESSION LOSSES: what each one's minimiser actually is. ---
def squared(r): return r ** 2
def absolute(r): return np.abs(r)
def huber(r, delta=1.35):
    a = np.abs(r)
    # Quadratic inside delta, linear outside: gradients stay bounded.
    return np.where(a <= delta, 0.5 * r**2, delta * (a - 0.5 * delta))
def quantile(r, q=0.9):
    # Penalise under-prediction (r > 0) by q and over-prediction by (1-q).
    return np.maximum(q * r, (q - 1) * r)

skewed = np.concatenate([rng.normal(50, 8, 900), rng.normal(160, 25, 100)])
grid = np.linspace(skewed.min(), skewed.max(), 4000)
print("WHAT EACH LOSS PREDICTS on a right-skewed target")
print(f"  data: mean {skewed.mean():.2f}, median {np.median(skewed):.2f},"
      f" p90 {np.percentile(skewed, 90):.2f}")
for name, fn, expect in [("squared error", squared, "the MEAN"),
                         ("absolute error", absolute, "the MEDIAN"),
                         ("huber", huber, "between the two"),
                         ("quantile q=0.9", lambda r: quantile(r, 0.9),
                          "the 90th PERCENTILE")]:
    # Minimise total loss over a grid of candidate constant predictions.
    best = grid[np.argmin([fn(skewed - c).sum() for c in grid])]
    print(f"  {name:16s} minimiser {best:7.2f}   ({expect})")
print("\nThe loss is not a technical detail: it decides WHICH summary of the")
print("conditional distribution your model predicts.")

# --- OUTLIER SENSITIVITY, measured. ---
clean = rng.normal(100, 10, 500)
contaminated = np.append(clean, [900.0])           # one absurd value
print("\nEFFECT OF ONE OUTLIER on the fitted constant")
for name, fn in [("squared", squared), ("absolute", absolute),
                 ("huber", huber)]:
    g = np.linspace(80, 200, 3000)
    a = g[np.argmin([fn(clean - c).sum() for c in g])]
    b = g[np.argmin([fn(contaminated - c).sum() for c in g])]
    print(f"  {name:9s} clean {a:7.2f} -> contaminated {b:7.2f}"
          f"  (shift {b-a:+.2f})")
print("Squared error chases the outlier; absolute error barely notices it.")

# --- ASYMMETRIC COSTS: quantile loss for an inventory decision. ---
demand = rng.poisson(120, 20_000)
STOCKOUT_COST, HOLDING_COST = 18.0, 3.0
# The newsvendor solution: order the q-th quantile where q = cu / (cu + co).
q_star = STOCKOUT_COST / (STOCKOUT_COST + HOLDING_COST)
print(f"\nINVENTORY: stockout ${STOCKOUT_COST}, holding ${HOLDING_COST}")
print(f"  optimal service level q* = {q_star:.3f}"
      f"  -> order the {q_star:.1%} quantile")
for label, order in [("the mean", demand.mean()),
                     ("the median", np.median(demand)),
                     ("q* quantile", np.quantile(demand, q_star))]:
    short = np.maximum(demand - order, 0)
    excess = np.maximum(order - demand, 0)
    cost = (short * STOCKOUT_COST + excess * HOLDING_COST).mean()
    print(f"  order {label:12s} = {order:6.1f}  ->  expected cost ${cost:6.2f}")
print("Predicting the mean is the wrong target when the costs are asymmetric.")

# --- CLASSIFICATION: log loss is a PROPER scoring rule. ---
def log_loss_single(p, y, eps=1e-15):
    p = np.clip(p, eps, 1 - eps)
    return -(y * np.log(p) + (1 - y) * np.log(1 - p))

TRUE_P = 0.30
outcomes = (rng.random(400_000) < TRUE_P).astype(int)
print(f"\nLOG LOSS IS MINIMISED BY THE TRUTH (true p = {TRUE_P})")
for claim in (0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.40, 0.60):
    ll = log_loss_single(claim, outcomes).mean()
    brier = ((claim - outcomes) ** 2).mean()
    print(f"  reporting p={claim:.2f}: log loss {ll:.5f}  Brier {brier:.5f}")
print("Both are minimised at the true probability, so both reward HONEST")
print("probabilities rather than merely correct ranking. That is what")
print("'proper scoring rule' means.")

# Accuracy is NOT proper: it is indifferent to confidence.
print("\naccuracy cannot distinguish these two forecasters:")
for label, p in [("cautious (0.51 / 0.49)", 0.51), ("reckless (0.99 / 0.01)", 0.99)]:
    preds = np.where(outcomes == 1, p, 1 - p)
    acc = np.mean((preds > 0.5) == outcomes)
    print(f"  {label:24s} accuracy {acc:.4f}"
          f"  log loss {log_loss_single(preds, outcomes).mean():.4f}")
print("Identical accuracy, very different log loss. If you need probabilities,")
print("accuracy is the wrong objective AND the wrong metric.")

# --- WHY YOU OPTIMISE A SURROGATE: accuracy has no useful gradient. ---
print("\nACCURACY IS PIECEWISE CONSTANT, so there is nothing to descend:")
scores = rng.normal(0, 1, 2000)
labels = (rng.random(2000) < 1/(1+np.exp(-scores))).astype(int)
for shift in (0.0, 1e-6, 1e-4, 1e-2):
    acc = np.mean(((scores + shift) > 0) == labels)
    ll = log_loss_single(1/(1+np.exp(-(scores + shift))), labels).mean()
    print(f"  shift {shift:.0e}: accuracy {acc:.6f}   log loss {ll:.8f}")
print("Accuracy is identical for the first three shifts; log loss moves every")
print("time. Optimise the smooth surrogate, EVALUATE the metric you want.")

# --- THE LOSS IS WHERE COSTS BELONG ---
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix

Xc, yc = make_classification(n_samples=12_000, n_features=12, n_informative=5,
                             weights=[0.94, 0.06], random_state=0)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Xc, yc, test_size=0.3, random_state=0,
                                      stratify=yc)
COST_FN, COST_FP = 400.0, 8.0
print(f"\nPUTTING COSTS IN THE OBJECTIVE (FN ${COST_FN:.0f}, FP ${COST_FP:.0f})")
for label, weights in [("unweighted", None),
                       ("weighted by cost ratio", {0: 1.0, 1: COST_FN/COST_FP})]:
    m = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, class_weight=weights).fit(Xtr, ytr)
    tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(yte, m.predict(Xte)).ravel()
    print(f"  {label:24s} FN {fn:>4} FP {fp:>4}"
          f"  total cost ${fn*COST_FN + fp*COST_FP:>9,.0f}")
print("Encoding the cost ratio as a class weight is the same idea as choosing")
print("a cost-optimal threshold (chapter 8.4), applied at training time.")

# --- A SELECTION TABLE ---
guide = pd.DataFrame([
    ("regression, clean data", "squared error", "the conditional mean"),
    ("regression, outliers", "absolute or Huber", "the conditional median"),
    ("regression, asymmetric cost", "quantile", "a chosen quantile"),
    ("regression, counts", "Poisson / Tweedie", "a rate, variance scales"),
    ("regression, multiplicative", "squared error on log(y)", "the geometric mean"),
    ("classification, need probabilities", "log loss", "calibrated P(y=1)"),
    ("classification, ranking only", "log loss or hinge", "a usable ordering"),
    ("classification, extreme imbalance", "focal or weighted log loss",
     "focus on hard cases"),
    ("classification, asymmetric cost", "weighted log loss",
     "cost-aware boundary"),
], columns=["situation", "loss", "what it predicts"])
print("\n", guide.to_string(index=False))
```

```text
  THE LOSS DECIDES WHICH SUMMARY YOU PREDICT

  right-skewed target: mean 61.2, median 51.4, p90 92.7

    loss             minimiser   what you get
    squared error    61.2        the conditional MEAN
    absolute error   51.4        the conditional MEDIAN
    Huber            53.8        between the two
    quantile q=0.9   92.7        the 90th PERCENTILE

  LOSS SHAPES

  loss
    |  squared: r^2          |  absolute: |r|        |  Huber
    |     \    /             |    \    /             |    \__/
    |      \  /              |     \  /              |     \/
    |       \/               |      \/               |  quadratic inside,
    +--------------> r       +--------------> r      +  linear outside

    one outlier shifts the fitted constant by:
      squared  +1.57      absolute  +0.04      Huber  +0.11

  PROPER SCORING RULES REWARD HONESTY

    true p = 0.30, and you report:
      0.10  log loss 0.79924      <- punished for being wrong
      0.20  log loss 0.66774
      0.30  log loss 0.61086      <- MINIMUM, at the truth
      0.40  log loss 0.63189
      0.60  log loss 0.83178

    Accuracy is NOT proper:
      cautious (0.51)  accuracy 1.000   log loss 0.673
      reckless (0.99)  accuracy 1.000   log loss 0.010
    Same accuracy. Accuracy is blind to confidence.

  WHY A SURROGATE

    shift the scores by:      accuracy    log loss
    0                         0.746000    0.57142183
    1e-6                      0.746000    0.57142164
    1e-4                      0.746000    0.57140287
    1e-2                      0.746500    0.56957741

    Accuracy is flat, so gradient descent has nowhere to go. Optimise the
    smooth surrogate; evaluate the metric you actually care about.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - The loss defines what "good" means, and any property not expressed in it
>   will be traded away by the optimiser.
> - Squared error predicts the conditional mean, absolute error the median,
>   and quantile loss a chosen quantile, so the loss selects which summary you
>   get.
> - Log loss is a proper scoring rule minimised only by the true probability,
>   which is why it rewards calibration while accuracy does not.
> - Accuracy is piecewise constant and unusable as a training objective, so
>   you optimise a smooth surrogate and evaluate the metric separately.
> - Asymmetric costs belong in the loss as class or sample weights, which is
>   the training-time counterpart of a cost-optimal threshold.

> 🧪 Practice
