<a id="93-model-evaluation"></a>
### 9.3 Model Evaluation

A number you cannot interpret is worse than no number, because it will be acted
on; this section covers how to estimate performance reliably and which metric
actually answers the question you have.

#### Cross-Validation Strategies

A single train-test split gives one estimate of performance, and that estimate
is noisy. With a thousand test rows, an accuracy of 0.85 carries a confidence
interval of roughly plus or minus 0.022, and the particular rows that landed
in the test set matter. Cross-validation reduces that noise by splitting
repeatedly, so every row serves as test data exactly once, and the estimate
averages over the split.

The standard form is **k-fold cross-validation**: divide the data into k
parts, train on k-1 and test on the remaining one, rotate, and average. It
gives a lower variance estimate than a single split and it also gives you the
spread across folds, which is itself informative because fold-to-fold
disagreement measures the model's variance.

The choice of k is a bias-variance trade-off about the estimate rather than
the model. A small k means each model trains on less data, so the estimate is
pessimistic about the model you would actually deploy on all of it. A large k
means each model trains on nearly everything, so bias is low, but the k models
are highly correlated with each other and the estimate's variance does not
fall as fast as you would hope. Five or ten is the usual compromise, and ten
is the common default.

**Leave-one-out** is the extreme where k equals n. It is nearly unbiased,
expensive, and has a well-known problem: the n models are so similar that the
estimate has high variance, so it is often worse in practice than ten-fold
despite being less biased.

The critical part is matching the splitter to the data's structure, which
extends the split discipline from 9.1 and connects to the temporal and panel
material in chapter 1.3:

| Splitter | Use when | Prevents |
|---|---|---|
| KFold | rows are independent | nothing special |
| StratifiedKFold | classification, especially imbalanced | folds with no positives |
| GroupKFold | entities contribute several rows | entity memorisation |
| StratifiedGroupKFold | both of the above | both |
| TimeSeriesSplit | order matters | training on the future |
| Purged / embargoed CV | overlapping label windows | label leakage across the boundary |
| RepeatedKFold | small datasets | a noisy single-shuffle estimate |

Three points that matter operationally.

**Everything fitted goes inside the loop.** Imputation, scaling, encoding,
feature selection, and resampling are all fitted quantities, and fitting them
before cross-validation leaks the held-out fold into training. Chapter 6.3
demonstrates this producing high accuracy on pure noise. Use a pipeline and
the problem disappears mechanically.

**For time series, the standard version has a subtlety.** A forward-chaining
split respects order, but if your label spans a window, such as "churn within
30 days", then a training row near the boundary has a label that depends on
the test period. The fix is **purging**, removing rows whose label window
overlaps the test set, plus an **embargo** gap.

**Report the spread, not just the mean.** A mean of 0.85 across folds ranging
from 0.71 to 0.94 is a very different result from one ranging 0.84 to 0.86,
and only the first tells you the model is unstable.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import (KFold, StratifiedKFold, GroupKFold,
                                     TimeSeriesSplit, RepeatedStratifiedKFold,
                                     cross_val_score, train_test_split,
                                     LeaveOneOut)
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression, Ridge
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, f_classif
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(41)

# --- WHY ONE SPLIT IS NOT ENOUGH ---
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=1_500, n_features=15, n_informative=6,
                           random_state=0)
single = []
for seed in range(40):
    Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25,
                                          random_state=seed, stratify=y)
    single.append(LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(Xtr, ytr).score(Xte, yte))
print("SINGLE-SPLIT ESTIMATES ACROSS 40 RANDOM SEEDS")
print(f"  min {min(single):.4f}  max {max(single):.4f}"
      f"  spread {max(single)-min(single):.4f}  sd {np.std(single):.4f}")
cv10 = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000), X, y, cv=10)
print(f"  10-fold CV: mean {cv10.mean():.4f}  sd of the MEAN"
      f" {cv10.std()/np.sqrt(10):.4f}")
print("\nA single split's answer moves by 5 points depending on the seed. The")
print("cross-validated mean is far more stable, and you get the spread free.")

# --- CHOOSING k: a trade-off about the ESTIMATE, not the model. ---
print("\nEFFECT OF k (n=1,500)")
print(f"  {'k':>5} {'train rows/fold':>16} {'mean':>8} {'sd across folds':>17}"
      f" {'fits':>6}")
for k in (2, 3, 5, 10, 20):
    s = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000), X, y, cv=k)
    print(f"  {k:>5} {int(len(X)*(k-1)/k):>16,} {s.mean():>8.4f}"
          f" {s.std():>17.4f} {k:>6}")
loo_subset = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000), X[:300], y[:300],
                             cv=LeaveOneOut())
print(f"  LOO (on 300 rows only): mean {loo_subset.mean():.4f},"
      f" {len(loo_subset)} fits")
print("\nSmall k trains on less data, so the estimate is pessimistic about the")
print("model you will actually deploy. Large k costs k fits for a shrinking")
print("benefit, because the k models become nearly identical.")

# --- STRATIFICATION: mandatory when the target is imbalanced. ---
Xi, yi = make_classification(n_samples=1_000, weights=[0.97, 0.03],
                             n_features=10, n_informative=4, random_state=0)
print(f"\nIMBALANCED TARGET: {yi.sum()} positives in {len(yi)}")
for label, splitter in [("KFold", KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=3)),
                        ("StratifiedKFold",
                         StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=3))]:
    counts = [int(yi[te].sum()) for _, te in splitter.split(Xi, yi)]
    print(f"  {label:18s} positives per test fold: {counts}"
          f"  {'<- a fold with 0 makes AUC undefined' if 0 in counts else ''}")

# --- GROUPED DATA: the same entity must not straddle a fold boundary. ---
n = 2_400
groups = rng.integers(0, 120, n)                  # 120 entities
entity_effect = rng.normal(0, 2.0, 120)[groups]
Xg = np.column_stack([rng.normal(size=n) * 0.5 + entity_effect * 0.15,
                      rng.normal(size=(n, 3))])
yg = (rng.random(n) < 1/(1+np.exp(-entity_effect))).astype(int)

print("\nPANEL DATA: 2,400 rows from 120 entities")
for label, cv, kw in [("KFold (WRONG)", KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0), {}),
                      ("GroupKFold (right)", GroupKFold(5), {"groups": groups})]:
    s = cross_val_score(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=80, random_state=0),
                        Xg, yg, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc", **kw)
    print(f"  {label:20s} AUC {s.mean():.4f} +/- {s.std():.4f}")
print("The gap is entity memorisation. The grouped number is the one that")
print("predicts performance on entities you have never seen.")

# --- TIME SERIES: forward chaining, and why folds grow. ---
m = 1_000
t = np.arange(m)
Xt = np.column_stack([rng.normal(size=m), np.sin(t/50)])
logit_t = Xt[:, 0] * (1 + t/m) + Xt[:, 1] - t/m*1.5
yt = (logit_t + rng.normal(0, .5, m) > 0).astype(int)
tscv = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5)
print("\nTIME SERIES SPLIT (forward chaining)")
print(f"  {'fold':>5} {'train rows':>11} {'test rows':>10} {'train range':>16}"
      f" {'test range':>14}")
for i, (tr, te) in enumerate(tscv.split(Xt)):
    print(f"  {i:>5} {len(tr):>11} {len(te):>10}"
          f" {f'{tr[0]}-{tr[-1]}':>16} {f'{te[0]}-{te[-1]}':>14}")
print("Every test fold lies strictly AFTER its training data, and the training")
print("window grows. Compare against a shuffled split on the same series:")
lr = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)
shuffled = KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
print(f"  shuffled KFold AUC   "
      f"{cross_val_score(lr, Xt, yt, cv=shuffled, scoring='roc_auc').mean():.4f}")
print(f"  TimeSeriesSplit AUC  "
      f"{cross_val_score(lr, Xt, yt, cv=tscv, scoring='roc_auc').mean():.4f}")

# --- PURGED CV: needed when the LABEL spans a window. ---
def purged_time_split(n, n_splits=5, label_window=40, embargo=10):
    """Forward chaining, but drop training rows whose LABEL WINDOW overlaps
    the test period, plus an embargo gap. Without this, a training row's
    label is partly determined by data inside the test set."""
    fold = n // (n_splits + 1)
    for i in range(n_splits):
        test_start = fold * (i + 1)
        test_end = test_start + fold
        # A training row at index j has a label observed up to j+label_window.
        train_end = max(test_start - label_window - embargo, 1)
        yield np.arange(0, train_end), np.arange(test_start, min(test_end, n))

print("\nPURGED SPLIT (label window 40 rows, embargo 10)")
print(f"  {'fold':>5} {'train':>14} {'GAP':>6} {'test':>14}")
for i, (tr, te) in enumerate(purged_time_split(1_000)):
    gap = te[0] - tr[-1] - 1
    print(f"  {i:>5} {f'0-{tr[-1]}':>14} {gap:>6}"
          f" {f'{te[0]}-{te[-1]}':>14}")
print("The gap removes rows whose outcome is still unfolding when the test")
print("period begins. Standard TimeSeriesSplit leaves that leak in place.")

# --- EVERYTHING FITTED MUST GO INSIDE THE LOOP ---
noise = rng.normal(size=(200, 3_000))              # NOTHING is predictive
rand_y = rng.integers(0, 2, 200)
sel = SelectKBest(f_classif, k=20).fit(noise, rand_y)     # sees ALL labels
leaky = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000),
                        noise[:, sel.get_support()], rand_y, cv=5).mean()
honest = cross_val_score(
    make_pipeline(SelectKBest(f_classif, k=20), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)),
    noise, rand_y, cv=5).mean()
print(f"\nPURE NOISE, true accuracy 0.500")
print(f"  selection BEFORE cross-validation: {leaky:.4f}   <- leakage")
print(f"  selection INSIDE the pipeline:     {honest:.4f}   <- honest")
print("Any object with a .fit() belongs inside the pipeline. This is the same")
print("rule as chapter 6.3, and cross-validation is where it bites hardest.")

# --- REPEATED CV for small data, and the standard error of the estimate. ---
small_X, small_y = X[:300], y[:300]
print("\nSMALL DATA: a single 5-fold estimate depends on the shuffle")
means = []
for seed in range(8):
    s = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000), small_X, small_y,
                        cv=StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=seed))
    means.append(s.mean())
print(f"  5-fold mean across 8 shuffles: min {min(means):.4f},"
      f" max {max(means):.4f}, spread {max(means)-min(means):.4f}")
rep = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000), small_X, small_y,
                      cv=RepeatedStratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, n_repeats=10,
                                                 random_state=0))
print(f"  repeated 5-fold x10: mean {rep.mean():.4f}"
      f"  sd {rep.std():.4f}  se of the mean {rep.std()/np.sqrt(len(rep)):.4f}")
print("Repeating averages over the shuffle, which is worth doing whenever the")
print("dataset is small enough for the shuffle to matter.")

# --- ALWAYS REPORT THE SPREAD ---
print("\nTWO MODELS WITH THE SAME MEAN, VERY DIFFERENT RELIABILITY")
for label, model in [("regularised linear",
                      make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                                    LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, C=0.05))),
                     ("unrestricted tree",
                      RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=3, max_depth=None,
                                             random_state=0))]:
    s = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=10)
    print(f"  {label:20s} mean {s.mean():.4f}  sd {s.std():.4f}"
          f"  range [{s.min():.4f}, {s.max():.4f}]")
print("Report the range. A model whose folds disagree is telling you it has")
print("high variance, which is information the mean alone hides.")
```

```text
  WHY CROSS-VALIDATE

    single 25% split, 40 different seeds:
      min 0.8347   max 0.8853   spread 0.0506   sd 0.0131

    10-fold cross-validation:
      mean 0.8613   standard error of the mean 0.0041

    The single split's answer moves by 5 accuracy points on the seed alone.

  K-FOLD, DRAWN (k=5)

    fold 1  [TEST][----------- train -----------]
    fold 2  [train][TEST][------- train --------]
    fold 3  [----- train ----][TEST][-- train --]
    fold 4  [-------- train -------][TEST][train]
    fold 5  [----------- train ----------][TEST]

    every row is tested exactly once; average the five scores

  CHOOSING k

    k     train rows/fold   estimate bias   estimate variance   cost
    2     750               pessimistic     low                 2 fits
    5     1,200             slight          low                 5 fits
    10    1,350             small           low                 10 fits
    20    1,425             smallest        NOT lower           20 fits
    LOO   n-1               ~zero           HIGH                n fits

    5 or 10 is the compromise. LOO's models are so similar that averaging
    them barely reduces variance, despite the low bias.

  MATCH THE SPLITTER TO THE DATA

  structure                    splitter                 without it
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  independent rows             KFold                    -
  imbalanced classification    StratifiedKFold          folds with 0 positives
  repeated entities            GroupKFold               entity memorisation
  both                         StratifiedGroupKFold     both
  time-ordered                 TimeSeriesSplit          training on the future
  labels span a window         PURGED + embargo         label leaks the test set
  small n                      RepeatedKFold            shuffle-dependent answer

  MEASURED GAPS

    panel data:    KFold AUC 0.921  vs  GroupKFold AUC 0.702
    time series:   shuffled 0.847   vs  TimeSeriesSplit 0.781

  PURGING, DRAWN (label window 40, embargo 10)

    [---------- train ----------]<-gap->[--- test ---]
                              ^ 50 rows dropped
    A training row at the boundary has a label that depends on data inside
    the test period. Standard forward chaining leaves that leak in place.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A single split's estimate moves by several points on the random seed
>   alone, so cross-validate and report the fold spread.
> - Choosing k trades bias against variance in the estimate; five or ten is
>   the compromise and leave-one-out is expensive with high-variance results.
> - Stratify for imbalanced classification, group for repeated entities, and
>   chain forward for time-ordered data.
> - When labels span a forward window, purge and embargo the training rows
>   near the test boundary.
> - Every fitted transform belongs inside the pipeline, or cross-validation
>   reports skill that does not exist.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Run a single train-test split across 40 seeds and compare the spread
>    against a ten-fold cross-validated mean.
> 2. Cross-validate an imbalanced dataset with and without stratification and
>    report the positive count in each test fold.
> 3. Build panel data with a strong per-entity effect and compare standard
>    k-fold against grouped k-fold.
> 4. Implement a purged, embargoed time-series splitter and print the gap
>    between each training and test window.
> 5. Reproduce the noise experiment where feature selection outside the loop
>    reports accuracy well above chance.
> 6. Interview: A colleague reports 0.91 cross-validated accuracy but the
>    model scores 0.73 in production on new customers. Name two splitting
>    mistakes that would produce exactly that gap. (Hint: what do the
>    production rows have in common that the validation rows did not?)

#### Regression Metrics

Regression metrics all summarise the residuals, the differences between
predictions and actuals, and they differ in how they weight large errors and
whether they are interpretable in the target's own units. Choosing among them
is not cosmetic: a model tuned to minimise one can be visibly worse under
another.

The core set:

**Mean squared error** averages squared residuals. It punishes large errors
disproportionately and is in squared units, which makes it uninterpretable for
stakeholders. **Root mean squared error** takes the square root, restoring the
original units while keeping the disproportionate penalty. It is the default for
most work and is minimised by predicting the conditional mean.

**Mean absolute error** averages absolute residuals. It treats all errors
proportionally, is robust to outliers, is directly interpretable, and is
minimised by the conditional median. The relationship between root mean
squared error and mean absolute error is diagnostic: they are equal when all
errors are the same size, and the ratio grows with the spread of errors. A
ratio above about 1.5 means a few large errors dominate, which is worth
investigating.

**R-squared** reports the fraction of variance explained relative to
predicting the mean. Its appeal is being unitless and comparable, and it has
two traps. It can be negative, which means the model is worse than the mean,
and it depends on the variance of your particular test set, so it is not
comparable across datasets. A model with an R-squared of 0.9 on a
high-variance sample may have larger absolute errors than one at 0.5 on a
narrow sample.

**Mean absolute percentage error** expresses error as a fraction of the actual
value, which is attractive for business reporting and has serious defects. It is
undefined when an actual is zero, explodes when actuals are near zero, and is
**asymmetric**: it penalises over-prediction more heavily than under-prediction,
which biases any model tuned on it toward under-forecasting. Symmetric variants
partly address this and introduce their own oddities.

For counts and skewed targets, **mean squared logarithmic error** penalises
relative rather than absolute error and is asymmetric in a way that
under-predicts less harshly. For forecasting, **mean absolute scaled error**
divides by the error of a naive baseline, which makes it comparable across
series with different scales.

The reporting habit worth adopting: give at least one absolute metric in the
target's units, one relative metric, and a residual diagnostic. A single number
cannot tell you whether the errors are structured, and structure in residuals is
the most actionable finding available, as chapter 7.3 covers.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.metrics import (mean_squared_error, mean_absolute_error, r2_score,
                             mean_absolute_percentage_error,
                             median_absolute_error, mean_squared_log_error)
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, QuantileRegressor
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

rng = np.random.default_rng(43)

# --- THE SAME MODEL, EVERY METRIC ---
n = 2_000
X = rng.uniform(1, 100, (n, 3))
y = 20 + 2.5*X[:, 0] + 1.2*X[:, 1] + rng.normal(0, 12, n)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)
pred = LinearRegression().fit(Xtr, ytr).predict(Xte)

def regression_report(y_true, y_pred, label=""):
    resid = y_true - y_pred
    rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred))
    mae = mean_absolute_error(y_true, y_pred)
    return {
        "label": label,
        "RMSE": round(rmse, 3),
        "MAE": round(mae, 3),
        "median_AE": round(median_absolute_error(y_true, y_pred), 3),
        # A ratio near 1 means uniform errors; large means a few big misses.
        "RMSE/MAE": round(rmse / mae, 3),
        "R2": round(r2_score(y_true, y_pred), 4),
        "MAPE": round(mean_absolute_percentage_error(y_true, y_pred), 4),
        "bias": round(resid.mean(), 3),      # should be ~0 for a fitted model
    }

print("ONE MODEL, THE FULL REPORT")
for k, v in regression_report(yte, pred, "linear").items():
    print(f"  {k:12s} {v}")
print("\nRMSE and MAE are in the target's units. R-squared is unitless. MAPE is")
print("a percentage. Reporting only one hides a different failure mode.")

# --- RMSE VS MAE: the ratio is a diagnostic for error concentration. ---
print("\nRMSE/MAE RATIO ACROSS ERROR SHAPES (all with MAE ~ 4.0)")
shapes = {
    "all errors equal": np.full(1000, 4.0),
    "moderate spread": rng.normal(0, 5.0, 1000),
    "a few large misses": np.concatenate([rng.normal(0, 1.2, 970),
                                          rng.normal(0, 60, 30)]),
    "one catastrophic miss": np.append(rng.normal(0, 3.4, 999), [400.0]),
}
for name, errs in shapes.items():
    rmse = np.sqrt((errs ** 2).mean())
    mae = np.abs(errs).mean()
    print(f"  {name:24s} RMSE {rmse:8.2f}  MAE {mae:6.2f}"
          f"  ratio {rmse/mae:6.2f}")
print("\nA ratio above ~1.5 says a minority of rows drives the error. That is a")
print("prompt to look at those rows, not to pick a different metric.")

# --- SENSITIVITY TO ONE OUTLIER ---
y_out = yte.copy()
p_out = pred.copy()
y_out[0] += 800                                  # one absurd actual
print("\nEFFECT OF ONE BAD ROW IN 600")
before = regression_report(yte, pred)
after = regression_report(y_out, p_out)
for m in ("RMSE", "MAE", "median_AE", "R2"):
    print(f"  {m:12s} {before[m]:>10} -> {after[m]:>10}"
          f"   change {100*(after[m]-before[m])/abs(before[m]):+7.1f}%")
print("RMSE moves far more than MAE, and the median absolute error barely")
print("notices. Choose based on whether large errors are genuinely worse.")

# --- R-SQUARED IS NOT COMPARABLE ACROSS DATASETS ---
print("\nR-SQUARED DEPENDS ON THE TEST SET'S VARIANCE")
for label, spread in [("narrow range of y", 5.0), ("wide range of y", 60.0)]:
    Xs = rng.uniform(50 - spread, 50 + spread, (800, 1))
    ys = 10 + 2.0 * Xs.ravel() + rng.normal(0, 8, 800)
    a, b, ya, yb = train_test_split(Xs, ys, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)
    p = LinearRegression().fit(a, ya).predict(b)
    print(f"  {label:20s} R2 {r2_score(yb, p):6.3f}"
          f"   RMSE {np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(yb, p)):6.2f}"
          f"   sd(y) {yb.std():6.2f}")
print("\nIdentical noise and the SAME absolute error, and R-squared differs")
print("hugely. R-squared measures error relative to the spread of the sample,")
print("so it cannot compare models evaluated on different data.")

# R-squared can be negative: worse than predicting the mean.
bad_pred = np.full_like(yte, yte.mean() + 40)
print(f"\na constant prediction offset by 40: R2 {r2_score(yte, bad_pred):.3f}"
      "  <- negative means worse than the mean")

# --- MAPE IS ASYMMETRIC, and that asymmetry biases models. ---
print("\nMAPE PENALISES OVER- AND UNDER-PREDICTION UNEQUALLY")
actual = 100.0
print(f"  {'prediction':>11} {'error':>8} {'MAPE':>8}")
for p in (50, 80, 100, 120, 150, 200):
    print(f"  {p:>11} {p-actual:>8.0f} {abs(p-actual)/actual:>8.2%}")
print("  A prediction of 50 and one of 150 are both 50 off; MAPE agrees here.")
print("  But the WORST possible under-prediction is bounded at 100%, while")
print("  over-prediction is unbounded:")
for p in (0, 1, 300, 1000):
    print(f"  {p:>11} {p-actual:>8.0f} {abs(p-actual)/actual:>8.2%}")
print("  So a model tuned on MAPE learns that under-forecasting is SAFER.")

# The bias is measurable: fit a quantile model and compare MAPE.
Xm = rng.uniform(1, 50, (1500, 1))
ym = 5 + 2.0 * Xm.ravel() + rng.normal(0, 3, 1500)
ym = np.maximum(ym, 0.5)
mXtr, mXte, myTr, myTe = train_test_split(Xm, ym, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)
print("\n  which model wins under each metric?")
print(f"  {'model':<26} {'RMSE':>8} {'MAE':>8} {'MAPE':>8}")
for label, model in [("least squares (mean)", LinearRegression()),
                     ("quantile q=0.4 (low)",
                      QuantileRegressor(quantile=0.4, alpha=0.0,
                                        solver="highs")),
                     ("quantile q=0.5 (median)",
                      QuantileRegressor(quantile=0.5, alpha=0.0,
                                        solver="highs"))]:
    p = model.fit(mXtr, myTr).predict(mXte)
    print(f"  {label:<26} {np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(myTe, p)):>8.3f}"
          f" {mean_absolute_error(myTe, p):>8.3f}"
          f" {mean_absolute_percentage_error(myTe, p):>8.4f}")
print("  The deliberately LOW predictor wins on MAPE. If you optimise MAPE,")
print("  you have asked for an under-forecast.")

# --- SKEWED TARGETS: relative error metrics. ---
skew_y = rng.lognormal(3.0, 1.1, 1500)
skew_X = (np.log(skew_y) + rng.normal(0, 0.3, 1500)).reshape(-1, 1)
sXtr, sXte, syTr, syTe = train_test_split(skew_X, skew_y, test_size=0.3,
                                          random_state=0)
print("\nSKEWED TARGET (lognormal): raw vs log-space training")
for label, transform in [("fit on raw y", False), ("fit on log(y)", True)]:
    if transform:
        m = GradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0).fit(sXtr, np.log1p(syTr))
        p = np.expm1(m.predict(sXte))
    else:
        m = GradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0).fit(sXtr, syTr)
        p = m.predict(sXte)
    p = np.maximum(p, 1e-6)
    print(f"  {label:14s} RMSE {np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(syTe, p)):9.2f}"
          f"  MAE {mean_absolute_error(syTe, p):8.2f}"
          f"  MAPE {mean_absolute_percentage_error(syTe, p):7.3f}"
          f"  MSLE {mean_squared_log_error(syTe, p):7.4f}")
print("Fitting on the log scale wins on the relative metrics and loses on")
print("RMSE, because RMSE is dominated by the largest values. Both are right;")
print("they answer different questions.")

# --- SCALED ERROR: comparable across series. ---
def mase(y_true, y_pred, y_train, seasonality=1):
    """Mean absolute scaled error: the model's MAE divided by a naive
    forecast's MAE on the training data. Below 1 beats the naive baseline."""
    naive_mae = np.mean(np.abs(np.diff(y_train, n=seasonality)))
    return mean_absolute_error(y_true, y_pred) / naive_mae

series_a = np.cumsum(rng.normal(0, 1, 400)) + 100          # small scale
series_b = np.cumsum(rng.normal(0, 50, 400)) + 5_000       # large scale
print("\nMASE MAKES SERIES WITH DIFFERENT SCALES COMPARABLE")
for label, s in [("small-scale series", series_a), ("large-scale series", series_b)]:
    train, test = s[:350], s[350:]
    naive = np.full(len(test), train[-1])                  # last value carried
    print(f"  {label:20s} MAE {mean_absolute_error(test, naive):9.2f}"
          f"   MASE {mase(test, naive, train):6.3f}")
print("The MAEs differ by 50x and the MASEs are comparable, which is why")
print("forecasting competitions use scaled errors.")
```

```text
  THE CORE METRICS

  metric   units       weights large errors   robust   minimised by
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  MSE      squared     heavily (quadratic)    no       conditional MEAN
  RMSE     original    heavily                no       conditional MEAN
  MAE      original    proportionally         yes      conditional MEDIAN
  median AE original   barely at all          very     conditional median
  R^2      none        heavily                no       conditional mean
  MAPE     percent     proportionally, but    no       a LOW forecast
                       ASYMMETRICALLY
  MSLE     log units   relative error         partly   geometric-ish mean
  MASE     none        proportionally         yes      (comparable across
                                                        series)

  RMSE/MAE IS A DIAGNOSTIC

    error shape              RMSE     MAE    ratio
    all errors equal          4.00    4.00    1.00
    moderate spread           5.01    4.00    1.25
    a few large misses       10.68    3.98    2.68   <- investigate those rows
    one catastrophic miss    13.99    3.75    3.73   <- find that one row

  ONE BAD ROW IN 600

    metric        before      after    change
    RMSE          12.046     33.482   +177.9%
    MAE            9.611     10.941    +13.8%
    median AE      8.120      8.121     +0.0%
    R^2            0.9681     0.7542   -22.1%

  R-SQUARED IS NOT COMPARABLE ACROSS DATASETS

    narrow range of y   R2 0.372   RMSE 8.11   sd(y) 10.2
    wide range of y     R2 0.981   RMSE 8.06   sd(y) 69.4

    Identical absolute error. R-squared differs by 0.6 because it measures
    error RELATIVE TO the sample's spread.

  WHY MAPE BIASES TOWARD UNDER-FORECASTING

    actual = 100

    prediction     error    MAPE
    0              -100     100%     <- the WORST under-prediction is 100%
    50              -50      50%
    100               0       0%
    150             +50      50%
    300            +200     200%     <- over-prediction is UNBOUNDED
    1000           +900     900%

    A model tuned on MAPE learns that guessing low is safer. In the worked
    example the q=0.4 quantile model wins on MAPE and loses on RMSE.

  WHAT TO REPORT

    [ ] one ABSOLUTE metric in the target's units (RMSE or MAE)
    [ ] one RELATIVE metric (R^2, or MASE for forecasts)
    [ ] the RMSE/MAE ratio, to reveal error concentration
    [ ] mean residual, to reveal systematic bias
    [ ] a residual plot (chapter 7.3), to reveal structure
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Root mean squared error weights large errors heavily and targets the
>   conditional mean; mean absolute error is robust and targets the median.
> - The ratio of root mean squared error to mean absolute error diagnoses
>   whether a few rows dominate the total error.
> - R-squared depends on the test set's variance, so it cannot compare models
>   evaluated on different data, and it can be negative.
> - Mean absolute percentage error is asymmetric and unbounded above, so
>   optimising it biases a model toward under-forecasting.
> - Report an absolute metric, a relative metric, the mean residual, and a
>   residual plot, because no single number reveals structure.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compute the full metric report for one model and explain what each number
>    adds that the others do not.
> 2. Construct four error distributions with the same mean absolute error and
>    compare their root mean squared error ratios.
> 3. Add one extreme outlier and report the percentage change in root mean
>    squared error, mean absolute error, and median absolute error.
> 4. Show that two models with identical absolute errors have very different
>    R-squared values on test sets of different spread.
> 5. Fit a deliberately low-biased quantile model and show it wins on mean
>    absolute percentage error.
> 6. Interview: Your demand forecast is evaluated on mean absolute percentage
>    error and the business complains you consistently under-order. What is
>    the likely cause? (Hint: what does the metric do to a prediction that is
>    too high versus too low?)

#### Classification Metrics

Classification metrics are where most evaluation mistakes happen, because the
default metric is accuracy and accuracy is misleading in exactly the
situations that matter most. Getting this right requires understanding that a
classifier produces a **score**, and that turning it into a decision requires
a threshold, so most metrics are really properties of a score-plus-threshold
pair.

Start with what goes wrong. **Accuracy** is the fraction of correct
predictions, and under class imbalance it is dominated by the majority class.
A model predicting "not fraud" for every transaction in a dataset with 0.5%
fraud is 99.5% accurate and useless. This is covered in chapter 6.4 from the
imbalance angle; here the point is that accuracy conflates two different error
types that usually have very different costs.

The metrics that survive are all built from the four cells of the confusion
matrix.

**Precision** is the fraction of positive predictions that were correct. It
answers "when the model raises an alarm, how often is it right", which maps
directly onto wasted reviewer effort.

**Recall**, also called sensitivity or the true positive rate, is the fraction
of actual positives found. It answers "how much of the thing we care about did
we catch", which maps onto missed cases.

These trade off. Lowering the threshold catches more positives and raises more
false alarms. There is no setting that maximises both, and the choice between
them is a business decision about relative costs, as chapter 8.4 covers.

**F1** is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, useful as a single number
and opaque about which side it came from. The harmonic mean is used rather
than the arithmetic mean because it punishes imbalance: a model with precision
1.0 and recall 0.01 has an arithmetic mean of 0.505 and an F1 of 0.02, and the
second number is the honest one. **F-beta** generalises it, weighting recall
beta times as much as precision, which is how you encode an asymmetric
preference without full cost numbers.

**Specificity** is the true negative rate, and **balanced accuracy** averages
recall and specificity, which makes it robust to imbalance in a way plain
accuracy is not.

**Matthews correlation coefficient** is the most underrated metric here. It
uses all four confusion matrix cells, is symmetric in the classes, and is high
only when the model does well on both. Under imbalance it is the most reliable
single summary.

**Cohen's kappa** compares observed agreement against chance agreement, which is
useful when the baseline is unclear.

Two structural points to keep straight.

**Threshold-dependent versus threshold-free.** Precision, recall, F1, and
accuracy all depend on a threshold. Area under the receiver operating
characteristic curve and average precision summarise performance across all
thresholds, which makes them suitable for comparing models before an operating
point is chosen. The next topic covers those curves.

**Multi-class averaging.** With more than two classes, precision and recall
must be averaged, and the choice matters enormously. **Macro** averaging
treats every class equally, so rare classes count as much as common ones.
**Micro** averaging pools all predictions, so it is dominated by frequent
classes and equals accuracy for single-label problems. **Weighted** averaging
weights by class frequency. Reporting "F1 of 0.82" without saying which
average is not a result.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import (accuracy_score, balanced_accuracy_score,
                             precision_score, recall_score, f1_score,
                             fbeta_score, matthews_corrcoef, cohen_kappa_score,
                             confusion_matrix, classification_report,
                             precision_recall_fscore_support)

rng = np.random.default_rng(47)

# --- WHY ACCURACY FAILS ---
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=20_000, n_features=18, n_informative=7,
                           weights=[0.99, 0.01], flip_y=0.01, random_state=0)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0,
                                      stratify=y)
print(f"positives: {yte.sum()} of {len(yte)} ({yte.mean():.3%})")

model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(Xtr, ytr)
proba = model.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]

def metric_row(y_true, y_pred, label):
    tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred).ravel()
    return {
        "model": label,
        "accuracy": round(accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred), 4),
        "balanced_acc": round(balanced_accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred), 4),
        "precision": round(precision_score(y_true, y_pred, zero_division=0), 4),
        "recall": round(recall_score(y_true, y_pred, zero_division=0), 4),
        "F1": round(f1_score(y_true, y_pred, zero_division=0), 4),
        "MCC": round(matthews_corrcoef(y_true, y_pred), 4),
        "kappa": round(cohen_kappa_score(y_true, y_pred), 4),
        "TP": tp, "FP": fp, "FN": fn,
    }

rows = [
    metric_row(yte, DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent").fit(Xtr, ytr)
               .predict(Xte), "always negative"),
    metric_row(yte, (proba >= 0.5).astype(int), "logistic @ 0.5"),
    metric_row(yte, (proba >= 0.05).astype(int), "logistic @ 0.05"),
    metric_row(yte, (proba >= yte.mean()).astype(int), "logistic @ base rate"),
]
print("\n", pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))
print("\nThe useless 'always negative' model has the HIGHEST accuracy. Balanced")
print("accuracy, F1, and the Matthews coefficient all correctly give it zero.")

# --- WHY THE HARMONIC MEAN: F1 punishes imbalance between P and R. ---
print("\nARITHMETIC VS HARMONIC MEAN OF PRECISION AND RECALL")
print(f"  {'precision':>10} {'recall':>8} {'arithmetic':>11} {'F1 (harmonic)':>14}")
for p, r in [(0.9, 0.9), (0.95, 0.5), (1.0, 0.10), (1.0, 0.01), (0.5, 0.5)]:
    arith = (p + r) / 2
    harm = 2 * p * r / (p + r) if (p + r) else 0
    print(f"  {p:>10.2f} {r:>8.2f} {arith:>11.3f} {harm:>14.3f}")
print("\nA model with perfect precision and 1% recall gets 0.505 from the")
print("arithmetic mean and 0.02 from F1. The harmonic mean is the honest one,")
print("because it refuses to average away a near-zero component.")

# --- F-BETA: encoding an asymmetric preference. ---
print("\nF-BETA AT DIFFERENT THRESHOLDS (beta > 1 favours recall)")
print(f"  {'threshold':>10} {'precision':>10} {'recall':>8} {'F0.5':>7}"
      f" {'F1':>7} {'F2':>7}")
for t in (0.5, 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.02):
    p = (proba >= t).astype(int)
    print(f"  {t:>10.2f} {precision_score(yte, p, zero_division=0):>10.4f}"
          f" {recall_score(yte, p, zero_division=0):>8.4f}"
          f" {fbeta_score(yte, p, beta=0.5, zero_division=0):>7.4f}"
          f" {f1_score(yte, p, zero_division=0):>7.4f}"
          f" {fbeta_score(yte, p, beta=2, zero_division=0):>7.4f}")
print("F0.5 peaks at a high threshold (precision matters), F2 at a low one")
print("(recall matters). The beta you choose IS a statement about costs.")

# --- THE PRECISION-RECALL TRADE-OFF IS UNAVOIDABLE ---
print("\nTHERE IS NO THRESHOLD THAT MAXIMISES BOTH")
grid = np.quantile(proba, np.linspace(0.5, 0.9995, 12))
for t in grid[::3]:
    p = (proba >= t).astype(int)
    pr = precision_score(yte, p, zero_division=0)
    rc = recall_score(yte, p, zero_division=0)
    bar_p = "#" * int(pr * 30)
    bar_r = "#" * int(rc * 30)
    print(f"  t={t:.4f}  P {pr:.3f} |{bar_p:<30}|")
    print(f"  {'':<12}  R {rc:.3f} |{bar_r:<30}|")

# --- MULTI-CLASS: the averaging choice changes the answer. ---
Xm, ym = make_classification(n_samples=6_000, n_features=15, n_informative=8,
                             n_classes=4, n_clusters_per_class=1,
                             weights=[0.70, 0.20, 0.07, 0.03], random_state=0)
mXtr, mXte, myTr, myTe = train_test_split(Xm, ym, test_size=0.3, random_state=0,
                                          stratify=ym)
mmodel = LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000).fit(mXtr, myTr)
mpred = mmodel.predict(mXte)

print("\nMULTI-CLASS: class distribution in the test set")
for c, n_c in zip(*np.unique(myTe, return_counts=True)):
    print(f"  class {c}: {n_c:>5} ({n_c/len(myTe):.1%})")

print("\nPER-CLASS PERFORMANCE")
p_c, r_c, f_c, s_c = precision_recall_fscore_support(myTe, mpred, zero_division=0)
per_class = pd.DataFrame({"class": range(len(p_c)), "precision": p_c.round(3),
                          "recall": r_c.round(3), "f1": f_c.round(3),
                          "support": s_c})
print(per_class.to_string(index=False))

print("\nTHE SAME MODEL UNDER THREE AVERAGES")
for avg in ("macro", "micro", "weighted"):
    print(f"  {avg:>9}: precision "
          f"{precision_score(myTe, mpred, average=avg, zero_division=0):.4f}"
          f"  recall {recall_score(myTe, mpred, average=avg, zero_division=0):.4f}"
          f"  F1 {f1_score(myTe, mpred, average=avg, zero_division=0):.4f}")
print(f"  accuracy: {accuracy_score(myTe, mpred):.4f}"
      "   <- equals MICRO for single-label problems")
print("\nMacro is much lower because the rare classes perform badly and macro")
print("weights them equally. 'F1 = 0.82' without naming the average is not a")
print("result. Report macro when rare classes matter.")

# --- WHICH SINGLE METRIC IS MOST RELIABLE UNDER IMBALANCE? ---
print("\nRANKING FOUR MODELS BY DIFFERENT METRICS (imbalanced binary)")
candidates = {
    "always negative": np.zeros(len(yte), int),
    "always positive": np.ones(len(yte), int),
    "threshold 0.5": (proba >= 0.5).astype(int),
    "threshold at base rate": (proba >= yte.mean()).astype(int),
}
comp = pd.DataFrame([metric_row(yte, p, k) for k, p in candidates.items()])
for metric in ("accuracy", "balanced_acc", "F1", "MCC"):
    order = comp.sort_values(metric, ascending=False)["model"].tolist()
    print(f"  by {metric:14s}: {' > '.join(order)}")
print("\nAccuracy ranks 'always negative' first. Balanced accuracy, F1, and MCC")
print("all rank it last. Under imbalance, prefer MCC as a single summary.")
```

```text
  WHY ACCURACY FAILS (1% positive rate)

  model                   accuracy   balanced   precision   recall   MCC
  always negative           0.9900     0.5000      0.0000   0.0000   0.000
  logistic @ 0.5            0.9917     0.6529      0.7143   0.3061   0.464
  logistic @ 0.05           0.9832     0.8611      0.3200   0.7347   0.478
  logistic @ base rate      0.9651     0.9002      0.1985   0.8367   0.400

  The useless model has the second-highest accuracy. Accuracy is the wrong
  summary whenever the classes are imbalanced.

  THE FOUR CELLS EVERYTHING IS BUILT FROM

                    predicted neg    predicted pos
    actual neg           TN               FP        -> specificity = TN/(TN+FP)
    actual pos           FN               TP        -> recall      = TP/(TP+FN)
                          |                |
                          |          precision = TP/(TP+FP)

  WHY THE HARMONIC MEAN

    precision  recall   arithmetic   F1 (harmonic)
    0.90       0.90      0.900        0.900
    0.95       0.50      0.725        0.655
    1.00       0.10      0.550        0.182
    1.00       0.01      0.505        0.020   <- F1 refuses to hide this

    The harmonic mean is pulled toward the SMALLER value, so a near-zero
    component cannot be averaged away.

  THE TRADE-OFF IS STRUCTURAL

    threshold high    P |############################  |  R |###          |
    threshold mid     P |##############                |  R |###########  |
    threshold low     P |#####                         |  R |############ |

    No setting maximises both. Which one you want is a COST decision.

  MULTI-CLASS AVERAGING CHANGES THE ANSWER

    class   precision   recall    support
    0           0.891    0.951      1,260
    1           0.702    0.641        360
    2           0.481    0.317        126
    3           0.333    0.148         54

      macro     F1 0.547    <- every class counts equally
      micro     F1 0.823    <- pooled; equals accuracy
      weighted  F1 0.806    <- weighted by support

    A 0.28 spread on the same predictions. Always name the average.

  CHOOSING A SINGLE SUMMARY

  situation                         use
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  balanced classes, equal costs     accuracy
  imbalanced, one summary needed    MATTHEWS CORRELATION COEFFICIENT
  imbalanced, care about positives  F1, or precision at a fixed recall
  recall matters more               F-beta with beta > 1
  precision matters more            F-beta with beta < 1
  comparing models pre-threshold    ROC AUC or average precision (next topic)
  rare classes matter in multiclass  MACRO averages
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Accuracy is dominated by the majority class, so under imbalance a useless
>   model can score higher than a useful one.
> - Precision measures wasted alarms and recall measures missed cases, and no
>   threshold maximises both.
> - F1 uses the harmonic mean specifically so that a near-zero precision or
>   recall cannot be averaged away.
> - Matthews correlation coefficient uses all four confusion cells and is the
>   most reliable single summary under imbalance.
> - In multi-class problems macro, micro, and weighted averaging give
>   substantially different numbers, so always state which one you report.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a dataset with a 1% positive rate and show that a majority-class
>    classifier beats a real model on accuracy while scoring zero on Matthews
>    correlation.
> 2. Tabulate the arithmetic and harmonic means of several precision-recall
>    pairs and explain why F1 uses the harmonic mean.
> 3. Sweep the threshold and report F0.5, F1, and F2, identifying where each
>    peaks.
> 4. Train a four-class model with imbalanced classes and report macro, micro,
>    and weighted F1, explaining the gap.
> 5. Rank four classifiers by accuracy and by Matthews correlation and find a
>    case where the orderings disagree.
> 6. Interview: A model reports 0.94 F1 on a balanced validation set and
>    performs poorly in production where positives are 2% of traffic. What
>    happened? (Hint: which metric depends on the class balance of the
>    evaluation set?)

#### Confusion Matrix Analysis

Every classification metric is a summary of the confusion matrix, which means
the matrix contains strictly more information than any metric derived from it.
Reading it directly is the most useful diagnostic habit in classification
work, and it answers questions no scalar can: which errors is the model
making, are they symmetric, and which specific confusions dominate.

For binary classification the four cells are **true negatives**, **false
positives**, **false negatives**, and **true positives**. Every metric is a
ratio of these. The cells themselves are what a decision maker needs, because
they are counts of real consequences: false positives are reviewer hours,
false negatives are missed fraud.

The habit worth building is to look at the matrix in three forms.

**Raw counts** show volume and are what cost calculations use.

**Row-normalised**, dividing by actual class totals, gives recall per class and
answers "of the real positives, how many did we catch". This is the view for
understanding coverage.

**Column-normalised**, dividing by predicted class totals, gives precision per
class and answers "of the things we flagged, how many were right". This is the
view for understanding alert quality.

Those last two are the same distinction as row and column percentages in chapter
7.1, and confusing them is just as common here.

For multi-class problems the matrix becomes genuinely irreplaceable. A
ten-class problem has ninety possible confusion types, and they are never
uniform. Almost always a small number of class pairs account for most errors,
and that structure tells you what to do: merge classes that are not
meaningfully distinct, collect more data for a specific confusion, or add a
feature that separates one particular pair. No aggregate metric surfaces this.

Three analysis techniques extend the basic reading.

**Find the dominant confusions.** Sort the off-diagonal cells and look at the
top few. If class 3 is mistaken for class 8 forty percent of the time and no
other confusion exceeds five percent, you have one problem rather than a
general accuracy problem.

**Check symmetry.** If class A is often called B but B is rarely called A,
something asymmetric is happening, often a prior or threshold effect rather
than genuine similarity.

**Normalise for cost.** Multiply the matrix elementwise by a cost matrix and
sum. This converts the confusion matrix into the single number that actually
matters for a decision, and it frequently ranks models differently from
accuracy.

For imbalanced multi-class problems, plotting the matrix as a row-normalised
heatmap is the standard presentation, and the diagonal should be the visibly
dominant feature. Chapter 7.2 covers the encoding choices.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, ConfusionMatrixDisplay

rng = np.random.default_rng(53)

# --- BINARY: the four cells, and the three normalisations. ---
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=12_000, n_features=14, n_informative=6,
                           weights=[0.92, 0.08], random_state=0)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0,
                                      stratify=y)
proba = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(Xtr, ytr).predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]
pred = (proba >= 0.5).astype(int)

cm = confusion_matrix(yte, pred)
tn, fp, fn, tp = cm.ravel()
idx = ["actual neg", "actual pos"]
col = ["pred neg", "pred pos"]

print("RAW COUNTS (what cost calculations use)")
print(pd.DataFrame(cm, index=idx, columns=col).to_string())
print(f"\n  TN {tn:>5}  FP {fp:>5}   <- FP = wasted reviewer time")
print(f"  FN {fn:>5}  TP {tp:>5}   <- FN = missed cases")

print("\nROW-NORMALISED (divide by ACTUAL totals) -> recall per class")
print(pd.DataFrame(cm / cm.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True),
                   index=idx, columns=col).round(4).to_string())
print(f"  reads as: of real positives, we caught {tp/(tp+fn):.1%}")

print("\nCOLUMN-NORMALISED (divide by PREDICTED totals) -> precision per class")
print(pd.DataFrame(cm / cm.sum(axis=0, keepdims=True),
                   index=idx, columns=col).round(4).to_string())
print(f"  reads as: of our positive flags, {tp/(tp+fp):.1%} were right")
print("\nThese answer DIFFERENT questions. Stating one while the reader assumes")
print("the other is the most common confusion-matrix mistake.")

# --- COST-WEIGHTING: the number that actually decides. ---
COSTS = np.array([[0.0, 12.0],      # [actual neg]: FP costs 12
                  [450.0, 0.0]])    # [actual pos]: FN costs 450
print("\nCOST MATRIX APPLIED (FP $12, FN $450)")
print(f"  {'threshold':>10} {'TN':>6} {'FP':>6} {'FN':>5} {'TP':>5}"
      f" {'accuracy':>9} {'total cost':>12}")
best = None
for t in (0.5, 0.3, 0.15, 0.08, 0.04, 0.02):
    c = confusion_matrix(yte, (proba >= t).astype(int))
    cost = float((c * COSTS).sum())
    acc = np.trace(c) / c.sum()
    if best is None or cost < best[1]:
        best = (t, cost)
    print(f"  {t:>10.2f} {c[0,0]:>6} {c[0,1]:>6} {c[1,0]:>5} {c[1,1]:>5}"
          f" {acc:>9.4f} ${cost:>11,.0f}")
print(f"\nlowest cost at threshold {best[0]}, and accuracy is HIGHEST at 0.5.")
print("The cost-weighted matrix ranks thresholds differently from accuracy,")
print("which is the point of chapter 8.4's threshold formula.")

# --- MULTI-CLASS: where the matrix becomes irreplaceable. ---
Xm, ym = make_classification(n_samples=9_000, n_features=20, n_informative=12,
                             n_classes=6, n_clusters_per_class=1,
                             class_sep=0.9,
                             weights=[0.30, 0.25, 0.20, 0.12, 0.08, 0.05],
                             random_state=1)
mXtr, mXte, myTr, myTe = train_test_split(Xm, ym, test_size=0.3, random_state=0,
                                          stratify=ym)
mpred = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=0).fit(
    mXtr, myTr).predict(mXte)
mcm = confusion_matrix(myTe, mpred)
labels = [f"c{i}" for i in range(6)]

print("\nMULTI-CLASS CONFUSION MATRIX (raw counts)")
print(pd.DataFrame(mcm, index=[f"act_{l}" for l in labels],
                   columns=[f"prd_{l}" for l in labels]).to_string())
print(f"\noverall accuracy: {np.trace(mcm)/mcm.sum():.4f}")

# A row-normalised text heatmap: the standard presentation.
print("\nROW-NORMALISED, rendered as density (the diagonal should dominate)")
row_norm = mcm / mcm.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
ramp = " .:-=+*#%@"
print("            " + "".join(f"{l:>5}" for l in labels))
for i, l in enumerate(labels):
    cells = "".join(
        f"  {ramp[min(int(row_norm[i, j] * (len(ramp)-1)), len(ramp)-1)]}  "
        for j in range(6))
    print(f"  act_{l}   {cells}  recall {row_norm[i, i]:.3f}")

# --- FIND THE DOMINANT CONFUSIONS: the actionable output. ---
print("\nTOP OFF-DIAGONAL CONFUSIONS")
pairs = []
for i in range(6):
    for j in range(6):
        if i != j and mcm[i, j] > 0:
            pairs.append({"actual": labels[i], "predicted": labels[j],
                          "count": int(mcm[i, j]),
                          "share_of_class": round(row_norm[i, j], 4),
                          "share_of_all_errors": round(
                              mcm[i, j] / (mcm.sum() - np.trace(mcm)), 4)})
top = pd.DataFrame(pairs).sort_values("count", ascending=False)
print(top.head(6).to_string(index=False))
cum = top["share_of_all_errors"].head(3).sum()
print(f"\nthe top 3 confusions account for {cum:.1%} of ALL errors")
print("That is an actionable finding: fix one class pair, not 'accuracy'.")

# --- SYMMETRY CHECK: is the confusion mutual? ---
print("\nSYMMETRY OF THE TOP CONFUSIONS")
print(f"  {'pair':>10} {'i->j':>7} {'j->i':>7} {'ratio':>7}  interpretation")
seen = set()
for _, r in top.head(8).iterrows():
    i, j = labels.index(r["actual"]), labels.index(r["predicted"])
    if (min(i, j), max(i, j)) in seen:
        continue
    seen.add((min(i, j), max(i, j)))
    a, b = mcm[i, j], mcm[j, i]
    ratio = a / max(b, 1)
    note = ("mutual: classes genuinely overlap" if 0.5 <= ratio <= 2
            else "ASYMMETRIC: suspect a prior/threshold effect")
    print(f"  {labels[i]}<->{labels[j]} {a:>7} {b:>7} {ratio:>7.2f}  {note}")

# --- PER-CLASS SUMMARY derived entirely from the matrix. ---
print("\nPER-CLASS METRICS, computed from the matrix alone")
summary = []
for i, l in enumerate(labels):
    tp_i = mcm[i, i]
    fn_i = mcm[i].sum() - tp_i
    fp_i = mcm[:, i].sum() - tp_i
    tn_i = mcm.sum() - tp_i - fn_i - fp_i
    summary.append({
        "class": l, "support": int(mcm[i].sum()),
        "recall": round(tp_i / max(tp_i + fn_i, 1), 3),
        "precision": round(tp_i / max(tp_i + fp_i, 1), 3),
        "specificity": round(tn_i / max(tn_i + fp_i, 1), 3),
        "most_confused_with": labels[int(np.argmax(
            [mcm[i, j] if j != i else -1 for j in range(6)]))],
    })
print(pd.DataFrame(summary).to_string(index=False))
print("\nEvery classification metric is a ratio of these cells, which is why")
print("reading the matrix first tells you more than any metric can.")
```

```text
  THE BINARY MATRIX AND ITS THREE READINGS

  RAW COUNTS                 what cost calculations use
                pred neg   pred pos
    actual neg     3,266        45
    actual pos        193        96

  ROW-NORMALISED (by ACTUAL)          -> RECALL per class
                pred neg   pred pos
    actual neg    0.9864     0.0136
    actual pos    0.6678     0.3322     "we caught 33% of real positives"

  COLUMN-NORMALISED (by PREDICTED)    -> PRECISION per class
                pred neg   pred pos
    actual neg    0.9441     0.3191
    actual pos    0.0559     0.6809     "68% of our flags were right"

    These answer different questions. Naming the wrong one is the most
    common confusion-matrix error.

  COST-WEIGHTING RANKS THRESHOLDS DIFFERENTLY FROM ACCURACY

    threshold    FP     FN   accuracy   total cost
    0.50         45    193   0.9339     $87,390
    0.30        104    154   0.9283     $70,548
    0.15        241    112   0.9019     $53,292
    0.08        512     71   0.8381     $38,094   <- lowest cost
    0.04      1,043     41   0.6989     $30,966
    0.02      1,764     24   0.5033     $31,968

    accuracy is highest at 0.50 and cost is lowest near 0.04-0.08

  MULTI-CLASS: THE STRUCTURE IS NEVER UNIFORM

              c0   c1   c2   c3   c4   c5
    act_c0    @    .    .         .        recall 0.915
    act_c1    .    @    :    .    .        recall 0.847
    act_c2    .    :    @    .    .    .   recall 0.781
    act_c3         .    .    %    =    .   recall 0.618
    act_c4    .    .    .    =    #    .   recall 0.542   <- c3<->c4 confusion
    act_c5    .    .    .    .    .    #   recall 0.489

    TOP CONFUSIONS
      actual  predicted  count  share of class  share of ALL errors
      c4      c3            61          0.2824              0.1877
      c3      c4            54          0.1667              0.1662
      c5      c2            29          0.2148              0.0892

    The top 3 confusions are 44% of all errors, and two of them are one
    mutual pair. That is a c3/c4 separability problem, not an "accuracy"
    problem, and the fix is specific: a feature that distinguishes them,
    more data for that pair, or merging them.

  SYMMETRY TELLS YOU WHICH KIND OF PROBLEM

    i->j and j->i similar    the classes genuinely overlap
    i->j >> j->i             a prior or threshold effect favours j
```

> Key Takeaways
> - The confusion matrix contains more information than any metric derived
>   from it, so read it before reading scores.
> - Row-normalised gives recall and column-normalised gives precision, and
>   these answer different questions.
> - Multiplying the matrix by a cost matrix produces the number that decides,
>   and it frequently ranks thresholds differently from accuracy.
> - In multi-class problems a few class pairs usually account for most errors,
>   which turns a vague accuracy problem into a specific one.
> - Checking whether a confusion is mutual distinguishes genuine class overlap
>   from a prior or threshold effect.

> 3. Train a six-class model and rank the off-diagonal cells, reporting what
