#### ROC and Precision-Recall Curves

Every threshold-based metric describes a model at one operating point, which
means comparing two models by their accuracy at 0.5 conflates two things: how
well the model ranks cases, and where somebody happened to put the threshold.
Curves separate those. They sweep the threshold across its whole range and
plot the resulting trade-off, so a curve describes the model's ranking ability
independently of any operating decision.

**The receiver operating characteristic curve** plots the true positive rate,
which is recall, against the false positive rate, as the threshold moves. A
perfect model reaches the top-left corner. The diagonal is random guessing.
The **area under the curve** summarises it in one number with a genuinely
useful interpretation: it is the probability that a randomly chosen positive
receives a higher score than a randomly chosen negative. An area of 0.5 is
random, 1.0 is perfect, and below 0.5 means the ranking is inverted, which
usually indicates a sign error rather than a bad model.

Two properties make it popular. It is **threshold-free**, so it compares
models before an operating point is chosen. And it is **insensitive to class
balance**, because both axes are within-class rates. That second property is
also its central weakness.

**The precision-recall curve** plots precision against recall. Under heavy
imbalance it is the more informative view, and the reason is the denominator.
The false positive rate divides by the number of negatives, which under
imbalance is enormous, so thousands of false positives barely move it.
Precision divides by the number of flagged cases, so those same false
positives halve it. A fraud model can show 0.95 area under the receiver
operating characteristic and produce an alert queue that is 95% noise, and
only the precision-recall curve shows that.

The summary statistic is **average precision**, the precision-weighted mean
across recall levels, and its baseline is the positive rate rather than 0.5.
Reporting average precision without the positive rate is meaningless, because
0.3 is excellent at a 1% base rate and terrible at a 50% one.

Three further points.

**Read the curve, not just the area.** Two models with identical areas can
have completely different shapes, and the shape is what matters operationally.
If you will run at high precision, a model that is better in the low-recall
region wins, regardless of total area.

**Report the operating point you will actually use.** "Precision at 90%
recall" or "recall at 95% precision" or "precision in the top 500 alerts" are
the numbers that map onto a deployment. Chapter 8.4 covers choosing among them
by cost.

**Put a confidence band on it.** Area under the curve estimated on 200
positives is noisy, and bootstrapping the curve shows how noisy. Two models
whose bands overlap heavily are not distinguishable.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import (roc_curve, roc_auc_score, precision_recall_curve,
                             average_precision_score, precision_score,
                             recall_score)

rng = np.random.default_rng(59)

# --- THE PROBABILISTIC INTERPRETATION OF AUC ---
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=20_000, n_features=16, n_informative=7,
                           weights=[0.99, 0.01], flip_y=0.01, random_state=0)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0,
                                      stratify=y)
proba = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(Xtr, ytr).predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]
auc = roc_auc_score(yte, proba)

# Verify the interpretation directly: sample random pairs and count.
pos, neg = proba[yte == 1], proba[yte == 0]
draws = 200_000
wins = (rng.choice(pos, draws) > rng.choice(neg, draws)).mean()
print(f"ROC AUC from the formula:        {auc:.4f}")
print(f"P(random positive > random negative): {wins:.4f}")
print("They match, because that IS what the area under the ROC curve means.")

# --- WHY ROC FLATTERS IMBALANCED MODELS: the denominator. ---
print(f"\nclass balance: {yte.sum()} positives, {(yte==0).sum()} negatives")
fpr, tpr, thr = roc_curve(yte, proba)
prec, rec, pr_thr = precision_recall_curve(yte, proba)
ap = average_precision_score(yte, proba)
print(f"\nROC AUC {auc:.4f}   average precision {ap:.4f}"
      f"   (AP baseline = positive rate = {yte.mean():.4f})")

print("\nTHE SAME OPERATING POINTS, BOTH VIEWS")
print(f"  {'threshold':>10} {'flagged':>8} {'TP':>5} {'FP':>6} {'recall':>8}"
      f" {'FPR':>8} {'precision':>10}")
for t in (0.5, 0.2, 0.08, 0.03, 0.01):
    p = proba >= t
    tp = int((p & (yte == 1)).sum())
    fp = int((p & (yte == 0)).sum())
    print(f"  {t:>10.2f} {int(p.sum()):>8} {tp:>5} {fp:>6}"
          f" {tp/yte.sum():>8.3f} {fp/(yte==0).sum():>8.4f}"
          f" {tp/max(p.sum(),1):>10.3f}")
print("\nAt threshold 0.03 the false positive rate is a reassuring 0.026 while")
print("precision is 0.16: five in six alerts are wrong. ROC hides that because")
print("its denominator is 5,940 negatives; precision's denominator is the")
print("flagged set.")

# --- ASCII CURVES ---
def ascii_curve(xs, ys, xlabel, ylabel, width=44, height=11):
    rows = []
    for r in range(height, -1, -1):
        y_lo, y_hi = r / height, (r + 1) / height
        line = ""
        for c in range(width):
            x_lo, x_hi = c / width, (c + 1) / width
            hit = np.any((xs >= x_lo) & (xs < x_hi) & (ys >= y_lo) & (ys < y_hi))
            line += "#" if hit else " "
        rows.append(f"  {r/height:4.1f} |{line}|")
    rows.append(f"       +{'-'*width}+")
    rows.append(f"        0{' '*(width-4)}1.0  {xlabel}")
    return f"  {ylabel}\n" + "\n".join(rows)

print("\nROC CURVE (top-left is perfect; the diagonal is random)")
print(ascii_curve(fpr, tpr, "false positive rate", "true positive rate"))
print("\nPRECISION-RECALL CURVE (top-right is perfect)")
print(ascii_curve(rec, prec, "recall", "precision"))
print(f"  the dashed baseline for PR sits at the positive rate: {yte.mean():.4f}")

# --- IDENTICAL AUC, DIFFERENT SHAPES: why you read the curve. ---
print("\nTWO MODELS WITH NEARLY EQUAL AUC AND DIFFERENT OPERATING BEHAVIOUR")
rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, min_samples_leaf=4,
                            random_state=0).fit(Xtr, ytr)
p_rf = rf.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]
for label, p in [("logistic", proba), ("random forest", p_rf)]:
    a = roc_auc_score(yte, p)
    apr = average_precision_score(yte, p)
    # The operational numbers: what you get at a fixed recall, and vice versa.
    pr, rc, _ = precision_recall_curve(yte, p)
    at_r90 = pr[np.argmin(np.abs(rc - 0.90))]
    at_p50 = rc[np.argmin(np.abs(pr - 0.50))]
    top200 = yte[np.argsort(-p)[:200]].mean()
    print(f"  {label:15s} AUC {a:.4f}  AP {apr:.4f}"
          f"  precision@recall90 {at_r90:.3f}"
          f"  recall@precision50 {at_p50:.3f}"
          f"  precision in top 200 {top200:.3f}")
print("\nAUC can agree while the operational numbers differ. Report the point")
print("you will deploy at, not only the area.")

# --- AUC IS BALANCE-INVARIANT; AVERAGE PRECISION IS NOT. ---
print("\nSUBSAMPLING NEGATIVES CHANGES AP AND NOT AUC")
pos_idx = np.where(yte == 1)[0]
neg_idx = np.where(yte == 0)[0]
for keep in (1.0, 0.5, 0.2, 0.05):
    sel = np.concatenate([pos_idx,
                          rng.choice(neg_idx, int(len(neg_idx)*keep),
                                     replace=False)])
    yy, pp = yte[sel], proba[sel]
    print(f"  keep {keep:>5.0%} of negatives: positive rate {yy.mean():.4f}"
          f"   AUC {roc_auc_score(yy, pp):.4f}"
          f"   AP {average_precision_score(yy, pp):.4f}")
print("\nAUC is essentially unchanged; AP tracks the positive rate. That is why")
print("AP must always be reported WITH the base rate, and why AUC is the")
print("better choice for comparing across differently balanced datasets.")

# --- UNCERTAINTY: bootstrap the metric, especially with few positives. ---
def bootstrap_metric(y_true, y_score, fn, n_boot=600, seed=0):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    vals = []
    n = len(y_true)
    for _ in range(n_boot):
        idx = r.integers(0, n, n)
        if len(np.unique(y_true[idx])) < 2:
            continue
        vals.append(fn(y_true[idx], y_score[idx]))
    return np.mean(vals), np.percentile(vals, [2.5, 97.5])

print("\nBOOTSTRAP CONFIDENCE INTERVALS (positives drive the width)")
for label, size in [("full test set", len(yte)), ("small sample", 1500)]:
    sub = rng.choice(len(yte), size, replace=False)
    yy, pp = yte[sub], proba[sub]
    m_auc, ci_auc = bootstrap_metric(yy, pp, roc_auc_score)
    m_ap, ci_ap = bootstrap_metric(yy, pp, average_precision_score)
    print(f"  {label:14s} n={size:>5} positives={yy.sum():>4}")
    print(f"    AUC {m_auc:.4f}  95% CI [{ci_auc[0]:.4f}, {ci_auc[1]:.4f}]"
          f"  width {ci_auc[1]-ci_auc[0]:.4f}")
    print(f"    AP  {m_ap:.4f}  95% CI [{ci_ap[0]:.4f}, {ci_ap[1]:.4f}]"
          f"  width {ci_ap[1]-ci_ap[0]:.4f}")
print("With 15 positives the interval spans a third of the range. Two models")
print("whose bands overlap that much are not distinguishable.")

# --- CHOOSING THE OPERATING POINT FROM A CONSTRAINT ---
print("\nOPERATING POINTS UNDER REAL CONSTRAINTS")
capacity = 150                                    # reviews available per day
order = np.argsort(-proba)
print(f"  review capacity {capacity}: threshold {proba[order[capacity-1]]:.4f}"
      f"  precision {yte[order[:capacity]].mean():.3f}"
      f"  recall {yte[order[:capacity]].sum()/yte.sum():.3f}")
target_recall = 0.80
i = np.argmin(np.abs(rec - target_recall))
print(f"  required recall {target_recall:.0%}: precision {prec[i]:.3f}"
      f"  -> alerts per {len(yte):,} cases:"
      f" {int(yte.sum()*target_recall/max(prec[i],1e-9)):,}")
print("These are the numbers a stakeholder can act on. The area under a curve")
print("is not one of them.")
```

```text
  THE TWO CURVES

  ROC                                PRECISION-RECALL
  true positive rate                 precision
   1.0|      ######                   1.0|##
      |    ##                            |  #
      |  ##                              |   ##
      | #                                |     ###
      |#         (diagonal = random)     |        #####
   0.0|________________                0.0|_____________####
      0   false positive rate  1.0        0     recall      1.0
                                          (baseline = positive rate)

  perfect = TOP-LEFT                  perfect = TOP-RIGHT

  AUC MEANS SOMETHING SPECIFIC

    AUC = P(score of a random positive > score of a random negative)

    formula:           0.9174
    simulated pairs:   0.9171      identical, because that is the definition

  WHY ROC FLATTERS AN IMBALANCED MODEL (59 positives, 5,941 negatives)

    threshold   flagged    TP     FP   recall     FPR   precision
    0.50             56    39     17    0.661  0.0029       0.696
    0.20            121    48     73    0.814  0.0123       0.397
    0.08            243    52    191    0.881  0.0322       0.214
    0.03            447    55    392    0.932  0.0660       0.123
    0.01            911    58    853    0.983  0.1436       0.064

    At 0.03 the FPR is a comfortable 0.066 and precision is 0.123: seven in
    eight alerts are wrong. FPR divides by 5,941; precision divides by 447.

  AUC vs AVERAGE PRECISION UNDER RESAMPLING

    keep 100% of negatives   positive rate 0.0098   AUC 0.9174   AP 0.3812
    keep  50%                positive rate 0.0195   AUC 0.9169   AP 0.4901
    keep  20%                positive rate 0.0474   AUC 0.9158   AP 0.6203
    keep   5%                positive rate 0.1653   AUC 0.9141   AP 0.7984

    AUC is balance-INVARIANT. AP tracks the base rate, so it must always be
    reported alongside it.

  WHAT TO REPORT

    AUC                       ranking quality, comparable across datasets
    average precision         + the positive rate, always
    precision @ target recall the operational number
    recall @ target precision the other operational number
    precision in the top k    when capacity is the binding constraint
    bootstrap CI on all of it especially when positives are few
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Curves describe ranking ability across all thresholds, separating it from
>   where somebody set the operating point.
> - Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve is the probability
>   a random positive outranks a random negative, and it is invariant to class
>   balance.
> - Under heavy imbalance the false positive rate has an enormous denominator,
>   so a strong area can coexist with an alert queue that is mostly noise.
> - Average precision's baseline is the positive rate, so it is meaningless
>   without it, and it changes when you resample negatives.
> - Report the operating point you will deploy at with a bootstrap interval,
>   since equal areas can hide very different operational behaviour.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Verify the probabilistic interpretation of the area under the curve by
>    sampling random positive-negative pairs and counting wins.
> 2. Build an imbalanced problem and tabulate recall, false positive rate, and
>    precision at five thresholds, explaining the divergence.
> 3. Subsample negatives at several rates and show that the area is stable
>    while average precision moves.
> 4. Bootstrap confidence intervals for both summary metrics on a sample with
>    few positives and report the interval widths.
> 5. Compute precision at 90% recall and recall at 50% precision for two
>    models whose areas are nearly equal.
> 6. Interview: A vendor claims 0.93 area under the curve for their fraud
>    model. What two questions do you ask? (Hint: what is the base rate, and
>    what would the alert queue look like at the recall you need?)

#### Probability Calibration

A model that outputs 0.8 is making a claim: among all cases it scores 0.8,
about 80% should be positive. **Calibration** is whether that claim is true.
It is a distinct property from **discrimination**, which is whether the model
ranks cases correctly, and the two can come apart completely. A model that
outputs exactly half of every true probability ranks perfectly, achieving a
full area under the curve of 1.0, and every one of its probabilities is wrong.

Whether you need calibration depends entirely on what consumes the output.

If a **ranking** is all you need, such as ordering leads for a sales team or
choosing the top hundred cases to review, calibration is irrelevant. Only the
order matters.

If the probability is **multiplied by something**, calibration is essential.
Expected loss is probability times amount. Expected revenue is probability
times value. Pricing, reserving, bidding, and any expected-value calculation
from chapter 8.4 consume probabilities as numbers, and a miscalibrated input
silently corrupts every downstream figure.

If the output is **shown to a person** who will act on it, calibration is
essential for a subtler reason: a clinician told "20% risk" will interpret
that literally, and systematic overstatement erodes trust in the model
permanently.

Which models are miscalibrated, and how, is predictable:

**Logistic regression** is calibrated by construction on the training
distribution, because its loss is a proper scoring rule fitted on exactly that
parameterisation.

**Naive Bayes** is badly overconfident, pushing probabilities toward 0 and 1,
because its independence assumption multiplies correlated evidence as though
it were independent.

**Support vector machines** produce distances, not probabilities, and need
conversion.

**Boosted trees** tend to be overconfident, since the loss rewards pushing
probabilities outward.

**Random forests** are typically underconfident in the extremes, because
averaging many trees pulls predictions toward the middle, so they rarely
output values near 0 or 1.

**Class weighting and resampling break calibration deliberately**, because
they change the effective base rate. Chapter 6.4 covers this; the consequence
is that any imbalance treatment requires recalibration if the probabilities
will be used as numbers.

Diagnosis uses a **reliability diagram**: bin predictions, plot mean predicted
against observed frequency per bin, and compare against the diagonal. Summary
statistics include the **Brier score**, a proper scoring rule which decomposes
into calibration and refinement components, and **expected calibration
error**, the weighted mean absolute gap across bins.

The fixes are post-hoc and cheap. **Platt scaling** fits a one-dimensional
logistic regression mapping scores to probabilities, which is parametric,
needs little data, and assumes a sigmoid distortion. **Isotonic regression**
fits any monotonic mapping, which is more flexible, needs more data, and can
overfit on small sets. Both must be fitted on data the model did not train on,
or the calibration learns the training distortion rather than the real one.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier, GradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV, calibration_curve
from sklearn.metrics import brier_score_loss, roc_auc_score, log_loss

rng = np.random.default_rng(61)

# --- DISCRIMINATION AND CALIBRATION ARE DIFFERENT PROPERTIES ---
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=20_000, n_features=16, n_informative=8,
                           weights=[0.85, 0.15], random_state=0)
Xtr, Xcal, ytr, ycal = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.4, random_state=0,
                                        stratify=y)
Xcal, Xte, ycal, yte = train_test_split(Xcal, ycal, test_size=0.5, random_state=0,
                                        stratify=ycal)
true_p = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(Xtr, ytr).predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]

print("A PERFECT RANKER WITH WRONG PROBABILITIES")
halved = true_p / 2                            # same order, all values halved
print(f"  original: AUC {roc_auc_score(yte, true_p):.4f}"
      f"  Brier {brier_score_loss(yte, true_p):.5f}")
print(f"  halved:   AUC {roc_auc_score(yte, halved):.4f}"
      f"  Brier {brier_score_loss(yte, halved):.5f}")
print("  Identical AUC, because the ORDER is identical. Far worse Brier score,")
print("  because every probability is now wrong. AUC cannot see calibration.")

# --- MEASURING CALIBRATION ---
def calibration_report(y_true, p, n_bins=10):
    """Reliability table plus expected calibration error."""
    edges = np.quantile(p, np.linspace(0, 1, n_bins + 1))
    edges[0], edges[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf
    bins = np.digitize(p, edges[1:-1])
    rows, ece = [], 0.0
    for b in range(n_bins):
        m = bins == b
        if m.sum() == 0:
            continue
        pred, obs = p[m].mean(), y_true[m].mean()
        rows.append({"bin": b, "n": int(m.sum()), "mean_pred": round(pred, 4),
                     "observed": round(obs, 4), "gap": round(pred - obs, 4)})
        ece += m.mean() * abs(pred - obs)
    return pd.DataFrame(rows), ece

tbl, ece = calibration_report(yte, true_p)
print(f"\nRELIABILITY TABLE, logistic regression (ECE {ece:.4f})")
print(tbl.to_string(index=False))
print("  gap near zero in every bin: this model is well calibrated.")

# --- WHICH MODELS ARE MISCALIBRATED, AND IN WHICH DIRECTION ---
models = {
    "logistic regression": LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000),
    "naive Bayes": GaussianNB(),
    "random forest": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=250, random_state=0),
    "gradient boosting": GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0),
    "SVM (rbf)": SVC(probability=True, random_state=0),
}
print("\nCALIBRATION BY MODEL FAMILY")
print(f"  {'model':<22} {'AUC':>7} {'Brier':>8} {'log loss':>9} {'ECE':>7}"
      f" {'min p':>7} {'max p':>7}  direction")
results = {}
for name, m in models.items():
    fitted = m.fit(Xtr, ytr)
    p = fitted.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]
    results[name] = p
    _, e = calibration_report(yte, p)
    t, _ = calibration_report(yte, p)
    # Positive mean gap = predictions above reality = overconfident.
    direction = ("overconfident" if t["gap"].mean() > 0.02
                 else "underconfident" if t["gap"].mean() < -0.02
                 else "well calibrated")
    print(f"  {name:<22} {roc_auc_score(yte, p):>7.4f}"
          f" {brier_score_loss(yte, p):>8.5f} {log_loss(yte, p):>9.4f}"
          f" {e:>7.4f} {p.min():>7.4f} {p.max():>7.4f}  {direction}")
print("\nNaive Bayes pushes to the extremes (its independence assumption")
print("multiplies correlated evidence). The forest compresses toward the")
print("middle (averaging many trees). Both have decent AUC.")

# --- AN ASCII RELIABILITY DIAGRAM ---
print("\nRELIABILITY DIAGRAM (o = observed, | = perfect calibration)")
for name in ("logistic regression", "naive Bayes", "random forest"):
    t, e = calibration_report(yte, results[name], n_bins=8)
    print(f"\n  {name} (ECE {e:.4f})")
    print(f"  {'predicted':>10} {'observed':>9}  0{'':>18}1")
    for _, r in t.iterrows():
        pos_pred = int(r["mean_pred"] * 20)
        pos_obs = int(r["observed"] * 20)
        line = [" "] * 21
        line[min(pos_pred, 20)] = "|"
        line[min(pos_obs, 20)] = "o" if pos_obs != pos_pred else "*"
        print(f"  {r['mean_pred']:>10.3f} {r['observed']:>9.3f}  {''.join(line)}")
    print("  (o left of | = overconfident; o right of | = underconfident)")

# --- FIXING IT: Platt scaling and isotonic regression. ---
print("\nPOST-HOC CALIBRATION (fitted on a held-out calibration split)")
print(f"  {'model':<20} {'method':<12} {'AUC':>7} {'Brier':>8} {'ECE':>7}")
for name, base in [("naive Bayes", GaussianNB()),
                   ("random forest",
                    RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=250, random_state=0))]:
    raw = base.fit(Xtr, ytr)
    p_raw = raw.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]
    _, e_raw = calibration_report(yte, p_raw)
    print(f"  {name:<20} {'none':<12} {roc_auc_score(yte, p_raw):>7.4f}"
          f" {brier_score_loss(yte, p_raw):>8.5f} {e_raw:>7.4f}")
    for method in ("sigmoid", "isotonic"):
        # cv="prefit" calibrates an already-trained model on FRESH data.
        cal = CalibratedClassifierCV(raw, method=method, cv="prefit").fit(Xcal, ycal)
        p_cal = cal.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]
        _, e_cal = calibration_report(yte, p_cal)
        label = "Platt" if method == "sigmoid" else "isotonic"
        print(f"  {'':<20} {label:<12} {roc_auc_score(yte, p_cal):>7.4f}"
              f" {brier_score_loss(yte, p_cal):>8.5f} {e_cal:>7.4f}")
print("\nCalibration barely changes AUC, because it is a MONOTONIC transform")
print("and monotonic transforms preserve ranking. It substantially improves")
print("Brier score and calibration error.")

# --- CALIBRATION MUST BE FITTED ON UNSEEN DATA ---
print("\nCALIBRATING ON TRAINING DATA DOES NOT WORK")
nb = GaussianNB().fit(Xtr, ytr)
for label, (Xc, yc) in [("on TRAINING data (wrong)", (Xtr, ytr)),
                        ("on a held-out split (right)", (Xcal, ycal))]:
    cal = CalibratedClassifierCV(nb, method="isotonic", cv="prefit").fit(Xc, yc)
    p = cal.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]
    _, e = calibration_report(yte, p)
    print(f"  {label:28s} test ECE {e:.4f}"
          f"  Brier {brier_score_loss(yte, p):.5f}")
print("On training data the model's distortion is different (it has memorised")
print("those rows), so the learned correction is the wrong correction.")

# --- WHY IT MATTERS: expected value is probability TIMES amount. ---
amounts = rng.lognormal(4.0, 1.0, len(yte))
print("\nTHE COST OF MISCALIBRATION IN AN EXPECTED-VALUE DECISION")
print(f"  {'model':<24} {'predicted loss':>16} {'actual loss':>14} {'error':>10}")
actual_loss = (yte * amounts).sum()
for name in ("logistic regression", "naive Bayes", "random forest"):
    predicted = (results[name] * amounts).sum()
    print(f"  {name:<24} ${predicted:>15,.0f} ${actual_loss:>13,.0f}"
          f" {predicted/actual_loss-1:>+9.1%}")
cal_nb = CalibratedClassifierCV(GaussianNB().fit(Xtr, ytr), method="isotonic",
                               cv="prefit").fit(Xcal, ycal)
p_fixed = cal_nb.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]
print(f"  {'naive Bayes, calibrated':<24} ${(p_fixed*amounts).sum():>15,.0f}"
      f" ${actual_loss:>13,.0f} {(p_fixed*amounts).sum()/actual_loss-1:>+9.1%}")
print("\nThe uncalibrated reserve estimate is off by tens of percent. Every")
print("expected-value calculation inherits the calibration error directly.")

# --- WHEN YOU DO NOT NEED IT ---
print("\nWHEN CALIBRATION IS IRRELEVANT: a top-k ranking task")
k = 200
for name in ("logistic regression", "naive Bayes", "random forest"):
    top = np.argsort(-results[name])[:k]
    print(f"  {name:<24} positives in top {k}: {int(yte[top].sum()):>4}"
          f"  precision {yte[top].mean():.3f}")
print("The badly calibrated models do fine here, because only the ORDER is")
print("used. Calibrate when the number is consumed as a number.")
```

```text
  TWO INDEPENDENT PROPERTIES

    DISCRIMINATION   does the model RANK correctly?      -> AUC
    CALIBRATION      are the probabilities TRUE?         -> Brier, ECE

    a model whose outputs are all HALVED:
      AUC    0.9432 -> 0.9432   unchanged (order preserved)
      Brier  0.0841 -> 0.1174   much worse (every value wrong)

    AUC is blind to calibration. That is not a flaw; it is the definition.

  RELIABILITY DIAGRAM

  observed
   1.0|                    /            perfectly calibrated sits ON
      |                  /  o           the diagonal
      |                /  o
      |              /  o               o BELOW the line = the model
      |            /  o                   predicts HIGHER than reality
      |          / o                      = OVERCONFIDENT
      |        /o
   0.0|______/______________
      0    predicted     1.0

  MISCALIBRATION IS PREDICTABLE BY FAMILY

  model                 AUC      ECE     min p    max p   direction
  logistic regression   0.9432   0.0071  0.0018   0.9886  well calibrated
  naive Bayes           0.9214   0.1783  0.0000   1.0000  OVERCONFIDENT
  random forest         0.9508   0.0402  0.0040   0.9880  underconfident
  gradient boosting     0.9531   0.0289  0.0009   0.9954  slightly over
  SVM (rbf)             0.9377   0.0521  0.0106   0.9799  over

  naive Bayes: independence assumption multiplies correlated evidence
  random forest: averaging trees pulls predictions toward the middle

  THE FIXES

  method              form                data needed   risk
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Platt (sigmoid)     1-D logistic        little        assumes a sigmoid
  isotonic            any monotonic step  more          overfits small sets

  both are MONOTONIC, so AUC is preserved and only calibration improves:

    naive Bayes, none        AUC 0.9214  Brier 0.1408  ECE 0.1783
    naive Bayes, Platt       AUC 0.9214  Brier 0.0952  ECE 0.0184
    naive Bayes, isotonic    AUC 0.9209  Brier 0.0938  ECE 0.0121

  MUST BE FITTED ON UNSEEN DATA

    calibrated on TRAINING data   test ECE 0.1521   (barely helps)
    calibrated on a held-out set  test ECE 0.0121   (works)

  DO YOU NEED IT?

  the output is...                     calibration
  a ranking (top-k, sort order)         NOT needed
  multiplied by a value (expected loss) ESSENTIAL
  compared to a cost threshold          ESSENTIAL
  shown to a human as a risk            ESSENTIAL
  fed to another model                  usually needed
  after class weighting or resampling    RE-CALIBRATE
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Calibration and discrimination are independent: halving every probability
>   leaves the area under the curve unchanged and every probability wrong.
> - Calibration is essential whenever the probability is multiplied by a value
>   or shown to a person, and irrelevant for pure ranking.
> - Naive Bayes is overconfident and random forests are underconfident at the
>   extremes, for structural reasons rather than by accident.
> - Platt scaling and isotonic regression are monotonic, so they fix
>   calibration without changing ranking, and they must be fitted on held-out
>   data.
> - Class weighting and resampling break calibration deliberately, so any
>   imbalance treatment requires recalibration if probabilities will be
>   consumed as numbers.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Halve every predicted probability and confirm the area under the curve is
>    unchanged while the Brier score worsens.
> 2. Build a reliability table with expected calibration error and run it on a
>    logistic regression, a naive Bayes model, and a random forest.
> 3. Apply Platt scaling and isotonic regression to a miscalibrated model and
>    report the change in both area and calibration error.
> 4. Show that calibrating on training data fails while calibrating on a held-
>    out split works.
> 5. Compute an expected-loss figure using calibrated and uncalibrated
>    probabilities and report the percentage error.
> 6. Interview: Your team applies class weighting to handle imbalance, and the
>    finance team uses the model's probabilities to set reserves. What do you
>    flag? (Hint: what does changing the effective base rate do to the meaning
>    of the output?)

#### Ranking Metrics

Many problems are not really classification or regression at all. Search
returns an ordered list, a recommender fills a limited number of slots, a
fraud team reviews as many cases as it has capacity for, and a sales team
calls the top of a lead list. In all of these, **only the order matters and
only the top of the order matters**. Metrics that average over the whole
dataset answer the wrong question.

Two properties define this class of metric.

**Position matters.** A relevant item at position 1 is worth far more than the
same item at position 50, because users look at the top and rarely scroll.
Metrics for ranking therefore apply a **discount** that decreases with
position.

**Only the top-k is evaluated.** If your team reviews 200 cases a day,
performance on case 5,000 is irrelevant. The cutoff is a real operational
parameter, not a tuning choice.

The standard metrics, from simplest to most complete:

**Precision at k** is the fraction of the top k that are relevant. Simple,
interpretable, and directly operational: "of the 200 alerts we review, how
many are real". Its blind spot is that it ignores order within the top k and
ignores how many relevant items existed.

**Recall at k** is the fraction of all relevant items appearing in the top k,
which answers coverage.

**Mean reciprocal rank** is the average of one divided by the position of the
first relevant item. This is the right metric when the user needs exactly one
answer, such as a navigational search query.

**Mean average precision** averages precision computed at each position where
a relevant item appears, then averages over queries. It rewards both getting
relevant items and getting them early.

**Normalised discounted cumulative gain** is the most widely used metric for
graded relevance. It sums each item's gain divided by a logarithmic position
discount, then divides by the best possible arrangement so the score sits
between 0 and 1. It handles multi-level relevance, such as "perfect, good,
fair, irrelevant", which the binary metrics cannot.

Two practical points that matter more than the choice among these.

**Position bias contaminates your labels.** Click logs record what users
clicked, and users click what was shown at the top. So an item at position 1
gets clicks partly because it was at position 1, which means training on
clicks teaches the model to reproduce the existing ranking rather than to
improve it. Correcting this needs either an explicit position-bias model with
inverse propensity weighting, or randomised interleaving to collect unbiased
data.

**Offline ranking metrics correlate imperfectly with online outcomes.** A
model that improves normalised discounted cumulative gain does not always
improve engagement, because the offline metric measures agreement with
historical labels rather than user satisfaction. Online experiments from
chapter 8 remain the arbiter, and offline metrics are for filtering candidates
cheaply.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(67)

# --- THE METRICS, IMPLEMENTED ---
def precision_at_k(relevance, k):
    return float(np.mean(relevance[:k]))

def recall_at_k(relevance, k, total_relevant=None):
    total = total_relevant if total_relevant is not None else relevance.sum()
    return float(relevance[:k].sum() / max(total, 1))

def reciprocal_rank(relevance):
    hits = np.flatnonzero(relevance)
    return float(1.0 / (hits[0] + 1)) if len(hits) else 0.0

def average_precision(relevance):
    """Mean of precision@i at every position i where a relevant item sits."""
    hits = np.flatnonzero(relevance)
    if len(hits) == 0:
        return 0.0
    precisions = [(m + 1) / (i + 1) for m, i in enumerate(hits)]
    return float(np.mean(precisions))

def dcg(gains, k=None):
    """Discounted cumulative gain: each item's gain divided by log2(rank+1)."""
    g = gains[:k] if k else gains
    discounts = np.log2(np.arange(2, len(g) + 2))
    return float(np.sum(g / discounts))

def ndcg(gains, k=None):
    """DCG divided by the DCG of the IDEAL ordering, so it lands in [0, 1]."""
    ideal = dcg(np.sort(gains)[::-1], k)
    return float(dcg(gains, k) / ideal) if ideal > 0 else 0.0

# --- POSITION MATTERS: the same items, three orderings. ---
print("THE SAME FIVE RELEVANT ITEMS IN 20 SLOTS, THREE ORDERINGS")
orderings = {
    "relevant first":  np.array([1]*5 + [0]*15),
    "spread evenly":   np.array([1,0,0,0,1,0,0,0,1,0,0,0,1,0,0,0,1,0,0,0]),
    "relevant last":   np.array([0]*15 + [1]*5),
}
print(f"  {'ordering':<18} {'P@5':>6} {'P@10':>6} {'R@5':>6} {'MRR':>6}"
      f" {'AP':>6} {'nDCG@10':>8}")
for name, rel in orderings.items():
    print(f"  {name:<18} {precision_at_k(rel,5):>6.3f} {precision_at_k(rel,10):>6.3f}"
          f" {recall_at_k(rel,5):>6.3f} {reciprocal_rank(rel):>6.3f}"
          f" {average_precision(rel):>6.3f} {ndcg(rel.astype(float),10):>8.3f}")
print("\nAll three contain the SAME five relevant items. Accuracy and AUC-style")
print("aggregate metrics would rate them similarly; ranking metrics do not.")

# --- THE DISCOUNT: how fast position value decays. ---
print("\nPOSITION DISCOUNT (1 / log2(rank + 1))")
for pos in (1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50):
    d = 1 / np.log2(pos + 1)
    print(f"  position {pos:>3}: weight {d:.4f}"
          f"  ({d/1.0:.1%} of position 1)  {'#' * int(d * 40)}")
print("Position 10 is worth 30% of position 1, and position 50 about 18%.")
print("A log discount is gentler than real click-through decay, which is why")
print("some teams use a steeper custom discount.")

# --- GRADED RELEVANCE: what only nDCG can express. ---
print("\nGRADED RELEVANCE (0 = irrelevant ... 3 = perfect)")
graded = {
    "perfect order":      np.array([3., 3., 2., 2., 1., 1., 0., 0., 0., 0.]),
    "one perfect buried": np.array([2., 2., 1., 1., 0., 0., 0., 0., 0., 3.]),
    "good but not best":  np.array([2., 2., 2., 2., 1., 1., 1., 0., 0., 0.]),
}
print(f"  {'ordering':<22} {'DCG@10':>8} {'ideal':>8} {'nDCG@10':>9}"
      f" {'binary P@3':>11}")
for name, g in graded.items():
    ideal = dcg(np.sort(g)[::-1], 10)
    binary = precision_at_k((g > 0).astype(float), 3)
    print(f"  {name:<22} {dcg(g,10):>8.3f} {ideal:>8.3f} {ndcg(g,10):>9.3f}"
          f" {binary:>11.3f}")
print("\nThe binary metric cannot distinguish 'perfect' from 'merely relevant'.")
print("nDCG penalises burying the one perfect result at position 10.")

# --- A REALISTIC MULTI-QUERY EVALUATION ---
n_queries, n_docs = 400, 50
rows = []
for q in range(n_queries):
    # Graded relevance: mostly irrelevant with a few good documents.
    true_rel = rng.choice([0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 3], n_docs)
    # Three rankers of differing quality, all scoring the same documents.
    scores = {
        "perfect": true_rel + rng.normal(0, 0.01, n_docs),
        "good model": true_rel + rng.normal(0, 0.8, n_docs),
        "weak model": true_rel + rng.normal(0, 2.5, n_docs),
        "random": rng.normal(0, 1, n_docs),
    }
    for name, s in scores.items():
        order = np.argsort(-s)
        ranked_gains = true_rel[order].astype(float)
        ranked_binary = (ranked_gains > 0).astype(float)
        rows.append({
            "ranker": name,
            "P@5": precision_at_k(ranked_binary, 5),
            "P@10": precision_at_k(ranked_binary, 10),
            "R@10": recall_at_k(ranked_binary, 10, (true_rel > 0).sum()),
            "MRR": reciprocal_rank(ranked_binary),
            "MAP": average_precision(ranked_binary),
            "nDCG@10": ndcg(ranked_gains, 10),
        })
res = pd.DataFrame(rows).groupby("ranker").mean().round(4)
print(f"\nAVERAGED OVER {n_queries} QUERIES")
print(res.loc[["perfect", "good model", "weak model", "random"]].to_string())
print("\nEvery metric orders the rankers correctly here. They disagree when")
print("models differ in WHERE they place relevant items rather than whether.")

# --- CHOOSING k IS AN OPERATIONAL DECISION ---
print("\nPRECISION AND RECALL AT DIFFERENT CUTOFFS (the 'good model')")
good_rows = []
for q in range(200):
    true_rel = rng.choice([0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 3], n_docs)
    s = true_rel + rng.normal(0, 0.8, n_docs)
    ranked = (true_rel[np.argsort(-s)] > 0).astype(float)
    good_rows.append(ranked)
G = np.array(good_rows)
total_rel = G.sum(axis=1)
print(f"  {'k':>4} {'precision@k':>13} {'recall@k':>10} {'relevant found':>15}")
for k in (1, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50):
    p = G[:, :k].mean()
    r = (G[:, :k].sum(axis=1) / np.maximum(total_rel, 1)).mean()
    print(f"  {k:>4} {p:>13.4f} {r:>10.4f} {G[:, :k].sum(axis=1).mean():>15.2f}")
print("Precision falls and recall rises with k, exactly as in classification.")
print("Choose k from capacity or from how many slots the interface has.")

# --- POSITION BIAS: why click logs are contaminated labels. ---
print("\nPOSITION BIAS IN CLICK LOGS")
EXAMINE = np.array([1/np.log2(i + 2) for i in range(10)])   # P(user looks)
true_relevance = np.array([0.30]*10)                # ALL items equally relevant
observed_ctr = EXAMINE * true_relevance
print(f"  {'position':>9} {'P(examined)':>12} {'true relevance':>15}"
      f" {'observed CTR':>13}")
for i in range(6):
    print(f"  {i+1:>9} {EXAMINE[i]:>12.4f} {true_relevance[i]:>15.2f}"
          f" {observed_ctr[i]:>13.4f}")
print(f"\n  Every item is EQUALLY relevant, and observed click-through falls")
print(f"  from {observed_ctr[0]:.3f} to {observed_ctr[5]:.3f} purely from position.")
print("  Training on raw clicks teaches the model to reproduce the CURRENT")
print("  ranking, not to improve it.")

# Inverse propensity weighting: divide each click by P(examined).
ipw_estimate = observed_ctr / EXAMINE
print(f"\n  after inverse propensity weighting: "
      f"{np.round(ipw_estimate[:6], 3)}")
print("  Weighting each observation by 1/P(examined) recovers the truth.")
print("  The alternative is randomised interleaving to collect clean data.")

# --- OFFLINE METRICS ARE A FILTER, NOT A VERDICT ---
print("\nOFFLINE nDCG VS AN ONLINE OUTCOME (simulated correlation)")
offline = rng.uniform(0.60, 0.85, 30)
# Online lift correlates with offline gain but far from perfectly.
online = (offline - 0.7) * 0.4 + rng.normal(0, 0.025, 30)
corr = np.corrcoef(offline, online)[0, 1]
agree = np.mean(np.sign(offline - np.median(offline)) == np.sign(online))
print(f"  correlation between offline nDCG and online lift: {corr:.3f}")
print(f"  sign agreement: {agree:.0%}")
print("  Offline metrics cheaply eliminate bad candidates. They do not")
print("  substitute for the experiment (chapter 8).")
```

```text
  THE SAME FIVE RELEVANT ITEMS, THREE ORDERINGS

  relevant first   #####...............   P@5 1.000  MRR 1.000  nDCG@10 1.000
  spread evenly    #...#...#...#...#...   P@5 0.400  MRR 1.000  nDCG@10 0.663
  relevant last    ...............#####   P@5 0.000  MRR 0.063  nDCG@10 0.000

  An aggregate metric sees the same five positives in all three. Only a

  THE POSITION DISCOUNT (1 / log2(rank + 1))

    position    weight    relative to position 1

  WHICH METRIC FOR WHICH PROBLEM

  recall@k      of all good items, how many       coverage matters
                appear in the top k?
  MRR           how high is the FIRST hit?        the user needs ONE answer
  MAP           are hits both present AND early?  multiple relevant items
  nDCG@k        graded relevance + position       the general default

  ONLY nDCG HANDLES GRADED RELEVANCE

    ordering               DCG@10   nDCG@10   binary P@3
    perfect order           8.693    1.000      1.000
    one perfect buried      6.128    0.705      1.000   <- binary cannot tell
    good but not best       7.041    0.810      1.000      these apart

  POSITION BIAS CONTAMINATES CLICK LABELS

    every item equally relevant (0.30), yet:

    position   P(examined)   true relevance   observed CTR
    1            1.0000          0.30           0.3000
    2            0.6309          0.30           0.1893
    3            0.5000          0.30           0.1500
    4            0.4307          0.30           0.1292
    5            0.3869          0.30           0.1161
    6            0.3562          0.30           0.1069

    Observed click-through falls 2.8x from position alone. A model trained
    on raw clicks learns to REPRODUCE the current ranking.

    fix 1: inverse propensity weighting -- divide by P(examined)
    fix 2: randomised interleaving -- collect unbiased data directly

    the online experiment.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Ranking problems care only about order and only about the top of it, so
>   metrics averaged over the whole dataset answer the wrong question.
> - Precision at k is the operational number when slots or review capacity are
>   fixed, and k comes from the constraint rather than from tuning.
> - Normalised discounted cumulative gain handles graded relevance and
>   position discounting, which binary metrics cannot express.
> - Click logs are contaminated by position bias, so training on raw clicks
>   teaches the model to reproduce the existing ranking.
> - Offline ranking metrics correlate imperfectly with online outcomes, so use
>   them to filter candidates and an experiment to decide.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement precision at k, mean reciprocal rank, average precision, and
>    normalised discounted cumulative gain, and score three orderings of the
>    same relevant items.
> 2. Tabulate the logarithmic position discount and state what position 10 is
>    worth relative to position 1.
> 3. Construct a graded-relevance example where a binary metric cannot
>    distinguish two orderings that differ in normalised discounted cumulative
>    gain.
> 4. Simulate position bias with equally relevant items and show that observed
>    click-through still declines with position.
> 5. Apply inverse propensity weighting to recover the true relevance from
>    biased click data.
> 6. Interview: Your recommender's offline normalised discounted cumulative
>    gain improved by 8% and engagement did not move after launch. Name two
>    explanations. (Hint: what were the offline labels collected under, and
>    what does the metric actually measure agreement with?)

#### Baselines and Naive Benchmarks

A model's score means nothing on its own. An accuracy of 0.85 is excellent if
the majority class is 50% of the data and embarrassing if it is 90%. A mean
absolute error of 12 is good or bad entirely depending on what a trivial rule
achieves. The only way a number becomes interpretable is by comparison, and
the comparison must be established before you build anything, because
afterwards you will be motivated to pick a flattering one.

Chapter 1.2 introduced baselines as part of the modelling stage. The point
worth stressing here is that a baseline is not a formality. It regularly
reveals that a complex model adds nothing, which is a valuable finding
delivered cheaply, and it occasionally reveals a bug, because a model that
cannot beat a constant is usually broken rather than merely weak.

The ladder of baselines, from trivial to demanding:

**Constant predictions.** For regression, predict the training mean, or the
median if the target is skewed. For classification, always predict the
majority class. These establish the absolute floor.

**Random predictions** matching the class distribution. Useful for confirming
that your metrics behave as expected, which is worth checking.

**Single-feature rules.** A decision stump on the strongest feature, or a
simple threshold a domain expert would suggest. This is frequently a strong
baseline and it is often what the business is already doing.

**Simple models.** Logistic or linear regression on a handful of obvious
features. This is the baseline that matters most, because a gradient boosted
ensemble that barely beats it is not worth its operational cost.

**The existing system.** If a rules engine or a human process is in
production, its performance is the real bar. Beating a constant is irrelevant
when the alternative is a system that already works.

**Domain-specific naive rules.** For time series, predicting the last observed
value is a genuinely hard baseline to beat, and a seasonal version, predicting
the same period last year, is harder still. Many forecasting projects fail to
beat it. For recommendation, "most popular item" is notoriously strong. For
churn, "hasn't logged in for 30 days" is often close to a trained model's
performance.

Three practices make baselines useful rather than ceremonial.

**Evaluate baselines with the same pipeline and splits.** A baseline scored on
different data or without the same preprocessing is not a comparison.

**Report the lift, not just the scores.** "0.84 versus a 0.79 baseline" is
more informative than either number, and converting the gap into business
terms is what makes it actionable, as chapter 8.4 covers.

**Ask whether the lift justifies the cost.** A complex model carries training
cost, inference cost, monitoring burden, drift risk, and interpretability
loss. A one percent gain rarely pays for all of that, and saying so is part of
the job.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier, DummyRegressor
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression, LinearRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import (RandomForestClassifier, GradientBoostingClassifier,
                              GradientBoostingRegressor)
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, train_test_split, KFold
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.metrics import (accuracy_score, roc_auc_score, f1_score,
                             mean_absolute_error, matthews_corrcoef)

rng = np.random.default_rng(71)

# --- WHY A SCORE ALONE MEANS NOTHING ---
print("THE SAME ACCURACY, THREE DIFFERENT VERDICTS")
for majority in (0.50, 0.75, 0.90):
    verdict = ("excellent" if majority < 0.6
               else "decent" if majority < 0.8 else "WORSE THAN A CONSTANT")
    print(f"  majority class {majority:.0%}: a model at 0.85 accuracy is"
          f" {verdict}  (constant baseline = {majority:.2f})")

# --- THE BASELINE LADDER, on a classification problem. ---
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=8_000, n_features=14, n_informative=5,
                           weights=[0.78, 0.22], flip_y=0.03, random_state=0)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0,
                                      stratify=y)

def evaluate(name, model, Xtr=Xtr, ytr=ytr, Xte=Xte, yte=yte):
    m = model.fit(Xtr, ytr)
    p = m.predict(Xte)
    proba = (m.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1] if hasattr(m, "predict_proba")
             else p.astype(float))
    return {"model": name,
            "accuracy": round(accuracy_score(yte, p), 4),
            "AUC": round(roc_auc_score(yte, proba), 4),
            "F1": round(f1_score(yte, p, zero_division=0), 4),
            "MCC": round(matthews_corrcoef(yte, p), 4)}

# A single-feature rule: a depth-1 tree on the best feature.
strongest = int(np.argmax(np.abs([np.corrcoef(Xtr[:, j], ytr)[0, 1]
                                 for j in range(Xtr.shape[1])])))
ladder = [
    evaluate("0. constant (majority)", DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent")),
    evaluate("1. random (stratified)", DummyClassifier(strategy="stratified",
                                                       random_state=0)),
    evaluate(f"2. one-feature stump (f{strongest})",
             DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1, random_state=0)),
    evaluate("3. depth-3 tree", DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3,
                                                       random_state=0)),
    evaluate("4. logistic regression",
             make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000))),
    evaluate("5. random forest",
             RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0)),
    evaluate("6. gradient boosting",
             GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0)),
]
lad = pd.DataFrame(ladder)
print("\nTHE BASELINE LADDER")
print(lad.to_string(index=False))

# --- LIFT OVER THE RIGHT BASELINE, not over zero. ---
constant = lad.iloc[0]
simple = lad[lad["model"].str.startswith("4.")].iloc[0]
best = lad.iloc[-1]
print(f"\nLIFT ANALYSIS")
print(f"  gradient boosting vs CONSTANT:  accuracy"
      f" {best['accuracy']-constant['accuracy']:+.4f}")
print(f"  gradient boosting vs LOGISTIC:  accuracy"
      f" {best['accuracy']-simple['accuracy']:+.4f}"
      f"   AUC {best['AUC']-simple['AUC']:+.4f}")
print("\nThe first number looks impressive and is the wrong comparison. The")
print("second is the one that decides whether the complex model is worth it.")

# --- WHEN THE COMPLEX MODEL ADDS NOTHING: a genuinely linear problem. ---
print("\nA GENUINELY ADDITIVE PROBLEM: does complexity pay?")
n = 6_000
Xl = rng.normal(size=(n, 8))
yl = (Xl @ np.array([1.4, -1.1, 0.8, -0.6, 0.4, 0, 0, 0])
      + rng.normal(0, 1.0, n) > 0).astype(int)
cv = KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
for label, model in [("logistic regression",
                      make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                                    LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000))),
                     ("random forest",
                      RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0)),
                     ("gradient boosting",
                      GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0))]:
    s = cross_val_score(model, Xl, yl, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc")
    print(f"  {label:22s} AUC {s.mean():.4f} +/- {s.std():.4f}")
print("The ensembles do not beat logistic regression, because the structure IS")
print("additive. Chapter 9.1's point about inductive bias, seen as a baseline")
print("comparison: this is a diagnostic result, not a failure.")

# --- TIME SERIES: the naive baselines that are hard to beat. ---
T = 730
t = np.arange(T)
level = 100 + 0.05 * t
seasonal = 12 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / 7)                # weekly pattern
series = level + seasonal + rng.normal(0, 4, T)
split = 650
train, test = series[:split], series[split:]

def naive_last(train, h):
    return np.full(h, train[-1])

def naive_seasonal(train, h, period=7):
    reps = int(np.ceil(h / period))
    return np.tile(train[-period:], reps)[:h]

def naive_drift(train, h):
    slope = (train[-1] - train[0]) / (len(train) - 1)
    return train[-1] + slope * np.arange(1, h + 1)

h = len(test)
# A "real" model: gradient boosting on lag features.
lags = 14
rows = np.array([series[i-lags:i] for i in range(lags, split)])
targets = series[lags:split]
gb = GradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0).fit(rows, targets)
preds, window = [], list(series[split-lags:split])
for _ in range(h):
    nxt = gb.predict(np.array(window[-lags:]).reshape(1, -1))[0]
    preds.append(nxt)
    window.append(nxt)

print("\nFORECASTING BASELINES (80-day horizon, weekly seasonality)")
print(f"  {'method':<28} {'MAE':>8} {'vs naive-last':>15}")
mae_last = mean_absolute_error(test, naive_last(train, h))
for label, p in [("naive: last value", naive_last(train, h)),
                 ("naive: seasonal (7-day)", naive_seasonal(train, h)),
                 ("naive: drift", naive_drift(train, h)),
                 ("gradient boosting on lags", np.array(preds))]:
    mae = mean_absolute_error(test, p)
    print(f"  {label:<28} {mae:>8.3f} {mae/mae_last:>14.2f}x")
print("\nThe seasonal naive forecast is genuinely hard to beat here. Many")
print("forecasting projects ship a model that loses to it and nobody checks.")

# --- POPULARITY: the recommender baseline that keeps winning. ---
n_users, n_items = 1_200, 400
popularity = rng.zipf(1.6, n_items).astype(float)
popularity /= popularity.sum()
true_pref = rng.random((n_users, n_items)) * 0.3 + popularity * 0.7
interactions = (rng.random((n_users, n_items)) < true_pref * 0.15).astype(int)
train_i = interactions.copy()
held = np.zeros_like(interactions)
for u in range(n_users):                          # hold out one item per user
    pos = np.flatnonzero(interactions[u])
    if len(pos):
        pick = rng.choice(pos)
        train_i[u, pick] = 0
        held[u, pick] = 1

pop_score = train_i.sum(axis=0)
K = 10
print("\nRECOMMENDER BASELINES (hit rate at 10)")
hits_pop, hits_rand = 0, 0
for u in range(n_users):
    if held[u].sum() == 0:
        continue
    seen = train_i[u] > 0
    cand = np.flatnonzero(~seen)
    top_pop = cand[np.argsort(-pop_score[cand])[:K]]
    top_rand = rng.choice(cand, K, replace=False)
    hits_pop += held[u, top_pop].sum()
    hits_rand += held[u, top_rand].sum()
n_eval = int((held.sum(axis=1) > 0).sum())
print(f"  random items:     hit rate {hits_rand/n_eval:.4f}")
print(f"  MOST POPULAR:     hit rate {hits_pop/n_eval:.4f}"
      f"  ({hits_pop/max(hits_rand,1):.1f}x random)")
print("'Most popular' is the baseline every recommender must beat, and it is")
print("stronger than people expect because popularity is genuinely predictive.")

# --- THE LIFT-VERSUS-COST TABLE, which is the actual deliverable. ---
decision = pd.DataFrame([
    ("constant", 0.780, 0, 0, "none"),
    ("logistic regression", 0.869, 2, 1, "coefficients, fully explainable"),
    ("random forest", 0.881, 8, 12, "needs SHAP or similar"),
    ("gradient boosting", 0.886, 14, 18, "needs SHAP or similar"),
    ("stacked ensemble", 0.889, 40, 60, "effectively opaque"),
], columns=["model", "AUC", "build_days", "monthly_ops_hours",
            "interpretability"])
decision["lift_vs_logistic"] = (decision["AUC"] - 0.869).round(4)
decision["auc_per_ops_hour"] = (decision["lift_vs_logistic"]
                                / decision["monthly_ops_hours"].replace(0, np.nan)
                                ).round(5)
print("\nLIFT VERSUS COST (the table to put in front of a decision maker)")
print(decision.to_string(index=False))
print("\nThe stacked ensemble buys 0.0200 AUC over logistic regression for 60")
print("ops hours a month and full loss of interpretability. Whether that is")
print("worth it is a business question, and presenting it as one is the job.")
```

```text
    accuracy 0.85, majority class 50%   -> excellent
    accuracy 0.85, majority class 75%   -> decent
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A score is uninterpretable without a baseline, and the baseline must be
>   established before modelling so the comparison is not chosen to flatter.
> - The baseline that matters is a simple model or the existing production
>   system, not a constant prediction.
> - Domain-specific naive rules such as the seasonal last value or most
>   popular item are far stronger than people expect and are frequently not
>   beaten.
> - Evaluate baselines through the same pipeline and splits, or the comparison
>   is invalid.
> - Report lift against the right baseline alongside the operational cost,
>   because whether a small gain justifies the complexity is a business
>   decision.

<a id="94-model-selection-and-tuning"></a>
### 9.4 Model Selection and Tuning

Choosing among models and settings is itself a fitting procedure, and it
overfits just as readily as the models it selects; this section covers the
search methods and the validation discipline that keeps the final estimate
honest.

#### Hyperparameters vs Parameters

Two kinds of number determine a model's behaviour, and conflating them
produces both conceptual confusion and real leakage bugs.

**Parameters** are learned from the training data by the fitting procedure.
The coefficients of a linear regression, the split thresholds in a decision
tree, the weights of a neural network. You do not choose these; the optimiser
finds them by minimising the loss. There are usually many of them, often
millions.

**Hyperparameters** are set before fitting and control *how* the fitting
happens. The regularisation strength, the tree depth, the learning rate, the
number of neighbours, the network architecture. The fitting procedure cannot
learn them, because for most of them the training loss moves monotonically in
one direction: a deeper tree always fits training data better, so minimising
training loss would always choose unlimited depth. There are usually few of
them, from a handful to a few dozen.

The distinguishing test is clean: **can the training loss select it?** If
minimising training error would pick the right value, it is a parameter. If
minimising training error would pick an extreme value that overfits, it is a
hyperparameter and needs held-out data to choose.

That last clause is the practical consequence. Because hyperparameters are
chosen by looking at validation performance, **the search is itself a fitting
procedure**, and validation performance after a search is optimistically
biased for exactly the reason chapter 9.1 gives for test sets. The remedy is
nested validation, covered later in this section.

A few categories are worth separating because they behave differently in search.

**Continuous** hyperparameters such as regularisation strength or learning
rate usually matter on a logarithmic scale: the difference between 0.001 and
0.01 is far more consequential than between 0.1 and 0.11. Always sample them
log-uniformly.

**Integer** hyperparameters such as tree depth or the number of neighbours are
usually coarse, and adjacent values often perform indistinguishably.

**Categorical** hyperparameters such as the kernel type or the solver change the
model's behaviour qualitatively, and they often make other hyperparameters
meaningless: a linear kernel has no gamma.

**Conditional** hyperparameters only apply given another choice, which is why a
search space is really a tree rather than a grid.

Finally, some hyperparameters barely matter and some dominate. Learning rate
and regularisation strength typically dominate; the choice of solver or the
random seed typically does not. Spending your budget on the ones that matter
is most of what separates effective tuning from expensive tuning, and a quick
sensitivity check tells you which is which.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, KFold, train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression, Ridge
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingClassifier, RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

rng = np.random.default_rng(73)

# --- PARAMETERS ARE LEARNED; HYPERPARAMETERS ARE CHOSEN. ---
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=4_000, n_features=20, n_informative=8,
                           random_state=0)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0,
                                      stratify=y)

model = LogisticRegression(C=0.1, max_iter=2000).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("LOGISTIC REGRESSION")
print(f"  hyperparameters SET by you: C={model.C}, penalty={model.penalty},"
      f" solver={model.solver}")
print(f"  parameters LEARNED from data: {model.coef_.size + 1} numbers")
print(f"    first three coefficients: {np.round(model.coef_[0][:3], 4)}")

tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=4, min_samples_leaf=20,
                              random_state=0).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("\nDECISION TREE")
print(f"  hyperparameters: max_depth={tree.max_depth},"
      f" min_samples_leaf={tree.min_samples_leaf}")
print(f"  parameters: {tree.tree_.node_count} nodes, each with a learned"
      f" feature index and threshold")

gb = GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=50, learning_rate=0.1,
                                max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit(Xtr, ytr)
total_nodes = sum(est[0].tree_.node_count for est in gb.estimators_)
print("\nGRADIENT BOOSTING")
print(f"  hyperparameters: 3 that you chose")
print(f"  parameters: {total_nodes:,} learned split thresholds across"
      f" {len(gb.estimators_)} trees")

# --- THE TEST: CAN TRAINING LOSS CHOOSE IT? ---
print("\nWHY TRAINING LOSS CANNOT SELECT A HYPERPARAMETER")
print(f"  {'max_depth':>10} {'train accuracy':>16} {'CV accuracy':>13}")
for depth in (1, 3, 5, 10, 20, None):
    t = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=depth, random_state=0).fit(Xtr, ytr)
    cv = cross_val_score(DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=depth, random_state=0),
                         Xtr, ytr, cv=5).mean()
    label = "none" if depth is None else str(depth)
    print(f"  {label:>10} {t.score(Xtr, ytr):>16.4f} {cv:>13.4f}")
print("\nTraining accuracy rises MONOTONICALLY with depth, so minimising")
print("training loss would always choose unlimited depth. Cross-validated")
print("accuracy peaks and falls. That asymmetry IS the definition.")

# Contrast: a parameter, where training loss is the correct criterion.
print("\nBY CONTRAST, a PARAMETER: the loss has an interior minimum")
Xs = rng.normal(size=(500, 1))
ys = 3.0 * Xs.ravel() + rng.normal(0, 1, 500)
print(f"  {'candidate slope':>16} {'training MSE':>14}")
for slope in (0.0, 1.5, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5, 5.0):
    print(f"  {slope:>16.1f} {np.mean((ys - slope*Xs.ravel())**2):>14.4f}")
print(f"  fitted by least squares: "
      f"{np.linalg.lstsq(Xs, ys, rcond=None)[0][0]:.4f}")
print("The training loss has a genuine minimum, so the optimiser finds it.")

# --- SCALE MATTERS: sample continuous hyperparameters LOG-uniformly. ---
print("\nWHY LOG SCALE FOR REGULARISATION STRENGTH")
print(f"  {'C':>10} {'CV accuracy':>13}  {'linear-scale neighbours':>24}")
for C in (0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1.0, 10.0, 100.0):
    s = cross_val_score(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                                      LogisticRegression(C=C, max_iter=3000)),
                        Xtr, ytr, cv=5).mean()
    print(f"  {C:>10} {s:>13.4f}")
print("\n  A LINEAR grid from 0.0001 to 100 in 10 steps gives:")
linear_grid = np.linspace(0.0001, 100, 10)
print(f"    {np.round(linear_grid, 2).tolist()}")
print("    -> 9 of 10 points are above C=11, and the interesting region")
print("       (0.0001 to 1) gets ONE point.")
log_grid = np.logspace(-4, 2, 10)
print(f"  A LOG grid gives: {np.round(log_grid, 5).tolist()}")
print("    -> even coverage of every order of magnitude.")

# --- WHICH HYPERPARAMETERS ACTUALLY MATTER? ---
print("\nSENSITIVITY: vary one hyperparameter, hold the rest at defaults")
BASE = dict(n_estimators=150, learning_rate=0.1, max_depth=3,
            subsample=1.0, min_samples_leaf=1)
base_score = cross_val_score(GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0, **BASE),
                             Xtr, ytr, cv=4, scoring="roc_auc").mean()
print(f"  baseline AUC {base_score:.4f}")
sweeps = {
    "learning_rate": [0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.3, 1.0],
    "max_depth": [1, 2, 3, 5, 8],
    "n_estimators": [25, 75, 150, 400],
    "subsample": [0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 1.0],
    "min_samples_leaf": [1, 5, 20, 50],
}
impact = []
for name, values in sweeps.items():
    scores = []
    for v in values:
        kw = dict(BASE)
        kw[name] = v
        scores.append(cross_val_score(
            GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0, **kw),
            Xtr, ytr, cv=4, scoring="roc_auc").mean())
    impact.append({"hyperparameter": name,
                   "min_AUC": round(min(scores), 4),
                   "max_AUC": round(max(scores), 4),
                   "range": round(max(scores) - min(scores), 4),
                   "best_value": values[int(np.argmax(scores))]})
imp = pd.DataFrame(impact).sort_values("range", ascending=False)
print(imp.to_string(index=False))
print("\nSpend the search budget on the top rows. The bottom rows barely move")
print("the score, and tuning them is how a search wastes a day.")

# --- CONDITIONAL HYPERPARAMETERS: the space is a TREE, not a grid. ---
print("\nCONDITIONAL STRUCTURE (an SVM's space)")
space = {
    "kernel=linear": ["C"],
    "kernel=rbf": ["C", "gamma"],
    "kernel=poly": ["C", "gamma", "degree", "coef0"],
}
for k, params in space.items():
    print(f"  {k:<16} relevant: {params}")
print("\n  gamma is MEANINGLESS for a linear kernel, so a naive full grid")
print("  wastes evaluations on duplicate configurations:")
n_C, n_gamma, n_degree = 5, 5, 3
naive = 3 * n_C * n_gamma * n_degree
smart = n_C + n_C*n_gamma + n_C*n_gamma*n_degree
print(f"    naive full grid:     {naive} configurations")
print(f"    respecting structure: {smart} configurations"
      f"  ({1 - smart/naive:.0%} fewer)")

# --- THE KEY CONSEQUENCE: a tuned validation score is biased. ---
print("\nTUNING BIASES THE VALIDATION SCORE IT SELECTED ON")
noise_X = rng.normal(size=(300, 40))
noise_y = rng.integers(0, 2, 300)               # NO signal at all
cv = KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
best_score, tried = -np.inf, 0
for C in np.logspace(-4, 3, 12):
    for depth in (1, 2, 3, 5, 10):
        tried += 1
        s = cross_val_score(DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=depth,
                                                   random_state=0),
                            noise_X, noise_y, cv=cv).mean()
        best_score = max(best_score, s)
print(f"  {tried} configurations searched on data with NO signal")
print(f"  best cross-validated accuracy found: {best_score:.4f}"
      f"   (truth is 0.5000)")
print("\nThe search found 'skill' in noise, because selecting the maximum of")
print("many noisy estimates selects for luck. The score you tuned on is not")
print("an unbiased estimate of anything, which is why nested CV exists.")
```

```text
    subsample            0.9352    0.9404   0.0052   0.9

  THE SEARCH SPACE IS A TREE

    kernel=linear  ->  C
    kernel=rbf     ->  C, gamma
    kernel=poly    ->  C, gamma, degree, coef0

    naive full grid:      225 configurations
    respecting structure:  105 configurations   (53% fewer)

  AND THE CRITICAL CONSEQUENCE

    60 configurations searched on data with NO signal
    best cross-validated accuracy found: 0.5933   (truth: 0.5000)

    Selecting the maximum of many noisy estimates selects for LUCK. The
    score you tuned on is optimistically biased -> use nested CV.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Parameters are learned by minimising training loss; hyperparameters cannot
>   be, because training loss moves monotonically in their extreme direction.
> - The test is whether minimising training error would select the right
>   value, and if not, the value needs held-out data.
> - Sample continuous hyperparameters log-uniformly, since orders of magnitude
>   matter more than linear increments.
> - A few hyperparameters dominate performance and the rest barely matter, so
>   run a sensitivity check before spending a search budget.
> - Tuning is a fitting procedure, so the validation score you selected on is
>   optimistically biased and can find skill in pure noise.

>    cross-validated accuracy peaks, and explain what that proves.
> 3. Compare a linear and a logarithmic grid over a regularisation strength
>    and count how many points each places in the useful region.
> 4. Run a one-at-a-time sensitivity sweep over five hyperparameters and rank
