```text
    1.66  1.40  2.17  2.13  3.16  3.07  3.56  5.14
     |                                          |
     +----------- spread TRIPLES ---------------+

    Breusch-Pagan LM = 25.81, p = 2.5e-06

    residual
       |        .      .   . :  .::  .:|:.        a FAN. constant-variance
       |    . : . : .:. ::.::.:|::.::.:|::        inference is invalid here,
     0 +----:-:---:--:--:--:---:-------:----      but the coefficients are
       |  . : . .: .: .::  .:.:|.::.:.:|:.        still unbiased.
       |        .      .    .: .  .::  .:|
       +------------------------------------> fitted

  3. MULTICOLLINEARITY: THE FIT IS FINE, THE SPLIT IS NOT

    model            R^2      x1        x2        x3
    x1 + x2        0.9454   + 6.499   +1.442      -
    x1 + x2 + x3   0.9459   +31.315   +1.428   -8.270
                      ^         ^                  ^
              barely moves   explodes      large and negative

    VIF:  x1 26401   x2 1.0   x3 26401      (x3 = 3*x1 + noise)

    The two collinear columns cancel each other. Predictions are
    unaffected; the individual coefficients are now meaningless.

  4. INFLUENCE

    mean leverage 0.0060 (= p/n)
    row  19: leverage 0.0081  residual +20.10  Cook's D 0.0547
    row 483: leverage 0.0195  residual +11.90  Cook's D 0.0474

    leverage answers "is this row unusual in X"
    Cook's D answers "would deleting it move the model"

  5. NORMALITY: STANDARDISED RESIDUAL QUANTILES

    q      observed   normal
    0.01     -1.91     -2.33     tails slightly off, which at n=500
    0.50     -0.17     +0.00     changes essentially nothing about
    0.99     +2.66     +2.33     the intervals

  THE FIX: ROBUST STANDARD ERRORS KEEP THE COEFFICIENTS

    term     classical    robust   ratio
    const       0.4014    0.2218    0.55
    x1          0.1837    0.1655    0.90
    x2          0.1355    0.1355    1.00
    x1^2        0.0178    0.0191    1.08

    Robust SEs can be smaller OR larger. "Robust" means correct under
    heteroscedasticity, not conservative.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - Only the linearity assumption makes coefficients wrong. Independence and
>   constant variance break the standard errors but leave the estimates
>   usable.
> - Plot residuals against fitted values first. A curve in that plot means
>   the model has the wrong shape.
> - Fix non-constant variance with robust standard errors, not by dropping the
>   model. Robust errors can be smaller as well as larger.
> - Near-collinearity gives no warning: the fit stays good while individual
>   coefficients become unstable and meaningless.
> - Collinearity hurts interpretation, not prediction, so it only matters if
>   you plan to read the coefficients.
> - High leverage only matters together with a large residual. Cook's
>   distance combines the two into one number.
> - Normal errors are the least important assumption at realistic sample
>   sizes, and the one people test most.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Simulate data with a real quadratic relationship, fit a straight line,
>    and build the binned residual table that shows the curve.
> 2. Compute VIFs for a design where one column is almost a copy of another.
>    Show that predictions are fine while the two coefficients blow up in
>    opposite directions.
> 3. Implement HC0 robust standard errors from the sandwich formula and
>    compare them with the classical ones on data with non-constant variance.
> 4. Compute leverage and Cook's distance by hand, remove the most
>    influential row, and report how far each coefficient moves.
> 5. Interview: Your model has an R^2 of 0.94 and a residual plot that fans
>    out to the right. Your manager asks whether the 95% confidence interval
>    on the key coefficient can be trusted. What do you say? (Hint: separate
>    what the problem does to the estimate from what it does to the interval.)


#### Ridge and Lasso Regression

Least squares has one goal: make the training residuals small. With sixty
features and only a hundred and twenty rows, it can make them very small by
bending itself to fit the noise. The model has more freedom than the data can
control.

**Regularisation** adds a second term that penalises large coefficients. Now
every bit of coefficient size has to be paid for with a real drop in error.
Features that only help by fitting noise cannot pay. This is the bias-variance
trade-off from chapter 9.2, made explicit and adjustable: you accept a little
bias to get a big drop in variance.

There are two main penalties. The only difference between them is their shape.

**Ridge** (L2) penalises the sum of squared coefficients:
`minimise ||y - Xb||^2 + alpha * sum(b_j^2)`. The pull towards zero is
proportional to the coefficient's size, so it gets weaker as the coefficient
shrinks and never reaches zero. Ridge shrinks all coefficients smoothly and
keeps every feature.

**Lasso** (L1) penalises the sum of absolute values:
`minimise ||y - Xb||^2 + alpha * sum(|b_j|)`. The pull towards zero has the
same strength no matter how small the coefficient is. So coefficients reach
exactly zero and stay there. As a side effect, lasso does **feature
selection**.

A picture helps. Draw the squared-error surface as ellipses around the
unpenalised answer, and draw the region the penalty allows. For L2, that region
is a circle. For L1, it is a diamond with its corners on the axes. The
penalised answer is where the growing ellipse first touches the region. A
circle has no corners, so the touch point usually has every coordinate
non-zero. A diamond's corners lie on the axes, and touching a corner means some
coefficient is exactly zero.

Three practical rules:

**Always standardise first.** The penalty is measured in coefficient units. A
feature in cents has coefficients a hundred times smaller than the same feature
in dollars, so it gets penalised a hundred times less. Put the scaler inside
your pipeline so it is refitted on every cross-validation fold.

**Do not penalise the intercept.** It shifts every prediction, and shrinking it
towards zero just pulls all predictions towards zero.

**Lasso is unstable when features are correlated.** If two predictors are near
copies that share one effect, lasso picks one of them more or less at random,
and *which* one changes from sample to sample. Ridge splits the effect between
them and gives the same split each time. So a lasso's chosen features are not a
discovery about the world. **Elastic net** exists for this reason: it mixes
both penalties, so correlated features enter or leave the model together.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, Ridge, Lasso, ElasticNet
from sklearn.linear_model import RidgeCV, LassoCV
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)

# 60 features, only 5 of which matter, and 120 training rows: the regime where
# unregularised least squares has more freedom than the data can support.
n, p, k = 160, 60, 5
X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, p))
X[:, 1] = X[:, 0] + rng.normal(0, 0.1, n)      # a correlated pair, on purpose
true = np.zeros(p)
true[:k] = [1.5, 1.5, -2.5, 1.8, 2.2]          # x0 and x1 SHARE one effect
y = X @ true + rng.normal(0, 1.5, n)

Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=40, random_state=0)

def rmse(m):
    return float(np.sqrt(np.mean((yte - m.predict(Xte)) ** 2)))

# --- WHY PENALISE AT ALL: the unregularised fit memorises. ---
ols = LinearRegression().fit(Xtr, ytr)
print(f"{'model':22s} {'train RMSE':>10s} {'test RMSE':>10s} {'nonzero':>8s}")
tr = float(np.sqrt(np.mean((ytr - ols.predict(Xtr)) ** 2)))
print(f"{'least squares':22s} {tr:10.3f} {rmse(ols):10.3f} {p:8d}")

# ALWAYS standardise before penalising: the penalty is in coefficient units, so
# a feature measured in cents would be penalised 100x less than one in dollars.
for name, est in [("ridge (alpha=10)", Ridge(alpha=10)),
                  ("lasso (alpha=0.1)", Lasso(alpha=0.1, max_iter=10000)),
                  ("elastic net (0.5)", ElasticNet(alpha=0.1, l1_ratio=0.5,
                                                   max_iter=10000))]:
    pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), est).fit(Xtr, ytr)
    coef = pipe[-1].coef_
    tr = float(np.sqrt(np.mean((ytr - pipe.predict(Xtr)) ** 2)))
    print(f"{name:22s} {tr:10.3f} {rmse(pipe):10.3f} "
          f"{int((np.abs(coef) > 1e-8).sum()):8d}")

# --- THE PATH: how coefficients move as the penalty grows. ---
print("\nRIDGE PATH  (coefficients shrink together, none reach zero)")
print(f"  {'alpha':>8s} " + " ".join(f"x{i}".rjust(7) for i in range(6))
      + "   ||b||")
for a in [0.01, 1, 10, 100, 1000]:
    m = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), Ridge(alpha=a)).fit(Xtr, ytr)
    c = m[-1].coef_
    print(f"  {a:8.2f} " + " ".join(f"{v:+7.3f}" for v in c[:6])
          + f"   {np.linalg.norm(c):6.2f}")

print("\nLASSO PATH  (coefficients hit zero exactly, and stay there)")
print(f"  {'alpha':>8s} " + " ".join(f"x{i}".rjust(7) for i in range(6))
      + "   nonzero")
for a in [0.01, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0]:
    m = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                      Lasso(alpha=a, max_iter=10000)).fit(Xtr, ytr)
    c = m[-1].coef_
    print(f"  {a:8.2f} " + " ".join(f"{v:+7.3f}" for v in c[:6])
          + f"   {int((np.abs(c) > 1e-8).sum()):7d}")

# --- LASSO IS UNSTABLE WHEN FEATURES ARE CORRELATED. ---
# x0 and x1 are near-duplicates. Lasso picks ONE of them, and which one it
# picks flips with the sample. Ridge splits the credit and is stable.
print("\nSTABILITY UNDER RESAMPLING (x0 and x1 are 0.99-correlated)")
picks = {"lasso": [], "ridge": []}
for seed in range(12):
    idx = np.random.default_rng(seed).choice(len(Xtr), len(Xtr), replace=True)
    for name, est in [("lasso", Lasso(alpha=0.3, max_iter=10000)),
                      ("ridge", Ridge(alpha=10))]:
        c = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), est).fit(Xtr[idx], ytr[idx])[-1].coef_
        picks[name].append((c[0], c[1]))
for name in ("lasso", "ridge"):
    arr = np.array(picks[name])
    zeroed = int(np.sum(np.abs(arr) < 1e-8))
    print(f"  {name}: x0 {arr[:,0].mean():+.2f} +/- {arr[:,0].std():.2f}   "
          f"x1 {arr[:,1].mean():+.2f} +/- {arr[:,1].std():.2f}   "
          f"zeros across 24 slots: {zeroed}")

# --- CHOOSING ALPHA IS A CROSS-VALIDATION PROBLEM, NOT A GUESS. ---
rcv = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                    RidgeCV(alphas=np.logspace(-3, 3, 40), cv=5)).fit(Xtr, ytr)
lcv = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                    LassoCV(cv=5, random_state=0, max_iter=20000)).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print(f"\nRidgeCV alpha {rcv[-1].alpha_:.3f}  test RMSE {rmse(rcv):.3f}")
print(f"LassoCV alpha {lcv[-1].alpha_:.3f}  test RMSE {rmse(lcv):.3f}"
      f"  kept {int((np.abs(lcv[-1].coef_) > 1e-8).sum())}/{p} features")
print("\ntrue nonzero features: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4")
print("lasso kept:", [int(i) for i in np.flatnonzero(np.abs(lcv[-1].coef_) > 1e-8)])
```

```text
  WHY PENALISE: 60 FEATURES, 120 TRAINING ROWS, 5 THAT MATTER

    model                 train RMSE   test RMSE   nonzero
    least squares              0.986       2.132        60
    ridge (alpha=10)           1.109       1.901        60
    lasso (alpha=0.1)          1.261       1.650        23
    elastic net (0.5)          1.202       1.704        43
                                   ^           ^
                            worse on train, BETTER on test.
                            that trade IS regularisation.

  THE TWO PENALTY SHAPES

      L2 (ridge): a circle              L1 (lasso): a diamond
           b2                                 b2
           |      ___                         |     /\
           |    /     \                       |    /  \
       ----+---(   *   )----- b1          ----+---<  * >----- b1
           |    \ ___ /                       |    \  /
           |                                  |     \/
      no corners, so contact at a       corners ON the axes, so contact
      point with both coords nonzero    often means b2 = 0 exactly

  THE PATHS

    ridge: everything shrinks together, nothing vanishes
      alpha        x0       x1       x2      ||b||
       0.01    +5.327   -2.176   -2.853       7.17
       1.00    +2.331   +0.796   -2.790       4.82
      10.00    +1.534   +1.354   -2.463       4.16
    1000.00    +0.267   +0.265   -0.252       0.59

    lasso: coefficients hit zero exactly and stay there
      alpha        x0       x1       x2    nonzero
       0.01    +3.106   +0.000   -2.794        51
       0.10    +2.901   +0.000   -2.541        23
       0.50    +2.476   +0.000   -2.097         4
       2.00    +0.889   +0.000   -0.445         3

  STABILITY: x0 AND x1 ARE 0.99-CORRELATED AND SHARE ONE TRUE EFFECT
  (truth: x0 = +1.5, x1 = +1.5)

    lasso   x0 +2.50 +/- 0.35    x1 +0.22 +/- 0.28    5 of 24 slots zeroed
    ridge   x0 +1.48 +/- 0.10    x1 +1.39 +/- 0.11    0 of 24 slots zeroed

    Lasso assigns the shared effect to ONE feature and drops the other,
    recovering neither true value. Ridge splits it and recovers both.
    A lasso's selected set is a modelling artefact, not a finding.

  CHOOSING ALPHA IS CROSS-VALIDATION, NOT INTUITION

    RidgeCV alpha 4.924   test RMSE 1.984
    LassoCV alpha 0.164   test RMSE 1.689   kept 11 of 60 features
    lasso kept: 0, 2, 3, 4, 12, 19, 28, 33, 35, 41, 56
                ^^^^^^^^^^        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
            4 of the 5 true      7 false positives, and x1 missed
```

|                         | Ridge (L2)                       | Lasso (L1)                      | Elastic net                      |
| ----------------------- | -------------------------------- | ------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| Coefficients reach zero | Never                            | Yes                             | Yes                              |
| Selects features        | No                               | Yes                             | Yes, in groups                   |
| Works with p > n        | Yes                              | Yes, keeps at most n            | Yes                              |
| Correlated predictors   | Splits the effect                | Picks one at random             | Keeps them together              |
| Stable selection        | N/A                              | No                              | Better                           |
| Direct formula          | Yes                              | No, needs coordinate descent    | No                               |
| Use when                | Many small effects, collinearity | Few real effects, want sparsity | Correlated groups, want sparsity |

> Key Takeaways
> - Regularisation trades a small increase in bias for a large drop in
>   variance. That is why a penalised model can fit the training set worse
>   and the test set better.
> - Ridge shrinks coefficients in proportion and never reaches zero. Lasso's
>   constant pull sets some coefficients to exactly zero, which selects
>   features.
> - The L1 region has corners on the axes and the L2 region does not. That is
>   the whole geometric reason lasso produces zeros.
> - Standardise inside the pipeline before penalising, because the penalty
>   depends on the units of each feature.
> - Among correlated predictors, lasso's choice is random and changes with
>   the sample, so never present lasso's selected features as a discovery.
> - Elastic net keeps correlated features together. Always choose alpha by
>   cross-validation, not by rule of thumb.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Fit ridge with alphas across six orders of magnitude and plot or
>    tabulate the coefficient paths. Confirm that none reaches zero.
> 2. Do the same for lasso and report the alpha at which each feature drops
>    out.
> 3. Fit lasso with and without a `StandardScaler` on data where one feature
>    is multiplied by a thousand. Explain why the selected features differ.
> 4. Build two features with correlation 0.99 that share one true effect.
>    Bootstrap the fit fifty times and report how often lasso picks each one.
> 5. Compare `RidgeCV` with 5-fold cross-validation against its default
>    leave-one-out on a small noisy dataset. Explain why they can disagree.
> 6. Interview: A stakeholder wants "the ten features that drive churn", and
>    your lasso selected exactly ten. What warning do you give before they act
>    on it? (Hint: refit on a bootstrap sample and see whether the same ten
>    come back.)


#### Generalized Linear Models

Linear regression, logistic regression and Poisson regression look like three
different methods. They are really one method with three settings. Seeing this
makes each one easier to use, and tells you what to do when the target does
not fit the usual shapes. (Logistic regression is covered in detail in 10.2.)

A **generalized linear model (GLM)** has three parts:

1. A **linear predictor**: `z = b0 + b1*x1 + ... + bp*xp`. This is the same in
   every GLM, and it is the part you fit.
2. A **link function** `g` that connects the target's mean to the linear
   predictor: `g(mu) = z`. Its job is to stretch the allowed range of `mu`
   over the whole number line, so the linear part has no limits.
3. A **distribution** that describes how the target varies around its mean.
   It sets the variance function, which decides how much weight each row
   gets.

Fill in the three parts and you get the familiar models:

- Normal distribution + identity link = linear regression.
- Binomial distribution + logit link = logistic regression.
- Poisson distribution + log link = count regression.

Nothing else changes. The same algorithm (iteratively reweighted least squares)
fits all of them.

**Choose the link to match the target's range.** Counts cannot be negative, so
a log link keeps predictions positive. It also makes coefficients
multiplicative, so `exp(b)` is a rate ratio. Probabilities lie between 0 and 1,
so a logit link maps them onto the whole number line. Positive, skewed amounts
(such as spend) also use a log link, for the same reason as counts.

**The variance function** is the part people skip, and should not. It is what
makes a GLM different from transforming the target and running least squares.
In a Poisson model, the variance equals the mean. So a row expected to have 10
events should vary much more than a row expected to have 0.5. The GLM knows
this and weights rows to match. Ordinary least squares assumes every row has
the same variance and gets the weights wrong.

Two extras come up all the time.

**Offsets handle exposure.** Suppose insurance policies are watched for
different lengths of time. The number of claims grows with the length of the
window, and you want coefficients that describe the claim *rate*. Add
`log(exposure)` to the linear predictor with its coefficient fixed at 1. That
is an offset, not a feature. If you add it as a feature, the model estimates
its own slope for exposure, which answers a different (and usually wrong)
question.

**Overdispersion** is the common way Poisson models fail. "Variance equals
mean" is a strong assumption. Real count data usually varies more, because of
differences between rows that you did not measure. To check, divide the Pearson
chi-squared statistic by the residual degrees of freedom; the result should be
close to 1. If it is 2, your standard errors are too small by about `sqrt(2)`,
so a coefficient that looks significant at p = 0.01 may not be. The
coefficients themselves stay roughly correct. Fix it with a quasi-Poisson
correction or, better, a **negative binomial** model, which adds a parameter
for the extra variation.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import (LinearRegression, PoissonRegressor,
                                  GammaRegressor, TweedieRegressor)

rng = np.random.default_rng(13)

# --- COUNTS: claims per policy, with an EXPOSURE that varies by row. ---
n = 4000
age = rng.integers(18, 75, n)
urban = rng.integers(0, 2, n)
years = rng.uniform(0.25, 3.0, n)                 # exposure: policy-years at risk
rate = np.exp(-0.4 - 0.015 * age + 0.55 * urban)  # claims PER YEAR
claims = rng.poisson(rate * years)                 # counts scale with exposure

X = np.column_stack([age, urban])
print(f"claims: mean {claims.mean():.3f}  variance {claims.var():.3f}"
      f"  max {claims.max()}  zeros {np.mean(claims == 0):.1%}")

# --- WHY NOT ORDINARY LEAST SQUARES ON A COUNT. ---
ols = LinearRegression().fit(X, claims)
print(f"\nleast squares on the count: min prediction {ols.predict(X).min():+.3f}"
      f", and at age 100 rural it predicts {ols.predict([[100, 0]])[0]:+.3f}")
print("Nothing stops the fitted plane from going below zero -- an impossible")
print("count -- because an identity link puts no constraint on the range.")
# The deeper problem: a Poisson's variance EQUALS its mean, so the constant-
# variance assumption is wrong in a way that misweights every row.
res = claims - ols.predict(X)
dec = pd.qcut(ols.predict(X), 5, labels=False, duplicates="drop")
print("  fitted quintile:  " + " ".join(f"{ols.predict(X)[dec==d].mean():5.2f}"
                                        for d in range(5)))
print("  residual variance:" + " ".join(f"{res[dec==d].var():6.2f}"
                                        for d in range(5)))
print("  Variance tracks the mean, which is exactly what OLS assumes away.")

# --- THE GLM: log link, and exposure enters as an OFFSET, not a feature. ---
# log(mu) = log(exposure) + b0 + b1*age + ...  so the coefficients describe the
# RATE. Passing exposure as a feature would estimate a slope for it instead of
# fixing it at 1, which is a different and usually wrong model.
pois = PoissonRegressor(alpha=1e-8, max_iter=2000).fit(
    X, claims / years, sample_weight=years)       # equivalent to an offset
print(f"\nPoisson GLM (log link)   intercept {pois.intercept_:+.4f}"
      f"  age {pois.coef_[0]:+.5f}  urban {pois.coef_[1]:+.4f}")
print(f"truth                    intercept {-0.4:+.4f}"
      f"  age {-0.015:+.5f}  urban {0.55:+.4f}")
print(f"\nexp(urban) = {np.exp(pois.coef_[1]):.3f}: urban policies claim"
      f" {(np.exp(pois.coef_[1]) - 1) * 100:.0f}% more often per policy-year.")
print("A log link makes coefficients MULTIPLICATIVE on the rate.")

# --- OVERDISPERSION: the assumption variance == mean is testable. ---
mu = pois.predict(X) * years
pearson = ((claims - mu) ** 2 / np.maximum(mu, 1e-9)).sum()
dispersion = pearson / (n - 3)                    # ~1 if Poisson is adequate
print(f"\ndispersion (Pearson chi2 / df) = {dispersion:.3f}")

# Inject extra variation and watch the diagnostic catch it.
gamma_noise = rng.gamma(0.7, 1 / 0.7, n)          # unobserved heterogeneity
claims_od = rng.poisson(rate * years * gamma_noise)
pois_od = PoissonRegressor(alpha=1e-8, max_iter=2000).fit(
    X, claims_od / years, sample_weight=years)
mu_od = pois_od.predict(X) * years
disp_od = ((claims_od - mu_od) ** 2 / np.maximum(mu_od, 1e-9)).sum() / (n - 3)
print(f"dispersion with unobserved heterogeneity = {disp_od:.3f}  -> > 1")
print("Coefficients stay roughly unbiased; the STANDARD ERRORS are too small by")
print(f"about sqrt({disp_od:.2f}) = {np.sqrt(disp_od):.2f}x. Fix with a")
print("quasi-Poisson scale factor or a negative binomial model.")

# --- POSITIVE, RIGHT-SKEWED, MULTIPLICATIVE: claim SEVERITY wants Gamma. ---
sev_mu = np.exp(6.0 + 0.02 * age + 0.3 * urban)
severity = rng.gamma(shape=2.0, scale=sev_mu / 2.0)   # variance grows as mu^2
print(f"\nseverity: mean {severity.mean():,.0f}  median"
      f" {np.median(severity):,.0f}  skew present")
gam = GammaRegressor(alpha=1e-8, max_iter=2000).fit(X, severity)
lin_log = LinearRegression().fit(X, np.log(severity))
print(f"  Gamma GLM (log link)  age {gam.coef_[0]:+.5f}"
      f"  urban {gam.coef_[1]:+.4f}")
print(f"  OLS on log(y)         age {lin_log.coef_[0]:+.5f}"
      f"  urban {lin_log.coef_[1]:+.4f}")
print(f"  truth                 age {0.02:+.5f}  urban {0.3:+.4f}")
print("Both handle skew, but they target different things: the Gamma GLM models")
print("E[y] directly, while OLS on log(y) models E[log y], whose exponential is")
print("the GEOMETRIC mean and is biased low for E[y].")
gm = np.exp(lin_log.predict(X)).mean()
print(f"  mean of exp(OLS fit) {gm:,.0f}   Gamma GLM mean prediction"
      f" {gam.predict(X).mean():,.0f}   actual mean {severity.mean():,.0f}")

# --- PURE PREMIUM: zero-inflated and continuous at once -> Tweedie. ---
pure = claims * severity / years                  # loss cost per policy-year
tw = TweedieRegressor(power=1.5, alpha=1e-8, max_iter=5000).fit(X, pure)
print(f"\npure premium: {np.mean(pure == 0):.0%} exact zeros,"
      f" continuous above 0")
print(f"  Tweedie(p=1.5) age {tw.coef_[0]:+.5f}  urban {tw.coef_[1]:+.4f}"
      f"  (truth {-0.015+0.02:+.5f} / {0.55+0.3:+.4f})")

# --- THE FAMILY TABLE ---
table = pd.DataFrame([
    ("continuous, symmetric", "Gaussian", "identity", "variance constant"),
    ("binary / proportion", "Binomial", "logit", "variance mu(1-mu)"),
    ("count", "Poisson", "log", "variance = mu"),
    ("count, overdispersed", "Negative binomial", "log", "variance > mu"),
    ("positive, skewed", "Gamma", "log", "variance ~ mu^2"),
    ("positive with exact zeros", "Tweedie 1<p<2", "log", "mass at 0 + skew"),
    ("time to event", "Gamma / Weibull", "log", "censoring needs survival"),
], columns=["target looks like", "family", "usual link", "variance story"])
print("\n", table.to_string(index=False))
```

```text
  THE THREE SLOTS

    z = b0 + b1*x1 + ...        (identical in every GLM)
           |
           | inverse link
           v
         mu = E[y | x]          (range enforced by the link)
           |
           | variance function
           v
      how y scatters around mu  (sets the weights during fitting)

  WHY NOT LEAST SQUARES ON A COUNT

    min prediction +0.208, and at age 100 rural it predicts -0.113
      -> an identity link puts no constraint on the range

    fitted quintile:    0.36   0.61   0.75   0.90   1.13
    residual variance:  0.43   0.67   0.88   1.03   1.58
                          |                           |
                          +--- variance tracks the mean

    That is the Poisson property (variance = mean), and it is exactly
    what OLS assumes away.

  POISSON GLM WITH EXPOSURE AS AN OFFSET

                  intercept       age     urban
    fitted          -0.3292  -0.01695   +0.5062
    truth           -0.4000  -0.01500   +0.5500

    exp(+0.5062) = 1.659: urban policies claim 66% more per policy-year.
    A log link makes coefficients MULTIPLICATIVE on the rate.

  OVERDISPERSION IS TESTABLE

    dispersion (Pearson chi2 / df), clean Poisson data      1.004
    dispersion with unobserved heterogeneity added          2.060

    standard errors are too small by about sqrt(2.06) = 1.44x
    coefficients stay roughly unbiased; the INFERENCE is broken

  GAMMA VS OLS-ON-LOG: THEY TARGET DIFFERENT THINGS

    severity: mean 1,242   median 971   (right-skewed)

    Gamma GLM (log link)   age +0.01885   urban +0.3699
    OLS on log(y)          age +0.01885   urban +0.3624
    truth                  age +0.02000   urban +0.3000

    Coefficients agree, but the PREDICTIONS do not:
      mean of exp(OLS fit)        941
      Gamma GLM mean prediction 1,242
      actual mean               1,242

    exp(E[log y]) is the GEOMETRIC mean, biased low for E[y]. If you
    need an expected amount, model E[y] directly.

  THE FAMILY TABLE

    target looks like            family              link       variance
    continuous, symmetric        Gaussian            identity   constant
    binary / proportion          Binomial            logit      mu(1-mu)
    count                        Poisson             log        = mu
    count, overdispersed         Negative binomial   log        > mu
    positive, skewed             Gamma               log        ~ mu^2
    positive with exact zeros    Tweedie 1<p<2       log        mass at 0
    time to event                Gamma / Weibull     log        censoring
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A GLM is a linear predictor, a link function that sets the range of the
>   mean, and a distribution that sets the variance. Linear, logistic and
>   Poisson regression are three choices of those parts.
> - Choose the link to match the target's range. A log link also makes
>   coefficients multiplicative, so `exp(b)` is a ratio.
> - The variance function is what separates a GLM from transforming the
>   target, because it decides how much weight each row gets.
> - Put exposure in the model as an offset with a coefficient fixed at 1, not
>   as a feature with its own slope.
> - Poisson assumes variance equals mean. Check the dispersion, and if it is
>   above 1, correct the standard errors or switch to negative binomial.
> - Overdispersion breaks p-values but leaves coefficients roughly correct.
> - A Gamma GLM models `E[y]`, while least squares on `log(y)` models
>   `E[log y]`. Exponentiating that gives the geometric mean, which is too low
>   as an estimate of the mean.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Fit a Poisson GLM with varying exposure, once with exposure as an offset
>    and once as a normal feature. Compare the coefficients with the true
>    values.
> 2. Compute the dispersion statistic on clean Poisson data and on data with
>    added variation between rows. Report how much the standard errors need
>    to be corrected.
> 3. Simulate right-skewed positive amounts, fit a Gamma GLM and least squares
>    on the log, and compare each model's average prediction with the true
>    average.
> 4. Fit least squares to a count target with low rates. Report the share of
>    negative predictions and the residual variance in each fifth of the
>    fitted values.
> 5. Fit a Tweedie model to a target that is exactly zero for most rows and
>    positive otherwise. Explain why neither Poisson nor Gamma alone would fit.
> 6. Interview: Your Poisson model of support tickets per account says a
>    feature is significant at p = 0.001, and the dispersion statistic is 3.4.
>    What do you do before reporting it? (Hint: what does dispersion do to the
>    standard error, and what does that do to the p-value?)


#### Interpreting Coefficients

A fitted linear model gives you a table of numbers, and there are many ways to
read that table wrongly. This topic lists the common mistakes. Interpretation
is the main reason to use a linear model, and also where it is most often
misused.

**Start with the units.** A coefficient is the change in `y` for one more unit
of `x`. Measure education in months instead of years and the coefficient
becomes twelve times smaller, even though nothing about the model changed. So
the *size* of a coefficient tells you nothing about how important a feature is
until you know the unit and the spread of that column.

**Logs change how you read coefficients.** This matters most, because log
targets and log features are everywhere.

| Form        | Regression         | Read the coefficient as | Meaning                            |
| ----------- | ------------------ | ----------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| level-level | `y` on `x`         | `b`                     | units of y per unit of x           |
| log-level   | `log y` on `x`     | `100*b` percent         | percent change in y per unit of x  |
| level-log   | `y` on `log x`     | `b/100`                 | units of y per 1% change in x      |
| log-log     | `log y` on `log x` | `b`                     | percent per percent (an elasticity) |

The log-level percentage is an approximation. The exact figure is
`exp(b) - 1`. The two agree closely when `b` is below about 0.10 and differ a
lot above that: a coefficient of 0.50 means a 65% increase, not 50%.

**Standardising makes sizes comparable.** Divide each predictor by its standard
deviation, and each coefficient becomes "the effect of a one-standard-deviation
change". Predictors in dollars and in years can then be compared. Two
warnings. Comparable does not mean causal: a bigger standardised coefficient
is not a stronger cause. And do not standardise binary predictors, because "a
one-SD change in being female" cannot happen to anyone. Leave 0/1 columns as
they are.

**Every categorical coefficient is a comparison.** One level is dropped as the
baseline, and each dummy coefficient is the difference from *that* level. The
baseline has no coefficient because it is the zero point. Drop a different
level and every number in the table changes, while the predictions stay the
same. Always say which level is the baseline.

**Interactions and polynomials do not have a single coefficient.** If the model
has `exper` and `exper^2`, the effect of one more year of experience is
`b_exper + 2*b_exper_sq*exper`, which depends on how much experience someone
already has. The `exper` coefficient alone is the slope at zero experience,
usually the least interesting point. Report the effect at meaningful values
instead.

**The Table 2 fallacy** is the most damaging mistake and the least known. It
means fitting one regression and reading every row as a causal effect. That
cannot work, because the controls needed to measure one variable's effect
correctly often *break* the measurement of another. Suppose education affects
wages partly through occupation. With occupation in the model, the education
coefficient is the **direct** effect. Without it, it is the **total** effect.
Both are valid, but neither is "the" effect. A regression table is designed to
answer one causal question; the other rows are adjustments, not findings.
Chapter 3.5 covers the theory. The practical rule here: name the one
coefficient you are reading causally, and treat the rest as controls.

**A coefficient without an interval is not a finding.** Report standard errors
and confidence intervals. Remember that with nearly collinear predictors, the
interval can be huge even when the model predicts well.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, LogisticRegression, Ridge
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

rng = np.random.default_rng(21)
n = 2500

# A wage model, because wage data makes every interpretation trap concrete.
educ = rng.integers(8, 21, n)                      # years of schooling
exper = rng.integers(0, 40, n)                     # years of experience
female = rng.integers(0, 2, n)
region = rng.choice(["north", "south", "west"], n, p=[0.4, 0.35, 0.25])
# Log wage is linear, so wage itself is MULTIPLICATIVE in the predictors.
log_wage = (1.6 + 0.085 * educ + 0.022 * exper - 0.0004 * exper ** 2
            - 0.12 * female + 0.05 * (region == "west")
            - 0.04 * (region == "south") + rng.normal(0, 0.30, n))
wage = np.exp(log_wage)
df = pd.DataFrame({"educ": educ, "exper": exper, "female": female,
                   "region": region, "wage": wage, "log_wage": log_wage})

# --- 1. UNITS. A coefficient is "change in y per one unit of x", and the unit
#        is whatever the column happens to be measured in.
X = df[["educ", "exper"]]
raw = LinearRegression().fit(X, df["wage"])
print("LEVEL-LEVEL  y in dollars, x in years")
print(f"  educ  {raw.coef_[0]:+.3f} dollars/hour per extra year of schooling")
print(f"  exper {raw.coef_[1]:+.3f} dollars/hour per extra year of experience")

# Rescale one column and the coefficient changes by exactly that factor. The
# model is identical; only the units of the answer moved.
Xc = X.assign(educ_months=X["educ"] * 12).drop(columns="educ")
rescaled = LinearRegression().fit(Xc, df["wage"])
print(f"  same model, educ in MONTHS: {rescaled.coef_[0]:+.4f}"
      f"  (= {raw.coef_[0]:+.3f} / 12)")
print("  Neither number is 'bigger'. Size of a coefficient says nothing until")
print("  you know the unit and the spread of the column.")

# --- 2. LOG TRANSFORMS change the reading to a PERCENTAGE. ---
logmod = LinearRegression().fit(X, np.log(df["wage"]))
b = logmod.coef_[0]
print(f"\nLOG-LEVEL  log(y) on x: coefficient {b:+.4f}")
print(f"  approximate reading: +{b*100:.1f}% per extra year of schooling")
print(f"  exact reading:       +{(np.exp(b) - 1)*100:.1f}%  (exp(b) - 1)")
print("  The approximation is fine below ~0.10 and drifts above it:")
for c in [0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 1.00]:
    print(f"    b={c:.2f}: approx {c*100:5.1f}%   exact {(np.exp(c)-1)*100:6.1f}%")

# log-log gives an ELASTICITY: a percentage per percentage, unit-free.
df["firm_size"] = rng.lognormal(4, 1, n)
df["log_wage2"] = df["log_wage"] + 0.06 * np.log(df["firm_size"])
ll = LinearRegression().fit(np.log(df[["firm_size"]]), df["log_wage2"])
print(f"\nLOG-LOG  elasticity {ll.coef_[0]:+.4f}: a firm 1% larger pays"
      f" {ll.coef_[0]:.3f}% more, and one 10% larger pays about"
      f" {ll.coef_[0] * 10:.2f}% more")

table = pd.DataFrame([
    ("level-level", "y on x", "b", "units of y per unit of x"),
    ("log-level", "log y on x", "100*b", "percent change in y per unit of x"),
    ("level-log", "y on log x", "b/100", "units of y per 1% change in x"),
    ("log-log", "log y on log x", "b", "percent per percent (elasticity)"),
], columns=["form", "regression", "read as", "meaning"])
print("\n", table.to_string(index=False))

# --- 3. CATEGORICAL BASELINES. Every dummy coefficient is a COMPARISON. ---
D = pd.get_dummies(df[["educ", "exper", "region"]], columns=["region"],
                   drop_first=True, dtype=float)
cat = LinearRegression().fit(D, df["log_wage"])
print("\nCATEGORICAL  region, with 'north' dropped as the baseline")
for name, c in zip(D.columns, cat.coef_):
    if name.startswith("region"):
        print(f"  {name:16s} {c:+.4f}  = {name.split('_')[1]} vs NORTH")
print("  There is no 'north' coefficient because north is the zero point. Drop")
print("  a different level and every number changes while the model does not.")

# --- 4. STANDARDISED COEFFICIENTS make magnitudes comparable, not causal. ---
cols = ["educ", "exper", "female"]
Z = StandardScaler().fit_transform(df[cols])
std = LinearRegression().fit(Z, df["log_wage"])
print(f"\nSTANDARDISED  effect of a one-SD move in each predictor")
for c, raw_b, z_b, sd in zip(cols,
                             LinearRegression().fit(df[cols], df["log_wage"]).coef_,
                             std.coef_, df[cols].std()):
    print(f"  {c:8s} raw {raw_b:+.4f} (per unit, sd {sd:5.2f})"
          f"   standardised {z_b:+.4f} (per sd)")
print("  Note 'female' is binary: a 'one-SD change' in it is not a thing that")
print("  can happen to a person, so leave binary predictors unstandardised.")

# --- 5. INTERACTIONS AND POLYNOMIALS: there is no single coefficient. ---
df["exper_sq"] = df["exper"] ** 2
quad = LinearRegression().fit(df[["educ", "exper", "exper_sq", "female"]],
                              df["log_wage"])
b_e, b_e2 = quad.coef_[1], quad.coef_[2]
print(f"\nPOLYNOMIAL  exper {b_e:+.4f}, exper^2 {b_e2:+.6f}")
print("  The effect of one more year depends on where you are:")
for yrs in [0, 5, 15, 25, 35]:
    marginal = b_e + 2 * b_e2 * yrs                # d/dexper of the fitted curve
    print(f"    at {yrs:2d} years: {marginal*100:+6.2f}% per extra year")
print(f"  peak wage at {-b_e / (2 * b_e2):.1f} years of experience")
print("  Reporting 'the' experience coefficient here would be meaningless.")

# --- 6. THE TABLE 2 FALLACY: adjusted coefficients are not all causal. ---
# Suppose occupation is a MEDIATOR of the education effect. Controlling for it
# does not make the education coefficient 'better'; it answers a different
# question, and the two numbers cannot both be the total effect.
occ_score = 0.7 * df["educ"] + rng.normal(0, 1.5, n)
df["log_wage3"] = df["log_wage"] + 0.09 * occ_score
tot = LinearRegression().fit(df[["educ"]], df["log_wage3"]).coef_[0]
dir_ = LinearRegression().fit(
    df[["educ"]].assign(occ=occ_score), df["log_wage3"]).coef_[0]
print(f"\nMEDIATION  educ coefficient WITHOUT occupation {tot:+.4f} (total)")
print(f"           educ coefficient WITH occupation    {dir_:+.4f} (direct)")
print("  Both are correct answers to different questions. Reading every row of")
print("  one regression table as a causal effect is the Table 2 fallacy: the")
print("  covariate set that identifies one effect generally ruins another.")

# --- 7. UNCERTAINTY. A coefficient without an interval is not a finding. ---
Xd = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), df["educ"], df["exper"], df["female"]])
beta = np.linalg.solve(Xd.T @ Xd, Xd.T @ df["log_wage"])
r = df["log_wage"] - Xd @ beta
s2 = (r ** 2).sum() / (n - Xd.shape[1])
se = np.sqrt(np.diag(s2 * np.linalg.inv(Xd.T @ Xd)))
print("\nUNCERTAINTY")
print(f"  {'term':10s} {'estimate':>9s} {'se':>7s} {'95% interval':>20s}")
for name, bb, ss in zip(["const", "educ", "exper", "female"], beta, se):
    print(f"  {name:10s} {bb:+9.4f} {ss:7.4f}"
          f"   [{bb - 1.96*ss:+.4f}, {bb + 1.96*ss:+.4f}]")
```

> Key Takeaways
> - The size of a coefficient means nothing without the column's unit and
>   spread, because rescaling a predictor rescales its coefficient.
> - With a log target, `100*b` is roughly a percentage change. The exact
>   figure is `exp(b)-1`, and the two differ noticeably above about 0.10.
> - A log-log coefficient is an elasticity: percent change per percent
>   change, with no units.
> - Standardised coefficients make sizes comparable but say nothing about
>   cause. Leave binary predictors unstandardised.
> - Every dummy coefficient is a difference from the dropped baseline level,
>   and you must state which level that is.
> - With polynomials or interactions, the effect of a predictor changes with
>   its value, so report effects at meaningful values rather than one number.
> - The Table 2 fallacy is reading every row of one regression as causal. The
>   controls that are right for one effect are usually wrong for another.
> - Controlling for a mediator turns a total effect into a direct effect.
>   Both are correct answers to different questions.

#### Decision Tree Construction

Linear models use one weighted sum for the whole dataset. Trees work
differently: they ask a series of yes-or-no questions, each about one feature.
Trees work for both regression and classification. This topic and the next use
a classification example because it is the easiest to picture. The tree
ensembles after them return to regression.

A decision tree is a chain of questions. Is income above 60? If yes, is the
debt ratio below 0.45? If yes, approve. Each question splits the data in two,
and the tree keeps splitting until it decides to stop. Each final region is
called a **leaf**. The prediction in a leaf is the most common class (for
classification) or the average target (for regression) of the training rows
that ended up there.

Trees are popular because this is how people already reason, and you can print
the fitted model and read it. The structure also gives you two things for free.

**Interactions are automatic.** In a linear model, "high income helps unless
debt is also high" must be added by hand as a product term. A tree splits on
debt ratio and then splits on income *inside* each branch, so it captures the
interaction without being told. Every path from the root to a leaf is a
combination of conditions, which is exactly what an interaction is.

**Rescaling features does not matter.** A split at income > 60 and a split at
log(income) > log(60) divide the data in exactly the same way. Any
transformation that keeps the order of values (standardising, taking logs,
clipping at percentiles) changes nothing. After all the care that penalised
linear models need, this is a relief.

How does the tree pick a split? **It tries every option at each step and keeps
the best.** For every feature and every possible threshold, it measures how
much the split reduces impurity (how mixed the classes are), and keeps the
best one. Then it repeats inside each child. Within one step the search is
complete, but across steps it is greedy: it never goes back to change an
earlier split based on what it found later. Finding the best possible tree
overall is computationally infeasible (NP-hard), so every library uses this
greedy approach.

The structure also has costs.

**Boundaries are made of straight, axis-aligned cuts.** Every split has the
form "feature <= threshold", so the regions are rectangles. A diagonal
boundary has to be approximated by a staircase. A line that logistic
regression describes with two parameters may take a tree dozens of leaves to
copy, and still poorly.

**Trees are unstable (high variance).** Because each split is chosen greedily,
a small change in the data can change an early split and rearrange everything
below it. Two samples from the same data source can produce completely
different-looking trees with similar accuracy. Ensembles exist to fix this
weakness, which is why a single tree is rarely the final model.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, export_text
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)

# A loan-approval problem with an INTERACTION: high income is fine unless the
# debt ratio is also high. A linear model needs that term written by hand; a
# tree discovers it by splitting twice.
n = 2000
income = rng.uniform(20, 140, n)         # thousands
debt_ratio = rng.uniform(0.0, 0.8, n)
approve = ((income > 60) & (debt_ratio < 0.45)).astype(int)
flip = rng.random(n) < 0.06              # 6% label noise, so nothing is perfect
approve = np.abs(approve - flip.astype(int))
X = pd.DataFrame({"income": income, "debt_ratio": debt_ratio})
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, approve, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)

# --- HOW ONE SPLIT IS CHOSEN: try every threshold, keep the purest. ---
def gini(y):
    if len(y) == 0:
        return 0.0
    p = np.mean(y)
    return 2 * p * (1 - p)               # 1 - p^2 - (1-p)^2, for two classes

def best_split(Xa, ya):
    """Exhaustive greedy search: every feature, every midpoint between values."""
    parent, best = gini(ya), None
    for col in Xa.columns:
        vals = np.unique(Xa[col])
        for thr in (vals[:-1] + vals[1:]) / 2:          # candidate midpoints
            mask = Xa[col] <= thr
            nl, nr = mask.sum(), (~mask).sum()
            if nl == 0 or nr == 0:
                continue
            # weighted child impurity: the WEIGHTING is the whole point
            child = (nl * gini(ya[mask.values])
                     + nr * gini(ya[~mask.values])) / len(ya)
            gain = parent - child
            if best is None or gain > best[0]:
                best = (gain, col, thr, nl, nr)
    return best

sub = Xtr.iloc[:400].reset_index(drop=True)
suby = pd.Series(ytr[:400])
gain, col, thr, nl, nr = best_split(sub, suby)
print(f"parent gini {gini(suby):.4f} on {len(suby)} rows")
print(f"best first split: {col} <= {thr:.3f}  gain {gain:.4f}"
      f"  ({nl} left / {nr} right)")

# Show the search surface: gain as a function of the threshold, per feature.
print("\nGAIN AS THE THRESHOLD SWEEPS (the greedy search, made visible)")
for c in X.columns:
    print(f"  {c}")
    lo, hi = sub[c].min(), sub[c].max()
    for t in np.linspace(lo, hi, 11)[1:-1]:
        mask = sub[c] <= t
        if mask.sum() in (0, len(sub)):
            continue
        g = gini(suby) - (mask.sum() * gini(suby[mask.values])
                          + (~mask).sum() * gini(suby[~mask.values])) / len(sub)
        print(f"    thr {t:7.3f}  gain {g:.4f}  {'#' * int(g * 120)}")

# --- THE FULL TREE: recursion, and a stopping rule. ---
tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=2, random_state=0).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("\n" + export_text(tree, feature_names=list(X.columns), decimals=2))
print(f"depth-2 tree: train {tree.score(Xtr, ytr):.4f}"
      f"  test {tree.score(Xte, yte):.4f}")
print("The tree recovered both thresholds (60 and 0.45) without being told")
print("that an interaction existed. That is what recursive partitioning buys.")

# --- DEPTH IS THE COMPLEXITY DIAL, AND IT OVERFITS FAST. ---
print(f"\n{'depth':>6s} {'leaves':>7s} {'train':>7s} {'test':>7s}")
for d in [1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 12, None]:
    t = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=d, random_state=0).fit(Xtr, ytr)
    label = "full" if d is None else str(d)
    print(f"{label:>6s} {t.get_n_leaves():7d} {t.score(Xtr, ytr):7.4f}"
          f" {t.score(Xte, yte):7.4f}")
print("A fully grown tree reaches 1.0 on train by isolating every noisy row in")
print("its own leaf. Perfect training accuracy is the SYMPTOM, not the goal.")

# --- WHAT A TREE CANNOT DO: a diagonal boundary needs many axis-aligned steps.
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

diag = (X["income"] / 140 + X["debt_ratio"] / 0.8 > 1.0).astype(int)
print("\nAN AXIS-ALIGNED MODEL ON A DIAGONAL BOUNDARY")
Xa, Xb, ya, yb = train_test_split(X, diag, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)
for d in [2, 4, 8, None]:
    t = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=d, random_state=0).fit(Xa, ya)
    lbl = "full" if d is None else f"depth {d}"
    print(f"  tree {lbl:8s} leaves {t.get_n_leaves():4d}"
          f"  test {t.score(Xb, yb):.4f}")
lg = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression()).fit(Xa, ya)
print(f"  logistic regression (2 parameters)   test {lg.score(Xb, yb):.4f}")
print("The tree needs dozens of leaves to approximate what one line does")
print("exactly. Trees are not universally better; they are differently biased.")
```

```text
    best first split: debt_ratio <= 0.446  gain 0.1614 (234 left / 166 right)

    income                        debt_ratio
      thr  32.2  gain 0.029 ###     thr 0.081  gain 0.012 #

  DEPTH IS THE COMPLEXITY DIAL AND IT OVERFITS FAST

         1       2  0.7614  0.7700
         2       4  0.9414  0.9450   <- the true structure, found
         3       8  0.9421  0.9450
         5      26  0.9486  0.9400
         8      63  0.9636  0.9283
        12     116  0.9871  0.9067
      full     142  1.0000  0.8900   <- memorised the label noise

  WHAT AN AXIS-ALIGNED MODEL CANNOT DO

    a diagonal boundary, approximated by a staircase:

      |  \                       |  +--+
      |    \    the truth        |  |  +--+     what a tree can express
      |      \                   |  |     +--+
      |        \                 |  |        +--+
      +----------\               +--+-----------+

    tree depth 2   leaves   4   test 0.8467
    tree depth 4   leaves  15   test 0.9483
    tree full      leaves  37   test 0.9683
    logistic regression, 2 parameters, test 0.9933

    Trees are not better than linear models. They are differently biased.
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A tree is a series of splits on one feature at a time. A leaf predicts the
>   most common class or the average target of the training rows that reach
>   it.
> - Interactions come for free, because every path from root to leaf is a
>   combination of conditions.
> - Trees are not affected by any order-preserving change to a feature, so
>   scaling and log transforms make no difference.
> - At each step the tree tries every split and keeps the best, but it never
>   revisits earlier steps, because finding the best tree overall is
>   infeasible.
> - Rectangular regions approximate a diagonal boundary badly. Here a
>   two-parameter linear model can beat a forty-leaf tree.
> - A fully grown tree reaches perfect training accuracy by isolating noisy
>   rows, so its depth must be limited.
> - Greedy splitting makes trees unstable, and that is exactly what ensembles
>   fix.

>    outside the training range?)


#### Splitting Criteria and Pruning

A tree algorithm is defined by two choices: how it scores a possible split, and
when it stops splitting. The first matters less than people expect. The second
matters a lot.

**Impurity measures** score how mixed a node is. For classification there are
three options, where `p_k` is the share of class `k` in the node:

- **Gini impurity**, `1 - sum(p_k^2)`: the chance that two rows picked at
  random from the node have different labels.
- **Entropy**, `-sum(p_k * log2(p_k))`: the number of bits needed to describe
  a label picked from the node.
- **Misclassification rate**, `1 - max(p_k)`: the error you make by always
  predicting the majority class.

Gini and entropy give almost the same trees in practice. Entropy reacts a
little more near the extremes, and Gini is slightly faster because it needs no
logarithms. The difference in accuracy is almost always smaller than the noise
in your evaluation. This is not a setting worth tuning.

Misclassification rate is different, and the reason is useful to understand.
It is the metric you actually care about, yet it is a *poor way to choose
splits*. Gini and entropy are curved (strictly concave), so any split that
makes the children purer earns some credit. Misclassification rate is made of
straight pieces, so it cannot tell apart a split that makes one child
perfectly pure from one that only shifts the majorities a little. The greedy
search gets stuck where the other two keep improving. So: split using Gini or
entropy, and evaluate using the metric you care about.

For **regression**, the tree uses variance reduction: pick the split that
minimises the sum of squared differences from the mean inside each child. It
is the same greedy idea with squared error in place of impurity. Splitting on
absolute error also exists; it gives leaves that predict the median, but it is
slower.

**Stopping** is what makes or breaks a tree. There are two approaches.

**Pre-pruning** (early stopping) prevents splits from happening:

- `max_depth` limits the number of questions in a row;
- `min_samples_leaf` refuses leaves below a minimum size;
- `min_samples_split` refuses to split small nodes;
- `max_leaf_nodes` limits the total number of leaves;
- `min_impurity_decrease` requires each split to improve impurity by a
  minimum amount.

Pre-pruning is cheap and is what people try first. Its weakness is the
**horizon effect**: a split that looks useless on its own may set up a very
useful split just below it, and pre-pruning cuts it off before the benefit is
visible. The classic example is an exclusive-or (XOR) pattern, where neither
feature on its own reduces impurity at all.

**Post-pruning** grows the full tree first, then removes branches that are not
worth keeping. **Cost-complexity pruning** makes "worth keeping" precise: it
minimises `error + alpha * (number of leaves)`. As `alpha` grows from zero,
the tree shrinks in a fixed sequence of steps, and only a limited number of
`alpha` values give different trees. Compute that sequence, cross-validate
over it, and pick the best. Post-pruning avoids the horizon effect completely,
because it has already seen what lies below every split. The price is growing
a large tree first.

In practice, trees inside boosted ensembles are pre-pruned to a shallow depth
and do not need post-pruning, because the ensemble controls complexity. For a
single tree that people will read, use cost-complexity pruning with `alpha`
chosen by cross-validation.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, DecisionTreeRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)

# --- THE THREE CLASSIFICATION IMPURITY MEASURES, SIDE BY SIDE. ---
def gini(p):
    return 1 - p ** 2 - (1 - p) ** 2

def entropy(p):
    p = np.clip(p, 1e-12, 1 - 1e-12)
    return -(p * np.log2(p) + (1 - p) * np.log2(1 - p))

def misclass(p):
    return np.minimum(p, 1 - p)

print(f"{'p(class 1)':>11s} {'gini':>7s} {'entropy':>8s} {'misclass':>9s}")
for p in [0.0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9, 1.0]:
    print(f"{p:11.2f} {gini(p):7.4f} {entropy(p):8.4f} {misclass(p):9.4f}")

# Why misclassification rate is a bad SPLITTING criterion even though it is the
# metric you care about: it is not strictly concave, so a split that improves
# purity can register zero gain and the greedy search stalls.
def weighted(fn, counts):
    tot = sum(a + b for a, b in counts)
    return sum((a + b) / tot * fn(a / (a + b)) for a, b in counts)

parent = [(400, 400)]
split_a = [(300, 100), (100, 300)]     # both children still predict a majority
split_b = [(400, 200), (0, 200)]       # one child made PURE
print("\nA SPLIT THAT MISCLASSIFICATION CANNOT SEE")
print(f"  {'criterion':12s} {'parent':>8s} {'split A':>9s} {'split B':>9s}")
for name, fn in [("gini", gini), ("entropy", entropy), ("misclass", misclass)]:
    p0, a, b = weighted(fn, parent), weighted(fn, split_a), weighted(fn, split_b)
    print(f"  {name:12s} {p0:8.4f} {a:9.4f} {b:9.4f}"
          f"   gains: A {p0-a:+.4f}  B {p0-b:+.4f}")
print("  Misclassification scores A and B IDENTICALLY (+0.2500 each), even")
print("  though B makes one child perfectly pure and therefore final. Gini and")
print("  entropy are strictly concave, so both prefer B. Split on gini or")
print("  entropy; EVALUATE with misclassification or your real metric.")

# --- REGRESSION TREES SPLIT ON VARIANCE, NOT PURITY. ---
# The reduction in sum of squared error is the same greedy idea; the leaf
# prediction is the mean of the rows that land there.
x = rng.uniform(0, 10, 300)
y = np.where(x < 4, 2.0, 8.0) + rng.normal(0, 1, 300)
best = None
for thr in np.linspace(0.5, 9.5, 91):
    l, r = y[x <= thr], y[x > thr]
    if len(l) < 5 or len(r) < 5:
        continue
    sse = ((l - l.mean()) ** 2).sum() + ((r - r.mean()) ** 2).sum()
    if best is None or sse < best[0]:
        best = (sse, thr)
print(f"\nREGRESSION SPLIT  parent SSE {((y - y.mean())**2).sum():.1f}"
      f"  best threshold x <= {best[1]:.2f}  child SSE {best[0]:.1f}")
print(f"  variance reduction {1 - best[0]/((y - y.mean())**2).sum():.1%}"
      "  (the true breakpoint is 4.00)")

# --- PRE-PRUNING VS POST-PRUNING ON A REAL-ISH PROBLEM. ---
n = 1500
Z = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, 8))
logit = 1.4 * Z[:, 0] - 1.1 * Z[:, 1] + 0.9 * Z[:, 0] * Z[:, 1]
yc = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit))).astype(int)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Z, yc, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)

print("\nPRE-PRUNING: stop growing early, using hyperparameters")
print(f"  {'setting':32s} {'leaves':>7s} {'train':>7s} {'test':>7s}")
settings = [
    ("no limits (grow to purity)", {}),
    ("max_depth=3", {"max_depth": 3}),
    ("min_samples_leaf=30", {"min_samples_leaf": 30}),
    ("min_samples_split=50", {"min_samples_split": 50}),
    ("max_leaf_nodes=12", {"max_leaf_nodes": 12}),
    ("min_impurity_decrease=0.005", {"min_impurity_decrease": 0.005}),
]
for label, kw in settings:
    t = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0, **kw).fit(Xtr, ytr)
    print(f"  {label:32s} {t.get_n_leaves():7d} {t.score(Xtr, ytr):7.4f}"
          f" {t.score(Xte, yte):7.4f}")

# --- POST-PRUNING: grow fully, then remove the splits that do not pay. ---
# Cost-complexity pruning minimises  error + ccp_alpha * (number of leaves).
# sklearn computes the alpha values at which each collapse becomes worthwhile.
full = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0).fit(Xtr, ytr)
path = full.cost_complexity_pruning_path(Xtr, ytr)
alphas = path.ccp_alphas[:-1]                     # drop the root-only tree
print(f"\nPOST-PRUNING: {len(alphas)} candidate alphas from"
      f" {alphas.min():.5f} to {alphas.max():.5f}")
print(f"  {'ccp_alpha':>10s} {'leaves':>7s} {'train':>7s} {'test':>7s} {'cv':>7s}")
rows = []
for a in [0.0, 0.0005, 0.002, 0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05]:
    t = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0, ccp_alpha=a).fit(Xtr, ytr)
    cv = cross_val_score(DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0, ccp_alpha=a),
                         Xtr, ytr, cv=5).mean()
    rows.append((a, t.get_n_leaves(), t.score(Xtr, ytr), t.score(Xte, yte), cv))
    print(f"  {a:10.4f} {t.get_n_leaves():7d} {t.score(Xtr, ytr):7.4f}"
          f" {t.score(Xte, yte):7.4f} {cv:7.4f}")
best_alpha = max(rows, key=lambda r: r[4])
print(f"  cross-validation picks alpha {best_alpha[0]:.4f}"
      f" -> {best_alpha[1]} leaves, test {best_alpha[3]:.4f}")
print("\nPost-pruning is the more principled procedure: it lets a weak split")
print("stand if a strong split sits underneath it. Pre-pruning would have cut")
print("the weak split and never discovered the strong one -- the horizon effect.")
```


|                 | Pre-pruning                      | Post-pruning                  |
| --------------- | -------------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| When it acts    | Before a split is made           | After the tree is grown       |
| Cost            | Cheap; never builds the big tree | Must grow the full tree first |
| Horizon effect  | Affected                         | Not affected                  |
| Main settings   | `max_depth`, `min_samples_leaf`  | `ccp_alpha`                   |
| How to choose   | Grid search the settings         | Cross-validate the alpha path |
| Typical use     | Trees inside ensembles           | A single readable tree        |

> Key Takeaways
> - Gini and entropy give almost the same trees, so choosing between them is
>   not a meaningful tuning decision.
> - Misclassification rate is the metric you care about but a poor splitting
>   rule, because it is not curved and cannot reward a split that purifies
>   one child.
> - Regression trees split to minimise squared error inside the children,
>   using the same greedy method.
> - Pre-pruning is cheap but suffers from the horizon effect: it can block a
>   useless-looking split that sets up a valuable one.
> - Cost-complexity post-pruning grows the tree first, so the horizon effect
>   cannot fool it.
> - Only a limited number of alpha values give different pruned trees, so you
>   can list them all and cross-validate.
> - Trees inside an ensemble are kept shallow with pre-pruning. A single
>   readable tree should use cost-complexity pruning.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Tabulate Gini, entropy and misclassification rate across class shares.
>    Check that all three peak at 0.5 but only two are strictly curved.
> 2. Rebuild the pair of splits from the example above and check that
>    misclassification rate scores them the same while Gini prefers one.
> 3. Fit trees with `criterion="gini"` and `criterion="entropy"` on one
>    dataset and compare test accuracy over ten random seeds. Is the
>    difference bigger than the seed-to-seed noise?
> 4. Build an XOR dataset and show that setting `min_impurity_decrease` too
>    high stops the tree from learning it at all.
> 5. Compute the full cost-complexity pruning path, cross-validate over it,
>    and plot the number of leaves against training and validation score.
> 6. Interview: Your single decision tree has 400 leaves and 100% training
>    accuracy. Your manager asks whether to cap the depth at 5 or prune
>    afterwards. Which do you recommend and why? (Hint: what happens to a
>    valuable split that sits below a useless-looking one?)


#### Bagging and Random Forests

A single deep tree has low bias and high variance. It can fit almost any
shape, but it fits a slightly different one every time the data changes.
Averaging is the fix for exactly this situation.

Here is why. If you average `k` independent models that each have variance
`v`, the average has variance `v/k`. The bias stays the same, because the
average of unbiased things is unbiased. So averaging many low-bias,
high-variance models gives a model with low bias *and* low variance, as long as
the models are independent.

You cannot get truly independent models from one dataset, but you can get
close. **Bagging** (bootstrap aggregating) works like this:

1. Draw a bootstrap sample: `n` rows picked at random *with replacement*.
2. Fit a tree on it.
3. Repeat many times.
4. Average the trees' predictions (regression) or take a vote
   (classification).

Each tree sees a slightly different dataset, so each makes different mistakes,
and the mistakes partly cancel out.

Bagging comes with a handy bonus. Sampling `n` rows with replacement leaves out
a fraction `(1 - 1/n)^n` of them, which approaches `1/e`, about 36.8%. That
tree never saw these **out-of-bag (OOB)** rows, so they can be used to test
it. Collect the OOB predictions across all trees and you get a validation
score without holding out any data.

The weakness of bagging is that the trees are not different enough. They all
see roughly the same data, so they all pick the same strong split at the root,
and their errors are correlated. If `k` models each have variance `v` and
pairwise correlation `rho`, the average has variance `rho*v + (1-rho)*v/k`,
not `v/k`. The second term shrinks as you add trees; **the first term does
not**. Correlation sets a floor on how much averaging can help.

**Random forests** lower that floor. On top of bootstrapping the rows, at
*every split* each tree may only look at a random subset of the features. If
the strongest feature is not in the subset, the tree has to find a different
split, so the trees become less alike.

This is a trade, not a free gain, and that is often missed. Limiting the
features makes each single tree worse. You pay some bias to buy less
correlation. The best setting is somewhere in the middle and depends on the
problem. That is why `max_features` is a hyperparameter, and why scikit-learn's
default for regression is *all* features (plain bagging) while its default for
classification is `sqrt(p)`. If you believe "random forests always beat
bagging", read the example below carefully.

**Extremely randomised trees** (Extra Trees) go further: they pick thresholds
at random instead of searching for the best one. This makes the trees even
less alike and much faster to fit.

Two properties of forests are worth stressing:

- **Adding trees almost never causes overfitting.** More trees only reduce
  variance; they never increase it. So `n_estimators` is a question of
  compute time, not of risk.
- **Forests cannot extrapolate.** A prediction is an average of leaf values,
  and a leaf can only report the average of rows it has seen. Beyond the
  training range the prediction goes flat.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor
from sklearn.ensemble import (BaggingRegressor, RandomForestRegressor,
                              ExtraTreesRegressor)
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

rng = np.random.default_rng(6)

# --- WHY AVERAGING WORKS: variance falls, bias does not. ---
# A deep tree is a low-bias, high-variance estimator. Fit it on 40 different
# samples from the same process and watch how far apart the fits are.
def make(n, seed):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X = r.uniform(-3, 3, (n, 1))
    y = np.sin(X[:, 0] * 1.5) + r.normal(0, 0.35, n)
    return X, y

grid = np.linspace(-3, 3, 200).reshape(-1, 1)
preds = np.array([DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=0).fit(*make(120, s))
                  .predict(grid) for s in range(40)])
truth = np.sin(grid[:, 0] * 1.5)
print("ONE DEEP TREE, 40 INDEPENDENT TRAINING SAMPLES")
print(f"  pointwise SD across the 40 fits    : {preds.std(axis=0).mean():.4f}"
      "   <- the variance term")
print(f"  MSE of a typical single tree       : {np.mean((preds - truth)**2):.4f}")
print(f"  MSE of the average of the 40 trees :"
      f" {np.mean((preds.mean(axis=0) - truth)**2):.4f}   <- bias^2 only")
print("Averaging removes the variance term and leaves the bias untouched. That")
print("is the entire theory of bagging, in two numbers.")

# --- BAGGING: bootstrap the rows, fit a tree on each, average. ---
X, y = make(600, 100)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)

def rmse(m, Xa, ya):
    return float(np.sqrt(np.mean((ya - m.predict(Xa)) ** 2)))

base = DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=0).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print(f"\nsingle unpruned tree   test RMSE {rmse(base, Xte, yte):.4f}")
print(f"{'n_estimators':>13s} {'bagged RMSE':>12s}")
for k in [1, 3, 10, 30, 100, 300]:
    bag = BaggingRegressor(DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=0),
                           n_estimators=k, random_state=0).fit(Xtr, ytr)
    print(f"{k:13d} {rmse(bag, Xte, yte):12.4f}")
print("Error drops steeply then flattens. More trees never HURT accuracy, they")
print("just stop helping, so n_estimators is a compute budget, not a risk.")

# --- OUT-OF-BAG ROWS: free validation data, from the bootstrap itself. ---
print(f"\neach bootstrap sample omits (1 - 1/n)^n of the rows -> 1/e ="
      f" {1/np.e:.4f}")
for n in [10, 100, 1000, 10000]:
    print(f"  n={n:5d}: {(1 - 1/n)**n:.4f}")

# --- RANDOM FORESTS: bagging PLUS a random feature subset at every split. ---
# The setup that makes the mechanism visible: 8 latent signals, each duplicated
# five times with a little noise. Every bagged tree keeps finding the SAME
# dominant column first, so the trees stay correlated and averaging saturates.
m = 1200
S = rng.normal(0, 1, (m, 8))                        # the 8 real signals
Z = np.column_stack([S[:, j] + rng.normal(0, 0.15, m)
                     for j in range(8) for _ in range(5)])   # 40 columns
w = np.array([3.0, 2.2, 1.8, 1.5, 1.2, 1.0, 0.8, 0.6])
t = S @ w + rng.normal(0, 1.2, m)
Ztr, Zte, ttr, tte = train_test_split(Z, t, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)

def tree_corr(est, Xa):
    """Mean pairwise correlation between the member trees' predictions."""
    P = np.array([tr.predict(Xa) for tr in est.estimators_])
    C = np.corrcoef(P)
    return float(C[np.triu_indices_from(C, 1)].mean())

print(f"\n40 columns carrying only 8 distinct signals")
print(f"  {'max_features':>13s} {'test RMSE':>10s} {'tree corr':>10s}")
for mf in [None, 20, 13, 6, 3]:
    est = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, max_features=mf,
                                random_state=0).fit(Ztr, ttr)
    label = "all 40" if mf is None else str(mf)
    print(f"  {label:>13s} {rmse(est, Zte, tte):10.4f} {tree_corr(est, Zte):10.3f}")
xt = ExtraTreesRegressor(n_estimators=300, max_features=13,
                         random_state=0).fit(Ztr, ttr)
print(f"  {'extra trees':>13s} {rmse(xt, Zte, tte):10.4f}"
      f" {tree_corr(xt, Zte):10.3f}   <- random thresholds too")
print("\nCorrelation falls monotonically as max_features shrinks, but RMSE has an")
print("INTERIOR optimum: subsampling also makes each tree worse. It is a")
print("bias-for-decorrelation trade, and the right amount is a tuned value --")
print("which is why sklearn's regressor default is all features, not sqrt(p).")

# The algebra behind the trade-off: averaging k estimators with pairwise
# correlation rho leaves a floor of rho*var that more trees cannot remove.
print("\nvariance of an average of k=200 estimators, each with variance 1:")
for rho in [1.0, 0.8, 0.5, 0.2, 0.0]:
    print(f"  rho={rho:.1f}  ->  rho*var + (1-rho)*var/k ="
          f" {rho + (1 - rho) / 200:.4f}")

# --- OOB VERSUS A HELD-OUT SET. ---
rf = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, max_features=13, oob_score=True,
                           random_state=0).fit(Ztr, ttr)
oob = float(np.sqrt(np.mean((ttr - rf.oob_prediction_) ** 2)))
print(f"\nOOB RMSE {oob:.4f}   held-out test RMSE {rmse(rf, Zte, tte):.4f}")
print("Each row is scored by only the ~37% of trees that excluded it, which")
print("biases OOB pessimistic in EXPECTATION -- but that bias is small next to")
print("the variation between one test split and another, which is why OOB came")
print("out lower here. Good enough to tune on when data is scarce; not a")
print("substitute for a held-out set when you are reporting a final number.")

# --- WHAT A FOREST CANNOT DO: extrapolate. ---
xr = np.linspace(0, 10, 300).reshape(-1, 1)
yr = 2.0 * xr[:, 0] + rng.normal(0, 0.5, 300)
rf1 = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=200, random_state=0).fit(xr, yr)
print(f"\nEXTRAPOLATION  (trained on x in [0, 10], max observed y"
      f" {yr.max():.1f})")
for v in [5.0, 10.0, 15.0, 50.0]:
    print(f"  x={v:5.1f}  forest {rf1.predict([[v]])[0]:7.3f}   true {2*v:7.3f}")
print("  Past the training range the prediction is a constant, because a leaf")
print("  can only report the mean of rows it actually saw. Linear models")
print("  extrapolate (sometimes wrongly); trees refuse to.")
```
