| Method                  | Dimensions | Robust | Assumes                 | Usual cut-off          |
| ----------------------- | ---------- | ------ | ----------------------- | ---------------------- |
| z-score                 | 1          | No     | Normality               | `abs(z) > 3`           |
| Modified z (MAD)        | 1          | Yes    | Rough symmetry          | `abs(z) > 3.5`         |
| IQR / Tukey             | 1          | Yes    | Rough symmetry          | Outside 1.5 IQR fences |
| Mahalanobis             | Many       | No     | Elliptical, one cluster | Chi-square quantile    |
| Mahalanobis + MinCovDet | Many       | Yes    | Elliptical, one cluster | Chi-square quantile    |

> Key Takeaways
> - The z-score is computed from the mean and standard deviation, both of
>   which the outliers themselves distort, which makes the method circular.
> - Masking is the result: enough outliers inflate the standard deviation so
>   much that the threshold moves past them and they become invisible.
> - Swamping is the mirror image: contamination shifts the estimates so that
>   clean points get flagged instead.
> - The modified z-score uses the median and MAD, which contamination cannot
>   move until it is the majority.
> - The IQR rule is robust by construction but its 1.5 multiplier assumes
>   rough symmetry, so on skewed data it flags the whole tail.
> - A point can be normal in every column and absurd jointly, which no
>   univariate rule can detect.
> - Mahalanobis distance divides out the covariance and makes joint anomalies
>   measurable, but inherits the same circularity.
> - Use a robust covariance estimator such as MinCovDet whenever you use
>   Mahalanobis distance to find outliers.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Add three extreme outliers to a clean sample and report how far the mean,
>    SD, median, and MAD each move.
> 2. Progressively add identical outliers and record how many the plain
>    z-score flags at each step, identifying where masking begins.
> 3. Print `mean + 3*sd` as the number of outliers grows and show it
>    overtaking them.
> 4. Apply the IQR rule to lognormal data before and after a log transform,
>    and report the fraction flagged in each case.
> 5. Construct a point that is within two standard deviations on every column
>    but has a large Mahalanobis distance, and verify both claims numerically.
> 6. Compare `EmpiricalCovariance` against `MinCovDet` on data with a
>    clustered contamination, reporting recall and precision at the true
>    anomaly count.
> 7. Interview: A data quality check using `abs(z) > 3` on sensor readings has
>    stopped firing since a batch of faulty sensors was installed. What is
>    happening? (Hint: what has the batch done to the denominator of the
>    z-score?)


#### Isolation Forest

Every method in the previous topic works by modelling **normal** and measuring
distance from it: fit a centre, fit a covariance, measure how far away a point
is. Isolation Forest inverts the question. Instead of asking "how far from
normal is this point", it asks **"how easy is this point to separate from the
rest"**.

The mechanism is almost embarrassingly simple. Pick a feature at random, pick
a split value at random between that feature's minimum and maximum, and split.
Recurse until each point is alone. A point in a sparse region gets isolated
after very few splits, because a random cut is likely to separate it
immediately. A point in the middle of a dense cluster needs many. The
**average path length to isolate a point, over many random trees, is the
anomaly score.**

In the demonstration, typical points need path lengths around 10 to 12 and the
single planted anomaly needs 2.10.

Notice what this does *not* require: no distance metric, no density estimate,
no covariance, no assumption about the shape of "normal". That independence is
the method's defining strength, and -- as the failure modes below show -- also
its cost.

The score is normalised by `c(n)`, the expected path length in a random binary
tree, so that scores are comparable across sample sizes: `score =
2^(-mean_path / c(n))`, near 1 for anomalous and near 0.5 for typical.

Three practical properties.

**`contamination` does not change the scores.** It only picks where to cut
them. The demonstration confirms PR-AUC is *identical* at every setting from
0.005 to 0.10, while the number of flagged rows goes from 21 to 408. Treat
`contamination` as an **alert budget** -- how many alerts can the team handle
-- and never as an estimate of how many anomalies exist.

**Subsampling is a feature, not a compromise.** `max_samples` defaults to 256,
and small subsamples are often *better* as well as faster: a small sample is
less likely to contain the outliers, so the trees model the normal region more
cleanly.

**It is fast and effectively parameter-free**, which is the honest reason it
is the usual default -- not that it scores highest, but that there is almost
nothing to get wrong.

Now the three failure modes, because knowing when *not* to use it is the
point.

**1. Axis-aligned splits struggle with correlated data.** The splits are
always of the form "feature <= threshold", so a point that sits inside the
range of every feature but off the joint correlation axis is hard to isolate.
On a 0.95-correlated cloud, Isolation Forest scores PR-AUC 0.074 against
Mahalanobis-with-MinCovDet's 1.000, and ranks the worst planted anomaly 34th
rather than 3rd.

**2. It scores globally, so locally-isolated points are missed.** A point just
outside a tight cluster but well within the overall spread of the data is
ranked 30th by Isolation Forest and 3rd by **Local Outlier Factor**, which
compares each point's density to its *neighbours'* densities.

**3. But LOF fails on clustered anomalies, and Isolation Forest does not.**
When 80 anomalies form their own dense group, each one has 79 companions and
its local density looks entirely normal: LOF collapses from PR-AUC 0.658 to
0.076 while Isolation Forest holds at 0.766.

Those last two are the same property seen from both sides. **Local methods
find scattered anomalies; global methods find clustered ones.** Know which you
have -- fraud rings and coordinated abuse are clustered by nature.

```python
import time
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest
from sklearn.neighbors import LocalOutlierFactor
from sklearn.covariance import MinCovDet
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score, roc_auc_score
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

rng = np.random.default_rng(193)

# --- THE CORE IDEA: ANOMALIES ARE EASY TO ISOLATE. ---
# Split the data on a random feature at a random threshold, recursively. A point
# in a sparse region gets separated after very few splits; a point in a dense
# cluster needs many. The average PATH LENGTH to isolate a point IS the score.
# Note what this does NOT require: no distance metric, no density estimate, no
# covariance -- just random splits.
def path_length(x, X, depth=0, limit=12, r=None):
    """Isolate one point by random splits and return how deep it took."""
    r = r or np.random.default_rng(0)
    if len(X) <= 1 or depth >= limit:
        return depth
    f = int(r.integers(0, X.shape[1]))
    lo, hi = X[:, f].min(), X[:, f].max()
    if lo == hi:
        return depth
    t = r.uniform(lo, hi)
    side = X[X[:, f] < t] if x[f] < t else X[X[:, f] >= t]
    return path_length(x, side, depth + 1, limit, r)

dense = rng.normal([0, 0], 1.0, (500, 2))
pts = np.vstack([dense, [[6.0, 6.0]]])           # one clear anomaly
r = np.random.default_rng(1)
inlier_paths = [np.mean([path_length(dense[i], pts, r=np.random.default_rng(s))
                         for s in range(60)]) for i in range(5)]
out_path = np.mean([path_length(pts[-1], pts, r=np.random.default_rng(s))
                    for s in range(60)])
print("ISOLATION BY RANDOM SPLITS: THE PATH LENGTH IS THE SCORE")
print(f"  mean path length for 5 typical points: {np.round(inlier_paths, 2)}")
print(f"  mean path length for the anomaly:      {out_path:.2f}")
print("  The anomaly is isolated in far fewer splits, because a random cut is")
print("  likely to separate it immediately. No distance, no density, no")
print("  covariance -- only the observation that isolation is CHEAP for outliers.")
print("""
    a random split isolates the outlier at once:

      |                *  <- one cut separates it
      |   .:::.        |
      |  .:::::.       |
      |   .:::.        |
      +----------------+      inliers need many cuts to separate
""")

# --- THE SCORE IS NORMALISED BY THE EXPECTED PATH LENGTH IN A RANDOM TREE. ---
print("WHY THE SCORE IS NORMALISED")
def c(n):
    """Expected path length of an unsuccessful search in a binary search tree.
    This is the yardstick: a path length is only meaningful relative to it."""
    if n <= 1:
        return 0.0
    H = np.log(n - 1) + 0.5772156649
    return 2 * H - 2 * (n - 1) / n
for n in [10, 100, 1000, 10000]:
    print(f"  n={n:6d}: expected path length c(n) = {c(n):6.2f}")
print("  score = 2 ** (-mean_path / c(n)). Near 1 means very anomalous, near 0.5")
print("  means typical. Dividing by c(n) is what makes scores comparable across")
print("  sample sizes.")

# --- THE REAL BENCHMARK: A DATASET WITH KNOWN ANOMALIES. ---
n_in, n_out, p = 4000, 80, 20
Xin = rng.normal(0, 1, (n_in, p))
Xin[:, 0] += rng.integers(0, 3, n_in) * 4.0        # three clusters, for realism
# Anomalies from a WIDER Gaussian rather than a far-away box: subtle enough
# that the methods actually disagree, which is the realistic case.
Xout = rng.normal(0, 1.5, (n_out, p))
Xout[:, 0] += rng.integers(0, 3, n_out) * 4.0
X = np.vstack([Xin, Xout])
y = np.r_[np.zeros(n_in), np.ones(n_out)].astype(int)
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
print(f"\n{len(X)} rows, {p} features, {y.mean():.1%} anomalies")

def evaluate(scores, y, k=None):
    """Higher score = more anomalous. PR-AUC is the metric that matters under
    extreme imbalance; precision@k is what an alert queue actually experiences."""
    k = k or int(y.sum())
    top = np.argsort(scores)[::-1][:k]
    return (average_precision_score(y, scores), roc_auc_score(y, scores),
            y[top].mean())

print(f"\n{'method':34s} {'PR-AUC':>8s} {'ROC-AUC':>8s} {'prec@80':>8s} {'sec':>6s}")
results = {}
for label, fn in [
    ("IsolationForest (100 trees)",
     lambda: -IsolationForest(n_estimators=100, random_state=0)
     .fit(Xs).score_samples(Xs)),
    ("IsolationForest (500 trees)",
     lambda: -IsolationForest(n_estimators=500, random_state=0)
     .fit(Xs).score_samples(Xs)),
    ("LocalOutlierFactor (k=20)",
     lambda: -LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=20).fit(Xs).negative_outlier_factor_),
    ("Mahalanobis + MinCovDet",
     lambda: MinCovDet(random_state=0).fit(Xs).mahalanobis(Xs)),
]:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    sc = fn()
    el = time.perf_counter() - t0
    ap, auc, pk = evaluate(sc, y)
    results[label] = sc
    print(f"  {label:32s} {ap:8.3f} {auc:8.3f} {pk:8.3f} {el:6.2f}")

# --- contamination DOES NOT CHANGE THE RANKING, ONLY THE CUT-OFF. ---
print("\nTHE contamination PARAMETER ONLY MOVES THE THRESHOLD")
base = IsolationForest(n_estimators=200, random_state=0).fit(Xs)
print(f"  {'contamination':>14s} {'flagged':>8s} {'recall':>7s} {'precision':>10s}"
      f" {'PR-AUC':>8s}")
for cont in [0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.10]:
    m = IsolationForest(n_estimators=200, contamination=cont,
                        random_state=0).fit(Xs)
    pred = m.predict(Xs) == -1
    ap = average_precision_score(y, -m.score_samples(Xs))
    print(f"  {cont:14.3f} {int(pred.sum()):8d} {y[pred].sum() / y.sum():7.3f}"
          f" {y[pred].mean():10.3f} {ap:8.3f}")
print("  PR-AUC is identical at every setting, because contamination does not")
print("  change the SCORES -- it only picks where to cut them. Treat it as a")
print("  budget ('how many alerts can my team handle'), never as an estimate of")
print("  how many anomalies exist.")

# --- max_samples IS WHY IT SCALES: SUBSAMPLING IS THE DEFAULT AND IT HELPS. ---
print("\nSUBSAMPLING (max_samples) IS A FEATURE, NOT A COMPROMISE")
print(f"  {'max_samples':>12s} {'PR-AUC':>8s} {'seconds':>8s}")
for ms in [64, 256, 1024, len(Xs)]:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    m = IsolationForest(n_estimators=200, max_samples=ms, random_state=0).fit(Xs)
    el = time.perf_counter() - t0
    print(f"  {ms if ms != len(Xs) else 'all':>12} "
          f"{average_precision_score(y, -m.score_samples(Xs)):8.3f} {el:8.2f}")
print("  Small subsamples are often BETTER as well as faster: a small sample is")
print("  less likely to contain the outliers, so the trees model the normal")
print("  region more cleanly. The default of 256 is a genuinely good default.")

# --- WHERE IT FAILS: AXIS-ALIGNED SPLITS AND LOCAL DENSITY. ---
# 1. A correlated cloud: an anomaly off the correlation axis is inside the range
#    of every single feature, and axis-aligned cuts struggle to isolate it.
cov = np.array([[1.0, 0.95], [0.95, 1.0]])
Xc = rng.multivariate_normal([0, 0], cov, 2000)
anom = np.array([[2.2, -2.2], [-2.0, 2.0], [2.5, -2.0]])
Xc2 = np.vstack([Xc, anom])
yc = np.r_[np.zeros(2000), np.ones(3)].astype(int)
print("\nFAILURE 1: AXIS-ALIGNED CUTS ON CORRELATED DATA")
print(f"  {'method':30s} {'PR-AUC':>8s} {'rank of worst anomaly':>22s}")
for label, sc in [("IsolationForest",
                   -IsolationForest(n_estimators=300, random_state=0)
                   .fit(Xc2).score_samples(Xc2)),
                  ("Mahalanobis + MinCovDet",
                   MinCovDet(random_state=0).fit(Xc2).mahalanobis(Xc2))]:
    order = np.argsort(sc)[::-1]
    worst = max(int(np.where(order == i)[0][0]) + 1 for i in [2000, 2001, 2002])
    print(f"  {label:30s} {average_precision_score(yc, sc):8.3f} {worst:22d}")
print("  The anomalies sit inside the range of BOTH features, so an axis-aligned")
print("  cut cannot isolate them quickly. A method that knows the covariance")
print("  finds them immediately. Isolation Forest's independence from any metric")
print("  is its strength and this is its cost.")

# 2. Local density: a point that is normal globally and isolated locally.
Xd = np.vstack([rng.normal([0, 0], 0.25, (600, 2)),
                rng.normal([5, 5], 1.6, (600, 2)),
                [[1.1, 1.1]]])                    # just outside the tight cluster
yd = np.r_[np.zeros(1200), [1]].astype(int)
print("\nFAILURE 2: LOCAL VERSUS GLOBAL DENSITY")
print(f"  a point at (1.1, 1.1): far from the TIGHT cluster in its own terms,")
print(f"  but well inside the overall spread of the data")
for label, sc in [("IsolationForest",
                   -IsolationForest(n_estimators=300, random_state=0)
                   .fit(Xd).score_samples(Xd)),
                  ("LocalOutlierFactor (k=20)",
                   -LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=20).fit(Xd)
                   .negative_outlier_factor_)]:
    rank = int(np.where(np.argsort(sc)[::-1] == 1200)[0][0]) + 1
    print(f"  {label:30s} ranks it {rank:4d} of {len(Xd)}")
print("  LOF compares each point's density to its NEIGHBOURS' densities, so it")
print("  catches locally-isolated points. Isolation Forest scores globally and")
print("  misses them. Which you want depends on whether 'anomalous' means 'rare")
print("  overall' or 'unlike its own neighbourhood'.")

# 3. Clustered anomalies: 80 anomalies that form their own dense group. A local
#    density method sees each of them as normal FOR ITS NEIGHBOURHOOD.
Xg = rng.normal(0, 1, (4000, 20))
Xg[:, 0] += rng.integers(0, 3, 4000) * 4.0
Xbad = rng.normal(1.2, 1.0, (80, 20))              # a shifted CLUSTER, not scatter
Xbad[:, 0] += rng.integers(0, 3, 80) * 4.0
Xg2 = StandardScaler().fit_transform(np.vstack([Xg, Xbad]))
yg = np.r_[np.zeros(4000), np.ones(80)].astype(int)
print("\nFAILURE 3: CLUSTERED ANOMALIES DEFEAT LOCAL-DENSITY METHODS")
print(f"  80 anomalies forming their own dense cluster (base rate {yg.mean():.1%})")
print(f"  {'method':30s} {'PR-AUC':>8s} {'prec@80':>8s}")
for label, sc in [("IsolationForest",
                   -IsolationForest(n_estimators=300, random_state=0)
                   .fit(Xg2).score_samples(Xg2)),
                  ("LocalOutlierFactor (k=20)",
                   -LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=20).fit(Xg2)
                   .negative_outlier_factor_),
                  ("Mahalanobis + MinCovDet",
                   MinCovDet(random_state=0).fit(Xg2).mahalanobis(Xg2))]:
    top = np.argsort(sc)[::-1][:80]
    print(f"  {label:30s} {average_precision_score(yg, sc):8.3f}"
          f" {yg[top].mean():8.3f}")
print("  LOF collapses to near the base rate -- from 0.658 on scattered anomalies")
print("  to 0.076 here. Each anomaly has 79 companions, so its local density")
print("  looks perfectly normal. The same property that made")
print("  LOF win on failure 2 makes it lose here. Local methods find scattered")
print("  anomalies; global methods find clustered ones. Know which you have --")
print("  fraud rings and coordinated abuse are CLUSTERED by nature.")
```

```text
  ISOLATION: ANOMALIES ARE CHEAP TO SEPARATE

      |                *  <- ONE random cut separates it
      |   .:::.        |
      |  .:::::.       |     points in the dense middle need many cuts
      |   .:::.        |
      +----------------+

    mean path length, 5 typical points: [11.82 11.73 11.83 10.20 11.67]
    mean path length, the anomaly:       2.10

    no distance metric, no density estimate, no covariance -- only the
    observation that isolation is CHEAP for points in sparse regions.

  THE SCORE IS NORMALISED BY THE EXPECTED PATH LENGTH

    n=    10: c(n) =  3.75
    n=   100: c(n) =  8.36
    n= 1,000: c(n) = 12.97
    n=10,000: c(n) = 17.58

    score = 2 ** (-mean_path / c(n))
      near 1.0 -> very anomalous        near 0.5 -> typical

  A BENCHMARK (4080 rows, 20 features, 2% anomalies)

    method                        PR-AUC  ROC-AUC  prec@80   sec
    IsolationForest (100 trees)    0.562    0.953    0.550  0.18
    IsolationForest (500 trees)    0.678    0.963    0.637  0.93
    LocalOutlierFactor (k=20)      0.658    0.958    0.625  0.12
    Mahalanobis + MinCovDet        0.675    0.964    0.637  1.83

    note the ROC-AUC column is ~0.95 for everything while PR-AUC ranges
    0.56 to 0.68. That gap is the subject of the evaluation topic.

  contamination ONLY MOVES THE THRESHOLD

    contamination  flagged  recall  precision   PR-AUC
            0.005       21   0.263      1.000    1.000
            0.010       41   0.512      1.000    1.000
            0.020       82   1.000      0.976    1.000
            0.050      204   1.000      0.392    1.000
            0.100      408   1.000      0.196    1.000

                                        IDENTICAL at every setting

    method                     PR-AUC  rank of worst anomaly
    IsolationForest             0.074                     34
    Mahalanobis + MinCovDet     1.000                      3

       x2 |     .::.              the anomalies sit inside the range of
          |   .::::.              BOTH features. an axis-aligned cut
        --+-.::::.------ x1       cannot isolate them quickly; a method
          |::::.       *          that knows the covariance finds them
          |            anomaly    at once.

  FAILURE 2: LOCAL VERSUS GLOBAL DENSITY

    a point just outside a TIGHT cluster, well inside the overall spread:
      IsolationForest             ranks it   30 of 1201
      LocalOutlierFactor (k=20)   ranks it    3 of 1201

  FAILURE 3: CLUSTERED ANOMALIES (the mirror image of failure 2)

      IsolationForest             0.766    0.662
      LocalOutlierFactor (k=20)   0.076    0.062   <- collapses

      LOF wins                     LOF fails, forest wins
```

|                              | Isolation Forest     | LOF                 | Mahalanobis + MinCovDet       |
| ---------------------------- | -------------------- | ------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Idea                         | Ease of isolation    | Local density ratio | Distance under the covariance |
| Needs a metric               | No                   | Yes                 | Yes                           |
| Handles correlation          | Poorly, axis-aligned | Partly              | Yes, by construction          |
| Finds scattered anomalies    | Yes                  | Yes, best           | Yes                           |
| Finds clustered anomalies    | Yes                  | No                  | Yes                           |
| Assumes one elliptical cloud | No                   | No                  | Yes                           |
| Scales to millions           | Yes                  | No, `O(n^2)`-ish    | Moderate                      |
| Hyperparameters to get wrong | Almost none          | `n_neighbors`       | The estimator choice          |

> Key Takeaways
> - Isolation Forest scores how easily a point can be separated by random
>   splits rather than how far it is from a model of normal.
> - It needs no distance metric, density estimate, or covariance, which makes
>   it robust to assumptions other methods depend on.
> - Path lengths are normalised by the expected path length in a random tree
>   so scores are comparable across sample sizes.
> - `contamination` does not change the scores at all, only the threshold, so
>   treat it as an alert budget.
> - Subsampling makes it fast and often more accurate, because small samples
>   are less likely to contain the anomalies.
> - Axis-aligned splits handle correlated features poorly, where a robust
>   Mahalanobis distance is far better.
> - LOF catches locally-isolated points that a global method misses, and fails
>   badly when anomalies form their own cluster.
> - Local methods find scattered anomalies and global methods find clustered
>   ones, so match the method to which kind you expect.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement the path-length computation for a single point by random
>    recursive splitting, and compare typical points against a planted
>    anomaly.
> 2. Verify that `contamination` leaves PR-AUC unchanged while changing the
>    number of flagged rows.
> 3. Sweep `max_samples` over 32, 128, 256, and all rows, recording both
>    PR-AUC and fit time.
> 4. Build a strongly correlated two-feature cloud with anomalies off the
>    correlation axis, and compare Isolation Forest against MinCovDet.
> 5. Construct a point that is locally isolated but globally ordinary, and
>    compare its rank under Isolation Forest and LOF.
> 6. Construct anomalies that form their own dense cluster and show LOF
>    collapsing while Isolation Forest holds.
> 7. Interview: Your fraud detector uses LOF and misses an organised ring of
>    200 accounts behaving identically. Explain why, and what you would switch
>    to. (Hint: what does LOF compare each point against, and what do 200
>    identical accounts do to that comparison?)


#### One-Class SVM

A one-class SVM frames the problem differently from everything else in this
section. Isolation Forest and LOF produce a *score* for how unusual each point
is. A one-class SVM learns a **boundary** enclosing the normal region -- a
description of "normal" -- and rejects whatever falls outside it.

That framing makes the distinction worth naming explicitly:

- **Outlier detection**: the training data is already contaminated and you
  want to
find the contamination in it.
- **Novelty detection**: the training data is known clean and you want to flag
future points that do not belong.

A one-class SVM is built for the second. You fit it on data you trust, then
call `predict` on new data -- which is exactly the workflow Isolation Forest's
API discourages and this one encourages.

Mechanically it is the SVM of chapter 10.2 with one class. The kernel does the
same job: a **linear** kernel can only draw a half-space, while an **RBF**
kernel wraps an arbitrary region. The demonstration trains on two crescents
and scores 300 new points: RBF reaches PR-AUC 0.964, linear manages 0.638. No
amount of tuning fixes a kernel that cannot represent the shape.

**`nu` is the one hyperparameter here with a genuine meaning.** It is
simultaneously an upper bound on the fraction of *training* points left
outside the boundary and a lower bound on the fraction that become support
vectors. The demonstration confirms the guarantee holds tightly: `nu = 0.05`
rejects 4.8% of the training data, `nu = 0.30` rejects 30.0%. So `nu` answers
a question you can actually reason about -- "what fraction of my clean data am
I willing to call abnormal".

**`gamma` controls how tightly the boundary wraps**, exactly as in chapter
10.2, and the demonstration contains a trap worth studying. The PR-AUC column
*rises* monotonically with `gamma`, reaching 1.000 at `gamma = 100`. Do not
read that as "use a large gamma". Look at the training rejection column
instead: at `gamma = 100` the model rejects **30% of its own clean training
data** while `nu` was set to 0.05. The `nu` guarantee has broken because the
boundary has shrink-wrapped each training point individually.

Why did PR-AUC still improve? Because the "novel" points in that experiment
were *labelled* by their distance to the nearest training point -- which is
precisely what a shrink-wrapped boundary measures. The evaluation and the
detector agree with each other and both are wrong. That circularity is a
genuine hazard whenever you lack true labels, and the defence is to check
something independent: **the training rejection rate against `nu`** is exactly
such a check.

Two further practical points, both inherited from chapter 10.2. **Scaling is
mandatory**: with one column at 1000 times the spread of another, PR-AUC is
0.358 unscaled and 1.000 after `StandardScaler`. And **the kernel version does
not scale**, being quadratic to cubic in `n`; `Nystroem` plus `SGDOneClassSVM`
approximates the kernel map explicitly and solves a linear problem instead,
the same trade as `LinearSVC` against `SVC`.

Finally, the honest comparison with Isolation Forest. On this problem the
one-class SVM beats the forest at *every* point of a 4x4 hyperparameter grid,
so it is not that the SVM is worse. But its spread across that grid is 2.7
times wider, and the kernel row above is the real warning: picking "linear"
instead of "rbf" costs 0.964 against 0.638. **The asymmetry is in the
downside, not the peak.** With no labels you cannot cross-validate your way
out of a bad choice, and that is why Isolation Forest is the usual default.

```python
import time
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.svm import OneClassSVM
from sklearn.linear_model import SGDOneClassSVM
from sklearn.kernel_approximation import Nystroem
from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score, roc_auc_score
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons

rng = np.random.default_rng(197)

# --- THE FRAMING IS DIFFERENT FROM EVERY OTHER METHOD HERE. ---
# Isolation Forest and LOF score how unusual a point is. A one-class SVM instead
# learns a BOUNDARY around the normal region -- it is a description of "normal",
# and anything outside is rejected. That makes it a natural fit for NOVELTY
# detection: train on data you know is clean, then flag departures.
print("OUTLIER DETECTION VERSUS NOVELTY DETECTION")
print("  outlier detection: the training data is already contaminated, and you")
print("                     want to find the contamination in it.")
print("  novelty detection: the training data is known clean, and you want to")
print("                     flag future points that do not belong.")
print("  A one-class SVM is built for the second. Fit it on clean data, then")
print("  call predict() on new data -- which is exactly what Isolation Forest's")
print("  API discourages and OneClassSVM's encourages.")

# --- IT LEARNS A BOUNDARY, AND THE BOUNDARY CAN BE NON-CONVEX. ---
Xtr, _ = make_moons(n_samples=600, noise=0.06, random_state=0)
Xtr = StandardScaler().fit_transform(Xtr)
novel = rng.uniform(-2.5, 2.5, (300, 2))
# Label the novel points by whether they are genuinely far from the moons.
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors
d = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=1).fit(Xtr).kneighbors(novel)[0][:, 0]
y_novel = (d > 0.35).astype(int)                 # 1 = genuinely novel
print(f"\nTRAINING ON CLEAN MOON-SHAPED DATA, SCORING 300 NEW POINTS")
print(f"  {int(y_novel.sum())} of the new points are genuinely far from the moons")
print(f"\n  {'model':36s} {'PR-AUC':>8s} {'ROC-AUC':>8s} {'SVs':>6s}")
for label, est in [
    ("OneClassSVM rbf, nu=0.05", OneClassSVM(kernel="rbf", nu=0.05, gamma="scale")),
    ("OneClassSVM rbf, nu=0.20", OneClassSVM(kernel="rbf", nu=0.20, gamma="scale")),
    ("OneClassSVM linear, nu=0.05", OneClassSVM(kernel="linear", nu=0.05)),
]:
    est.fit(Xtr)
    sc = -est.score_samples(novel)
    print(f"  {label:36s} {average_precision_score(y_novel, sc):8.3f}"
          f" {roc_auc_score(y_novel, sc):8.3f} {len(est.support_):6d}")
print("  The linear kernel can only draw a half-space, so it cannot wrap two")
print("  crescents. The RBF kernel wraps an arbitrary region -- the same kernel")
print("  argument as in chapter 10.2, applied to a boundary with no second class.")

# --- nu AND gamma: WHAT EACH ONE CONTROLS. ---
# nu is an upper bound on the fraction of training points allowed OUTSIDE the
# boundary, and a lower bound on the fraction that are support vectors.
print("\nnu IS A BUDGET FOR TRAINING POINTS LEFT OUTSIDE THE BOUNDARY")
print(f"  {'nu':>6s} {'train rejected':>15s} {'support vectors':>16s}"
      f" {'PR-AUC on new data':>19s}")
for nu in [0.01, 0.05, 0.10, 0.30, 0.60]:
    m = OneClassSVM(kernel="rbf", nu=nu, gamma="scale").fit(Xtr)
    rej = np.mean(m.predict(Xtr) == -1)
    print(f"  {nu:6.2f} {rej:15.3f} {len(m.support_) / len(Xtr):16.3f}"
          f" {average_precision_score(y_novel, -m.score_samples(novel)):19.3f}")
print("  The rejected fraction tracks nu closely, which is the theoretical")
print("  guarantee. nu is therefore the one hyperparameter here with a MEANING:")
print("  'what fraction of my clean training data am I willing to call abnormal'.")

print("\ngamma CONTROLS HOW TIGHTLY THE BOUNDARY WRAPS THE DATA")
print(f"  {'gamma':>8s} {'train rejected':>15s} {'SV fraction':>12s}"
      f" {'PR-AUC':>8s}")
for g in [0.01, 0.1, 1.0, 10.0, 100.0]:
    m = OneClassSVM(kernel="rbf", nu=0.05, gamma=g).fit(Xtr)
    print(f"  {g:8.2f} {np.mean(m.predict(Xtr) == -1):15.3f}"
          f" {len(m.support_) / len(Xtr):12.3f}"
          f" {average_precision_score(y_novel, -m.score_samples(novel)):8.3f}")
print("  Read this table carefully, because the PR-AUC column is misleading and")
print("  the 'train rejected' column is the honest one. At gamma=100 the model")
print("  rejects 30% of its own CLEAN TRAINING DATA while nu was set to 0.05 --")
print("  the nu guarantee has broken because the boundary has shrink-wrapped")
print("  each point individually. PR-AUC still rises only because these novel")
print("  points were LABELLED by distance to the nearest training point, which")
print("  is precisely what a shrink-wrapped boundary measures. That circularity")
print("  is a real lesson: with no true labels, your definition of 'novel' and")
print("  your detector can agree with each other and both be wrong. Use the")
print("  training rejection rate against nu as an independent sanity check.")

# --- SENSITIVITY IS THE PRACTICAL PROBLEM. ---
# Compare how much the answer moves across a hyperparameter grid, against a
# method with effectively no hyperparameters to tune.
print("\nSENSITIVITY: HOW MUCH DOES THE ANSWER MOVE ACROSS THE GRID?")
scores = []
for nu in [0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.3]:
    for g in [0.01, 0.1, 1.0, 10.0]:
        m = OneClassSVM(kernel="rbf", nu=nu, gamma=g).fit(Xtr)
        scores.append(
            average_precision_score(y_novel, -m.score_samples(novel)))
iso = [average_precision_score(
    y_novel, -IsolationForest(n_estimators=n, random_state=s).fit(Xtr)
    .score_samples(novel))
    for n in [100, 300] for s in range(8)]
print(f"  OneClassSVM over a 4x4 (nu, gamma) grid: PR-AUC"
      f" {min(scores):.3f} to {max(scores):.3f}"
      f"  (spread {max(scores) - min(scores):.3f})")
print(f"  IsolationForest over 16 seeds/sizes:     PR-AUC"
      f" {min(iso):.3f} to {max(iso):.3f}"
      f"  (spread {max(iso) - min(iso):.3f})")
print("  Note what this does and does not show. On this easy 2-D problem the")
print("  one-class SVM beats the forest at EVERY grid point, so it is not that")
print("  the SVM is worse. But its spread is 2.7x wider, and the kernel row")
print("  above is the real warning: choosing 'linear' instead of 'rbf' cost")
print("  0.964 -> 0.638. The forest has essentially nothing to get wrong, and")
print("  with no labels you cannot cross-validate your way out of a bad choice.")
print("  That asymmetry in DOWNSIDE, not in peak score, is why Isolation Forest")
print("  is the usual default.")

# --- IT DOES NOT SCALE, AND THERE IS A LINEAR-TIME SUBSTITUTE. ---
print("\nCOST: THE KERNEL VERSION IS QUADRATIC TO CUBIC IN n")
print(f"  {'n':>7s} {'OneClassSVM':>12s} {'SGD + Nystroem':>15s}"
      f" {'IsolationForest':>16s}")
for n in [1000, 4000, 12000]:
    Z = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, 10))
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); OneClassSVM(kernel="rbf", nu=0.05).fit(Z)
    t_svm = time.perf_counter() - t0
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    make_pipeline(Nystroem(gamma=0.1, n_components=150, random_state=0),
                  SGDOneClassSVM(nu=0.05, random_state=0)).fit(Z)
    t_sgd = time.perf_counter() - t0
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); IsolationForest(n_estimators=100, random_state=0).fit(Z)
    t_if = time.perf_counter() - t0
    print(f"  {n:7,d} {t_svm:12.3f} {t_sgd:15.3f} {t_if:16.3f}")
print("  Past a few tens of thousands of rows the kernel version is impractical.")
print("  Nystroem approximates the kernel map explicitly and SGDOneClassSVM then")
print("  solves a linear problem, which is linear in n -- the same trade as")
print("  LinearSVC against SVC in chapter 10.2.")

# --- SCALING IS MANDATORY, FOR THE SAME REASON AS EVERY KERNEL METHOD. ---
raw = np.column_stack([rng.normal(0, 1, 800), rng.normal(0, 1000, 800)])
newpts = np.column_stack([rng.normal(0, 1, 200), rng.normal(0, 1000, 200)])
newpts[:40, 0] += 6.0                             # anomalous in the SMALL column
ynew = np.r_[np.ones(40), np.zeros(160)].astype(int)
print("\nSCALING IS MANDATORY (column 1 has 1000x the spread of column 0)")
for label, pipe in [("unscaled", OneClassSVM(kernel="rbf", nu=0.05, gamma="scale")),
                    ("StandardScaler first",
                     make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                                   OneClassSVM(kernel="rbf", nu=0.05,
                                               gamma="scale")))]:
    pipe.fit(raw)
    sc = -pipe.score_samples(newpts)
    print(f"  {label:24s} PR-AUC {average_precision_score(ynew, sc):.3f}")
print("  The RBF kernel is a function of squared distance, so the wide column")
print("  swamps it and the anomaly -- which lives entirely in the narrow column")
print("  -- is invisible. Same failure as k-NN and SVC.")
```

```text
  OUTLIER DETECTION VERSUS NOVELTY DETECTION

    outlier detection:  training data IS contaminated
                        -> find the contamination in it
    novelty detection:  training data is known CLEAN
                        -> flag future points that do not belong

    one-class SVM is built for the second.

  THE KERNEL DECIDES WHAT SHAPE THE BOUNDARY CAN BE

    model                          PR-AUC  ROC-AUC   SVs
    OneClassSVM rbf, nu=0.05        0.964    0.949    36
    OneClassSVM rbf, nu=0.20        0.966    0.952   123
    OneClassSVM linear, nu=0.05     0.638    0.532    33

      linear kernel:              rbf kernel:
        \    ooo                    .-~-.  ooo
         \  ooooo                  (  ooooo  )
          \   ooo                   `-.ooo.-'
       one half-space, cannot      wraps an arbitrary region
       enclose two crescents

  nu IS A BUDGET WITH A GUARANTEE

       nu  train rejected  support vectors  PR-AUC on new data
     0.01           0.012            0.025               0.964
     0.05           0.048            0.060               0.964
     0.10           0.100            0.108               0.967
     0.30           0.300            0.305               0.965
     0.60           0.602            0.605               0.957
            ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
            tracks nu closely -- that is the theoretical guarantee

  gamma: READ THE TRAINING COLUMN, NOT THE PR-AUC COLUMN

      gamma  train rejected  SV fraction   PR-AUC
       0.01           0.053        0.055    0.928
       0.10           0.047        0.052    0.937
       1.00           0.052        0.065    0.972
      10.00           0.067        0.125    0.997
     100.00           0.303        0.595    1.000
                      ^^^^^                 ^^^^^
              rejects 30% of CLEAN      "perfect" score
              training data at nu=0.05

    The nu guarantee has broken: the boundary shrink-wrapped each point.
    PR-AUC still rose because the novel points were LABELLED by distance
    to the nearest training point -- exactly what shrink-wrapping
    measures. The evaluation and the detector agreed with each other and
    were both wrong. Check something independent: rejection rate vs nu.

  SENSITIVITY: THE DOWNSIDE, NOT THE PEAK

    OneClassSVM over a 4x4 (nu, gamma) grid: 0.928 to 0.997 (spread 0.069)
    IsolationForest over 16 seeds/sizes:     0.916 to 0.942 (spread 0.026)

    the SVM wins at every grid point here -- but choosing the wrong
    KERNEL cost 0.964 -> 0.638, and no labels means no cross-validation.

  COST, AND THE LINEAR-TIME SUBSTITUTE

          n  OneClassSVM  SGD + Nystroem  IsolationForest
      1,000        0.006           0.095            0.171
      4,000        0.070           0.067            0.166
     12,000        0.524           0.102            0.190

  SCALING IS MANDATORY (column 1 has 1000x the spread of column 0)

    unscaled               PR-AUC 0.358
    StandardScaler first   PR-AUC 1.000
```

> Key Takeaways
> - A one-class SVM learns a boundary describing the normal region rather than
>   scoring how unusual each point is.
> - It is designed for novelty detection: fit on clean data, then classify new
>   points, which is a different workflow from outlier detection.
> - The kernel decides what shapes the boundary can take, and a linear kernel
>   cannot enclose a non-convex region.
> - `nu` bounds the fraction of training points left outside the boundary,
>   which is a parameter you can reason about directly.
> - `gamma` controls how tightly the boundary wraps, and too large a value
>   shrink-wraps individual points and breaks the `nu` guarantee.
> - A rising evaluation score can be an artefact of how you defined "novel";
>   check the training rejection rate against `nu` as an independent signal.
> - Scaling is mandatory because the RBF kernel is a function of squared
>   distance.
> - The kernel version does not scale past tens of thousands of rows; Nystroem
>   plus `SGDOneClassSVM` is the linear-time substitute.
> - Isolation Forest is the usual default not because it scores higher but
>   because its downside is bounded when you cannot tune.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Fit a one-class SVM on clean crescent-shaped data with linear and RBF
>    kernels and compare PR-AUC on new points.
> 2. Sweep `nu` over five values and verify that the fraction of rejected
>    training points tracks it.
> 3. Sweep `gamma` over five orders of magnitude, recording both PR-AUC and
>    the training rejection rate, and identify where the `nu` guarantee
>    breaks.
> 4. Define "novel" two different ways -- distance to nearest training point,
>    and membership of a held-out different distribution -- and show that the
>    best `gamma` differs between them.
> 5. Fit with and without `StandardScaler` on data with one wide-range column,
>    and report the difference.
> 6. Time `OneClassSVM` against `Nystroem` plus `SGDOneClassSVM` at 1,000,
>    10,000, and 50,000 rows.
> 7. Interview: You are asked to detect unusual network traffic and you have a
>    month of logs from a period believed to be clean. Which of the methods in
>    this section fits that description best, and what would worry you about
>    the assumption? (Hint: the phrase is "believed to be clean" -- what
>    happens to a novelty detector if that belief is wrong?)


#### Reconstruction-Based Detection

This approach reuses the dimensionality reduction of section 11.2 directly.
Fit a compression model on normal data; it learns the manifold that normal
data occupies. Then compress and reconstruct each point and measure the
**reconstruction error**. A point on the manifold reconstructs almost
perfectly; a point off it does not. The error is the anomaly score, and
computing it requires no anomaly labels.

The demonstration builds the case this method exists for. Normal data lies on
a *curved* 3-dimensional manifold inside 20 dimensions. The anomalies have the
**same per-column distributions** -- each column is independently shuffled --
so every marginal is untouched and only the relationships between columns are
destroyed. The result: **86% of the anomalies have every single `abs(z)` below
3**. No univariate rule can find these; they are anomalous only jointly.

**PCA reconstruction** is the linear version, and it performs badly here in an
instructive way. At the true intrinsic dimension of 3 it scores PR-AUC 0.044,
barely above the 2% base rate. It only reaches 1.000 at 18 of 20 components.
The reason is curvature: a flat 3-dimensional subspace does not contain a
curved 3-dimensional surface, so normal points reconstruct badly too and the
score cannot discriminate. PCA only works here by keeping enough components
that the residual captures just the two dimensions of genuinely impossible
variation.

**An autoencoder** at a bottleneck of 3 -- the true intrinsic dimension --
reaches **PR-AUC 1.000**. It can follow the curve, so normal points
reconstruct almost perfectly and anything off the manifold does not. This is
the clearest case in the chapter for preferring a non-linear model, and it is
worth contrasting with the autoencoder topic in 11.2, where the advantage was
a matter of degree. Here it is 0.044 against 1.000.

For reference, Isolation Forest scores 0.029 on the same data. It has no
notion of a manifold at all, so "inconsistent with the other columns" is not
something it can represent.

Now the requirement everyone states and few state precisely. The usual version
is "train on clean data". The demonstration shows the real rule is sharper.

**Case 1, unstructured anomalies**: contamination barely matters. Even at 30%
contamination PR-AUC stays at 1.000, because these anomalies fill all 20
dimensions and a 3-unit bottleneck cannot encode them however many it sees.
**The bottleneck is itself the protection.**

**Case 2, structured anomalies**: contamination is devastating. When the
anomalies form their own 3-dimensional manifold, PR-AUC falls from 0.976
clean, to 0.678 at 1% contamination, to 0.040 at 20% -- twice the base rate
and no more. A 3-unit bottleneck learns that second manifold happily and then
reconstructs the anomalies as well as it reconstructs normal points.

So: **contamination hurts in proportion to how learnable the anomalies are
within your bottleneck.** Scattered noise is self-protecting. Fraud rings and
coordinated abuse are exactly the structured case, and there a clean reference
set is essential.

The final advantage is operational and easy to overlook. **Reconstruction
error is attributable per feature.** The residual says *which columns* the
model could not explain -- in the demonstration, three of twenty columns carry
61% of each anomaly's error. The alert arrives with a reason attached: "these
three fields are inconsistent with the rest of this record". Isolation Forest
returns one opaque number. For anything a human has to investigate, that
difference is often worth more than a better PR-AUC.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score, roc_auc_score

torch.manual_seed(0)
rng = np.random.default_rng(199)

# --- THE IDEA: MODEL 'NORMAL', THEN MEASURE WHAT THE MODEL CANNOT EXPLAIN. ---
# Compress and reconstruct. A model fitted on normal data learns the normal
# manifold, so a point OFF that manifold reconstructs badly. The reconstruction
# error is the anomaly score, and computing it needs no anomaly labels at all.
n_in, n_out, k_true = 5000, 100, 3

def embed(u, shift=0.0):
    """20 smooth functions of 3 latent variables: a curved 3-D manifold in 20-D.
    A non-zero shift moves the latents, producing a DIFFERENT manifold."""
    u = u + shift
    return np.column_stack([
        u[:, 0], u[:, 1], u[:, 2],
        np.sin(1.5 * u[:, 0]), np.cos(1.5 * u[:, 1]), np.tanh(u[:, 2]),
        u[:, 0] * u[:, 1], u[:, 1] * u[:, 2], u[:, 0] ** 2, u[:, 2] ** 2,
        np.sin(u[:, 0] + u[:, 1]), np.cos(u[:, 1] - u[:, 2]),
        np.tanh(u[:, 0] * u[:, 2]), u[:, 1] ** 2, np.sin(2 * u[:, 2]),
        u[:, 0] - u[:, 2], u[:, 0] + u[:, 1] + u[:, 2], np.exp(u[:, 1] / 2),
        np.abs(u[:, 0]), u[:, 2] ** 3 / 3])

Xin = embed(rng.normal(0, 1, (n_in, k_true)))
# Anomalies with the SAME per-column distributions and NO joint structure:
# shuffle each column independently, which destroys every relationship while
# leaving every marginal untouched. This is the case a per-column rule cannot see.
base = embed(rng.normal(0, 1, (n_out, k_true)))
Xout = np.column_stack([base[rng.permutation(n_out), j]
                        for j in range(base.shape[1])])
X = np.vstack([Xin, Xout])
y = np.r_[np.zeros(n_in), np.ones(n_out)].astype(int)

sc = StandardScaler().fit(Xin)          # fit the scaler on NORMAL data only
Xs, Xins = sc.transform(X), sc.transform(Xin)

print(f"{len(X)} rows, {X.shape[1]} columns, {y.mean():.1%} anomalies")
print("  Normal data lies on a CURVED 3-dimensional manifold in 20 dimensions.")
print("  The anomalies have identical per-column distributions and no joint")
print("  structure at all.")
zmax = np.abs(Xs[y == 1]).max(1)
print(f"\n  per-column check: median max|z| over 20 columns = {np.median(zmax):.2f},")
print(f"  and {np.mean(zmax < 3):.0%} of anomalies have EVERY |z| below 3.")
print("  No univariate rule can find these. They are anomalous only jointly.")

# --- PCA RECONSTRUCTION ERROR: THE LINEAR VERSION. ---
print("\nPCA RECONSTRUCTION ERROR (fitted on normal data only)")
print(f"  {'components':>11s} {'variance kept':>14s} {'PR-AUC':>8s} {'ROC-AUC':>8s}")
for kk in [2, 3, 5, 8, 12, 18]:
    p = PCA(n_components=kk).fit(Xins)
    err = ((Xs - p.inverse_transform(p.transform(Xs))) ** 2).sum(1)
    print(f"  {kk:11d} {p.explained_variance_ratio_.sum():14.3f}"
          f" {average_precision_score(y, err):8.3f} {roc_auc_score(y, err):8.3f}")
print("  At the TRUE intrinsic dimension of 3, PCA scores 0.044 -- barely above")
print("  the 2% base rate. It only works at 18 of 20 components. The reason is")
print("  curvature: a flat 3-D subspace does not contain a curved 3-D surface, so")
print("  normal points reconstruct badly too and the score cannot discriminate.")

# --- THE AUTOENCODER VERSION: THE SAME IDEA, NON-LINEAR. ---
class AE(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, p, k, h=96):
        super().__init__()
        self.enc = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(p, h), nn.ReLU(),
                                 nn.Linear(h, h), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(h, k))
        self.dec = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(k, h), nn.ReLU(),
                                 nn.Linear(h, h), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(h, p))

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.dec(self.enc(x))

def train_ae(Xtrain, k, epochs=1500, lr=3e-3):
    m = AE(Xtrain.shape[1], k)
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(m.parameters(), lr=lr)
    T = torch.tensor(Xtrain, dtype=torch.float32)
    for _ in range(epochs):
        opt.zero_grad()
        ((m(T) - T) ** 2).mean().backward()
        opt.step()
    return m

def ae_error(m, Xa):
    with torch.no_grad():
        T = torch.tensor(Xa, dtype=torch.float32)
        return ((m(T) - T) ** 2).sum(1).numpy()

print("\nAUTOENCODER RECONSTRUCTION ERROR (trained on normal data only)")
print(f"  {'bottleneck':>11s} {'PR-AUC':>8s} {'ROC-AUC':>8s}")
for kk in [2, 3, 5, 8]:
    err = ae_error(train_ae(Xins, kk), Xs)
    print(f"  {kk:11d} {average_precision_score(y, err):8.3f}"
          f" {roc_auc_score(y, err):8.3f}")
print("  At a bottleneck of 3 -- the true intrinsic dimension -- the autoencoder")
print("  reaches a PR-AUC of 1.000 where PCA managed 0.044. It can follow the")
print("  curve, so normal points reconstruct almost perfectly and anything off")
print("  the manifold does not. This is the clearest case in the chapter for")
print("  preferring a non-linear model.")

# --- THE HEADLINE COMPARISON. ---
ae3 = train_ae(Xins, k_true)
ae_err = ae_error(ae3, Xs)
pca3 = PCA(n_components=k_true).fit(Xins)
pca_err = ((Xs - pca3.inverse_transform(pca3.transform(Xs))) ** 2).sum(1)
pca18 = PCA(n_components=18).fit(Xins)
pca18_err = ((Xs - pca18.inverse_transform(pca18.transform(Xs))) ** 2).sum(1)
iso = -IsolationForest(n_estimators=300, random_state=0).fit(Xins).score_samples(Xs)
print(f"\n{'method':38s} {'PR-AUC':>8s} {'ROC-AUC':>8s} {'prec@100':>9s}")
for label, s_ in [("PCA reconstruction, 3 components", pca_err),
                  ("PCA reconstruction, 18 components", pca18_err),
                  ("Autoencoder reconstruction, 3", ae_err),
                  ("IsolationForest (for reference)", iso)]:
    top = np.argsort(s_)[::-1][:int(y.sum())]
    print(f"  {label:36s} {average_precision_score(y, s_):8.3f}"
          f" {roc_auc_score(y, s_):8.3f} {y[top].mean():9.3f}")

# --- CONTAMINATION: IT MATTERS ONLY IF THE MODEL CAN LEARN THE ANOMALIES. ---
# Case 1: the anomalies are unstructured (shuffled columns), so they fill 20
# dimensions. A 3-unit bottleneck cannot represent them even if it trains on them.
print("\nCONTAMINATION, CASE 1: UNSTRUCTURED ANOMALIES")
print(f"  {'contamination':>14s} {'PR-AUC':>8s}")
for frac in [0.0, 0.05, 0.30]:
    nadd = int(frac * n_in)
    if nadd:
        b = embed(rng.normal(0, 1, (nadd, k_true)))
        extra = np.column_stack([b[rng.permutation(nadd), j]
                                 for j in range(b.shape[1])])
        Xtrain = np.vstack([Xin, extra])
    else:
        Xtrain = Xin
    s2 = StandardScaler().fit(Xtrain)
    e = ae_error(train_ae(s2.transform(Xtrain), k_true), s2.transform(X))
    print(f"  {frac:14.2f} {average_precision_score(y, e):8.3f}")
print("  Barely affected, even at 30%. The bottleneck is the protection: three")
print("  units cannot encode 20-dimensional noise, so the model cannot learn to")
print("  reconstruct these anomalies however many it sees.")

# Case 2: the anomalies are STRUCTURED -- a second, shifted manifold of the same
# low dimension. Now the bottleneck CAN represent them, and contamination bites.
print("\nCONTAMINATION, CASE 2: STRUCTURED ANOMALIES (a second manifold)")
Xout2 = embed(rng.normal(0, 1, (n_out, k_true)), shift=3.0)
X2 = np.vstack([Xin, Xout2])
print(f"  {'contamination':>14s} {'PR-AUC':>8s}")
for frac in [0.0, 0.01, 0.05, 0.20]:
    nadd = int(frac * n_in)
    Xtrain = (np.vstack([Xin, embed(rng.normal(0, 1, (nadd, k_true)), shift=3.0)])
              if nadd else Xin)
    s2 = StandardScaler().fit(Xtrain)
    e = ae_error(train_ae(s2.transform(Xtrain), k_true), s2.transform(X2))
    print(f"  {frac:14.2f} {average_precision_score(y, e):8.3f}")
print("  From 0.976 down to 0.040 -- twice the base rate and no more. These")
print("  anomalies form their own 3-D manifold, so a 3-unit bottleneck learns it")
print("  happily and then reconstructs them as well as it reconstructs normal")
print("  points. At 20% contamination they are no longer anomalous TO THE MODEL.")
print("\n  The rule is sharper than 'train on clean data': contamination hurts in")
print("  proportion to how LEARNABLE the anomalies are within your bottleneck.")
print("  Scattered noise is self-protecting; fraud rings and coordinated abuse are")
print("  exactly the structured case, and there a clean reference set is essential.")

# --- THE OPERATIONAL PAYOFF: THE ERROR IS ATTRIBUTABLE PER FEATURE. ---
with torch.no_grad():
    T = torch.tensor(Xs, dtype=torch.float32)
    resid = ((ae3(T) - T) ** 2).numpy()
print("\nRECONSTRUCTION ERROR IS ATTRIBUTABLE; A TREE SCORE IS NOT")
for i in np.argsort(ae_err)[::-1][:3]:
    cols = np.argsort(resid[i])[::-1][:4]
    print(f"  row {i:4d}  score {ae_err[i]:8.1f}  truly anomalous {bool(y[i])!s:5s}"
          f"  driven by columns {cols.tolist()}")
share = np.sort(resid[y == 1], axis=1)[:, -3:].sum(1) / resid[y == 1].sum(1)
print(f"\n  for the true anomalies, the top 3 of 20 columns carry"
      f" {share.mean():.0%} of the error")
print("  So the alert arrives with a reason attached: 'these three fields are")
print("  inconsistent with the rest of the record'. Isolation Forest returns one")
print("  opaque number. For anything a human has to investigate, attributability")
print("  is often worth more than a slightly better PR-AUC.")
```

```text
  THE IDEA

    fit a compression model on NORMAL data
                  |
    x  ->  encode -> bottleneck -> decode  ->  x_hat
                                                |
                       score = || x - x_hat ||^2

    on the manifold -> reconstructs well -> low score
    off it          -> reconstructs badly -> high score

```

|                           | PCA reconstruction | Autoencoder                        | Isolation Forest  |
| ------------------------- | ------------------ | ---------------------------------- | ----------------- |
| Captures curvature        | No                 | Yes                                | Not as a manifold |
| Needs clean training data | Yes                | Yes                                | No                |
| Attributable per feature  | Yes                | Yes                                | No                |
| Hyperparameters           | `n_components`     | Architecture, bottleneck, training | Almost none       |
| Deterministic             | Yes                | No                                 | With a fixed seed |
| Cost                      | Instant            | A training loop                    | Fast              |

> Key Takeaways
> - Fit a compression model on normal data and use reconstruction error as the
>   anomaly score; no anomaly labels are needed.
> - This is the method for anomalies that are normal in every column and
>   abnormal only in the relationships between columns.
> - PCA reconstruction is defeated by curvature: at the true intrinsic
>   dimension a flat subspace leaves normal points with large residuals too.
> - An autoencoder at the true intrinsic dimension follows the curve and
>   separates perfectly where PCA does not.
> - Contamination hurts in proportion to how learnable the anomalies are
>   within the bottleneck, not simply in proportion to how much there is.
> - Unstructured anomalies are self-protecting, because a tight bottleneck
>   cannot encode them; structured anomalies are learned and then become
>   invisible.
> - Reconstruction error decomposes per feature, so alerts carry a reason,
>   which Isolation Forest's single score cannot provide.
> - The number of components or bottleneck units is an explicit assumption
>   about how many dimensions "normal" occupies.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Generate data on a curved low-dimensional manifold, create anomalies by
>    shuffling each column independently, and confirm the marginals are
>    unchanged.
> 2. Compute PCA reconstruction error for components from 2 to `p` and plot
>    PR-AUC against the number of components.
> 3. Train an autoencoder at several bottleneck sizes and compare its PR-AUC
>    curve with PCA's.
> 4. Contaminate the training set with unstructured anomalies and then with
>    structured ones, and show the two behave completely differently.
> 5. Decompose the reconstruction error by feature for your top ten alerts and
>    report what share the top three columns carry.
> 6. Compare a reconstruction detector against Isolation Forest on data whose
>    anomalies violate only the correlation structure.
> 7. Interview: Your autoencoder-based detector worked well at launch and its
>    alert volume has quietly fallen to near zero over six months of weekly
>    retraining. What do you suspect? (Hint: what is in each week's training
>    data, and what has the model been slowly learning to reconstruct?)


#### Evaluating Anomaly Detectors

Everything in this section produces a score. Deciding which score is better is
genuinely harder than producing one, for two reasons that compound: anomalies
are rare, which breaks the usual metrics, and you normally have no labels,
which breaks the usual procedure.

Start with what rarity does. At a 0.2% base rate, a detector that flags
**nothing** achieves 99.8% accuracy. That much is widely known.

Less widely appreciated is that **ROC-AUC is nearly as misleading**. On the
demonstration's data, Isolation Forest reaches ROC-AUC 0.9634 -- which reads
as an excellent model -- while PR-AUC is 0.5480. The discrepancy is entirely
in the denominators. The false positive *rate* divides by the number of
negatives, which is enormous, so it stays tiny while the absolute count of
false alarms is large:

- to catch 52% of anomalies: FPR 0.0007, meaning 14 false alarms for 21 real
  ones
- to catch 80%: FPR 0.0222, meaning **445 false alarms for 32 real ones**
- to catch 90%: FPR 0.0807, meaning **1,613 false alarms for 36 real ones**

An FPR of 0.02 sounds negligible and is 445 alerts out of 20,000 rows. With 40
anomalies in existence, the queue is 93% noise. **Precision** divides by the
number of *alerts*, which is what the analyst experiences, so **PR-AUC is the
metric to report under imbalance.** Its baseline is the base rate itself:
0.002 here, against which 0.548 is a real achievement and 0.9634 was flattery.

That also makes ROC-AUC the worst choice for *comparing* candidates. In the
demonstration the ROC-AUC column spans 0.9634 to 0.9809 while PR-AUC spans
0.5480 to 0.7522 -- the same ranking, but ROC-AUC compresses a 37% relative
difference into a 2% one.

**Precision@k is the metric that matches operational reality.** Nobody reviews
20,000 rows; a team reviews the top `k`, and `k` is a staffing decision. The
demonstration's table -- precision 1.000 at `k=10`, 0.525 at `k=40`, 0.075 at
`k=400` -- is the conversation to have with whoever will work the alerts: "we
can send you 40 a day and about half will be real, or 100 a day and about a
quarter". No single number communicates that.

Now the harder problem: **you usually have no labels at all**, so none of the
above is computable. Four things are still available.

**1. Agreement between independent detectors.** Not correctness, but
disagreement is a reason to look harder. And read the *top-k overlap*, not the
rank correlation. In the demonstration all pairwise rank correlations exceed
0.93, which suggests broad consensus -- while the top-40 overlap reveals that
the three distance- and density-based methods agree with each other at 0.90 to
0.93 and agree with Isolation Forest at only 0.62 to 0.68. Roughly a third of
the forest's top 40 appears in nobody else's list. The methods cluster by
inductive bias, "the anomalies" is not a well-defined set, and the rank
correlations hide that completely.

**2. Synthetic anomaly injection.** Inject anomalies of a type you care about
and measure recall on those. It validates the detector against *your*
definition, which is the only one available. Recall@60 in the demonstration
goes 0.300, 0.867, 1.000 for anomalies at 1.5x, 2.5x, and 4.0x the normal
spread -- which tells you roughly how extreme a deviation must be before you
will see it. Note the honest limitation: this measures performance on the
anomalies you thought to simulate.

**3. Stability under resampling.** Refit on bootstrap samples and check the
top-k overlap; the demonstration gets 0.48 across eight refits. A detector
whose top-40 changes substantially between refits is not reporting a stable
property of the data.

**4. Label the top `k`.** This is the only thing that actually settles it.
Send the highest-scoring alerts to a human, record the verdicts, and you have
precision@k for real -- plus a labelled set that grows and eventually supports
a supervised model. Every mature anomaly system ends up here, because
unsupervised evaluation cannot close the loop on its own.

One last practical point: **anomaly detection is a ranking problem wearing a
classification costume.** The threshold is a business decision about alert
capacity and the cost of a miss, exactly as in chapter 8.4, and it should be
set from those costs rather than from a `contamination` default.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest
from sklearn.neighbors import LocalOutlierFactor
from sklearn.covariance import MinCovDet
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import (roc_auc_score, average_precision_score,
                             precision_recall_curve, roc_curve)

rng = np.random.default_rng(211)

# --- THE SETUP: EXTREME IMBALANCE, WHICH IS THE NORMAL CASE. ---
n_in, n_out, p = 20_000, 40, 15          # 0.2% anomalies
Xin = rng.normal(0, 1, (n_in, p))
Xin[:, 0] += rng.integers(0, 3, n_in) * 3.0
Xout = rng.normal(0, 1.9, (n_out, p))
Xout[:, 0] += rng.integers(0, 3, n_out) * 3.0
X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(np.vstack([Xin, Xout]))
y = np.r_[np.zeros(n_in), np.ones(n_out)].astype(int)
print(f"{len(X):,} rows, {y.sum()} anomalies, base rate {y.mean():.3%}")

# --- WHY ACCURACY IS USELESS, AND WHY ROC-AUC IS NEARLY SO. ---
scores = -IsolationForest(n_estimators=300, random_state=0).fit(X).score_samples(X)
print("\nA DETECTOR THAT FLAGS NOTHING")
print(f"  accuracy of 'always normal': {1 - y.mean():.3%}")
print(f"  it finds 0 of {y.sum()} anomalies.")
print("  Accuracy is unusable below a few percent prevalence. That part is well")
print("  known. The next part is not.")

print("\nROC-AUC LOOKS EXCELLENT WHILE THE ALERT QUEUE IS USELESS")
print(f"  ROC-AUC {roc_auc_score(y, scores):.4f}")
print(f"  PR-AUC  {average_precision_score(y, scores):.4f}")
print(f"  base rate (a random detector's PR-AUC) {y.mean():.4f}")
print("\n  The reason is the false positive RATE's denominator:")
fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y, scores)
for target in [0.5, 0.8, 0.9]:
    i = int(np.searchsorted(tpr, target))
    i = min(i, len(fpr) - 1)
    n_fp = int(fpr[i] * (len(y) - y.sum()))
    tp = int(tpr[i] * y.sum())
    prec = tp / max(tp + n_fp, 1)
    print(f"    to catch {tpr[i]:.0%} of anomalies: FPR {fpr[i]:.4f}"
          f"  ->  {n_fp:5d} false alarms for {tp:2d} real ones"
          f"  (precision {prec:.3f})")
print("  An FPR of 0.02 sounds negligible and means 400 false alarms out of")
print("  20,000 normal rows. With 40 anomalies in total, the queue is 90% noise.")
print("  ROC-AUC divides false positives by the huge negative count, so it stays")
print("  flattering. Precision divides by the number of ALERTS, which is what the")
print("  analyst experiences. Report PR-AUC under imbalance.")

# --- PRECISION@k IS THE METRIC THAT MATCHES THE OPERATIONAL REALITY. ---
# Nobody reviews 20,000 rows. They review the top k, and k is a staffing decision.
print("\nPRECISION@k: THE METRIC THAT MATCHES AN ALERT QUEUE")
order = np.argsort(scores)[::-1]
print(f"  {'k':>6s} {'precision@k':>12s} {'recall@k':>9s} {'anomalies found':>16s}")
for k in [10, 20, 40, 100, 400, 1000]:
    top = order[:k]
    print(f"  {k:6d} {y[top].mean():12.3f} {y[top].sum() / y.sum():9.3f}"
          f" {int(y[top].sum()):16d}")
print("  This table is the conversation to have with the team that will work the")
print("  alerts: 'we can send you 40 a day and about half will be real, or 100 a")
print("  day and about a quarter'. No")
print("  single-number metric communicates that.")

# --- COMPARING DETECTORS: THE RANKING DEPENDS ON THE METRIC. ---
print("\nTHE CHOICE OF METRIC CHANGES THE RANKING")
print(f"  {'method':30s} {'ROC-AUC':>8s} {'PR-AUC':>8s} {'prec@40':>8s}"
      f" {'rec@400':>8s}")
detectors = {
    "IsolationForest": scores,
    "LocalOutlierFactor (k=20)":
        -LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=20).fit(X).negative_outlier_factor_,
    "LocalOutlierFactor (k=100)":
        -LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=100).fit(X).negative_outlier_factor_,
    "Mahalanobis + MinCovDet": MinCovDet(random_state=0).fit(X).mahalanobis(X),
}
for label, sc in detectors.items():
    o = np.argsort(sc)[::-1]
    print(f"  {label:30s} {roc_auc_score(y, sc):8.4f}"
          f" {average_precision_score(y, sc):8.4f} {y[o[:40]].mean():8.3f}"
          f" {y[o[:400]].sum() / y.sum():8.3f}")
print("  Note how much tighter the ROC-AUC column is than the PR-AUC column. Under")
print("  imbalance ROC-AUC compresses real differences, so it is the worst metric")
print("  for choosing between candidates.")

# --- WITHOUT LABELS: WHAT YOU CAN AND CANNOT DO. ---
print("\nTHE USUAL SITUATION: NO LABELS AT ALL")
print("  You cannot compute any of the above. What you CAN do:")
print("\n  1. AGREEMENT between independent detectors. Not correctness, but")
print("     disagreement is a reason to look harder.")
ranks = {k: np.argsort(np.argsort(-v)) for k, v in detectors.items()}
names = list(detectors)
print(f"     {'pair':58s} {'rank corr':>10s} {'top-40 overlap':>15s}")
from scipy.stats import spearmanr
for i in range(len(names)):
    for j in range(i + 1, len(names)):
        a, b = detectors[names[i]], detectors[names[j]]
        ta = set(np.argsort(a)[::-1][:40])
        tb = set(np.argsort(b)[::-1][:40])
        print(f"     {names[i] + ' vs ' + names[j]:58s}"
              f" {spearmanr(a, b).statistic:10.3f} {len(ta & tb) / 40:15.2f}")
print("     Read the top-40 overlap column. The three distance- and density-based")
print("     methods agree with each other at 0.90 to 0.93, and all three agree")
print("     with the FOREST at only 0.62 to 0.68. The methods cluster by their")
print("     inductive bias, and roughly a third of the forest's top 40 appears in")
print("     nobody else's. 'The anomalies' is not a well-defined set, and the rank")
print("     correlations (all above 0.93) hide that completely -- always compare")
print("     the top-k sets you would actually act on, not the full ranking.")

print("\n  2. A SYNTHETIC-ANOMALY sanity check. Inject known anomalies of a type")
print("     you care about and measure recall on those. It validates the")
print("     detector against YOUR definition, which is the only one available.")
for scale in [1.5, 2.5, 4.0]:
    inj = rng.normal(0, scale, (60, p))
    inj[:, 0] += rng.integers(0, 3, 60) * 3.0
    Xa = StandardScaler().fit_transform(np.vstack([Xin, inj]))
    ya = np.r_[np.zeros(n_in), np.ones(60)].astype(int)
    s_ = -IsolationForest(n_estimators=300, random_state=0).fit(Xa).score_samples(Xa)
    o = np.argsort(s_)[::-1][:60]
    print(f"     injected anomalies at {scale}x the normal spread:"
          f" recall@60 = {ya[o].mean():.3f}")
print("     Recall degrades smoothly as anomalies get subtler, which tells you")
print("     roughly how extreme a deviation must be before you will see it.")

print("\n  3. STABILITY. Refit on bootstrap samples and check the top-k overlap.")
tops = []
for s_ in range(8):
    idx = rng.choice(len(X), len(X), replace=True)
    m = IsolationForest(n_estimators=200, random_state=s_).fit(X[idx])
    tops.append(set(np.argsort(-m.score_samples(X))[:40]))
ov = [len(tops[i] & tops[j]) / 40 for i in range(len(tops))
      for j in range(i + 1, len(tops))]
print(f"     mean pairwise top-40 overlap across 8 bootstrap refits:"
      f" {np.mean(ov):.2f}")
print("     A detector whose top-40 changes completely between refits is not")
print("     reporting a property of the data.")

print("\n  4. The only thing that actually settles it: LABEL THE TOP k. Send the")
print("     highest-scoring alerts to a human, record the verdicts, and you now")
print("     have precision@k for real -- plus a labelled set that grows over time")
print("     and eventually supports a supervised model. Every mature anomaly")
print("     system ends up here, because unsupervised evaluation cannot close.")
```

```text

    accuracy of "always normal": 99.800%, finding 0 of 40 anomalies

  ROC-AUC IS NEARLY AS MISLEADING
    ROC-AUC 0.9634        <- reads as an excellent model
    PR-AUC  0.5480
    PR-AUC of a random detector = the base rate = 0.0020

    the false positive RATE hides the false positive COUNT:

       52%    0.0007             14         21      0.600

                          spans 2%        spans 37% relative

  1. AGREEMENT -- and read the TOP-k OVERLAP, not the rank correlation

     pair                                    rank corr  top-40 overlap

     IsolationForest vs LOF (k=100)              0.964            0.68
     IsolationForest vs Mahalanobis+MCD          0.970            0.62

     the forest is a different one.

     anomalies at 4.0x the normal spread: recall@60 = 1.000

  3. STABILITY -- mean top-40 overlap across 8 bootstrap refits: 0.48

     section with a supervised model.
```

| Metric      | Baseline        | Robust to imbalance | What it tells you                                 |
| ----------- | --------------- | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| Accuracy    | `1 - base rate` | No                  | Nothing useful below a few percent prevalence     |
| ROC-AUC     | 0.5             | Barely              | Ranking quality, but flattering and compressed    |
| PR-AUC      | The base rate   | Yes                 | Ranking quality as the alert queue experiences it |
| Precision@k | The base rate   | Yes                 | What fraction of `k` alerts are real              |
| Recall@k    | 0               | Yes                 | What fraction of anomalies `k` alerts catch       |

> Key Takeaways
> - At low prevalence accuracy is meaningless, and ROC-AUC is nearly as
>   misleading because the false positive rate has an enormous denominator.
> - The same FPR that looks negligible can mean hundreds of false alarms per
>   handful of real anomalies.
> - PR-AUC is the metric to report under imbalance, and its baseline is the
>   base rate rather than 0.5.
> - ROC-AUC compresses genuine differences between candidates, making it the
>   worst choice for model selection here.
> - Precision@k and recall@k match how alerts are actually consumed and make
>   the staffing trade-off explicit.
> - Without labels, compare the top-k sets you would act on rather than rank
>   correlations, which hide substantial disagreement.
> - Synthetic anomaly injection validates a detector against your own
>   definition of anomalous, which is its strength and its limit.
> - Stability under resampling and labelling the top `k` are the remaining
>   honest checks, and only labelling closes the loop.
> - The threshold is a business decision about alert capacity and the cost of
>   a miss, not a default parameter.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. On a dataset with a 0.5% base rate, compute accuracy, ROC-AUC, and PR-AUC
>    for the same detector and explain the gap between the last two.
> 2. From the ROC curve, convert FPR into an absolute count of false alarms at
>    50%, 80%, and 95% recall.
> 3. Produce a precision@k and recall@k table for `k` from 10 to 1000 and
>    write the one-sentence summary you would give an operations team.

>    spread of each column.
> 5. Compute pairwise rank correlations and top-50 overlaps between three
>    detectors, and describe where the two measures disagree.
> 6. Inject synthetic anomalies at three severities and report recall at a
>    fixed `k` for each.
> 7. Bootstrap-refit a detector ten times and report the mean pairwise overlap
>    of the top 100.
> 8. Interview: Your anomaly detector has ROC-AUC 0.97 and the fraud team says
>    the alerts are useless. Reconcile those two statements, and say what you
>    would measure instead. (Hint: work out how many false alarms an FPR of
>    0.03 produces on a million transactions with 500 genuine frauds.)
