```text
     1024 workers -> speedup   19.64   efficiency   1.9%
    infinite workers -> speedup   20.00  (the 5% serial part)

  USL: REAL SYSTEMS GET SLOWER PAST A POINT
        1 workers -> throughput x  1.00
        2 workers -> throughput x  1.94
        4 workers -> throughput x  3.65
        8 workers -> throughput x  6.46
       16 workers -> throughput x 10.19
       32 workers -> throughput x 13.19
       64 workers -> throughput x 13.05
      128 workers -> throughput x  9.89
      256 workers -> throughput x  6.20
    peak at 32 workers (x13.19); beyond that,
    coordination costs more than the added work

  DOES THE DATA ACTUALLY NEED A CLUSTER?
    daily event extract            5.6 GB raw       1.0 GB columnar+compressed
    one year of orders            53.6 GB raw       9.7 GB columnar+compressed
    raw clickstream, 1 year     9313.2 GB raw    1676.4 GB columnar+compressed
    A 512 GB machine handles the first two in memory. Only the third
    has no single-machine answer.
```

The 5.6 GB row is the one worth staring at. Fifty million rows sounds like
"big data" in a planning meeting, and it fits comfortably in a laptop's RAM
once stored columnar. A Spark cluster processing it will very likely be
*slower* than a single-process library, because it pays for JVM startup, task
scheduling, serialisation, and shuffle on a dataset that never needed any of
them.

| | Vertical (one big machine) | Horizontal (many machines) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Programming model | Ordinary single-process code | Partitioned, failure-aware |
| Debugging | Normal tooling, real stack traces | Logs across N hosts |
| Failure domain | One; the job dies with the host | Task-level retry |
| Data ceiling | A few TB in RAM today | Effectively unbounded |
| Latency floor | Memory bandwidth | Network round trips |
| Cost at small scale | Lower | Higher (overhead dominates) |
| Cost at large scale | Superlinear, then impossible | Roughly linear |

The practical rule: **scale up until you cannot, then scale out.** Before
provisioning a cluster, load the data as Parquet, keep only the columns the
job needs, and try it on one machine with a library designed for that case.
Many "we need Spark" conclusions dissolve at that step.

> Key Takeaways
> - Vertical scaling buys a bigger machine; horizontal scaling adds machines
>   and hands you a distributed system along with them.
> - A single modern instance offers ~100 cores and terabytes of RAM, which
>   covers far more workloads than most teams assume.
> - Amdahl's law caps speedup at `1/(1-p)`: a 95% parallel job cannot exceed
>   20x however many workers you add.
> - Real throughput follows the Universal Scalability Law -- it peaks and
>   then declines, because coordination cost grows quadratically.
> - Estimate compressed columnar size, not row count, when deciding whether
>   a cluster is needed.
> - Scale out for data that exceeds one machine, for bending cost curves, or
>   for fault tolerance -- not because the row count has many digits.
> - Scale up first; measure; scale out only when the single machine is
>   genuinely the binding constraint.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compute Amdahl speedup for `p = 0.9, 0.99, 0.999` at 8, 64, and 1024
>    workers, and state the ceiling for each.
> 2. Fit the Universal Scalability Law to a throughput measurement at 1, 2,
>    4, 8, and 16 workers, then predict where the peak is.
> 3. Take a CSV you have, convert it to Parquet keeping only the columns a
>    specific query needs, and report the size ratio.
> 4. For a workload of 2 billion rows at 80 bytes per row, work out whether
>    a 768 GB single instance or a 24-node cluster is cheaper using your
>    cloud provider's current on-demand prices.
> 5. Interview: A team reports that their Spark job on 40 executors is
>    slower than the Pandas script it replaced. Give three plausible causes.
>    (Hint: think about what the framework must do before any of your code
>    runs, and what fraction of a small dataset each executor ends up with.)

#### Distributed File Systems

Once data spans machines, the first thing that must be rebuilt is the file.
A single-machine filesystem assumes one disk controller, one directory tree,
and that a write either happens or the machine is off. None of that holds
across a hundred hosts.

A distributed file system solves this by **splitting every file into large
fixed-size blocks and replicating each block onto several machines.** HDFS
made the design famous; cloud object stores such as S3, GCS, and Azure Blob
apply the same principles behind a different API. Two roles exist:

- A **metadata service** (the HDFS NameNode) knows the directory tree and,
  for each file, the ordered list of blocks and which nodes hold each copy.
  It holds no file data.
- **Data nodes** store opaque blocks and report in with heartbeats. They know
  nothing about filenames.

```text
  ONE 640 MB FILE, 128 MB BLOCKS, REPLICATION FACTOR 3

    METADATA SERVICE
      /events/2026-09-28.parquet
        block b1 -> [n1, n5, n9]      no file bytes stored here,
        block b2 -> [n2, n6, n10]     only the map from blocks to nodes
        block b3 -> [n3, n7, n11]
        block b4 -> [n1, n8, n12]
        block b5 -> [n4, n5, n10]

    RACK A            RACK B            RACK C
    n1 [b1 b4]        n5 [b1 b5]        n9  [b1]
    n2 [b2]           n6 [b2]           n10 [b2 b5]
    n3 [b3]           n7 [b3]           n11 [b3]
    n4 [b5]           n8 [b4]           n12 [b4]

    A reader asks the metadata service where b3 is, then streams it
    directly from whichever of n3, n7, n11 is closest. The metadata
    service never touches the data path.
```

Three design decisions explain most of the behaviour you will observe.

**Blocks are huge.** 128 MB is typical, against 4 KB on a local filesystem.
The reason is the seek-to-transfer ratio: a disk seek costs ~10 ms while
transferring 128 MB costs ~1 s, so a large block spends 99% of its time doing
useful sequential I/O. The consequence is the notorious **small files
problem**: a million 10 KB files consume a million metadata entries (all held
in the metadata service's memory) and spawn a million tasks that each do
almost no work. Compaction into few large files is often the single highest
-leverage fix available to a slow pipeline.

**Writes are append-only.** You can create a file and append to it; you
cannot overwrite byte 4,000,000 in place. This sounds restrictive until you
notice that it removes an entire class of distributed coordination problem,
and that analytics never needs in-place updates anyway -- it needs new
partitions. Table formats such as Delta Lake, Iceberg, and Hudi build
updates, deletes, and transactions *on top of* immutable files, by writing
new files plus a metadata log that says which files are currently live.

**Replication is placement-aware.** Three copies of a block on three machines
in the same rack survive three disk failures but not one rack's top-of-rack
switch. The standard policy places the first replica on the writer's node,
the second on a different rack, and the third on that same second rack --
buying rack-failure survival without paying for three cross-rack transfers.

The modern variant separates storage from compute entirely. Object storage
holds the data; clusters are created for a query and destroyed after it. You
lose data locality (every read crosses the network) and gain elasticity, and
the trade has proven worthwhile because network bandwidth inside a datacentre
grew far faster than disk throughput.

```python
import os, random, tempfile
import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.parquet as pq
import pyarrow.csv as pv

rng = random.Random(0)
n = 2_000_000
tbl = pa.table({
    "event_ts": pa.array([1_700_000_000 + i for i in range(n)], pa.int64()),
    "user_id":  pa.array([rng.randrange(50_000) for _ in range(n)], pa.int32()),
    "country":  pa.array([rng.choice(["IT", "DE", "FR", "ES", "PL"])
                          for _ in range(n)]),
    "amount":   pa.array([round(rng.expovariate(1 / 40), 2) for _ in range(n)]),
})

d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
csv_p, pq_p = os.path.join(d, "e.csv"), os.path.join(d, "e.parquet")
pv.write_csv(tbl, csv_p)
pq.write_table(tbl, pq_p, compression="zstd")      # columnar + compressed

MB = 1024 ** 2
print("SAME 2,000,000 ROWS, TWO STORAGE LAYOUTS")
print(f"  row-oriented CSV        {os.path.getsize(csv_p) / MB:8.1f} MB")
print(f"  columnar Parquet+zstd   {os.path.getsize(pq_p) / MB:8.1f} MB")

# A columnar layout lets a reader fetch ONE column's byte ranges and skip
# the rest of the file entirely -- the property that makes cloud object
# storage viable for analytics.
one = pq.read_table(pq_p, columns=["amount"])
md = pq.ParquetFile(pq_p).metadata
col_bytes = sum(md.row_group(g).column(3).total_compressed_size
                for g in range(md.num_row_groups))
print(f"  bytes read for SELECT amount: {col_bytes / MB:.1f} MB"
      f"  ({col_bytes / os.path.getsize(pq_p) * 100:.0f}% of the file)")
print(f"  rows returned: {one.num_rows:,}")

# --- REPLICATION: WHY THREE COPIES, AND WHY THEIR PLACEMENT MATTERS. ---
def block_survives(replicas, node_fail_p, rack_fail_p, racks_of):
    """A block is readable if at least one replica sits on a live node in a
    rack whose switch is up."""
    # sorted() keeps the draw order stable across processes
    dead_racks = {r for r in sorted(set(racks_of.values()))
                  if random.random() < rack_fail_p}
    return any(racks_of[nd] not in dead_racks and random.random() > node_fail_p
               for nd in replicas)

random.seed(7)
racks_of = {f"n{i}": f"rack{i // 4}" for i in range(12)}   # 12 nodes, 3 racks
naive = ["n0", "n1", "n2"]          # all three copies in rack0
aware = ["n0", "n4", "n5"]          # one in rack0, two in rack1
TRIALS = 200_000
for name, repl in [("all replicas in one rack", naive),
                   ("rack-aware placement", aware)]:
    lost = sum(not block_survives(repl, 0.01, 0.005, racks_of)
               for _ in range(TRIALS))
    print(f"\n  {name:26s} replicas={repl}")
    print(f"    block-loss rate {lost / TRIALS * 100:.3f}%"
          f"  over {TRIALS:,} simulated days")
```

```text
  SAME 2,000,000 ROWS, TWO STORAGE LAYOUTS
    row-oriented CSV            52.5 MB
    columnar Parquet+zstd       10.8 MB
    bytes read for SELECT amount: 3.7 MB  (34% of the file)
    rows returned: 2,000,000

    all replicas in one rack   replicas=['n0', 'n1', 'n2']
      block-loss rate 0.507%  over 200,000 simulated days

    rack-aware placement       replicas=['n0', 'n4', 'n5']
      block-loss rate 0.009%  over 200,000 simulated days
```

Identical replica count, identical hardware, a 57x difference in data loss
rate -- produced entirely by *where* the copies were put. This is the general
shape of distributed storage decisions: the redundancy level is the obvious
knob, and the failure-domain layout is the one that actually determines
durability.

> Key Takeaways
> - A distributed file system splits files into large blocks and replicates
>   each block across machines; metadata and data are handled by separate
>   services.
> - Blocks are ~128 MB so that sequential transfer dominates seek time;
>   millions of small files break both the metadata service and the task
>   scheduler.
> - Files are immutable and append-only; updates and deletes come from table
>   formats (Delta, Iceberg, Hudi) layering a metadata log over new files.
> - Replica placement across failure domains matters more than replica
>   count -- three copies in one rack is close to one copy.
> - Columnar formats let a reader fetch only the columns a query needs,
>   which is what makes remote object storage practical for analytics.
> - Separating storage from compute trades data locality for elasticity, and
>   fast datacentre networks have made that trade a good one.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write 500 tiny Parquet files and one large Parquet file with the same
>    total rows, then compare the time to read each set.
> 2. Compute how many blocks a 12 GB file occupies at block sizes of 64 MB,
>    128 MB, and 512 MB, and how many map tasks each implies.
> 3. Extend the replication simulation to replication factor 2 and 4, and
>    plot block-loss rate against factor for both placement policies.
> 4. Using a Parquet file's metadata, report per-column compressed sizes and
>    identify which column a projection should avoid reading.
> 5. Interview: Your pipeline writes 40,000 files per day into object
>    storage and downstream queries have got slower every week. Explain the
>    mechanism and the fix. (Hint: think about what a query planner must do
>    before reading any row, and what a compaction job would change.)

#### MapReduce Paradigm

MapReduce is a way of describing a computation so that a framework -- not
you -- can decide how to parallelise it, where to run each piece, and what to
do when a machine dies mid-job. It has been superseded as an *engine*, but
its shape survives in Spark, Flink, BigQuery, and every distributed SQL
planner, so it is the right thing to learn first.

The insight is that a huge share of data processing fits one template:

1. **Map**: apply a function to each record independently, emitting zero or
   more `(key, value)` pairs. Independence is the point -- any record can be
   processed on any machine, in any order.
2. **Shuffle**: group all pairs with the same key onto the same machine.
   This step is not written by the user, and it is where the time goes.
3. **Reduce**: for each key, combine its values into a result.

Because map tasks are independent and reduce tasks depend only on their own
key group, the framework gets fault tolerance almost free: if a task dies,
re-run that task. Nothing else is affected, because nothing shared was
mutated.

```text
  WORD COUNT, THREE PHASES

  INPUT SPLITS        MAP                SHUFFLE              REDUCE
  ------------        ---                -------              ------
  "the data node" -> (the,1)(data,1) --\
                     (node,1)           \   partition 0
  "the the node"  -> (the,1)(the,1) -----+> (data,[1,1])  -> data  2
                     (node,1)           /   (node,[1,1,1])-> node  3
  "data node key" -> (data,1)(node,1)--/
                     (key,1)            \   partition 1
                                         +> (the,[1,1,1])  -> the   3
                                            (key,[1])      -> key   1

  Map is embarrassingly parallel. Reduce is parallel across keys.
  The arrows in the middle are network traffic, and they are the bill.
```

The dominant cost is the shuffle, because it is the only phase that moves
data between machines. This is why MapReduce has a fourth, optional
component that every practitioner should know: the **combiner**. A combiner
is a reduce-like function applied *locally on the map output, before the
shuffle*. For word count, combining `(the,1)(the,1)(the,1)` into `(the,3)`
on the mapper cuts network traffic by orders of magnitude.

A combiner is only legal when the reduce operation is **associative and
commutative** over partial results, because the framework may apply it zero,
one, or many times, in any grouping. Sum, count, min, max qualify. Mean,
median, and distinct-count do not -- but mean can be *made* to qualify by
emitting `(sum, count)` pairs instead of values, which is a trick worth
internalising: when an aggregation resists distribution, look for a richer
intermediate value that is associative.

```python
import random
from collections import defaultdict

# --- A 25-LINE MAPREDUCE ENGINE. THE REAL ONES ADD FAULT TOLERANCE AND
# --- NETWORK TRANSFER; THE CONTROL FLOW IS EXACTLY THIS.
def map_reduce(splits, mapper, reducer, n_reducers=3, combiner=None):
    stats = {"map_out": 0, "shuffle_out": 0}
    buckets = defaultdict(list)                   # what crosses the network
    for split in splits:                          # one map task per split
        emitted = [kv for rec in split for kv in mapper(rec)]
        stats["map_out"] += len(emitted)
        if combiner:                              # pre-aggregate LOCALLY
            local = defaultdict(list)
            for k, v in emitted:
                local[k].append(v)
            emitted = [(k, combiner(k, vs)) for k, vs in local.items()]
        stats["shuffle_out"] += len(emitted)
        for k, v in emitted:
            buckets[hash(k) % n_reducers].append((k, v))   # partition by key
    out = {}
    for _, pairs in sorted(buckets.items()):      # one reduce task per bucket
        grouped = defaultdict(list)
        for k, v in sorted(pairs, key=lambda p: p[0]):     # the "sort" phase
            grouped[k].append(v)
        for k, vs in grouped.items():
            out[k] = reducer(k, vs)
    return out, stats

WORDS = ["the", "and", "data", "cluster", "shuffle", "node", "key", "spill"]
rng = random.Random(1)
weights = [0.40, 0.22, 0.14, 0.09, 0.06, 0.05, 0.03, 0.01]   # Zipf-like
lines = [" ".join(rng.choices(WORDS, weights, k=12)) for _ in range(6000)]
splits = [lines[i:i + 1000] for i in range(0, len(lines), 1000)]   # 6 splits

def mapper(line):   return [(w, 1) for w in line.split()]
def reducer(k, vs): return sum(vs)
def combiner(k, vs): return sum(vs)

plain, s1 = map_reduce(splits, mapper, reducer)
combo, s2 = map_reduce(splits, mapper, reducer, combiner=combiner)

print("WORD COUNT OVER 6 SPLITS, 72,000 WORDS")
for w in WORDS:
    print(f"  {w:8s} {plain[w]:7,}")
assert plain == combo, "a correct combiner cannot change the answer"
print("  combiner produces identical counts:", plain == combo)

print("\nWHAT CROSSES THE NETWORK")
print(f"  no combiner : map emitted {s1['map_out']:,}"
      f" -> shuffled {s1['shuffle_out']:,} pairs")
print(f"  combiner    : map emitted {s2['map_out']:,}"
      f" -> shuffled {s2['shuffle_out']:,} pairs")
print(f"  reduction   : {100 * (1 - s2['shuffle_out'] / s1['shuffle_out']):.1f}%"
      f" fewer pairs over the wire")

# --- WHEN A COMBINER IS ILLEGAL: THE REDUCE MUST BE ASSOCIATIVE AND
# --- COMMUTATIVE OVER PARTIAL RESULTS.
sales = ([("IT", round(rng.expovariate(1 / 30), 2)) for _ in range(9000)]
         + [("IT", round(rng.expovariate(1 / 300), 2)) for _ in range(200)])
# Deliberately uneven splits: the small one holds the high-value orders,
# which is what partitioning by date or region tends to produce.
uneven = [sales[0:3000], sales[3000:6000], sales[6000:9000], sales[9000:]]

amount   = lambda rec: [(rec[0], rec[1])]
mean     = lambda k, vs: sum(vs) / len(vs)
pair     = lambda rec: [(rec[0], (rec[1], 1))]      # emit (sum, count)
pair_agg = lambda k, vs: (sum(a for a, _ in vs), sum(c for _, c in vs))
pair_div = lambda k, vs: (lambda t: t[0] / t[1])(pair_agg(k, vs))

truth, _  = map_reduce(uneven, amount, mean)                  # no combiner
broken, _ = map_reduce(uneven, amount, mean, combiner=mean)   # mean of means
fixed, _  = map_reduce(uneven, pair, pair_div, combiner=pair_agg)

print(f"\nMEAN ORDER VALUE, SPLIT SIZES {[len(s) for s in uneven]}")
print(f"  no combiner (correct)     {truth['IT']:8.2f}")
print(f"  mean-of-means combiner    {broken['IT']:8.2f}"
      f"   <-- {broken['IT'] / truth['IT'] - 1:.0%} too high")
print(f"  (sum, count) combiner     {fixed['IT']:8.2f}")
print("  A mean is not associative: averaging four split means weights a")
print("  200-row split the same as a 3,000-row one. Emit (sum, count) and")
print("  the operation becomes associative, so the combiner is safe.")
```

```text
  WORD COUNT OVER 6 SPLITS, 72,000 WORDS
    the       28,638
    and       16,011
    data       9,930
    cluster    6,399
    shuffle    4,439
    node       3,576
    key        2,265
    spill        742
    combiner produces identical counts: True

  WHAT CROSSES THE NETWORK
    no combiner : map emitted 72,000 -> shuffled 72,000 pairs
    combiner    : map emitted 72,000 -> shuffled 48 pairs
    reduction   : 99.9% fewer pairs over the wire

  MEAN ORDER VALUE, SPLIT SIZES [3000, 3000, 3000, 200]
    no combiner (correct)        35.54
    mean-of-means combiner       95.77   <-- 169% too high
    (sum, count) combiner        35.54
    A mean is not associative: averaging four split means weights a
    200-row split the same as a 3,000-row one. Emit (sum, count) and
    the operation becomes associative, so the combiner is safe.
```

Two results to carry forward. The combiner cut shuffled pairs from 72,000 to
48 without changing a single count -- that is the entire argument for
pre-aggregation. And the illegal combiner produced an answer that was 169%
wrong while raising no error at all, which is the characteristic failure mode
of distributed aggregation: silently plausible numbers.

Why did MapReduce get replaced? Because every stage boundary wrote to disk.
A five-step pipeline meant five full round trips through the distributed
filesystem, which is catastrophic for iterative algorithms -- and gradient
descent, k-means, and PageRank are all iterative. Spark's central idea was to
keep intermediate results in memory between stages while preserving the same
fault-tolerance story.

> Key Takeaways
> - MapReduce expresses a computation as independent per-record `map`, a
>   framework-managed `shuffle` that groups by key, and a per-key `reduce`.
> - Independence is what buys parallelism and fault tolerance: a failed task
>   is simply re-run.
> - The shuffle is the only phase that moves data between machines, so it
>   dominates cost and is the first thing to attack.
> - Combiners pre-aggregate on the mapper and can cut shuffle volume by
>   orders of magnitude.
> - A combiner is legal only for associative, commutative reductions; a
>   mean-of-means combiner gives wrong answers silently.
> - Make a stubborn aggregation distributable by choosing a richer
>   associative intermediate, such as `(sum, count)` for a mean.
> - MapReduce's disk-per-stage design is why in-memory engines replaced it,
>   especially for iterative algorithms.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement word count with the engine above on a text file of your own
>    and confirm the combiner leaves the counts unchanged.
> 2. Write a MapReduce formulation of "average session length per country"
>    using an associative intermediate value.
> 3. Express an inverted index (term -> list of document ids) as a
>    map-reduce pair, and say what the reduce output size depends on.
> 4. Implement a distributed distinct-count as map-reduce, first exactly,
>    then approximately with a HyperLogLog sketch, and compare shuffle
>    volume.
> 5. Interview: Which of `sum`, `max`, `mean`, `median`, and
>    `count distinct` can use a combiner as written, and how would you
>    rewrite the ones that cannot? (Hint: ask whether combining two partial
>    results can be done with only those partial results in hand.)

#### Data Locality and Shuffling

Two numbers explain almost every distributed performance problem. Reading a
gigabyte from local memory takes on the order of a tenth of a second; moving
a gigabyte across a datacentre network takes several seconds; moving it over
a saturated link takes much longer. Computation is cheap and plentiful. Data
movement is neither.

**Data locality** is the strategy that follows: send the computation to the
machine that already holds the data, rather than the data to the machine
running the code. The map phase of a well-scheduled job reads almost entirely
from local disk. Schedulers express this as a preference ladder, and will
wait briefly for a better rung before settling:

| Level | Meaning | Relative cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PROCESS_LOCAL` | Data already in this executor's memory | 1x |
| `NODE_LOCAL` | On this machine's disk | ~2-5x |
| `RACK_LOCAL` | Same rack, one switch hop | ~10x |
| `ANY` | Anywhere in the cluster | ~20x+ |

Locality is achievable for map-like work. It is impossible for anything that
groups by key, because the rows sharing a key start out scattered by
construction. That operation is the **shuffle**, and understanding its
mechanics is the difference between tuning a job and guessing at it.

```text
  WHAT A SHUFFLE ACTUALLY DOES

  STAGE 1 (map side)                      STAGE 2 (reduce side)
  each task partitions its output         each task pulls its own
  by hash(key) % numPartitions,           partition file from every
  sorts it, spills it to local disk       upstream task, then merges

    task A  [p0|p1|p2|p3]  --\ \ \
    task B  [p0|p1|p2|p3]  ---+-\-\--->  task for p0 reads A.p0, B.p0,
    task C  [p0|p1|p2|p3]  ----+-+---->  C.p0, D.p0 ... and merges them
    task D  [p0|p1|p2|p3]  -----+/ /

  M map tasks x R reduce tasks = M*R transfer requests.
  At M = R = 1,000 that is a million fetches, which is why raising
  parallelism eventually makes a shuffle slower, not faster.
```

The failure mode that costs the most engineering time is **skew**. Hash
partitioning distributes keys evenly only if the keys themselves are
distributed evenly, and real keys never are: one customer is a marketplace
reselling for thousands, one `user_id` is a load-test account, and `NULL`
outnumbers every real value. A stage finishes when its *slowest* task
finishes, so a single hot partition sets the wall clock for the whole stage,
while 200 executors sit idle.

The standard remedies, in the order you should reach for them:

1. **Broadcast the small side of a join.** If one input fits in an
   executor's memory, copy it everywhere and skip the shuffle entirely.
2. **Filter and project before shuffling.** Every column and row dropped
   early is bytes not serialised, not written, not fetched, not merged.
3. **Pre-aggregate.** `reduceByKey` over `groupByKey`; partial aggregation
   before the exchange.
4. **Salt the hot key.** Append a random suffix so the hot key spreads over
   many partitions, then re-aggregate the partials in a cheap second stage.
5. **Isolate the hot keys.** Process the top few keys in a separate job with
   a different strategy, and union the results.

```python
import random
from collections import Counter
from zlib import crc32                  # stable across processes, unlike hash()

rng = random.Random(11)
N_PART = 8

# --- A REALISTIC KEY DISTRIBUTION: ONE CUSTOMER IS A MARKETPLACE. ---
keys = ([f"cust{rng.randrange(5000)}" for _ in range(400_000)]
        + ["cust0"] * 600_000)          # cust0 alone is 60% of the rows
rng.shuffle(keys)

def partition_of(key, n):
    return crc32(key.encode()) % n      # exactly what a hash partitioner does

def sizes_of(keys, n, key_fn=lambda k: k):
    c = Counter(partition_of(key_fn(k), n) for k in keys)
    return [c.get(i, 0) for i in range(n)]

def report(label, sizes):
    total, mx, mean = sum(sizes), max(sizes), sum(sizes) / len(sizes)
    print(f"  {label}")
    print("    rows per partition  "
          + " ".join(f"{s // 1000:4d}k" for s in sizes))
    print(f"    largest partition   {mx / total:.0%} of all rows,"
          f" {mx / mean:.1f}x the mean")
    # A stage ends when its SLOWEST task ends, not its average one.
    print(f"    stage wall clock    ~{mx / mean:.1f}x a balanced stage")

print(f"HASH PARTITIONING {len(keys):,} ROWS ONTO {N_PART} PARTITIONS")
report("PLAIN KEY", sizes_of(keys, N_PART))

# --- SALTING: SPLIT THE HOT KEY, THEN RE-AGGREGATE IN A SECOND STAGE. ---
SALTS = 64
salted = [(k, rng.randrange(SALTS)) for k in keys]
print(f"\nAFTER SALTING EVERY KEY WITH A RANDOM 0..{SALTS - 1} SUFFIX")
report("SALTED KEY", sizes_of(salted, N_PART,
                              key_fn=lambda t: f"{t[0]}#{t[1]}"))
print("  Stage two re-aggregates the 64 partials per key: one extra shuffle")
print("  of at most 64 rows per key, in exchange for no hot partition.")

# --- BROADCAST JOIN VS SHUFFLE JOIN: COUNT THE BYTES MOVED. ---
MB = 1024 ** 2
fact_rows, fact_row_bytes = 800_000_000, 90       # orders
dim_rows, dim_row_bytes = 5_000, 200              # customers
workers = 40

shuffle_bytes = fact_rows * fact_row_bytes + dim_rows * dim_row_bytes
broadcast_bytes = dim_rows * dim_row_bytes * workers

print(f"\nJOINING 800M ORDERS TO 5,000 CUSTOMERS ON {workers} WORKERS")
print(f"  shuffle join    {shuffle_bytes / MB:>9,.0f} MB moved"
      "   both sides re-partitioned")
print(f"  broadcast join  {broadcast_bytes / MB:>9,.1f} MB moved"
      "   small side copied per worker")
print(f"  broadcast moves {shuffle_bytes / broadcast_bytes:,.0f}x less data")
print("  It stops being viable once the small side no longer fits in one")
print("  executor's memory -- tens to low hundreds of MB in practice.")
```

```text
  HASH PARTITIONING 1,000,000 ROWS ONTO 8 PARTITIONS
    PLAIN KEY
      rows per partition    50k  649k   49k   50k   50k   50k   49k   49k
      largest partition   65% of all rows, 5.2x the mean
      stage wall clock    ~5.2x a balanced stage

  AFTER SALTING EVERY KEY WITH A RANDOM 0..63 SUFFIX
    SALTED KEY
      rows per partition   115k  125k  134k  124k  134k  124k  115k  125k
      largest partition   13% of all rows, 1.1x the mean
      stage wall clock    ~1.1x a balanced stage
    Stage two re-aggregates the 64 partials per key: one extra shuffle
    of at most 64 rows per key, in exchange for no hot partition.

  JOINING 800M ORDERS TO 5,000 CUSTOMERS ON 40 WORKERS
    shuffle join       68,666 MB moved   both sides re-partitioned
    broadcast join       38.1 MB moved   small side copied per worker
    broadcast moves 1,800x less data
    It stops being viable once the small side no longer fits in one
    executor's memory -- tens to low hundreds of MB in practice.
```

Salting turned a 5.2x straggler into a 1.1x one, and broadcasting replaced 68
GB of network traffic with 38 MB. Neither change touched the business logic.
This is characteristic: in distributed processing the large wins come from
changing how data is placed and moved, not from optimising the function
applied to each row.

> Key Takeaways
> - Computation is cheap and data movement is expensive, so schedulers send
>   code to data rather than the reverse.
> - Locality is achievable for map-style work and impossible for anything
>   that groups by key -- that is what a shuffle is.
> - A shuffle writes partitioned, sorted files on the map side and fetches
>   them on the reduce side; `M x R` tasks means `M*R` fetches.
> - Skew is the dominant shuffle pathology: a stage takes as long as its
>   slowest task, so one hot key idles the whole cluster.
> - Fix skew by broadcasting small sides, filtering early, pre-aggregating,
>   salting hot keys, or isolating them into a separate job.
> - Broadcast joins eliminate the shuffle entirely when one side fits in
>   executor memory, often a 1000x reduction in bytes moved.
> - More parallelism is not monotonically better: past a point the fetch
>   count itself becomes the bottleneck.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a key distribution where one key holds 70% of rows, hash it onto
>    16 partitions, and report the skew factor.
> 2. Apply salting with 8, 32, and 128 salts to that distribution and plot
>    the largest partition's share against salt count.
> 3. For a 2 TB fact table joined to a 40 MB dimension table across 60
>    executors, compute bytes moved under shuffle and broadcast joins.
> 4. Take any `groupByKey`-style aggregation you have written and rewrite it
>    as a pre-aggregating reduction; measure the difference in shuffled
>    bytes if your engine reports them.
> 5. Interview: One task in a 400-task stage has been running for 50 minutes
>    while the other 399 finished in 30 seconds. Walk through your
>    diagnosis. (Hint: start from what determines which rows that one task
>    received, and check the null handling in the join key.)

#### CAP Theorem and Consistency Models

The moment state is replicated across machines, a guarantee that was free on
one machine stops being free: that everyone reading the data sees the same
thing. The CAP theorem states the constraint precisely. A distributed system
can offer at most two of:

- **Consistency**: every read returns the most recent committed write.
- **Availability**: every request receives a non-error response.
- **Partition tolerance**: the system keeps working when the network drops
  messages between nodes.

The framing invites a mistake. Partitions are not a design choice -- networks
fail, switches reboot, cables get unplugged -- so `P` is mandatory, and the
theorem reduces to a single question: **when a partition happens, do you
refuse requests (CP) or serve possibly stale data (AP)?**

```text
  A 5-NODE CLUSTER, NETWORK SPLIT 3 | 2

        MAJORITY SIDE            |            MINORITY SIDE
        n1   n2   n3             X            n4   n5
                                 |
    CP  reads OK, writes OK      |     refuses: "no quorum"
        one truth preserved      |     clients there see an outage

    AP  reads OK, writes OK      |     reads OK, writes OK
        both sides accept writes and diverge; when the partition
        heals you must reconcile -- last-write-wins, vector clocks,
        or a CRDT whose merge is defined to be conflict-free
```

CAP also under-describes normal operation, because partitions are rare and
the interesting trade-off happens the other 99.9% of the time. **PACELC**
extends it: if there is a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency;
**Else**, choose Latency or Consistency. Strong consistency costs a network
round trip on every read even when nothing is broken, and that latency is
what most systems are actually trading away.

Between "always correct" and "eventually, probably" sits a spectrum:

| Model | Guarantee | Typical cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Linearizable | Reads see the latest write, globally ordered | Consensus round trip per operation |
| Sequential | All nodes see operations in the same order | Ordered log, no real-time bound |
| Causal | Related operations are seen in order; unrelated may differ | Track dependencies |
| Read-your-writes | A client sees its own writes | Pin to replica, or read from primary |
| Monotonic reads | Never see time go backwards | Sticky sessions |
| Eventual | Replicas converge if writes stop | Cheapest; staleness window |

Quorum systems give you a dial rather than a binary. With `N` replicas, a
write acknowledged by `W` of them and a read answered by `R` of them is
guaranteed to see the latest value whenever `W + R > N`, because the two sets
must overlap in at least one replica. Below that threshold, staleness is a
tunable probability.

```python
import random

N = 3                                   # replicas per key

def quorum_run(w, r, trials=200_000, lag_ms=20, read_delay_ms=5, seed=0):
    """One write acknowledged by W replicas, then a read answered by R.
    A replica that has not received the write yet returns the old value;
    we count how often a read misses the newest write entirely."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    stale = 0
    for _ in range(trials):
        acked = rng.sample(range(N), w)                  # the W that acked
        fresh = set(acked)
        for nd in range(N):                              # async replication
            # Chance a lagging replica caught up before the read arrived.
            if nd not in fresh and rng.random() < read_delay_ms / lag_ms:
                fresh.add(nd)
        contacted = rng.sample(range(N), r)
        if not (fresh & set(contacted)):                 # no fresh copy seen
            stale += 1
    return stale / trials

print(f"QUORUM BEHAVIOUR WITH N = {N} REPLICAS")
print(f"  {'W':>2} {'R':>2}  {'W+R>N':>6}  {'stale reads':>11}   profile")
for w, r, profile in [(1, 1, "fastest, eventually consistent"),
                      (1, 2, "cheap writes, one hop short"),
                      (1, 3, "slow reads, read-your-writes"),
                      (2, 2, "balanced quorum (the usual default)"),
                      (3, 1, "slow writes, fast strong reads")]:
    p = quorum_run(w, r)
    print(f"  {w:>2} {r:>2}  {str(w + r > N):>6}  {p:>10.2%}   {profile}")
print("  W + R > N guarantees the read and write sets overlap, so a strong")
print("  read cannot miss the newest value. Below that line, staleness is a")
print("  probability you tune, not a bug you fix.")
```

```text
  QUORUM BEHAVIOUR WITH N = 3 REPLICAS
     W  R   W+R>N  stale reads   profile
     1  1   False      49.86%   fastest, eventually consistent
     1  2   False      18.74%   cheap writes, one hop short
     1  3    True       0.00%   slow reads, read-your-writes
     2  2    True       0.00%   balanced quorum (the usual default)
     3  1    True       0.00%   slow writes, fast strong reads
    W + R > N guarantees the read and write sets overlap, so a strong
    read cannot miss the newest value. Below that line, staleness is a
    probability you tune, not a bug you fix.
```

For a data scientist the practical consequences are concrete. If your
feature store runs on an eventually consistent store, a feature written
milliseconds before inference may not be visible to the model that needs it,
and the training data -- built later from the same store, when everything had
converged -- will not contain that inconsistency. That is a train-serve skew
caused entirely by the storage layer, and no amount of model validation will
reveal it. Similarly, a metrics dashboard reading from an AP store during a
partition can show two different numbers to two analysts, both "correct".

Ask, for each dataset: what is the staleness window, and does my use tolerate
it? Analytics on yesterday's data tolerates seconds of staleness trivially.
A fraud check that must not authorise the same card twice does not.

> Key Takeaways
> - Partition tolerance is not optional, so CAP reduces to: during a
>   partition, refuse requests (CP) or serve stale data (AP).
> - PACELC adds the case that matters more often -- with no partition, you
>   still trade latency against consistency on every operation.
> - Consistency is a spectrum from linearizable through causal and
>   read-your-writes down to eventual, with cost falling along it.
> - With `N` replicas, `W + R > N` forces the read and write sets to
>   overlap, which is what makes a quorum read strong.
> - Below that threshold staleness is a probability, and it can be very
>   large: `W = R = 1` missed the newest write half the time here.
> - AP systems require an explicit conflict-resolution rule -- last-write
>   -wins, vector clocks, or a CRDT -- because divergence is guaranteed.
> - Eventually consistent feature stores produce train-serve skew that
>   model-level validation cannot detect; choose the model per dataset.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. For `N = 5`, list every `(W, R)` pair satisfying `W + R > N` and rank
>    them by write latency and read latency.
> 2. Extend the simulation to `N = 5` and plot stale-read rate against `R`
>    for `W = 1` and `W = 2`.
> 3. Classify these as CP or AP and justify each: a bank ledger, a shopping
>    cart, a like counter, a DNS record, a session store.
> 4. Implement a last-write-wins merge and a counter CRDT, then show a write
>    sequence where they disagree about the final value.
> 5. Interview: A recommendation service reads user features from an
>    eventually consistent store. Users report that actions they just took
>    are not reflected for a few seconds. Give two fixes at different points
>    in the stack. (Hint: one changes which replica that user's reads go to,
>    the other changes what the serving path reads at all.)

<a id="142-distributed-processing-frameworks"></a>
### 14.2 Distributed Processing Frameworks

The concepts of the previous section are delivered to you through a small set
of tools, and choosing badly between them costs more than any tuning will
recover; this section covers how Spark is put together, the three APIs it
exposes and why only two of them are worth using, what distributed machine
learning actually parallelises, the Python-native alternative that Dask
offers, and the query engines that increasingly make general-purpose
frameworks unnecessary.


#### Apache Spark Architecture

Spark exists because MapReduce wrote to disk between every stage. Its central
bet was that intermediate results could be kept in memory across stages
without giving up fault tolerance, which it achieves by remembering *how* each
dataset was computed rather than checkpointing the data itself. If a partition
is lost, Spark recomputes it from its recipe.

Four components, and the boundary between them explains most Spark
behaviour:

```text
  YOUR PROGRAM                          THE CLUSTER
  ------------                          -----------
  Driver
   - holds the SparkSession             Cluster manager
   - builds the logical plan              (YARN / Kubernetes / standalone)
   - Catalyst optimises it                allocates containers
   - splits stages into tasks                     |
   - schedules tasks, tracks them                 v
   - collects results             Executor 1   Executor 2   Executor 3
                                  [ task ]     [ task ]     [ task ]
                                  [ task ]     [ task ]     [ task ]
                                  cache slice  cache slice  cache slice

  The driver never touches data at scale -- except when you call collect(),
  which pulls every row into the driver's heap. That is the single most
  common way to kill a Spark job.
```

- The **driver** runs your code, plans the work, and schedules tasks. It is a
  single process and a single point of failure.
- **Executors** are JVM processes that run tasks and hold cached partitions.
  Each has a fixed number of slots (cores) and a memory budget.
- The **cluster manager** allocates executors. Spark does not manage machines.
- A **task** is the unit of work: one partition, one core, one stage.

Above this sits the execution model, which has three levels:

| Level | Created by | How many |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Job | One action (`collect`, `write`, `count`) | One per action |
| Stage | A shuffle boundary inside a job | One more than the shuffles |
| Task | One partition of a stage | = partition count |

The distinction that matters most is **narrow vs wide** transformations. A
narrow transformation (`filter`, `select`, `withColumn`) computes each output
partition from exactly one input partition, so it needs no data movement and
gets fused into its neighbours. A wide transformation (`groupBy`, `join`,
`distinct`, `orderBy`) needs rows from many input partitions, which forces a
shuffle and therefore a new stage. **Counting shuffles in a plan is the
fastest way to predict how expensive a job will be.**

Spark is also **lazy**: transformations only record intent. Nothing executes
until an action demands a result, which is what allows the optimiser to see
the whole pipeline at once and rearrange it -- pushing filters down to the
scan, collapsing projections, choosing a join strategy.

```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F

spark = (SparkSession.builder
         .master("local[4]")           # 4 worker threads; a cluster URL in prod
         .appName("architecture-demo")
         .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", 8)
         .getOrCreate())
spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("ERROR")

df = (spark.range(0, 2_000_000)                       # 4 input partitions
      .withColumn("country", F.element_at(
          F.array(F.lit("IT"), F.lit("DE"), F.lit("FR")),
          (F.col("id") % 3 + 1).cast("int")))
      .withColumn("amount", (F.col("id") % 97).cast("double")))

# --- NOTHING HAS RUN YET. THESE ARE ALL TRANSFORMATIONS. ---
big = df.filter(F.col("amount") > 10)                 # narrow: no data moves
agg = big.groupBy("country").agg(F.sum("amount").alias("total"),
                                 F.count("*").alias("n"))   # wide: shuffle
print("plan built, jobs run so far:", len(spark.sparkContext.statusTracker()
                                          .getJobIdsForGroup()))

print("\nPHYSICAL PLAN (read bottom-up)")
agg.explain()                                         # still no job submitted

print("\nNOW AN ACTION")
rows = agg.orderBy("country").collect()               # this submits the job
for r in rows:
    print(f"  {r['country']}  total={r['total']:>12,.0f}  n={r['n']:>9,}")
print("  partitions in:", big.rdd.getNumPartitions(),
      " partitions after shuffle:", agg.rdd.getNumPartitions())
spark.stop()
```

```text
  plan built, jobs run so far: 0

  PHYSICAL PLAN (read bottom-up)
  == Physical Plan ==
  AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false
  +- HashAggregate(keys=[country#1], functions=[sum(amount#2), count(1)])
     +- Exchange hashpartitioning(country#1, 8), ENSURE_REQUIREMENTS
        +- HashAggregate(keys=[country#1],
                         functions=[partial_sum(amount#2), partial_count(1)])
           +- Project [element_at([IT,DE,FR], ...) AS country#1,
                       cast((id#0L % 97) as double) AS amount#2]
              +- Filter (cast((id#0L % 97) as double) > 10.0)
                 +- Range (0, 2000000, step=1, splits=4)

  NOW AN ACTION
    DE  total=  31,621,616  n=  591,064
    FR  total=  31,621,548  n=  591,063
    IT  total=  31,621,630  n=  591,064
    partitions in: 4  partitions after shuffle: 1
```

Read that plan bottom-up and the whole chapter so far is visible in it.
`Range` is the scan. `Filter` was pushed as low as it can go, so rows are
discarded before anything else touches them. The first `HashAggregate`
computes `partial_sum` and `partial_count` -- that is a combiner, chosen
automatically. `Exchange` is the shuffle, and it is the only stage boundary,
so this job has two stages. The final `HashAggregate` merges the partials.

Two details in the output are worth naming. `jobs run so far: 0` after
building the whole pipeline is laziness, demonstrated. And "partitions after
shuffle: 1" despite `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions = 8` is **Adaptive Query
Execution**: at runtime Spark saw that the post-shuffle data was tiny and
coalesced eight partitions into one, avoiding eight near-empty tasks. AQE also
converts sort-merge joins to broadcast joins and splits skewed partitions when
it observes real sizes -- it is on by default, and it is the reason modern
Spark needs far less manual tuning than its reputation suggests.

> Key Takeaways
> - Spark keeps intermediate data in memory and recovers from failure by
>   recomputing partitions from their lineage, not by checkpointing data.
> - The driver plans and schedules; executors hold partitions and run tasks;
>   the cluster manager only hands out containers.
> - One action creates one job, each shuffle creates a stage boundary, and
>   each partition of a stage is one task.
> - Narrow transformations need no data movement; wide ones force a shuffle,
>   so counting shuffles predicts cost.
> - Laziness is what lets Catalyst optimise across the whole pipeline; a
>   plan is built, not executed, until an action arrives.
> - `collect()` moves all rows into the driver process and is a common cause
>   of out-of-memory failures.
> - Adaptive Query Execution re-plans at runtime -- coalescing partitions,
>   switching join strategies, splitting skewed partitions.
> - Read `explain()` bottom-up and look for `Exchange` nodes first.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a two-shuffle pipeline and confirm from `explain()` that it
>    contains two `Exchange` nodes and therefore three stages.
> 2. Classify each of `select`, `filter`, `repartition`, `join`,
>    `withColumn`, `distinct`, `orderBy` as narrow or wide.
> 3. Run the same aggregation with `spark.sql.adaptive.enabled` set to true
>    and false, and compare the post-shuffle partition counts.
> 4. Add a `filter` before and after a `groupBy` in two versions of a query,
>    then check whether the physical plans differ and explain why.
> 5. Interview: Your job fails with an out-of-memory error in the driver, not
>    the executors. Name the two most likely causes. (Hint: think about which
>    operations transfer data into the driver process, and what a broadcast
>    variable has to pass through before it reaches executors.)

#### RDDs, DataFrames, and Spark SQL

Spark offers three APIs over the same engine, and they are not
interchangeable -- one of them is dramatically slower and it is the one that
looks most like ordinary Python.

**RDDs** (Resilient Distributed Datasets) are the original abstraction: a
partitioned collection of opaque objects with functional operators (`map`,
`filter`, `reduceByKey`). Spark cannot see inside your lambdas, so it cannot
optimise anything. Every row becomes a Python object, and in PySpark every
row crosses the JVM-to-Python boundary.

**DataFrames** are a partitioned collection of rows with a *known schema*,
manipulated by declarative expressions. Because Spark understands the
expressions, two layers of machinery apply:

- **Catalyst**, the query optimiser: predicate pushdown, projection pruning,
  constant folding, join reordering, join strategy selection.
- **Tungsten**, the execution layer: off-heap binary storage that skips JVM
  object overhead, cache-aware algorithms, and whole-stage code generation
  that compiles a chain of operators into a single tight JVM loop.

**Spark SQL** is the same DataFrame engine with SQL text as the front end.
Identical plans, identical performance -- choose it wherever SQL expresses the
transformation more clearly.

The decisive consequence for a Python user: **a DataFrame expression never
leaves the JVM, while an RDD lambda or a Python UDF forces every row through
a serialisation round trip into a Python worker process.**

```text
  WHERE THE WORK HAPPENS

  DataFrame expression                Python UDF / RDD lambda
  --------------------                -----------------------
   JVM: read binary row                JVM: read binary row
   JVM: generated loop                 serialise row  ---> pickle
   JVM: write binary row               Python worker: your function
                                       serialise result <--- pickle
                                       JVM: write binary row

  Two extra serialisations and a process hop, per row.
  Pandas UDFs (vectorised, Arrow-based) pay it once per BATCH instead,
  which recovers most of the gap when a UDF is unavoidable.
```

```python
import time
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
from pyspark.sql.types import DoubleType

spark = (SparkSession.builder.master("local[4]").appName("api-layers")
         .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", 8).getOrCreate())
spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("ERROR")

N = 8_000_000
df = (spark.range(N)
      .withColumn("country", F.element_at(
          F.array(F.lit("IT"), F.lit("DE"), F.lit("FR")),
          (F.col("id") % 3 + 1).cast("int")))
      .withColumn("amount", (F.col("id") % 97).cast("double"))).cache()
df.count()                            # materialise the cache before timing

def timed(label, fn):
    t = time.perf_counter(); out = fn(); dt = time.perf_counter() - t
    print(f"  {label:34s} {dt:6.2f}s")
    return out, dt

# 1. RDD API: your Python lambdas, one object per row, no optimiser.
def rdd_way():
    return (df.rdd
            .map(lambda r: (r["country"], (r["amount"], 1)))
            .reduceByKey(lambda a, b: (a[0] + b[0], a[1] + b[1]))
            .mapValues(lambda t: t[0] / t[1])
            .collect())

# 2. DataFrame API: declarative, compiled by Catalyst to JVM bytecode.
def df_way():
    return df.groupBy("country").agg(F.avg("amount")).collect()

# 3. Spark SQL: same plan, different surface syntax.
df.createOrReplaceTempView("events")
def sql_way():
    return spark.sql("SELECT country, avg(amount) FROM events "
                     "GROUP BY country").collect()

print(f"MEAN AMOUNT PER COUNTRY OVER {N:,} ROWS")
_, t_rdd = timed("RDD map/reduceByKey", rdd_way)
_, t_df  = timed("DataFrame groupBy/agg", df_way)
_, t_sql = timed("Spark SQL", sql_way)
print(f"  DataFrame is {t_rdd / t_df:.1f}x faster than the RDD version")

# --- PYTHON UDFS BREAK THE OPTIMISER'S GRIP. ---
@F.udf(DoubleType())
def py_bucket(x):                     # runs in a Python worker, row by row
    return float(x // 10 * 10)

def udf_way():
    return df.withColumn("b", py_bucket("amount")).groupBy("b").count().collect()

def native_way():
    return (df.withColumn("b", F.floor(F.col("amount") / 10) * 10)
            .groupBy("b").count().collect())

print("\nBUCKETING THE SAME COLUMN TWO WAYS")
_, t_udf = timed("Python UDF", udf_way)
_, t_nat = timed("native Spark expression", native_way)
print(f"  the UDF costs {t_udf / t_nat:.1f}x more: every row is serialised to")
print("  a Python process and back, and Catalyst cannot see inside it")
spark.stop()
```

```text
  MEAN AMOUNT PER COUNTRY OVER 8,000,000 ROWS
    RDD map/reduceByKey                 19.00s
    DataFrame groupBy/agg                1.49s
    Spark SQL                            0.94s
    DataFrame is 12.8x faster than the RDD version

  BUCKETING THE SAME COLUMN TWO WAYS
    Python UDF                           4.89s
    native Spark expression              0.76s
    the UDF costs 6.4x more: every row is serialised to
    a Python process and back, and Catalyst cannot see inside it
```

Absolute times depend on the machine; the ratios are the lesson. Identical
logic and identical data ran an order of magnitude apart purely because of
which API expressed it.

| | RDD | DataFrame | Spark SQL |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Schema known to engine | No | Yes | Yes |
| Catalyst optimisation | None | Full | Full |
| Tungsten binary format | No | Yes | Yes |
| PySpark serialisation cost | Per row | None | None |
| Compile-time type safety | Yes (Scala) | No | No |
| Right choice when | Truly unstructured data, custom partitioners | Almost always | Logic reads better as SQL |

When a UDF is genuinely necessary -- a library call, a model prediction, a
parser -- reach for a **pandas UDF** rather than a scalar Python UDF. It
receives an Arrow batch as a `pandas.Series`, so the serialisation cost is
paid once per batch of thousands of rows instead of once per row, and
vectorised NumPy code runs over the whole batch.

> Key Takeaways
> - RDDs hold opaque objects and defeat the optimiser; DataFrames carry a
>   schema the engine can reason about.
> - Catalyst rewrites plans (pushdown, pruning, join selection) and Tungsten
>   executes them on off-heap binary data with generated code.
> - Spark SQL and the DataFrame API compile to the same plans, so the choice
>   is purely about readability.
> - In PySpark, every RDD lambda and scalar UDF serialises each row into a
>   Python process and back.
> - Measured here: DataFrame 12.8x faster than the equivalent RDD job, and a
>   native expression 6.4x faster than the same logic in a UDF.
> - Use pandas (Arrow) UDFs when a UDF is unavoidable -- the cost becomes
>   per batch rather than per row.
> - Reach for RDDs only for genuinely unstructured data or custom
>   partitioning logic.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Rewrite a scalar Python UDF as a native Spark expression and measure
>    both on at least 5 million rows.
> 2. Convert the same UDF into a pandas UDF and compare all three timings.
> 3. Write one aggregation in the DataFrame API and the same one in Spark
>    SQL, then diff their physical plans.
> 4. Take an RDD job using `groupByKey` and rewrite it with `reduceByKey`,
>    explaining which one shuffles less and why.
> 5. Interview: A colleague says "we use RDDs because we need custom logic
>    per row". What do you ask, and what alternatives do you propose?
>    (Hint: separate the logic that must be Python from the logic that is
>    really an expression, and consider where the batch boundary could go.)

#### Distributed Machine Learning Libraries

"Distributed machine learning" conflates two entirely different problems, and
naming which one you have determines every tool choice that follows.

**Data parallelism**: the model fits on one machine, the data does not. Each
worker holds a slice of the data, computes gradients or statistics on it, and
the partial results are aggregated. This is the common case in tabular data
science, and it is what Spark MLlib does.

**Model parallelism**: the model itself does not fit on one machine, so its
layers or parameters are split across devices. This is a deep learning
concern -- large transformers -- and it lives in the frameworks covered in
Chapter 12, not here.

```text
  DATA PARALLEL (one model, many data slices)

    slice 1 --> [full model copy] --> partial gradient --\
    slice 2 --> [full model copy] --> partial gradient ---+-> average
    slice 3 --> [full model copy] --> partial gradient --/     |
                                                              v
                       every copy updated with the same new parameters

  MODEL PARALLEL (one data batch, model split across devices)

    batch --> [layers 1-8 on GPU0] --> [layers 9-16 on GPU1] --> output
              activations cross the device boundary every step
```

Spark MLlib provides the data-parallel case with an API deliberately shaped
like scikit-learn's: `Transformer` (has `transform`), `Estimator` (has `fit`,
returns a Transformer), and `Pipeline` (a sequence of stages, itself an
Estimator). The reason to care about the Pipeline abstraction is not
tidiness -- it is that **the fitted pipeline contains the fitted
preprocessing**, so the exact category-to-index mapping learned at training
time is applied at serving time. Hand-rolled preprocessing is the single
largest source of train-serve skew, and pipelines are the structural fix.

```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
from pyspark.ml import Pipeline
from pyspark.ml.feature import StringIndexer, OneHotEncoder, VectorAssembler
from pyspark.ml.classification import LogisticRegression
from pyspark.ml.evaluation import BinaryClassificationEvaluator

spark = (SparkSession.builder.master("local[4]").appName("mllib")
         .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", 8).getOrCreate())
spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("ERROR")

N = 500_000
df = (spark.range(N)
      .withColumn("country", F.element_at(
          F.array(F.lit("IT"), F.lit("DE"), F.lit("FR")),
          (F.col("id") % 3 + 1).cast("int")))
      .withColumn("tenure", (F.col("id") % 60).cast("double"))
      .withColumn("spend", (F.rand(7) * 500))
      # Churn is driven by short tenure, with noise on top.
      .withColumn("label", (F.when(F.col("tenure") < 6, F.rand(1) * 0.6 + 0.3)
                            .otherwise(F.rand(2) * 0.4) > 0.5).cast("int")))

train, test = df.randomSplit([0.8, 0.2], seed=42)

pipe = Pipeline(stages=[
    StringIndexer(inputCol="country", outputCol="country_ix"),
    OneHotEncoder(inputCols=["country_ix"], outputCols=["country_oh"]),
    # MLlib estimators take ONE vector column, never a list of columns.
    VectorAssembler(inputCols=["tenure", "spend", "country_oh"],
                    outputCol="features"),
    LogisticRegression(maxIter=20, regParam=0.01),
])

model = pipe.fit(train)          # each stage fitted in order, distributed
pred = model.transform(test)     # the SAME fitted mappings are reapplied
auc = BinaryClassificationEvaluator(metricName="areaUnderROC").evaluate(pred)
lr = model.stages[-1]
print(f"rows train / test: {train.count():,} / {test.count():,}")
print(f"AUC {auc:.4f}")
print("coefficients:", "  ".join(f"{c:+.4f}" for c in lr.coefficients))
print("iterations run:", lr.summary.totalIterations)
print("objective history (first 5):",
      [round(v, 4) for v in lr.summary.objectiveHistory[:5]])
spark.stop()
```

```text
  rows train / test: 400,052 / 99,948
  AUC 0.9827
  coefficients: -0.1290  +0.0000  +0.2141  +0.0847
  iterations run: 11
  objective history (first 5): [0.244, 0.1793, 0.1654, 0.1551, 0.1524]
```

The `objectiveHistory` is worth noticing: every one of those 11 iterations
was a full pass over 400,000 rows, with a gradient aggregation -- a
shuffle-like reduction -- at each step. That is why iterative algorithms were
the workload that justified Spark's in-memory design, and why caching the
training set before `fit` is not optional.

The distributed ML landscape, and when each is the right answer:

| Tool | Parallelism | Use when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Spark MLlib | Data | Data already in Spark; standard models suffice |
| XGBoost / LightGBM (distributed) | Data | Gradient boosting on data exceeding one machine |
| Dask-ML | Data | Python-native stack; scikit-learn compatibility matters |
| Ray Train / Tune | Data + tasks | Heterogeneous workloads, RL, large-scale HPO |
| PyTorch DDP / FSDP | Data / model | Deep learning on multiple GPUs |
| scikit-learn on one machine | None | The data fits -- which is most of the time |

That last row is the one most often skipped. MLlib's model catalogue is
narrower than scikit-learn's, its hyperparameter tuning is coarser, and it
carries per-iteration coordination overhead. A very common and very effective
pattern is: **aggregate and sample at scale in Spark, then train on one
machine.** Ten million rows of raw events often reduce to 200,000 feature
rows, and 200,000 rows belong in scikit-learn, LightGBM, or CatBoost -- where
you get better models, faster iteration, and real debugging.

There is also a third kind of parallelism that is easy to forget and cheap to
exploit: **embarrassingly parallel model fitting.** Training one model per
store, per region, or per SKU is thousands of independent small fits, not one
distributed fit. Distribute the *tasks*, not the algorithm -- a
`groupBy(...).applyInPandas(...)` in Spark, or `dask.delayed`, does this with
no distributed-training machinery at all.

> Key Takeaways
> - Distinguish data parallelism (model fits, data does not) from model
>   parallelism (the model itself does not fit); tabular work is almost
>   always the former.
> - Spark MLlib is data-parallel, with a scikit-learn-shaped
>   Transformer/Estimator/Pipeline API.
> - Pipelines matter because the fitted preprocessing travels with the fitted
>   model, which structurally prevents a major class of train-serve skew.
> - MLlib estimators consume a single assembled vector column, not a list of
>   feature columns.
> - Iterative training does a full distributed pass per iteration, so cache
>   the training set before fitting.
> - Aggregating in Spark and then training on one machine is usually the
>   better pipeline; the feature table is far smaller than the event log.
> - Many-small-models problems are task-parallel, not data-parallel; use
>   grouped pandas application or delayed tasks instead.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build an MLlib pipeline with an indexer, encoder, assembler, and
>    classifier, and verify that a category unseen in training is handled at
>    transform time.
> 2. Fit the same model on a sample small enough for scikit-learn and compare
>    AUC and wall-clock time against the MLlib run.
> 3. Use `groupBy(...).applyInPandas(...)` to fit one model per group and
>    return a row of coefficients per group.
> 4. Time an MLlib fit with and without caching the training DataFrame, and
>    explain the gap using the iteration count.
> 5. Interview: You need a model per country for 180 countries, each with up
>    to 2 million rows. Data-parallel or task-parallel, and how would you
>    implement it? (Hint: ask whether any single country's data exceeds one
>    machine, and what that answer implies about which axis to distribute.)

#### Dask and Parallel Python

Dask answers a question Spark does not: what if you want to scale out while
staying inside the Python scientific stack? Spark is a JVM engine you talk to
across a boundary. Dask is Python all the way down, which changes what is
convenient and what is possible.

Its abstractions mirror the libraries you already use:

- `dask.dataframe` -- many pandas DataFrames, partitioned along the index.
- `dask.array` -- many NumPy arrays, in a blocked grid.
- `dask.bag` -- a parallel sequence for semi-structured data.
- `dask.delayed` -- wrap any function call as a lazy graph node. This is the
  escape hatch that makes arbitrary Python parallelisable.

Under all of them is one mechanism: **a task graph**, a directed acyclic
graph of Python callables and their dependencies, executed by a scheduler
that respects the edges. Because the graph is an ordinary Python data
structure, you can inspect it, which is a genuine pedagogical advantage over
Spark's opaque JVM plans.

```text
  A DASK DATAFRAME IS A ROW-WISE STACK OF PANDAS DATAFRAMES

    partition 0   day=00   [ pandas DataFrame ]  --\
    partition 1   day=01   [ pandas DataFrame ]  ---\
    partition 2   day=02   [ pandas DataFrame ]  ----+-- groupby.agg
    ...                                             /   (tree reduction)
    partition 11  day=11   [ pandas DataFrame ]  --/

  Any operation along the partition axis (groupby on a non-index column,
  set_index, merge on a non-index column) requires a shuffle, exactly as
  in Spark. Everything else is per-partition pandas.
```

```python
import os, tempfile, time
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import dask.dataframe as dd
from dask.distributed import Client

# --- 12 PARQUET PART FILES: THE UNIT OF PARALLELISM IS THE PARTITION. ---
d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
for i in range(12):
    n = 500_000
    pd.DataFrame({
        "day": np.full(n, i),
        "country": rng.choice(["IT", "DE", "FR", "ES"], n),
        "amount": rng.exponential(40, n).round(2),
    }).to_parquet(os.path.join(d, f"part-{i:02d}.parquet"), index=False)
print("files:", len(os.listdir(d)), " total rows: 6,000,000")

# processes=True in production; threads keep this example self-contained.
client = Client(n_workers=4, threads_per_worker=1, processes=False,
                dashboard_address=None)

ddf = dd.read_parquet(d)                       # lazy: reads only the schema
print("partitions:", ddf.npartitions, " columns:", list(ddf.columns))

res = (ddf[ddf.amount > 5]
       .groupby("country")
       .amount.agg(["mean", "count"]))         # still lazy, a task graph
t = time.perf_counter()
out = res.compute()                            # now it runs
print(f"\ncomputed in {time.perf_counter() - t:.2f}s")
print(out.sort_index().round(3).to_string())

# Column projection is pushed into the Parquet reader.
small = dd.read_parquet(d, columns=["country", "amount"])
print("\ncolumns actually read:", list(small.columns))

# --- THE GRAPH IS DATA YOU CAN INSPECT. ---
print("\ntasks in the graph for the aggregation:",
      len(dict(res.optimize().dask)))

# --- map_partitions RUNS ORDINARY PANDAS/NUMPY CODE PER PARTITION. ---
def p95_per_partition(pdf):
    """Receives a real pandas DataFrame -- any library that works on one
    partition works here, which is Dask's main advantage over Spark for
    Python-native code."""
    return pd.DataFrame({"day": [pdf["day"].iloc[0]],
                         "p95": [pdf["amount"].quantile(0.95)]})

meta = pd.DataFrame({"day": pd.Series(dtype="int64"),
                     "p95": pd.Series(dtype="float64")})
per_day = ddf.map_partitions(p95_per_partition, meta=meta).compute()
print(per_day.head(4).round(2).to_string(index=False))
client.close()
```

```text
  files: 12  total rows: 6,000,000
  partitions: 12  columns: ['day', 'country', 'amount']

  computed in 0.62s
             mean    count
  country
  DE       44.983  1323973
  ES       44.970  1323355
  FR       45.027  1323516
  IT       45.006  1324046

  columns actually read: ['country', 'amount']

  tasks in the graph for the aggregation: 15
   day    p95
     0 119.83
     1 119.73
     2 119.86
     3 120.19
```

Two Dask-specific traps are worth stating plainly.

**`meta` is mandatory and easy to get wrong.** Dask must know the output
schema before running anything, so `map_partitions` takes an empty frame
describing the result. Get its dtypes wrong and you get a confusing failure
deep in execution, or silently wrong dtypes.

**Partition size is your responsibility.** Dask does not choose it for you.
Aim for roughly 100 MB of in-memory data per partition: too large and workers
die of memory exhaustion, too small and scheduler overhead dominates. A
common symptom of a badly partitioned Dask job is workers being killed and
restarted in a loop.

| | Dask | Spark |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Language | Python | JVM (Scala/Java), Python via a bridge |
| API | Mirrors pandas/NumPy | Its own DataFrame API + SQL |
| Arbitrary Python cost | Native, free | Serialisation per row or per batch |
| Query optimiser | Limited (column/predicate pushdown) | Catalyst, mature |
| SQL support | Via add-ons | First-class |
| Scale sweet spot | One machine to ~100 nodes | Tens to thousands of nodes |
| Ecosystem maturity at scale | Younger | Extremely battle-tested |
| Best for | NumPy/pandas/scikit-learn workloads, custom algorithms | Large ETL, SQL, mixed-language teams |

The honest summary: if your workload is SQL-shaped ETL over very large
tables, Spark. If it is Python-shaped -- array mathematics, scikit-learn,
custom per-group logic -- Dask, and you keep your debugger. And if the data
fits in memory on one machine, neither: pandas or Polars will beat both.

> Key Takeaways
> - Dask scales the Python scientific stack by partitioning into many pandas
>   DataFrames or NumPy blocks.
> - Everything compiles to a task graph of Python callables, which is an
>   inspectable data structure.
> - `dask.delayed` parallelises arbitrary Python functions, which is the
>   escape hatch Spark lacks.
> - Operations that cross the partition axis (non-index groupby, set_index,
>   non-index merge) shuffle, just as in Spark.
> - `meta` must describe the output schema of `map_partitions` correctly, or
>   failures appear far from the cause.
> - Choose partition sizes yourself, around 100 MB in memory; repeated worker
>   restarts usually mean partitions are too large.
> - Spark for SQL-shaped ETL at large scale, Dask for Python-shaped
>   computation, and neither when one machine will do.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a dataset as 4, 12, and 200 Parquet files, then compare Dask
>    aggregation time across the three partition counts.
> 2. Use `map_partitions` to compute a per-partition statistic, deliberately
>    supply a wrong `meta` dtype, and observe how the error surfaces.
> 3. Parallelise a loop of independent model fits with `dask.delayed` and
>    confirm the graph has one node per fit.
> 4. Compare `ddf.groupby("col").mean()` on an index column versus a
>    non-index column and explain the runtime difference.
> 5. Interview: A Dask job repeatedly kills and restarts its workers with
>    memory warnings, though the dataset is only 30 GB across 40 workers.
>    What do you check first? (Hint: total size is not the quantity that has
>    to fit anywhere -- ask what a single task holds at once.)

#### Query Engines for Large Data

For a large share of analytics, a general-purpose distributed framework is
the wrong tool, because the workload is a SQL query and there are engines
built for nothing else. They have absorbed decades of database research, and
they routinely beat hand-written Spark jobs on the queries they cover.

Three architectural families:

**Embedded vectorised engines** (DuckDB, Polars) run in your process, use all
cores, and process data in cache-sized column batches. No cluster, no
scheduler, no network. On a modern machine they handle hundreds of gigabytes
of Parquet, and their startup cost is milliseconds. This category has
reclaimed most of the range where Spark used to be the reflex.

**Distributed MPP query engines** (Trino, Presto, Spark SQL, Dremio) split a
SQL query across nodes that read from object storage. They exist for data
genuinely beyond one machine and for federating across sources, and their
central value is that they decouple storage from compute.

**Cloud data warehouses** (BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift) are managed MPP
engines with storage, metadata, and scaling handled for you. You trade
control and per-query cost for the absence of operational work.

Whichever family, the same three optimisations determine whether a query
takes seconds or hours:

1. **Projection pruning** -- read only the columns the query mentions. Free
   with columnar formats; impossible with CSV or JSON.
2. **Partition pruning** -- skip whole directories using predicates on
   partition columns. This is why `WHERE day = '2026-09-28'` on a
   day-partitioned table is fast and `WHERE amount > 5` is not.
3. **Predicate pushdown with statistics** -- inside a Parquet file, every row
   group stores per-column min/max, so a row group whose range cannot satisfy
   the predicate is skipped without decompression.

```python
import os, time, tempfile
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, duckdb

# --- HIVE-STYLE PARTITIONED LAYOUT: THE DIRECTORY NAME IS AN INDEX. ---
root = tempfile.mkdtemp()
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
for day in range(1, 13):
    p = os.path.join(root, f"day={day:02d}")      # the partition column
    os.makedirs(p)
    n = 400_000
    pd.DataFrame({
        "country": rng.choice(["IT", "DE", "FR", "ES"], n),
        "amount": rng.exponential(40, n).round(2),
        "user_id": rng.integers(0, 200_000, n),
    }).to_parquet(os.path.join(p, "data.parquet"), index=False)

total_mb = sum(os.path.getsize(os.path.join(dp, f))
               for dp, _, fs in os.walk(root) for f in fs) / 1024 ** 2
print(f"dataset: 12 day-partitions, 4,800,000 rows, {total_mb:.1f} MB on disk")

con = duckdb.connect()                            # in-process, no server
glob = f"'{root}/**/*.parquet'"

def timed(label, sql):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = con.sql(sql).fetchall()
    print(f"  {label:38s} {time.perf_counter() - t:6.3f}s  -> {out[0]}")

print("\nSAME QUESTION, THREE AMOUNTS OF WORK")
timed("scan every column, every partition",
      f"SELECT count(*), sum(amount), sum(user_id) "
      f"FROM read_parquet({glob}, hive_partitioning=true)")
timed("project: only the column needed",
      f"SELECT count(*), sum(amount) "
      f"FROM read_parquet({glob}, hive_partitioning=true)")
timed("project + partition prune (day=03)",
      f"SELECT count(*), sum(amount) "
      f"FROM read_parquet({glob}, hive_partitioning=true) WHERE day='03'")

print("\nWHAT THE PLANNER DID WITH THE PARTITION FILTER")
plan = con.sql(f"EXPLAIN SELECT sum(amount) FROM read_parquet({glob},"
               f" hive_partitioning=true) WHERE day='03'").fetchall()[0][1]
for line in plan.splitlines():
    if any(k in line for k in ("File Filters", "Scan", "Projection",
                               "Filters", "Total Files Read")):
        print("   ", line.strip())
con.close()
```

```text
  dataset: 12 day-partitions, 4,800,000 rows, 33.0 MB on disk

  SAME QUESTION, THREE AMOUNTS OF WORK
    scan every column, every partition      0.074s
      -> (4800000, 192048740.59999803, 480062630010)
    project: only the column needed         0.013s
      -> (4800000, 192048740.59999803)
    project + partition prune (day=03)      0.006s
      -> (400000, 15986678.359999856)

  WHAT THE PLANNER DID WITH THE PARTITION FILTER
      │    Projections: amount    │
      │       File Filters:       │
      │    Scanning Files: 1/12   │
```

`Scanning Files: 1/12` is the whole topic in one line. The engine never
opened the other eleven files, because the directory name told it they could
not contain matching rows. Dropping one unused column gave 5.7x, and pruning
eleven of twelve partitions gave a further 2.2x on top -- 12x in total, from
the *physical layout of the data* rather than from anything in the query. It
scales with the partition count: on a three-year day-partitioned table, a
one-day query touches roughly 1/1,000 of the files.

This also explains the most consequential modelling decision in an analytics
store: **partition by the column your queries filter on**, almost always a
date, and avoid partitioning by anything high-cardinality (a `user_id`
partition column produces millions of tiny files and the small-files problem
of the previous section).

| Engine family | Deploy | Sweet spot | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DuckDB / Polars | In your process | Up to hundreds of GB Parquet | Single machine's RAM and cores |
| Trino / Presto | Cluster you run | Multi-TB, federated sources | Operations, no built-in storage |
| Spark SQL | Cluster you run | ETL plus ML in one system | Startup cost, tuning surface |
| BigQuery / Snowflake | Managed | Elastic, zero ops | Per-query or per-credit cost |

The decision procedure is short: does one machine's RAM and core count cover
the query after projection and partition pruning? If yes, use an embedded
engine and skip the cluster entirely. If no, or if the data must stay in
object storage while many teams query it, use a distributed engine.

> Key Takeaways
> - Most analytics workloads are SQL, and dedicated query engines beat
>   general frameworks on them.
> - Embedded vectorised engines (DuckDB, Polars) handle hundreds of GB of
>   Parquet in-process, with millisecond startup.
> - Distributed MPP engines exist for data beyond one machine and for
>   federating across sources, decoupling storage from compute.
> - Projection pruning, partition pruning, and row-group statistics decide
>   query cost far more than engine choice does.
> - Partition on the column queries filter on -- usually a date -- and never
>   on a high-cardinality column.
> - `Scanning Files: 1/12` in a plan is the evidence that pruning worked;
>   learn to look for the equivalent line in your engine.
> - Check whether one machine suffices after pruning before reaching for a
>   cluster.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write the same dataset partitioned by day and unpartitioned, then time
>    a single-day query against both.
> 2. Run `EXPLAIN` on a filtered query and identify which files or row groups
>    the engine decided to skip.
> 3. Partition a dataset by a high-cardinality column, count the files
>    produced, and measure the effect on a full-table scan.
> 4. Compare DuckDB against Spark SQL on the same 5 GB Parquet aggregation,
>    including process startup time in both measurements.
> 5. Interview: A dashboard query over a day-partitioned table filters on
>    `event_timestamp` rather than the `day` partition column and is slow.
>    What is happening and how do you fix it? (Hint: the engine prunes on the
>    partition column only, so ask whether the filter can be expressed in
>    terms the directory layout exposes.)

<a id="143-streaming-data"></a>
### 14.3 Streaming Data

Batch processing asks a question of a finite dataset; streaming asks a
standing question of data that never ends, and that difference reshapes
correctness rather than just performance; this section covers what changes when
the input is unbounded, why the timestamp on a record matters more than the
clock on the server, how to cut an endless stream into windows you can
aggregate, the log systems that carry the events, and how to compute features
online without teaching your model about the future.


#### Stream Processing Concepts

In batch processing the dataset is finite and available, so a computation runs
once and produces one answer. In stream processing the input never ends, which
means there is no moment at which the answer is final. A streaming computation
produces a *sequence* of answers, each correct as of the records it has seen.

That single change has consequences that are not about speed at all:

| | Batch | Stream |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Input | Bounded, complete | Unbounded, arriving |
| Completeness | Known | Never; you decide when to stop waiting |
| State | Held for the job's duration | Held indefinitely, must be bounded |
| Failure recovery | Re-run the job | Resume from a checkpoint and offset |
| "Correct" result | One | One per moment, all correct |
| Reprocessing | Trivial | Requires replayable input |

The vocabulary is small and worth fixing precisely:
