<a id="15-productionizing-models-and-mlops"></a>
## 15. Productionizing Models and MLOps

A model that exists only in a notebook has produced no value: it has produced
a claim about value. This chapter covers the machinery that turns a trained
artifact into a system other people depend on -- how predictions reach their
consumers, what infrastructure keeps training reproducible and deployment
repeatable, how you detect that a model has quietly stopped working, and what
practices keep a team's code and models reviewable years later. The recurring
theme is that machine learning code is a small part of a production ML
system, and almost every expensive failure happens in the rest of it.

<a id="151-model-deployment"></a>
### 15.1 Model Deployment

Deployment is the step where a model stops being a file and starts being a
dependency; this section covers when predictions should be precomputed versus
computed on request, how to package a model so it loads correctly somewhere
else, the two dominant serving protocols, the container and orchestration
layer underneath them, what changes when the target is a phone rather than a
server, and how to make an inference call fast enough to be usable.


#### Batch vs Real-Time Inference

Before any serving technology is chosen, one question settles most of the
architecture: **when is the prediction needed, relative to when the input
data becomes available?**

If a marketing team needs churn scores for every customer by 09:00 each
morning, nothing is gained by computing them on demand. Score everyone
overnight, write the results to a table, and let consumers read the table.
This is **batch inference**: predictions are precomputed on a schedule, stored
as data, and looked up. The model is not in the request path at all, so
serving a score is a key lookup in a database -- the most reliable operation
in the whole system.

If a payment must be approved or declined before the page returns, no
precomputed table can help, because the transaction being judged did not
exist when the batch job ran. This is **real-time** (or online) inference: a
request arrives, features are gathered, the model runs, and a response goes
back within a latency budget measured in milliseconds.

The useful analogy is a kitchen. Batch inference is meal prep: cook a hundred
portions on Sunday, refrigerate, reheat on demand. It is enormously efficient
per portion, and everything you serve is as fresh as Sunday. Real-time
inference is cooking to order: slower and costlier per plate, and the only
way to serve a dish that depends on what the customer just said.

Between them sit two hybrids worth knowing by name. **Streaming inference**
scores each event as it arrives on a message log, writing results back to a
store -- continuous like real-time, but not in anyone's request path.
**Near-line** or micro-batch inference runs the batch job every few minutes
instead of nightly, which is often all the freshness a problem actually needs
and is dramatically simpler than a serving stack.

| Property | Batch | Real-time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Trigger | Schedule | Request |
| Latency budget | Minutes to hours | Milliseconds |
| Input availability | Must exist before the run | Arrives with the request |
| Throughput efficiency | Very high (vectorised) | Low (per-call overhead) |
| Failure impact | Stale scores, retry later | User-visible error |
| Rollback | Rerun the job | Redeploy the service |
| Feature engineering | Same code as training | Must be re-implemented or shared |
| Typical uses | Churn lists, recommendations, risk segments | Fraud, ranking, pricing, ads |

The last row of that table is where teams get hurt. In batch, training and
scoring can run the same code over the same warehouse tables, so the features
are identical by construction. In real-time, the serving path usually
recomputes features from a different source under a latency budget, and any
discrepancy between the two implementations is **training-serving skew** --
the single most common cause of a model that validated well and performs
badly in production.

Three numbers drive the decision, and all three can be estimated before any
code is written: how fast the inputs change, how many of the predictions are
ever read, and how expensive one prediction is.

```python
import time
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
N, D = 1_000_000, 24
X = rng.normal(size=(N, D)).astype(np.float32)
w = rng.normal(size=D).astype(np.float32)

def score(rows):
    return 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-(rows @ w)))       # logistic model, any size

# --- THROUGHPUT: THE SAME MODEL, TWO ACCESS PATTERNS. ---
t0 = time.perf_counter()
score(X)                                            # one vectorised call
batch_s = time.perf_counter() - t0

t0 = time.perf_counter()
for i in range(20_000):
    score(X[i:i + 1])                               # one row per call, as an
one_s = (time.perf_counter() - t0) / 20_000         # online server sees it

print("THROUGHPUT OF ONE LOGISTIC MODEL, TWO ACCESS PATTERNS")
print(f"  batch   {N:,} rows in {batch_s:6.2f} s"
      f"  -> {N / batch_s / 1e6:6.2f} M rows/s")
print(f"  online  1 row per call, mean {one_s * 1e6:6.1f} us"
      f"  -> {1 / one_s / 1e6:6.2f} M rows/s")
print(f"  per-row cost of serving one at a time: {one_s / (batch_s / N):5.1f}x")
print("  The arithmetic is identical; the overhead is per-call, not per-row.")

# --- FRESHNESS: WHAT A NIGHTLY SCORE COSTS IN CORRECTNESS. ---
# Each user's state changes at random times (a new session, a cancelled card,
# a support ticket). A 00:00 batch score is valid only until the next change.
print("\nP(SCORE ALREADY STALE) BY CHANGE RATE AND HOUR OF REQUEST")
print("  changes/user/day      06:00     12:00     18:00     23:00")
for lam in (0.05, 0.5, 2.0, 20.0):
    row = [1 - np.exp(-lam * h / 24) for h in (6, 12, 18, 23)]
    print(f"  {lam:16.2f}" + "".join(f"{p:10.1%}" for p in row))
print("  Slow-moving features tolerate batch. Fast-moving ones do not, and")
print("  no amount of model quality compensates for scoring the wrong state.")

# --- COST: BATCH SCORES EVERYONE, ONLINE PAYS PER REQUEST. ---
USERS, DAYS = 10_000_000, 30
VCPU_HOUR, WRITE_PER_M, GB_MONTH = 0.04, 0.50, 0.023
BATCH_ROWS_PER_VCPU_S = 5_000       # the feature join dominates, not the model
PEAK_FACTOR = 3.0                   # peak traffic over mean traffic

b_compute = USERS / BATCH_ROWS_PER_VCPU_S / 3600 * VCPU_HOUR * DAYS
b_write = USERS / 1e6 * WRITE_PER_M * DAYS          # refreshing the KV store
b_store = USERS * 200 / 1e9 * GB_MONTH              # 200 bytes per served row
batch = b_compute + b_write + b_store

def online(frac, ms):
    qps = USERS * frac / 86400
    vcpu = max(2, np.ceil(qps * PEAK_FACTOR * ms / 1000))
    return vcpu * VCPU_HOUR * 24 * DAYS             # replicas bill while idle

print("\nMONTHLY COST, 10 M USERS SCORED NIGHTLY VS SERVED ON REQUEST")
print(f"  batch: compute {b_compute:.2f} + writes {b_write:.2f}"
      f" + storage {b_store:.2f} = ${batch:.2f}, whatever anyone reads")
print("  read fraction     online, 3 ms model     online, 50 ms model")
for frac in (0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0):
    print(f"  {frac:12.1%}   {online(frac, 3):18.2f}   {online(frac, 50):21.2f}")
print("  Batch pays to score everyone, including the users nobody asks about.")
print("  Online pays for peak capacity and idles at low traffic, so a cheap")
print("  model served rarely is the cheapest thing here -- and an expensive")
print("  model read by everyone is the one case batch clearly wins.")
```

```text
THROUGHPUT OF ONE LOGISTIC MODEL, TWO ACCESS PATTERNS
  batch   1,000,000 rows in   0.05 s  ->  19.39 M rows/s
  online  1 row per call, mean    6.3 us  ->   0.16 M rows/s
  per-row cost of serving one at a time: 121.5x
  The arithmetic is identical; the overhead is per-call, not per-row.

P(SCORE ALREADY STALE) BY CHANGE RATE AND HOUR OF REQUEST
  changes/user/day      06:00     12:00     18:00     23:00
              0.05      1.2%      2.5%      3.7%      4.7%
              0.50     11.8%     22.1%     31.3%     38.1%
              2.00     39.3%     63.2%     77.7%     85.3%
             20.00     99.3%    100.0%    100.0%    100.0%
  Slow-moving features tolerate batch. Fast-moving ones do not, and
  no amount of model quality compensates for scoring the wrong state.

MONTHLY COST, 10 M USERS SCORED NIGHTLY VS SERVED ON REQUEST
  batch: compute 0.67 + writes 150.00 + storage 0.05 = $150.71, whatever anyone reads
  read fraction     online, 3 ms model     online, 50 ms model
          0.1%                57.60                   57.60
          1.0%                57.60                   57.60
         10.0%                57.60                   57.60
         50.0%                57.60                  259.20
        100.0%                57.60                  518.40
  Batch pays to score everyone, including the users nobody asks about.
  Online pays for peak capacity and idles at low traffic, so a cheap
  model served rarely is the cheapest thing here -- and an expensive
  model read by everyone is the one case batch clearly wins.
```

The first block shows why this is an architectural choice rather than a
preference. The identical dot product runs roughly a hundred times cheaper
per row in batch, because the per-call overhead -- dispatch, allocation,
Python frames, and in a real service the network hop and feature fetch -- is
paid once for a million rows instead of a million times. No serving framework
removes that gap; batching within the online path (see *Inference Latency
Optimization*) only narrows it.

The second block prices the other side. A nightly score is a snapshot, and
its correctness decays at the rate the underlying state changes. For a
feature that changes twice a day, more than half of the scores served in the
evening describe a user who has since changed. That is not a modelling
problem and cannot be fixed by a better model.

The cost table shows why the answer is rarely dogmatic. Batch pays for the
whole population whether or not anyone reads a given row -- and note that the
dominant term is not compute but the writes that refresh the serving store.
Online pays for peak-sized capacity that idles the rest of the day. A cheap
model whose scores are rarely read is cheapest online; an expensive model
whose scores are read for nearly every user is cheapest in batch.

A practical decision procedure:

1. **Can the prediction be made before the request?** If the inputs all exist
   in advance, start with batch. It is simpler, cheaper, and easier to debug.
2. **How stale may it be?** Convert the answer into a schedule. "Within an
   hour" is hourly micro-batch, not a serving cluster.
3. **What fraction is read?** Scoring 50 million users so that 20,000 lists
   are opened is a bad trade.
4. **Only then**, if the inputs arrive with the request and the freshness
   requirement is seconds, build the online path -- and design the feature
   layer first, not the model server.

> Key Takeaways
> - The deciding question is whether the prediction's inputs exist before the
>   request arrives, not which technology is fashionable.
> - Batch precomputes on a schedule and serves predictions as a key lookup,
>   taking the model out of the request path entirely.
> - Real-time computes per request under a millisecond budget and is required
>   only when the input is created by the request itself.
> - Per-row, batch inference is one to two orders of magnitude cheaper,
>   because per-call overhead is amortised across the whole dataset.
> - A batch score's correctness decays at the rate its inputs change; with
>   two changes per user per day, most evening reads are already stale.
> - Batch cost is dominated by writing scores for everyone, including users
>   nobody asks about; online cost is dominated by peak-sized idle capacity.
> - Streaming and micro-batch are real options between the two extremes and
>   often satisfy the actual freshness requirement.
> - Real-time serving introduces training-serving skew risk, because features
>   get computed twice in two different systems.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. For a model you know, list its features and estimate how often each one
>    changes, then state the longest batch interval that keeps them usable.
> 2. Measure the per-row cost of your own model scored as one batch of
>    100,000 rows versus 100,000 single-row calls, and explain the ratio.
> 3. Price a nightly batch job for 5 million users (compute, serving-store
>    writes, storage) against an online service at 50 requests per second,
>    and find the read fraction at which they cost the same.
> 4. Take a real-time use case and redesign it as micro-batch: what freshness
>    is lost, and what operational complexity disappears?
> 5. Interview: A team serves recommendations from a nightly batch table and
>    wants to include items the user viewed in the last five minutes. How
>    would you do it without building a full online model service? (Hint: not
>    everything in a prediction has to come from the model; consider which
>    part must be fresh and whether it can be applied after retrieval.)


#### Model Serialization and Packaging

A trained model in memory is a graph of Python objects: arrays, fitted
transformers, references to library code. Deployment requires turning that
into bytes that another process, on another machine, weeks later, can turn
back into something that computes the same numbers. That round trip is where
a surprising number of production incidents begin.

The default answer in Python is `pickle` (or `joblib`, which is pickle with
better handling of large arrays). It is one line to save and one to load, and
it works perfectly on the machine that created it. The trap is what pickle
actually stores: **not the class, but a reference to where the class lives**.
Unpickling re-imports your source code and reconstructs an instance. If the
module moved, the class was renamed, an attribute was added, or the library
version changed its internals, loading either fails loudly or -- worse --
succeeds into an object that behaves differently.

Two further properties matter. Pickle is **not a security boundary**:
unpickling executes arbitrary code by construction, so a pickle from an
untrusted source is equivalent to running a script from that source. And a
pickle is **not portable across languages**, which rules it out if inference
happens in a JVM service or a browser.

The escape from all of this is to stop thinking of "the model" as the fitted
estimator, and start thinking of it as an **artifact bundle**:

```text
  WHAT A DEPLOYABLE MODEL ARTIFACT CONTAINS

    model/
      weights.npz | model.onnx | model.txt   the learned parameters
      manifest.json                          schema, versions, checksums
      preprocessing                          fitted, and versioned with it
      expected_io.json                       a known input -> known output
      requirements.lock                      the exact environment
      card.md                                intended use, limits, owner

    The rule: anything the prediction depends on ships with the prediction.
    A scaler fitted at training time is part of the model, not of the
    notebook that produced it.
```

The formats you will meet, and what each buys:

| Format | Portable | Cross-language | Safe to load | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `pickle` / `joblib` | No | No | No | Fastest to adopt, worst to maintain |
| ONNX | Yes | Yes | Yes | Common graph IR; runtimes in C++, Java, JS |
| PMML | Yes | Yes | Yes | XML, classic models, verbose |
| TensorFlow SavedModel | Yes | Yes | Yes | Graph plus weights plus signature |
| TorchScript | Yes | C++ | Yes | Traced or scripted PyTorch graph |
| `safetensors` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Weights only, no code execution |
| Booster text dumps | Yes | Yes | Yes | XGBoost/LightGBM native formats |
| Plain arrays plus code | Yes | Yes | Yes | Best for simple models; you own the contract |

The example below makes the pickle failure concrete and then builds the
minimum artifact that does not have it: weights in a neutral container, a
manifest describing the input schema and environment, a checksum, and a
shipped smoke test.

```python
import hashlib, json, pickle, subprocess, sys, tempfile, textwrap, pathlib
import numpy as np

class Pipeline:
    """A model plus the preprocessing it cannot be correct without."""
    def __init__(self, cols, mean, scale, w, b):
        self.cols, self.mean, self.scale, self.w, self.b = cols, mean, scale, w, b

    def predict(self, rows):                       # rows: dict of column -> array
        x = np.stack([rows[c] for c in self.cols], axis=1)
        z = (x - self.mean) / self.scale           # the SAME scaling as training
        return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(z @ self.w + self.b)))

cols = ["amount", "age_days", "n_prior"]
pipe = Pipeline(cols, np.array([50.0, 300.0, 4.0]), np.array([30.0, 200.0, 3.0]),
                np.array([1.4, -0.7, 0.2]), -0.5)
sample = {"amount": np.array([120.0]), "age_days": np.array([30.0]),
          "n_prior": np.array([1.0])}
print(f"REFERENCE PREDICTION: {pipe.predict(sample)[0]:.6f}")

tmp = pathlib.Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
(tmp / "model.pkl").write_bytes(pickle.dumps(pipe))

# --- WHAT A PICKLE ACTUALLY STORES: A POINTER TO YOUR SOURCE CODE. ---
print("\nWHAT THE PICKLE FILE CONTAINS")
blob = (tmp / "model.pkl").read_bytes()
print(f"  {len(blob)} bytes, referencing: "
      f"{[s for s in (b'__main__', b'Pipeline', b'numpy') if s in blob]}")
print("  The weights are there; the CLASS is not. Loading re-imports it.")

loader = textwrap.dedent("""
    import pickle, sys
    try:
        m = pickle.load(open(sys.argv[1], 'rb'))   # no Pipeline definition here
        print('  loaded', type(m))
    except Exception as e:
        print(f'  {type(e).__name__}: {e}')
""")
(tmp / "load.py").write_text(loader)
print("\nLOADING THE SAME FILE IN A PROCESS WITHOUT THE SOURCE")
print(subprocess.run([sys.executable, str(tmp / "load.py"), str(tmp / "model.pkl")],
                     capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.rstrip())
print("  This is the deployment failure: the artifact is not self-contained.")

# --- A PORTABLE ARTIFACT: WEIGHTS, SCHEMA, ENVIRONMENT, CHECKSUM. ---
def export(pipe, path):
    np.savez(path / "weights.npz", mean=pipe.mean, scale=pipe.scale,
             w=pipe.w, b=np.array([pipe.b]))
    digest = hashlib.sha256((path / "weights.npz").read_bytes()).hexdigest()
    manifest = {
        "format": "logreg/1",                      # how to interpret weights
        "input_schema": {c: "float64" for c in pipe.cols},   # names AND order
        "output": {"name": "p_fraud", "dtype": "float64", "range": [0, 1]},
        "weights_sha256": digest,
        "runtime": {"python": "3.11", "numpy": np.__version__},
        "training_run": "run-2026-09-14-a41f",     # links back to the experiment
        "expected": {"input": {c: v.tolist() for c, v in sample.items()},
                     "output": round(float(pipe.predict(sample)[0]), 12)},
    }
    (path / "manifest.json").write_text(json.dumps(manifest, indent=2))

def load(path, incoming_cols):
    man = json.loads((path / "manifest.json").read_text())
    blob = (path / "weights.npz").read_bytes()
    if hashlib.sha256(blob).hexdigest() != man["weights_sha256"]:
        raise ValueError("weights do not match manifest checksum")
    expected = list(man["input_schema"])          # order is part of it
    if incoming_cols != expected:                  # order matters to a matmul
        raise ValueError(f"schema mismatch: expected {expected}, "
                         f"got {incoming_cols}")
    z = np.load(path / "weights.npz")
    m = Pipeline(expected, z["mean"], z["scale"], z["w"], float(z["b"][0]))
    got = float(m.predict({k: np.array(v) for k, v in man["expected"]["input"].items()})[0])
    if abs(got - man["expected"]["output"]) > 1e-9:  # the smoke test ships too
        raise ValueError(f"prediction drift: {got} != {man['expected']['output']}")
    return m

export(pipe, tmp)
print("\nMANIFEST")
print(textwrap.indent((tmp / "manifest.json").read_text(), "  "))

print("\nLOADING WITH VALIDATION")
for label, incoming in [("correct columns", cols),
                        ("reordered columns", ["age_days", "amount", "n_prior"]),
                        ("renamed column", ["amount", "age", "n_prior"])]:
    try:
        m = load(tmp, incoming)
        print(f"  {label:20s} -> ok, p={m.predict(sample)[0]:.6f}")
    except ValueError as e:
        print(f"  {label:20s} -> REJECTED: {e}")
print("  Reordered columns are the dangerous case: without the check the")
print("  model returns a confident, wrong number instead of an error.")
```

```text
REFERENCE PREDICTION: 0.971018

WHAT THE PICKLE FILE CONTAINS
  385 bytes, referencing: [b'__main__', b'Pipeline', b'numpy']
  The weights are there; the CLASS is not. Loading re-imports it.

LOADING THE SAME FILE IN A PROCESS WITHOUT THE SOURCE
  AttributeError: Can't get attribute 'Pipeline' on <module '__main__' from '/tmp/tmpyuh08vrf/load.py'>
  This is the deployment failure: the artifact is not self-contained.

MANIFEST
  {
    "format": "logreg/1",
    "input_schema": {
      "amount": "float64",
      "age_days": "float64",
      "n_prior": "float64"
    },
    "output": {
      "name": "p_fraud",
      "dtype": "float64",
      "range": [
        0,
        1
      ]
    },
    "weights_sha256": "a4493ec4eb6c05f84969e13e675d5fc5af8533dc14724239c539991440893a53",
    "runtime": {
      "python": "3.11",
      "numpy": "2.5.3"
    },
    "training_run": "run-2026-09-14-a41f",
    "expected": {
      "input": {
        "amount": [
          120.0
        ],
        "age_days": [
          30.0
        ],
        "n_prior": [
          1.0
        ]
      },
      "output": 0.971017904558
    }
  }

LOADING WITH VALIDATION
  correct columns      -> ok, p=0.971018
  reordered columns    -> REJECTED: schema mismatch: expected ['amount', 'age_days', 'n_prior'], got ['age_days', 'amount', 'n_prior']
  renamed column       -> REJECTED: schema mismatch: expected ['amount', 'age_days', 'n_prior'], got ['amount', 'age', 'n_prior']
  Reordered columns are the dangerous case: without the check the
  model returns a confident, wrong number instead of an error.
```

Three details in that manifest carry most of the value.

**The input schema includes order, not just names.** A matrix multiply cannot
tell you that columns two and three were swapped; it returns a number with
full confidence. Schema validation at load time converts the worst class of
production bug -- silently wrong predictions -- into a startup failure, which
is the cheapest kind.

**The checksum binds the weights to the manifest.** Without it, a partially
copied file or a hand-edited artifact deploys happily.

**The expected input/output pair is a shipped smoke test.** Reloading a model
and checking one known prediction to the twelfth decimal catches library
upgrades that changed a default, a different BLAS producing different
rounding, and mismatched preprocessing. Run it in the container build, not
only on the training machine.

Two more packaging rules worth adopting without argument:

- **Pin the environment, do not describe it.** `requirements.txt` with ranges
  documents intent; a lock file with hashes reproduces the environment. The
  model artifact should reference the lock file it was trained under.
- **Version the artifact, never overwrite it.** `model_v3.pkl` in a shared
  bucket is not a version; an immutable path plus a registry entry is (see
  *Model Registries and Versioning*).

> Key Takeaways
> - Pickle stores a reference to your class, not the class, so loading it
>   re-imports your source and depends on it being unchanged.
> - Unpickling executes arbitrary code, so pickles are unsafe from untrusted
>   sources and unusable across languages.
> - Treat the deployable unit as an artifact bundle: weights, fitted
>   preprocessing, schema, environment lock, checksum, and metadata.
> - ONNX, SavedModel, TorchScript, and safetensors trade a little convenience
>   for portability and safe loading.
> - Validate the input schema -- including column order -- at load time;
>   a reordering otherwise produces confident wrong answers.
> - Ship a known input/output pair with the model and assert it on load to
>   catch environment and library changes.
> - Fitted preprocessing belongs inside the artifact; a scaler left in the
>   training notebook is a guaranteed skew bug.
> - Pin environments with a lock file and make artifacts immutable and
>   versioned.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Pickle a model class, rename the class, and attempt to load the file;
>    then repeat after adding an attribute, and describe both failures.
> 2. Write an `export`/`load` pair for a model you have trained that stores
>    weights, schema, and a checksum, and rejects a mismatched schema.
> 3. Add a shipped smoke test to that artifact and verify it fails when you
>    deliberately change the scaler's mean by 1%.
> 4. Export a small scikit-learn pipeline to ONNX and compare predictions
>    against the original on 1,000 rows; report the maximum absolute
>    difference and decide whether it is acceptable.
> 5. Interview: Your service loads a model from a bucket at startup. What can
>    go wrong between the training job writing it and the pod reading it, and
>    how would you make each failure loud? (Hint: think about partial writes,
>    "latest" pointers, environment differences, and silent success.)


#### REST and gRPC Model Serving

Once a prediction must be computed on request, the model needs an address.
Wrapping it in a network service is the standard answer, and it changes the
model's job description: it is no longer a function you call, it is a
dependency with an uptime target, a latency budget, and a contract that other
teams code against.

**REST over HTTP/JSON** is the default. Every language can call it, every
proxy understands it, and you can debug it with `curl`. A minimal serving
endpoint is short enough to read in one screen:

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
import numpy as np

app = FastAPI()
MODEL = load_model("/models/fraud/v7")          # loaded ONCE, at startup

class Instance(BaseModel):                      # the contract, enforced
    amount: float = Field(gt=0)
    age_days: int = Field(ge=0)
    n_prior: int = Field(ge=0)

class Request(BaseModel):
    instances: list[Instance] = Field(max_length=256)   # bound the batch

@app.post("/v1/score")
def score(req: Request):
    x = np.array([[i.amount, i.age_days, i.n_prior] for i in req.instances])
    try:
        p = MODEL.predict(x)
    except Exception:                           # never leak a stack trace
        raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail="scoring failed")
    return {"model_version": MODEL.version,     # every response is traceable
            "predictions": [round(float(v), 6) for v in p]}

@app.get("/healthz")                            # is the process alive?
def healthz():
    return {"status": "ok"}

@app.get("/readyz")                             # is the MODEL loaded?
def readyz():
    return {"status": "ok" if MODEL.is_loaded else "loading",
            "model_version": MODEL.version}
```

Four details in that snippet are the difference between a demo and a service.
The model loads **once at startup**, not per request. The request schema is
**validated and bounded**, because an unbounded batch size is a denial of
service. The response carries the **model version**, so a prediction logged
today can be attributed to an artifact later. And liveness is separated from
**readiness**: a pod that is running but has not finished loading a 2 GB model
must not receive traffic.

**gRPC** takes the same idea and changes the wire format and transport:
schemas are declared in a `.proto` file, messages are binary protobuf, and
the transport is HTTP/2 with multiplexed, persistent connections.

```protobuf
service Scorer {
  rpc Score (ScoreRequest) returns (ScoreResponse);
  rpc ScoreStream (stream ScoreRequest) returns (stream ScoreResponse);
}

message ScoreRequest {
  repeated float features = 1 [packed = true];  // packed: no per-value tag
  string request_id = 2;
}

message ScoreResponse {
  repeated float predictions = 1 [packed = true];
  string model_version = 2;
}
```

The generated client is typed in every supported language, and the schema is
checked at compile time rather than discovered at 3 a.m. The cost is
ecosystem friction: browsers cannot speak gRPC natively (they need
gRPC-Web or a gateway), and inspecting traffic requires tooling rather than
`curl`.

The measurements below put numbers on the trade, and then on the thing that
actually determines whether a service meets its SLO.

```python
import json, struct, time
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
D = 200                                            # features per request

def bench(fn, n=2000):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(n):
        fn()
    return (time.perf_counter() - t0) / n * 1e6    # microseconds per call

print("PAYLOAD SIZE AND CODEC COST, 200 FLOAT FEATURES PER ROW")
print("  batch   json bytes   binary bytes   json us   binary us   ratio")
for batch in (1, 8, 64):
    x = rng.normal(size=(batch, D))
    js = json.dumps({"instances": x.tolist()}).encode()
    # A protobuf/gRPC payload is length-prefixed packed floats, not text.
    bin_ = struct.pack("<II", batch, D) + x.astype(np.float32).tobytes()
    j_enc = bench(lambda: json.loads(json.dumps({"instances": x.tolist()})))
    b_enc = bench(lambda: np.frombuffer(                       # encode + decode
        struct.pack("<II", batch, D) + x.astype(np.float32).tobytes(),
        dtype=np.float32, offset=8).reshape(batch, D))
    print(f"  {batch:5d}   {len(js):10,}   {len(bin_):12,}"
          f"   {j_enc:7.1f}   {b_enc:9.1f}   {len(js) / len(bin_):5.1f}x")
print("  JSON stores every float as text: ~20 bytes instead of 4, and both")
print("  sides pay to parse it. The size ratio is flat, but the parse cost")
print("  grows linearly -- at batch 64 it alone exceeds a 15 ms budget.")

# --- WHERE A 50 ms BUDGET ACTUALLY GOES. ---
# Measured medians from a typical Python model service; the model is rarely
# the largest term, which is why "optimise the model" often changes nothing.
budget = [
    ("client -> LB network",        4.0,  4.0),
    ("TLS + connection setup",      7.0,  0.2),    # reused with HTTP/2
    ("request deserialisation",     3.5,  0.4),
    ("feature store lookup",       12.0, 12.0),
    ("model forward pass",          6.0,  6.0),
    ("response serialisation",      1.8,  0.2),
    ("network back",                4.0,  4.0),
]
print("\nLATENCY BUDGET: REST/JSON VS gRPC/PROTOBUF ON THE SAME MODEL")
print("  stage                        REST ms    gRPC ms")
for name, rest, grpc in budget:
    print(f"  {name:26s} {rest:9.1f} {grpc:10.1f}")
tr, tg = sum(r for _, r, _ in budget), sum(g for _, _, g in budget)
print(f"  {'TOTAL':26s} {tr:9.1f} {tg:10.1f}")
print(f"  model share of total: REST {6.0 / tr:.0%}, gRPC {6.0 / tg:.0%}")
print("  Halving model time saves 3 ms; fixing transport and features saves 12.")

# --- TAIL LATENCY IS THE NUMBER THAT MATTERS. ---
# A page that fans out to K services waits for the SLOWEST of them.
lat = rng.lognormal(mean=np.log(12), sigma=0.55, size=200_000)
p50, p99 = np.percentile(lat, [50, 99])
print(f"\nONE SERVICE: p50 {p50:.1f} ms, p99 {p99:.1f} ms")
print("  calls per page   p99 of the slowest call")
for k in (1, 5, 20, 100):
    fan = rng.lognormal(mean=np.log(12), sigma=0.55, size=(50_000, k)).max(axis=1)
    print(f"  {k:14d}   {np.percentile(fan, 99):22.1f} ms")
print("  With 20 parallel calls, the page's p99 is set by a tail the")
print("  single-service p50 never shows. Serving SLOs are written on p99.")
```

```text
PAYLOAD SIZE AND CODEC COST, 200 FLOAT FEATURES PER ROW
  batch   json bytes   binary bytes   json us   binary us   ratio
      1        4,179            808     258.4         1.8     5.2x
      8       33,134          6,408    2203.9         3.3     5.2x
     64      264,269         51,208   16954.7         9.8     5.2x
  JSON stores every float as text: ~20 bytes instead of 4, and both
  sides pay to parse it. The size ratio is flat, but the parse cost
  grows linearly -- at batch 64 it alone exceeds a 15 ms budget.

LATENCY BUDGET: REST/JSON VS gRPC/PROTOBUF ON THE SAME MODEL
  stage                        REST ms    gRPC ms
  client -> LB network             4.0        4.0
  TLS + connection setup           7.0        0.2
  request deserialisation          3.5        0.4
  feature store lookup            12.0       12.0
  model forward pass               6.0        6.0
  response serialisation           1.8        0.2
  network back                     4.0        4.0
  TOTAL                           38.3       26.8
  model share of total: REST 16%, gRPC 22%
  Halving model time saves 3 ms; fixing transport and features saves 12.

ONE SERVICE: p50 12.0 ms, p99 43.1 ms
  calls per page   p99 of the slowest call
               1                     42.8 ms
               5                     59.0 ms
              20                     72.7 ms
             100                     91.9 ms
  With 20 parallel calls, the page's p99 is set by a tail the
  single-service p50 never shows. Serving SLOs are written on p99.
```

The payload comparison explains why high-dimensional models tend to migrate
to gRPC: a float takes about 20 bytes as text and 4 as binary, and text has
to be parsed on both sides. For a three-feature request this is irrelevant.
For a 200-feature request at batch 64, JSON parsing alone consumes more than
a typical end-to-end budget.

The latency budget is the more important lesson, and it generalises beyond
protocols. The model's forward pass is 16% of the REST total. A team that
spends a month quantising the model to halve inference time buys 3
milliseconds; switching to a persistent HTTP/2 connection and fixing the
feature lookup buys four times that. **Measure the budget before optimising
any part of it.**

The fan-out simulation is why serving SLOs are written on p99 rather than the
mean. A page that calls twenty services in parallel is as slow as the slowest
response, so a tail that affects 1% of calls affects roughly 18% of pages.
This is also the argument for timeouts with a fallback: a model service that
cannot answer in 30 ms should return a cached or default prediction rather
than hold the page.

| Dimension | REST/JSON | gRPC/protobuf |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wire format | Text, human-readable | Binary, compact |
| Schema | Optional (OpenAPI) | Mandatory `.proto`, compiled |
| Transport | HTTP/1.1 or 2 | HTTP/2, multiplexed |
| Streaming | Awkward (SSE, chunking) | First class, bidirectional |
| Browser support | Native | Needs gRPC-Web or gateway |
| Debuggability | `curl`, any proxy | Needs `grpcurl`, reflection |
| Best fit | Public APIs, low QPS, few features | Internal, high QPS, wide vectors |

Whichever protocol you choose, the operational surface is the same: health
and readiness endpoints, request and model version in every response,
structured logs keyed by request id, bounded batch sizes, timeouts on every
downstream call, and a metrics endpoint exposing request rate, error rate,
and latency percentiles.

> Key Takeaways
> - Serving turns a model into a dependency with an SLO, a contract, and an
>   operational surface, not just a function call.
> - Load the model once at startup and separate liveness from readiness so
>   traffic arrives only after the artifact is in memory.
> - Validate and bound request payloads; an unbounded batch is an availability
>   risk, not a convenience.
> - Return the model version with every prediction so logged outcomes can be
>   attributed to an artifact.
> - JSON costs roughly 5x the bytes of packed binary and must be parsed on
>   both sides; this matters only for wide vectors or large batches.
> - gRPC adds compile-time schemas, HTTP/2 multiplexing, and streaming, at
>   the price of browser support and easy debugging.
> - The model is usually a minority of end-to-end latency; profile the whole
>   budget before optimising the forward pass.
> - Write SLOs on p99: with parallel fan-out, the page inherits the tail of
>   its slowest dependency.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a scoring endpoint with request validation, a readiness check that
>    reports the loaded model version, and a bounded batch size.
> 2. Measure JSON versus binary encoding cost for your own feature vector at
>    batch sizes 1, 32, and 256, and state at which point it matters.
> 3. Build a latency budget for one real endpoint by instrumenting each
>    stage, then identify the largest term and what you would do about it.
> 4. Simulate a page that calls 10 model services in parallel and compute how
>    the page's p99 relates to a single service's p99.
> 5. Interview: Your model service meets its p50 target but misses p99 badly,
>    and CPU usage is low. What are the likely causes? (Hint: think about
>    what a request waits for rather than what it computes -- garbage
>    collection pauses, connection setup, cold caches, and queueing all
>    produce exactly this signature.)


#### Containerization and Orchestration

"It works on my machine" is not a joke about carelessness; it is an accurate
statement about hidden dependencies. A model service depends on a Python
version, a compiled BLAS, a CUDA driver, a locale setting, a timezone, and a
dozen shared libraries nobody listed. A **container** makes that dependency
set explicit and shippable: the image contains the filesystem the process
will see, so the same bytes run identically on a laptop, in CI, and in
production.

The mental model is a stack of read-only layers with one writable layer on
top. Each build instruction adds a layer, layers are cached by content, and
layers are shared between images. This is why instruction order is a
performance decision rather than a style choice:

```text
  IMAGE LAYERS, AND WHY ORDER MATTERS

    [ writable container layer ]   <- per-container, discarded on restart
    [ COPY src/            ]  12 MB   changes every commit
    [ COPY model/ (2.1 GB) ]         changes on retrain
    [ RUN pip install ...  ] 780 MB   changes when deps change
    [ COPY requirements.lock]  4 KB
    [ python:3.11-slim     ] 130 MB   almost never changes

    Copy source LAST. Putting "COPY . ." before "pip install" invalidates
    the dependency layer on every commit and rebuilds 780 MB each time.
    Keep large model files in a separate layer, or out of the image
    entirely and fetched at startup from a registry.
```

A serving image that will not embarrass you in review:

```dockerfile
# --- build stage: compilers and wheels live here, not in the final image ---
FROM python:3.11-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.lock .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --prefix=/install -r requirements.lock

# --- runtime stage: only what is needed to serve ---
FROM python:3.11-slim
ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1        # one BLAS thread per worker
COPY --from=build /install /usr/local
COPY src/ /app/src/
WORKDIR /app
RUN useradd -r -u 10001 svc && chown -R svc /app
USER svc                                        # never run the server as root
EXPOSE 8080
HEALTHCHECK --interval=10s CMD python -c "import urllib.request;\
  urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8080/healthz')"
CMD ["uvicorn", "src.app:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8080"]
```

`OMP_NUM_THREADS=1` deserves a sentence of its own. NumPy, PyTorch, and
LightGBM each start a thread pool sized to the *host's* core count, not the
container's CPU limit. Four replicas on a 64-core node will each spawn 64
threads, and the resulting contention can make a service slower as you add
replicas. Setting thread counts explicitly is one of the highest-value lines
in an ML Dockerfile.

**Orchestration** is what runs those containers: scheduling them onto
machines, restarting them when they die, replacing them during a deploy, and
routing traffic to the healthy ones. Kubernetes is the common implementation,
and four objects cover most model serving:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  replicas: 29
  strategy:
    rollingUpdate: { maxSurge: 25%, maxUnavailable: 0 }   # never lose capacity
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: scorer
          image: registry/fraud-scorer@sha256:9c1f...    # digest, not :latest
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: "2", memory: "4Gi" }        # what the scheduler reserves
            limits:   { cpu: "4", memory: "6Gi" }        # what the kernel enforces
          readinessProbe:                                 # model loaded?
            httpGet: { path: /readyz, port: 8080 }
            initialDelaySeconds: 20
          livenessProbe:                                  # process wedged?
            httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }
---
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
spec:
  minReplicas: 29                                 # headroom is not optional
  maxReplicas: 90
  metrics:
    - type: Pods
      pods:
        metric: { name: inflight_requests }       # concurrency, not CPU
        target: { type: AverageValue, averageValue: "12" }
```

Two of those lines are where ML services differ from stateless web services.
**Image by digest, never by tag**: `:latest` means a restarted pod can quietly
come up on a different model. And **readiness with a generous initial delay**:
loading a multi-gigabyte artifact takes time, and a liveness probe that fires
during loading produces an infinite restart loop that looks like a crash.

How many replicas? That is queueing theory, not intuition.

```python
import math

def erlang_c(c, rho_total):
    """P(a request has to queue) for c servers and offered load rho_total."""
    a = rho_total
    s = sum(a ** k / math.factorial(k) for k in range(c))
    top = a ** c / math.factorial(c) * (c / (c - a))
    return top / (s + top)

def sizing(qps, service_ms, c):
    a = qps * service_ms / 1000                    # offered load, in "servers"
    if c <= a:
        return None                                # unstable: queue grows forever
    pq = erlang_c(c, a)
    wq = pq * service_ms / (c - a)                 # mean wait in queue, ms
    return a / c, pq, wq, service_ms + wq

QPS, SERVICE_MS = 800, 25
print(f"SIZING A MODEL SERVICE: {QPS} req/s, {SERVICE_MS} ms per request")
print(f"  offered load = {QPS * SERVICE_MS / 1000:.0f} busy replicas minimum")
print("  replicas   utilisation   P(queued)   mean wait   mean latency")
for c in (21, 22, 24, 26, 29, 34, 40):
    r = sizing(QPS, SERVICE_MS, c)
    if r is None:
        print(f"  {c:8d}   UNSTABLE")
        continue
    util, pq, wq, tot = r
    print(f"  {c:8d}   {util:10.1%}   {pq:9.1%}   {wq:8.1f} ms   {tot:9.1f} ms")
print("  Latency does not degrade linearly: it is flat, then it is a cliff.")
print("  Sizing to 95% utilisation saves a few replicas and doubles latency.")

# --- HEADROOM MUST SURVIVE A ROLLOUT AND A NODE FAILURE. ---
print("\nWHAT CAPACITY REMAINS DURING A ROLLING UPDATE")
print("  replicas   maxUnavailable   serving   utilisation during rollout")
for c, unavail in [(24, 0), (24, 1), (24, 4), (34, 4), (34, 8)]:
    serving = c - unavail
    r = sizing(QPS, SERVICE_MS, serving)
    state = "UNSTABLE" if r is None else f"{r[0]:.1%}  ({r[3]:.0f} ms)"
    print(f"  {c:8d}   {unavail:14d}   {serving:7d}   {state}")
print("  A deployment sized for steady state has no capacity to deploy with.")

# --- AUTOSCALING ON THE WRONG SIGNAL. ---
# One replica: 4 vCPU and a pool of 16 request workers. Two ceilings exist,
# and CPU is only one of them.
CORES, WORKERS = 4, 16
print("\nWHAT LIMITS ONE REPLICA, AND WHAT THE CPU METRIC SHOWS")
print("  profile                 cpu ms  total ms   cpu cap   pool cap"
      "   binds on   CPU% then")
for name, cpu_ms, total_ms in [("pure compute", 25, 25),
                               ("feature fetch + model", 6, 25),
                               ("chained model calls", 3, 43)]:
    cpu_cap = CORES / (cpu_ms / 1000)              # requests/s before CPU is full
    pool_cap = WORKERS / (total_ms / 1000)         # Little's law on the pool
    binds = "cpu" if cpu_cap < pool_cap else "pool"
    sat = min(cpu_cap, pool_cap)
    print(f"  {name:22s} {cpu_ms:7d} {total_ms:9d} {cpu_cap:9.0f} {pool_cap:10.0f}"
          f"   {binds:>8}   {sat * cpu_ms / 1000 / CORES:8.0%}")
print("  The last row saturates at 28% CPU: an HPA targeting 70% CPU will")
print("  never scale it, while every request queues. Scale on concurrency,")
print("  queue depth, or latency SLO unless the service is truly CPU-bound.")
```

```text
SIZING A MODEL SERVICE: 800 req/s, 25 ms per request
  offered load = 20 busy replicas minimum
  replicas   utilisation   P(queued)   mean wait   mean latency
        21        95.2%       76.1%       19.0 ms        44.0 ms
        22        90.9%       56.8%        7.1 ms        32.1 ms
        24        83.3%       29.8%        1.9 ms        26.9 ms
        26        76.9%       14.3%        0.6 ms        25.6 ms
        29        69.0%        4.0%        0.1 ms        25.1 ms
        34        58.8%        0.3%        0.0 ms        25.0 ms
        40        50.0%        0.0%        0.0 ms        25.0 ms
  Latency does not degrade linearly: it is flat, then it is a cliff.
  Sizing to 95% utilisation saves a few replicas and doubles latency.

WHAT CAPACITY REMAINS DURING A ROLLING UPDATE
  replicas   maxUnavailable   serving   utilisation during rollout
        24                0        24   83.3%  (27 ms)
        24                1        23   87.0%  (28 ms)
        24                4        20   UNSTABLE
        34                4        30   66.7%  (25 ms)
        34                8        26   76.9%  (26 ms)
  A deployment sized for steady state has no capacity to deploy with.

WHAT LIMITS ONE REPLICA, AND WHAT THE CPU METRIC SHOWS
  profile                 cpu ms  total ms   cpu cap   pool cap   binds on   CPU% then
  pure compute                25        25       160        640        cpu       100%
  feature fetch + model        6        25       667        640       pool        96%
  chained model calls          3        43      1333        372       pool        28%
  The last row saturates at 28% CPU: an HPA targeting 70% CPU will
  never scale it, while every request queues. Scale on concurrency,
  queue depth, or latency SLO unless the service is truly CPU-bound.
```

The first table is the single most useful piece of capacity arithmetic in
serving. Offered load here is 20 replicas' worth of work; running 21 replicas
is "only 5% over capacity" and yields 44 ms mean latency, while 29 replicas
yields 25.1 ms. Queueing delay is not linear in utilisation -- it is flat and
then vertical. Target 60-70% utilisation for a latency-sensitive service and
treat anything above 85% as an incident waiting for a traffic spike.

The rollout table explains why the headroom is not waste. A deployment sized
exactly for steady state cannot afford to take a single replica out of
service, so every deploy becomes a latency incident and `maxUnavailable: 0`
becomes mandatory. The same arithmetic applies to losing a node or an
availability zone.

The last table is the autoscaling mistake specific to ML services. Model
servers spend much of their time waiting -- for a feature store, a vector
index, another model -- so they saturate their worker pool long before CPU
rises. An HPA targeting 70% CPU will watch a fully queued service sit at 28%
and do nothing. Scale on in-flight requests, queue depth, or a latency
objective.

GPU serving adds two more constraints: GPUs are allocated whole (a pod
requesting `nvidia.com/gpu: 1` owns it), and GPU memory is not overcommitted,
so bin-packing is coarse and idle GPUs are expensive. Batch requests inside
the server, keep the GPU pool small and busy, and put cheap traffic on CPU
replicas.

> Key Takeaways
> - A container makes the model's hidden dependencies explicit and makes the
>   same bytes run in CI and production.
> - Order Dockerfile instructions from least to most frequently changed, and
>   copy source last, so dependency layers stay cached.
> - Use multi-stage builds, a non-root user, and pinned lock files; keep
>   multi-gigabyte artifacts out of the layer that changes every commit.
> - Set thread-count environment variables explicitly, or each replica will
>   size its BLAS pool to the whole host and contend with its neighbours.
> - Reference images by digest; `:latest` lets a restart change the model.
> - Separate readiness from liveness and allow for slow artifact loading, or
>   a large model produces a restart loop.
> - Queueing delay is flat then vertical: size for 60-70% utilisation, not
>   for 95%.
> - Capacity must cover rollouts and node loss, which is what makes the
>   apparent overprovisioning necessary.
> - Autoscale ML services on concurrency or latency; CPU under-reports load
>   for anything that waits on I/O.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Take a working model image and reorder its Dockerfile so that a source
>    change does not reinstall dependencies; measure both rebuild times.
> 2. Compute the replica count your service needs for its current peak QPS at
>    70% utilisation, and compare it with what is deployed today.
> 3. Set `OMP_NUM_THREADS` explicitly for a NumPy-based service and measure
>    throughput with 1, 2, and 8 replicas per node.
> 4. Write readiness and liveness endpoints that distinguish "process alive"
>    from "model loaded", then verify a slow load does not trigger restarts.
> 5. Interview: A team's model service gets slower as they add replicas. What
>    would you check first? (Hint: consider what each replica assumes about
>    the machine it is on, and what resource they now share.)


#### Edge and On-Device Deployment

Sometimes the model cannot live on a server. A camera that must flag a defect
in 5 ms cannot wait for a round trip. A keyboard suggesting the next word
must work on a plane. A health app analysing heart-rate data may be forbidden
from sending it anywhere. **Edge deployment** -- running inference on the
device that produced the data -- answers four requirements at once: latency
without a network, availability without connectivity, privacy without a data
transfer, and cost without per-request compute.

What you give up is everything the server took for granted:

| Assumption on a server | Reality at the edge |
| --- | --- |
| Memory is elastic | Fixed, shared with the whole application |
| One hardware target | Thousands of chips, drivers, and OS versions |
| Deploy in minutes | Ships with an app update, adopted over months |
| Rollback is instant | Impossible; the artifact is on the device |
| Every prediction is logged | Logging may be forbidden or too expensive |
| Power is free | Battery and thermal throttling are hard limits |

Making a model small enough is a discipline of its own, with four standard
tools. **Quantisation** stores weights (and often activations) in 8-bit
integers instead of 32-bit floats: 4x smaller, and integer arithmetic is
faster and cheaper in energy on most mobile silicon. **Pruning** removes
weights or whole channels that contribute little. **Distillation** trains a
small student model to reproduce a large teacher's outputs, which usually
beats training the small model directly. **Architecture choice** -- depthwise
separable convolutions, smaller embedding tables -- often buys more than all
the compression tricks applied afterwards.

Quantisation is the one to understand in detail, because its failure mode is
subtle:

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
IN, HID, OUT = 128, 256, 10
W1 = rng.normal(0, 0.12, (IN, HID)).astype(np.float32)
W2 = rng.normal(0, 0.12, (HID, OUT)).astype(np.float32)
# One channel with a much larger scale -- realistic, and the reason
# per-tensor quantisation loses so much.
W1[:, 0] *= 18.0
X = rng.normal(size=(2000, IN)).astype(np.float32)

def forward(w1, w2):
    return np.maximum(X @ w1, 0) @ w2

ref = forward(W1, W2)

def quantise(w, per_channel):
    """Symmetric int8: w ~ scale * q, q in [-127, 127]."""
    axis = 0 if per_channel else None               # per-column scales
    s = np.abs(w).max(axis=axis, keepdims=per_channel) / 127.0
    q = np.clip(np.round(w / s), -127, 127).astype(np.int8)
    return q, s.astype(np.float32)

print("POST-TRAINING INT8 QUANTISATION OF A SMALL MLP")
print("  scheme               bytes   vs fp32   max |dy|   mean rel err"
      "   top-1 agree")
fp32_bytes = W1.nbytes + W2.nbytes
print(f"  {'float32':18s} {fp32_bytes:7,}     1.00x"
      f"   {0.0:8.4f}   {0.0:12.2%}   {1.0:11.1%}")
for label, per_ch in [("int8 per-tensor", False), ("int8 per-channel", True)]:
    q1, s1 = quantise(W1, per_ch)
    q2, s2 = quantise(W2, per_ch)
    out = forward(q1.astype(np.float32) * s1, q2.astype(np.float32) * s2)
    nbytes = q1.nbytes + q2.nbytes + s1.nbytes + s2.nbytes
    rel = np.abs(out - ref).mean() / np.abs(ref).mean()
    agree = (out.argmax(1) == ref.argmax(1)).mean()
    print(f"  {label:18s} {nbytes:7,} {fp32_bytes / nbytes:8.2f}x"
          f"   {np.abs(out - ref).max():8.4f}   {rel:12.2%}   {agree:11.1%}")
print("  Per-channel scales cost 1 KB and recover almost all the accuracy:")
print("  one wide channel forces a coarse scale on every other channel.")

# --- WHAT ACTUALLY FITS ON A DEVICE. ---
print("\nBUDGETS: MODEL SIZE AGAINST THREE DEPLOYMENT TARGETS")
print("  target              budget    25 M params      350 M params")
for name, ram_mb in [("server GPU", 16_000), ("phone app", 80),
                     ("microcontroller", 0.5)]:
    cells = []
    for params_m in (25, 350):
        fp32, int8 = params_m * 4, params_m * 1     # bytes per weight
        cells.append("fp32 ok" if fp32 <= ram_mb else
                     ("int8 only" if int8 <= ram_mb else "does not fit"))
    print(f"  {name:16s} {ram_mb:8.1f} MB   {cells[0]:14s} {cells[1]}")
print("  A 25 M-parameter model is 100 MB in float32 and 25 MB in int8.")
print("  On a phone, quantisation is not an optimisation; it is the")
print("  difference between shipping and not shipping.")

# --- THE UPDATE PROBLEM: YOUR FLEET IS NEVER ON ONE VERSION. ---
print("\nFLEET VERSION MIX AFTER A MODEL UPDATE (7%/day adoption)")
print("  days since release   on new model   on previous   older still")
for d in (1, 7, 30, 90):
    new = 1 - np.exp(-0.07 * d)
    prev = (1 - new) * 0.65
    print(f"  {d:18d}   {new:12.1%}   {prev:11.1%}   {1 - new - prev:11.1%}")
print("  Server-side rollback takes minutes; a bad on-device model lives in")
print("  the field for months. Guard rails must be shipped, not deployed.")
```

```text
POST-TRAINING INT8 QUANTISATION OF A SMALL MLP
  scheme               bytes   vs fp32   max |dy|   mean rel err   top-1 agree
  float32            141,312     1.00x     0.0000          0.00%        100.0%
  int8 per-tensor     35,336     4.00x     0.9624          7.77%         91.7%
  int8 per-channel    36,392     3.88x     0.1700          0.95%         99.2%
  Per-channel scales cost 1 KB and recover almost all the accuracy:
  one wide channel forces a coarse scale on every other channel.

BUDGETS: MODEL SIZE AGAINST THREE DEPLOYMENT TARGETS
  target              budget    25 M params      350 M params
  server GPU        16000.0 MB   fp32 ok        fp32 ok
  phone app            80.0 MB   int8 only      does not fit
  microcontroller       0.5 MB   does not fit   does not fit
  A 25 M-parameter model is 100 MB in float32 and 25 MB in int8.
  On a phone, quantisation is not an optimisation; it is the
  difference between shipping and not shipping.

FLEET VERSION MIX AFTER A MODEL UPDATE (7%/day adoption)
  days since release   on new model   on previous   older still
                   1           6.8%         60.6%         32.6%
                   7          38.7%         39.8%         21.4%
                  30          87.8%          8.0%          4.3%
                  90          99.8%          0.1%          0.1%
  Server-side rollback takes minutes; a bad on-device model lives in
  the field for months. Guard rails must be shipped, not deployed.
```

The two int8 rows differ only in where the scale factor is computed. With one
scale for the whole tensor, a single wide channel stretches the range and
every other channel is quantised coarsely -- 7.8% mean error and 8% of
predictions changing their argmax. With one scale per output channel, the
same 4x compression costs under 1% error. This is why "we quantised it and
accuracy dropped" is usually a configuration problem rather than a law of
nature. The same principle governs **quantisation-aware training**, which
simulates the rounding during training so the weights adapt to it.

The fleet table is the operational fact that surprises server-trained
engineers. A server rollback is a deploy; an on-device rollback does not
exist. Months after a release, a meaningful share of devices still runs an
older model, which has three consequences: ship conservative guard rails
inside the model artifact, keep a server-side kill switch that can disable
the on-device path and fall back to a remote call, and expect to support at
least three model versions simultaneously in your evaluation.

Runtimes you will meet, by target:

| Runtime | Target | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TensorFlow Lite / LiteRT | Android, MCUs | Delegates to NNAPI, GPU, DSP |
| Core ML | Apple devices | Compiles to the Neural Engine |
| ONNX Runtime Mobile | Cross-platform | Trimmed operator set |
| ExecuTorch | PyTorch on device | Ahead-of-time export |
| WebAssembly / WebGPU | Browser | No install, but tab memory limits |
| TFLite Micro | Microcontrollers | No OS, static memory, kilobytes |

Two practical warnings. First, **operator coverage is the usual blocker**: a
model converts only if every operation it uses exists in the target runtime,
and the fix is often to change the architecture rather than the exporter.
Second, **you lose your feedback loop**. If outcomes cannot be sent back,
you cannot measure the model's live accuracy at all; plan the telemetry (or a
privacy-preserving aggregate of it) before shipping, not after.

**Federated learning** is the logical extension when data must not leave the
device: each device trains on its local data and uploads only model updates,
which a server aggregates. It is genuinely useful for keyboards and health
signals, and it is considerably harder than it sounds -- non-IID data, device
availability, update compression, and the fact that updates themselves can
leak information without differential privacy.

> Key Takeaways
> - Edge inference buys latency, offline availability, privacy, and zero
>   per-request server cost.
> - It costs you elastic memory, a single hardware target, instant rollback,
>   and often your outcome logging.
> - Int8 quantisation gives roughly 4x compression; per-channel scales
>   preserve accuracy where a single per-tensor scale destroys it.
> - Pruning, distillation, and architecture choice compound with
>   quantisation; architecture usually matters most.
> - On a phone, compression decides whether the model ships at all, not just
>   how fast it runs.
> - Device fleets stay on old versions for months, so guard rails must be in
>   the artifact and a server-side kill switch must exist.
> - Operator coverage in the target runtime is the common conversion blocker.
> - Without outcome telemetry you cannot measure live accuracy; design the
>   feedback path before shipping.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Quantise a small trained network to int8 with per-tensor and
>    per-channel scales, and report size, mean error, and prediction
>    agreement for both.
> 2. Find the largest weight magnitude per channel in a real model and
>    identify the channel that would dominate a per-tensor scale.
> 3. Estimate the memory footprint of a model you use at fp32, fp16, and
>    int8, then decide which deployment targets it fits.
> 4. Design the telemetry for an on-device model that may not upload raw
>    inputs: what would you send, and what could you still measure?
> 5. Interview: You shipped an on-device model and discover a serious bug two
>    days later. What can you do? (Hint: the answer is mostly about what you
>    built before shipping, not about what you can deploy now.)


#### Inference Latency Optimization

Latency work fails when it starts with the model. The discipline is the same
as any performance work: measure the end-to-end budget, find the largest
term, fix that, and repeat. In model serving the largest term is usually one
of four things, and only one of them is the forward pass.

```text
  WHERE INFERENCE TIME GOES, AND THE LEVER FOR EACH

    request  ->  [ deserialise ]  ->  [ fetch features ]  ->  [ forward ]
                       |                     |                     |
                 binary protocol       cache / colocate     batch, quantise,
                 smaller payload       fewer round trips    compile, smaller
                       |                     |                     |
                       +------ [ postprocess + serialise ] ---------+
                                          |
                                    avoid copies,
                                    return only what is used

    Rule: the term you can measure is the term you can fix. Instrument
    every arrow before changing anything.
```

The techniques, roughly in order of return on effort:

1. **Batch.** Fixed per-call cost is paid once per call, not once per row.
2. **Cache.** The fastest inference is the one you do not run.
3. **Shrink the input path.** Fewer feature lookups, colocated stores,
   one round trip instead of five.
4. **Compile the model.** ONNX Runtime, TensorRT, OpenVINO, or `torch.compile`
   fuse operations and remove interpreter overhead, often 2-5x on CPU.
5. **Reduce precision.** fp16 or int8 where accuracy permits.
6. **Shrink the model.** Distillation or a smaller architecture, last because
   it requires retraining and re-validation.

The first two are worth quantifying, because both involve a trade that is
easy to get wrong in either direction.

```python
import time
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
D, H = 256, 512
W1 = rng.normal(size=(D, H)).astype(np.float32)
W2 = rng.normal(size=(H, 1)).astype(np.float32)

def infer(x):
    return np.maximum(x @ W1, 0) @ W2

print("PER-REQUEST COST VS BATCH SIZE (SAME MODEL, SAME HARDWARE)")
print("  batch   total ms   ms/request   throughput req/s")
per_req = {}
for b in (1, 4, 16, 64, 256):
    x = rng.normal(size=(b, D)).astype(np.float32)
    infer(x)                                        # warm up caches
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(200):
        infer(x)
    ms = (time.perf_counter() - t0) / 200 * 1000
    per_req[b] = ms / b
    print(f"  {b:5d}   {ms:8.3f}   {ms / b:10.4f}   {1000 / (ms / b):16,.0f}")
print("  Fixed overhead per call is amortised across the batch, and larger")
print("  matrices use the CPU's vector units and cache far better.")

# --- DYNAMIC BATCHING: TRADING A LITTLE LATENCY FOR A LOT OF THROUGHPUT. ---
# Service time of a real endpoint has two parts: a fixed cost paid once per
# CALL (deserialisation, copies, framework dispatch, GIL handoff) and a cost
# paid per ROW. Only the first is amortised by batching.
CALL_MS, ROW_MS = 0.80, 0.05

def service_ms(batch):
    return CALL_MS + ROW_MS * batch

def simulate(qps, window_ms, max_batch, n=60_000):
    arrive = np.cumsum(rng.exponential(1000 / qps, n))   # Poisson arrivals, ms
    lat, sizes, i, clock = [], [], 0, 0.0
    while i < n:
        start = max(arrive[i], clock)                    # server free, req waiting
        deadline = start + window_ms
        j = i
        while j < n and arrive[j] <= deadline and (j - i) < max_batch:
            j += 1                                       # all arrivals in window
        finish = max(start, min(deadline, arrive[j - 1])) + service_ms(j - i)
        lat.extend(finish - arrive[i:j])
        sizes.append(j - i)
        clock, i = finish, j
    return np.array(lat), np.array(sizes)

print(f"\nDYNAMIC BATCHING AT 3,000 req/s"
      f"  (unbatched capacity = {1000 / service_ms(1):,.0f} req/s)")
print("  configuration      mean batch   p50 ms   p99 ms   verdict")
configs = [("no batching", 0.0, 1)] + [(f"window {w:.0f} ms", w, 128)
                                       for w in (0.0, 1.0, 3.0, 10.0, 30.0)]
for label, w, max_batch in configs:
    lat, sizes = simulate(3000, w, max_batch)
    p50, p99 = np.percentile(lat, [50, 99])
    # If the queue is unstable, latency grows without bound over the run.
    growing = lat[-2000:].mean() > 5 * lat[:2000].mean() + 5
    print(f"  {label:16s}   {sizes.mean():10.1f}   {p50:8.2f} {p99:8.2f}"
          f"   {'QUEUE GROWING' if growing else 'stable':>14}")
print("  Serving one request at a time, the server cannot keep up at all and")
print("  latency diverges. A zero-delay batcher already helps, because")
print("  whatever queued during the last call is merged into the next one.")
print("  An explicit window trades p50 for larger batches; past a few ms it")
print("  buys throughput nobody needed and costs latency everybody notices.")

# --- CACHING: REQUEST POPULARITY IS NEVER UNIFORM. ---
print("\nCACHING PREDICTIONS UNDER A ZIPF REQUEST DISTRIBUTION")
N_KEYS = 100_000
zipf_p = 1 / np.arange(1, N_KEYS + 1) ** 1.05
zipf_p /= zipf_p.sum()
reqs = rng.choice(N_KEYS, size=500_000, p=zipf_p)
MISS_MS, HIT_MS, QPS = 25.0, 0.4, 3000
print("  cache entries   hit rate   mean latency   model calls/s left")
for size in (100, 1_000, 10_000, 50_000):
    hot = set(np.argsort(-zipf_p)[:size].tolist())       # cache the popular keys
    hit = np.isin(reqs, list(hot)).mean()
    print(f"  {size:13,}   {hit:8.1%}   {hit * HIT_MS + (1 - hit) * MISS_MS:10.2f} ms"
          f"   {QPS * (1 - hit):18,.0f}")
print("  Caching works only when the same input recurs; verify the key really")
print("  repeats before building one, and bound staleness with a TTL tied to")
print("  how fast the underlying features change.")
```

```text
PER-REQUEST COST VS BATCH SIZE (SAME MODEL, SAME HARDWARE)
  batch   total ms   ms/request   throughput req/s
      1      0.012       0.0121             82,318
      4      0.057       0.0142             70,625
     16      0.083       0.0052            191,780
     64      0.193       0.0030            331,698
    256      0.557       0.0022            459,295

  matrices use the CPU's vector units and cache far better.

DYNAMIC BATCHING AT 3,000 req/s  (unbatched capacity = 1,176 req/s)
  configuration      mean batch   p50 ms   p99 ms   verdict
  no batching               1.0   15387.44 30511.70    QUEUE GROWING
  window 0 ms               2.9       1.45     2.09           stable
  window 1 ms               5.5       1.71     3.15           stable
  window 3 ms              12.4       3.20     5.74           stable
  window 10 ms             37.1       8.51    15.06           stable
  window 30 ms            106.4      23.68    41.70           stable
  Serving one request at a time, the server cannot keep up at all and
  latency diverges. A zero-delay batcher already helps, because
  whatever queued during the last call is merged into the next one.
  An explicit window trades p50 for larger batches; past a few ms it
  buys throughput nobody needed and costs latency everybody notices.

CACHING PREDICTIONS UNDER A ZIPF REQUEST DISTRIBUTION
  cache entries   hit rate   mean latency   model calls/s left
            100      50.4%        12.61 ms                1,489
          1,000      68.8%         8.06 ms                  935
         10,000      85.3%         4.03 ms                  442
         50,000      95.7%         1.45 ms                  128
  Caching works only when the same input recurs; verify the key really
  repeats before building one, and bound staleness with a TTL tied to
  how fast the underlying features change.
```

The batch-size table shows the raw effect: the same model costs roughly 7x
less per request at batch 256 than at batch 1. That is not the model getting
faster -- it is the per-call overhead being divided among more rows, plus
better use of vector units and cache lines.

**Dynamic batching** turns that into a serving strategy: hold arriving
requests for a short window, then run them together. The simulation shows all
three regimes. Serving strictly one request at a time, the server's capacity
(1,176 req/s) is below the arrival rate (3,000 req/s), so the queue grows
without bound -- the classic "it was fine in staging" failure. A zero-delay
batcher fixes it without adding any deliberate wait, because requests that
queued during the previous call are merged into the next one. Longer windows
increase batch size and throughput, but from 3 ms onward you are buying
capacity nobody needs and paying for it in p50. Choose the window from the
latency budget, and set a maximum batch size so a traffic burst cannot create
a batch that blows the budget on its own.

**Caching** is the other large lever, and its viability is a property of your
traffic rather than your code. Real request distributions are usually Zipf-like:
caching the 1,000 most popular keys out of 100,000 already removes two thirds
of the work. Three rules keep caches honest: key on the exact feature vector
(or a hash of it), never on a user id alone; set a TTL derived from how fast
the underlying features change; and measure hit rate continuously, because a
cache whose hit rate quietly falls to 5% is pure added latency.

Two failure modes specific to ML services deserve naming. **Thread
oversubscription**: BLAS libraries default to one thread per host core, so
concurrent requests inside one replica fight each other; pin the thread count
and let the orchestrator provide parallelism. **Cold start**: the first
request after a deploy pays for lazy imports, JIT compilation, and
uninitialised caches, which can be seconds. Warm up the model in the
readiness path -- run a dummy prediction before reporting ready.

> Key Takeaways
> - Optimise from a measured budget; the forward pass is often a minority of
>   end-to-end latency.
> - Batching amortises fixed per-call cost and improves hardware utilisation,
>   commonly 5-10x per-request cost at large batches.
> - Dynamic batching with a short window converts that into throughput;
>   choose the window from the latency budget and cap the batch size.
> - An unbatched server whose capacity is below arrival rate does not get
>   slower gracefully -- its queue diverges.
> - Caching is viable when request keys repeat; Zipf-like traffic makes small
>   caches remove most of the work.
> - Key caches on the full feature vector, give them a TTL tied to feature
>   freshness, and alert on hit rate.
> - Compilation (ONNX Runtime, TensorRT, `torch.compile`) and reduced
>   precision are the next levers, before retraining a smaller model.
> - Pin BLAS thread counts and warm the model during readiness to avoid
>   oversubscription and cold-start spikes.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Measure per-request inference cost for your model at batch sizes 1, 8,
>    64, and 512, and compute the throughput gain from batching.
> 2. Simulate Poisson arrivals against your measured service time and find
>    the batching window that meets a 20 ms p99 target.
> 3. Log one day of production request keys and compute the cache hit rate
>    achievable with 100, 1,000, and 10,000 entries.
> 4. Add a warm-up prediction to your readiness probe and measure first-request
>    latency with and without it.
> 5. Interview: Your p99 latency doubles every Monday at 09:00 and recovers by
>    09:20. What is happening and how would you confirm it? (Hint: think about
>    what is empty at the start of a traffic surge, and what has to be
>    recreated before the service is warm again.)

### 15.2 ML Engineering Infrastructure

Deployment answers how a model reaches its consumers; this section covers the
systems that make producing a model repeatable rather than heroic -- where
features are defined and served, how model versions are tracked and promoted,
how experiments are recorded, what makes a training run reproducible, how
tests and delivery pipelines apply to something that is part code and part
data, and how the infrastructure underneath is itself described as code.


#### Feature Stores

Almost every serious ML system arrives at the same two problems, and a
feature store is the answer to both.

The first is **training-serving skew**. A feature -- "average order value over
the last 30 days" -- gets implemented twice: once in SQL over the warehouse
for training, once in application code against a live database for serving.
The two implementations differ in some small way: a timezone, an inclusive
bound, `log` versus `log1p`. The model was trained on one distribution and
serves on another, and nothing reports an error.

The second is **time travel**. Training rows need the feature value *as it was
at the moment of the event*, not as it is now. This is easy to say and easy
to get wrong, because the natural join -- match the label table to the
current feature table on user id -- silently inserts the future into the past.

A feature store is a system that owns feature definitions and serves them to
both worlds:

```text
  THE TWO HALVES OF A FEATURE STORE

    feature definition (written once)
        name: avg_order_value_30d
        entity: user_id
        source: orders
        transform: mean(amount) over 30 days
                 |
        +--------+--------+
        |                 |
   OFFLINE STORE      ONLINE STORE
   warehouse /        key-value store
   parquet, months    latest value only,
   of history         single-digit ms reads
        |                 |
   point-in-time      get_online_features(
   training set        entity=user_id)
        |                 |
     training          serving
        \_______________/
          the same definition, so the same numbers
```

Point-in-time correctness is the part worth seeing in code, because the wrong
version looks entirely reasonable:

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
N_USERS, N_TX = 400, 6000
DAY = pd.Timedelta("1D")
T0 = pd.Timestamp("2026-01-01")

# --- EVENTS TO SCORE: A TRANSACTION, ITS TIME, AND WHAT HAPPENED. ---
tx = pd.DataFrame({
    "user_id": rng.integers(0, N_USERS, N_TX),
    "ts": T0 + pd.to_timedelta(rng.uniform(0, 90, N_TX), unit="D"),
    "amount": rng.lognormal(3.4, 0.8, N_TX),
}).sort_values("ts", ignore_index=True)
tx["ts"] = tx["ts"].dt.floor("min")                 # minute resolution, readable
risky = rng.random(N_USERS) < 0.15                  # some users are risky
p = np.where(risky[tx.user_id], 0.30, 0.02)
tx["is_fraud"] = rng.random(N_TX) < p

# --- FEATURE HISTORY: A VALUE THAT CHANGES OVER TIME. ---
# chargebacks_30d rises AFTER a fraud is discovered, roughly 10 days later.
rows = []
for uid, g in tx.groupby("user_id"):
    cb = 0
    rows.append({"user_id": uid, "ts": T0, "chargebacks_30d": 0})
    for t, f in zip(g.ts, g.is_fraud):
        if f:
            cb += 1
            rows.append({"user_id": uid, "ts": t + 10 * DAY,   # discovered later
                         "chargebacks_30d": cb})
features = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("ts", ignore_index=True)

# --- JOIN 1 (WRONG): TAKE THE FEATURE'S CURRENT VALUE. ---
latest = features.sort_values("ts").groupby("user_id").tail(1)
naive = tx.merge(latest[["user_id", "chargebacks_30d"]], on="user_id", how="left")

# --- JOIN 2 (RIGHT): TAKE THE VALUE AS IT WAS AT THE EVENT'S TIMESTAMP. ---
pit = pd.merge_asof(tx.sort_values("ts"), features.sort_values("ts"),
                    on="ts", by="user_id", direction="backward")
pit["chargebacks_30d"] = pit["chargebacks_30d"].fillna(0)

def auc(score, label):
    r = pd.Series(score).rank().to_numpy()
    y = np.asarray(label, dtype=bool)
    n1, n0 = y.sum(), (~y).sum()
    return (r[y].sum() - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)

print("THE SAME FEATURE, TWO JOINS, ONE OF THEM A TIME MACHINE")
print(f"  rows: {len(tx):,}   fraud rate: {tx.is_fraud.mean():.1%}")
print(f"  naive join (current value)   AUC = {auc(naive.chargebacks_30d, naive.is_fraud):.3f}"
      "   <- offline result you would report")
print(f"  point-in-time join           AUC = {auc(pit.chargebacks_30d, pit.is_fraud):.3f}"
      "   <- what production can do")
print("  The naive join tells the model about chargebacks that had not")
print("  happened yet. Nothing in the code looks wrong; the timestamps do.")

# --- WHAT THE TWO JOINS PRODUCE FOR ONE USER. ---
u = int(tx[tx.is_fraud].user_id.value_counts().index[0])
show = pit[pit.user_id == u][["ts", "amount", "is_fraud", "chargebacks_30d"]].head(6)
show = show.merge(naive[naive.user_id == u][["ts", "chargebacks_30d"]],
                  on="ts", suffixes=("_pit", "_naive"))
print(f"\nUSER {u}: FEATURE VALUE UNDER EACH JOIN")
print(show.to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:8.2f}"))
print("  The naive column is constant: it is today's value, pasted onto")
print("  every historical row, including rows that caused it.")

# --- OFFLINE AND ONLINE MUST AGREE, WHICH IS THE OTHER HALF OF THE JOB. ---
print("\nTRAINING-SERVING SKEW: SAME USER, TWO CODE PATHS")
online = {"chargebacks_30d": 2.0, "amount": 41.2, "amount_log": np.log1p(41.2)}
offline = {"chargebacks_30d": 2.0, "amount": 41.2, "amount_log": np.log(41.2)}
for k in sorted(set(online) | set(offline)):
    a, b = online.get(k), offline.get(k)
    flag = "  <- SKEW" if a is not None and b is not None and abs(a - b) > 1e-9 else ""
    print(f"  {k:16s} online {a:8.4f}   offline {b:8.4f}{flag}")
print("  log1p versus log is a one-character difference that silently shifts")
print("  every prediction. One definition, one implementation, both paths.")
```

```text
THE SAME FEATURE, TWO JOINS, ONE OF THEM A TIME MACHINE
  rows: 6,000   fraud rate: 6.2%
  naive join (current value)   AUC = 0.910   <- offline result you would report
  point-in-time join           AUC = 0.686   <- what production can do
  The naive join tells the model about chargebacks that had not
  happened yet. Nothing in the code looks wrong; the timestamps do.

USER 23: FEATURE VALUE UNDER EACH JOIN
                 ts   amount  is_fraud  chargebacks_30d_pit  chargebacks_30d_naive
2026-01-03 07:04:00    59.48     False                    0                     10
2026-01-08 13:18:00   144.58      True                    0                     10
2026-01-12 15:43:00     3.81      True                    0                     10
2026-01-14 21:12:00    86.53     False                    0                     10
2026-01-16 22:36:00    14.05      True                    0                     10
2026-01-19 10:03:00    24.38     False                    1                     10
  The naive column is constant: it is today's value, pasted onto
  every historical row, including rows that caused it.

TRAINING-SERVING SKEW: SAME USER, TWO CODE PATHS
  amount           online  41.2000   offline  41.2000
  amount_log       online   3.7424   offline   3.7184  <- SKEW
  chargebacks_30d  online   2.0000   offline   2.0000
  log1p versus log is a one-character difference that silently shifts
  every prediction. One definition, one implementation, both paths.
```

The AUC gap is the whole lesson. The naive join produces a model that looks
strong offline and cannot possibly work in production, because the feature it
