relies on -- chargebacks recorded ten days *after* the transaction -- does not
exist at scoring time. The per-user table shows the mechanism: today's value
pasted onto every historical row, including the rows that caused it.

`merge_asof` is the correct primitive, and its arguments encode the rules:
join on time, group by entity, and search **backward** only. A feature store
does this for you across dozens of features with different update frequencies,
which is the part that is tedious rather than difficult -- and therefore the
part people skip.

The skew demonstration is the other half. Once definitions live in one place,
the online and offline paths compute the same expression, and a one-character
difference cannot get between them.

What a feature store gives you, beyond correctness:

| Capability | What it prevents |
| --- | --- |
| Single definition, two paths | Training-serving skew |
| Point-in-time joins | Label leakage from future values |
| Feature versioning | Silent redefinition breaking old models |
| Shared catalogue | Five teams building `days_since_signup` five times |
| Freshness monitoring | Serving a feature whose pipeline died yesterday |
| Backfill | New feature, months of training history, one command |

When do you need one? Not on day one. A single team with a batch model and
one warehouse gets most of the benefit from a shared SQL module and an
`as_of` parameter. The store earns its operational cost when you have
real-time serving *and* offline training, or several teams reusing features,
or features that are expensive to compute and worth computing once.

Two implementation notes that matter more than the vendor choice. **Decide
the freshness contract per feature** and monitor it: a feature that should
update hourly and last updated yesterday is a silent, model-wide bug.
And **treat feature definitions as versioned code** -- changing the window of
`avg_order_value_30d` from 30 to 28 days does not modify a feature, it
creates a new one, and models trained on the old definition must either be
retrained or keep reading the old version.

> Key Takeaways
> - Feature stores exist to solve training-serving skew and point-in-time
>   correctness, not to be a fashionable box in an architecture diagram.
> - Skew comes from computing a feature twice in two languages; one
>   definition serving both paths removes the category of bug.
> - Training rows need feature values as of the event timestamp; joining on
>   the current value inserts the future into the past.
> - `merge_asof` with `by=entity` and `direction="backward"` is the correct
>   join primitive; leaky joins look completely ordinary in code.
> - A leaky feature inflates offline metrics and produces a model that cannot
>   work in production, which is worse than a weak model.
> - The offline store holds history for training; the online store holds the
>   latest value for millisecond reads.
> - Give every feature a freshness contract and monitor it; a dead feature
>   pipeline is invisible to the model.
> - Feature definitions are versioned code: changing a window creates a new
>   feature rather than editing an old one.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a labelled event table and a feature history table, then compute a
>    training set both ways and compare a metric under each join.
> 2. Write a point-in-time join with `merge_asof` that also enforces a
>    maximum feature age, dropping rows whose latest value is too old.
> 3. Take one feature from your own project and write down its definition
>    precisely enough that two engineers would implement it identically.
> 4. Design freshness monitoring for three features with different update
>    frequencies, and state what alert each one needs.
> 5. Interview: A model's offline AUC is 0.94 and its production AUC is 0.71.
>    Where do you look first? (Hint: rank your candidate causes by how
>    cheaply you can test them, and start with the timestamps in the
>    training-set join.)


#### Model Registries and Versioning

`model_final_v3_REALLY_final.pkl` is a joke because it is a memory. The
underlying problem is real: a trained model is produced many times, by
several people, from changing data, and exactly one of those artifacts is
answering requests right now. A **model registry** is the system of record
that answers four questions at any moment:

1. **What is in production?** Not "which code" -- which artifact.
2. **Where did it come from?** Which commit, which data, which parameters.
3. **How did it get there?** Who promoted it, against which evaluation.
4. **What do we roll back to?** And is that artifact still loadable?

Note that version control does not answer these. Git versions code; the model
is a function of code *and* data *and* hyperparameters *and* a random seed.
Two runs of the same commit produce different artifacts, and both may be
legitimate.

The registry's core discipline is **immutability plus staging**. A registered
version is never edited: new training produces a new version. What changes is
a version's *stage* -- `none`, `staging`, `production`, `archived` -- and every
transition is logged with a reason. Promotion is guarded by rules, not by
judgement in a chat thread.

```python
import hashlib, json, time
from dataclasses import dataclass, field, asdict

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Version:
    """Immutable record of one trained artifact and everything it came from."""
    name: str
    version: int
    uri: str                      # content-addressed, never overwritten
    git_sha: str                  # code that produced it
    data_snapshot: str            # table version or dataset hash
    params: dict
    metrics: dict
    stage: str = "none"
    created: float = field(default_factory=time.time)

class Registry:
    GATES = {"auc": 0.78, "latency_p99_ms": 40}     # absolute floors

    def __init__(self):
        self.versions, self.log = {}, []

    def register(self, name, uri, git_sha, data_snapshot, params, metrics):
        n = len([v for v in self.versions.values() if v.name == name]) + 1
        v = Version(name, n, uri, git_sha, data_snapshot, params, metrics)
        self.versions[(name, n)] = v
        self.log.append(f"registered {name} v{n} from {git_sha[:7]}")
        return v

    def production(self, name):
        return next((v for v in self.versions.values()
                     if v.name == name and v.stage == "production"), None)

    def promote(self, name, version, to):
        v = self.versions[(name, version)]
        reasons = []
        if v.metrics.get("auc", 0) < self.GATES["auc"]:
            reasons.append(f"auc {v.metrics['auc']:.3f} below floor "
                           f"{self.GATES['auc']}")
        if v.metrics.get("latency_p99_ms", 1e9) > self.GATES["latency_p99_ms"]:
            reasons.append(f"p99 {v.metrics['latency_p99_ms']} ms over budget")
        cur = self.production(name)
        if to == "production" and cur and v.metrics["auc"] < cur.metrics["auc"]:
            reasons.append(f"auc {v.metrics['auc']:.3f} worse than live "
                           f"v{cur.version} ({cur.metrics['auc']:.3f})")
        if not v.data_snapshot or not v.git_sha:
            reasons.append("incomplete lineage")
        if reasons:
            self.log.append(f"BLOCKED {name} v{version} -> {to}: "
                            + "; ".join(reasons))
            return False
        if to == "production" and cur:                # only one at a time
            self.versions[(name, cur.version)] = replace_stage(cur, "archived")
            self.log.append(f"archived {name} v{cur.version}")
        self.versions[(name, version)] = replace_stage(v, to)
        self.log.append(f"promoted {name} v{version} -> {to}")
        return True

    def rollback(self, name, to_version):
        cur = self.production(name)
        if cur:
            self.versions[(name, cur.version)] = replace_stage(cur, "archived")
        self.versions[(name, to_version)] = replace_stage(
            self.versions[(name, to_version)], "production")
        self.log.append(f"ROLLBACK {name} -> v{to_version} "
                        f"(was v{cur.version if cur else '-'})")

def replace_stage(v, stage):
    d = asdict(v) | {"stage": stage}
    return Version(**d)

reg = Registry()
runs = [
    ("s3://models/fraud/9a1c", "4f2b9e1c", "orders@2026-08-01",
     {"depth": 6, "lr": 0.08}, {"auc": 0.802, "latency_p99_ms": 31}),
    ("s3://models/fraud/1de7", "7c19aa03", "orders@2026-09-01",
     {"depth": 9, "lr": 0.05}, {"auc": 0.771, "latency_p99_ms": 28}),
    ("s3://models/fraud/55b2", "7c19aa03", "orders@2026-09-01",
     {"depth": 8, "lr": 0.05}, {"auc": 0.818, "latency_p99_ms": 52}),
    ("s3://models/fraud/e004", "b2d40f77", "orders@2026-09-20",
     {"depth": 8, "lr": 0.05}, {"auc": 0.826, "latency_p99_ms": 33}),
]
for uri, sha, snap, params, metrics in runs:
    reg.register("fraud", uri, sha, snap, params, metrics)

for n in (1, 2, 3, 4):
    reg.promote("fraud", n, "production")
reg.rollback("fraud", 1)                             # incident: v4 misbehaves

print("REGISTRY TRANSITION LOG")
for line in reg.log:
    print(f"  {line}")

print("\nREGISTRY STATE")
print("  version   stage        auc    p99    git        data snapshot")
for (_, n), v in sorted(reg.versions.items()):
    print(f"  v{v.version:<8} {v.stage:11s} {v.metrics['auc']:.3f}"
          f" {v.metrics['latency_p99_ms']:5d}   {v.git_sha[:7]}   {v.data_snapshot}")

live = reg.production("fraud")
print(f"\nSERVING NOW: v{live.version} at {live.uri}")
print("  Every field needed to reproduce or audit this prediction is here:")
print("  the artifact, the code that built it, the data it saw, its")
print("  hyperparameters, its measured metrics, and how it got promoted.")

fingerprint = hashlib.sha256(
    json.dumps({"uri": live.uri, "git": live.git_sha,
                "data": live.data_snapshot}, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
print(f"  lineage fingerprint: {fingerprint[:16]}  (log this with predictions)")
```

```text
REGISTRY TRANSITION LOG
  registered fraud v1 from 4f2b9e1
  registered fraud v2 from 7c19aa0
  registered fraud v3 from 7c19aa0
  registered fraud v4 from b2d40f7
  promoted fraud v1 -> production
  BLOCKED fraud v2 -> production: auc 0.771 below floor 0.78; auc 0.771 worse than live v1 (0.802)
  BLOCKED fraud v3 -> production: p99 52 ms over budget
  archived fraud v1
  promoted fraud v4 -> production
  ROLLBACK fraud -> v1 (was v4)

REGISTRY STATE
  version   stage        auc    p99    git        data snapshot
  v1        production  0.802    31   4f2b9e1   orders@2026-08-01
  v2        none        0.771    28   7c19aa0   orders@2026-09-01
  v3        none        0.818    52   7c19aa0   orders@2026-09-01
  v4        archived    0.826    33   b2d40f7   orders@2026-09-20

SERVING NOW: v1 at s3://models/fraud/9a1c
  Every field needed to reproduce or audit this prediction is here:
  the artifact, the code that built it, the data it saw, its
  hyperparameters, its measured metrics, and how it got promoted.
  lineage fingerprint: 1e2ed102ac3d8eb8  (log this with predictions)
```

Read the transition log as an audit trail, which is exactly what it is. v2
was blocked twice over: it failed the absolute quality floor *and* was worse
than the live model. v3 passed on quality and failed on latency -- a reminder
that "better" is multi-dimensional and the registry is where those dimensions
get enforced. v4 passed and displaced v1, which was archived rather than
deleted, which is what made the rollback possible thirty seconds later.

Four properties of that design are worth adopting whatever tool you use
(MLflow Model Registry, Weights & Biases, SageMaker, Vertex, or a table you
write yourself):

- **Content-addressed artifact URIs.** `s3://models/fraud/9a1c`, not
  `s3://models/fraud/latest`. A pointer that can be overwritten means a
  restarted pod can silently change models.
- **Lineage is mandatory, not optional metadata.** Code commit and data
  snapshot must be present for promotion to be allowed; without them the
  version cannot be reproduced or audited.
- **Gates are code.** Absolute floors plus a comparison against the incumbent,
  evaluated automatically. A human approval step can sit *after* the gates,
  never instead of them.
- **Archive, never delete.** Rollback requires the previous artifact to exist
  and still load, which is worth testing periodically rather than assuming.

Versioning in ML has one more dimension than software versioning, and being
explicit about it prevents confusion:

| What is versioned | Mechanism | Changes when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Code | Git commit | Someone edits the pipeline |
| Data | Snapshot, table version, DVC hash | The source is refreshed |
| Features | Definition version in the feature store | A window or formula changes |
| Model artifact | Registry version | Any training run completes |
| Deployment | Image digest plus config | Anything is released |

The last line ties back to serving: **log the model version and the lineage
fingerprint with every prediction**. When someone asks in six months why a
particular customer was declined, that logged fingerprint is the difference
between an answer and an apology. In regulated settings it is not optional.

> Key Takeaways
> - A registry answers what is live, where it came from, how it got promoted,
>   and what to roll back to.
> - Git versions code, but a model is code plus data plus parameters plus
>   seed, so code versioning alone cannot identify an artifact.
> - Registered versions are immutable; retraining creates a new version and
>   only the stage changes.
> - Promotion gates belong in code: absolute floors plus a comparison with
>   the incumbent on every dimension that matters, including latency.
> - Use content-addressed artifact URIs; a mutable "latest" pointer lets a
>   restart change the model silently.
> - Require lineage (commit, data snapshot, parameters) for promotion, or
>   reproduction and audit become impossible.
> - Archive rather than delete, and verify periodically that the rollback
>   target still loads.
> - Log the model version and lineage fingerprint with every prediction.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement a minimal registry with immutable versions, stages, and a
>    promotion gate, then show it blocking a worse model.
> 2. Add a rule that blocks promotion if the candidate was trained on an
>    older data snapshot than the incumbent, and test it.
> 3. Take your last three trained models and write down, for each, the exact
>    commit and data snapshot used; note which ones you cannot reconstruct.
> 4. Design the prediction log schema for an audit that must reconstruct any
>    decision made in the past two years.
> 5. Interview: Production is serving a model nobody can reproduce, and the
>    person who trained it has left. What do you do, in what order? (Hint:
>    separate "make the current state safe and documented" from "recreate the
>    artifact", and consider which one is actually urgent.)


#### Experiment Tracking

Model development is a search. You try a feature set, a model family, a
learning rate; you look at a number; you try again. Fifty runs later somebody
asks which configuration produced the result in the slide, and the honest
answer is a shrug. **Experiment tracking** is the practice of recording every
run automatically, so that the search is a dataset rather than a memory.

A run record has four parts, and leaving any of them out makes the rest less
useful:

| Part | Examples | Why it is needed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Parameters | depth, learning rate, seed, feature set | Reproduce and compare |
| Metrics | val AUC, test AUC, training time, cost | Judge the run |
| Context | git commit, dataset version, environment | Trace back to inputs |
| Artifacts | model file, plots, confusion matrix | Inspect without rerunning |

The temptation is to log only the winner. Resist it: the value of tracking
comes from the *population* of runs, which supports questions a single run
cannot answer -- which hyperparameter actually matters, how much variance a
seed contributes, whether last quarter's result is still reproducible.

```python
import itertools, json, time
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

class Tracker:
    """The smallest experiment tracker that is still useful."""
    def __init__(self):
        self.runs = []

    def log(self, params, metrics, tags):
        self.runs.append({"run_id": f"r{len(self.runs):03d}",
                          "params": params, "metrics": metrics, "tags": tags,
                          "ts": time.time()})

    def best(self, metric, k=5):
        return sorted(self.runs, key=lambda r: -r["metrics"][metric])[:k]

# --- A SWEEP: EVERY RUN IS RECORDED, NOT JUST THE ONE THAT WON. ---
tr = Tracker()
TRUE = {"depth": {4: 0.780, 6: 0.800, 8: 0.802, 10: 0.801},   # real effect
        "lr": {0.01: 0.795, 0.05: 0.797, 0.2: 0.796}}         # near-none
for depth, lr, seed in itertools.product([4, 6, 8, 10], [0.01, 0.05, 0.2],
                                         range(8)):
    true_auc = TRUE["depth"][depth] + TRUE["lr"][lr] - 0.796
    val = true_auc + rng.normal(0, 0.012)         # small validation set noise
    test = true_auc + rng.normal(0, 0.012)        # independent, unseen
    tr.log({"depth": depth, "lr": lr, "seed": seed},
           {"val_auc": round(val, 4), "test_auc": round(test, 4)},
           {"dataset": "orders@2026-09-01", "git": "7c19aa0"})

print(f"LOGGED {len(tr.runs)} RUNS")
print("  run    depth     lr   seed   val_auc   test_auc")
for r in tr.best("val_auc", 5):
    p, m = r["params"], r["metrics"]
    print(f"  {r['run_id']}   {p['depth']:5d} {p['lr']:6.2f} {p['seed']:6d}"
          f"   {m['val_auc']:7.4f}   {m['test_auc']:8.4f}")

# --- WHAT THE SWEEP ACTUALLY LEARNED, WHICH IS NOT THE TOP ROW. ---
print("\nMARGINAL EFFECT OF EACH HYPERPARAMETER (MEAN OVER ALL OTHER SETTINGS)")
for key in ("depth", "lr"):
    vals = sorted({r["params"][key] for r in tr.runs})
    print(f"  {key:6s}" + "".join(f"{v:>10}" for v in vals))
    means = [np.mean([r["metrics"]["val_auc"] for r in tr.runs
                      if r["params"][key] == v]) for v in vals]
    print("        " + "".join(f"{m:10.4f}" for m in means))
print("  depth matters and saturates after 6; the lr spread is smaller than")
print("  the per-run noise (sd 0.012), so it is not evidence of anything.")
print("  A single best run cannot tell you this; the population of runs can.")

# --- THE WINNER'S CURSE: SELECTING ON VALIDATION OVERFITS VALIDATION. ---
print("\nSELECTING THE BEST OF N RUNS BY VALIDATION SCORE")
print("  runs considered   best val_auc   its test_auc   optimism")
for n in (1, 5, 20, 96):
    picks = []
    for _ in range(3000):                          # repeat the whole selection
        sub = rng.choice(len(tr.runs), size=n, replace=False)
        i = max(sub, key=lambda j: tr.runs[j]["metrics"]["val_auc"])
        picks.append((tr.runs[i]["metrics"]["val_auc"],
                      tr.runs[i]["metrics"]["test_auc"]))
    v, t = np.mean([p[0] for p in picks]), np.mean([p[1] for p in picks])
    print(f"  {n:15d}   {v:12.4f}   {t:12.4f}   {v - t:+8.4f}")
print("  The more runs you compare, the more the winner's validation score is")
print("  luck. Report the held-out test score of the selected run, once.")

print("\nWHAT EVERY RUN RECORD MUST CONTAIN")
print(json.dumps({k: v for k, v in tr.best("val_auc", 1)[0].items()
                  if k != "ts"}, indent=2)[:420])
print("  Params, metrics, dataset version, and code version. Without the last")
print("  two, a run is a number with no way back to what produced it.")
```

```text
LOGGED 96 RUNS
  run    depth     lr   seed   val_auc   test_auc
  r081      10   0.05      1    0.8275     0.7921
  r069       8   0.20      5    0.8260     0.8370
  r059       8   0.05      3    0.8222     0.8001
  r095      10   0.20      7    0.8217     0.7988
  r063       8   0.05      7    0.8206     0.7887

MARGINAL EFFECT OF EACH HYPERPARAMETER (MEAN OVER ALL OTHER SETTINGS)
  depth          4         6         8        10
            0.7829    0.7966    0.8016    0.8016
  lr          0.01      0.05       0.2
            0.7918    0.7996    0.7957
  depth matters and saturates after 6; the lr spread is smaller than
  the per-run noise (sd 0.012), so it is not evidence of anything.
  A single best run cannot tell you this; the population of runs can.

SELECTING THE BEST OF N RUNS BY VALIDATION SCORE
  runs considered   best val_auc   its test_auc   optimism
                1         0.7956         0.7950    +0.0006
                5         0.8116         0.8013    +0.0103
               20         0.8214         0.8037    +0.0177
               96         0.8275         0.7921    +0.0354
  The more runs you compare, the more the winner's validation score is
  luck. Report the held-out test score of the selected run, once.

WHAT EVERY RUN RECORD MUST CONTAIN
{
  "run_id": "r081",
  "params": {
    "depth": 10,
    "lr": 0.05,
    "seed": 1
  },
  "metrics": {
    "val_auc": 0.8275,
    "test_auc": 0.7921
  },
  "tags": {
    "dataset": "orders@2026-09-01",
    "git": "7c19aa0"
  }
}
  Params, metrics, dataset version, and code version. Without the last
  two, a run is a number with no way back to what produced it.
```

The marginal-effect table is the first payoff. Reading the leaderboard, you
would conclude that `depth=10, lr=0.05` is the answer. Averaging over the
whole grid shows something more useful and more durable: depth matters up to
6 and then saturates, while the learning-rate spread is smaller than the
noise between seeds. That conclusion survives the next dataset; the winning
row does not.

The winner's-curse table is the second, and it is the part most teams learn
late. When runs differ only by noise, the maximum of N validation scores is
biased upward, and the bias grows with N. Selecting the best of 96 runs here
produces a validation score 0.035 too optimistic -- larger than most reported
model improvements. Three defences follow directly:

- **Select on validation, report on test**, and touch the test set once.
- **Repeat seeds** and compare configurations by their mean, not by their
  best run.
- **Treat a small improvement from a large sweep as unproven** until it
  survives a fresh split or a live test.

Practical habits that make tracking worth its cost:

- **Log automatically, from inside the training code.** Anything requiring a
  person to remember will be skipped on the run that matters.
- **Log the dataset version and the commit**, or runs cannot be reproduced.
- **Log failures too.** "This configuration diverges" is a result, and
  rediscovering it three months later is a waste.
- **Name experiments after the question**, not after the model. `2026-09
  does-adding-device-features-help` beats `xgb_test7`.
- **Record cost and training time** alongside accuracy; a 0.2% gain for four
  times the training cost is a decision, and it needs both numbers.

Tools (MLflow, Weights & Biases, Neptune, Comet, or a database table) differ
in the interface, not in the idea. The minimum viable version is the class in
the example plus a JSON file per run in object storage.

> Key Takeaways
> - Tracking turns model development from a memory into a queryable dataset
>   of runs.
> - A run record needs parameters, metrics, context (commit, dataset), and
>   artifacts; missing context makes the rest unreproducible.
> - Log every run, including failures, automatically from inside the training
>   code.
> - The population of runs answers which hyperparameters matter; the
>   leaderboard's top row does not.
> - Selecting the best of N runs biases the validation score upward, and the
>   bias grows with N.
> - Select on validation, report on test, and treat small gains from big
>   sweeps as unproven.
> - Repeat seeds and compare configurations by their means when differences
>   are near the noise level.
> - Record cost and runtime with accuracy so the trade is visible at decision
>   time.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Instrument a training script so every run writes parameters, metrics,
>    commit, and dataset version to a file without any manual step.
> 2. Run a small grid with three seeds per configuration and compute each
>    hyperparameter's marginal effect and the seed-to-seed standard deviation.
> 3. Simulate selecting the best of N runs where all configurations are
>    equally good, and plot the optimism as a function of N.
> 4. Take a recent experiment of yours and try to reproduce its number from
>    the record alone; list everything that was missing.
> 5. Interview: A colleague reports that their new model improves validation
>    AUC from 0.802 to 0.818 after a 400-run sweep. What do you ask? (Hint:
>    one question is about the test set, one is about seeds, and one is about
>    how many other things were also tried.)


#### Reproducible Training Pipelines

Reproducibility is not a virtue for its own sake. It is the property that
makes three ordinary requests answerable: "why is this quarter's model worse
than last quarter's?", "can you retrain it with the fraud cases included?",
and "the regulator wants to know how this decision was made". Without it,
each of those becomes a research project.

A training pipeline is reproducible when the same inputs produce the same
artifact. That requires nailing down more than most people expect:

| Source of variation | How it bites | Control |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Data snapshot | Table refreshed between runs | Versioned snapshot or hash |
| Row order | Upstream query without `ORDER BY` | Deterministic sort key |
| Split assignment | Reshuffles when data grows | Hash of a stable key |
| Sampling, init, dropout | Different draws | Seed every RNG in use |
| Thread count | Changes summation order | Pin thread environment variables |
| Library versions | Changed defaults, changed kernels | Lock file, container digest |
| Hardware | Different GPU kernels, different FMA | Record it; do not assume it away |
| Wall-clock logic | `today()` inside a feature | Pass the run date as a parameter |

Two of those rows are worth seeing, because they are the ones people believe
they have already handled.

```python
import hashlib
import numpy as np

# --- SPLIT STABILITY: THE SAME CODE, A WEEK LATER, DIFFERENT SPLIT. ---
users_v1 = [f"user-{i}" for i in range(10_000)]
users_v2 = users_v1 + [f"user-{i}" for i in range(10_000, 12_000)]  # a week of growth

def random_split(users, seed=0, frac=0.8):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)               # seeded, and still unstable
    idx = rng.permutation(len(users))
    train = set(np.array(users)[idx[:int(frac * len(users))]])
    return {u: ("train" if u in train else "test") for u in users}

def hash_split(users, salt="split-v1", frac=0.8):
    out = {}
    for u in users:                                 # depends on the KEY only
        h = int(hashlib.md5(f"{salt}:{u}".encode()).hexdigest()[:8], 16)
        out[u] = "train" if (h % 10_000) / 10_000 < frac else "test"
    return out

reordered = list(np.random.default_rng(1).permutation(users_v1))  # no ORDER BY
print("USERS THAT SWITCHED BETWEEN TRAIN AND TEST, SAME CODE AND SEED")
print("  split strategy      2,000 new rows arrive   upstream returns rows"
      " in a new order")
for name, fn in [("seeded shuffle", random_split), ("hash of user id", hash_split)]:
    base = fn(users_v1)
    grown = fn(users_v2)
    shuffled = fn(reordered)
    g = sum(1 for u in users_v1 if base[u] != grown[u]) / len(users_v1)
    r = sum(1 for u in users_v1 if base[u] != shuffled[u]) / len(users_v1)
    print(f"  {name:18s} {g:21.1%} {r:33.1%}")
print("  A seeded shuffle is reproducible only for a FIXED dataset. Hashing")
print("  the key is reproducible for a growing one, which is the real case.")

# --- SEEDS ARE NECESSARY AND NOT SUFFICIENT. ---
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.normal(size=1_000_000).astype(np.float32)
serial = np.float32(0)
for v in x[:200_000]:                               # strict left-to-right
    serial += v
chunked = x[:200_000].reshape(8, -1).sum(axis=1).sum()   # 8 partial sums
print(f"\nFLOAT ADDITION IS NOT ASSOCIATIVE")
print(f"  serial sum      {serial:.8f}")
print(f"  8 partial sums  {chunked:.8f}")
print(f"  difference      {abs(serial - chunked):.8f}"
      "  <- same data, same seed, different order")
print("  Thread counts, GPU kernels, and library versions all change summation")
print("  order. 'Set the seed' controls sampling, not arithmetic.")

# --- WHAT REPRODUCIBILITY ACTUALLY REQUIRES: A FINGERPRINT PER STEP. ---
def fp(*parts):
    return hashlib.sha256("|".join(map(str, parts)).encode()).hexdigest()[:10]

pipeline = [
    ("load_raw",      {"snapshot": "orders@2026-09-01"}, "def load_raw(): ..."),
    ("clean",         {"drop_nulls": True},              "def clean(df): ..."),
    ("features",      {"window_days": 30},               "def features(df): ..."),
    ("train",         {"depth": 8, "lr": 0.05, "seed": 7}, "def train(X, y): ..."),
    ("evaluate",      {"split": "time", "cutoff": "2026-08-15"}, "def eval(m): ..."),
]

def run(pipeline, cache):
    upstream, fired = "root", []
    for name, params, code in pipeline:
        key = fp(name, sorted(params.items()), code, upstream)
        hit = key in cache
        if not hit:
            cache.add(key)
            fired.append(name)
        upstream = key                              # each step depends on the last
    return fired

cache = set()
print("\nCONTENT-ADDRESSED PIPELINE CACHE")
print(f"  first run             re-executes: {run(pipeline, cache)}")
print(f"  unchanged rerun       re-executes: {run(pipeline, cache) or ['nothing']}")
changed = [(n, dict(p, **({"lr": 0.08} if n == "train" else {})), c)
           for n, p, c in pipeline]
print(f"  learning rate changed re-executes: {run(changed, cache)}")
newdata = [(n, dict(p, **({"snapshot": "orders@2026-09-08"} if n == "load_raw"
                          else {})), c) for n, p, c in pipeline]
print(f"  new data snapshot     re-executes: {run(newdata, cache)}")
print("  Downstream steps rerun because their fingerprint includes the")
print("  upstream one. This is what makes a pipeline both fast and honest:")
print("  nothing is reused unless every input that produced it is identical.")
```

```text
USERS THAT SWITCHED BETWEEN TRAIN AND TEST, SAME CODE AND SEED
  split strategy      2,000 new rows arrive   upstream returns rows in a new order
  seeded shuffle                      5.0%                             32.1%
  hash of user id                     0.0%                              0.0%
  A seeded shuffle is reproducible only for a FIXED dataset. Hashing
  the key is reproducible for a growing one, which is the real case.

FLOAT ADDITION IS NOT ASSOCIATIVE
  serial sum      26.13436699
  8 partial sums  26.13507843
  difference      0.00071144  <- same data, same seed, different order
  Thread counts, GPU kernels, and library versions all change summation
  order. 'Set the seed' controls sampling, not arithmetic.

CONTENT-ADDRESSED PIPELINE CACHE
  first run             re-executes: ['load_raw', 'clean', 'features', 'train', 'evaluate']
  unchanged rerun       re-executes: ['nothing']
  learning rate changed re-executes: ['train', 'evaluate']
  new data snapshot     re-executes: ['load_raw', 'clean', 'features', 'train', 'evaluate']
  Downstream steps rerun because their fingerprint includes the
  upstream one. This is what makes a pipeline both fast and honest:
  nothing is reused unless every input that produced it is identical.
```

**The split.** A seeded shuffle is reproducible only over a fixed dataset.
Add a week of users and 5% of the old ones silently change sides; let an
upstream query return rows in a different order and a third of them do. Once
a user who was in test is in train, every comparison across those two runs is
invalid, and nothing anywhere reports an error. Hashing a stable key gives an
assignment that depends only on the key -- stable under growth, reordering,
and reruns, and identical in SQL, Python, and Spark. Include a salt so you
can deliberately create a fresh split when you want one.

**The seed.** Seeding is necessary and not sufficient. Floating-point
addition is not associative, so the order in which partial sums are combined
changes the result in the seventh decimal. Change the thread count, the GPU,
or the library version, and summation order changes with it. Those
differences are usually irrelevant -- and occasionally they flip a threshold
comparison or a tie-break. The practical rule: aim for **bitwise
reproducibility on identical hardware and environment**, and for **statistical
reproducibility** (the same conclusions within a stated tolerance) across
environments. Pin what you can, record what you cannot, and assert on
tolerances rather than on exact equality.

**Fingerprinting steps** is what makes a reproducible pipeline usable day to
day. Each step's cache key combines its code, its parameters, and its
upstream key, so an unchanged rerun does nothing, a hyperparameter change
reruns training and evaluation only, and a new data snapshot correctly
invalidates everything. This is the mechanism behind Make, DVC, Dagster,
Airflow's data-aware scheduling, and Kubeflow -- and it is worth understanding
independently of any of them, because a hand-rolled version in fifty lines
is often enough.

Practices that follow from all of this:

- **Parameterise the run date.** A feature computed with `today()` produces a
  different training set every day, and backfills are impossible.
- **Put configuration in files, not in code.** One config per run, committed
  or logged with the run.
- **Make steps idempotent and rerunnable.** Writing to a partition keyed by
  the run date beats appending to a table.
- **Separate the pipeline from the notebook.** A notebook is where you decide
  what the pipeline should do; it is not the pipeline.

> Key Takeaways
> - Reproducibility exists so that comparison, retraining, and audit are
>   routine rather than heroic.
> - Data version, row order, split assignment, seeds, thread counts, library
>   versions, and hardware all change results.
> - A seeded shuffle is stable only for a fixed dataset; hashing a stable key
>   survives growth and reordering.
> - Once rows migrate between train and test, cross-run comparisons are
>   invalid and nothing raises an error.
> - Seeds control sampling, not arithmetic; float addition is not
>   associative, so thread count and hardware change results slightly.
> - Target bitwise reproducibility within one environment and statistical
>   reproducibility across environments, with explicit tolerances.
> - Fingerprint each step by code, parameters, and upstream key so caching is
>   both fast and correct.
> - Parameterise the run date, keep configuration in files, and make steps
>   idempotent.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Replace a random train/test split with a hash-based one and verify that
>    assignments are unchanged after adding rows and reordering them.
> 2. Run the same training twice with different thread counts and report the
>    largest difference in predictions.
> 3. Write a fingerprint function for a three-step pipeline and demonstrate
>    which steps rerun for each kind of change.
> 4. Find every use of the current date or time in one of your pipelines and
>    convert them into explicit parameters.
> 5. Interview: Your model scored 0.81 AUC in March and the same code scores
>    0.78 today. List the possible causes in the order you would check them.
>    (Hint: only one of them is "the model got worse"; most involve something
>    that changed underneath the code.)


#### CI/CD for Machine Learning

Continuous integration for ordinary software asks one question: does the code
still do what the tests say it should? For machine learning there are three
inputs -- code, data, and the trained artifact -- and each needs its own
answer. A green test suite that only covers the code proves very little about
the model.

The pipeline has more stages than a web service's, and they run at different
times:

```text
  WHAT RUNS WHEN

  on every commit           on data arrival           on model candidate
  -----------------         ----------------          ------------------
  lint, type check          schema validation         behavioural tests
  unit tests (features)     null/range/volume         metric gates
  pipeline smoke test       distribution checks       fairness slices
  (tiny sample, minutes)    freshness                 latency + memory
        |                         |                         |
        +-------------------------+-------------------------+
                                  |
                          registry: register version
                                  |
                          promote -> staging
                                  |
                       shadow / canary (see 15.3)
                                  |
                              production
```

The distinctively ML part is the middle column of tests. Model quality is not
binary, so "does it pass?" has to be turned into explicit, arguable claims.
Four kinds are standard, and the last two are the ones teams usually lack:

| Test type | Question | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit | Is this transformation correct? | `days_since()` handles month ends |
| Data | Is the input sane? | No nulls in `amount`, volume within 20% |
| Metric gate | Is it good enough? | AUC above floor and near the incumbent |
| Behavioural | Does it behave sensibly? | New device must not reduce fraud risk |

Behavioural tests deserve the emphasis. They come in three flavours, borrowed
from the CheckList methodology: **minimum functionality** (obvious cases the
model must get right), **invariance** (changes that must not alter the
prediction), and **directional expectation** (changes that must move the
prediction a known way). They encode domain knowledge as executable claims,
which is exactly what an aggregate metric cannot do.

```python
import time
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(13)
FEATURES = ["amount", "hour", "n_prior", "device_is_new"]

def make_model(weights):
    w = np.array(weights, dtype=float)
    def predict(rows):                              # rows: (n, 4) array
        return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(rows @ w - 3.0)))
    return predict

# The candidate has a sign error on device_is_new: a new device now LOWERS
# risk. Offline AUC barely notices, because the feature is rare.
good = make_model([0.010, 0.02, -0.15, 1.50])
candidate = make_model([0.010, 0.02, -0.15, -1.50])

def golden_set(n=4000):
    x = np.column_stack([rng.lognormal(3.6, 0.9, n), rng.integers(0, 24, n),
                         rng.poisson(3, n), (rng.random(n) < 0.01).astype(float)])
    logit = 0.010 * x[:, 0] + 0.02 * x[:, 1] - 0.15 * x[:, 2] + 1.50 * x[:, 3] - 3
    y = rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit))
    return x, y

X, y = golden_set()

def auc(s, label):
    order = np.argsort(s)
    r = np.empty(len(s)); r[order] = np.arange(1, len(s) + 1)
    n1, n0 = label.sum(), (~label).sum()
    return (r[label].sum() - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)

# --- THE TEST SUITE THAT RUNS ON EVERY MODEL CANDIDATE. ---
def test_minimum_functionality(m):
    """Obvious cases the model must get right."""
    tiny = np.array([[5.0, 14, 40, 0]])             # small, known, many priors
    huge = np.array([[9000.0, 3, 0, 1]])            # large, 3 a.m., new device
    return float(m(tiny)[0]) < 0.2 and float(m(huge)[0]) > 0.8

def test_directional_new_device(m, n=500):
    """Everything else equal, a new device must not REDUCE risk."""
    base = X[:n].copy(); base[:, 3] = 0
    alt = base.copy();   alt[:, 3] = 1
    return bool(np.all(m(alt) >= m(base) - 1e-9))

def test_invariance_row_order(m):
    """Predictions must not depend on the order rows arrive in."""
    idx = rng.permutation(len(X))
    return bool(np.allclose(m(X)[idx], m(X[idx])))

def test_performance_floor(m, floor=0.65):
    return auc(m(X), y) >= floor

def test_no_regression(m, live, margin=0.02):   # run-to-run tolerance
    return auc(m(X), y) >= auc(live(X), y) - margin

def test_latency(m, budget_ms=5.0):
    one = X[:1]
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(2000):
        m(one)
    return (time.perf_counter() - t0) / 2000 * 1000 < budget_ms

def test_schema(m):
    """The model must reject the wrong number of columns, not guess."""
    try:
        m(np.zeros((1, len(FEATURES) - 1)))
        return False
    except ValueError:
        return True

SUITE = [("minimum functionality", test_minimum_functionality),
         ("directional: new device", test_directional_new_device),
         ("invariance: row order", test_invariance_row_order),
         ("performance floor", test_performance_floor),
         ("no regression vs live", lambda m: test_no_regression(m, good)),
         ("latency budget", test_latency),
         ("schema rejection", test_schema)]

for label, model in [("LIVE MODEL", good), ("CANDIDATE (sign error)", candidate)]:
    print(f"{label}   golden-set AUC = {auc(model(X), y):.4f}")
    failed = 0
    for name, fn in SUITE:
        ok = fn(model)
        failed += not ok
        print(f"  [{'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}] {name}")
    print(f"  -> {'promote' if not failed else f'BLOCKED, {failed} test(s) failed'}\n")

print("The candidate's AUC is 0.016 lower -- inside the 0.02 tolerance teams")
print("use for run-to-run noise, because the broken feature is rare. Every")
print("metric gate passes. Only the behavioural test, which states the")
print("expectation in words a human can argue about, catches the sign error.")
```

```text
LIVE MODEL   golden-set AUC = 0.6904
  [PASS] minimum functionality
  [PASS] directional: new device
  [PASS] invariance: row order
  [PASS] performance floor
  [PASS] no regression vs live
  [PASS] latency budget
  [PASS] schema rejection
  -> promote

CANDIDATE (sign error)   golden-set AUC = 0.6747
  [PASS] minimum functionality
  [FAIL] directional: new device
  [PASS] invariance: row order
  [PASS] performance floor
  [PASS] no regression vs live
  [PASS] latency budget
  [PASS] schema rejection
  -> BLOCKED, 1 test(s) failed

The candidate's AUC is 0.016 lower -- inside the 0.02 tolerance teams
use for run-to-run noise, because the broken feature is rare. Every
metric gate passes. Only the behavioural test, which states the
expectation in words a human can argue about, catches the sign error.
```

That is the argument for behavioural tests in one run. A sign error on a rare
but important feature moved AUC by 0.016 -- comfortably inside the tolerance
any team would set for run-to-run variation. Every metric gate passed. The
only thing that caught it was a test asserting something a human believes
about the world: a brand-new device does not make a transaction *safer*.

The delivery half is more mundane, and mostly consists of not skipping steps:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/model-ci.yml (shape, not a full file)
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  code:
    steps:
      - run: ruff check . && mypy src/
      - run: pytest tests/unit -q                 # feature logic, seconds
      - run: pytest tests/pipeline -q --sample 1000   # end-to-end, minutes
  model:
    needs: code
    steps:
      - run: python -m pipeline.train --config configs/ci.yaml --seed 7
      - run: pytest tests/behavioural -q          # invariance, directional
      - run: python -m pipeline.gate              # metric + latency floors
      - run: python -m pipeline.register --stage staging
```

Four rules that separate a useful ML pipeline from a slow one:

- **Tier the tests by cost.** Unit tests on every commit, a small-sample
  pipeline run on every pull request, a full training run nightly or on
  demand. If CI takes two hours, people will stop running it.
- **Version the test data.** A golden evaluation set must be fixed and
  checked in (or snapshotted), or your gates move on their own.
- **Deploy the artifact, not the notebook.** The thing that passed the gates
  is the thing that ships, by digest.
- **Automate promotion, keep a human for the decision.** Gates run
  automatically; a person can still be required to approve production, but
  only after everything mechanical has passed.

**Continuous training** extends the same pipeline to run on a schedule or a
trigger (drift detected, enough new labels accumulated). It is only safe if
the gates are strong -- automated retraining without behavioural tests and
metric floors is an automated way to deploy a bad model at 3 a.m.

> Key Takeaways
> - ML CI must cover code, data, and the trained artifact; code tests alone
>   prove almost nothing about model quality.
> - Metric gates check magnitude; behavioural tests check meaning, and only
>   the latter catches a plausible-looking sign error.
> - Use minimum functionality, invariance, and directional expectation tests
>   to encode domain knowledge as assertions.
> - Tier tests by cost: fast unit tests per commit, sampled pipeline runs per
>   PR, full training on a schedule.
> - Fix and version the golden evaluation set, or gates drift silently.
> - Promote the artifact that passed the gates, by digest, rather than
>   retraining at deploy time.
> - Automate gates; a human approval may follow them but must not replace
>   them.
> - Continuous training is safe only in proportion to the strength of those
>   gates.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write three behavioural tests for a model you know: one minimum
>    functionality, one invariance, one directional expectation.
> 2. Add a metric gate that compares a candidate against the live model with
>    an explicit tolerance, and justify the tolerance you chose.
> 3. Introduce a deliberate sign error into a feature and check which of your
>    existing tests catch it; add one that does if none do.
> 4. Split your test suite into per-commit, per-PR, and nightly tiers and
>    measure the runtime of each tier.
> 5. Interview: How would you design CI for a pipeline whose full training
>    run takes six hours? (Hint: think about what a pull request actually
>    needs to prove, and what can be proven on a sample or deferred.)


#### Infrastructure as Code Basics

Data scientists inherit infrastructure whether they want it or not: a
training cluster, a bucket, a scheduled job, a serving deployment, a
monitoring alert. The question is only whether that infrastructure exists as
**a sequence of things somebody clicked** or as **a file in the repository**.

Infrastructure as code (IaC) means the second. The configuration is
declarative -- it states the desired end state rather than the steps to reach
it -- and a tool computes the difference between that state and reality, then
reconciles them. Terraform, Pulumi, CloudFormation, and Kubernetes manifests
are all instances of the same loop:

```text
  THE RECONCILIATION LOOP

    desired state (in git)  ----+
                                |
                             [ plan ]  <---- actual state (the real world)
                                |
                        list of differences
                                |
                            [ apply ]
                                |
                       actual state == desired state

    Run it twice and the second run does nothing. That is idempotence,
    and it is what makes the loop safe to automate.
```

The whole idea fits in a page of code, which is worth writing once to
understand what the tools are doing:

```python
import json, copy

# --- DESIRED STATE: WHAT THE CODE SAYS THE WORLD SHOULD LOOK LIKE. ---
desired = {
    "bucket:models":        {"type": "s3", "versioning": True, "encryption": "kms"},
    "service:fraud-scorer": {"type": "deployment", "replicas": 29,
                             "image": "registry/fraud@sha256:9c1f",
                             "cpu": "2", "memory": "4Gi"},
    "job:nightly-train":    {"type": "schedule", "cron": "0 2 * * *",
                             "timeout_min": 180},
    "alert:drift":          {"type": "monitor", "metric": "psi_score",
                             "threshold": 0.2},
}

# --- ACTUAL STATE: WHAT IS RUNNING RIGHT NOW. ---
actual = {
    "bucket:models":        {"type": "s3", "versioning": False, "encryption": "kms"},
    "service:fraud-scorer": {"type": "deployment", "replicas": 12,
                             "image": "registry/fraud@sha256:4a02",
                             "cpu": "2", "memory": "4Gi"},
    "job:legacy-export":    {"type": "schedule", "cron": "0 5 * * *",
                             "timeout_min": 60},
}

def plan(desired, actual):
    """The whole idea of declarative infrastructure, in fifteen lines."""
    out = []
    for key, want in desired.items():
        have = actual.get(key)
        if have is None:
            out.append(("create", key, want))
        elif have != want:
            diff = {k: (have.get(k), v) for k, v in want.items() if have.get(k) != v}
            out.append(("update", key, diff))
    for key in actual:
        if key not in desired:                      # code is the source of truth
            out.append(("destroy", key, actual[key]))
    return out

def show(p):
    if not p:
        print("  No changes. Infrastructure matches configuration.")
    for action, key, detail in p:
        mark = {"create": "+", "update": "~", "destroy": "-"}[action]
        print(f"  {mark} {action:8s} {key}")
        if action == "update":
            for field, (old, new) in detail.items():
                print(f"      {field}: {old!r} -> {new!r}")

def apply(p, actual, desired):
    for action, key, _ in p:
        if action in ("create", "update"):
            actual[key] = copy.deepcopy(desired[key])
        else:
            del actual[key]
    return actual

print("PLAN (what would change, before anything changes)")
show(plan(desired, actual))
print(f"  {len(plan(desired, actual))} changes")

actual = apply(plan(desired, actual), actual, desired)
print("\nPLAN AGAIN, IMMEDIATELY AFTER APPLY")
show(plan(desired, actual))
print("  Idempotence is the property that makes this safe to run in CI:")
print("  applying twice does the same thing as applying once.")

# --- DRIFT: SOMEBODY FIXED AN INCIDENT IN THE CONSOLE AT 2 A.M. ---
actual["service:fraud-scorer"]["replicas"] = 60
actual["service:fraud-scorer"]["memory"] = "8Gi"
print("\nPLAN AFTER A MANUAL CHANGE IN THE CONSOLE")
show(plan(desired, actual))
print("  The next apply will silently revert the emergency fix. That is not")
print("  a flaw -- it is the guarantee. The fix belongs in the config file,")
print("  where it is reviewed, versioned, and survives the next deploy.")

# --- ENVIRONMENTS ARE THE SAME CODE WITH DIFFERENT NUMBERS. ---
def env(base, **overrides):
    out = copy.deepcopy(base)
    for path, value in overrides.items():
        key, field = path.split(".")
        out[key][field] = value
    return out

staging = env(desired, **{"service:fraud-scorer.replicas": 2,
                          "job:nightly-train.timeout_min": 30})
print("\nSTAGING FROM THE SAME MODULE")
print(json.dumps({k: v for k, v in staging.items()
                  if k.startswith("service") or k.startswith("job:n")}, indent=2))
print("  One definition, per-environment values. Copy-pasted environments")
print("  diverge within weeks and then 'it works in staging' means nothing.")
```

```text
PLAN (what would change, before anything changes)
  ~ update   bucket:models
      versioning: False -> True
  ~ update   service:fraud-scorer
      replicas: 12 -> 29
      image: 'registry/fraud@sha256:4a02' -> 'registry/fraud@sha256:9c1f'
  + create   job:nightly-train
  + create   alert:drift
  - destroy  job:legacy-export
  5 changes

PLAN AGAIN, IMMEDIATELY AFTER APPLY
  No changes. Infrastructure matches configuration.
  Idempotence is the property that makes this safe to run in CI:
  applying twice does the same thing as applying once.

PLAN AFTER A MANUAL CHANGE IN THE CONSOLE
  ~ update   service:fraud-scorer
      replicas: 60 -> 29
      memory: '8Gi' -> '4Gi'
  The next apply will silently revert the emergency fix. That is not
  a flaw -- it is the guarantee. The fix belongs in the config file,
  where it is reviewed, versioned, and survives the next deploy.

STAGING FROM THE SAME MODULE
{
  "service:fraud-scorer": {
    "type": "deployment",
    "replicas": 2,
    "image": "registry/fraud@sha256:9c1f",
    "cpu": "2",
    "memory": "4Gi"
  },
  "job:nightly-train": {
    "type": "schedule",
    "cron": "0 2 * * *",
    "timeout_min": 30
  }
}
  One definition, per-environment values. Copy-pasted environments
  diverge within weeks and then 'it works in staging' means nothing.
```

Four behaviours in that output define the practice.

**The plan comes before the apply.** You see that the deployment will move
from 12 to 29 replicas and change image digest *before* anything happens.
Requiring a reviewed plan for production changes catches the destructive
surprise -- note the `- destroy job:legacy-export`, which is exactly the line
you want a human to read before it runs.

**Idempotence.** Applying twice changes nothing the second time, which is
what makes it safe to run from CI on every merge.

**Drift detection.** The 2 a.m. console fix shows up as a difference, and the
next apply reverts it. This feels hostile the first time it happens, and it
is the point: the repository is the source of truth, so the fix must be made
there. The good version of that incident is: change the replica count in the
config, open a pull request, merge, apply -- three minutes, and the change
survives the next deploy.

**Environments are parameters, not copies.** Staging and production differ in
numbers, not in structure. Copy-pasted environments diverge, and then a
staging test tells you nothing about production.

In practice, for an ML platform, expect to declare: object storage for
artifacts and datasets (with versioning and encryption turned on in code),
the training compute (cluster, node pools, GPU quotas), the serving
deployment and its autoscaler, the scheduled jobs and their triggers, the
feature store or database, the monitors and alerts, and the IAM roles that
connect them. The IAM roles are the ones most worth having in code: least
privilege is only auditable if it is written down.

Two cautions specific to this territory:

- **State is a real thing you can lose.** Terraform's state file maps
  configuration to real resources; store it remotely with locking, never on a
  laptop, and never edit it by hand.
- **Secrets are not configuration.** Keys and passwords go in a secret
  manager and are referenced by name; putting them in the repository -- or in
  the state file -- is the classic way to publish them.

> Key Takeaways
> - IaC replaces console clicks with a declarative file that is reviewed,
>   versioned, and repeatable.
> - The core loop is plan (diff desired against actual) then apply
>   (reconcile); running it twice changes nothing the second time.
> - Always read the plan before applying to production, especially for
>   destroy actions.
> - Manual console changes show up as drift and get reverted; make the fix in
>   the repository instead.
> - Parameterise environments from one module rather than copying
>   configurations, or staging stops predicting production.
> - For ML platforms, declare storage, compute, serving, schedules, monitors,
>   and IAM roles -- especially IAM.
> - Store remote state with locking and never hand-edit it.
> - Keep secrets in a secret manager and reference them; never in the repo or
>   the state file.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a declarative description of one piece of infrastructure you use
>    today, and diff it against what actually exists.
> 2. Implement the plan/apply loop for a small configuration and prove it is
>    idempotent.
> 3. Parameterise that configuration into development and production variants
>    that differ only in values.
> 4. List every resource your current ML project depends on and mark which
>    ones exist only because somebody clicked.
> 5. Interview: An engineer fixes a production outage by editing settings in
>    the cloud console. What should happen next, and why? (Hint: the fix
>    itself was fine; think about what happens on the next deploy and how the
>    team would ever know.)


<a id="153-monitoring-and-maintenance"></a>
### 15.3 Monitoring and Maintenance

A deployed model is the only kind of software that can fail without anything
breaking: no exception, no error rate, no alert -- just decisions that get
worse. This section covers how to notice that happening (drift in the inputs
and in the relationship), how to measure live performance when labels are
late or missing, how to keep the data feeding the model trustworthy, what to
do when something fires, when and how to retrain, and how to release a new
model without betting the business on it.


#### Data Drift and Concept Drift

Models assume the future resembles the past. Production's job is to violate
that assumption, and it does so in two distinct ways that require different
responses.

**Data drift** (covariate shift) means the inputs have moved: `P(X)` changed
while `P(Y|X)` stayed the same. A marketing campaign brings in younger users,
a new country launches, a currency changes. The relationship the model
learned is still valid; it is simply being applied to a population it saw
less of during training.

**Concept drift** means the relationship itself changed: `P(Y|X)` is
different. The same customer profile that predicted churn last year no longer
does, because a competitor changed their pricing. The model is now wrong
about the world, and no amount of input monitoring will tell you so.

The distinction is not academic, because the standard drift dashboards
measure `P(X)`:

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(21)

def psi(ref, cur, bins=10):
    """Population Stability Index: how far a distribution moved."""
    edges = np.quantile(ref, np.linspace(0, 1, bins + 1))
    edges[0], edges[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf
    r = np.histogram(ref, edges)[0] / len(ref) + 1e-6
    c = np.histogram(cur, edges)[0] / len(cur) + 1e-6
    return float(np.sum((c - r) * np.log(c / r)))

def ks(ref, cur):
    """Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic: largest gap between the two CDFs."""
    allv = np.sort(np.concatenate([ref, cur]))
    return float(np.max(np.abs(np.searchsorted(np.sort(ref), allv, "right") / len(ref)
                             - np.searchsorted(np.sort(cur), allv, "right") / len(cur))))

N = 20_000
x_ref = rng.normal(0, 1, N)
y_ref = (rng.random(N) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(1.5 * x_ref)))).astype(int)
model = lambda x: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(1.5 * x)))      # the deployed relationship

def accuracy(x, y):
    return float(((model(x) > 0.5).astype(int) == y).mean())

scenarios = {
    # Inputs move; the relationship between x and y is unchanged.
    "covariate shift": (rng.normal(0.8, 1.0, N), 1.5),
    # Inputs identical; what x MEANS for y has changed. This is the dangerous one.
    "concept drift":   (rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, N), -0.4),
    # Both move.
    "both":            (rng.normal(0.8, 1.4, N), 0.3),
    # Nothing moves: the control.
    "stable":          (rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, N), 1.5),
}

print("DRIFT DETECTORS SEE THE INPUTS. THE DAMAGE IS IN THE RELATIONSHIP.")
print(f"  reference accuracy = {accuracy(x_ref, y_ref):.3f}\n")
base = accuracy(x_ref, y_ref)
print("  scenario           PSI(x)   KS(x)   accuracy   change   input alarm?")
for name, (x_cur, beta) in scenarios.items():
    y_cur = (rng.random(N) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(beta * x_cur)))).astype(int)
    p_in, k_in = psi(x_ref, x_cur), ks(x_ref, x_cur)
    acc = accuracy(x_cur, y_cur)
    fires = "FIRES" if p_in > 0.2 else "silent"
    print(f"  {name:16s} {p_in:7.3f} {k_in:7.3f} {acc:10.3f}"
          f"  {acc - base:+7.3f}   {fires:>12}")
print("\n  PSI rule of thumb: <0.1 stable, 0.1-0.2 watch, >0.2 investigate.")
print("  Covariate shift fired the alarm and the model got BETTER: the inputs")
print("  moved into a region where the decision is easier. Input drift is a")
print("  reason to look, not a failure. Concept drift moved nothing")
print("  measurable in the inputs and cost 31 points of accuracy -- no")
print("  input-only monitor can see it. Only labels can.")

# --- DRIFT IS NOT ALWAYS GRADUAL. KNOW THE SHAPES. ---
print("\nSHAPES OF DRIFT, AND WHAT EACH IMPLIES")
shapes = [
    ("sudden", "policy change, new competitor, pandemic", "retrain now, on new data only"),
    ("gradual", "slow change in customer mix", "scheduled retraining keeps up"),
    ("incremental", "prices creeping upward", "recalibrate or add a trend feature"),
    ("recurring", "seasonality, weekday effects", "do NOT retrain; add the feature"),
]
for name, cause, action in shapes:
    print(f"  {name:12s} {cause:40s} -> {action}")
print("  Mistaking seasonality for drift produces a model that chases noise")
print("  and is retrained every December for no reason.")

# --- HOW LONG BEFORE YOU KNOW? LABEL DELAY SETS THE DETECTION FLOOR. ---
print("\nLABEL DELAY VS DETECTION DELAY")
print("  use case            label arrives after   what you can watch meanwhile")
for case, delay, proxy in [
        ("ad click", "minutes", "the labels themselves, almost live"),
        ("churn", "30 days", "engagement proxies, score distribution"),
        ("fraud chargeback", "30-90 days", "analyst review queue, alert rate"),
        ("loan default", "6-24 months", "early-payment behaviour, input drift")]:
    print(f"  {case:20s} {delay:19s}   {proxy}")
print("  When labels are slow, input drift and prediction drift are the only")
print("  signals you have -- which is exactly why you monitor them too.")
```

```text
DRIFT DETECTORS SEE THE INPUTS. THE DAMAGE IS IN THE RELATIONSHIP.
  reference accuracy = 0.737

  scenario           PSI(x)   KS(x)   accuracy   change   input alarm?
  covariate shift    0.586   0.309      0.780   +0.043          FIRES
  concept drift      0.001   0.010      0.426   -0.311         silent
  both               0.505   0.291      0.595   -0.142          FIRES
  stable             0.000   0.005      0.733   -0.004         silent

  PSI rule of thumb: <0.1 stable, 0.1-0.2 watch, >0.2 investigate.
  Covariate shift fired the alarm and the model got BETTER: the inputs
  moved into a region where the decision is easier. Input drift is a
  reason to look, not a failure. Concept drift moved nothing
  measurable in the inputs and cost 31 points of accuracy -- no
  input-only monitor can see it. Only labels can.

SHAPES OF DRIFT, AND WHAT EACH IMPLIES
  sudden       policy change, new competitor, pandemic  -> retrain now, on new data only
  gradual      slow change in customer mix              -> scheduled retraining keeps up
  incremental  prices creeping upward                   -> recalibrate or add a trend feature
  recurring    seasonality, weekday effects             -> do NOT retrain; add the feature
  Mistaking seasonality for drift produces a model that chases noise
  and is retrained every December for no reason.

LABEL DELAY VS DETECTION DELAY
  use case            label arrives after   what you can watch meanwhile
  ad click             minutes               the labels themselves, almost live
  churn                30 days               engagement proxies, score distribution
  fraud chargeback     30-90 days            analyst review queue, alert rate
  loan default         6-24 months           early-payment behaviour, input drift
  When labels are slow, input drift and prediction drift are the only
  signals you have -- which is exactly why you monitor them too.
```

Read those four rows carefully, because they contradict the usual intuition.

Covariate shift produced a large PSI, fired every alarm -- and *improved*
accuracy, because the inputs moved into a region where the decision boundary
is easier. **Input drift is a reason to investigate, not evidence of harm.**
Treating every PSI alarm as an incident trains a team to ignore the
dashboard.

Concept drift produced PSI of 0.001 -- indistinguishable from a stable
population -- while accuracy collapsed by 31 points. Every input-based monitor
stayed silent. This is the failure mode that makes label-based monitoring
non-negotiable wherever labels can be obtained at all.

The standard measures, and when each is appropriate:

| Measure | Applies to | Interpretation | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| PSI | Binned numeric or categorical | <0.1 stable, >0.2 investigate | Sensitive to bin choice |
| KS statistic | Continuous, univariate | Max CDF gap; has a p-value | Tiny shifts are "significant" at scale |
| Chi-square | Categorical | Tests frequency change | Same large-sample problem |
| Jensen-Shannon | Any distribution | Symmetric, bounded 0-1 | Needs density estimation |
| Wasserstein | Continuous | Distance in units of the variable | Interpretable, scale-dependent |
| Null and cardinality rates | Any | Schema or pipeline failure | Often the real cause |

Two practical notes. With large production volumes, **every** statistical test
rejects; use effect sizes (PSI, Wasserstein) with thresholds, not p-values.
And multivariate drift can hide in a set of individually stable features -- if
that risk matters, train a **drift classifier**: if a model can distinguish
reference rows from current rows better than chance, the joint distribution
has moved.

The shapes table matters for the response. Sudden drift needs immediate
retraining on recent data; recurring drift needs a *feature*, not a
retraining -- a model retrained every December to handle Christmas is a model
that should have had a seasonality feature.

Finally, label delay sets a floor on how fast you can detect concept drift.
If chargebacks arrive 60 days later, you cannot know a fraud model degraded
until 60 days after it did. That is precisely why input and prediction drift
are monitored anyway: they are the only early signals available, even though
they are imperfect.

> Key Takeaways
> - Data drift changes `P(X)`; concept drift changes `P(Y|X)`, and only the
>   second necessarily harms the model.
> - Input drift monitors cannot detect concept drift -- in the example PSI was
>   0.001 while accuracy fell 31 points.
> - Input drift can coincide with improved accuracy; treat an alarm as a
>   prompt to investigate, not an incident.
> - Use effect-size measures (PSI, Wasserstein, JS) with thresholds, because
>   p-values reject everything at production volume.
> - Watch prediction distributions and null/cardinality rates alongside
>   inputs; pipeline breakage often shows there first.
> - A drift classifier catches multivariate shift that per-feature tests miss.
> - Classify drift by shape: sudden, gradual, incremental, recurring -- and
>   handle recurring drift with a feature rather than retraining.
> - Label delay sets the floor on concept-drift detection, which is why
>   imperfect early signals are still worth monitoring.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement PSI and apply it to one feature across two months of your own
>    data; state which bins drive the score.
> 2. Simulate covariate shift and concept drift separately and confirm which
>    detectors fire in each case.
> 3. Train a drift classifier between a reference window and a current window
>    and report its AUC; interpret a value of 0.52 and one of 0.85.
> 4. For a model you know, write down the label delay and the earliest date a
>    concept drift starting today could be detected.
> 5. Interview: Your PSI dashboard is green but business metrics dropped. How
>    do you investigate? (Hint: consider which quantity each of your monitors
>    actually measures, and which one nobody is measuring.)


#### Model Performance Monitoring

Monitoring a model means answering "is it still working?" continuously, for a
system whose failures are quiet. It has four layers, and teams reliably build
the first and skip the third:

| Layer | Examples | Fails loudly? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Service | Latency, error rate, saturation, restarts | Yes |
| Data | Null rates, schema, volume, freshness, drift | Sometimes |
| Model | Accuracy, AUC, calibration, per-segment quality | No |
| Business | Approval rate, fraud loss, revenue per session | Eventually, expensively |

The model layer is where the interesting problems are, and three properties
make it harder than ordinary monitoring: labels arrive late or never,
aggregate metrics conceal segment failures, and the noise floor is high
enough that naive alerting produces mostly false alarms.

```python
import math
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(31)

# --- AGGREGATE METRICS HIDE SEGMENT FAILURES. ---
# Traffic mix and per-segment accuracy, before and after a mobile SDK change.
segments = [
    ("web / desktop",  0.55, 0.812, 0.815),
    ("mobile / iOS",   0.22, 0.798, 0.794),
    ("mobile/Android", 0.18, 0.803, 0.617),   # broken feature in the new SDK
    ("partner API",    0.05, 0.771, 0.769),
]
print("PER-SEGMENT ACCURACY, BEFORE AND AFTER A RELEASE")
print("  segment          share   before    after   change")
for name, share, before, after in segments:
    print(f"  {name:15s} {share:6.0%} {before:8.3f} {after:8.3f} {after - before:+8.3f}")
agg_b = sum(s * b for _, s, b, _ in segments)
agg_a = sum(s * a for _, s, _, a in segments)
print(f"  {'AGGREGATE':15s} {1.0:6.0%} {agg_b:8.3f} {agg_a:8.3f} {agg_a - agg_b:+8.3f}")
print("  A 19-point collapse for 18% of users shows up as 3 points overall --")
print("  inside the range a weekly dashboard is routinely noisy by.")

# --- HOW MANY LABELS BEFORE A DROP IS DETECTABLE? ---
def n_needed(p0, drop, alpha=0.05, power=0.80):
    """Two-proportion test: labels needed per window to see p0 -> p0-drop."""
    p1 = p0 - drop
    za, zb = 1.959964, 0.8416212
    pbar = (p0 + p1) / 2
    return math.ceil(2 * (za * math.sqrt(2 * pbar * (1 - pbar))
                          + zb * math.sqrt(p0 * (1 - p0) + p1 * (1 - p1))) ** 2
                     / (2 * (p0 - p1) ** 2))

print("\nLABELS NEEDED TO DETECT AN ACCURACY DROP (80% POWER, 5% ALPHA)")
print("  baseline   -1 pt     -2 pt     -5 pt    -10 pt")
for p0 in (0.80, 0.95, 0.99):
    row = "".join(f"{n_needed(p0, d):10,}" for d in (0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.10))
    print(f"  {p0:8.0%} {row}")
print("  At 500 labels/day, a 2-point drop from a 95% baseline takes about")
print(f"  {n_needed(0.95, 0.02) / 500:.0f} days to confirm. Daily alerting on it is not")
print("  monitoring; it is a random number generator.")

# --- A CONTROL CHART SEPARATES NOISE FROM A REAL SHIFT. ---
days, n_per_day = 60, 400
true_acc = np.where(np.arange(days) < 40, 0.80, 0.755)      # a real step at day 40
obs = rng.binomial(n_per_day, true_acc) / n_per_day
ref_mu, ref_sd = obs[:30].mean(), obs[:30].std(ddof=1)
print(f"\nCONTROL CHART: baseline {ref_mu:.3f} +/- {ref_sd:.3f} (first 30 days)")
print("  day   accuracy   z      3-sigma   7-day mean below baseline?")
alerted = None
for d in range(30, days, 5):
    win = obs[max(0, d - 6):d + 1]
    z = (obs[d] - ref_mu) / ref_sd
    run = win.mean() < ref_mu - ref_sd        # sustained, not a single point
    flag = "BREACH" if abs(z) > 3 else "-"
    if alerted is None and run and z < -1:
        alerted = d
    print(f"  {d:4d}   {obs[d]:8.3f} {z:6.2f}   {flag:7s}   {'yes' if run else 'no'}")
print(f"  A single point beyond 3 sigma never fires here; the sustained")
print(f"  7-day shift is detected at day {alerted}, {alerted - 40} days after the change.")
print("  Alert on sustained deviation, not on single days.")

# --- WITHOUT LABELS, MONITOR WHAT YOU STILL HAVE. ---
print("\nSIGNALS AVAILABLE BEFORE LABELS ARRIVE")
for name, what in [
        ("prediction mean", "shifts when inputs or the model change"),
        ("score histogram", "bimodality or pile-ups reveal broken features"),
        ("alert/approval rate", "the operational consequence of the scores"),
        ("feature null rate", "upstream breakage, usually the real cause"),
        ("override rate", "humans disagreeing with the model, a live signal"),
        ("latency and errors", "a service failure looks like a quality failure")]:
    print(f"  {name:20s} {what}")
```

```text
PER-SEGMENT ACCURACY, BEFORE AND AFTER A RELEASE
  segment          share   before    after   change
  web / desktop      55%    0.812    0.815   +0.003
  mobile / iOS       22%    0.798    0.794   -0.004
  mobile/Android     18%    0.803    0.617   -0.186
  partner API         5%    0.771    0.769   -0.002
  AGGREGATE         100%    0.805    0.772   -0.033
  A 19-point collapse for 18% of users shows up as 3 points overall --
  inside the range a weekly dashboard is routinely noisy by.

LABELS NEEDED TO DETECT AN ACCURACY DROP (80% POWER, 5% ALPHA)
  baseline   -1 pt     -2 pt     -5 pt    -10 pt
       80%     25,583     6,510     1,094       294
       95%      8,158     2,213       435       141
       99%      2,319       769       211        88
  At 500 labels/day, a 2-point drop from a 95% baseline takes about
  4 days to confirm. Daily alerting on it is not
  monitoring; it is a random number generator.

CONTROL CHART: baseline 0.798 +/- 0.020 (first 30 days)
  day   accuracy   z      3-sigma   7-day mean below baseline?
    30      0.802   0.23   -         no
    35      0.830   1.59   -         no
    40      0.785  -0.64   -         no
    45      0.750  -2.37   -         yes
    50      0.770  -1.38   -         yes
    55      0.743  -2.74   -         yes
  A single point beyond 3 sigma never fires here; the sustained
  7-day shift is detected at day 45, 5 days after the change.
  Alert on sustained deviation, not on single days.

SIGNALS AVAILABLE BEFORE LABELS ARRIVE
  prediction mean      shifts when inputs or the model change
  score histogram      bimodality or pile-ups reveal broken features
  alert/approval rate  the operational consequence of the scores
  feature null rate    upstream breakage, usually the real cause
  override rate        humans disagreeing with the model, a live signal
  latency and errors   a service failure looks like a quality failure
```

**Segments first.** The Android collapse -- 19 points of accuracy for nearly a
fifth of users -- appears as a 3-point aggregate decline, which is
indistinguishable from an ordinary bad week. Aggregate metrics are for
reporting; monitoring belongs at the segment level. Choose segments before
the incident: platform, country, customer tier, new versus returning, and any
group with a fairness obligation. Track a small number of them with explicit
thresholds rather than a hundred without.

**Then statistical power.** The table converts a wish ("alert me if accuracy
drops") into an arithmetic fact: detecting a 2-point drop from a 95% baseline
needs roughly 2,200 labelled outcomes. At 500 labels a day, a daily alert on
that threshold is noise, and the correct design is a weekly comparison or a
sequential test. Knowing this number prevents both false alarms and the
opposite failure -- a threshold so wide that a genuine collapse takes a month
to trip it.

**Then sustained-deviation alerting.** The control chart shows a real 4.5-point
step at day 40 that never produces a single 3-sigma point, because daily noise
is larger than the shift. A rolling-window rule detects it five days later.
That five-day delay is not a flaw to be engineered away; it is the price of
not paging someone every Tuesday. Where faster detection genuinely matters,
use a sequential method (CUSUM, page-Hinkley, or a Bayesian changepoint test)
which accumulates evidence rather than testing each day independently.

**Calibration deserves separate tracking** from discrimination. A model can
keep its ranking quality (AUC unchanged) while its probabilities become
systematically too high -- which breaks every downstream threshold and
expected-value calculation. Monitor mean predicted probability against mean
observed outcome per bucket, and treat a widening gap as its own alert; it is
also the cheapest thing to fix, since recalibration does not require
retraining.

When labels are slow, monitor the signals you still have -- prediction
distribution, alert rate, null rates, human override rate. The override rate
in particular is an underused live signal: when analysts start disagreeing
with the model more often, something has changed, and they knew before the
labels did.

Two principles for the alerts themselves. **Alert on consequences, not on
statistics**: "approval rate fell 8% for Android users" is actionable, "KS
statistic on feature 17 is 0.13" is not. And **every alert needs an owner and
a runbook**, or it becomes a notification that people filter.

> Key Takeaways
> - Model monitoring has four layers; the model layer fails silently and is
>   the one most often missing.
> - Aggregate metrics hide segment failures -- a 19-point collapse for 18% of
>   traffic looks like a 3-point wobble.
> - Define monitored segments in advance, with thresholds, and keep the list
>   short enough to act on.
> - Compute the labels needed to detect the drop you care about; alerting
>   faster than that is noise generation.
> - Alert on sustained deviation (rolling windows, CUSUM) rather than single
>   points beyond a sigma band.
> - Track calibration separately from ranking; probabilities can degrade
>   while AUC is unchanged, and recalibration is cheap.
> - Before labels arrive, monitor prediction distributions, null rates,
>   operational rates, and human override rates.
> - Every alert needs a consequence-level description, an owner, and a
>   runbook.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Split one model's live accuracy by three segments and compare each
>    against the aggregate over the last month.
> 2. Compute how many labelled examples you need to detect a 2-point drop
>    from your model's current baseline, and convert it into a time window.
> 3. Build a control chart on a real metric and tune a rolling rule so it
>    would have caught the last known incident without firing in the previous
>    quarter.
> 4. Plot predicted versus observed rates by score decile for a live model
>    and decide whether it needs recalibration.
> 5. Interview: You can log only one number per prediction for monitoring
>    purposes. What do you log and why? (Hint: think about which single
>    quantity lets you reconstruct both distribution shifts and, once labels
>    arrive, performance.)


#### Data Quality Checks in Production

Ask experienced ML engineers where production incidents come from and the
answer is rarely "the model". It is an upstream table that started arriving
six hours late, a column that changed units, a join that silently duplicated
rows, a team that replaced nulls with `-1` as a favour. The model consumes
whatever it is given and returns confident numbers either way.

The remedy is to make expectations about data **explicit and executable**,
and to run them where the data enters -- the same principle as type checking,
applied to rows instead of variables. Six families cover most real failures:

| Check family | Catches | Typical rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Schema | Renamed, dropped, retyped columns | Column set and dtypes match |
| Volume | Partial loads, duplicated loads | Row count within X% of recent |
| Uniqueness | Fan-out from a bad join | Primary key is unique |
| Nullness | Broken upstream field | Null rate below threshold |
| Range / set | Unit changes, sentinels, new categories | Value bounds, allowed values |
| Freshness | Stalled pipelines | Max timestamp within an interval |

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(17)

def batch(n, day, broken=None):
    df = pd.DataFrame({
        "event_id": np.arange(n) + day * 100_000,
        "ts": pd.Timestamp("2026-09-01") + pd.Timedelta(days=day)
```
