```text
  avg_order_30d     also read by: finance-report
  'analytics-dashboard' and 'finance-report' now depend on outputs
  nobody promised to keep stable. The next threshold change breaks a
  report somebody presents to the board. Publish an interface or
  deprecate the access -- but know that it exists.

THE ML-SPECIFIC DEBT CATALOGUE
  entanglement (CACE)   one feature, many models           -> isolate, version features
  undeclared consumers  outputs read by unknown systems    -> publish contracts
  pipeline jungle       scripts calling scripts            -> one orchestrated DAG
  dead features         computed, never used               -> ablate and delete
  glue code             90% of the repo is plumbing        -> standard interfaces
  configuration debt    50 flags, 3 documented             -> typed, validated config
  correction cascades   model B patches model A            -> retrain A properly
  feedback loops        the model shapes its own data      -> control groups, logging
  None of these appear in code quality metrics. All of them determine
  how long the next change takes.
```

Three patterns in that report recur in every mature ML codebase.

**Entanglement.** A feature read by several models cannot be changed by one
team alone. The fix is not to avoid sharing -- sharing is the point of a
feature store -- but to **version feature definitions**, so a change creates
`avg_order_30d@v2` and each model migrates deliberately.

**Dead and overpriced features.** Nearly a third of the daily feature spend
here supports features with importance below 0.03, plus one that no model
reads at all. They persist because removing a feature is not free: you must
retrain without it, measure the loss, and be willing to accept it. Nobody
schedules that work, so the pipeline grows monotonically. Budget a periodic
**ablation review** -- and note that the same review usually finds a pipeline
that can be deleted entirely, which is where the real saving is.

**Undeclared consumers.** This is the most dangerous item on the list. Once a
model's output lands in a table, other systems read it, and none of them
appear in your design document. Your next threshold change breaks a finance
report. The remedies are ordinary interface discipline applied to data:
publish a stable, documented output contract; version it; log who reads it;
and use access controls so that new consumers must ask rather than discover.

The rest of the catalogue in the output is worth periodically walking as a
checklist. Add to it two habits that keep debt visible rather than
accumulating:

- **Track the cost of the pipeline, not only its accuracy.** A feature's value
  is its contribution minus its daily cost and its maintenance burden.
- **Give every model an end date.** A scheduled review -- is this still used,
  still correct, still worth its cost? -- is the only reliable mechanism for
  deleting models, and undeleted models are where most of this debt lives.

> Key Takeaways
> - ML debt is dominated by data dependencies, which are invisible to
>   compilers and to code review.
> - CACE: models have no internal modularity, so any input change moves every
>   output.
> - A shared feature cannot be changed by one team alone; version feature
>   definitions so migration is deliberate.
> - Dead and low-importance features persist because removing them requires
>   an ablation nobody schedules.
> - Undeclared consumers turn every output change into an unplanned breakage;
>   publish contracts and log readers.
> - Watch for pipeline jungles, glue code, configuration debt, correction
>   cascades, and feedback loops.
> - Track pipeline cost alongside accuracy so a feature's net value is
>   visible.
> - Review models on a schedule and delete the ones that are no longer worth
>   their cost.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build the feature-to-model dependency map for your project and identify
>    every feature used by more than one model.
> 2. Estimate the daily cost of your three most expensive features and
>    compare it with their importance.
> 3. Ablate one low-importance feature, measure the change, and decide
>    whether to remove it.
> 4. Search access logs for consumers of one model's output table and compare
>    them with the documented consumers.
> 5. Interview: You want to change how a widely used feature is computed.
>    What is your plan? (Hint: the technical change is the easy part; think
>    about versions, migration, and who must agree.)


#### Team Workflows and Handoffs

Most ML work crosses a boundary at some point: from an analyst who built a
model to engineers who will run it, from one team to another during a
reorganisation, from a person leaving to whoever is left. What survives that
crossing is determined long before it happens, by how the work was organised.

Start with the workflow, because ML repositories accumulate a specific mess:
exploratory code and production code in the same place, indistinguishable.
The convention that works is a **one-way path** -- code moves from notebook to
module, never back:

```text
  notebooks/     exploration only, never imported, outputs stripped in git
  src/           importable modules: features, training, evaluation, serving
  configs/       one file per run; no constants buried in code
  tests/         unit, behavioural, pipeline
  pipelines/     orchestration definitions (DAGs, schedules)
  docs/          ADRs, model cards, runbooks, data dictionary

  Rule: if a notebook cell has been run more than twice by two people,
  it belongs in src/ with a test. Notebooks are for questions, not
  for answers other people depend on.
```

Branching and release conventions can be borrowed wholesale from software
engineering -- short-lived branches, small pull requests, trunk-based
development -- with two ML-specific additions. **Data changes need their own
review path**, because a change to a source table is a change to every model
that reads it. And **experiments do not need branches**: they need tracked
runs, since a branch per experiment produces fifty stale branches and no
comparison.

The handoff itself deserves an explicit review, run before the transfer
rather than after:

```python
# --- A PRODUCTION-READINESS REVIEW, RUN BEFORE A HANDOFF, NOT AFTER. ---
CHECKS = {
    "ownership": [
        ("named owning team and on-call rota", True, "blocker"),
        ("second person can retrain it unaided", False, "blocker"),
        ("runbook exists and was used in a drill", False, "blocker"),
    ],
    "reproducibility": [
        ("training runs from a committed config", True, "blocker"),
        ("data snapshot and commit recorded per run", True, "blocker"),
        ("rebuild from scratch verified this quarter", False, "major"),
    ],
    "operability": [
        ("dashboards for latency, errors, action rate", True, "blocker"),
        ("alerts route to the on-call rota", True, "blocker"),
        ("rollback tested in production", False, "blocker"),
        ("cost per 1k predictions is known", False, "minor"),
    ],
    "quality": [
        ("behavioural tests in CI", True, "major"),
        ("sliced evaluation published", False, "major"),
        ("model card current for the live version", False, "major"),
    ],
    "data": [
        ("expectation suite on inputs", True, "blocker"),
        ("drift monitoring with owners", True, "major"),
        ("label delay documented", False, "minor"),
    ],
}
WEIGHT = {"blocker": 3, "major": 2, "minor": 1}

print("PRODUCTION-READINESS REVIEW: intent_v7 handover to platform-ops")
print("  area              score   open items")
total, earned, blockers = 0, 0, []
for area, items in CHECKS.items():
    w = sum(WEIGHT[sev] for _, _, sev in items)
    got = sum(WEIGHT[sev] for _, ok, sev in items if ok)
    total, earned = total + w, earned + got
    open_items = [name for name, ok, sev in items if not ok]
    blockers += [(area, name) for name, ok, sev in items
                 if not ok and sev == "blocker"]
    print(f"  {area:16s} {got:3d}/{w:<3d}   {'; '.join(open_items) or '-'}")
print(f"  {'TOTAL':16s} {earned:3d}/{total:<3d}   {earned / total:.0%} ready")
print("\nBLOCKING GAPS (handover does not proceed until these close)")
for area, name in blockers:
    print(f"  [{area}] {name}")
print("  Two of the three blockers are about PEOPLE, not code: a single")
print("  person who can retrain the model and an untested rollback are how")
print("  a working system becomes an incident three months after handover.")

# --- WHERE WORK LIVES AS IT MATURES. ---
print("\nTHE PATH FROM NOTEBOOK TO PRODUCTION, AND WHAT CHANGES AT EACH STEP")
for stage, artifact, owner, rule in [
        ("explore", "notebook, ad-hoc data", "the analyst", "no reuse expected"),
        ("formalise", "module + config + test", "the analyst", "it must run twice"),
        ("schedule", "orchestrated DAG", "the team", "it must run unattended"),
        ("serve", "service or batch job", "the team", "it must have an SLO"),
        ("operate", "same code, on-call rota", "on-call", "somebody is paged")]:
    print(f"  {stage:10s} {artifact:24s} {owner:12s} {rule}")
print("  The common failure is jumping from column one to column four. The")
print("  'formalise' step -- extracting a module, parameterising the config,")
print("  writing one test -- is what makes everything after it possible.")
```

```text
PRODUCTION-READINESS REVIEW: intent_v7 handover to platform-ops
  area              score   open items
  ownership          3/9     second person can retrain it unaided; runbook exists and was used in a drill
  reproducibility    6/8     rebuild from scratch verified this quarter
  operability        6/10    rollback tested in production; cost per 1k predictions is known
  quality            2/6     sliced evaluation published; model card current for the live version
  data               5/6     label delay documented
  TOTAL             22/39    56% ready

BLOCKING GAPS (handover does not proceed until these close)
  [ownership] second person can retrain it unaided
  [ownership] runbook exists and was used in a drill
  [operability] rollback tested in production
  Two of the three blockers are about PEOPLE, not code: a single
  person who can retrain the model and an untested rollback are how
  a working system becomes an incident three months after handover.

THE PATH FROM NOTEBOOK TO PRODUCTION, AND WHAT CHANGES AT EACH STEP
  explore    notebook, ad-hoc data    the analyst  no reuse expected
  formalise  module + config + test   the analyst  it must run twice
  schedule   orchestrated DAG         the team     it must run unattended
  serve      service or batch job     the team     it must have an SLO
  operate    same code, on-call rota  on-call      somebody is paged
  The common failure is jumping from column one to column four. The
  'formalise' step -- extracting a module, parameterising the config,
  writing one test -- is what makes everything after it possible.
```

Notice what the blockers are. The model works; the metrics are fine; the
pipeline runs. What is missing is a second person who can retrain it, a
rehearsed runbook, and a tested rollback. Those three gaps are what convert a
working system into an incident a quarter later, when the author is on
holiday and a feature pipeline dies. **Production readiness is mostly a
property of the team, not of the code.**

The maturity table at the end names the step that teams skip. Moving from a
notebook straight to a scheduled production job means the formalisation --
extracting a module, parameterising the configuration, writing at least one
test -- never happens, and the resulting pipeline is a notebook running
unattended at 2 a.m.

Two more practices that reduce handoff pain:

| Practice | What it prevents |
| --- | --- |
| Named owner per model, in the registry | "Whose model is this?" during an incident |
| Two people per critical pipeline | Bus factor of one |
| Rotating on-call including model owners | Unoperable designs, because the author is paged |
| Definition of done that includes docs, tests, monitoring | Work declared finished at the demo |
| Quarterly model review | Zombie models nobody uses and nobody deletes |

The last row is the cheapest high-value habit in this chapter. Once a
quarter, list every model in production and ask: is it still used, is it
still correct, is it still worth its cost, and who would notice if it stopped?
Models that fail all four questions are deleted, and the team gets time back.

> Key Takeaways
> - Code moves one way: notebooks for questions, modules for anything anyone
>   depends on.
> - Keep exploration, source, configuration, tests, pipelines, and docs
>   separate, and strip notebook outputs in version control.
> - Use tracked experiment runs rather than branches for experiments.
> - Treat changes to shared data sources as changes to every model that reads
>   them.
> - Run a production-readiness review before a handoff; blockers are usually
>   about people, not code.
> - A second person who can retrain the model, a rehearsed runbook, and a
>   tested rollback are non-negotiable.
> - Do not skip formalisation: a notebook running unattended is not a
>   pipeline.
> - Name an owner per model, rotate on-call through model authors, and review
>   every production model quarterly.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Audit your repository against the directory convention above and list
>    everything that is in the wrong place.
> 2. Run a production-readiness review on one of your models and record the
>    blocking gaps.
> 3. Have a colleague retrain one of your models from documentation alone,
>    and fix whatever they had to ask you about.
> 4. Write a definition of done for model work that includes documentation,
>    tests, monitoring, and rollback.
> 5. Interview: You are inheriting a model from a team that is being
>    dissolved next week. What do you ask for, in priority order? (Hint:
>    think about what you cannot reconstruct later versus what you can, and
>    which single document would let you operate it on day one.)

---

<a id="16-interpretability-ethics-and-governance"></a>
## 16. Interpretability, Ethics, and Governance

A model that cannot be explained cannot be argued with, a model that cannot
be audited cannot be trusted, and a model that handles personal data without
a lawful basis cannot be deployed at all. This chapter covers the four
disciplines that decide whether a technically correct model is allowed to
influence real decisions: making predictions explainable, measuring and
constraining unequal treatment, protecting the people in the data, and
building the organisational machinery that keeps all of it true over time.
The recurring theme is that none of these are add-ons applied after
modelling -- each one changes what you are permitted to build, and each one
is cheapest to satisfy before the first model is trained.

<a id="161-model-interpretability"></a>
### 16.1 Model Interpretability

Interpretability is the ability to answer "why did the model produce that
number?" in terms a human can check; this section covers the choice between
models that are readable by construction and explanations bolted on
afterwards, the difference between describing a model overall and describing
one prediction, the four workhorse post-hoc methods (permutation importance,
partial dependence, SHAP, LIME), explanations phrased as actionable changes,
and the failure modes that make every method above misleading if used
without care.

Most examples in this section share one setup: a loan-default model on
synthetic data, deliberately containing a nonlinear interaction and a pair
of nearly duplicate features, because those two properties are what break
naive explanations.

```python
import numpy as np

def make_data(n=6000, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    income = rng.lognormal(10.6, 0.45, n)
    debt_ratio = np.clip(rng.beta(2, 5, n) * 1.4, 0, 1.2)
    age = rng.integers(21, 70, n).astype(float)
    late = rng.poisson(0.8, n).astype(float)
    verified = income * rng.normal(1.0, 0.05, n)   # near-duplicate of income
    z = (-1.9 - 1.0*np.log(income/40000) + 2.6*debt_ratio + 0.45*late
         + 1.3*(age < 25)                          # a threshold effect
         - 2.8*np.log(income/40000)*debt_ratio)    # and an interaction
    y = (rng.random(n) < 1/(1+np.exp(-z))).astype(int)      # 1 = defaulted
    X = np.column_stack([np.log(income), debt_ratio, age, late,
                         np.log(verified)])
    return X, y, ["log_income", "debt_ratio", "age", "late_pmts",
                  "log_verified"]

def auc(y, s):                       # rank-based AUC, no sklearn needed
    o = np.argsort(s); r = np.empty(len(s)); r[o] = np.arange(1, len(s)+1)
    n1 = y.sum(); n0 = len(y) - n1
    return (r[y == 1].sum() - n1*(n1+1)/2) / (n0*n1)

def logistic(X, y, iters=3000, lr=0.5):
    Xs = (X - X.mean(0)) / X.std(0)                # coefficients comparable
    w = np.zeros(X.shape[1]); b = 0.0
    for _ in range(iters):
        p = 1/(1+np.exp(-(Xs @ w + b)))
        g = (p - y) / len(y)
        w -= lr * (Xs.T @ g); b -= lr * g.sum()
    return w, b, X.mean(0), X.std(0)
```

A minimal gradient-boosted model plays the role of "the black box" -- 60
depth-3 regression trees fitted to the residuals, which is enough structure
that no human can read it directly.

```python
class Tree:                                   # CART on a squared-error split
    def __init__(self, depth=3, min_leaf=20):
        self.depth, self.min_leaf = depth, min_leaf
    def fit(self, X, g):
        self.node = self._build(X, g, 0); return self
    def _build(self, X, g, d):
        if d >= self.depth or len(g) < 2*self.min_leaf:
            return ("leaf", g.mean())
        best = None
        for j in range(X.shape[1]):
            for t in np.unique(np.quantile(X[:, j], np.linspace(.1, .9, 9))):
                m = X[:, j] <= t
                if min(m.sum(), (~m).sum()) < self.min_leaf: continue
                sse = g[m].var()*m.sum() + g[~m].var()*(~m).sum()
                if best is None or sse < best[0]: best = (sse, j, t, m)
        if best is None: return ("leaf", g.mean())
        _, j, t, m = best
        return ("split", j, t, self._build(X[m], g[m], d+1),
                               self._build(X[~m], g[~m], d+1))
    def predict(self, X):
        out = np.empty(len(X))
        for i, x in enumerate(X):
            nd = self.node
            while nd[0] == "split":
                nd = nd[3] if x[nd[1]] <= nd[2] else nd[4]
            out[i] = nd[1]
        return out

class GBM:
    def __init__(self, n=60, lr=0.2, depth=3):
        self.n, self.lr, self.depth = n, lr, depth
    def fit(self, X, y):
        self.base = np.log(y.mean()/(1-y.mean())); self.trees = []
        f = np.full(len(y), self.base)
        for _ in range(self.n):
            p = 1/(1+np.exp(-f))
            t = Tree(self.depth).fit(X, y - p)     # fit the gradient
            f += self.lr * t.predict(X); self.trees.append(t)
        return self
    def predict_proba(self, X):
        f = np.full(len(X), self.base)
        for t in self.trees: f += self.lr * t.predict(X)
        return 1/(1+np.exp(-f))
```


#### Intrinsic vs Post-Hoc Interpretability

There are exactly two ways to be able to explain a prediction. Either the
model is simple enough that its mechanism *is* the explanation, or the model
is not, and you build a second, separate artifact whose job is to describe
it. The first is **intrinsic** interpretability; the second is **post-hoc**.

The distinction matters because the second option carries a hidden cost that
the first does not. An intrinsic explanation is the model: if a logistic
regression says the coefficient on `debt_ratio` is +0.53, then the model
genuinely adds 0.53 log-odds per standard deviation of debt ratio, in every
case, forever. A post-hoc explanation is an **approximation of a different
object**, and approximations have error. When the explanation and the model
disagree, the model is what runs in production and the explanation is what
you showed the regulator.

The analogy is the difference between a recipe and a restaurant review. A
recipe *is* the dish's construction -- follow it and you reproduce the dish
exactly. A review describes the dish from outside: often useful, sometimes
insightful, and occasionally wrong in ways you cannot detect from the review
alone.

Interpretability is not a binary property but a rough ordering, and it is
not the same thing as simplicity. A linear model with 4,000 features is
technically transparent and practically unreadable; a depth-3 tree with
five features can be read aloud in a meeting.

```text
  MORE READABLE                                        LESS READABLE
  |                                                                |
  scorecard --- linear/logistic --- shallow --- GAM --- random --- deep
  (integer     (one coefficient     tree      (one     forest/    network
   points)      per feature)                   curve    boosting
                                               per
                                               feature)
  <---------- intrinsic: the model is the explanation ---------->
                        <-------- post-hoc required -------->
```

The decision procedure is not "always use the interpretable model". It is:
**measure what the opacity buys you**, then decide whether that is worth the
explanation debt.

```python
X, y, names = make_data(); tr, te = slice(0, 4000), slice(4000, None)
w, b, mu, sd = logistic(X[tr], y[tr])
lin = lambda Z: 1/(1+np.exp(-(((Z-mu)/sd) @ w + b)))
tree = Tree(depth=3).fit(X[tr], y[tr].astype(float))
gbm = GBM(n=60, depth=3).fit(X[tr], y[tr])

print("MODEL FAMILY vs WHAT YOU CAN SAY ABOUT IT")
print(f"{'model':22}{'test AUC':>10}{'params to read':>16}")
for nm, s, k in [("logistic regression", lin(X[te]), "6 numbers"),
                 ("depth-3 tree", tree.predict(X[te]), "8 rules"),
                 ("60-tree boosted", gbm.predict_proba(X[te]), "~480 splits")]:
    print(f"{nm:22}{auc(y[te], s):10.3f}{k:>16}")

# THE CLASSIC POST-HOC SHORTCUT: FIT AN INTERPRETABLE MODEL TO THE BLACK
# BOX'S OUTPUT, NOT TO THE LABELS. THE QUESTION IS ALWAYS: HOW FAITHFUL?
sur = Tree(depth=3).fit(X[tr], gbm.predict_proba(X[tr]))
pg, ps = gbm.predict_proba(X[te]), sur.predict(X[te])
r2 = 1 - ((pg-ps)**2).sum()/((pg-pg.mean())**2).sum()
print(f"\nsurrogate tree fidelity: R2={r2:.2f}, same decision on "
      f"{((pg>0.5) == (ps>0.5)).mean():.1%} of rows")
big = np.abs(pg-ps) > 0.15
print(f"rows where the surrogate is off by >0.15: {big.mean():.1%}"
      f"  (mean |error| there {np.abs(pg-ps)[big].mean():.2f})")
```

```text
MODEL FAMILY vs WHAT YOU CAN SAY ABOUT IT
model                   test AUC  params to read
logistic regression        0.770       6 numbers
depth-3 tree               0.738         8 rules
60-tree boosted            0.778     ~480 splits

surrogate tree fidelity: R2=0.80, same decision on 89.8% of rows
rows where the surrogate is off by >0.15: 6.3%  (mean |error| there 0.19)
```

Read the numbers carefully, because they are typical of real tabular
problems and they cut against the usual instinct. The boosted ensemble beats
the logistic regression by 0.008 AUC. In exchange for that, nobody can state
the model's rule, and every explanation you produce will be an inference
about a 480-split object.

The surrogate row is the warning. A global surrogate tree reproduces the
boosted model's decision on 90% of rows -- which sounds excellent until you
invert it. One applicant in ten receives a decision the explanation cannot
account for, and those are disproportionately the borderline cases, which
are exactly the ones who complain, appeal, or sue.

| | Intrinsic | Post-hoc |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What you explain | The model itself | A model of the model |
| Fidelity | Exact by definition | Measured, always below 1.0 |
| Cost of adding | Chosen up front | Extra pipeline, extra tests |
| Stability | Same answer every time | Depends on sampling, seeds, background data |
| Failure mode | Underfits the problem | Explains confidently and wrongly |
| Regulatory posture | Easiest to defend | Requires a fidelity argument |

The practical rule used in regulated settings: **if a decision materially
affects a person's rights, money, health, or liberty, start intrinsic and
force the black box to justify itself against a measured accuracy gap.**
Elsewhere, take the accuracy and invest in post-hoc tooling.

> Key Takeaways
> - Intrinsic interpretability means the model's mechanism is the
>   explanation; post-hoc means you build a second artifact that describes
>   the model.
> - Post-hoc explanations are approximations, so they have error, and the
>   model -- not the explanation -- is what runs in production.
> - Interpretability is an ordering, not a binary, and it is not the same as
>   having few parameters.
> - Always measure the accuracy the opacity buys; on tabular problems it is
>   frequently a fraction of a point.
> - A global surrogate's fidelity must be reported as a number; "90% of
>   decisions match" means one in ten explanations is unaccounted for.
> - Surrogate error concentrates on borderline cases, which are the cases
>   most likely to be challenged.
> - For high-stakes decisions, default to intrinsic and require the complex
>   model to justify the explanation debt.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Fit a logistic regression and a boosted model on the same dataset and
>    report the AUC gap; state whether you would accept the opacity for that
>    gap and why.
> 2. Fit a depth-3 surrogate tree to your black box's predictions and report
>    both R-squared and the fraction of flipped decisions.
> 3. Take the 5% of rows where your surrogate disagrees most with the model
>    and characterise them: are they near the decision threshold, in a sparse
>    region, or a distinct subgroup?
> 4. Rewrite a logistic regression as an integer scorecard (points per band)
>    and measure how much AUC the rounding costs.
> 5. Interview: A stakeholder asks for "an interpretable version" of a
>    production neural network. What do you deliver, and what do you refuse
>    to promise? (Hint: separate a faithful description of the model from a
>    replacement for the model, and think about what number you must attach
>    to whatever you hand over.)


#### Global vs Local Explanations

Two very different questions get called "explanation", and confusing them
produces answers that are technically correct and practically useless.

**Global**: how does this model behave, in general, across the population?
This is what you need to validate a model, document it, brief a risk
committee, or notice that it depends on something it should not.

**Local**: why did this model produce *this* number for *this* row? This is
what you need to answer an applicant's appeal, debug a surprising
prediction, or comply with a rule that requires giving individuals reasons.

The analogy: global explanation is climate, local explanation is weather.
Knowing the average August temperature does not tell you whether to carry
an umbrella today, and today's rain does not describe the climate. Both are
real; neither substitutes for the other.

The trap is that global explanations feel like they answer local questions.
"Income is the most important feature in this model" is a statement about
the population. For a specific applicant with an unremarkable income and
four late payments, income contributed nothing and the reason is the
payment history. Handing that applicant the global feature ranking is
giving them the wrong reason.

```text
  GLOBAL                              LOCAL
  one statement per feature           one statement per feature PER ROW
  "debt_ratio matters most"           "for applicant #8812, late_pmts
                                       pushed the score up by 1.61"

  audience: modellers, risk,          audience: the affected person,
  regulators reviewing the model      support agents, the appeals process

  built from: coefficients,           built from: SHAP, LIME,
  permutation importance, PDP         counterfactuals, coef x deviation
```

For a linear model both are available exactly and cheaply, which makes it
the clearest place to see the distinction. The global explanation is the
coefficient vector. The local explanation is the coefficient multiplied by
*this row's* deviation from the mean -- the contributions sum to the
prediction's log-odds, so nothing is hidden.

```python
X, y, names = make_data(); tr, te = slice(0, 4000), slice(4000, None)
w, b, mu, sd = logistic(X[tr], y[tr])
Z = (X - mu) / sd

print("GLOBAL: one number per feature, valid on average")
for n, c in sorted(zip(names, w), key=lambda t: -abs(t[1])):
    print(f"  {n:14}{c:+.2f}  ({'raises' if c > 0 else 'lowers'} log-odds)")

# LOCAL: THE SAME COEFFICIENTS, WEIGHTED BY HOW UNUSUAL THIS ROW IS.
rows = {"A (low income, high debt)": int(np.argmax(Z[te] @ w)),
        "B (rejected, but why?)":    int(np.argsort(Z[te] @ w)[-40]),
        "C (approved)":              int(np.argmin(Z[te] @ w))}
print("\nLOCAL: coefficient x this applicant's deviation, in log-odds")
print(f"  {'applicant':28}" + "".join(f"{n[:11]:>13}" for n in names))
for label, i in rows.items():
    contrib = w * Z[te][i]                       # sums to the row's log-odds
    print(f"  {label:28}" + "".join(f"{c:+13.2f}" for c in contrib))
for label, i in rows.items():
    top = names[int(np.argmax(np.abs(w * Z[te][i])))]
    print(f"  top driver for {label:26} -> {top}")
```

```text
GLOBAL: one number per feature, valid on average
  log_income    -0.68  (lowers log-odds)
  debt_ratio    +0.53  (raises log-odds)
  late_pmts     +0.35  (raises log-odds)
  log_verified  -0.29  (lowers log-odds)
  age           -0.22  (lowers log-odds)

LOCAL: coefficient x this applicant's deviation, in log-odds
  applicant                      log_income   debt_ratio          age    late_pmts  log_verifie
  A (low income, high debt)           +1.80        +1.11        +0.26        +0.07        +0.77
  B (rejected, but why?)              +0.60        -0.12        +0.07        +1.61        +0.30
  C (approved)                        -2.11        -0.21        -0.14        -0.32        -0.85
  top driver for A (low income, high debt)  -> log_income
  top driver for B (rejected, but why?)     -> late_pmts
  top driver for C (approved)               -> log_income
```

Applicant B is the whole point. Globally, `late_pmts` is only the third most
important feature. For B it is the dominant reason by a factor of two and a
half, and `debt_ratio` -- the second most important feature globally --
actually *helped* B. A reason code generated from the global ranking would
tell B to reduce their debt ratio, which for B is already good.

Two consequences follow for practice. First, **adverse action notices,
appeal responses, and support scripts must be generated per row**, never
from a global table. Second, a global explanation can be *aggregated up*
from local ones (average the absolute contributions), but never
*disaggregated down*; the arrow only points one way.

| Question you are asked | Explanation type | Typical tool |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Is this model using something it shouldn't? | Global | Permutation importance, coefficient review |
| What relationship did it learn for income? | Global | PDP, GAM shape function |
| Why was this person declined? | Local | SHAP, coefficient x deviation |
| What would change this person's outcome? | Local | Counterfactual search |
| Does it behave differently for subgroups? | Cohort (global within a slice) | Grouped SHAP, per-slice metrics |

That third row -- **cohort explanation** -- is the useful middle ground:
global explanation computed within a slice. It is how you discover that a
model relies on one feature for urban applicants and another for rural
ones, which no single global table will reveal.

> Key Takeaways
> - Global explanations describe the model over the population; local
>   explanations describe one prediction.
> - Global importance rankings are the wrong source for individual reason
>   codes, and can name a feature that contributed nothing to that row.
> - In a linear model the local explanation is the coefficient times the
>   row's deviation from the mean, and the contributions sum exactly to the
>   prediction.
> - Local explanations aggregate into global ones; global explanations
>   cannot be disaggregated into local ones.
> - Individual-facing outputs -- adverse action notices, appeals, support
>   scripts -- must be computed per row.
> - Cohort explanations (global within a slice) reveal behaviour that
>   whole-population summaries hide.
> - Match the explanation type to the question: model validation is global,
>   answering a person is local.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. For a linear model of yours, print the global coefficients and the local
>    contributions for three rows, and find a row whose top driver differs
>    from the global top feature.
> 2. Aggregate your local contributions into a global ranking by mean
>    absolute value and compare it with the coefficient ranking; explain any
>    difference.
> 3. Compute global importance separately within two subgroups and report any
>    feature whose rank changes by more than two positions.
> 4. Write the adverse-action template your system would send, and identify
>    exactly which numbers must come from the row rather than the model.
> 5. Interview: A product manager wants a single "top 3 reasons" panel to
>    display for every user, and proposes computing it once from global
>    importance to save latency. What do you tell them? (Hint: think about
>    which users the shortcut is wrong for, and whether that set is random
>    or systematic.)


#### Permutation Feature Importance

Suppose you have a model you cannot read and you want one number per feature
answering "how much does the model rely on this?" The cheapest honest answer
is destructive: **break the feature and see how much worse the model gets.**

Concretely, take the evaluation set, shuffle one column so its values no
longer line up with the rows they came from, re-score, and record the drop
in your metric. The feature's values are still present and their
distribution is unchanged -- only the *relationship* to the outcome has been
destroyed. If the metric collapses, the model depended on that relationship.
If nothing happens, the model was ignoring it.

The analogy is testing which cables matter by unplugging one at a time and
watching what stops working. It is crude, it is model-agnostic, and it is
usually the first diagnostic worth running because it requires nothing but a
predict function and a metric.

```text
  original          debt_ratio shuffled
  income debt y     income debt y
  38k    0.16 1     38k    0.61 1      <- values kept, pairing destroyed
  92k    0.61 0     92k    0.08 0
  51k    0.08 0     51k    0.16 0

  importance(j) = metric(original) - metric(column j shuffled)
```

Two decisions change the meaning of the result and are routinely made by
accident.

**Which dataset?** Permuting on the *training* set measures how much the
model used the feature to fit, including to fit noise. Permuting on a
held-out set measures how much the feature contributes to performance that
generalises. A feature with a large training drop and a near-zero test drop
is a memorisation channel, not a signal.

**How many repeats?** A single shuffle is one draw from a random process.
Report the mean over several repeats with its spread, or you will rank
features by noise.

```python
X, y, names = make_data(); tr, te = slice(0, 4000), slice(4000, None)
gbm = GBM(n=60, depth=3).fit(X[tr], y[tr])
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)

def perm_imp(Xe, ye, reps=5):
    base = auc(ye, gbm.predict_proba(Xe)); out = []
    for j in range(Xe.shape[1]):
        drops = []
        for _ in range(reps):
            Xp = Xe.copy()
            Xp[:, j] = rng.permutation(Xp[:, j])   # break only column j
            drops.append(base - auc(ye, gbm.predict_proba(Xp)))
        out.append((np.mean(drops), np.std(drops)))
    return base, out

base_te, imp_te = perm_imp(X[te], y[te])
base_tr, imp_tr = perm_imp(X[tr], y[tr])
print(f"baseline AUC   train {base_tr:.3f}   test {base_te:.3f}")
print(f"{'feature':14}{'test drop':>12}{'+/-':>7}{'train drop':>12}")
for n, (m, s), (mt, _) in sorted(zip(names, imp_te, imp_tr),
                                 key=lambda t: -t[1][0]):
    print(f"{n:14}{m:12.4f}{s:7.4f}{mt:12.4f}")

# THE CORRELATED-PAIR TRAP: PERMUTE THE TWO INCOME COLUMNS TOGETHER.
Xp = X[te].copy(); p = rng.permutation(len(Xp))
Xp[:, 0], Xp[:, 4] = Xp[p, 0], Xp[p, 4]            # same shuffle, both cols
print(f"\nlog_income + log_verified permuted TOGETHER: drop "
      f"{base_te - auc(y[te], gbm.predict_proba(Xp)):.4f}")
print(f"correlation of the pair: {np.corrcoef(X[:, 0], X[:, 4])[0, 1]:.3f}")
```

```text
baseline AUC   train 0.790   test 0.778
feature          test drop    +/-  train drop
debt_ratio          0.0625 0.0046      0.0655
log_income          0.0613 0.0093      0.0565
log_verified        0.0511 0.0051      0.0625
late_pmts           0.0224 0.0013      0.0247
age                 0.0142 0.0038      0.0289

log_income + log_verified permuted TOGETHER: drop 0.1902
correlation of the pair: 0.994
```

The last two lines are the single most important thing to understand about
this method. Individually, the two income columns look worth 0.061 and 0.051
AUC. Permuted together they are worth 0.190 -- more than three times their
sum. The reason is that when you break one, the model reads the other, so
each shuffle understates both. **With correlated features, permutation
importance systematically attributes too little to every member of the
correlated group.**

There is a second, subtler problem. Shuffling a column independently of the
others creates rows that cannot exist: a 23-year-old with 40 years of credit
history, a studio apartment with six bedrooms. The model is then evaluated
on inputs from outside the data distribution, where its behaviour is
undefined and arbitrary. The measured drop mixes "the model needed this
feature" with "the model was asked nonsense".

Both problems have standard mitigations:

| Problem | Mitigation |
| --- | --- |
| Correlated features split credit | Permute correlated groups jointly; report group importance |
| Impossible rows created | Permute within strata of the correlated features (conditional permutation) |
| Ranking driven by noise | Repeat 5-20 times, report mean and standard deviation |
| Train/test confusion | Report both; treat a large gap as an overfitting signal |
| Metric insensitivity | Use a metric that reacts to your actual decision (recall at threshold, not accuracy) |

One more property worth stating explicitly: permutation importance measures
**importance to this fitted model**, not importance in the world. If two
features carry the same information and the model happened to key on one,
permutation importance will say the other is worthless. That is a true
statement about the model and a false statement about the problem, and the
difference has misled a great many feature-selection exercises.

> Key Takeaways
> - Permutation importance shuffles one column and measures the metric drop;
>   it needs only a predict function and a metric.
> - Permuting on training data measures fitting; permuting on held-out data
>   measures generalisation, and a large gap between them indicates
>   overfitting to that feature.
> - Always repeat the shuffle and report the spread, or the ranking is noise.
> - Correlated features split the credit between them, understating every
>   member of the group; permute the group jointly to see its true weight.
> - Independent shuffling creates impossible rows, so the drop partly
>   measures the model's behaviour off the data distribution.
> - The result describes the fitted model, not the problem: a redundant
>   feature scores near zero even if it is perfectly predictive on its own.
> - Choose a metric that matches the decision, since importance is defined
>   relative to whatever you measure.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compute permutation importance on train and test for one of your models
>    with 10 repeats, and report mean and standard deviation for each feature.
> 2. Find the two most correlated features in your data, permute them
>    jointly, and compare the group drop with the sum of the individual drops.
> 3. Recompute importance using two different metrics (for example AUC and
>    recall at your production threshold) and explain any reordering.
> 4. Construct a dataset with a duplicated column and demonstrate that both
>    copies score near zero individually.
> 5. Interview: A colleague drops every feature whose permutation importance
>    is below 0.001 and the model's AUC falls noticeably. What happened?
>    (Hint: consider what happens to a group of features that were each
>    individually redundant but jointly necessary.)


#### Partial Dependence and ICE Plots

Feature importance tells you *how much* a feature matters. It says nothing
about *which direction* or *what shape*. A feature can be enormously
important and its effect can be U-shaped, stepped, or reversed in the tails
-- and those are the facts you need to sanity-check a model or explain it to
a domain expert.

A **partial dependence plot** (PDP) answers: if I could set this feature to
value *v* for everybody, leaving all their other characteristics alone, what
would the model predict on average? Mechanically, you take a sample of real
rows, overwrite the feature of interest with *v* in every one, score them
all, and average. Repeat across a grid of *v*.

The analogy is a clinical trial run inside the model: everyone gets the same
dose, the population is otherwise unchanged, and you record the average
response. And, as with a trial, **the average response can hide that half
the patients improved and half got worse.**

That is what an **ICE plot** (individual conditional expectation) fixes.
Instead of averaging, keep one curve per row. The PDP is exactly the mean of
the ICE curves, so nothing is added -- what is removed is the averaging that
conceals disagreement.

```text
  ICE: one line per individual        PDP: the average of those lines

  p  |          ___/                 p  |
     |      ___/                        |        ____/
     |  ___/        low income          |    ___/
     |--------------                    |___/
     |\___                               |
     |     \____    high income         |
     +---------------- debt_ratio       +---------------- debt_ratio
       two populations, opposite            one curve, both stories
       slopes                               averaged away
```

```python
X, y, names = make_data(); tr, te = slice(0, 4000), slice(4000, None)
gbm = GBM(n=60, depth=3).fit(X[tr], y[tr])
grid = np.linspace(0.05, 0.9, 12)
bg = X[te][:400]                          # background sample of real rows

def ice(rows):
    out = np.empty((len(rows), len(grid)))
    for k, v in enumerate(grid):
        Z = rows.copy(); Z[:, 1] = v      # force debt_ratio, keep the rest
        out[:, k] = gbm.predict_proba(Z)
    return out

curves = ice(bg)
pdp = curves.mean(0)                      # PDP == mean of the ICE curves
print("PARTIAL DEPENDENCE OF P(default) ON debt_ratio")
print("  debt_ratio " + "".join(f"{v:6.2f}" for v in grid))
print("  PDP        " + "".join(f"{p:6.2f}" for p in pdp))
lo = X[te][:, 0] < np.quantile(X[:, 0], 0.25)       # bottom income quartile
hi = X[te][:, 0] > np.quantile(X[:, 0], 0.75)       # top income quartile
print("  low income " + "".join(f"{p:6.2f}" for p in ice(X[te][lo][:200]).mean(0)))
print("  high income" + "".join(f"{p:6.2f}" for p in ice(X[te][hi][:200]).mean(0)))

sl = curves[:, -1] - curves[:, 0]                   # per-individual slope
print(f"\nindividual slopes across the grid: mean {sl.mean():+.2f}, "
      f"min {sl.min():+.2f}, max {sl.max():+.2f}")
print(f"share of individuals whose curve goes DOWN: {(sl < 0).mean():.1%}")
cnt, _ = np.histogram(X[:, 1], bins=np.r_[grid - 0.0386, 0.9])
print("  rows near grid point " + "".join(f"{c:6d}" for c in cnt))
```

```text
PARTIAL DEPENDENCE OF P(default) ON debt_ratio
  debt_ratio   0.05  0.13  0.20  0.28  0.36  0.44  0.51  0.59  0.67  0.75  0.82  0.90
  PDP          0.32  0.32  0.32  0.36  0.37  0.44  0.46  0.46  0.50  0.54  0.54  0.54
  low income   0.44  0.45  0.45  0.54  0.55  0.70  0.72  0.73  0.75  0.79  0.79  0.79
  high income  0.20  0.20  0.20  0.20  0.20  0.21  0.22  0.22  0.23  0.25  0.25  0.25

individual slopes across the grid: mean +0.22, min -0.02, max +0.47
share of individuals whose curve goes DOWN: 1.0%
  rows near grid point    287   546   791   808   791   708   595   515   323   255   156    68
```

The PDP says debt ratio raises default probability by 22 points across its
range. True on average, and badly incomplete. For low-income applicants the
effect is 35 points; for high-income applicants it is 5. Anyone who reads
only the PDP will build a policy -- "cap debt ratio at 0.5" -- that is far
too weak for the group it is meant to protect and pointless for the other.

Three practical cautions follow directly from the mechanics.

**The step shape is the model, not the world.** The PDP is flat from 0.05 to
0.20 and jumps at 0.28 because tree ensembles are piecewise constant. Those
plateaus are artifacts of the splits, and reading a real threshold into them
is a mistake.

**The last grid points are extrapolation.** Only 68 of 6,000 rows lie near
debt_ratio = 0.9. The curve is still drawn there, at full visual weight, on
almost no evidence. Always plot the feature's distribution beneath the PDP,
or restrict the grid to the 5th-95th percentile.

**Correlated features make the query points impossible.** Setting
`debt_ratio = 0.9` for a high-income applicant with no late payments creates
a combination the model never saw. This is the same off-distribution problem
as permutation importance, and it has the same fix: **accumulated local
effects** (ALE), which measure the model's *local* differences within narrow
bins of the feature and integrate them, instead of extrapolating globally.

| Method | Answers | Handles interactions | Robust to correlation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| PDP | Average effect of setting a feature | No -- averages them away | No |
| ICE | Per-individual effect | Yes -- shows heterogeneity | No |
| Centred ICE | Effect relative to each row's start | Yes | No |
| 2-D PDP | Joint effect of a feature pair | Only that pair | No |
| ALE | Local effect within observed bins | Partially | Yes |

A workable default: plot ICE with the PDP overlaid, colour a few curves by
a suspected interacting feature, add a rug or histogram of the feature's
distribution, and switch to ALE the moment the feature is strongly
correlated with another.

> Key Takeaways
> - A PDP shows the model's average prediction as one feature is forced
>   across a grid, with all other features left as they are.
> - ICE keeps one curve per row; the PDP is exactly the average of the ICE
>   curves, so ICE strictly adds information.
> - A flat or modest PDP can hide opposite effects in different subgroups --
>   here 35 points for low income against 5 for high income.
> - Plateaus and steps in a tree ensemble's PDP are artifacts of split
>   locations, not thresholds in the world.
> - The tails of a PDP are drawn on very few observations; always show the
>   feature's distribution alongside the curve.
> - Forcing a feature value creates impossible rows when features are
>   correlated; ALE avoids this by working within observed bins.
> - Colour ICE curves by a suspected interacting feature to find
>   heterogeneity you would otherwise average away.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Plot the PDP and ICE curves for your model's most important feature and
>    report the fraction of individuals whose curve slopes opposite to the
>    PDP.
> 2. Overlay a histogram of that feature and mark which part of the PDP rests
>    on fewer than 1% of rows.
> 3. Split the ICE curves by a second feature's quartiles and report the
>    difference in average slope between the top and bottom quartile.
> 4. Implement a one-dimensional ALE plot (differences within bins,
>    cumulatively summed) and compare it with the PDP for a correlated
>    feature.
> 5. Interview: A PDP for "number of previous claims" is almost flat, but the
>    feature has the highest permutation importance in the model. Give two
>    explanations that could both be true. (Hint: one involves the shape of
>    the effect across subgroups, the other involves interactions with other
>    features.)


#### SHAP Values

Every local explanation method is trying to do the same thing: split a
prediction into per-feature parts. The obvious approaches all fail in ways
that are easy to demonstrate. "Remove the feature and see how the prediction
changes" gives a different answer depending on which other features you
removed first. "Coefficient times value" only works for linear models.

SHAP starts from a different question: **is there a unique fair way to
divide a prediction among its features?** That question was answered in
1953, in cooperative game theory, by Lloyd Shapley -- and it was not about
models at all. It was about dividing a payout among players who achieved it
together.

Map the game onto the model:

- the **players** are the features,
- the **payout** is the prediction minus the average prediction,
- a **coalition** *S* is a subset of features whose values you reveal,
- the coalition's **value** *v(S)* is the model's expected output when only
  the features in *S* are set to this row's values and the rest are drawn
  from the data.

A feature's Shapley value is its average marginal contribution across every
possible order in which features could join the coalition. Averaging over
all orders is what removes the arbitrariness of "which feature did we remove
first".

```text
  ONE ROW, THREE FEATURES: ALL 3! = 6 JOINING ORDERS

  {}  --income-->  {inc}  --debt-->  {inc,debt}  --late-->  all
  {}  --income-->  {inc}  --late-->  {inc,late}  --debt-->  all
  {}  --debt-->    {debt} --income-->{inc,debt}  --late-->  all
  ...
  phi(income) = average of income's step size over all six orders
  and: phi(income) + phi(debt) + phi(late) = f(x) - E[f(X)]
```

That last line is the **efficiency** (or local accuracy) property, and it is
what makes SHAP usable in a regulated setting: the contributions add up to
the prediction exactly, so no part of the decision is unexplained. Shapley
values are the unique attribution satisfying efficiency plus symmetry
(identical contributions get identical credit), dummy (a feature the model
ignores gets zero), and additivity across ensembled models.

The cost is combinatorial: *2^d* coalitions. With five features that is 32
and we can compute it exactly; in practice you use KernelSHAP (sampled
coalitions, weighted regression) or TreeSHAP (an exact polynomial-time
algorithm for tree ensembles).

```python
from itertools import combinations
from math import factorial

X, y, names = make_data(); tr, te = slice(0, 4000), slice(4000, None)
gbm = GBM(n=60, depth=3).fit(X[tr], y[tr])
bg = X[tr][np.random.default_rng(3).choice(4000, 80, replace=False)]
d = X.shape[1]

def value(x, S):
    """v(S): expected model output with features in S fixed to x's values
    and every other feature replaced from the background sample."""
    Z = bg.copy()
    for j in S: Z[:, j] = x[j]
    return gbm.predict_proba(Z).mean()

def shap(x):
    v = {frozenset(S): value(x, S)                  # all 2^d coalitions
         for k in range(d+1) for S in combinations(range(d), k)}
    phi = np.zeros(d)
    for j in range(d):
        for k in range(d):                          # |S| = k, j not in S
            for S in combinations([i for i in range(d) if i != j], k):
                wt = factorial(k)*factorial(d-k-1)/factorial(d)
                phi[j] += wt*(v[frozenset(S+(j,))] - v[frozenset(S)])
    return phi, v[frozenset()], v[frozenset(range(d))]

x = X[te][np.argsort(gbm.predict_proba(X[te]))[-25]]
phi, base, full = shap(x)
print("SHAP DECOMPOSITION OF ONE PREDICTION")
print(f"  base value E[f(X)]        {base:+.3f}")
for n, p in sorted(zip(names, phi), key=lambda t: -abs(t[1])):
    print(f"  {n:24}{p:+.3f}")
print(f"  sum of contributions      {phi.sum():+.3f}")
print(f"  base + sum                {base+phi.sum():.3f}")
print(f"  model prediction f(x)     {full:.3f}   <- identical, by design")

G = np.array([shap(r)[0] for r in X[te][:30]])      # local -> global
print("\nGLOBAL IMPORTANCE = MEAN |SHAP| OVER 30 ROWS")
for n, m in sorted(zip(names, np.abs(G).mean(0)), key=lambda t: -t[1]):
    print(f"  {n:14}{m:.4f}")
print("\nSIGN DISAGREEMENT ACROSS ROWS (same feature, opposite direction)")
for n, col in zip(names, G.T):
    print(f"  {n:14} positive for {(col > 0).mean():5.0%} of rows, "
          f"negative for {(col < 0).mean():5.0%}")
```

```text
SHAP DECOMPOSITION OF ONE PREDICTION
  base value E[f(X)]        +0.420
  debt_ratio              +0.200
  log_verified            +0.119
  log_income              +0.101
  late_pmts               -0.019
  age                     -0.009
  sum of contributions      +0.392
  base + sum                0.812
  model prediction f(x)     0.812   <- identical, by design

GLOBAL IMPORTANCE = MEAN |SHAP| OVER 30 ROWS
  debt_ratio    0.0670
  log_income    0.0653
  log_verified  0.0651
  age           0.0354
  late_pmts     0.0289

SIGN DISAGREEMENT ACROSS ROWS (same feature, opposite direction)
  log_income     positive for   40% of rows, negative for   60%
  debt_ratio     positive for   20% of rows, negative for   80%
  age            positive for   17% of rows, negative for   83%
  late_pmts      positive for   50% of rows, negative for   50%
  log_verified   positive for   30% of rows, negative for   70%
```

Three things to read out of that output.

**The additivity is exact.** 0.420 + 0.392 = 0.812, which is the model's
prediction to three decimals. That is not an empirical finding; it is a
mathematical guarantee, and it is why SHAP is the default for
individual-level reason codes.

**Averaging the absolute values turns local explanations into a global
one.** The ranking it produces is generally more trustworthy than
permutation importance because it is not confounded by metric choice -- but
note that the correlated income pair still splits roughly evenly (0.065 and
0.065), so SHAP does not escape the correlated-feature problem either. The
`shap` interventional formulation spreads credit across the group; the
`tree_path_dependent` formulation spreads it differently. Neither is wrong,
and they disagree.

**Signs vary by row.** `debt_ratio` pushes 80% of rows down and 20% up. This
is the local/global distinction reappearing: a global bar chart of mean
|SHAP| tells you *how much* a feature moves predictions, and deliberately
discards *which way*. Use a beeswarm plot (one dot per row, coloured by
feature value) when direction matters.

Four caveats that matter in production:

| Caveat | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| The base value depends on the background set | Explanations against "all customers" and "declined customers" differ; state which |
| Cost grows with features and background size | KernelSHAP is sampled and therefore noisy; TreeSHAP is exact but tree-only |
| Attribution is in the model's output units | SHAP on log-odds is additive; SHAP on probability is not; pick one and label it |
| Correlated features share credit | A feature can look moderately important while being individually irreplaceable |

And the one misreading to guard against above all: **a SHAP value is not a
causal effect.** It says how much this feature's value moved *this model's
output* relative to a baseline. It does not say what would happen in the
world if the feature changed. That question needs the counterfactual and
causal machinery, not an attribution.

> Key Takeaways
> - SHAP divides a prediction into per-feature contributions using Shapley
>   values from cooperative game theory, averaging over all orders in which
>   features could be revealed.
> - Contributions plus the base value equal the prediction exactly, which is
>   what makes SHAP defensible for individual reason codes.
> - Shapley values are the unique attribution satisfying efficiency,
>   symmetry, dummy, and additivity.
> - Exact computation is exponential in the number of features; use TreeSHAP
>   for tree ensembles and sampled KernelSHAP otherwise.
> - Mean absolute SHAP aggregates local explanations into a global ranking
>   while discarding direction; beeswarm plots retain it.
> - The explanation is relative to a chosen background distribution, so the
>   baseline must be stated alongside the numbers.
> - Correlated features still share credit, and different SHAP variants split
>   it differently.
> - A SHAP value is an attribution of the model's output, not a causal effect
>   in the world.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compute exact Shapley values for one row of a 4-feature model by brute
>    force and verify that the contributions plus the base value equal the
>    prediction.
> 2. Recompute SHAP for the same row against two different background sets
>    (all rows, then only approved rows) and explain why the numbers move.
> 3. Compare mean absolute SHAP with permutation importance on the same model
>    and account for any disagreement in the ranking.
> 4. Compute SHAP on log-odds and on probability for the same row and show
>    that only one of them sums to the prediction gap.
> 5. Interview: A stakeholder reads that "income contributed +0.10 to this
>    applicant's default probability" and concludes that raising the
>    applicant's income by any amount will lower their risk by 0.10. Correct
>    them. (Hint: distinguish attribution relative to a baseline population
>    from the effect of an intervention on one person.)


#### LIME

SHAP's guarantees come from evaluating the model over every coalition of
features, which is expensive and requires deciding how to "hide" a feature.
LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) takes a completely
different route, with a simpler intuition: **any smooth function looks
linear if you zoom in far enough.**

So: pick the row you want to explain, generate a cloud of synthetic points
around it, ask the black box for its prediction on each, weight those points
by how close they are to your row, and fit a sparse linear model to the
weighted cloud. The linear model's coefficients are the explanation. You are
not describing the model; you are describing a small neighbourhood of it.

The analogy is surveying a hillside. You cannot describe an entire mountain
range with a plane, but you can describe the patch of ground you are
standing on with a slope and a direction -- and that is precisely what you
need to answer "which way is downhill from here?"

```text
  the black box's decision surface       LIME's local linear fit

     ___                                       /
    /   \___                                  /
   /        \__     x                    o o x   <- weighted samples
  /            \___/ \                  o  /  o     near x only
 /                     \                  /
 +---------------------------          +------------------------
 global behaviour: nonlinear           local behaviour: a slope
```

Four choices define a LIME explanation, and all four are yours to make:
how to sample perturbations, how to measure distance, the **kernel width**
that decides what "local" means, and how many features the surrogate may
use. Different choices give different explanations of the same prediction.

```python
X, y, names = make_data(); tr, te = slice(0, 4000), slice(4000, None)
gbm = GBM(n=60, depth=3).fit(X[tr], y[tr])
mu, sd = X[tr].mean(0), X[tr].std(0)
x = X[te][np.argsort(gbm.predict_proba(X[te]))[-25]]

def lime(x, n=800, width=0.75, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    Xp = mu + rng.normal(0, 1, (n, X.shape[1])) * sd      # sample the space
    dist = np.linalg.norm((Xp - x) / sd, axis=1)          # distance to x
    wts = np.exp(-(dist**2) / (2*width*len(x)))           # locality kernel
    yq = gbm.predict_proba(Xp)                            # black box answers
    A = np.c_[np.ones(n), (Xp - x) / sd]
    W = np.diag(wts)                                      # weighted ridge fit
    beta = np.linalg.solve(A.T @ W @ A + 1e-3*np.eye(A.shape[1]), A.T @ W @ yq)
    ybar = (wts*yq).sum()/wts.sum()
    r2 = 1 - (wts*(yq - A @ beta)**2).sum()/(wts*(yq - ybar)**2).sum()
    return beta[0], beta[1:], r2, wts

b0, coef, r2, wts = lime(x)
print(f"LIME AROUND ONE APPLICANT   f(x)={gbm.predict_proba(x[None])[0]:.3f}"
      f"   local R2={r2:.2f}")
print(f"effective sample size = {wts.sum()**2/(wts**2).sum():.0f} of 800")
for n, c in sorted(zip(names, coef), key=lambda t: -abs(t[1])):
    print(f"  {n:14}{c:+.3f} per standard deviation")

print("\nSTABILITY AT A SMALLER PERTURBATION BUDGET (n=100)")
print(f"  {'seed':>6}" + "".join(f"{n[:11]:>13}" for n in names) + f"{'R2':>7}")
for s in range(4):
    _, c, r, _ = lime(x, n=100, seed=s)
    print(f"  {s:6}" + "".join(f"{v:+13.3f}" for v in c) + f"{r:7.2f}")

print("\nSENSITIVITY TO THE KERNEL WIDTH (a free parameter you must pick)")
print(f"  {'width':>6}" + "".join(f"{n[:11]:>13}" for n in names) + f"{'R2':>7}")
for wd in (0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 4.0):
    _, c, r, _ = lime(x, width=wd, seed=0)
    print(f"  {wd:6.2f}" + "".join(f"{v:+13.3f}" for v in c) + f"{r:7.2f}")
```

```text

effective sample size = 363 of 800
  debt_ratio    +0.085 per standard deviation
  log_income    -0.083 per standard deviation
  log_verified  -0.083 per standard deviation
  late_pmts     +0.032 per standard deviation
  age           -0.022 per standard deviation

STABILITY AT A SMALLER PERTURBATION BUDGET (n=100)
    seed   log_income   debt_ratio          age    late_pmts  log_verifie     R2
       0       -0.086       +0.087       -0.021       +0.042       -0.086   0.86
       1       -0.089       +0.109       -0.011       +0.037       -0.083   0.80
       2       -0.070       +0.083       -0.020       +0.024       -0.080   0.82
       3       -0.110       +0.080       -0.025       +0.024       -0.078   0.81

SENSITIVITY TO THE KERNEL WIDTH (a free parameter you must pick)
   width   log_income   debt_ratio          age    late_pmts  log_verifie     R2
    0.25       -0.073       +0.051       -0.001       +0.010       -0.066   0.65
    0.50       -0.084       +0.081       -0.018       +0.026       -0.082   0.77
    1.00       -0.081       +0.084       -0.023       +0.034       -0.082   0.79
```
