The first block is a perfectly reasonable explanation: debt ratio pushes this
applicant's risk up, income pushes it down, and the local linear
approximation captures 79% of the model's variation in the neighbourhood.
Report that R-squared always -- it is LIME's fidelity measure, and a low
value means the explanation does not describe the model even locally.

The next two blocks are the reason LIME is used with caution in high-stakes
settings. At 100 perturbations, the same applicant, the same model, and only
a different random seed produce income coefficients from -0.070 to -0.110, a
57% swing, and the top-driver ranking between `log_income` and `debt_ratio`
flips between seeds. At kernel width 0.25 the effect of `late_pmts` is
+0.010; at width 4.0 it is +0.038, nearly four times larger. Nothing about
the model changed. **Two applicants with identical files can receive
different reason codes, and an applicant who appeals can receive a different
answer than the first time.**

| | SHAP | LIME |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Foundation | Game theory, axioms | Local linear approximation |
| Adds up to the prediction | Yes, exactly | No, only approximately |
| Free parameters | Background set | Kernel width, distance, sample size, sparsity |
| Stability | High (exact variants) | Low to moderate; must be measured |
| Cost per explanation | High (or tree-specialised) | Moderate, one model fit |
| Works on text/images | Yes, with segmentations | Yes, natively via superpixels/tokens |
| Fidelity report | Guaranteed | Local R-squared, must be reported |

LIME still earns its place. It is the easiest method to apply to text and
images, where "features" are tokens or superpixels and turning them off is
natural. It produces a genuinely sparse explanation ("these three words
drove the classification"), which is often more useful to a human than
attributions over 30,000 dimensions. And it is fast enough to run
interactively during debugging.

The rule for using it responsibly: **fix the seed, fix the kernel width,
and report the local fidelity with every explanation.** If the explanation
is destined for a person affected by the decision, run it several times and
verify the top reasons do not move.

> Key Takeaways
> - LIME explains one prediction by fitting a sparse linear model to
>   perturbed samples around that row, weighted by proximity.
> - It describes a neighbourhood of the model, not the model, and its
>   contributions do not sum to the prediction.
> - Local R-squared is LIME's fidelity measure and must be reported with
>   every explanation.
> - The explanation depends on four free choices: sampling scheme, distance
>   metric, kernel width, and surrogate sparsity.
> - With small perturbation budgets, different seeds change coefficients by
>   tens of percent and can reorder the top drivers.
> - Kernel width materially changes the answer, and there is no principled
>   way to choose it from the model alone.
> - LIME's practical advantage is text and image data, where perturbation by
>   removing tokens or superpixels is natural and the sparse output is
>   readable.
> - For individual-facing use, pin the seed and parameters and verify that
>   repeated runs give the same top reasons.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Run LIME 20 times on one row with different seeds and report the
>    standard deviation of each coefficient and how often the top feature
>    changes.
> 2. Sweep the kernel width over two orders of magnitude and plot how the
>    explanation and the local R-squared change.
> 3. Compare LIME and SHAP explanations for the same three rows and
>    characterise where they disagree.
> 4. Apply LIME to a text classifier by deleting random words, and inspect
>    whether the highlighted words are plausible causes.
> 5. Interview: Your compliance team asks whether LIME explanations can be
>    used as adverse action reasons. What conditions would you require first?
>    (Hint: think about reproducibility of the same answer for the same
>    person, and about what fidelity number you would have to commit to.)


#### Counterfactual Explanations

Attribution methods answer "what drove this outcome?" People affected by a
decision almost never ask that. They ask **"what do I have to do
differently?"** Those are different questions, and a SHAP value does not
answer the second one.

A **counterfactual explanation** is the answer to the second question: the
nearest set of feature values that would have produced a different outcome.
"Your application was declined. It would have been approved with an annual
income of 43,800 instead of 38,100, all else equal." That statement is
checkable by the applicant, actionable, and does not require them to
understand the model at all.

The analogy is the difference between a post-mortem and a set of directions.
A post-mortem tells you why you are where you are; directions tell you how to
get somewhere else. Both are useful; only one is what you want when you are
lost.

Formally, you search for x' minimising a cost that combines three things:

```text
  minimise    cost(x, x')
  subject to  model(x') crosses the decision threshold
              x' is plausible     (a real combination of values)
              x' is actionable    (only features the person can change)

  cost = sum over changed features of  (effort_j x size of change_j)
```

Each constraint corresponds to a real failure. Drop plausibility and you
produce "approved if your debt ratio were negative". Drop actionability and
you produce "approved if you were 26 instead of 23", which is not recourse,
it is an insult -- and in several jurisdictions, evidence of a problem.

```python
X, y, names = make_data(); tr, te = slice(0, 4000), slice(4000, None)
gbm = GBM(n=60, depth=3).fit(X[tr], y[tr])
p_te = gbm.predict_proba(X[te])
cand = np.where((p_te > 0.58) & (p_te < 0.66) & (X[te][:, 3] >= 1))[0]
x = X[te][cand[0]]                              # a borderline decline
THRESH = 0.5
print(f"applicant: income {np.exp(x[0]):,.0f}, debt_ratio {x[1]:.2f}, "
      f"age {x[2]:.0f}, late {x[3]:.0f}")
print(f"p(default) = {gbm.predict_proba(x[None])[0]:.3f}  -> DECLINED "
      f"(threshold {THRESH})\n")

# EFFORT WEIGHTS AND ALLOWED DIRECTIONS ENCODE ACTIONABILITY. AGE IS ABSENT
# FROM THIS TABLE ON PURPOSE: IT IS NOT A THING THE APPLICANT CAN CHANGE.
COST = {1: ("debt_ratio", 4.0, -1), 0: ("income", 3.0, +1),
        3: ("late_pmts", 9.0, -1)}
best = None
for dd in np.arange(0, 0.81, 0.02):             # cut debt ratio
    for di in np.arange(0, 0.81, 0.02):         # raise log income
        for dl in (0, 1, 2, 3):                 # wait out late payments
            z = x.copy()
            z[1] = max(0.0, x[1]-dd)
            z[0] = x[0]+di; z[4] = z[0]         # verified income moves too
            z[3] = max(0.0, x[3]-dl)
            if gbm.predict_proba(z[None])[0] >= THRESH: continue
            cost = 4.0*dd/0.1 + 3.0*di/0.1 + 9.0*dl
            if best is None or cost < best[0]: best = (cost, dd, di, dl, z)

cost, dd, di, dl, z = best
print("NEAREST ACTIONABLE COUNTERFACTUAL (age and history treated as fixed)")
print(f"  reduce debt_ratio by {dd:.2f}  ({x[1]:.2f} -> {z[1]:.2f})")
print(f"  raise income by {np.exp(di)-1:.1%}  "
      f"({np.exp(x[0]):,.0f} -> {np.exp(z[0]):,.0f})")
print(f"  clear {dl} late payment(s)")
print(f"  new p(default) = {gbm.predict_proba(z[None])[0]:.3f} -> APPROVED"
      f"   (effort score {cost:.0f})")

print("\nSINGLE-FEATURE COUNTERFACTUALS: IS ANY ONE CHANGE ENOUGH?")
for j, (nm, _, sign) in COST.items():
    found = None
    for step in np.arange(0.02, 3.0, 0.02):
        z2 = x.copy(); z2[j] = max(0.0, x[j] + sign*step)
        if j == 0: z2[4] = z2[0]
        if gbm.predict_proba(z2[None])[0] < THRESH: found = z2[j]; break
    print(f"  {nm:12} alone: " + (f"reach {found:.2f}" if found is not None
          else "no reachable value flips the decision"))
```

```text
applicant: income 38,079, debt_ratio 0.16, age 23, late 1
p(default) = 0.618  -> DECLINED (threshold 0.5)

NEAREST ACTIONABLE COUNTERFACTUAL (age and history treated as fixed)
  reduce debt_ratio by 0.00  (0.16 -> 0.16)
  raise income by 15.0%  (38,079 -> 43,801)
  clear 0 late payment(s)
  new p(default) = 0.492 -> APPROVED   (effort score 4)

SINGLE-FEATURE COUNTERFACTUALS: IS ANY ONE CHANGE ENOUGH?
  debt_ratio   alone: no reachable value flips the decision
  income       alone: reach 10.69
  late_pmts    alone: no reachable value flips the decision
```

This example contains the lesson that makes counterfactuals worth the effort.
A SHAP explanation of this applicant would put `age` near the top: they are
23, and the model learned a sharp penalty below 25. That is a true statement
about the model and a useless statement to the applicant. The counterfactual
search, told that age is not actionable, finds the only route that exists:
15% more income. Note also that reducing debt ratio cannot flip the decision
at all -- it is already 0.16, so there is nothing left to give.

Several properties are worth knowing before you ship this.

**Counterfactuals are not unique.** There are usually many minimal-ish
changes, and which one you show is a design decision. Presenting a *diverse
set* ("any one of these three would have worked") is more useful and more
honest than presenting one.

**The distance metric is a policy statement.** Declaring that a 10% income
rise is "cheaper" than clearing a late payment encodes a claim about human
effort. Write those weights down, have them reviewed, and do not let them be
an accident of feature scaling.

**A counterfactual is not a causal promise.** The model says it would have
scored the applicant differently with that income. Whether earning more
income actually reduces their default risk is a causal question the model
cannot answer, and if the feature is a proxy rather than a cause, the advice
may be gameable without being beneficial -- the "recourse versus gaming"
problem.

**They must remain valid.** If the model is retrained next week, the advice
you gave may no longer hold. Serious deployments version the model behind
every counterfactual and honour the advice for a stated period.

| Property | Attribution (SHAP/LIME) | Counterfactual |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Question answered | Why this score? | What would change it? |
| Output | A number per feature | An alternative input row |
| Needs actionability model | No | Yes -- which features can change, at what cost |
| Uniqueness | One answer | Many; diversity is a feature |
| Directly usable by a layperson | Rarely | Usually |
| Legal framing | Reason codes | Recourse |

> Key Takeaways
> - A counterfactual explanation gives the nearest input that would have
>   produced a different decision, answering "what must I change?" rather
>   than "why?".
> - The search needs three constraints: it must flip the decision, be
>   plausible, and only touch features the person can act on.
> - Immutable attributes must be excluded from the search; recourse that
>   requires being older or a different sex is not recourse.
> - The cost function encodes a human-effort policy and should be written
>   down and reviewed, not left to feature scaling.
> - Counterfactuals are not unique; presenting a diverse set is more useful
>   and more honest than presenting one.
> - A counterfactual describes the model's behaviour, not a causal guarantee
>   about the world, and proxy features make the advice gameable.
> - Advice tied to a model version stops being true when the model is
>   retrained, so version and time-bound it.
> - Some features offer no recourse at all; discovering that is itself a
>   finding worth escalating.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement a grid or random search for the nearest counterfactual on a
>    model of yours and report the change it finds for three declined rows.
> 2. Add a constraint that one feature is immutable and report how much the
>    required effort increases.
> 3. Generate three diverse counterfactuals for the same row and write the
>    customer-facing message you would send.
> 4. Retrain the model on a different data sample and check whether the
>    counterfactuals you produced earlier still flip the decision.
> 5. Interview: An applicant follows your counterfactual advice exactly,
>    reapplies, and is declined again. List the possible causes. (Hint:
>    consider what changed between the two scoring events, and whether the
>    features the applicant changed were the only ones that moved.)


#### Limits of Explanation Methods

Every method in this section produces confident, plausible, well-formatted
output whether or not it is telling you something true. The final skill is
knowing what the output cannot establish -- because explanation tooling
fails silently, and a wrong explanation is worse than none: it manufactures
confidence.

**Limit 1: many different models fit the data equally well, and they
disagree about why.** This is the *Rashomon effect*, named for the film in
which several witnesses describe the same event incompatibly. When two
features carry overlapping information, which one the model keys on is
decided by accidents of regularisation, seed, and sample -- not by the world.

**Limit 2: importance rankings are estimates, and estimates have variance.**
The ranking that a report presents as a fact is a statistic with a confidence
interval that is almost never shown.

```python
X, y, names = make_data(); tr, te = slice(0, 4000), slice(4000, None)
print("TWO MODELS, INDISTINGUISHABLE ACCURACY, DIFFERENT STORY")
for label, cols in [("uses reported income ", [0, 1, 2, 3]),
                    ("uses verified income ", [4, 1, 2, 3]),
                    ("uses both            ", [0, 1, 2, 3, 4])]:
    w, b, mu, sd = logistic(X[tr][:, cols], y[tr])
    a = auc(y[te], ((X[te][:, cols]-mu)/sd) @ w + b)
    top = [names[cols[k]] for k in np.argsort(-np.abs(w))[:2]]
    print(f"  {label} AUC {a:.3f}   top drivers: {', '.join(top)}")
print("  The two income columns correlate at "
      f"{np.corrcoef(X[:, 0], X[:, 4])[0, 1]:.3f}; a reviewer reading either")
print("  report would name a different variable as the deciding factor.\n")

print("SAME ALGORITHM, DIFFERENT BOOTSTRAP: HOW STABLE IS THE RANKING?")
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
for rep in range(5):
    idx = rng.choice(4000, 400, replace=True)      # a small-data regime
    g = GBM(n=40, depth=3).fit(X[tr][idx], y[tr][idx])
    base = auc(y[te], g.predict_proba(X[te])); drops = []
    for j in range(X.shape[1]):
        Xp = X[te].copy(); Xp[:, j] = rng.permutation(Xp[:, j])
        drops.append(base - auc(y[te], g.predict_proba(Xp)))
    order = np.argsort(-np.array(drops))
    print(f"  replicate {rep}: " + " > ".join(names[k] for k in order))

print("\nHOW MANY PDP QUERY POINTS RESEMBLE A REAL APPLICANT?")
Z = (X - X.mean(0)) / X.std(0); bg = X[te][:300]
print(f"  {'debt_ratio':>12}{'median dist to 10th NN':>26}{'% with no close row':>22}")
for v in (0.05, 0.3, 0.6, 0.9):
    Q = bg.copy(); Q[:, 1] = v                     # the PDP's query points
    Qz = (Q - X.mean(0)) / X.std(0)
    d = np.sqrt(((Qz[:, None, :] - Z[tr][:600][None, :, :])**2).sum(-1))
    nn10 = np.sort(d, axis=1)[:, 9]                # distance to 10th neighbour
    print(f"  {v:12.2f}{np.median(nn10):26.2f}{(nn10 > 1.5).mean():22.1%}")
```

```text
TWO MODELS, INDISTINGUISHABLE ACCURACY, DIFFERENT STORY
  uses reported income  AUC 0.771   top drivers: log_income, debt_ratio
  uses verified income  AUC 0.768   top drivers: log_verified, debt_ratio
  uses both             AUC 0.770   top drivers: log_income, debt_ratio
  The two income columns correlate at 0.994; a reviewer reading either
  report would name a different variable as the deciding factor.

SAME ALGORITHM, DIFFERENT BOOTSTRAP: HOW STABLE IS THE RANKING?
  replicate 0: log_income > debt_ratio > log_verified > age > late_pmts
  replicate 1: log_verified > debt_ratio > log_income > late_pmts > age
  replicate 2: log_income > debt_ratio > log_verified > age > late_pmts
  replicate 3: log_income > debt_ratio > log_verified > late_pmts > age
  replicate 4: log_verified > debt_ratio > late_pmts > log_income > age

HOW MANY PDP QUERY POINTS RESEMBLE A REAL APPLICANT?
    debt_ratio    median dist to 10th NN   % with no close row
          0.05                      1.19                 12.7%
          0.30                      0.89                  7.0%
          0.60                      1.06                  8.7%
          0.90                      1.40                 34.0%
```

Three models with AUC 0.768, 0.770, and 0.771 -- differences well inside
sampling noise -- name different top drivers. Resample the training data and
the *most important feature* changes between replicates. And a third of the
PDP's query points at debt_ratio = 0.9 have no close analogue in the training
data at all, so the model's behaviour there is extrapolation being reported
as description.

The remaining limits do not need code to state, only discipline to remember.

| Limit | What it means in practice |
| --- | --- |
| Not causal | Every method describes the model's input-output mapping, not the world's mechanism |
| Off-manifold evaluation | Permutation, PDP, and SHAP all query impossible rows; the model's answers there are arbitrary |
| Correlated features | Credit is split or shifted arbitrarily among near-duplicates |
| Explanation does not validate | A model with a leaked feature produces a beautiful, coherent explanation of its leakage |
| Interactions are collapsed | A single number per feature cannot express "matters only when X is high" |
| Fairwashing | Explanations can be optimised to look acceptable while the model is unchanged |
| Human over-trust | People accept plausible explanations without checking fidelity, especially when presented graphically |

The **fairwashing** row deserves emphasis because it is an adversarial risk,
not just an error. Given freedom over the background set, kernel width,
surrogate family, and which features to display, a motivated analyst can
produce an explanation that omits the uncomfortable variable without changing
a single model weight. This is why explanation *configuration* must be
version-controlled and reviewed like model code.

A defensible practice, then, is not "run SHAP" but:

1. **Report fidelity with every explanation** -- surrogate R-squared, local
   R-squared, or the exactness guarantee you are relying on.
2. **Report stability** -- rerun with different seeds, background sets, and
   bootstrap samples, and publish the variation rather than one draw.
3. **Report support** -- state how many real observations back the region
   being explained; refuse to plot where there is no data.
4. **Cross-check with a second method** -- agreement between SHAP,
   permutation importance, and a fitted GAM is weak evidence of truth;
   disagreement is strong evidence of a problem.
5. **Never present an explanation as a causal claim** without a causal
   design behind it.
6. **Version the explanation configuration** with the model, so the reasons
   given to a person can be reproduced years later.

> Key Takeaways
> - Many models fit the data equally well and attribute the outcome to
>   different features; near-identical accuracy does not imply a shared story.
> - Importance rankings are statistics with variance; in small-data regimes
>   the top feature can change between bootstrap samples.
> - Permutation, PDP, and SHAP all evaluate the model on inputs that do not
>   occur in reality, especially in the tails.
> - No explanation method is causal; all describe the model's mapping, not
>   the world.
> - A coherent explanation of a leaking or biased model is still coherent --
>   explanations do not validate models.
> - Single numbers per feature cannot express interactions, so conditional
>   effects are silently collapsed.
> - Explanation configuration is adversarially exploitable (fairwashing) and
>   must be version-controlled and reviewed.
> - Defensible practice means reporting fidelity, stability, and data support
>   with every explanation, and cross-checking with a second method.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Train five models on bootstrap resamples of your data and report how
>    often the top-ranked feature changes.
> 2. Fit two models on overlapping feature subsets with near-identical
>    accuracy and write the two contradictory explanation summaries they
>    produce.
> 3. For your PDP grid, measure the distance from each query point to its
>    tenth nearest real row and mark the region you should refuse to plot.
> 4. Take a model with a deliberately leaked feature, generate a SHAP summary,
>    and show that the explanation looks entirely reasonable.
> 5. Interview: You are asked to sign off that a model's explanations are
>    "accurate". What would you insist the sign-off statement actually say?
>    (Hint: accuracy of an explanation is fidelity to the model, not truth
>    about the world, and it is a measured quantity with a range.)


<a id="162-fairness-and-bias"></a>
### 16.2 Fairness and Bias

Fairness in machine learning is not one property but a family of
incompatible ones, and choosing between them is a normative decision that
cannot be delegated to a metric; this section covers where bias enters
before any model is fitted, the standard statistical definitions of fairness
and what each one actually asserts, how regulators test for disparate
impact, the three families of mitigation and what each costs, the
mathematical reason you cannot have everything at once, and how to keep
watching after deployment.

The examples share a hiring model on synthetic data constructed so that the
two groups have *almost identical* true success rates, while every observed
feature is measured less favourably for one of them. That is the hard case,
and it is the common one.

```python
import numpy as np

def make_hiring(n=20000, seed=4):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    g = (rng.random(n) < 0.35).astype(int)         # 1 = group B (minority)
    skill = rng.normal(0, 1, n)                    # unobserved true ability
    # measurement bias: the test under-measures group B and is noisier
    test = skill - 0.35*g + rng.normal(0, 1, n)*(0.9 + 0.2*g)
    # access bias: prestige tracks skill for A, barely for B
    prestige = skill*(1.3 - 1.2*g) - 0.5*g + rng.normal(0, 0.5, n)
    referral = (rng.random(n) < np.where(g == 1, 0.10, 0.30)).astype(float)
    perform = (skill + rng.normal(0, 0.7, n) > 0.4).astype(int)   # true label
    # historical labels: past humans hired with a penalty against group B
    hist = ((0.9*test + 0.6*prestige + 0.8*referral - 0.7*g
             + rng.normal(0, 0.7, n)) > 0.6).astype(int)
    X = np.column_stack([test, prestige, referral])
    return X, perform, hist, g, ["test_score", "prestige", "referral"]

def auc(y, s):
    o = np.argsort(s); r = np.empty(len(s)); r[o] = np.arange(1, len(s)+1)
    n1 = y.sum(); n0 = len(y) - n1
    return (r[y == 1].sum() - n1*(n1+1)/2)/(n0*n1)

def logistic(X, y, sw=None, iters=4000, lr=0.6):
    Xs = (X - X.mean(0))/X.std(0)
    sw = np.ones(len(y)) if sw is None else sw*len(y)/sw.sum()
    w = np.zeros(X.shape[1]); b = 0.0
    for _ in range(iters):
        p = 1/(1+np.exp(-(Xs @ w + b)))
        gr = sw*(p - y)/len(y)
        w -= lr*(Xs.T @ gr); b -= lr*gr.sum()
    return lambda Z: 1/(1+np.exp(-(((Z-X.mean(0))/X.std(0)) @ w + b))), w

def rates(y, yhat, g):
    """The confusion matrix by group, as the rates fairness criteria use."""
    out = {}
    for k in (0, 1):
        m = g == k
        tp = ((yhat==1) & (y==1) & m).sum(); fn = ((yhat==0) & (y==1) & m).sum()
        fp = ((yhat==1) & (y==0) & m).sum(); tn = ((yhat==0) & (y==0) & m).sum()
        out[k] = dict(sel=(yhat[m]==1).mean(), tpr=tp/max(tp+fn, 1),
                      fpr=fp/max(fp+tn, 1), ppv=tp/max(tp+fp, 1),
                      base=y[m].mean(), n=int(m.sum()))
    return out
```


#### Sources of Bias in Data

The phrase "biased algorithm" is almost always wrong about the location of
the problem. Learning algorithms are indifferent: they minimise a loss over
whatever they are given. If the output is unequal, the inequality was in the
inputs, the labels, the sampling, the framing, or the deployment -- and
knowing which one is the difference between a fix that works and a
post-processing patch that hides the symptom.

The useful mental model is a chain of measurements between the world and the
model, where each link can distort:

```text
  the world          -> who gets recorded   -> what is measured
  (true ability)        (sampling bias)        (measurement bias)
                                                     |
  what decision        <- what label is kept  <------+
  gets deployed           (historical/label bias)
  (deployment bias)
       |
       +-> feeds back into next year's data (feedback loop)
```

Six named sources, each with a distinct fix:

| Source | What it is | Example | Fix direction |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Historical bias | The world itself is unequal, and the data records it faithfully | Past managers hired fewer B candidates | Change the target, not the model |
| Representation bias | A group is too small in the sample to be learned well | 2% of training rows are group B | Collect or oversample; report per-group sample size |
| Measurement bias | The proxy measures the construct differently by group | A test that under-measures B's skill | Fix or drop the instrument; validate per group |
| Aggregation bias | One model imposed on populations with different relationships | Prestige predicts success for A but not B | Per-group models, interactions, or hierarchical models |
| Label bias | The label is a record of a biased decision, not the outcome | "Was hired" instead of "performed well" | Relabel with the outcome you actually care about |
| Deployment bias | The model is used differently from how it was validated | A risk score built for triage used for sentencing | Governance, not modelling |

The single most consequential of these is **label bias**, because it is
invisible to every diagnostic that treats the label as ground truth. If the
label is "was hired" and past hiring was discriminatory, a model with perfect
accuracy reproduces discrimination perfectly, and every validation metric
says it is excellent.

```python
X, y, hist, g, names = make_hiring()
tr, te = slice(0, 14000), slice(14000, None)

print("THE SAME FEATURES, TWO DIFFERENT LABELS")
print(f"  true on-the-job success rate   A {y[g==0].mean():.3f}"
      f"   B {y[g==1].mean():.3f}")
print(f"  historical hiring decision     A {hist[g==0].mean():.3f}"
      f"   B {hist[g==1].mean():.3f}")
for lab, target in [("trained on historical decisions", hist),
                    ("trained on measured performance", y)]:
    f, _ = logistic(X[tr], target[tr])
    yhat = (f(X[te]) > 0.5).astype(int)
    a, b = yhat[g[te]==0].mean(), yhat[g[te]==1].mean()
    print(f"  {lab:34} select A {a:.3f}  B {b:.3f}  ratio {b/a:.2f}")

print("\nMEASUREMENT BIAS: THE FEATURE, NOT THE PERSON")
for j, n in enumerate(names):
    print(f"  mean {n:12} A {X[g==0, j].mean():+.3f}   B {X[g==1, j].mean():+.3f}")
print("  ...while true success rates differ by only "
      f"{abs(y[g==0].mean()-y[g==1].mean()):.3f}")

print("\nAGGREGATION BIAS: ONE MODEL FOR TWO DIFFERENT POPULATIONS")
mA, mB = g[te]==0, g[te]==1
f, _ = logistic(X[tr], y[tr]); sp = f(X[te])
print(f"  pooled model        AUC on A {auc(y[te][mA], sp[mA]):.3f}"
      f"   AUC on B {auc(y[te][mB], sp[mB]):.3f}")
fa, wa = logistic(X[tr][g[tr]==0], y[tr][g[tr]==0])
fb, wb = logistic(X[tr][g[tr]==1], y[tr][g[tr]==1])
print(f"  per-group models    AUC on A {auc(y[te][mA], fa(X[te][mA])):.3f}"
      f"   AUC on B {auc(y[te][mB], fb(X[te][mB])):.3f}")
print("  weights A: " + "  ".join(f"{n}={v:+.2f}" for n, v in zip(names, wa)))
print("  weights B: " + "  ".join(f"{n}={v:+.2f}" for n, v in zip(names, wb)))

print("\nREPRESENTATION BIAS: HOW MUCH GROUP-B DATA BUYS A GROUP-B MODEL")
print(f"  {'B rows in training':>20}{'mean AUC on B':>16}{'sd over 8 seeds':>18}")
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); iB = np.where(g[tr]==1)[0]
for nB in (40, 150, 600, 2400):
    aucs = []
    for _ in range(8):
        idx = rng.choice(iB, nB, replace=False)
        fbb, _ = logistic(X[tr][idx], y[tr][idx])
        aucs.append(auc(y[te][mB], fbb(X[te][mB])))
    print(f"  {nB:20}{np.mean(aucs):16.3f}{np.std(aucs):18.3f}")
```

```text
THE SAME FEATURES, TWO DIFFERENT LABELS
  true on-the-job success rate   A 0.374   B 0.363
  historical hiring decision     A 0.433   B 0.125
  trained on historical decisions    select A 0.397  B 0.166  ratio 0.42
  trained on measured performance    select A 0.383  B 0.164  ratio 0.43

MEASUREMENT BIAS: THE FEATURE, NOT THE PERSON
  mean test_score   A +0.001   B -0.362
  mean prestige     A +0.003   B -0.502
  mean referral     A +0.300   B +0.101
  ...while true success rates differ by only 0.010

AGGREGATION BIAS: ONE MODEL FOR TWO DIFFERENT POPULATIONS
  pooled model        AUC on A 0.861   AUC on B 0.755
  per-group models    AUC on A 0.871   AUC on B 0.767
  weights A: test_score=+0.50  prestige=+1.75  referral=-0.00
  weights B: test_score=+1.09  prestige=+0.18  referral=-0.06

REPRESENTATION BIAS: HOW MUCH GROUP-B DATA BUYS A GROUP-B MODEL
    B rows in training   mean AUC on B   sd over 8 seeds
                    40           0.755             0.015
                   150           0.757             0.013
                   600           0.765             0.003
                  2400           0.767             0.001
```

The first block sets up the expectation and the second demolishes it.
Historical hiring favoured group A more than three to one (0.433 against
0.125) while true success rates differ by one percentage point. Fixing the
label -- training on measured performance rather than on past hiring
decisions -- barely changes the outcome: the selection ratio moves from 0.42
to 0.43. **The bias has already been baked into the features.** Group B's
test scores average 0.36 standard deviations lower and their prestige scores
0.50 lower, for reasons that have nothing to do with their success rate.

This is the most important practical lesson in the whole topic: *relabelling
is necessary and not sufficient*. When the measuring instrument is biased, no
choice of target repairs it. You have to fix, replace, or drop the
instrument, or accept that your model encodes its bias.

The aggregation block shows a second, independent problem. The pooled model
assigns `prestige` a weight of +1.75; the group-B-only model assigns +0.18.
The pooled model is applying, to group B, a relationship that does not hold
for group B. And the representation block quantifies why you cannot always
just fit per-group models: with 40 group-B rows the per-group AUC is both
lower and three times more variable across samples.

A structured way to look for all six before modelling:

1. **Compare the label to the construct.** Write down what you wish you
   could measure and what you actually recorded. Every gap is a bias
   candidate.
2. **Tabulate sample size and outcome rate per group**, including
   intersections. Small cells are a finding, not a footnote.
3. **Test the features for group differences that the outcome does not
   justify.** A feature gap larger than the outcome gap is a measurement
   bias signal.
4. **Fit per-group models and compare coefficients.** Large differences mean
   aggregation bias.
5. **Ask who is missing entirely.** People who never applied, claims never
   filed, patients who never reached a clinic.
6. **Trace the feedback loop.** If the model's decisions generate next
   year's training data, the bias compounds.

> Key Takeaways
> - Bias almost always enters through data, labels, sampling, or use --
>   rarely through the learning algorithm itself.
> - Label bias is the most dangerous because it is invisible to accuracy
>   metrics: a perfect model reproduces a biased decision perfectly.
> - Relabelling to the true outcome is necessary but often insufficient,
>   because biased features carry the disparity on their own.
> - A feature gap between groups that is much larger than the outcome gap is
>   direct evidence of measurement bias.
> - Aggregation bias means one model is imposed on populations with different
>   feature-outcome relationships; compare per-group coefficients to detect it.
> - Per-group models are not a free fix: small groups give noisier, weaker
>   models, which is representation bias reappearing.
> - Always report sample size and outcome rate per group and per intersection
>   before reporting any fairness metric.
> - Deployment bias and feedback loops occur outside the model and need
>   governance, not tuning.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. For a dataset of yours, write down the construct you care about and the
>    label you actually have, then list every way they could diverge by group.
> 2. Tabulate row count, outcome rate, and missingness rate per group, and
>    flag every cell with fewer than 100 rows.
> 3. Fit separate models per group and report the two coefficient vectors;
>    identify the feature whose weight differs most.

>    only for the selected, retrain, and track the selection ratio over five
>    rounds.

>    and reports that the model is now fair. What is wrong with that claim?
>    (Hint: consider what remains in the data after the column is dropped,
>    and how you would test whether it is still there.)


#### Fairness Definitions and Metrics

"Is this model fair?" is not a question a metric can answer, because there
are at least a dozen formal definitions of fairness and they assert
different, sometimes contradictory, things. What a data scientist can do is
state each definition precisely, measure it, and force the choice between
them to be made explicitly by the people accountable for the decision.

Every group-fairness definition has the same shape: **pick a quantity from
the confusion matrix, and require it to be equal across groups.** The
definitions differ only in which quantity.

```text
                        actually succeeded?
                        yes          no
  model says   yes      TP           FP      -> precision = TP/(TP+FP)
  model says   no       FN           TN
                        |            |
                 recall = TP/(TP+FN) |
                            FPR = FP/(FP+TN)

  selection rate = (TP+FP)/all       base rate = (TP+FN)/all

  equalise selection rate  -> demographic parity
  equalise recall          -> equal opportunity
  equalise recall AND FPR  -> equalized odds
  equalise precision       -> predictive parity
  equalise P(y=1 | score)  -> calibration by group
```

| Definition | Requires equal | Assumes the label is | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Demographic parity (statistical parity) | Selection rate | Possibly biased | Outreach, quotas, advertising |
| Equal opportunity | TPR among the qualified | Trustworthy | Opportunity allocation: hiring, lending, admissions |
| Equalized odds | TPR and FPR | Trustworthy | Where false positives also harm |
| Predictive parity | Precision | Trustworthy | Risk scores consumed as probabilities |
| Calibration by group | P(y=1 given score) | Trustworthy | Any score published as a probability |
| Treatment equality | FN/FP ratio | Trustworthy | Where the error mix is the harm |
| Individual fairness | Similar individuals treated similarly | -- | Requires a defensible similarity metric |
| Counterfactual fairness | Outcome unchanged if group flipped | -- | Requires a causal model |

The column that decides most real arguments is the third one. Demographic
parity is the only definition that does not take the label at face value,
which is exactly why it is the right choice when the label is a record of a
biased decision -- and the wrong choice when the label is a genuine outcome
you have no reason to distrust.

```python
X, y, hist, g, names = make_hiring()
tr, te = slice(0, 14000), slice(14000, None)
f, _ = logistic(X[tr], y[tr])                 # trained on the TRUE outcome
s = f(X[te]); yt, gt = y[te], g[te]
r = rates(yt, (s > 0.5).astype(int), gt)

print("FAIRNESS MEASURES ON ONE MODEL AT THRESHOLD 0.5")
print(f"  {'quantity':34}{'group A':>10}{'group B':>10}{'ratio':>9}{'diff':>9}")
for lab, k in [("selection rate P(yhat=1)", "sel"),
               ("true positive rate (recall)", "tpr"),
               ("false positive rate", "fpr"),
               ("precision P(y=1|yhat=1)", "ppv"),
               ("base rate P(y=1)", "base")]:
    a, b = r[0][k], r[1][k]
    print(f"  {lab:34}{a:10.3f}{b:10.3f}{b/a:9.2f}{b-a:+9.3f}")
print(f"  {'group size':34}{r[0]['n']:10d}{r[1]['n']:10d}")

print("\nCALIBRATION: AMONG THOSE SCORED IN A BAND, WHO ACTUALLY SUCCEEDS?")
print(f"  {'score band':16}{'A: n':>8}{'A: rate':>9}{'B: n':>8}{'B: rate':>9}")
edges = [0, .2, .4, .6, .8, 1.0]
for lo, hi in zip(edges[:-1], edges[1:]):
    m = (s >= lo) & (s < hi)
    a, b = m & (gt == 0), m & (gt == 1)
    print(f"  [{lo:.1f}, {hi:.1f})      {a.sum():8d}{yt[a].mean():9.3f}"
          f"{b.sum():8d}{yt[b].mean():9.3f}")

print("\nWHICH CRITERIA DOES THIS MODEL SATISFY? (tolerance 0.05 absolute)")
for lab, a, b in [("demographic parity  (equal selection rate)",
                   r[0]['sel'], r[1]['sel']),
                  ("equal opportunity   (equal TPR)", r[0]['tpr'], r[1]['tpr']),
                  ("predictive parity   (equal precision)",
                   r[0]['ppv'], r[1]['ppv']),
                  ("FPR parity          (equal false alarm)",
                   r[0]['fpr'], r[1]['fpr'])]:
    verdict = 'PASS' if abs(a-b) <= 0.05 else 'FAIL'
    print(f"  {lab:44}{verdict}  |diff| {abs(a-b):.3f}")
```

```text
FAIRNESS MEASURES ON ONE MODEL AT THRESHOLD 0.5
  quantity                             group A   group B    ratio     diff
  selection rate P(yhat=1)               0.383     0.164     0.43   -0.219
  true positive rate (recall)            0.723     0.323     0.45   -0.400
  false positive rate                    0.184     0.075     0.41   -0.109
  precision P(y=1|yhat=1)                0.697     0.705     1.01   +0.008
  base rate P(y=1)                       0.369     0.357     0.97   -0.012
  group size                              3853      2147

CALIBRATION: AMONG THOSE SCORED IN A BAND, WHO ACTUALLY SUCCEEDS?
  score band          A: n  A: rate    B: n  B: rate
  [0.0, 0.2)          1195    0.044     823    0.146
  [0.2, 0.4)           818    0.248     769    0.378
  [0.4, 0.6)           670    0.434     379    0.580
  [0.6, 0.8)           602    0.626     157    0.745
  [0.8, 1.0)           568    0.879      19    1.000

WHICH CRITERIA DOES THIS MODEL SATISFY? (tolerance 0.05 absolute)
  demographic parity  (equal selection rate)  FAIL  |diff| 0.219
  equal opportunity   (equal TPR)             FAIL  |diff| 0.400
  predictive parity   (equal precision)       PASS  |diff| 0.008
  FPR parity          (equal false alarm)     FAIL  |diff| 0.109
```

This single output contains the reason fairness debates are so confused. The
same model, at the same threshold, on the same data, **passes** predictive
parity almost perfectly and **fails** equal opportunity by 40 percentage
points. A vendor reporting "our model has equal precision across groups" is
telling the truth. So is a plaintiff reporting "qualified group-B candidates
are selected less than half as often". Both describe this model.

The calibration table explains the mechanism. In every score band, group B's
actual success rate is *higher* than group A's -- at scores of 0.2 to 0.4, B
succeeds 37.8% of the time against A's 24.8%. The model systematically
under-scores group B, because its features under-measure them. The base rates
are nearly identical (0.369 and 0.357), so this is not a difference in the
population; it is an error in the instrument.

Three practical rules follow.

**Report the whole table, never a single number.** Any one row can be
cherry-picked. The set of rows is the honest description.

**Report ratios and differences.** A ratio of 0.43 sounds different from a
difference of 0.219, and regulators use ratios (the four-fifths rule) while
harm scales with differences. Give both.

**State the tolerance and the group sizes.** With 19 group-B applicants in
the top score band, the "1.000" success rate is one number from nineteen
people and carries no information. Every fairness metric needs a confidence
interval.

Finally, note what none of these definitions do: they are all **group**
properties, satisfied on average, and a model can satisfy every one of them
while treating specific individuals arbitrarily. Individual and
counterfactual fairness address that, but require, respectively, a defensible
similarity metric and a causal model -- both of which are substantive
assumptions you must be prepared to defend.

> Key Takeaways
> - Every group-fairness definition equalises one quantity from the confusion
>   matrix across groups; they differ only in which quantity.
> - Demographic parity is the only common definition that does not treat the
>   label as trustworthy, which makes it right for biased labels and wrong
>   for genuine outcomes.
> - The same model can pass predictive parity and fail equal opportunity by
>   40 points; a single fairness number is always cherry-picked.
> - Group-wise calibration reveals whether the score means the same thing for
>   each group, and is the diagnostic closest to "is the instrument fair".
> - Report differences and ratios together: regulators reason in ratios, harm
>   scales with differences.
> - Every fairness metric needs a group size and a confidence interval; small
>   cells produce meaningless extremes.
> - Group fairness says nothing about individuals; individual and
>   counterfactual fairness require a similarity metric or a causal model.
> - Choosing the criterion is a normative decision for accountable owners, not
>   a modelling choice.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compute selection rate, TPR, FPR, precision, and base rate per group for
>    a model of yours and present them as one table with ratios and
>    differences.
> 2. Build a group-wise calibration table in five score bands and state
>    whether the score means the same thing for both groups.
> 3. Find a threshold at which your model passes the four-fifths rule and one
>    at which it fails, and report the accuracy at each.
> 4. Add bootstrap confidence intervals to every fairness number and identify
>    which comparisons are actually resolvable at your sample size.
> 5. Interview: A vendor's model card states "demographic parity difference:
>    0.01". What three follow-up questions do you ask before accepting it?
>    (Hint: think about the threshold, the population it was measured on, and
>    which other criteria were not reported.)


#### Disparate Impact Assessment

Disparate impact is a legal concept before it is a statistical one. The
distinction it rests on: **disparate treatment** is using a protected
attribute in a decision, and **disparate impact** is a neutral-looking rule
that nevertheless falls much more heavily on a protected group. A model that
never sees race can still produce disparate impact, and in United States
employment and lending law that alone can establish a prima facie case.

The standard screen is the **four-fifths rule** from the US Uniform
Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures: if the selection rate for a
group is less than 80% of the rate for the most-selected group, that is
treated as evidence of adverse impact requiring justification.

```text
  impact ratio = selection rate of group B / selection rate of group A

  ratio >= 0.80   ->  no adverse impact flagged
  ratio <  0.80   ->  flagged; employer must justify business necessity
                      AND show no less discriminatory alternative exists
```

The burden-shifting structure matters more than the arithmetic. Flagging does
not end the enquiry: the defendant may show the procedure is job-related and
consistent with business necessity, and the plaintiff may then show a **less
discriminatory alternative** exists with similar validity. That last step is
a modelling question, and it is where data scientists do the most useful
work.

Three things must accompany any impact ratio.

**Statistical significance.** A ratio computed on 40 applicants is not
evidence of anything.

**Practical significance.** The *shortfall* -- how many additional
selections would reach parity -- is what quantifies the harm and is what
courts and regulators actually respond to.

**The threshold.** The impact ratio is a function of where you cut the score,
and it can move from passing to failing across ordinary operating choices.

```python
from math import erf, sqrt
X, y, hist, g, names = make_hiring()
tr, te = slice(0, 14000), slice(14000, None)
f, _ = logistic(X[tr], y[tr])
s = f(X[te]); yt, gt = y[te], g[te]

def phi(z): return 0.5*(1 + erf(z/sqrt(2)))       # standard normal CDF

def impact(sel_a, n_a, sel_b, n_b):
    p = (sel_a*n_a + sel_b*n_b)/(n_a + n_b)       # pooled selection rate
    se = sqrt(p*(1-p)*(1/n_a + 1/n_b))            # two-proportion z test
    z = (sel_b - sel_a)/se
    return sel_b/sel_a, z, 2*(1 - phi(abs(z)))

print("FOUR-FIFTHS RULE AT SEVERAL THRESHOLDS")
print(f"  {'thr':>5}{'sel A':>8}{'sel B':>8}{'ratio':>8}{'4/5?':>6}"
      f"{'z':>8}{'p':>10}{'shortfall':>11}")
for thr in (0.20, 0.35, 0.50, 0.65):
    yhat = (s > thr).astype(int)
    a, b = yhat[gt==0].mean(), yhat[gt==1].mean()
    na, nb = (gt==0).sum(), (gt==1).sum()
    ratio, z, pv = impact(a, na, b, nb)
    short = int(round((a-b)*nb))                  # extra B selections to parity
    print(f"  {thr:5.2f}{a:8.3f}{b:8.3f}{ratio:8.2f}"
          f"{'ok' if ratio >= 0.8 else 'FAIL':>6}{z:8.1f}{pv:10.1e}{short:11d}")

print("\nSMALL SAMPLES: THE SAME RATIO, DIFFERENT EVIDENTIAL WEIGHT")
print(f"  {'n per group':>12}{'sel A':>8}{'sel B':>8}{'ratio':>8}{'z':>8}{'p':>10}")
for n in (40, 200, 1000, 5000):
    ratio, z, pv = impact(0.40, n, 0.28, n)
    print(f"  {n:12}{0.40:8.2f}{0.28:8.2f}{ratio:8.2f}{z:8.1f}{pv:10.1e}")

print("\nLESS DISCRIMINATORY ALTERNATIVE SEARCH")
print(f"  {'feature set':32}{'AUC':>7}{'ratio':>8}{'TPR gap':>10}")
for lab, cols in [("all three features", [0,1,2]), ("drop referral", [0,1]),
                  ("drop prestige", [0,2]), ("test_score only", [0])]:
    fs, _ = logistic(X[tr][:, cols], y[tr])
    ss = fs(X[te][:, cols])
    thr = np.quantile(ss, 1 - 0.30)               # hold the hire rate at 30%
    rr = rates(yt, (ss > thr).astype(int), gt)
    print(f"  {lab:32}{auc(yt, ss):7.3f}"
          f"{rr[1]['sel']/rr[0]['sel']:8.2f}{rr[1]['tpr']-rr[0]['tpr']:+10.3f}")
```

```text
FOUR-FIFTHS RULE AT SEVERAL THRESHOLDS
    thr   sel A   sel B   ratio  4/5?       z         p  shortfall
   0.20   0.690   0.617    0.89    ok    -5.8   8.9e-09        157
   0.35   0.523   0.326    0.62  FAIL   -14.7   0.0e+00        423
   0.50   0.383   0.164    0.43  FAIL   -17.7   0.0e+00        471
   0.65   0.266   0.055    0.21  FAIL   -19.9   0.0e+00        452

SMALL SAMPLES: THE SAME RATIO, DIFFERENT EVIDENTIAL WEIGHT
   n per group   sel A   sel B   ratio       z         p
            40    0.40    0.28    0.70    -1.1   2.6e-01
           200    0.40    0.28    0.70    -2.5   1.1e-02
          1000    0.40    0.28    0.70    -5.7   1.5e-08
          5000    0.40    0.28    0.70   -12.7   0.0e+00

LESS DISCRIMINATORY ALTERNATIVE SEARCH
  feature set                         AUC   ratio   TPR gap
  all three features                0.820    0.42    -0.401
  drop referral                     0.820    0.40    -0.426
  drop prestige                     0.774    0.84    -0.066
  test_score only                   0.774    0.83    -0.068
```

Read the first table as a warning about how fragile a pass is. At a
threshold of 0.20 this model passes the four-fifths rule at 0.89. At 0.65 it
is at 0.21. **Nothing about the model changed** -- only the operating point,
which is usually set by capacity, not by fairness. Any fairness claim must
name the threshold it was measured at, and any monitoring must re-measure
when the threshold moves. Note too that the flagged ratio and the shortfall
do not peak together: the worst ratio is at 0.65, the largest shortfall at
0.50, because a stricter rule selects fewer people overall.

The second table is the small-sample caveat in numbers: the identical ratio
of 0.70 is statistically unremarkable at 40 per group (p = 0.26) and
overwhelming at 5,000 (p < 1e-30). Ratios from small slices should be
reported with intervals and never acted on alone.

The third table is the most useful result in the topic. Dropping the
`prestige` feature moves the impact ratio from 0.42 to 0.84 -- through the
four-fifths threshold -- and shrinks the TPR gap from 40 points to 7, at a
cost of 0.046 AUC. That is a textbook less discriminatory alternative: a
model of materially similar validity with materially less adverse impact. If
this alternative exists and you deployed the other one, the business
necessity defence is in serious trouble.

The corresponding workflow:

1. Fix the operating point that will actually be used, and measure the ratio
   there -- plus at the range of thresholds operations might drift to.
2. Report ratio, z-statistic, p-value, shortfall count, and group sizes
   together.
3. Enumerate alternatives: feature subsets, different targets, different
   model families, different thresholds.
4. Plot validity against impact ratio across those alternatives and identify
   the frontier.
5. Document why the chosen point on that frontier was chosen, and who chose
   it. That document is the business necessity argument.

> Key Takeaways
> - Disparate treatment is using a protected attribute; disparate impact is a
>   neutral rule with heavily unequal effects, and a model that never sees the
>   attribute can still produce it.
> - The four-fifths rule flags a selection-rate ratio below 0.80 as evidence
>   requiring justification, not as a verdict.
> - The impact ratio depends strongly on the threshold; a model can pass at
>   one operating point and fail badly at another.
> - Always report statistical significance, shortfall count, and group sizes
>   alongside the ratio.
> - The worst ratio and the largest shortfall generally occur at different
>   thresholds, so both must be reported.
> - Identical ratios carry completely different evidential weight at
>   different sample sizes.
> - Searching for a less discriminatory alternative is the highest-value
>   technical work here; a small validity loss for a large impact improvement
>   usually defeats a business-necessity defence.
> - Document the validity-impact frontier and who chose the operating point.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compute the impact ratio, z-statistic, and shortfall for your model at
>    five thresholds spanning its operating range.
> 2. For each single feature, drop it and record the resulting AUC and impact
>    ratio; plot the frontier.
> 3. Determine the minimum sample size per group at which a ratio of 0.75
>    would be statistically significant at p < 0.05.
> 4. Compute the shortfall in people, not rates, for your worst-performing
>    slice, and write one sentence a non-technical reader would understand.
