>    one geography. How do you decide whether that matters? (Hint: think about
>    the unit at which decisions are actually made and the sample size of the
>    failing slice.)


#### Bias Mitigation Techniques

Mitigation techniques are organised by *where in the pipeline they
intervene*, and that placement determines their cost, their legal posture,
and what they can possibly fix. There are three families.

```text
  DATA  ----[pre-processing]---->  TRAINING  ----[in-processing]---->  MODEL
                                                                        |
                                                              [post-processing]
                                                                        v
                                                                    DECISION

  pre:   change the data        reweight, relabel, resample, repair features
  in:    change the objective   fairness penalty, constrained optimisation,
                                adversarial debiasing
  post:  change the decision    per-group thresholds, score calibration,
                                reject-option classification
```

| Family | Needs training access | Needs group at inference | Accuracy cost | Fixes root cause |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pre-processing | Yes | No | Low to moderate | Sometimes |
| In-processing | Yes | Only during training | Tunable | Partly |
| Post-processing | No | **Usually yes** | Low on ranking, high on accuracy | No |

That "needs group at inference" cell in the post-processing row is the most
consequential practical fact in the topic. Applying a different threshold by
group requires knowing each individual's group membership at decision time
and acting on it -- which in many jurisdictions is disparate treatment, the
thing that is most clearly prohibited. Post-processing is technically the
easiest family and legally the hardest.

```python
X, y, hist, g, names = make_hiring()
tr, te = slice(0, 14000), slice(14000, None)
Xtr, ytr, gtr = X[tr], y[tr], g[tr]
yt, gt = y[te], g[te]
mu, sd = Xtr.mean(0), Xtr.std(0)
Ztr, Zte = (Xtr-mu)/sd, (X[te]-mu)/sd

def fit(Z, yy, sw=None, gg=None, lam=0.0, iters=4000, lr=0.6):
    sw = np.ones(len(yy)) if sw is None else sw*len(yy)/sw.sum()
    w = np.zeros(Z.shape[1]); b = 0.0
    for _ in range(iters):
        p = 1/(1+np.exp(-(Z @ w + b)))
        gr = sw*(p - yy)/len(yy)
        if lam:                                   # demographic-parity penalty
            mA, mB = gg == 0, gg == 1
            gap = p[mA].mean() - p[mB].mean()     # squared gap in mean score
            dp = p*(1-p)                          # d sigmoid / d logit
            gr = gr + lam*2*gap*(dp*(mA/mA.sum() - mB/mB.sum()))
        w -= lr*(Z.T @ gr); b -= lr*gr.sum()
    return w, b

def report(lab, s, thrs):
    yh = np.where(gt == 0, s > thrs[0], s > thrs[1]).astype(int)
    r = rates(yt, yh, gt)
    print(f"  {lab:26}{auc(yt, s):8.3f}{(yh == yt).mean():10.3f}"
          f"{r[1]['sel']/r[0]['sel']:11.2f}{r[1]['tpr']-r[0]['tpr']:+10.3f}"
          f"{r[1]['ppv']-r[0]['ppv']:+9.3f}")

print("MITIGATION STRATEGIES, ALL AT A 30% OVERALL HIRE RATE")
print(f"  {'strategy':26}{'AUC':>8}{'accuracy':>10}{'sel ratio':>11}"
      f"{'TPR gap':>10}{'PPV gap':>9}")
w, b = fit(Ztr, ytr)
s0 = 1/(1+np.exp(-(Zte @ w + b))); t0 = np.quantile(s0, 0.70)
report("baseline", s0, (t0, t0))

# PRE: REWEIGHT SO GROUP AND LABEL ARE STATISTICALLY INDEPENDENT IN THE SAMPLE
sw = np.empty(len(ytr))
for gv in (0, 1):
    for yv in (0, 1):
        m = (gtr == gv) & (ytr == yv)
        sw[m] = (gtr == gv).mean()*(ytr == yv).mean()/m.mean()
w, b = fit(Ztr, ytr, sw=sw)
s1 = 1/(1+np.exp(-(Zte @ w + b))); t1 = np.quantile(s1, 0.70)
report("pre: reweighting", s1, (t1, t1))

# IN: PENALISE THE GAP IN MEAN PREDICTED SCORE BETWEEN GROUPS
for lam in (2.0, 10.0):
    w, b = fit(Ztr, ytr, gg=gtr, lam=lam)
    s2 = 1/(1+np.exp(-(Zte @ w + b))); t2 = np.quantile(s2, 0.70)
    report(f"in: parity penalty {lam:g}", s2, (t2, t2))

# POST: PER-GROUP THRESHOLDS
def tpr_at(s, mask, thr):
    m = mask & (yt == 1); return ((s > thr) & m).sum()/m.sum()
cand = np.linspace(0.02, 0.98, 400)
target = tpr_at(s0, gt == 0, t0)
tB = min(cand, key=lambda c: abs(tpr_at(s0, gt == 1, c) - target))
report("post: equal-opportunity", s0, (t0, tB))
print(f"  thresholds used: A {t0:.3f}   B {tB:.3f}")
selA = (s0[gt == 0] > t0).mean()
tB2 = min(cand, key=lambda c: abs((s0[gt == 1] > c).mean() - selA))
report("post: demographic parity", s0, (t0, tB2))
print(f"  thresholds used: A {t0:.3f}   B {tB2:.3f}")
```

```text
MITIGATION STRATEGIES, ALL AT A 30% OVERALL HIRE RATE
  strategy                       AUC  accuracy  sel ratio   TPR gap  PPV gap
  baseline                     0.820     0.756       0.42    -0.401   +0.005
  pre: reweighting             0.820     0.756       0.43    -0.398   +0.007
  in: parity penalty 2         0.813     0.752       0.56    -0.280   +0.005
  in: parity penalty 10        0.785     0.732       0.75    -0.147   -0.024
  post: equal-opportunity      0.820     0.743       1.29    +0.002   -0.173
  thresholds used: A 0.506   B 0.263
  post: demographic parity     0.820     0.750       1.00    -0.116   -0.136
  thresholds used: A 0.506   B 0.318
```

Four lessons are visible in that table.

**Reweighting did nothing.** It moved the selection ratio from 0.42 to 0.43.
This is not a bug: the Kamiran-Calders reweighting scheme makes group and
*label* independent in the training sample, and in this dataset they already
are (base rates 0.369 and 0.357). The disparity lives in the *features*, and
reweighting does not touch features. **Match the mitigation to the diagnosed
source of bias** -- a technique aimed at label imbalance cannot repair a
biased measuring instrument.

**In-processing gives a dial with a real price.** A penalty weight of 2
halves the TPR gap for 0.007 AUC; a weight of 10 cuts it to 0.147 for 0.035
AUC. This monotone trade is the honest shape of the problem, and the right
way to present it to a decision-maker is as a curve, not a single number.

**Post-processing is free in ranking quality and not free elsewhere.** AUC is
unchanged at 0.820 because the score is unchanged; only the cut moved. But
equalising TPR overshoots the selection ratio to 1.29 and opens a precision
gap of -0.173: group-B hires are now less likely to succeed than group-A
hires. Someone will notice that, and you need to have decided in advance
whether it is acceptable.

**Every row satisfies a different definition, and none satisfies all of
them.** That is not a failure of the techniques; it is the next topic.

Beyond these three families, two other interventions are often the most
effective and are frequently skipped:

- **Change the target.** Predicting the outcome you care about instead of a
  biased proxy is usually worth more than any algorithmic fix.
- **Change the features.** Removing or repairing the specific feature that
  carries the disparity -- as the previous topic's `prestige` result showed --
  can move the impact ratio further than any reweighting scheme, and it is far
  easier to explain and defend.

A note on **adversarial debiasing**, the most common in-processing method in
deep learning: train the predictor jointly with an adversary that tries to
recover the protected attribute from the representation, and penalise the
predictor when the adversary succeeds. It is powerful and notoriously
unstable, needs careful tuning, and its guarantee is only as good as the
adversary's capacity -- a weak adversary certifies nothing.

> Key Takeaways
> - Mitigations are classified by where they intervene: pre-processing on the
>   data, in-processing on the objective, post-processing on the decision.
> - Post-processing usually requires the protected attribute at decision time,
>   which can itself constitute disparate treatment.
> - Reweighting targets dependence between group and label; it does nothing
>   when the disparity lives in the features.
> - Match the technique to the diagnosed source of bias rather than reaching
>   for a standard library call.
> - In-processing penalties give a tunable accuracy-fairness trade that should
>   be presented as a curve, not a point.
> - Post-processing leaves ranking quality untouched but shifts other fairness
>   quantities, often opening a precision gap in the other direction.
> - Changing the target or repairing the offending feature often beats every
>   algorithmic mitigation and is easier to defend.
> - Adversarial debiasing is powerful, unstable, and certifies nothing beyond
>   what its adversary could detect.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement reweighting on a dataset where group and label ARE dependent
>    and verify it moves the selection ratio there.
> 2. Sweep an in-processing fairness penalty over a range and plot AUC against
>    the selection ratio to produce the trade-off frontier.
> 3. Apply per-group thresholds to equalise TPR and report every other
>    fairness quantity before and after.
> 4. Compare dropping the single most disparity-carrying feature against your
>    best in-processing result, on both accuracy and impact ratio.
> 5. Interview: Legal tells you that you may not use group membership at
>    decision time. Which mitigation families remain available, and what do
>    you lose? (Hint: think about which family needs the attribute at training
>    time only, and whether any post-processing variant can avoid it.)


#### Tradeoffs Between Fairness Criteria

Once you have several fairness definitions and several mitigations, the
natural instinct is to satisfy all of them. That instinct runs into a
theorem: **when base rates differ between groups, calibration, equal true
positive rates, and equal false positive rates cannot all hold
simultaneously unless the classifier is perfect.** This is the impossibility
result of Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan, and independently
Chouldechova, and it is arithmetic, not a limitation of current methods.

The intuition takes one line of algebra. Precision relates to base rate and
error rates by

```text
                      p * TPR
  PPV  =  ---------------------------------      where p = base rate
           p * TPR  +  (1 - p) * FPR
```

Fix TPR and FPR to be equal across groups. Then PPV is a strictly increasing
function of *p* alone -- so if *p* differs, PPV must differ. Equalising error
rates forces unequal precision; equalising precision forces unequal error
rates. There is no third option.

```python
X, y, hist, g, names = make_hiring()
tr, te = slice(0, 14000), slice(14000, None)
# USE THE HISTORICAL LABEL: ITS BASE RATE DIFFERS BY GROUP, WHICH IS THE
# CONDITION UNDER WHICH THE CRITERIA BECOME MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE.
f, _ = logistic(X[tr], hist[tr])
s = f(X[te]); yt, gt = hist[te], g[te]
print(f"base rates differ: A {yt[gt==0].mean():.3f}   B {yt[gt==1].mean():.3f}")

def at(ta, tb):
    return rates(yt, np.where(gt == 0, s > ta, s > tb).astype(int), gt)

def gapline(lab, ta, tb):
    r = at(ta, tb)
    print(f"  {lab:26}{ta:8.3f}{tb:8.3f}"
          f"{r[1]['sel']/max(r[0]['sel'], 1e-9):11.2f}"
          f"{r[1]['tpr']-r[0]['tpr']:+9.3f}{r[1]['fpr']-r[0]['fpr']:+9.3f}"
          f"{r[1]['ppv']-r[0]['ppv']:+9.3f}")

cand = np.linspace(0.02, 0.98, 300)
base = np.quantile(s, 0.70)
r0 = at(base, base)
print("\nENFORCE ONE CRITERION, MEASURE WHAT BREAKS")
print(f"  {'target':26}{'thr A':>8}{'thr B':>8}{'sel ratio':>11}"
      f"{'TPR gap':>9}{'FPR gap':>9}{'PPV gap':>9}")
gapline("single threshold", base, base)
for lab, key in [("demographic parity", "sel"), ("equal opportunity (TPR)", "tpr"),
                 ("FPR parity", "fpr"), ("predictive parity (PPV)", "ppv")]:
    tb = min(cand, key=lambda c: abs(at(base, c)[1][key] - r0[0][key]))
    gapline(lab, base, tb)
tb = min(cand, key=lambda c: (abs(at(base, c)[1]['tpr'] - r0[0]['tpr'])
                              + abs(at(base, c)[1]['fpr'] - r0[0]['fpr'])))
gapline("equalized odds (both)", base, tb)

print("\nTHE ALGEBRA: PPV = p*TPR / (p*TPR + (1-p)*FPR)")
print(f"  {'':8}{'base rate p':>13}{'TPR':>7}{'FPR':>7}{'implied PPV':>13}")
for lab, p in (("group A", yt[gt==0].mean()), ("group B", yt[gt==1].mean())):
    tpr, fpr = 0.70, 0.20                          # identical error rates
    print(f"  {lab:8}{p:13.3f}{tpr:7.2f}{fpr:7.2f}"
          f"{p*tpr/(p*tpr + (1-p)*fpr):13.3f}")
print("  Identical TPR and FPR, different base rates -> PPV cannot match.")
```

```text
base rates differ: A 0.431   B 0.129

ENFORCE ONE CRITERION, MEASURE WHAT BREAKS
  target                       thr A   thr B  sel ratio  TPR gap  FPR gap  PPV gap
  single threshold             0.548   0.548       0.40   -0.042   +0.003   -0.268
  demographic parity           0.548   0.081       1.01   +0.179   +0.236   -0.581
  equal opportunity (TPR)      0.548   0.498       0.44   +0.001   +0.012   -0.286
  FPR parity                   0.548   0.559       0.39   -0.057   +0.000   -0.262
  predictive parity (PPV)      0.548   0.913       0.14   -0.434   -0.054   +0.000
  equalized odds (both)        0.548   0.502       0.43   +0.001   +0.011   -0.285

THE ALGEBRA: PPV = p*TPR / (p*TPR + (1-p)*FPR)
            base rate p    TPR    FPR  implied PPV
  group A         0.431   0.70   0.20        0.726
  group B         0.129   0.70   0.20        0.341
  Identical TPR and FPR, different base rates -> PPV cannot match.
```

Every row is a legitimate policy and every row is unfair by some other row's
standard. Look at the two extremes. Enforcing **demographic parity** requires
dropping group B's threshold to 0.081, which achieves an equal selection rate
and a false positive rate 23.6 points higher for group B -- a large number of
group-B candidates selected who will not succeed, which harms them too.
Enforcing **predictive parity** requires raising group B's threshold to 0.913,
which achieves equal precision and a TPR gap of -0.434: qualified group-B
candidates are selected at a fraction of the rate of equally qualified group-A
candidates.

The algebra block shows why no cleverness escapes this. With base rates of
0.431 and 0.129 and identical error rates, precision *must* be 0.726 for one
group and 0.341 for the other.

So the trade-offs are structural, and the real questions become practical
ones:

| Question | Consequence for the choice |
| --- | --- |
| Do you believe the label? | If not, demographic parity; if yes, an error-rate criterion |
| Who is harmed by a false positive? | If the individual (a loan they cannot repay), do not maximise selection |
| Who is harmed by a false negative? | If the individual (a job they deserved), prioritise equal TPR |
| Is the score consumed as a probability downstream? | Then calibration is close to mandatory |
| Are base rates genuinely different, or an artefact? | If artefact, fix measurement first; criteria stop conflicting as base rates converge |

That last row is the escape hatch, and it is the one worth pursuing. The
impossibility bites *because* base rates differ. If the difference is an
artefact of measurement or of a biased label, then repairing the instrument
does not just improve one metric -- it dissolves the conflict. In our own
dataset with the true label, base rates were 0.369 and 0.357, and the
criteria are nearly reconcilable. With the biased historical label they are
0.431 and 0.129, and they are not.

And there is a second escape hatch: **improve the model**. The impossibility
holds for imperfect classifiers, and the tension shrinks as accuracy rises.
Better features -- especially features that measure the construct equally
well for both groups -- reduce the conflict in a way that no post-processing
can.

> Key Takeaways
> - When base rates differ, calibration, equal TPR, and equal FPR cannot hold
>   together unless the classifier is perfect; this is arithmetic, not a
>   technical limitation.
> - Precision is determined by base rate and error rates, so equalising error
>   rates forces unequal precision and vice versa.
> - Enforcing demographic parity on unequal base rates raises the false
>   positive rate for the disadvantaged group, which is itself a harm.
> - Enforcing predictive parity on unequal base rates collapses the
>   disadvantaged group's true positive rate.
> - There is no fairness criterion that is correct in general; the choice
>   follows from who is harmed by which error and whether the label is
>   trustworthy.
> - Calibration becomes near-mandatory when a score is consumed downstream as
>   a probability.
> - The conflict shrinks as base rates converge, so repairing biased labels
>   and measurement dissolves part of the problem.
> - Better accuracy also shrinks the conflict; improving features is the only
>   intervention that helps every criterion at once.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Reproduce the impossibility numerically: fix TPR and FPR equal across two
>    groups with base rates 0.1 and 0.4 and compute both precisions.
> 2. For your own model, find the per-group thresholds that equalise each
>    criterion in turn, and tabulate what each choice does to the others.
> 3. Write a one-page memo recommending a criterion for a concrete decision,
>    naming who bears each error type.
> 4. Simulate reducing the base rate gap (by fixing a biased label) and show
>    the conflict between criteria shrinking.
> 5. Interview: A stakeholder wants both equal selection rates and equal
>    precision across groups. Explain why you cannot deliver both, without
>    using the word "theorem". (Hint: talk about what the selection rate does
>    to who ends up in the selected pool when the groups' qualified fractions
>    differ.)


#### Auditing Deployed Models

A fairness assessment made at training time expires. The population changes,
the sourcing changes, upstream features change meaning, thresholds get
adjusted for capacity, and the model's own decisions reshape the data it will
be retrained on. A model that passed every check in March can be failing
badly in September without a single line of code having changed.

Auditing is therefore a *monitoring* discipline, and it has the same
structure as the model monitoring in the previous chapter -- with three
complications that make it harder.

**Ground truth is delayed or missing.** You learn whether a hire succeeded a
year later, and you never learn whether a rejected applicant would have
succeeded. Outcome-based metrics (TPR, precision) lag; decision-based metrics
(selection rate) are available immediately. Monitor both, at their own
cadences.

**Slices are small.** The whole point is to look at subgroups, and subgroups
have few rows, so every number is noisy. Without intervals you will chase
phantoms and miss real regressions.

**Intersections multiply.** Two protected attributes with four levels each
make sixteen cells; the group-level number can look fine while a cell is in
serious trouble.

```python
X, y, hist, g, names = make_hiring()
tr, te = slice(0, 14000), slice(14000, None)
f, _ = logistic(X[tr], y[tr])
rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
Xte, yt, gt = X[te].copy(), y[te].copy(), g[te]
month = rng.integers(0, 6, len(yt))
# SIMULATE A SOURCING CHANGE: FROM MONTH 3, GROUP B APPLICANTS ARRIVE WITH
# SYSTEMATICALLY LOWER PRESTIGE SCORES. THE MODEL IS UNCHANGED.
drift = (month >= 3) & (gt == 1)
Xte[drift, 1] -= 0.8
s = f(Xte)
thr = np.quantile(f(X[tr]), 0.70)                 # the threshold set in March

def boot_ratio(mask, reps=300):
    out = []; idx = np.where(mask)[0]
    for _ in range(reps):
        b = rng.choice(idx, len(idx), replace=True)   # resample the slice
        yh = (s[b] > thr).astype(int); gb = gt[b]
        a, bb = yh[gb == 0].mean(), yh[gb == 1].mean()
        out.append(bb/a if a > 0 else np.nan)
    return np.nanpercentile(out, [2.5, 50, 97.5])

print("MONTHLY DISPARATE IMPACT RATIO WITH A 95% BOOTSTRAP INTERVAL")
print(f"  {'month':>6}{'n':>7}{'n_B':>6}{'ratio':>8}{'95% CI':>18}{'flag':>7}")
for m in range(6):
    mask = month == m
    lo, md, hi = boot_ratio(mask)
    flag = "ALERT" if hi < 0.8 else ("watch" if lo < 0.8 else "ok")
    print(f"  {m:6}{mask.sum():7}{(mask & (gt==1)).sum():6}{md:8.2f}"
          f"   [{lo:.2f}, {hi:.2f}]{flag:>8}")

print("\nWHY SMALL SLICES CANNOT BE MONITORED THE SAME WAY")
print(f"  {'slice size':>12}{'ratio':>8}{'95% CI width':>15}")
for n in (30, 100, 400, 1600):
    sub = rng.choice(len(yt), n, replace=False)
    mask = np.zeros(len(yt), bool); mask[sub] = True
    lo, md, hi = boot_ratio(mask, reps=200)
    print(f"  {n:12}{md:8.2f}{hi-lo:15.2f}")

print("\nINTERSECTIONAL SLICES: THE GROUP-LEVEL NUMBER HIDES THE WORST CELL")
# A SECOND ATTRIBUTE THE MODEL NEVER SEES: APPLICANTS FROM NON-TARGET
# REGIONS HAVE LOWER PRESTIGE SCORES, AND THE EFFECT COMPOUNDS FOR GROUP B.
X2 = X[te].copy()
region = (rng.random(len(yt)) < 0.4)              # 1 = non-target region
X2[region, 1] -= 0.6
X2[region & (gt == 1), 1] -= 0.7                  # the compounding part
yh = (f(X2) > thr).astype(int)
base = yh[(gt == 0) & ~region].mean()
print(f"  {'slice':24}{'n':>7}{'sel rate':>10}{'ratio vs A/target':>20}")
for lab, m in [("A, target region", (gt==0) & ~region),
               ("A, other region", (gt==0) & region),
               ("B, target region", (gt==1) & ~region),
               ("B, other region", (gt==1) & region)]:
    print(f"  {lab:24}{m.sum():7}{yh[m].mean():10.3f}{yh[m].mean()/base:20.2f}")
print(f"  group-level only:  A {yh[gt==0].mean():.3f}   B {yh[gt==1].mean():.3f}"
      f"   ratio {yh[gt==1].mean()/yh[gt==0].mean():.2f}")
```

```text
MONTHLY DISPARATE IMPACT RATIO WITH A 95% BOOTSTRAP INTERVAL
   month      n   n_B   ratio            95% CI   flag
       0   1016   391    0.42   [0.33, 0.52]   ALERT
       1    950   324    0.46   [0.36, 0.61]   ALERT
       2    973   359    0.43   [0.34, 0.54]   ALERT
       3   1034   352    0.14   [0.08, 0.22]   ALERT
       4   1045   366    0.11   [0.06, 0.18]   ALERT
       5    982   355    0.15   [0.09, 0.22]   ALERT

WHY SMALL SLICES CANNOT BE MONITORED THE SAME WAY
    slice size   ratio   95% CI width
            30    0.51           1.67
           100    0.14           0.42
           400    0.34           0.36
          1600    0.35           0.14

INTERSECTIONAL SLICES: THE GROUP-LEVEL NUMBER HIDES THE WORST CELL
  slice                         n  sel rate   ratio vs A/target
  A, target region           2303     0.385                1.00
  A, other region            1550     0.278                0.72
  B, target region           1277     0.156                0.40
  B, other region             870     0.016                0.04
  group-level only:  A 0.342   B 0.099   ratio 0.29
```

The monthly table shows the regression clearly: a stable ratio around 0.43
for three months, then a drop to 0.11-0.15 once the upstream sourcing change
lands. Nothing about the model changed. What changed was the *input
distribution for one group*, and the fixed threshold turned that into a step
change in selection. This is why fairness monitoring must be continuous and
must be tied to feature drift monitoring: the root cause is visible in the
`prestige` distribution weeks before anyone queries the outcome data.

The confidence-interval table is the operational discipline. At 30 rows the
95% interval is 1.67 wide -- the ratio is essentially unmeasured. At 1,600
rows it is 0.14 wide and you can act on it. **Set a minimum slice size for
alerting and report "insufficient data" rather than a number below it.**

The intersectional table is the finding you would otherwise miss. At the
group level the ratio is 0.29 -- already bad. But the harm is not spread
evenly: group-B applicants in the target region are selected at 0.40 of the
reference rate, while group-B applicants from other regions are at 0.04. An
audit that reported only the group-level number would have described a
uniform 0.29 disadvantage that no individual actually experiences.

A workable audit programme:

1. **Log what you need.** Score, threshold, decision, model version,
   explanation configuration, and group attributes (stored separately with
   restricted access, since you need them to audit and must not use them to
   decide).
2. **Define the slice set in advance** -- protected groups, their pairwise
   intersections, geography, channel, and time -- so you are not accused of
   slicing until something looks acceptable.
3. **Monitor decision metrics daily and outcome metrics at their natural
   lag**, with the lag stated.
4. **Alert on intervals, not points**, with a minimum slice size below which
   you report insufficient data.
5. **Re-audit on every change** to the model, the threshold, the feature
   pipeline, or the upstream data source. A threshold change is a fairness
   change.
6. **Keep a decision log**: every alert, its investigation, and its
   resolution. This is the artifact a regulator asks for, and reconstructing
   it later is impossible.
7. **Watch the feedback loop.** If the model's decisions produce the next
   training set, compare the deployed population with the applicant
   population every cycle.

One organisational point that matters more than any of the above: **the
people who build the model should not be the only people who audit it.**
Independent review, with access to the data and a mandate to publish
findings, is the control that makes the rest credible.

> Key Takeaways
> - Fairness assessments expire; population, sourcing, thresholds, and
>   upstream features all change after deployment.
> - Decision metrics are available immediately, outcome metrics lag, and both
>   must be monitored at their own cadence with the lag documented.
> - A fairness regression can occur with no model change at all, driven by a
>   shift in one group's input distribution against a fixed threshold.
> - Tie fairness monitoring to feature drift monitoring, since drift is
>   visible before outcomes are.
> - Every slice metric needs a confidence interval and a minimum sample size;
>   below it, report insufficient data rather than a number.
> - Intersectional cells can be far worse than either group-level number, so
>   define the slice set in advance and audit the cells.
> - Log score, threshold, model version, and decision for every case, and keep
>   a decision log of every alert and its resolution.
> - Independent audit, separate from the build team, is what makes the rest of
>   the programme credible.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compute your model's impact ratio per month with bootstrap intervals and
>    identify the minimum slice size at which the interval is narrower than
>    0.15.
> 2. Simulate an upstream feature shift affecting one group and show how long
>    it takes your current alerting to detect it.
> 3. Enumerate every intersectional cell for two protected attributes in your
>    data, report selection rates, and flag the cells below the minimum size.
> 4. Write the alerting policy: which metrics, which slices, which thresholds,
>    which minimum sample sizes, and who is paged.
> 5. Interview: Your fairness dashboard is green but a journalist presents
>    three cases that look clearly unfair. How do you respond? (Hint: consider
>    what a group average can be true of while individual cases are still
>    indefensible, and which slice the three cases share.)


<a id="163-privacy-and-security"></a>
### 16.3 Privacy and Security

Data about people is the raw material of most data science, and it is also a
liability that grows with every copy; this section covers what actually
counts as identifying, why removing names is not anonymisation, the one
technique that offers a mathematical privacy guarantee, how to train without
centralising data, the attacks that target models rather than databases, and
the everyday engineering controls that prevent most real incidents. The
unifying idea is that privacy is a property of a *system's whole behaviour*,
not of a column, and that it must be designed in rather than certified
afterwards.


#### Personally Identifiable Information

The intuitive model of personal data -- "the name column is sensitive, the
rest is fine" -- is wrong in a way that has caused many of the largest
privacy failures on record. Identification does not require an identifier. It
requires only that the combination of attributes you publish be *unique
enough* to single someone out when joined against anything else.

Three categories matter, and the second is the dangerous one:

| Category | Examples | Risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Direct identifiers** | Name, national ID, email, phone, account number, device ID | Obvious; usually removed |
| **Quasi-identifiers** | Postcode, date of birth, sex, job title, employer, timestamps, GPS traces, browser fingerprint | Individually harmless, jointly identifying |
| **Sensitive attributes** | Diagnosis, salary, religion, sexual orientation, criminal record, biometrics | The thing you are protecting; special legal categories |

The canonical result: Latanya Sweeney showed that the combination of
five-digit postcode, date of birth, and sex uniquely identifies roughly 87%
of the United States population. The Netflix Prize dataset, released with all
identifiers removed, was de-anonymised by joining viewing histories with
public IMDb ratings. Anonymised taxi trip records were linked to named
celebrities using timestamped paparazzi photographs.

```text
  "de-identified" release            public voter roll
  +----------------------+           +-------------------------+
  | zip | dob | sex | dx |  <--JOIN--| zip | dob | sex | NAME  |
  +----------------------+           +-------------------------+
       the join key was never removed, because it was never
       recognised as a key
```

```python
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
N = 50000
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "zip": rng.choice([f"{z:05d}" for z in range(10001, 10201)], N),
    "birth_year": rng.integers(1940, 2006, N),
    "birth_month": rng.integers(1, 13, N),
    "sex": rng.choice(["F", "M"], N),
    "diagnosis": rng.choice(["asthma", "diabetes", "hypertension", "none"],
                            N, p=[.12, .13, .25, .50]),
})
print(f"a 'de-identified' table of {N:,} people, no name, no id\n")
print(f"  {'quasi-identifier set':44}{'unique (k=1)':>14}{'k<5':>8}")
for cols in [("zip",), ("zip", "sex"), ("zip", "birth_year"),
             ("zip", "birth_year", "sex"),
             ("zip", "birth_year", "birth_month", "sex")]:
    g = df.groupby(list(cols), observed=True).size()
    print(f"  {' + '.join(cols):44}{(g == 1).sum()/N:13.1%}"
          f"{g[g < 5].sum()/N:8.1%}")
print("\nNo single column is an identifier. The COMBINATION is.")

print("\nAND THE DIAGNOSIS LEAKS EVEN WHEN THE PERSON DOES NOT:")
g = df.groupby(["zip", "birth_year", "sex"], observed=True)["diagnosis"]
homog = g.nunique() == 1                        # every member shares a value
print(f"  groups where every member shares one diagnosis: {homog.mean():.1%}")
print(f"  people in such groups: {g.size()[homog].sum()/N:.1%}")
```

```text
a 'de-identified' table of 50,000 people, no name, no id

  quasi-identifier set                          unique (k=1)     k<5
  zip                                                  0.0%    0.0%
  zip + sex                                            0.0%    0.0%
  zip + birth_year                                     2.2%   47.8%
  zip + birth_year + sex                              14.9%   88.0%
  zip + birth_year + birth_month + sex                85.5%  100.0%

No single column is an identifier. The COMBINATION is.

AND THE DIAGNOSIS LEAKS EVEN WHEN THE PERSON DOES NOT:
  groups where every member shares one diagnosis: 47.8%
  people in such groups: 30.1%
```

Read down that first column. Postcode alone identifies nobody. Postcode plus
birth year plus sex uniquely identifies 14.9% of the table, and adding birth
month takes it to 85.5% -- reproducing Sweeney's result on synthetic data.
Nothing was added to the release except *precision*.

The second block makes the subtler point: even where individuals are not
unique, the *sensitive value* can still be determined. If everyone in your
quasi-identifier group has the same diagnosis, learning your group is enough.

Practical consequences for how you handle data:

1. **Classify columns, not tables.** Every column gets a label -- direct
   identifier, quasi-identifier, sensitive, or ordinary -- and that label
   drives access, masking, retention, and logging. Do this in the schema, not
   in a wiki.
2. **Count uniqueness before you release anything.** The query in the code
   above takes one line and is the single most informative privacy check
   available.
3. **Treat high-dimensional behavioural data as identifying by default.**
   Purchase histories, location traces, app-usage sequences, and clickstreams
   are effectively unique per person; there is no small set of columns to
   remove.
4. **Remember free text and images.** Notes fields, uploaded documents, and
   photographs carry identifiers that no column-level policy catches.
5. **Assume an auxiliary dataset exists.** Your release will be joined
   against voter rolls, social media, data brokers, and leaked breaches. The
   question is never "is this anonymous?" but "anonymous against what?"

A final legal note, because the definitions differ in ways that change what
you must do. **PII** (US-centric) generally refers to information that
identifies a specific individual. **Personal data** under the GDPR is much
broader: any information *relating to* an identified or identifiable natural
person, which includes IP addresses, cookie IDs, and pseudonymised records
where re-identification remains possible. **PHI** under HIPAA covers health
information along with 18 enumerated identifier types. If you build to the
narrowest definition, you will be non-compliant under the broadest.

> Key Takeaways
> - Identification does not require an identifier; a sufficiently precise
>   combination of ordinary attributes singles people out.
> - Postcode, date of birth, and sex identify the large majority of a
>   population; here 85.5% of rows were unique on four coarse columns.
> - Quasi-identifiers are the dangerous category precisely because each one
>   looks harmless in isolation.
> - Even without uniqueness, a homogeneous group leaks the sensitive value to
>   anyone who knows the group.
> - High-dimensional behavioural data (locations, purchases, clickstreams) is
>   identifying by default and cannot be fixed by dropping columns.
> - Classify columns in the schema, and count uniqueness before every release.
> - Privacy is always relative to the auxiliary data an attacker can join
>   against, so "anonymous" is meaningless without naming that threat model.
> - PII, personal data (GDPR), and PHI (HIPAA) have different scopes; build to
>   the broadest that applies.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. For a dataset you have, compute the fraction of rows that are unique on
>    each candidate quasi-identifier combination of two and three columns.
> 2. Write a column classification for that dataset and note which columns you
>    had to think about longest.
> 3. Identify one auxiliary dataset that is publicly available and could be
>    joined to yours, and name the join keys.
> 4. Take a free-text field and measure how often it contains something that
>    would identify a person.
> 5. Interview: A colleague proposes publishing "anonymous" hourly step counts
>    from a fitness app, with user IDs replaced by random numbers. What do you
>    say? (Hint: think about what a sequence of daily behaviour looks like
>    across a population, and how many days it takes to become unique.)


#### Anonymization and Pseudonymization

These two words are used interchangeably in conversation and mean completely
different things in law and in practice. The difference decides whether a
dataset is still regulated personal data.

**Pseudonymisation** replaces identifiers with surrogate values while keeping
the ability to link records -- and, crucially, keeping the possibility of
re-identification, whether through a key you hold or through the
quasi-identifiers you left behind. Under the GDPR, pseudonymised data *is
still personal data*. It is a risk-reduction control, not an exit from the
regulation.

**Anonymisation** means re-identification is no longer reasonably possible by
anyone, including you. Truly anonymised data falls outside the regulation --
and genuine anonymisation is much harder than people expect, because it
requires destroying enough information that the release stops being useful for
some of the analyses you wanted.

```text
  ORIGINAL           PSEUDONYMISED          ANONYMISED (k=5, generalised)
  Alice, 10001,      a91f3c, 10001,         *, 100**, 1980-1989, F,
  1984-03, F,        1984-03, F,            asthma
  asthma             asthma
                     ^                      ^
                     re-linkable with       no individual row corresponds
                     the key or by join     to one identifiable person
```

The tool of anonymisation is **generalisation**: replace a precise value with
a coarser one until every combination of quasi-identifiers is shared by at
least *k* people. That is **k-anonymity**. The complementary tools are
suppression (drop rare rows entirely) and perturbation (add noise).

```python
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, hashlib
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
N = 50000
zips = np.array([f"{z:05d}" for z in range(10001, 10201)])
# TRUE PREVALENCE VARIES BY AREA AND AGE -- THIS IS THE SIGNAL GENERALISATION
# WILL DESTROY, AND THE REASON ANONYMISATION HAS A COST.
area_rate = rng.uniform(0.10, 0.40, len(zips))
zi = rng.integers(0, len(zips), N)
birth = rng.integers(1940, 2006, N)
p_hyp = np.clip(area_rate[zi] + 0.004*(1980-birth), 0.02, 0.95)
df = pd.DataFrame({"zip": zips[zi], "birth_year": birth,
                   "sex": rng.choice(["F", "M"], N),
                   "hypertension": (rng.random(N) < p_hyp).astype(int)})
df["z3"] = df["zip"].str[:3]; df["z2"] = df["zip"].str[:2]
df["band5"] = (df["birth_year"]//5)*5
df["band10"] = (df["birth_year"]//10)*10

print("PSEUDONYMISATION IS NOT ANONYMISATION")
salt = b"per-dataset-salt"
h = lambda v: hashlib.sha256(salt + str(v).encode()).hexdigest()[:12]
df["zip_hash"] = df["zip"].map(h)
rainbow = {h(z): z for z in zips}          # attacker hashes the whole domain
print(f"  hashed zip looks like: {df['zip_hash'].iloc[0]}")
print(f"  domain size to brute force: {len(rainbow)}")
print(f"  share of hashes reversed by a table lookup: "
      f"{(df['zip_hash'].map(rainbow) == df['zip']).mean():.1%}")
print("  A hash of a low-entropy value is a pseudonym, not a secret.\n")

print("GENERALISATION: TRADING PRECISION FOR GROUP SIZE")
print(f"  {'scheme':28}{'min k':>8}{'cells k<5':>11}{'people k<5':>12}"
      f"{'area MAE':>10}")
truth = df.groupby("zip", observed=True)["hypertension"].mean()
levels = [("zip5 + year + sex", ["zip", "birth_year", "sex"], "zip"),
          ("zip3 + year + sex", ["z3", "birth_year", "sex"], "z3"),
          ("zip3 + 5y band + sex", ["z3", "band5", "sex"], "z3"),
          ("zip2 + 10y band + sex", ["z2", "band10", "sex"], "z2")]
for lab, cols, geo in levels:
    g = df.groupby(cols, observed=True).size()
    est = df.groupby(geo, observed=True)["hypertension"].mean()
    pred = df[geo].map(est)                 # best guess per original postcode
    mae = np.abs(pred.groupby(df["zip"]).mean() - truth).mean()
    print(f"  {lab:28}{g.min():8d}{(g < 5).mean():11.1%}"
          f"{g[g < 5].sum()/N:12.1%}{mae:10.4f}")

print("\nK-ANONYMITY IS NOT ENOUGH: THE HOMOGENEITY ATTACK")
# ONE CELL IS A RETIREMENT COMMUNITY: LARGE, AND ALMOST ALL POSITIVE.
mask = (df["z3"] == "101") & (df["band10"] == 1940)
df.loc[mask, "hypertension"] = (rng.random(mask.sum()) < 0.97).astype(int)
g = df.groupby(["z3", "band10", "sex"], observed=True)["hypertension"]
wk = g.mean().idxmax()
print(f"  smallest cell size k = {g.size().min()}  (well past 5-anonymity)")
print(f"  worst cell {(wk[0], int(wk[1]), wk[2])}: n={g.size()[wk]}, "
      f"positive rate {g.mean()[wk]:.1%}")
```

```text
PSEUDONYMISATION IS NOT ANONYMISATION
  hashed zip looks like: 8b66e715562c
  domain size to brute force: 200
  share of hashes reversed by a table lookup: 100.0%
  A hash of a low-entropy value is a pseudonym, not a secret.

GENERALISATION: TRADING PRECISION FOR GROUP SIZE
  scheme                         min k  cells k<5  people k<5  area MAE
  zip5 + year + sex                  1      95.0%       87.9%    0.0000
  zip3 + year + sex                  1      27.2%        0.4%    0.0792
  zip3 + 5y band + sex               2       3.6%        0.0%    0.0792
  zip2 + 10y band + sex           2230       0.0%        0.0%    0.0793

K-ANONYMITY IS NOT ENOUGH: THE HOMOGENEITY ATTACK
  smallest cell size k = 7  (well past 5-anonymity)
  worst cell ('101', 1940, 'F'): n=1957, positive rate 97.4%
```

The first block is the mistake that appears in production code constantly:
hashing a value with a low-entropy domain protects nothing. There are only
200 postcodes, so an attacker hashes all 200 and reverses every record. The
same applies to phone numbers, national ID numbers with checksums, email
addresses from a known list, and any small categorical. A hash is only a
secret when the input space is too large to enumerate -- which is why real
tokenisation uses a **keyed** function (HMAC) with the key stored separately,
as the last topic in this section shows.

The generalisation block quantifies the cost. Going from full postcode to a
three-digit prefix eliminates almost all small cells (87.9% of people were in
cells of fewer than 5, now 0.4%) -- and it takes the achievable accuracy of a
per-postcode prevalence estimate from exact to a mean absolute error of 0.079,
which on rates ranging from 0.10 to 0.40 destroys most of the geographic
signal. **Anonymisation is not free; it trades a specific analysis away.** The
right way to run this decision is to name the analyses the release must
support and check them at each generalisation level.

The last block is the reason k-anonymity alone is not a sufficient standard.
Every cell here has at least 7 members, so the release is 5-anonymous, and
yet one cell of 1,957 people has a 97.4% positive rate. Knowing only that
someone belongs to that cell tells you their diagnosis with near certainty.
This is the **homogeneity attack**, and it is what the successor definitions
address:

| Definition | Guarantees | Attack it blocks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| k-anonymity | Each quasi-identifier cell has >= k members | Direct re-identification by join |
| l-diversity | Each cell contains >= l distinct sensitive values | Homogeneity attack |
| t-closeness | Each cell's sensitive distribution is within t of the global one | Skewness / background-knowledge attack |
| Differential privacy | Bounded change in output from any one person's data | All of the above, plus unknown future attacks |

Each row up that table is strictly stronger and strictly more costly in
utility. And the crucial limitation of the first three is that they are
**syntactic**: they constrain the shape of a released table, and they do not
compose. Two separately k-anonymous releases of the same population can
jointly re-identify people. That non-composition is exactly what the next
topic fixes.

> Key Takeaways
> - Pseudonymised data is still personal data under the GDPR; anonymised data
>   is outside it, and genuine anonymisation is hard.
> - Hashing a low-entropy value protects nothing: the attacker enumerates the
>   domain, and here recovered 100% of postcodes.
> - Tokenisation needs a keyed function with the key stored separately, not a
>   plain hash.
> - k-anonymity is achieved by generalisation and suppression, and it always
>   costs a specific analysis; name those analyses before choosing the level.
> - k-anonymity does not prevent learning the sensitive value: a homogeneous
>   cell leaks it regardless of size.
> - l-diversity and t-closeness patch the homogeneity and skewness attacks at
>   further utility cost.
> - All of these are syntactic properties of one table and do not compose;
>   multiple releases can jointly re-identify.
> - Decide what the release must support analytically, then find the weakest
>   generalisation that still supports it.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement a k-anonymity check and find the coarsest generalisation of your
>    data that reaches k = 10.
> 2. Measure the utility cost of that generalisation on one concrete query you
>    care about, reported as an error, not as a feeling.
> 3. Find a cell in your generalised data with the least diverse sensitive
>    attribute and compute what an attacker learns from group membership alone.
> 4. Demonstrate the rainbow-table attack on a hashed column from your own
>    data, then repeat it with an HMAC and show the difference.
> 5. Interview: Your company publishes two k-anonymous extracts of the same
>    customer base for two different partners. What could go wrong? (Hint:
>    consider what happens when the two partners' quasi-identifier
>    generalisations do not nest inside each other.)


#### Differential Privacy

Every technique in the previous topic shares a weakness: it protects against
the attacks you thought of, using the auxiliary data you imagined. Each new
attack requires a new patch, and combining releases breaks guarantees that
held individually.

Differential privacy changes the question. Instead of asking "can someone be
re-identified from this output?", it asks: **would the output look
meaningfully different if any one person's data were removed?** If the answer
is no -- if the distribution of outputs is nearly the same whether you are in
the dataset or not -- then nothing anyone learns from the output can be
attributed to you, no matter what else they know.

Formally, a randomised mechanism *M* is **epsilon-differentially private** if
for any two datasets *D* and *D'* differing in one person's record, and any
set of outputs *S*:

```text
  P(M(D) in S)  <=  exp(eps) * P(M(D') in S)

  eps = 0     : output is independent of any individual -> useless but perfect
  eps small   : an attacker's belief about you barely moves
  eps large   : the guarantee is nominal

  (eps, delta)-DP adds a delta probability of the guarantee failing outright,
  which is what Gaussian noise and DP-SGD accounting use.
```

The analogy: imagine answering a sensitive yes/no question by first flipping a
coin in private. Heads, you answer truthfully; tails, you flip again and
answer yes or no according to that. Any individual answer is deniable -- you
can always say the coin made you say it -- yet the aggregate proportion is
recoverable, because you know the coin's bias. That is randomised response,
the oldest differentially private mechanism, invented for survey research in
1965.

The standard mechanism for numeric queries adds noise calibrated to
**sensitivity**: the largest amount the answer could change if one person's
record changed. For a count, that is 1.

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
N = 10000
disease = (rng.random(N) < 0.18).astype(int)
true_count = disease.sum()

def lap_count(data, eps, sens=1.0):
    return data.sum() + rng.laplace(0, sens/eps)   # sensitivity 1 for a count

print(f"true count = {true_count} of {N}")
print("\nLAPLACE MECHANISM: NOISE SCALE IS SENSITIVITY / EPSILON")
print(f"  {'epsilon':>9}{'noise scale':>13}{'mean |error|':>14}"
      f"{'95% of errors within':>22}")
for eps in (0.01, 0.1, 1.0, 10.0):
    errs = np.abs([lap_count(disease, eps) - true_count for _ in range(4000)])
    print(f"  {eps:9.2f}{1/eps:13.1f}{errs.mean():14.1f}"
          f"{np.percentile(errs, 95):22.1f}")

print("\nWHAT EPSILON MEANS: THE ATTACKER'S ADVANTAGE IS BOUNDED BY e^eps")
print(f"  {'epsilon':>9}{'max likelihood ratio':>22}"
      f"{'best posterior from 50% prior':>31}")
for eps in (0.01, 0.1, 1.0, 5.0, 10.0):
    r = np.exp(eps)
    print(f"  {eps:9.2f}{r:22.2f}{r/(1+r):31.1%}")

print("\nCOMPOSITION: A PRIVACY BUDGET IS SPENT, NOT RENEWED")
print(f"  {'queries':>9}{'eps each':>10}{'total eps (basic)':>19}"
      f"{'total eps (advanced)':>22}")
for q in (1, 10, 100, 1000):
    e = 0.1
    adv = np.sqrt(2*q*np.log(1/1e-5))*e + q*e*(np.exp(e)-1)
    print(f"  {q:9d}{e:10.2f}{q*e:19.1f}{adv:22.1f}")

print("\nSAME BUDGET, MORE PEOPLE: PRIVACY GETS CHEAPER AT SCALE")
print(f"  {'n':>9}{'true rate':>11}{'noisy rate (eps=1)':>20}{'rel error':>11}")
for n in (100, 1000, 10000, 1000000):
    d = (rng.random(n) < 0.18).astype(int)
    noisy = (d.sum() + rng.laplace(0, 1.0))/n
    print(f"  {n:9d}{d.mean():11.3f}{noisy:20.3f}"
          f"{abs(noisy-d.mean())/d.mean():11.1%}")
```

```text
true count = 1827 of 10000

LAPLACE MECHANISM: NOISE SCALE IS SENSITIVITY / EPSILON
    epsilon  noise scale  mean |error|  95% of errors within
       0.01        100.0          98.4                 287.2
       0.10         10.0          10.3                  30.6
       1.00          1.0           1.0                   3.0
      10.00          0.1           0.1                   0.3

WHAT EPSILON MEANS: THE ATTACKER'S ADVANTAGE IS BOUNDED BY e^eps
    epsilon  max likelihood ratio  best posterior from 50% prior
       0.01                  1.01                          50.2%
       0.10                  1.11                          52.5%
       1.00                  2.72                          73.1%
       5.00                148.41                          99.3%
      10.00              22026.47                         100.0%

COMPOSITION: A PRIVACY BUDGET IS SPENT, NOT RENEWED
    queries  eps each  total eps (basic)  total eps (advanced)
          1      0.10                0.1                   0.5
         10      0.10                1.0                   1.6
        100      0.10               10.0                   5.9
       1000      0.10              100.0                  25.7

SAME BUDGET, MORE PEOPLE: PRIVACY GETS CHEAPER AT SCALE
          n  true rate  noisy rate (eps=1)  rel error
        100      0.170               0.165       2.7%
       1000      0.184               0.183       0.5%
      10000      0.182               0.182       0.0%
    1000000      0.179               0.179       0.0%
```

Four readings, each with a practical consequence.

**Epsilon is an exchange rate, not a switch.** At eps = 1 the noise on a count
is about 1 person -- negligible against a count of 1,827. At eps = 0.01 it is
about 100 people, which destroys the answer. Real deployments sit between: the
US Census 2020 used a total budget in the range of tens; Apple and Google use
per-report epsilons of a few units per day.

**Epsilon has a direct interpretation.** The third column of the second table
is the most useful thing to tell a stakeholder: starting from a 50% belief
that you are in the dataset, an attacker who sees an eps = 1 output can reach
at most 73%. At eps = 5 they can reach 99.3%. **Epsilon values above about 5
provide a formal guarantee with very little practical content**, which is why
reported epsilons should always be read sceptically.

**The budget composes and does not reset.** A hundred queries at eps = 0.1
each cost eps = 10 in total under basic composition, or 5.9 under advanced
composition. This is differential privacy's greatest strength -- the guarantee
degrades *predictably* rather than silently, as k-anonymity does -- and its
greatest operational burden: you must track spend, and when the budget is
exhausted, the honest answer is to stop answering.

**Scale is free privacy.** The same absolute noise is 2.7% relative error on
100 people and invisible on a million. Differential privacy is nearly costless
for population-level statistics on large datasets, and expensive for small
subgroups -- which is unfortunately where the interesting questions often are.

For training models the standard method is **DP-SGD**: bound each example's
influence by clipping its gradient, then add noise to the summed gradient
before the update.

```python
X = rng.normal(0, 1, (4000, 5)); w_true = np.array([1.2,-0.8,0.5,0.0,0.3])
y = (rng.random(4000) < 1/(1+np.exp(-(X @ w_true)))).astype(int)
Xt = rng.normal(0, 1, (2000, 5))
yt = (rng.random(2000) < 1/(1+np.exp(-(Xt @ w_true)))).astype(int)

def train(clip=None, sigma=0.0, iters=300, lr=0.5, batch=64):
    w = np.zeros(5)
    for _ in range(iters):
        idx = rng.choice(len(X), batch, replace=False)
        p = 1/(1+np.exp(-(X[idx] @ w)))
        gi = (p - y[idx])[:, None]*X[idx]              # PER-EXAMPLE gradients
        if clip is not None:
            nrm = np.linalg.norm(gi, axis=1, keepdims=True)
            gi = gi*np.minimum(1.0, clip/nrm)          # bound each influence
        g = gi.sum(0)
        if sigma:
            g = g + rng.normal(0, sigma*(clip or 1.0), 5)   # then add noise
        w -= lr*g/batch
    return w

def acc(w): return ((1/(1+np.exp(-(Xt @ w))) > 0.5) == yt).mean()
print(f"  {'setting':32}{'test accuracy':>15}{'|w - w_true|':>14}")
for lab, kw in [("no privacy", dict()),
                ("clip only (C=1), no noise", dict(clip=1.0)),
                ("clip + noise sigma=2", dict(clip=1.0, sigma=2.0)),
                ("clip + noise sigma=10", dict(clip=1.0, sigma=10.0)),
                ("clip + noise sigma=40", dict(clip=1.0, sigma=40.0))]:
    w = train(**kw)
    print(f"  {lab:32}{acc(w):15.3f}{np.linalg.norm(w-w_true):14.2f}")
```

```text
  setting                           test accuracy  |w - w_true|
  no privacy                                0.719          0.17
  clip only (C=1), no noise                 0.721          0.60
  clip + noise sigma=2                      0.726          0.65
  clip + noise sigma=10                     0.713          0.79
  clip + noise sigma=40                     0.626          3.71
```

Both DP-SGD steps matter and they are not interchangeable. Clipping is what
*bounds sensitivity* -- without it, one outlier can move the gradient
arbitrarily far and no amount of noise gives a guarantee. Noise is what buys
the epsilon. The table shows the usual shape: modest noise is nearly free,
and there is a point (here sigma = 40) where the model degrades sharply. Note
also that clipping alone already costs parameter accuracy (0.17 to 0.60),
because it biases the gradient.

A last caution. Differential privacy protects **one person's record**. If a
person contributes many rows, the unit of protection must be the person, not
the row (*user-level* rather than *example-level* DP), or the guarantee you
advertise is not the guarantee you provide.

> Key Takeaways
> - Differential privacy bounds how much any single person's data can change
>   the distribution of outputs, which protects against unknown future attacks.
> - The noise scale is sensitivity divided by epsilon; sensitivity is the most
>   an answer could change if one record changed.
> - Epsilon is an exchange rate with a direct reading: from a 50% prior, an
>   attacker can reach at most exp(eps)/(1+exp(eps)).
> - Epsilons above roughly 5 are formally valid and practically weak; always
>   read a reported epsilon critically.
> - The budget composes across queries and does not reset; when it is spent,
>   the correct action is to stop answering.
> - Privacy is cheap at population scale and expensive for small subgroups,
>   which is often where the questions are.
> - DP-SGD needs both clipping (to bound sensitivity) and noise (to buy
>   epsilon); clipping alone gives no guarantee.
> - Protect at the level of the person, not the row, whenever one person can
>   contribute many rows.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement the Laplace mechanism for a mean rather than a count, deriving
>    the sensitivity yourself, and check the error at three epsilon values.
> 2. Implement randomised response and recover the true proportion from the
>    noisy answers, reporting the variance of your estimate.
> 3. Track a privacy budget across a sequence of queries and write the code
>    that refuses a query once the budget is exhausted.
> 4. Train a model with DP-SGD at several noise levels and plot accuracy
>    against noise, identifying the knee.
> 5. Interview: A vendor advertises "differentially private analytics with
>    epsilon = 12". What do you conclude? (Hint: compute the bound on an
>    attacker's posterior from a 50% prior, and ask whether it is per query or
>    in total.)


#### Federated Learning

Every privacy technique so far assumes the data has already been collected
into one place. Federated learning asks whether that step is necessary at all.
**The insight: to fit a model you need gradients, not rows.** If each
participant computes updates on their own data and only the updates are
shared, the raw data never leaves the device or the institution.

This matters in two very different settings. **Cross-device** federation
involves millions of phones with a few hundred examples each -- the original
motivating case, for keyboard prediction. **Cross-silo** federation involves a
handful of organisations with large datasets that they cannot legally pool --
hospitals, banks, or national statistical offices.

The standard algorithm is **FedAvg**:

```text
  for each round:
    server sends the current model to a sample of clients
    each client trains locally for a few steps on its own data
    each client uploads its updated weights (not its data)
    server averages the uploads, weighted by client dataset size

  server  --w-->  [client 1] --w1-->  \
          --w-->  [client 2] --w2-->   >  w <- weighted mean
          --w-->  [client k] --wk-->  /
```

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(8)
D, NC, NPER = 6, 20, 300                         # dims, clients, rows each
w_true = np.array([1.5, -1.0, 0.8, 0.0, 0.4, -0.6])

def make_clients(non_iid=0.0):
    """non_iid shifts each client's feature distribution and label balance."""
    cls = []
    for c in range(NC):
        shift = non_iid*rng.normal(0, 1, D)
        Xc = rng.normal(shift, 1.0, (NPER, D))
        z = Xc @ w_true + non_iid*rng.normal(0, 2)
        yc = (rng.random(NPER) < 1/(1+np.exp(-z))).astype(int)
        cls.append((Xc, yc))
    return cls

Xt = rng.normal(0, 1, (4000, D))
yt = (rng.random(4000) < 1/(1+np.exp(-(Xt @ w_true)))).astype(int)
def acc(w): return ((1/(1+np.exp(-(Xt @ w))) > 0.5) == yt).mean()

def local_steps(w, Xc, yc, steps, lr=0.5):
    w = w.copy()
    for _ in range(steps):
        p = 1/(1+np.exp(-(Xc @ w)))
        w -= lr*(Xc.T @ (p - yc))/len(yc)
    return w

def central(cls, iters=400, lr=0.5):             # the baseline: pool the data
    X = np.vstack([c[0] for c in cls]); y = np.concatenate([c[1] for c in cls])
    w = np.zeros(D)
    for _ in range(iters):
        p = 1/(1+np.exp(-(X @ w)))
        w -= lr*(X.T @ (p - y))/len(y)
    return w

def fedavg(cls, rounds, local, frac=1.0):
    w = np.zeros(D)
    for _ in range(rounds):
        sel = rng.choice(NC, max(1, int(frac*NC)), replace=False)
        ws = [local_steps(w, cls[i][0], cls[i][1], local) for i in sel]
        w = np.mean(ws, axis=0)                  # equal n, so equal weights
    return w

print("FEDAVG vs POOLING THE DATA (20 clients, 300 rows each)")
print(f"  {'setting':34}{'rounds':>8}{'local steps':>13}{'accuracy':>10}"
      f"{'uploads':>9}")
for label, non_iid in [("IID clients", 0.0), ("non-IID clients", 2.5)]:
    cls = make_clients(non_iid)
    print(f"  {label}")
    print(f"  {'  centralised (data pooled)':34}{'-':>8}{'-':>13}"
          f"{acc(central(cls)):10.3f}{0:9d}")
    for rounds, local in [(5, 1), (5, 20), (40, 5), (200, 5)]:
        print(f"  {'  fedavg':34}{rounds:8d}{local:13d}"
              f"{acc(fedavg(cls, rounds, local)):10.3f}{rounds*NC:9d}")

print("\nCLIENT SAMPLING: NOT EVERY DEVICE IS ONLINE EVERY ROUND")
cls = make_clients(2.5)
print(f"  {'fraction per round':>20}{'rounds':>8}{'accuracy':>10}{'uploads':>9}")
for frac in (0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0):
    print(f"  {frac:20.0%}{60:8d}{acc(fedavg(cls, 60, 5, frac=frac)):10.3f}"
          f"{int(60*NC*frac):9d}")

print("\nWHY THE UPDATE IS NOT PRIVATE: A GRADIENT LEAKS ITS BATCH")
Xc, yc = make_clients(0.0)[0]
w0 = np.zeros(D)
for n in (1, 2, 8, 32):
    sims = []
    for rep in range(40):                        # average over many batches
        idx = rng.choice(len(Xc), n, replace=False)
        p = 1/(1+np.exp(-(Xc[idx] @ w0)))
        g = (Xc[idx].T @ (p - yc[idx]))/n        # the uploaded gradient
        v = Xc[idx[0]]                           # one example in that batch
        sims.append(abs(g @ v)/(np.linalg.norm(g)*np.linalg.norm(v)))
    print(f"  batch of {n:4d}: mean |cosine| between the update and one of "
          f"its rows = {np.mean(sims):.3f}")
chance = np.mean([abs(a @ b)/(np.linalg.norm(a)*np.linalg.norm(b))
                  for a, b in zip(rng.normal(0, 1, (40, D)), Xc[:40])])
print(f"  chance level for unrelated vectors in {D} dimensions = {chance:.3f}")
```

FEDAVG vs POOLING THE DATA (20 clients, 300 rows each)
