```text
    fedavg                                 5            1     0.792      100
    fedavg                                 5           20     0.791      100
    fedavg                                40            5     0.791      800
    fedavg                               200            5     0.791     4000
  non-IID clients
    centralised (data pooled)              -            -     0.757        0
    fedavg                                 5            1     0.753      100
    fedavg                                 5           20     0.776      100
    fedavg                                40            5     0.763      800
    fedavg                               200            5     0.763     4000

CLIENT SAMPLING: NOT EVERY DEVICE IS ONLINE EVERY ROUND
    fraction per round  rounds  accuracy  uploads
                   10%      60     0.702      120
                   25%      60     0.719      300
                   50%      60     0.737      600
                  100%      60     0.757     1200

WHY THE UPDATE IS NOT PRIVATE: A GRADIENT LEAKS ITS BATCH
  batch of    1: mean |cosine| between the update and one of its rows = 1.000
  batch of    2: mean |cosine| between the update and one of its rows = 0.677
  batch of    8: mean |cosine| between the update and one of its rows = 0.525
  batch of   32: mean |cosine| between the update and one of its rows = 0.378
  chance level for unrelated vectors in 6 dimensions = 0.308
```

On IID clients FedAvg matches centralised training exactly -- 0.791 either way
-- which is the result that makes the approach attractive. On non-IID clients
it does not: centralised reaches 0.757 and FedAvg lands between 0.753 and
0.776 depending on how the round budget is spent, and client sampling costs
more still (0.702 at 10% participation against 0.757 pooled). **Heterogeneity,
not cryptography, is the main practical difficulty in federated learning.**

The last block is the point that must be understood before anyone describes
federated learning as private. A single-example update has cosine similarity
1.000 with that example -- the gradient of a logistic model on one row is a
scalar multiple of the row, so uploading it *is* uploading the data. Even at a
batch of 32, similarity remains above the chance level of 0.308. Published
gradient-inversion attacks reconstruct recognisable training images from
updates in realistic deep-learning settings.

Federated learning is therefore a **data minimisation** technique, not a
privacy guarantee. Making it private requires composing it with other
mechanisms:

| Mechanism | What it adds | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Secure aggregation | Server sees only the sum, never an individual update | Crypto protocol, dropout handling |
| DP noise (local or central) | A formal epsilon on what any update reveals | Accuracy, and needs many clients |
| Gradient clipping | Bounded per-client influence; also blocks poisoning | Slower convergence |
| Update compression | Less to intercept, less bandwidth | Some accuracy |
| Client-side validation | Resistance to malicious clients | Cannot fully solve it |

And two costs that are frequently underestimated: you cannot inspect the
training data, so **debugging is severely limited** -- no looking at the
distribution, no finding the mislabelled batch -- and a subset of clients can
**poison** the model by sending crafted updates, which requires robust
aggregation (trimmed means, median, norm bounds) rather than a plain average.

> Key Takeaways
> - Federated learning trains on decentralised data by sharing model updates
>   instead of rows, in cross-device (many small clients) or cross-silo (few
>   large ones) settings.
> - FedAvg matches centralised training on IID clients and falls short on
>   heterogeneous ones; heterogeneity is the main practical problem.
> - Partial client participation costs additional accuracy for the same number
>   of rounds.
> - Model updates leak their training data: a single-example gradient is the
>   example up to scale, and inversion attacks reconstruct inputs in practice.
> - Federated learning is data minimisation, not a privacy guarantee; it needs
>   secure aggregation and differential privacy to become one.
> - Gradient clipping bounds both privacy leakage and the influence of a
>   malicious client.
> - Plain averaging is vulnerable to poisoning; robust aggregation is required
>   when clients are not trusted.
> - You cannot inspect the data, so ordinary debugging and data-quality work
>   become much harder.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Implement FedAvg and compare it with centralised training under IID and
>    label-skewed client splits.
> 2. Measure the accuracy cost of reducing client participation from 100% to
>    10% at a fixed number of rounds.
> 3. Reconstruct a training row from a single-example gradient upload for a
>    linear model, and show how batching degrades the reconstruction.
> 4. Implement a trimmed-mean aggregator and show that it survives three
>    clients uploading large adversarial updates while the plain mean does not.
> 5. Interview: A hospital consortium wants federated learning so that "no
>    patient data is shared". What do you have to tell them before they
>    announce it? (Hint: distinguish what leaves the building from what can be
>    inferred from what leaves the building.)


#### Adversarial Attacks on Models

Once a model is exposed -- through an API, an app, or a decision it makes --
it becomes an attack surface in its own right. The model is not just software
that could have bugs; it is a **statistical object that leaks information
about its training data and can be manipulated through its inputs**. Four
attack families cover almost everything seen in practice, and they are
distinguished by what the attacker wants.

| Attack | Attacker's goal | Access needed | Primary defence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Evasion (adversarial examples) | Make one input be classified wrongly | Query access; gradients help | Adversarial training, input validation, ensembles |
| Poisoning / backdoor | Corrupt the model during training | Influence over training data | Data provenance, anomaly detection in training data |
| Membership inference | Learn whether a record was in training | Query access | Reduce overfitting, DP training |
| Model extraction / inversion | Steal the model, or reconstruct training inputs | Many queries | Rate limits, output coarsening, watermarking |

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(13)
D = 40
def feats(n):
    X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, D))
    w = np.r_[np.linspace(1.5, 0.2, 8), np.zeros(D-8)]
    y = (rng.random(n) < 1/(1+np.exp(-(X @ w)))).astype(int)
    return X, y
Xtr, ytr = feats(600); Xte, yte = feats(4000)

def train(X, y, iters=4000, lr=0.4, l2=0.0):
    w = np.zeros(X.shape[1]); b = 0.0
    for _ in range(iters):
        p = 1/(1+np.exp(-(X @ w + b)))
        g = (p - y)/len(y)
        w -= lr*(X.T @ g + l2*w); b -= lr*g.sum()
    return w, b
def prob(X, wb): return 1/(1+np.exp(-(X @ wb[0] + wb[1])))

print("1. EVASION: THE SMALLEST PERTURBATION THAT FLIPS A DECISION")
wb = train(Xtr, ytr, l2=1e-3)
p = prob(Xte, wb)
# FOR A LINEAR MODEL THE MINIMUM L2 PERTURBATION IS THE DISTANCE TO THE
# HYPERPLANE: |margin| / ||w||, APPLIED ALONG -sign(margin)*w.
margin = Xte @ wb[0] + wb[1]
need = np.abs(margin)/np.linalg.norm(wb[0])
print(f"  clean test accuracy: {((p > 0.5) == yte).mean():.3f}")
print(f"  {'perturbation L2 budget':>24}{'accuracy under attack':>24}")
for eps in (0.0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0):
    flipped = need <= eps
    print(f"  {eps:24.2f}{(((p > 0.5) == yte) & ~flipped).mean():24.3f}")
print(f"  median row sits {np.median(need):.3f} away from the boundary, while")
print(f"  a typical row has norm {np.median(np.linalg.norm(Xte, axis=1)):.1f}"
      f" -- the attack is "
      f"{np.median(need)/np.median(np.linalg.norm(Xte, axis=1)):.1%} of the input")

print("\n2. MEMBERSHIP INFERENCE: DID THIS ROW APPEAR IN TRAINING?")
def xent(X, y, wb):
    p = np.clip(prob(X, wb), 1e-9, 1-1e-9)
    return -(y*np.log(p) + (1-y)*np.log(1-p))
def auc(lab, sc):
    o = np.argsort(sc); r = np.empty(len(sc)); r[o] = np.arange(1, len(sc)+1)
    n1 = lab.sum(); n0 = len(lab)-n1
    return (r[lab == 1].sum() - n1*(n1+1)/2)/(n0*n1)
print(f"  {'training rows':>14}{'train acc':>11}{'test acc':>10}{'gap':>8}"
      f"{'attack AUC':>12}")
for n in (60, 150, 400, 1200, 4000):
    TR, TE, AT = [], [], []
    for _ in range(8):                            # average over 8 draws
        Xs, ys = feats(n); Xo, yo = feats(n)      # members and non-members
        wb = train(Xs, ys, iters=8000, lr=0.5, l2=1e-4)
        TR.append(((prob(Xs, wb) > 0.5) == ys).mean())
        TE.append(((prob(Xte, wb) > 0.5) == yte).mean())
        # THE ATTACK: SCORE EACH ROW BY ITS LOSS. LOW LOSS -> LIKELY A MEMBER.
        L = np.r_[xent(Xs, ys, wb), xent(Xo, yo, wb)]
        AT.append(auc(np.r_[np.ones(n), np.zeros(n)], -L))
    print(f"  {n:14d}{np.mean(TR):11.3f}{np.mean(TE):10.3f}"
          f"{np.mean(TR)-np.mean(TE):+8.3f}{np.mean(AT):12.3f}")

print("\n3. MODEL EXTRACTION: REBUILDING THE MODEL FROM ITS OWN ANSWERS")
wb = train(Xtr, ytr, l2=1e-3)
print(f"  {'queries':>9}{'agreement with victim':>24}{'cosine(w_hat, w)':>19}")
for q in (50, 200, 1000, 5000):
    Xq = rng.normal(0, 1, (q, D))                 # the attacker's own inputs
    yq = (prob(Xq, wb) > 0.5).astype(int)         # only HARD labels returned
    sur = train(Xq, yq, l2=1e-3)
    agree = ((prob(Xte, sur) > 0.5) == (prob(Xte, wb) > 0.5)).mean()
    cos = (sur[0] @ wb[0])/(np.linalg.norm(sur[0])*np.linalg.norm(wb[0]))
    print(f"  {q:9d}{agree:24.3f}{cos:19.3f}")
```

```text
1. EVASION: THE SMALLEST PERTURBATION THAT FLIPS A DECISION
  clean test accuracy: 0.801
    perturbation L2 budget   accuracy under attack
                      0.00                   0.801
                      0.05                   0.783
                      0.10                   0.766
                      0.25                   0.696
                      0.50                   0.569
                      1.00                   0.320
  median row sits 0.679 away from the boundary, while
  a typical row has norm 6.3 -- the attack is 10.8% of the input

2. MEMBERSHIP INFERENCE: DID THIS ROW APPEAR IN TRAINING?
   training rows  train acc  test acc     gap  attack AUC
              60      1.000     0.694  +0.306       0.649
             150      0.936     0.721  +0.215       0.570
             400      0.844     0.791  +0.053       0.523
            1200      0.826     0.819  +0.007       0.510
            4000      0.826     0.828  -0.002       0.507

3. MODEL EXTRACTION: REBUILDING THE MODEL FROM ITS OWN ANSWERS
    queries   agreement with victim   cosine(w_hat, w)
         50                   0.763              0.747
        200                   0.936              0.981
       1000                   0.979              0.998
       5000                   0.987              1.000
```

Each block carries a distinct lesson.

**Evasion is cheap and it is not a deep-learning phenomenon.** A perturbation
of L2 norm 1.0 -- about 16% of a typical input's norm -- halves the model's
accuracy, and even a budget of 0.1 costs 3.5 points. The reason is geometric,
not a quirk of neural networks: in high dimensions most points sit close to
the decision boundary relative to their own magnitude, and the shortest path
across is along the weight vector. Anything with a decision boundary can be
evaded; models trained on attacker-controlled inputs (spam, fraud, malware,
content moderation) must assume it.

**Membership inference power is the generalisation gap.** The attack is
embarrassingly simple -- compute each candidate's loss and guess "member" if
it is low -- and its AUC tracks the train-test gap almost perfectly: 0.649 at a
gap of 0.306, and 0.507 (chance) when the model does not overfit. The
practical implication is encouraging: **the main defence against membership
inference is not exotic, it is the regularisation you should already be
doing.** For genuinely sensitive training data -- medical records, private
messages -- add DP training on top.

**Extraction needs only the answers.** With 1,000 queries returning nothing
but hard labels, the copy agrees with the original on 97.9% of inputs and its
weight vector has cosine similarity 0.998. Returning probabilities or
explanations makes it dramatically faster. This is why rate limits, query
monitoring, coarsened outputs, and abuse detection are part of ML security,
not just of API design -- and why "we only return the label" is not a defence.

The fourth family, **poisoning**, does not appear in the code because it
requires control over training data rather than queries, but it is the most
serious for any pipeline that ingests public or user-supplied data. A backdoor
attack adds a small number of examples containing a trigger pattern paired with
the attacker's desired label; the model behaves normally except when the
trigger is present. Defences are about provenance and data validation: know
where every training row came from, detect distributional anomalies in incoming
data, hold out a trusted clean validation set, and treat any externally
sourced dataset or pretrained checkpoint as untrusted input.

> Key Takeaways
> - A deployed model is an attack surface: it leaks information about its
>   training data and can be manipulated through its inputs.
> - Evasion is geometric, not specific to deep learning; perturbations of ~10%
>   of an input's norm flip a large share of decisions for a linear model.
> - Any system whose inputs are controlled by an adversary must assume evasion
>   attempts.
> - Membership inference reduces to thresholding the per-example loss, and its
>   power tracks the train-test gap almost exactly.
> - Ordinary regularisation is the first and most effective defence against
>   membership inference; DP training is the second.
> - Model extraction works from hard labels alone: 1,000 queries produced a
>   copy agreeing on 97.9% of inputs.
> - Returning probabilities or explanations accelerates extraction, so output
>   coarsening and rate limiting are security controls.
> - Poisoning and backdoors require provenance controls and validation of
>   incoming training data, including third-party datasets and checkpoints.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Compute the minimum perturbation needed to flip each test prediction of a
>    linear model and plot accuracy against the attack budget.
> 2. Run a loss-threshold membership inference attack against two versions of
>    a model, one overfitted and one regularised, and report both AUCs.
> 3. Extract a copy of a model of yours using only hard labels, and find the
>    number of queries at which agreement exceeds 95%.
> 4. Insert a backdoor by adding 50 poisoned rows with a trigger feature
>    pattern, then verify that overall accuracy is unaffected.
> 5. Interview: Your public API returns a fraud probability to four decimal
>    places. What are the risks, and what would you change? (Hint: think about
>    what extra precision gives an attacker who can query repeatedly, and what
>    the legitimate consumer actually needs.)


#### Secure Data Handling Practices

Most real privacy incidents are not clever attacks. They are a notebook with
customer emails committed to a repository, an S3 bucket left public, a
production credential in a config file, a CSV of records emailed to a
contractor, or a dataset that should have been deleted two years ago and was
still sitting in a backup when the breach happened. The controls that prevent
these are unglamorous and they matter more than everything above.

Five principles organise them:

| Principle | What it means in a data science workflow |
| --- | --- |
| **Data minimisation** | Pull the columns and rows you need, not the whole table "in case" |
| **Least privilege** | Access matched to role and to a current, stated purpose |
| **Purpose limitation** | Data gathered for billing is not automatically available for modelling |
| **Defence in depth** | Encryption, access control, masking, and logging are layers, not alternatives |
| **Auditability** | Who accessed which records, when, and why -- retained and reviewable |

```python
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, hashlib, hmac, datetime as dt
rng = np.random.default_rng(21)
N = 200
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "user_id": range(1000, 1000+N),
    "email": [f"user{i}@example.com" for i in range(N)],
    "ssn": [f"{rng.integers(100,999)}-{rng.integers(10,99)}"
            f"-{rng.integers(1000,9999)}" for _ in range(N)],
    "card": [f"4111 1111 1111 {rng.integers(1000,9999)}" for _ in range(N)],
    "zip": rng.choice(["10001", "10002", "94107"], N),
    "spend": rng.normal(200, 60, N).round(2),
    "created": [dt.date(2021, 1, 1) + dt.timedelta(days=int(d))
                for d in rng.integers(0, 1700, N)],
})

print("1. A PII SCANNER YOU CAN PUT IN CI")
PATTERNS = {"email": r"[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.]+",
            "us_ssn": r"\b\d{3}-\d{2}-\d{4}\b",
            "card_like": r"\b(?:\d[ -]?){13,16}\b"}
for col in df.columns:
    vals = df[col].astype(str)
    hits = {k: vals.str.contains(p, regex=True).mean()
            for k, p in PATTERNS.items()}
    flags = [f"{k} {v:.0%}" for k, v in hits.items() if v > 0.5]
    print(f"  {col:10} {'CLASSIFY: ' + ', '.join(flags) if flags else 'ok'}")

print("\n2. TOKENISATION: STABLE JOIN KEY, NO RECOVERABLE VALUE")
KEY = b"kept-in-a-kms-not-in-git"                # rotate it; never commit it
def token(v):
    return hmac.new(KEY, str(v).encode(), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()[:16]
bad = lambda v: hashlib.sha256(str(v).encode()).hexdigest()[:16]
print(f"  plain sha256 of an email : {bad(df.email[0])}")
print(f"  keyed HMAC of the same   : {token(df.email[0])}")
print("  The plain hash is guessable from a wordlist of emails; the HMAC")
print("  is not, without the key. Both join consistently.")

print("\n3. COLUMN-LEVEL ACCESS BY ROLE")
CLASS = {"user_id": "internal", "email": "pii", "ssn": "sensitive",
         "card": "sensitive", "zip": "quasi", "spend": "internal",
         "created": "internal"}
ROLE_MAX = {"analyst": {"internal"},
            "ds_modeller": {"internal", "quasi", "pii"},
            "fraud_ops": {"internal", "quasi", "pii", "sensitive"}}
MASK = {"pii": token, "sensitive": lambda v: "***REDACTED***",
        "quasi": lambda v: str(v)[:3] + "**"}
def view(role):
    allowed = ROLE_MAX[role]; out = df.copy()
    for c in out.columns:
        cl = CLASS[c]
        if cl not in allowed:
            out[c] = out[c].map(MASK.get(cl, lambda v: "***"))
        elif cl == "pii":
            out[c] = out[c].map(token)           # pseudonymise even if allowed
    return out
for role in ROLE_MAX:
    r = view(role).iloc[0]
    print(f"  {role:12} email={r.email[:12]:14} ssn={r.ssn:14} zip={r.zip}")

print("\n4. RETENTION: DELETION AS A SCHEDULED JOB, NOT A PROMISE")
today = dt.date(2026, 9, 28)
POLICY = {"raw_events": 90, "enriched": 730, "aggregates": None}
print(f"  {'dataset':14}{'retention (days)':>18}{'rows kept of 200':>18}")
for ds, days in POLICY.items():
    if days is None:
        print(f"  {ds:14}{'indefinite':>18}{N:18d}")
    else:
        keep = (pd.to_datetime(df.created) >
                pd.Timestamp(today - dt.timedelta(days=days))).sum()
        print(f"  {ds:14}{days:18d}{keep:18d}")
```

```text
  ds_modeller  email=18691c13cdb0   ssn=***REDACTED*** zip=10001
  fraud_ops    email=18691c13cdb0   ssn=370-79-4474    zip=10001
```
