```text
  raw_events                    90                 0
  enriched                     730                33
  aggregates            indefinite               200
```

Four controls, each cheap and each preventing a whole class of incident.

**Automated classification** means the schema knows what each column is, so
masking and access rules can be enforced by code rather than remembered by
people. Run the scanner in CI over every new table and fail the build on an
unclassified match. The same scanner catches the accidental case: a "notes"
column that turns out to contain email addresses.

**Keyed tokenisation** replaces identifiers with values that still join
correctly -- essential, because analysis needs to link a customer's rows -- while
being useless to anyone without the key. The key lives in a key-management
service, is rotated on a schedule, and is never in the repository. A plain hash,
as the previous topic showed, is not a substitute.

**Column-level access by role** is the practical form of least privilege. The
analyst gets aggregate-safe columns and a masked postcode; the modeller gets a
pseudonymous customer key so features can be joined; only fraud operations, with
a documented purpose, sees the raw sensitive fields. Implement this in the
warehouse (views, row and column policies, dynamic masking) rather than in each
notebook, because a policy that depends on every analyst writing the right query
is not a policy.

**Retention as a scheduled job** is what makes a deletion promise real. The
policy is per dataset and per class of data, the job runs unattended, and it
must reach every copy: warehouse tables, feature store, training snapshots,
model artifacts that embedded the data, logs, exports, and backups. The copies
are what make subject-access deletion requests hard, and the only manageable
approach is to keep an inventory of where personal data flows.

Beyond the code, the checklist that catches most of the remainder:

1. **Encrypt in transit and at rest** by default; treat an unencrypted store as
   a finding.
2. **No secrets in code.** Use a secret manager, scan for credentials in
   pre-commit hooks, and rotate anything that has ever been committed.
3. **Never copy production data to a laptop.** Work in the environment where
   the data already is; if you must extract, extract a sampled, masked subset
   with an expiry.
4. **Use synthetic or masked data for development and tests.** Test fixtures
   containing real records are a recurring source of leaks.
5. **Strip notebook outputs before committing.** A cleared cell is not a
   cleared file.
6. **Log access, and review the logs.** An audit trail nobody reads deters
   nothing.
7. **Have an incident plan and rehearse it.** Who is called, what is disclosed,
   within what deadline (72 hours under the GDPR).
8. **Review third-party data flows.** A dashboard tool, an LLM API, or an
   analytics SDK receiving personal data is a processor relationship with
   contractual requirements.

That last item has become the most common new exposure: sending customer records
into an external model API is a data transfer, subject to the same rules as any
other, and "it is just for a prototype" is not an exemption.

> Key Takeaways
> - Most privacy incidents come from ordinary handling failures, not from
>   sophisticated attacks.
> - Minimise, restrict by role and purpose, layer defences, and make access
>   auditable.
> - Classify columns automatically in CI so masking and access can be enforced
>   by code instead of by memory.
> - Use keyed tokenisation (HMAC with a managed key) for join keys; a plain
>   hash is reversible for low-entropy values.
> - Enforce column-level access in the warehouse, not in each analyst's query.
> - Retention must be a scheduled, unattended job that reaches every copy,
>   including snapshots, logs, and backups.
> - Keep no secrets in code, no production data on laptops, and no real records
>   in test fixtures; strip notebook outputs before committing.
> - Sending personal data to an external model API is a data transfer with the
>   same obligations as any other, prototype or not.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write a scanner that classifies every column of one of your tables and run
>    it as a pre-commit or CI check.
> 2. Replace a plain-hash join key in an existing pipeline with an HMAC and
>    document where the key lives and how it rotates.
> 3. Define three roles for one of your datasets with the columns each may see,
>    and implement the masked views.
> 4. Trace one personal data field through every system it reaches and write the
>    deletion procedure that covers all of them.
> 5. Interview: You need to share a dataset with an external research partner
>    next week. Walk through your process. (Hint: think about the legal basis
>    first, then minimisation, then the technical release, and finally what
>    happens to their copy afterwards.)


<a id="164-governance-and-regulation"></a>
### 16.4 Governance and Regulation

Governance is the set of mechanisms that make everything in the previous three
sections *true in practice rather than in a document*; this section covers the
frameworks that assign accountability for data, the lineage and catalog
infrastructure that makes questions answerable, the regulatory landscape a
model must operate inside, what consent actually obliges you to do, how
responsible-AI principles become enforceable controls, and the additional
duties that apply when your work is research on people. The organising
insight: **a governance rule that cannot be executed by a machine or attached
to a named person is a preference, not a control.**


#### Data Governance Frameworks

Data governance is the answer to a question that has no technical answer: *who
decides?* Who decides what "active customer" means, whether a new field may be
collected, how long records are kept, who may see the salary column, and
whether a model may be retrained on last week's data. Without an answer,
every one of those decisions is made implicitly, by whoever wrote the query.

The recurring failure mode of governance programmes is that they produce
documents. A policy in a wiki that nobody can execute changes nothing; it just
shifts blame after an incident. Effective governance has three properties:
**named accountability**, **machine-checkable rules**, and **a gate that can
actually block something**.

The standard role model separates decision rights from execution:

| Role | Accountable for | Typical holder |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Data owner | The decision: who may use this data, for what, how long | A business leader, not a data team |
| Data steward | Day-to-day correctness: definitions, quality, metadata | A domain expert |
| Data custodian | The technical controls: storage, access, backups | Platform engineering |
| Data protection officer | Legal compliance, DPIAs, regulator contact | Legal/compliance (mandatory in some cases under GDPR) |
| Governance council | Cross-domain conflicts, standards, exceptions | A standing forum with authority |
| Consumer | Using data within its declared purpose | Every analyst and data scientist |

Two organisational patterns dominate, and the choice is about where the
bottleneck sits rather than about better and worse:

```text
  CENTRALISED                        FEDERATED (data mesh)
  one team owns the standards        each domain owns its data products
  and the catalog                   a central team owns the platform
                                    and the global rules
  + consistent, one throat to choke + scales; owners have context
  - bottleneck; lacks domain context- inconsistency; needs real enforcement
```

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import List, Optional
import datetime as dt

@dataclass
class Dataset:
    name: str
    owner: Optional[str] = None
    steward: Optional[str] = None
    classification: Optional[str] = None      # public|internal|pii|sensitive
    retention_days: Optional[int] = None
    lawful_basis: Optional[str] = None
    upstream: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    last_reviewed: Optional[dt.date] = None
    tests: int = 0

CLASSES = {"public", "internal", "pii", "sensitive"}
BASES = {"consent", "contract", "legal_obligation", "vital_interests",
         "public_task", "legitimate_interests"}
TODAY = dt.date(2026, 9, 28)

def check(d: Dataset):
    """Each rule is a policy statement that a machine can enforce."""
    out = []
    if not d.owner:                     out.append("no accountable owner")
    if not d.steward:                   out.append("no data steward")
    if d.classification not in CLASSES: out.append("unclassified")
    if d.classification in {"pii", "sensitive"}:
        if d.lawful_basis not in BASES: out.append("no lawful basis recorded")
        if d.retention_days is None:    out.append("no retention period")
        elif d.retention_days > 1095:   out.append("retention over 3 years")
    if not d.upstream and d.name != "raw_signup":
        out.append("no declared lineage")
    if d.last_reviewed is None or (TODAY - d.last_reviewed).days > 365:
        out.append("review overdue")
    if d.tests == 0:                    out.append("no quality tests")
    return out

catalog = [
  Dataset("raw_signup", "growth@", "a.rivera", "pii", 365, "consent",
          [], dt.date(2026, 4, 2), 6),
  Dataset("user_profile", "platform@", "j.chen", "pii", 730, "contract",
          ["raw_signup"], dt.date(2026, 1, 15), 4),
  Dataset("churn_features", "ds@", None, "internal", None, None,
          ["user_profile"], dt.date(2024, 11, 3), 0),
  Dataset("support_transcripts", None, None, None, 4000, None,
          ["raw_signup"], None, 0),
  Dataset("revenue_daily", "finance@", "m.okafor", "internal", None, None,
          ["user_profile"], dt.date(2026, 6, 30), 9),
  Dataset("churn_model_v3", "ds@", "s.haddad", "internal", None, None,
          ["churn_features"], dt.date(2026, 5, 20), 3),
  Dataset("retention_dashboard", "growth@", "a.rivera", "internal", None,
          None, ["churn_model_v3", "revenue_daily"], dt.date(2026, 7, 1), 2),
]

print("GOVERNANCE GATE: POLICY AS CODE OVER THE CATALOG")
print(f"  {'dataset':22}{'class':>11}{'findings':>10}  detail")
fail = 0
for d in catalog:
    f = check(d)
    fail += bool(f)
    print(f"  {d.name:22}{str(d.classification):>11}{len(f):10}  "
          f"{'; '.join(f) if f else 'compliant'}")
print(f"\n  {fail} of {len(catalog)} datasets fail the gate")

print("\nBLAST RADIUS: WHAT A POLICY BREACH UPSTREAM AFFECTS")
children = {d.name: [c.name for c in catalog if d.name in c.upstream]
            for d in catalog}
def downstream(n, seen=None):
    seen = seen or set()
    for c in children.get(n, []):
        if c not in seen:
            seen.add(c); downstream(c, seen)
    return seen
for d in catalog:
    if check(d):
        print(f"  {d.name:22} -> affects "
              f"{sorted(downstream(d.name)) or ['nothing']}")
```

```text
GOVERNANCE GATE: POLICY AS CODE OVER THE CATALOG
  dataset                     class  findings  detail
  raw_signup                    pii         0  compliant
  user_profile                  pii         0  compliant
  churn_features           internal         3  no data steward; review overdue; no quality tests
  support_transcripts          None         5  no accountable owner; no data steward; unclassified; review overdue; no quality tests
  revenue_daily            internal         0  compliant
  churn_model_v3           internal         0  compliant
  retention_dashboard      internal         0  compliant

  2 of 7 datasets fail the gate

BLAST RADIUS: WHAT A POLICY BREACH UPSTREAM AFFECTS
  churn_features         -> affects ['churn_model_v3', 'retention_dashboard']
  support_transcripts    -> affects ['nothing']
```

That check is fifteen lines and it is the difference between a governance
policy and a governance control. It runs in CI over the catalog, it names
specific gaps, and it can fail a build. Every rule inside it corresponds to a
sentence someone would otherwise have written in a document and hoped for:
"all personal data must have a documented lawful basis" becomes four lines
that can be violated visibly.

Notice what the blast radius query adds. `churn_features` has no steward, no
tests, and has not been reviewed in nearly two years -- and two production
assets depend on it. That combination is what turns a low-priority metadata
gap into an incident waiting to happen, and it is invisible if you look at
datasets one at a time.

A practical adoption sequence, in the order that actually works:

1. **Inventory first.** You cannot govern what you cannot list. An
   auto-discovered catalog of tables with row counts and last-write times
   beats a curated one that is three months stale.
2. **Assign owners before writing policies.** An unowned dataset cannot comply
   with anything.
3. **Classify.** Four levels is enough; more than six will not be used.
4. **Encode a small number of rules and enforce them.** Three enforced rules
   beat thirty aspirational ones.
5. **Report, do not police.** Publish a per-domain compliance score and let
   owners fix their own gaps; make exceptions explicit and time-bound.
6. **Attach governance to the pipeline, not to a review meeting.** A rule that
   only runs when someone remembers is not enforced.

Two framework names worth recognising because they structure many corporate
programmes: **DAMA-DMBOK** (a broad body of knowledge across eleven knowledge
areas including quality, metadata, security, and architecture) and **DCAM** (a
capability-maturity assessment model). Both are useful as checklists of what
you might be missing and useless as a substitute for the six steps above.

> Key Takeaways
> - Governance answers "who decides?" about definitions, access, retention, and
>   permitted use; without it those decisions are made implicitly by whoever
>   writes the query.
> - Effective governance needs named accountability, machine-checkable rules,
>   and a gate that can block a release.
> - Separate the roles: owner decides, steward maintains meaning, custodian
>   operates controls, DPO handles legal compliance.
> - Centralised governance is consistent but bottlenecked; federated
>   governance scales but needs real enforcement of global rules.
> - Encode policy as code that runs in CI over the catalog, so violations are
>   visible rather than remembered.
> - Combine compliance findings with lineage: an unowned dataset with
>   downstream production consumers is the real risk.
> - Adopt in order -- inventory, owners, classification, a few enforced rules,
>   published scores -- and keep exceptions explicit and time-bound.
> - DAMA-DMBOK and DCAM are useful checklists, not substitutes for enforcement.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a minimal catalog of five datasets you work with, listing owner,
>    steward, classification, and retention; note how many fields you cannot
>    fill in.
> 2. Write three executable governance rules for your environment and run them
>    over that catalog.
> 3. Compute the downstream blast radius of your least-governed dataset.
> 4. Draft a one-page exception process: who approves, for how long, and what
>    triggers a review.
> 5. Interview: Your company has a 40-page data governance policy and
>    persistent data quality problems. What do you change first? (Hint: think
>    about which of the three properties of effective governance the policy is
>    missing, and what the smallest enforceable version would be.)


#### Data Lineage and Cataloging

Every data organisation eventually faces the same four questions, and none of
them can be answered from code alone:

- *Where did this number come from?* (a dashboard figure someone disputes)
- *What breaks if I change this column?* (before you ship a schema change)
- *Where does this person's data live?* (a deletion request arrives)
- *Who is using this table?* (you want to deprecate it)

**Lineage** is the graph that answers them: nodes are datasets, tables, or
columns, and edges record derivation. A **catalog** is lineage plus metadata --
descriptions, owners, classifications, freshness, quality test results, usage
statistics -- made searchable.

The distinction that matters most in practice is granularity. **Table-level**
lineage is easy to capture and answers the coarse questions. **Column-level**
lineage is much harder and is what you need for deletion propagation, impact
analysis, and finding out that a "de-identified" feature was derived from an
email address.

```text
  TABLE-LEVEL                        COLUMN-LEVEL
  raw_signup -> profile -> feat      raw_signup.email -> profile.user_key
      -> churn_model                     -> feat.avg_session
                                     raw_signup.country -> profile.region
  "the model depends on signup"          -> feat.region_onehot
                                     "the model depends on country, not on
                                      email, except through the join key"
```

```python
import textwrap
EDGES = {                      # node -> the nodes it is derived FROM
  "raw_signup.email":        [],
  "raw_signup.country":      [],
  "raw_signup.signup_ts":    [],
  "events.user_key":         ["raw_signup.email"],
  "events.session_len":      [],
  "profile.user_key":        ["raw_signup.email"],
  "profile.tenure_days":     ["raw_signup.signup_ts"],
  "profile.region":          ["raw_signup.country"],
  "feat.tenure_bucket":      ["profile.tenure_days"],
  "feat.avg_session":        ["events.session_len", "events.user_key"],
  "feat.region_onehot":      ["profile.region"],
  "churn_model.score":       ["feat.tenure_bucket", "feat.avg_session",
                              "feat.region_onehot"],
  "dash.churn_by_region":    ["churn_model.score", "profile.region"],
  "campaign.target_list":    ["churn_model.score"],
}
CHILD = {}
for n, ups in EDGES.items():
    for u in ups: CHILD.setdefault(u, []).append(n)

def walk(start, graph):                       # transitive closure, either way
    seen, stack = set(), list(graph.get(start, []))
    while stack:
        n = stack.pop()
        if n in seen: continue
        seen.add(n); stack += graph.get(n, [])
    return sorted(seen)

def show(label, items):
    for i, line in enumerate(textwrap.wrap(", ".join(items), 48)):
        print(f"  {label if i == 0 else '':24}{'<- ' if i == 0 else '   '}{line}")

print("1. UPSTREAM: WHERE DID THIS NUMBER COME FROM?")
for n in ("churn_model.score", "campaign.target_list"):
    show(n, walk(n, EDGES))

print("\n2. DOWNSTREAM: WHAT BREAKS IF I CHANGE THIS COLUMN?")
print(f"  {'column':26}{'blast radius':>14}  affected")
for n in ("raw_signup.email", "raw_signup.country", "events.session_len",
          "profile.tenure_days"):
    d = walk(n, CHILD)
    print(f"  {n:26}{len(d):14}  "
          f"{', '.join(dict.fromkeys(x.split('.')[0] for x in d))}")

print("\n3. PROPAGATION: A DELETION REQUEST TOUCHES EVERY DERIVED ASSET")
touched = {"raw_signup.email"} | set(walk("raw_signup.email", CHILD))
print(f"  erasing one subject's email must be reflected in "
      f"{len(touched)} assets:")
for t in sorted(touched): print(f"    {t}")

print("\n4. ORPHANS AND DEAD ENDS: WHAT THE CATALOG SHOULD FLAG")
roots = [n for n, u in EDGES.items() if not u]
leaves = [n for n in EDGES if n not in CHILD]
no_consumer = [n for n in leaves if not n.startswith(("dash.", "campaign."))]
print(f"  source columns (no upstream):   {len(roots)}")
print(f"  terminal columns (no consumer): {len(leaves)}")
print(f"  computed but never consumed:    {no_consumer}")
```

```text
1. UPSTREAM: WHERE DID THIS NUMBER COME FROM?
  churn_model.score       <- events.session_len, events.user_key,
                             feat.avg_session, feat.region_onehot,
                             feat.tenure_bucket, profile.region,
                             profile.tenure_days, raw_signup.country,
                             raw_signup.email, raw_signup.signup_ts
  campaign.target_list    <- churn_model.score, events.session_len,
                             events.user_key, feat.avg_session,
                             feat.region_onehot, feat.tenure_bucket,
                             profile.region, profile.tenure_days,
                             raw_signup.country, raw_signup.email,
                             raw_signup.signup_ts

2. DOWNSTREAM: WHAT BREAKS IF I CHANGE THIS COLUMN?
  column                      blast radius  affected
  raw_signup.email                       6  campaign, churn_model, dash, events, feat, profile
  raw_signup.country                     5  campaign, churn_model, dash, feat, profile
  events.session_len                     4  campaign, churn_model, dash, feat
  profile.tenure_days                    4  campaign, churn_model, dash, feat

3. PROPAGATION: A DELETION REQUEST TOUCHES EVERY DERIVED ASSET
  erasing one subject's email must be reflected in 7 assets:
    campaign.target_list
    churn_model.score
    dash.churn_by_region
    events.user_key
    feat.avg_session
    profile.user_key
    raw_signup.email

4. ORPHANS AND DEAD ENDS: WHAT THE CATALOG SHOULD FLAG
  source columns (no upstream):   4
  terminal columns (no consumer): 3
  computed but never consumed:    ['profile.user_key']
```

The third query is the one that turns lineage from a nice-to-have into a
compliance requirement. A single deletion request reaches seven assets, and two
of them -- `churn_model.score` and `dash.churn_by_region` -- are *derived*
artifacts where deletion is not obvious. Does a trained model "contain" the
deleted person's data? That is a real and unsettled question, and the only
defensible position is a documented decision: either the model is retrained on
a schedule that bounds how long any record influences it, or you have a written
argument that the model output is not personal data. Both are acceptable;
having neither is not.

The fourth query illustrates the catalog's quieter value: `profile.user_key` is
computed and consumed by nothing. Either it is dead code costing money, or it is
an undocumented export somebody is reading outside the graph you modelled. Both
are findings.

How lineage actually gets captured, in rough order of reliability:

| Method | Coverage | Effort |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Query log parsing (warehouse) | Automatic, table and often column level | Low; the best default |
| Transformation-tool metadata (dbt, Spark plans, orchestrator) | Very good within the tool | Low if you already use it |
| Runtime instrumentation of jobs | Broad, including non-SQL | Moderate |
| Manual declaration | Whatever people remember | High, decays immediately |

**Prefer automatic capture and treat manual declaration as a gap-filler.** A
hand-maintained lineage diagram is out of date the week it is drawn, and --
worse -- it is believed.

Two final practices that make a catalog used rather than merely built. Make it
**searchable from where people work** (an IDE or notebook extension, a slash
command, a warehouse UI) because a catalog nobody opens documents nothing. And
**surface freshness and quality state on the asset itself**, so the person about
to use a table sees that its tests last failed yesterday.

> Key Takeaways
> - Lineage is the derivation graph that answers where a number came from, what
>   a change breaks, where a person's data lives, and who uses a table.
> - A catalog is lineage plus searchable metadata: owners, classifications,
>   freshness, quality results, and usage.
> - Column-level lineage is what deletion propagation and real impact analysis
>   require; table-level is only a start.
> - A deletion request reaches every derived asset, including models and
>   aggregates, and each needs a documented decision about what deletion means.
> - Assets computed but never consumed are either dead cost or undocumented
>   exports; both are findings.
> - Capture lineage automatically from query logs and transformation tooling;
>   manual diagrams decay immediately and are trusted anyway.
> - Combine lineage with governance metadata so risk can be ranked by blast
>   radius rather than by dataset.
> - Put the catalog where people already work and show freshness and quality on
>   the asset itself.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Build a column-level lineage graph for one pipeline you own and compute
>    the blast radius of each source column.
> 2. Trace one personal data field to every downstream asset and write what
>    deletion means for each.
> 3. Find an asset in your environment with no downstream consumer and
>    determine whether it can be removed.
> 4. Extract lineage automatically from your warehouse's query log for one day
>    and compare it with what you believed the dependencies were.
> 5. Interview: A dashboard number disagrees with a finance report. How does
>    lineage help, and what does it not tell you? (Hint: it shows the two
>    derivation paths but not which definition is correct -- think about what
>    other metadata you need.)


#### Regulatory Landscape: GDPR and Beyond

Regulation is a design constraint, not an afterthought, and the reason is
structural: several of the rules restrict things that are easy to change before
you collect data and nearly impossible afterwards. If you gather data without a
lawful basis, no amount of later engineering makes the resulting model lawful.

The **GDPR** is the reference framework because most later laws borrow from it.
Its core mechanics, in the order they bind you:

**You need a lawful basis** for every processing purpose, chosen *before*
processing and recorded. There are six, and they are not ranked -- but they have
very different consequences:

| Basis | When it applies | Consequence for data science |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Consent | Freely given, specific, informed, withdrawable | Must be withdrawable, which means data must be removable |
| Contract | Necessary to deliver what the person signed up for | Narrow: "necessary", not "useful" |
| Legal obligation | A law requires it | Often overrides erasure requests |
| Vital interests | Life-or-death | Rare |
| Public task | Public authority functions | Public sector |
| Legitimate interests | Your interest, balanced against their rights | Needs a documented balancing test; the usual basis for analytics |

**Special category data** -- health, race, ethnicity, political opinions,
religion, trade union membership, genetics, biometrics, sex life, sexual
orientation -- is prohibited by default and requires a specific additional
condition, usually explicit consent. Note the trap: **a model that infers a
special category creates special category data**, whether or not you collected
it.

**Data subjects have rights** with a one-month statutory deadline: access,
rectification, erasure, restriction, portability, objection, and rights
concerning automated decision-making.

**Article 22** restricts decisions based *solely* on automated processing that
have legal or similarly significant effects. Where it applies, you need an
explicit basis, must provide meaningful information about the logic involved,
and must offer human review.

Beyond the GDPR, the landscape a global model operates in:

| Regime | Scope | The thing that most often surprises teams |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GDPR (EU/EEA) | Personal data of people in the EU | Applies extraterritorially; fines up to 4% of global turnover |
| UK GDPR / DPA 2018 | Same structure, separate regulator | Divergence is growing |
| CCPA/CPRA (California) | Consumers of qualifying businesses | Opt-out of "sale/sharing"; broad definition of sharing |
| EU AI Act | AI systems by risk tier | Obligations attach to the *use case*, with bans and high-risk duties |
| HIPAA (US health) | Protected health information by covered entities | De-identification has a specified standard (Safe Harbor or expert determination) |
| ECOA / Reg B, FCRA (US credit) | Credit decisions | Adverse action notices must give specific principal reasons |
| Illinois BIPA | Biometric identifiers | Private right of action; written consent before collection |
| Brazil LGPD, India DPDP, China PIPL | National regimes | PIPL adds data localisation and export approval |

```python
import datetime as dt
TODAY = dt.date(2026, 9, 28)
DEADLINE_DAYS = 30                      # GDPR Art. 12(3): one month

REQUESTS = [
    dict(id="DSR-101", kind="access",      received=dt.date(2026, 9, 5),
         verified=True,  note=""),
    dict(id="DSR-102", kind="erasure",     received=dt.date(2026, 8, 20),
         verified=True,  note="tax records retained 7y (legal obligation)"),
    dict(id="DSR-103", kind="portability", received=dt.date(2026, 9, 20),
         verified=False, note="identity not yet verified; clock paused"),
    dict(id="DSR-104", kind="objection",   received=dt.date(2026, 6, 30),
         verified=True,  note="no response sent"),
]
print("1. DATA SUBJECT REQUESTS AGAINST THE STATUTORY CLOCK")
print(f"  {'id':9}{'type':13}{'day':>5}{'days left':>11}{'state':>16}  note")
for r in REQUESTS:
    age = (TODAY - r["received"]).days
    left = DEADLINE_DAYS - age
    if not r["verified"]:                       state = "on hold"
    elif r["note"] and "retained" in r["note"]: state = "partial refuse"
    elif left < 0:                              state = "BREACH"
    elif left <= 7:                             state = "urgent"
    else:                                       state = "in progress"
    print(f"  {r['id']:9}{r['kind']:13}{age:5}{left:11}{state:>16}  {r['note']}")

print("\n2. IS EACH PROCESSING ACTIVITY LAWFUL? (a minimal ROPA check)")
BASES = {"consent", "contract", "legal_obligation", "vital_interests",
         "public_task", "legitimate_interests"}
ROPA = [
    dict(purpose="billing",             basis="contract",
         special=False, dpia=False, transfer=None, retention=2555),
    dict(purpose="churn_model",         basis="legitimate_interests",
         special=False, dpia=True,  transfer=None, retention=730),
    dict(purpose="ad_targeting",        basis="legitimate_interests",
         special=False, dpia=False, transfer="US", retention=1095),
    dict(purpose="health_risk_score",   basis="consent",
         special=True,  dpia=False, transfer=None, retention=365),
    dict(purpose="employee_monitoring", basis=None,
         special=False, dpia=False, transfer="IN", retention=None),
]
ADEQUATE = {"CH", "JP", "KR", "UK", "CA"}      # illustrative adequacy list
print(f"  {'purpose':22}{'findings':>10}  detail")
for p in ROPA:
    f = []
    if p["basis"] not in BASES:                   f.append("no lawful basis")
    if p["basis"] == "legitimate_interests" and not p["dpia"]:
        f.append("LIA/DPIA missing")
    if p["special"] and p["basis"] != "consent":  f.append("Art.9 basis wrong")
    if p["special"] and not p["dpia"]:            f.append("DPIA required")
    if p["transfer"] and p["transfer"] not in ADEQUATE:
        f.append(f"transfer to {p['transfer']} needs SCCs + TIA")
    if p["retention"] is None:                    f.append("no retention limit")
    elif p["retention"] > 2000 and p["purpose"] != "billing":
        f.append("retention looks excessive")
    print(f"  {p['purpose']:22}{len(f):10}  {'; '.join(f) if f else 'ok'}")

print("\n3. AUTOMATED DECISION-MAKING: DOES ARTICLE 22 APPLY?")
SYSTEMS = [
    dict(name="churn score -> email", solely_automated=True,  legal_effect=False),
    dict(name="credit decline",       solely_automated=True,  legal_effect=True),
    dict(name="fraud hold + review",  solely_automated=False, legal_effect=True),
    dict(name="CV shortlisting",      solely_automated=True,  legal_effect=True),
]
print(f"  {'system':26}{'Art.22?':>9}  obligation")
for s in SYSTEMS:
    applies = s["solely_automated"] and s["legal_effect"]
    duty = ("explicit basis + logic disclosed + human review"
            if applies else
            "transparency only" if not s["legal_effect"]
            else "human step must be genuine, not a rubber stamp")
    print(f"  {s['name']:26}{'YES' if applies else 'no':>9}  {duty}")
```

```text
1. DATA SUBJECT REQUESTS AGAINST THE STATUTORY CLOCK
  id       type           day  days left           state  note
  DSR-101  access          23          7          urgent  
  DSR-102  erasure         39         -9  partial refuse  tax records retained 7y (legal obligation)
  DSR-103  portability      8         22         on hold  identity not yet verified; clock paused
  DSR-104  objection       90        -60          BREACH  no response sent

2. IS EACH PROCESSING ACTIVITY LAWFUL? (a minimal ROPA check)
  purpose                 findings  detail
  billing                        0  ok
  churn_model                    0  ok
  ad_targeting                   2  LIA/DPIA missing; transfer to US needs SCCs + TIA
  health_risk_score              1  DPIA required
  employee_monitoring            3  no lawful basis; transfer to IN needs SCCs + TIA; no retention limit

3. AUTOMATED DECISION-MAKING: DOES ARTICLE 22 APPLY?
  system                      Art.22?  obligation
  churn score -> email             no  transparency only
  credit decline                  YES  explicit basis + logic disclosed + human review
  fraud hold + review              no  human step must be genuine, not a rubber stamp
  CV shortlisting                 YES  explicit basis + logic disclosed + human review
```

Three observations that translate the law into engineering work.

**The clock is real and it starts on receipt.** DSR-104 is 90 days old with no
response: that is a regulatory breach independent of whether the underlying
request was reasonable. Request handling must be a tracked workflow with a
timer, not an inbox. Note also that DSR-102 is a legitimate *partial* refusal --
erasure yields to a legal retention obligation for the tax records, but the
other 88 records must still be deleted, and the refusal must be explained.

**The records of processing double as a compliance test.** The ROPA check flags
what an auditor would: analytics relying on legitimate interests with no
balancing assessment, a special-category model with no DPIA, and a transfer to a
country without an adequacy decision needing standard contractual clauses plus a
transfer impact assessment. All of these are answerable before a model exists.

**Article 22 hinges on two words: "solely" and "significant".** The fraud case
escapes it because a human reviews the hold -- but only if that review is
genuine. A human who approves 3,000 automated decisions an hour is not
meaningful involvement, and regulators have said so. If you build the human
step, you must give the human the information and the time to actually use it.

Two further instruments to know by name. A **DPIA** (data protection impact
assessment) is mandatory for high-risk processing -- large-scale profiling,
special category data, systematic monitoring -- and is the natural place to put
your fairness and privacy analysis. **Privacy by design and by default** is a
legal requirement, not a slogan: the default configuration must be the private
one.

A closing caution, which is also a professional boundary: this is a map, not
legal advice. Your job is to recognise when a modelling choice has legal
consequences and to bring it to someone qualified *early*, when the choice is
still cheap.

> Key Takeaways
> - Every processing purpose needs a lawful basis chosen and recorded before
>   processing begins; retrofitting one is not possible.
> - Consent must be withdrawable, which means the architecture must support
>   removing a person's data and its downstream effects.
> - Legitimate interests is the usual basis for analytics and requires a
>   documented balancing assessment.
> - Special category data is prohibited by default, and a model that *infers* a
>   special category creates it.
> - Data subject rights carry a one-month deadline from receipt; handle them as
>   a tracked workflow with a timer, and explain partial refusals.
> - Article 22 applies to solely automated decisions with significant effects; a
>   rubber-stamp human review does not remove it.
> - DPIAs are mandatory for high-risk processing and are the right place for
>   fairness and privacy analysis.
> - Cross-border transfers need an adequacy decision or safeguards such as SCCs
>   plus a transfer impact assessment.
> - Recognise legal consequences early and escalate; this is not legal advice.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Write the records of processing for one system you work on: purposes,
>    lawful bases, categories of data, retention, recipients, and transfers.
> 2. Determine whether Article 22 applies to a decision system you know, and
>    justify your answer on both "solely" and "significant".
> 3. Implement the data subject request workflow with a deadline timer and a
>    state for identity verification.
> 4. Identify one feature in a model of yours that could function as a proxy for
>    a special category, and state how you would test that.
> 5. Interview: Your team wants to fine-tune a model on support chat
>    transcripts. What do you check before starting? (Hint: work through
>    purpose, lawful basis, what might be inside free text, where the compute
>    runs, and what happens when someone asks to be deleted.)


#### Consent and Data Ownership

Consent looks like the simplest lawful basis and is in practice the most
demanding, because it creates an ongoing obligation that has to be respected at
*every* moment of use, not just at collection.

Valid consent under the GDPR has four properties, each with a concrete
engineering consequence:

| Property | What it means | What you must build |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Freely given** | No penalty for refusing; not bundled with service access | Separate toggles; the product must work without the optional ones |
| **Specific** | Per purpose, not a blanket "we use your data" | A purpose taxonomy, and consent stored per purpose |
| **Informed** | Plain language, before collection | Versioned notices, with the version recorded alongside the consent |
| **Withdrawable** | As easy to withdraw as to give, at any time | Withdrawal propagating to every downstream use, including models |

The consequence people underestimate: **consent is a time-varying state, not a
flag.** The question is never "did this user consent?" but "was this user
consented *for this purpose* at the moment I used their data?" That requires an
append-only ledger of grant and withdrawal events, not a boolean column.

```python
import numpy as np, datetime as dt
rng = np.random.default_rng(31)
TODAY = dt.date(2026, 9, 28)
N = 5000
PURPOSES = ["service", "analytics", "personalisation", "marketing",
            "third_party_sharing"]
GRANT_P  = [1.00,      0.72,        0.55,              0.38,       0.11]
ledger = []
for uid in range(N):
    signup = TODAY - dt.timedelta(days=int(rng.integers(30, 900)))
    for p, pr in zip(PURPOSES, GRANT_P):
        if rng.random() < pr:
            ledger.append((uid, p, "grant", signup))
            if rng.random() < 0.12:                    # some later withdraw
                d = signup + dt.timedelta(days=int(rng.integers(1, 800)))
                if d <= TODAY: ledger.append((uid, p, "withdraw", d))

def consent_at(events, when):
    """Latest event at or before `when` decides. Absence means NO consent."""
    state = False
    for kind, d in sorted(events, key=lambda t: t[1]):
        if d <= when: state = (kind == "grant")
    return state

index = {}
for uid, p, kind, d in ledger:
    index.setdefault((uid, p), []).append((kind, d))

print("1. HOW MUCH OF THE POPULATION MAY YOU ACTUALLY USE, PER PURPOSE?")
print(f"  {'purpose':22}{'granted ever':>14}{'valid today':>13}{'withdrawn':>11}")
for p in PURPOSES:
    ever = sum(1 for (u, pp) in index if pp == p)
    now = sum(1 for (u, pp), ev in index.items()
              if pp == p and consent_at(ev, TODAY))
    print(f"  {p:22}{ever/N:13.1%}{now/N:13.1%}{(ever-now)/N:11.1%}")

print("\n2. CONSENT IS EVALUATED AT THE TIME OF USE, NOT AT TRAINING TIME")
train_day = TODAY - dt.timedelta(days=180)
p = "personalisation"
cohort = {u for (u, pp), ev in index.items()
          if pp == p and consent_at(ev, train_day)}    # the training cohort
still = {u for u in cohort if consent_at(index[(u, p)], TODAY)}
print(f"  rows in the training cohort for '{p}': {len(cohort)}")
print(f"  of those, still consented today:                 {len(still)}")
print(f"  became unusable but remain inside the model:     {len(cohort-still)}")

print("\n3. THE COST OF PURPOSE LIMITATION ON A MODELLING DATASET")
print(f"  {'required purposes':56}{'usable rows':>13}{'share':>8}")
combos = [("service", ["service"]),
          ("service + analytics", ["service", "analytics"]),
          ("service + analytics + personalisation",
           ["service", "analytics", "personalisation"]),
          ("service + analytics + marketing",
           ["service", "analytics", "marketing"]),
          ("all five purposes", PURPOSES)]
for lab, c in combos:
    ok = sum(1 for uid in range(N)
             if all(consent_at(index.get((uid, p), []), TODAY) for p in c))
    print(f"  {lab:56}{ok:13}{ok/N:8.1%}")
```

```text
1. HOW MUCH OF THE POPULATION MAY YOU ACTUALLY USE, PER PURPOSE?
  purpose                 granted ever  valid today  withdrawn
  service                      100.0%        93.8%       6.2%
  analytics                     72.8%        67.8%       5.0%
  personalisation               55.1%        51.1%       4.1%
  marketing                     37.9%        34.9%       3.0%
  third_party_sharing           10.9%        10.3%       0.7%

2. CONSENT IS EVALUATED AT THE TIME OF USE, NOT AT TRAINING TIME
  rows in the training cohort for 'personalisation': 2194
  of those, still consented today:                 2124
  became unusable but remain inside the model:     70

3. THE COST OF PURPOSE LIMITATION ON A MODELLING DATASET
  required purposes                                         usable rows   share
  service                                                          4690   93.8%
  service + analytics                                              3187   63.7%
  service + analytics + personalisation                            1628   32.6%
  service + analytics + marketing                                  1074   21.5%
  all five purposes                                                  58    1.2%
```

Three consequences for how you plan a project.

**Consent rates are not 100% and they compound.** Requiring analytics consent
alone leaves 63.7% of the population; requiring four purposes leaves 21.5%; all
five leaves 1.2%. A model specified over a feature set that spans many purposes
quietly becomes a model of a tiny, self-selected subset -- which is also a
*sampling bias* problem, connecting directly back to section 16.2. **Design the
feature set around the consent you have, or go and ask for more, but do not
discover the shrinkage after building.**

**Withdrawal reaches into trained models.** Seventy people in the training
cohort have since withdrawn, and their influence remains in the model's
parameters until it is retrained. The workable answers are: retrain on a
schedule short enough to bound the exposure and say so in the notice; exclude
withdrawn users at scoring time as an immediate measure; and use machine
unlearning techniques where the stakes justify them. Doing nothing is a
position you would have to defend.

**The ledger must be queryable at the moment of use.** A pipeline should join
against the consent state *as of the processing timestamp*, and that join should
be in shared, reviewed code -- not reimplemented per project, where the first
mistake is silently using today's consent to justify a computation over last
year's data.

On **ownership**, a clarification that prevents a great deal of confused
discussion: in most legal systems, data is not property, and nobody "owns" it in
the way one owns a chair. What exists instead is a bundle of specific rights and
obligations:

| Actor | Role | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Data subject | The person the data is about | Rights: access, erasure, portability, objection |
| Controller | Decides why and how data is processed | The obligations; liability |
| Processor | Processes on the controller's instructions | Contractual duties, breach notification |
| Joint controllers | Decide together | Must allocate responsibilities in an arrangement |

Treating this as ownership leads to bad conclusions in both directions -- "the
user owns their data so they can demand anything" and "we collected it so we can
do anything with it". The accurate framing is stewardship: you hold data under
obligations, for declared purposes, for a limited time.

This also determines what happens with third parties. If you send data to a
vendor, you are the controller and they are usually the processor, which needs a
data processing agreement, a documented purpose, and a deletion commitment.
Sending customer records to an external model provider is exactly this
relationship.

> Key Takeaways
> - Valid consent is freely given, specific, informed, and withdrawable, and
>   each property maps to something you must build.
> - Consent is a time-varying state; store an append-only ledger of grants and
>   withdrawals per purpose, not a boolean.
> - Evaluate consent as of the moment of use, and keep that join in shared,
>   reviewed code.
> - Consent rates compound across purposes: requiring several purposes can
>   reduce a usable population to a small, self-selected fraction.
> - Population shrinkage from consent is also a sampling bias problem, so it
>   affects model validity, not just legality.
> - Withdrawal reaches trained models; bound the exposure with scheduled
>   retraining, exclude withdrawn users at scoring time, and document the
>   approach.
> - Nobody "owns" personal data; there are data subjects with rights and
>   controllers and processors with obligations.
> - Sending data to a vendor or an external model API creates a
>   controller-processor relationship needing an agreement and a deletion
>   commitment.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Design a consent ledger schema and write the query that returns whether a
>    user was consented for a purpose as of an arbitrary timestamp.
> 2. For a model you work on, list the purposes its features require and compute
>    the usable population under each combination.
> 3. Write the procedure for handling a withdrawal: what changes immediately,
>    what changes at the next retrain, and what you would tell the user.
> 4. Audit one pipeline for whether it filters on consent at all, and at which
>    timestamp.
> 5. Interview: Marketing wants to reuse churn model features for an
>    advertising campaign. What do you check? (Hint: think about the purpose the
>    data was collected under, and what fraction of the population would remain
>    if you filtered correctly.)


#### Responsible AI Principles

Nearly every organisation now publishes a set of AI principles: fairness,
transparency, accountability, privacy, safety, human oversight. They are almost
identical everywhere, they are almost always correct, and on their own they
change nothing. The reason is that a principle is a *statement of intent* and an
engineering organisation runs on *controls* -- things that happen automatically,
block something, or page someone.

The useful skill is therefore translation, in both directions: turning a
principle into a control, and recognising when a proposed control does not
actually serve the principle it is filed under.

Two things make that translation tractable. First, **obligations should scale
with risk**, which is the structure of the EU AI Act: a tier determined by the
*use case* rather than the algorithm. Second, **documentation should be a
structured artifact the pipeline can check**, which is what model cards are for.

```text
  RISK TIERS AND WHAT THEY ATTACH TO

  prohibited   social scoring, manipulative techniques, some biometric
               categorisation, emotion inference at work or school
  high         employment, credit, education, essential services, law
               enforcement, medical devices, critical infrastructure
  limited      systems interacting with people, deepfakes, chatbots
               -> transparency obligations
  minimal      spam filters, recommenders, forecasting -> voluntary codes

  The SAME model architecture sits in three different tiers depending on
  what decision it feeds.
```

```python
SYSTEMS = [
  dict(name="product recommender",   domain="retail",     affects_rights=False,
       safety_critical=False, human_in_loop=True,  vulnerable=False),
  dict(name="CV screening",          domain="employment", affects_rights=True,
       safety_critical=False, human_in_loop=False, vulnerable=False),
  dict(name="credit scoring",        domain="finance",    affects_rights=True,
       safety_critical=False, human_in_loop=True,  vulnerable=False),
  dict(name="sepsis early warning",  domain="health",     affects_rights=True,
       safety_critical=True,  human_in_loop=True,  vulnerable=True),
  dict(name="emotion inference at work", domain="employment",
       affects_rights=True, safety_critical=False, human_in_loop=False,
       vulnerable=True),
  dict(name="warehouse demand forecast", domain="logistics",
       affects_rights=False, safety_critical=False, human_in_loop=True,
       vulnerable=False),
]
BANNED = {("employment", "emotion inference at work")}
HIGH_RISK_DOMAINS = {"employment", "finance", "health", "education",
                     "law_enforcement", "essential_services"}

def tier(s):
    if (s["domain"], s["name"]) in BANNED:                 return "prohibited"
    if s["safety_critical"] or (s["affects_rights"]
                                and s["domain"] in HIGH_RISK_DOMAINS):
        return "high"
    if s["affects_rights"]:                                return "limited"
    return "minimal"

DUTIES = {
  "prohibited": "do not build; escalate",
  "high":       "risk mgmt, logging, oversight, conformity assmt",
  "limited":    "transparency to users, documentation, monitoring",
  "minimal":    "voluntary codes; normal engineering practice",
}
print("RISK TIER AND WHAT IT OBLIGES")
print(f"  {'system':28}{'tier':>12}  obligations")
for s in SYSTEMS:
    print(f"  {s['name']:28}{tier(s):>12}  {DUTIES[tier(s)]}")

print("\n2. A MODEL CARD IS A STRUCTURED ARTIFACT, NOT A README")
REQUIRED = ["intended_use", "out_of_scope_use", "training_data",
            "evaluation_data", "metrics_overall", "metrics_by_subgroup",
            "known_limitations", "ethical_considerations", "owner",
            "version", "review_date", "fairness_assessment"]
cards = {
  "churn_v3": {"intended_use": 1, "out_of_scope_use": 1, "training_data": 1,
               "evaluation_data": 1, "metrics_overall": 1, "owner": 1,
               "version": 1, "review_date": 1},
  "credit_v7": {k: 1 for k in REQUIRED},
  "resume_rank_v1": {"intended_use": 1, "metrics_overall": 1, "owner": 1},
}
print(f"  {'model':18}{'completeness':>14}  missing")
for name, card in cards.items():
    missing = [k for k in REQUIRED if k not in card]
    detail = ', '.join(missing[:4]) + (' ...' if len(missing) > 4 else '')
    print(f"  {name:18}{1-len(missing)/len(REQUIRED):13.0%}  "
          f"{detail or 'none'}")

print("\n3. FROM PRINCIPLE TO CONTROL: THE ONLY TRANSLATION THAT MATTERS")
MAP = [
  ("fairness",       "subgroup metrics with CIs in CI; block on regression"),
  ("transparency",   "model card required by the deploy pipeline"),
  ("accountability", "named owner in the registry; on-call rotation"),
  ("privacy",        "column classification + retention job + access logs"),
  ("robustness",     "drift monitors, adversarial test suite, rollback drill"),
  ("human oversight","appeal route with an SLA and a reviewer who can override"),
  ("contestability", "reason codes generated per decision and stored"),
]
for pr, control in MAP:
    print(f"  {pr:17} -> {control}")
```

```text
RISK TIER AND WHAT IT OBLIGES
  system                              tier  obligations
  product recommender              minimal  voluntary codes; normal engineering practice
  CV screening                        high  risk mgmt, logging, oversight, conformity assmt
  credit scoring                      high  risk mgmt, logging, oversight, conformity assmt
  sepsis early warning                high  risk mgmt, logging, oversight, conformity assmt
  emotion inference at work     prohibited  do not build; escalate
  warehouse demand forecast        minimal  voluntary codes; normal engineering practice

2. A MODEL CARD IS A STRUCTURED ARTIFACT, NOT A README
  model               completeness  missing
  churn_v3                    67%  metrics_by_subgroup, known_limitations, ethical_considerations, fairness_assessment
  credit_v7                  100%  none
  resume_rank_v1              25%  out_of_scope_use, training_data, evaluation_data, metrics_by_subgroup ...

3. FROM PRINCIPLE TO CONTROL: THE ONLY TRANSLATION THAT MATTERS
  fairness          -> subgroup metrics with CIs in CI; block on regression
  transparency      -> model card required by the deploy pipeline
  accountability    -> named owner in the registry; on-call rotation
  privacy           -> column classification + retention job + access logs
  robustness        -> drift monitors, adversarial test suite, rollback drill
  human oversight   -> appeal route with an SLA and a reviewer who can override
  contestability    -> reason codes generated per decision and stored
```

The tiering table makes the key conceptual point: **the same model is in
different tiers depending on what it decides.** A gradient boosting model
forecasting warehouse demand is minimal risk; the identical algorithm ranking
job applicants is high risk. Risk is a property of the deployment, which is why
model governance must be attached to *use cases*, and why "we already approved
this model" is not an answer when someone repurposes it.

The model card table is what converts documentation from good intentions into a
gate. Three fields are the ones that are almost always missing and almost always
matter most: **out-of-scope use** (the explicit list of things this model must
not be used for, which is your only defence against repurposing),
**metrics by subgroup** (without which no fairness claim is possible), and
**known limitations** (which is where the honest caveats live). Note the pattern
in the output: the credit model, which is regulated, is complete; the résumé
ranker, which is the highest-risk system in the list, is 25% complete. That
inversion is extremely common, because regulation forces documentation and
internal tools do not.

The third block is the discipline to internalise. For each principle, write the
control, then ask three questions: *what does it block?*, *who is paged when it
fires?*, and *how would I know if it silently stopped working?* A principle with
no answer to those is decoration.

Finally, three governance structures that make the controls stick:

1. **A model registry as the single source of truth** -- every production model
   with its owner, version, card, risk tier, and approval state. If a model can
   reach production without an entry, the registry is documentation, not a
   control.
2. **A review gate proportional to tier.** Minimal-risk models pass on automated
   checks; high-risk models require documented sign-off from someone who is not
   the author, plus fairness and privacy assessments.
3. **An incident and appeal path with a service level.** People affected by
   decisions need a route to contest them, and the organisation needs a record
   of the outcomes -- which is also the dataset that tells you where the model
   is wrong.

> Key Takeaways
> - Responsible AI principles are nearly identical everywhere and change nothing
>   until they become controls that block, alert, or require sign-off.
> - Obligations should scale with risk, and risk is a property of the use case,
>   not the algorithm: the same model can be minimal or high risk.
> - Approval must be per use case, so repurposing an approved model requires a
>   new assessment.
> - Model cards are structured artifacts whose completeness can be checked by
>   the deploy pipeline.
> - The most commonly missing and most valuable card fields are out-of-scope
>   use, subgroup metrics, and known limitations.
> - Regulated systems tend to be well documented and internal tools poorly
>   documented, which inverts the actual risk ordering.
> - For every control, know what it blocks, who is paged, and how you would
>   detect that it stopped working.
> - A model registry, tier-proportional review gates, and an appeal path with an
>   SLA are what make the rest durable.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Assign a risk tier to three systems you work on, justifying each from the
>    decision it feeds rather than the model type.
> 2. Write a model card for one of your models and mark every field you cannot
>    complete honestly.
> 3. Add a CI check that fails a deployment when a required model card field is
>    missing.
> 4. Take two of your organisation's published AI principles and write the
>    control, the owner, and the alert for each.
> 5. Interview: An internal tool built for triage is being used to make final
>    decisions. How did that happen and what do you do? (Hint: think about what
>    the original approval covered, and which single model card field would have
>    made the change visible.)


#### Research Ethics and IRB Considerations

Most data science is not research on human subjects, and some of it is -- and the
boundary is not where practitioners usually assume. If you are running an
experiment on people to produce generalisable knowledge, you are doing human
subjects research, whether it happens in a university or in a product A/B
testing framework.

The framework in use worldwide descends from the **Belmont Report**, written
after a series of abuses in medical research. Its three principles map cleanly
onto data work:

| Principle | Means | In a data science project |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Respect for persons** | Autonomy; informed consent; extra protection for those with diminished autonomy | Meaningful consent for the actual use; extra care with children, patients, employees, prisoners |
| **Beneficence** | Maximise benefit, minimise harm; the risk must be justified | A written risk analysis, a stopping rule, and an honest account of who benefits |
| **Justice** | Fair distribution of burdens and benefits | Do not experiment on the vulnerable while benefiting others; connect directly to section 16.2 |

An **IRB** (institutional review board, or research ethics committee) reviews
protocols against these before the work begins. Three routes exist, and
determining which applies is a screening question, not a judgement call:

```text
  is it human subjects research?   (living individuals AND
        |                            intervention/interaction OR
        |                            identifiable private information)
        no -> out of scope / exempt
        yes
        |
  minimal risk, no vulnerable group, no deception?
        yes -> expedited review (single reviewer)
        no  -> full board review (convened committee)
```

```python
STUDIES = [
  dict(name="public corpus, aggregate stats only",
       identifiable=False, interaction=False, intervention=False,
       sensitive=False, vulnerable=False, deception=False, minimal_risk=True),
  dict(name="survey of our own employees",
       identifiable=True,  interaction=True,  intervention=False,
       sensitive=False, vulnerable=True,  deception=False, minimal_risk=True),
  dict(name="newsfeed mood manipulation A/B test",
       identifiable=True,  interaction=False, intervention=True,
       sensitive=True,  vulnerable=False, deception=True,  minimal_risk=False),
  dict(name="retrospective de-identified chart review",
       identifiable=False, interaction=False, intervention=False,
       sensitive=True,  vulnerable=False, deception=False, minimal_risk=True),
  dict(name="wearable trial, paediatric clinic",
       identifiable=True,  interaction=True,  intervention=True,
       sensitive=True,  vulnerable=True,  deception=False, minimal_risk=False),
]

def route(s):
    """Human subjects research = living individuals, plus interaction or
    identifiable private information. Everything else is out of scope."""
    if not s["identifiable"] and not s["interaction"] and not s["intervention"]:
        return "exempt / not human subjects"
    if not s["minimal_risk"] or s["vulnerable"] or s["deception"]:
        return "full board review"
    return "expedited review"

def artifacts(s):
    a = ["protocol", "data mgmt plan"]
    if s["identifiable"]: a.append("informed consent")
    if s["deception"]:    a.append("debriefing")
    if s["vulnerable"]:   a.append("vulnerable-group safeguards")
    if s["sensitive"]:    a.append("restricted storage + breach plan")
    if s["intervention"]: a.append("stopping rule")
    return a

print(f"  {'study':40}{'route':>28}")
for s in STUDIES:
    print(f"  {s['name']:40}{route(s):>28}")
    print(f"    required: {', '.join(artifacts(s))}")
```

```text
  study                                                          route
  public corpus, aggregate stats only      exempt / not human subjects
    required: protocol, data mgmt plan
  survey of our own employees                        full board review
    required: protocol, data mgmt plan, informed consent, vulnerable-group safeguards
  newsfeed mood manipulation A/B test                full board review
    required: protocol, data mgmt plan, informed consent, debriefing, restricted storage + breach plan, stopping rule
  retrospective de-identified chart review exempt / not human subjects
    required: protocol, data mgmt plan, restricted storage + breach plan
  wearable trial, paediatric clinic                  full board review
    required: protocol, data mgmt plan, informed consent, vulnerable-group safeguards, restricted storage + breach plan, stopping rule
```

Two of these deserve comment because they are the cases practitioners get wrong.

**The employee survey goes to full review** because employees are a vulnerable
population in the technical sense: their consent is not freely given when their
employer is asking. The same logic applies to students, patients of the treating
clinician, and anyone in a dependent relationship with the researcher.

**The newsfeed experiment** is the well-known hard case. Product A/B tests are
ordinarily not research -- they are operational decisions about your own service,
and nobody expects an IRB to review a button colour. The line is crossed when
the intervention is designed to affect people's psychological state, when the
purpose is generalisable knowledge rather than a product decision, or when harm
is plausible. The 2014 Facebook emotional contagion study is the canonical
example of that line being crossed without review, and the resulting damage was
reputational as much as regulatory.

For everyday data science work that is *not* formal research, the useful
discipline is to borrow the structure without the paperwork:

1. **Write down who could be harmed and how**, before starting. One page, kept
   with the project.
2. **State the stopping rule.** Under what observed result do you halt the
   experiment? A test with no stopping rule has no harm bound.
3. **Ask whether the affected people would be surprised.** Surprise is a good
   proxy for a consent problem, and it is a question anyone can answer.
4. **Check the burden distribution.** Who bears the risk of the experiment and
   who gets the benefit? If they are different groups, that is the justice
   principle flagging.
5. **Do not experiment on vulnerable populations by default**, including
   employees, and be explicit when you must.
6. **Get an outside opinion for anything you would not describe publicly.** The
   reluctance to describe it is the finding.

Two further obligations that arise in research contexts and increasingly in
industry:

- **Secondary use.** Data collected for one study is not automatically available
  for the next. Reusing a research dataset for model training usually requires
  the original consent to have covered it, or a new approval.
- **Publication ethics.** Pre-registration, reporting negative results,
  declaring conflicts of interest, and releasing enough detail for replication
  -- which connects to the reproducibility practices in the next chapter.

> Key Takeaways
> - Human subjects research is defined by living individuals plus intervention,
>   interaction, or identifiable private information -- not by whether you work
>   at a university.
> - The Belmont principles are respect for persons, beneficence, and justice, and
>   each maps to concrete project artifacts.
> - Screening determines the route: out of scope, expedited review, or full board
>   review; vulnerable groups or deception force the last one.
> - Employees, students, and patients of the treating clinician are vulnerable
>   populations because their consent is not freely given.
> - Ordinary product A/B tests are not research, but manipulating psychological
>   state or seeking generalisable knowledge crosses the line.
> - Every experiment needs a stopping rule, or it has no bound on harm.
> - "Would the affected people be surprised?" is a practical, fast proxy for a
>   consent problem.
> - Secondary use of research data needs the original consent to cover it or a
>   fresh approval, and publication carries its own ethical duties.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Apply the screening logic above to three projects you have worked on and
>    state the route each would take.
> 2. Write a one-page harms analysis with a stopping rule for an experiment you
>    are planning.
> 3. Identify a dataset in your organisation that was collected for one purpose
>    and is now used for another, and determine what would make that lawful.
> 4. Draft the informed consent text for a study using your product's data, in
>    language a non-specialist would understand.
> 5. Interview: Your company wants to A/B test messages that increase urgency in
>    a financial product's checkout flow. Is this research, and what would you
>    require? (Hint: consider whether the intervention targets a psychological
>    state, who is most affected by urgency pressure, and what the stopping rule
>    would be.)

<a id="17-communication-and-professional-practice"></a>
## 17. Communication and Professional Practice

This chapter covers the work that surrounds the analysis: explaining a result
to someone who will not read the code, negotiating what the project is
actually for, and making the work solid enough that a colleague — or you in
six months — can rerun it and reach the same number. These skills decide
whether technically correct work changes anything, and they are the most
common reason strong analyses are ignored while weak ones get shipped.

<a id="171-communicating-results"></a>
### 17.1 Communicating Results

An analysis exists to change someone's mind or someone's decision. This
section covers how to carry a finding across the gap between the person who
computed it and the person who must act on it, without losing the caveats
that make it honest.

#### Knowing Your Audience

The instinct when presenting analysis is to describe what you did, in the
order you did it. This is the wrong instinct, and it comes from a real place:
you spent three weeks on the work, the hard parts were technical, and the
technical parts feel like the content. But the audience did not spend three
weeks on it. They have five minutes, a decision to make, and no reason to
care how the missing values were imputed.

The fix is to ask what the listener is *for*. Every audience has a decision
they own and a vocabulary they think in, and your job is to enter through
that door. An executive owns resource allocation and thinks in money and
risk. A product manager owns roadmap and thinks in user behavior and
tradeoffs. An engineer owns the system and thinks in latency, failure modes,
and interfaces. A fellow data scientist owns whether your work is correct and
thinks in assumptions and identification. The same finding — "the churn model
scores 0.81 AUC" — is useless to three of those four people until it is
translated.

An analogy: a doctor explaining the same MRI to a patient, a surgeon, and an
insurance adjuster says three different true things. The patient hears what
happens next. The surgeon hears where to cut. The adjuster hears a billing
code. None of them is being lied to, and none of them wants the other two
explanations.

```text
  SAME RESULT, FOUR TRANSLATIONS
  finding: churn model, AUC 0.81, top decile captures 44% of churners

  EXECUTIVE      -> "We can find nearly half of the customers who will
                     leave by contacting 10% of the base. At current
                     retention cost that is a 3.2x return; I need two
                     engineers for a quarter."

  PRODUCT        -> "The model flags at-risk users a month early. The
                     strongest signal is support tickets without
                     resolution, so the intervention is probably a
                     service fix, not a discount."

  ENGINEER       -> "Batch scoring nightly, 40ms p99, reads from the
                     events table, writes a score column. No online
                     features, so no feature store needed yet."

  DATA SCIENTIST -> "Time-based split, calibrated on the last fold,
                     AUC 0.81 +/- 0.02. Label is 30-day non-renewal.
                     Tenure leaks slightly; I capped it."
```

The practical technique is a translation table written before the meeting,
not improvised during it.

```python
# A finding is a fact plus an audience-specific frame. Keeping the fact in
# one place prevents the frames from drifting away from the numbers.

finding = {
    "metric": "top_decile_recall",
    "value": 0.44,
    "baseline": 0.10,          # random targeting captures 10% of churners
    "cost_per_contact": 12.0,
    "value_per_save": 340.0,
    "monthly_churners": 2_100,
}

def frame_for(audience, f):
    """Return the one sentence that audience can act on."""
    captured = int(f["monthly_churners"] * f["value"])
    contacts = int(f["monthly_churners"] / 0.10)   # decile of the base
    net = captured * 0.25 * f["value_per_save"] - contacts * f["cost_per_contact"]
    return {
        # Executives need the decision and its magnitude, not the metric.
        "executive": (
            f"Targeting 10% of customers reaches {captured} of the {f['monthly_churners']} "
            f"likely leavers each month; at a 25% save rate that is "
            f"${net:,.0f} net per month."
        ),
        # Product needs what to build, which means the driver, not the score.
        "product": (
            f"We can identify {f['value']:.0%} of churners a month ahead, "
            "which is enough lead time for an in-product intervention."
        ),
        # Engineering needs the contract: inputs, cadence, outputs.
        "engineering": (
            "Nightly batch job, one score per account, written to "
            "`accounts.churn_score`; no real-time path required."
        ),
        # Peers need what would falsify it.
        "peer": (
            f"Top-decile recall {f['value']:.2f} vs {f['baseline']:.2f} random, "
            "time-based split, label = 30-day non-renewal."
        ),
    }[audience]

print(frame_for("executive", finding))
```

Two failure modes bracket this skill. Under-translating buries the decision
under method and the audience disengages. Over-translating drops the
uncertainty and the audience acts on a number more confidently than the
evidence supports. The target is a sentence that is both actionable and
still true.

> Key Takeaways
> - Lead with the decision the audience owns, not the order in which you did
>   the work.
> - Executives think in money and risk, product in behavior and tradeoffs,
>   engineers in interfaces and failure modes, peers in assumptions.
> - Keep one canonical set of numbers and derive each audience's framing from
>   it, so the framings cannot drift apart.
> - Translating is not simplifying away the caveats; a frame that is
>   actionable but false is worse than silence.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Take a result you produced recently and write four one-sentence versions
>    of it, one each for an executive, a product manager, an engineer, and a
>    peer reviewer.
> 2. Find a technical blog post and rewrite its conclusion for a reader who
>    has budget authority but no statistics background.
> 3. List the three questions each of your actual stakeholders asked in the
>    last month. Identify what decision each question was really about.
> 4. Interview: You present a model to an executive who immediately asks
>    "what is AUC?" What went wrong, and what do you say next? (Hint: the
>    recovery and the root cause are different things; do not fix only one.)

#### Data Storytelling Structure

People remember narratives and forget lists. This is not a weakness to work
around; it is a constraint on how information reaches a decision. An analysis
presented as a sequence of findings — here is a chart, here is another chart,
here is a table — forces the audience to do the assembly themselves, and they
will assemble it wrong or not at all.

A *data story* imposes structure: a situation everyone accepts, a
complication that makes the situation unstable, a question that the
complication raises, and an answer supported by evidence. This is the SCQA
pattern from consulting, and it works because it earns attention before
spending it. The audience agrees with the situation, feels the tension of the
complication, and therefore wants the answer.

The contrast with the way analysis is *done* is important. Analysis is
exploratory and works forward: load data, look around, test ideas, arrive
somewhere. Communication works backward: state where you arrived, then show
only the evidence that supports it. The dead ends were necessary work and
they do not belong in the story. An appendix is the correct home for them.

```text
  ANALYSIS ORDER (how you worked)      STORY ORDER (how you present)

  1. pulled 14 months of orders        1. SITUATION
  2. found duplicate rows                 "Repeat purchase drives 70%
  3. rebuilt the cohort join               of revenue."
  4. tried 6 feature sets              2. COMPLICATION
  5. three models, two failed             "Second-order rate fell from
  6. the good one needs recency             31% to 24% since March."
  7. checked it holds by segment       3. QUESTION
  8. conclusion: delivery time            "What changed, and is it
     is the driver                          something we control?"
                                       4. ANSWER
  Presenting in this order forces         "Delivery time. Orders over
  the audience to hold 7 facts             4 days repeat at half the
  before hearing why they matter.          rate; volume shifted to a
                                           slower carrier in March."
                                       5. EVIDENCE + what would change it
```

The discipline shows up in artifacts. Chart titles carry the finding rather
than describing the axes, and the ordering of slides follows the argument
rather than the workflow.

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# WEAK: the title names the variables and leaves interpretation to the reader.
# ax.set_title("Repeat rate by delivery days")

# STRONG: the title states the claim; the chart becomes its evidence.
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.bar(buckets["delivery_days"], buckets["repeat_rate"], color="#4C6EF5")
ax.set_title("Orders delivered in over 4 days repeat at half the rate")
ax.set_xlabel("Days to delivery")
ax.set_ylabel("Repeat purchase rate")

# Annotate the specific comparison the sentence in the title refers to,
# so the eye lands where the argument is rather than wandering the bars.
ax.annotate(
    "31% -> 16%",
    xy=(4, buckets.loc[buckets["delivery_days"] == 4, "repeat_rate"].iat[0]),
    xytext=(5.2, 0.28),
    arrowprops={"arrowstyle": "->"},
)
plt.tight_layout()
```

One caution: narrative pressure and honesty pull in opposite directions. A
clean story wants a single cause, and real data usually has several partial
ones. The fix is to let the complication carry the mess — "three things
changed in March; two are noise and one is not" — rather than pretending the
mess was never there.

| Element      | Purpose                          | Common failure                     |
| ------------ | -------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| Situation    | Establish shared ground          | Starting with something disputed   |
| Complication | Create the need to know          | Omitted, so the answer feels moot  |
| Question     | Name what is being decided       | Vague ("how do we improve things") |
| Answer       | The finding, stated up front     | Withheld for suspense              |
| Evidence     | Support, in descending strength  | Every chart you made, in order     |

> Key Takeaways
> - Present backward from the conclusion; analysis order is not story order.
> - SCQA — situation, complication, question, answer — earns attention before
>   it spends attention.
> - Chart titles should state the finding, not name the axes.
> - Dead ends and robustness checks belong in an appendix, not the narrative.
> - Do not buy narrative cleanliness with a false single cause.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Rewrite the titles of five charts from a past report so each states a
>    claim rather than describing the axes.
> 2. Take an analysis you did and write its SCQA in four sentences before
>    looking at any of your slides.
> 3. Reorder an existing deck so that a reader who stops after slide two still
>    knows the conclusion and the recommended action.
> 4. Interview: A stakeholder says your presentation "did not go anywhere."
>    Which element of SCQA was most likely missing? (Hint: think about which
>    element creates the need for an answer.)

#### Presenting Uncertainty

Every estimate you produce is wrong by some amount. Communicating the estimate
without the amount transfers a false certainty to the decision maker, and they
have no way to detect the omission. This is the most common way honest
analysts mislead people.

The difficulty is that the standard vocabulary of uncertainty does not
survive contact with a general audience. "The 95% confidence interval is
[1.2%, 4.8%]" is precise and widely misunderstood — most listeners hear "95%
probability the answer is in there," which is a Bayesian credible interval,
not a frequentist confidence interval. Arguing about this in a business
meeting is a losing move. The productive response is to express uncertainty
in terms of the decision rather than in terms of the statistic.

Three techniques do most of the work. First, translate the interval into
outcomes: "somewhere between 400 and 1,600 extra signups per month" beats any
interval notation. Second, state what the uncertainty means for the decision:
"even the pessimistic end pays for the build" ends the conversation, while
"the interval spans both profit and loss" is itself the finding. Third, show
the distribution rather than a point when the shape matters — a fan chart or
a dot-and-whisker plot makes variance visible without requiring vocabulary.

```text
  POINT ESTIMATE              INTERVAL                DECISION FRAME

  "+3.0% conversion"          "+3.0%,                 "Worst case we
                               CI [1.2, 4.8]"          gain 1.2%, which
```
