```python
            # Sentinel values hide as legitimate numbers; they show up as
            # implausible modes at the extremes of the range.
            vc = s.value_counts().head(3)
            info["top_values"] = vc.to_dict()
            info["suspect_sentinels"] = [
                v for v in vc.index
                if v in (-1, 0, 999, 9999, -999) and vc[v] > 0.01 * len(s)
            ]

        if pd.api.types.is_datetime64_any_dtype(s):
            # All-midnight timestamps mean the time component is fabricated.
            info["all_midnight"] = bool((s.dt.time == pd.Timestamp("00:00").time()).all())
            info["range"] = (str(s.min()), str(s.max()))

        report[col] = info
    return pd.DataFrame(report).T

# Then check stability over time, which catches the drift a single profile misses.
monthly_nulls = df.groupby(df["created_at"].dt.to_period("M"))["plan_type"].apply(
    lambda s: s.isna().mean()
)
print(monthly_nulls)
# A null rate that jumps from 2% to 40% in one month is a schema change
# upstream, not a data quality problem to impute away.
```

Two judgments recur. First, decide whether a problem is worth fixing: a field
that is 60% missing and weakly related to the outcome should be dropped, not
rescued. Second, never silently impute without recording what you did and how
much — a null rate is itself a signal, and replacing it with a mean destroys
information about the process that generated it.

The most important habit is to find the person who generated the data and ask
them. Ten minutes with the operations team explaining why Tuesday's numbers
are always low beats a week of statistical detective work.

> Key Takeaways
> - Expect most project effort to go into understanding what the data means,
>   not into modeling.
> - Mess has recognizable causes — manual entry, schema drift, key mismatches,
>   process-correlated missingness — and the cause dictates the fix.
> - Profile null rates over time, not just overall; a jump is a schema change,
>   not noise.
> - Missingness is usually informative; record it before imputing anything.
> - Ask the people who generate the data; it is the highest-yield hour in the
>   project.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Run a profiling pass on an unfamiliar public dataset and list every
>    anomaly with a hypothesis about its cause.
> 2. Plot the null rate of three fields by month and explain any step changes.
> 3. Take a field you previously imputed and test whether its missingness
>    predicts the outcome.
> 4. Interview: You find that 15% of timestamps are exactly midnight. What do
>    you conclude and what do you stop doing? (Hint: some analyses become
>    invalid, not merely less accurate.)

#### Competition and Benchmark Practice

Competitions such as Kaggle and public benchmarks are a fast way to build
certain skills and a reliable way to distort others. Treating them as
representative of professional work produces a predictable set of bad habits,
so it is worth being explicit about what transfers and what does not.

What they teach well is genuine. You get fast feedback, a strong reference
point in the form of other competitors' scores, exposure to techniques you
would not have tried, and practice at the mechanics of validation — which is
where most beginners are weakest. Reading top solutions after a competition
closes is among the most efficient available forms of study.

What they distort is equally real. The problem is given, the metric is given,
the data is assembled, and the evaluation is fixed — which removes precisely
the parts of the job that determine whether a project succeeds. The
competitive equilibrium also rewards enormous ensembles for hundredths of a
point, which is almost always the wrong tradeoff in production.

| Aspect            | Competition               | Professional work              |
| ----------------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| Problem framing   | Given                     | The hardest part               |
| Metric            | Given and fixed           | Negotiated, often multiple     |
| Data              | Assembled for you         | You find and join it           |
| Leakage           | Something to exploit      | Something to eliminate         |
| Model complexity  | Rewarded without limit    | Constrained by latency and ops |
| Maintenance       | None                      | The majority of lifetime cost  |
| Result            | A score                   | A changed decision             |

```python
# The transferable skill: a validation scheme that mirrors the real
# deployment condition. Getting this right matters far more than the model.

# WRONG for a leaderboard split by time or by group — random KFold leaks
# information across the boundary and flatters every model equally.
# from sklearn.model_selection import KFold

from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, TimeSeriesSplit

# If the test set contains customers never seen in training, validate that way.
cv = GroupKFold(n_splits=5)
for tr, va in cv.split(X, y, groups=df["customer_id"]):
    ...

# If the test set is strictly later, validate that way.
cv = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5)

# The diagnostic that matters more than any single score: does local
# validation move together with the public leaderboard?
import numpy as np
cv_scores = [0.812, 0.818, 0.823, 0.827]
lb_scores = [0.809, 0.815, 0.816, 0.810]
print(f"corr(cv, lb) = {np.corrcoef(cv_scores, lb_scores)[0, 1]:.2f}")
# A weak or negative correlation means the validation scheme does not
# reflect the test distribution. Fix the scheme before tuning anything else.
```

Use competitions deliberately. Pick one for a technique you want to learn
rather than for the ranking, stop when the learning stops rather than when
the ranking plateaus, and read the winning write-ups regardless of your own
result. Then consciously re-acquire what the format removed: for a portfolio,
a competition entry is worth far more if you also state what the problem
would have required in production.

> Key Takeaways
> - Competitions build validation discipline and technique exposure with fast
>   feedback; that part transfers.
> - They remove framing, metric choice, data assembly, and maintenance — the
>   parts that decide real projects.
> - Ensembling for hundredths of a point is a competition-specific incentive,
>   not an engineering practice.
> - The core transferable skill is building a validation scheme that mirrors
>   the deployment condition.
> - Read winning write-ups; they are dense, free, and reviewed by thousands.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Enter a competition with the sole goal of building a validation scheme
>    whose scores track the leaderboard within 0.005.
> 2. Take a competition you worked on and write what the same problem would
>    require in production: metric, latency, retraining, monitoring.
> 3. Read three winning solutions and list techniques you had not considered.
> 4. Interview: Your cross-validation score improves but the leaderboard score
>    falls. What is happening? (Hint: two different explanations, one about
>    the split and one about how many times you looked.)

#### Continuous Learning and Staying Current

The field moves quickly enough that a fixed skill set depreciates, and slowly
enough at its foundations that chasing every new development is wasted
effort. Distinguishing the two is the actual skill, and it prevents both
stagnation and the exhausting sense of permanent catch-up.

The useful model is a layered one. The bottom layer — linear algebra,
probability, inference, causal reasoning, the mechanics of generalization —
changes on a timescale of decades and repays deep investment. The middle
layer, model families and architectures, changes over years. The top layer,
specific libraries and APIs, changes over months and should be learned on
demand rather than in advance.

```text
  DEPRECIATION RATE DETERMINES STUDY STRATEGY

  tools & APIs          months    learn when needed, do not stockpile
  ----------------------------------------------------------------
  frameworks            1-3 yrs   learn one deeply, others by analogy
  ----------------------------------------------------------------
  architectures         3-7 yrs   understand the problem each solves
  ----------------------------------------------------------------
  methods & statistics  decades   invest here; it makes the rest fast
  ----------------------------------------------------------------
  domain knowledge      career    compounds, and is rarely portable
                                  between industries

  A practitioner strong at the bottom learns a new top layer in a week.
  The reverse is not true.
```

A structural point about foundations: they are what make the top layer cheap.
Someone who understands attention as a learned weighted average over a set
can read a new architecture paper in an afternoon. Someone who learned the
API without the concept must relearn from scratch each time.

For keeping up without drowning, a few filters work. Prefer sources with
signal density — a well-run paper-reading group, a small number of practising
authors — over volume feeds. Give a new method a few weeks before evaluating
it; the discourse in the first fortnight is uninformative. And evaluate
anything new against a specific problem you have, which converts "should I
learn this?" into a question with an answer.

```python
# A concrete learning practice: reproduce, do not just read. The gap
# between understanding a method and being able to use it only closes here.

# Step 1: implement the mechanism from the description, minimally.
import numpy as np

def scaled_dot_product_attention(Q, K, V):
    d_k = Q.shape[-1]
    # Scaling by sqrt(d_k) keeps the softmax out of its saturated region,
    # where gradients vanish — the reason the scaling exists at all.
    scores = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(d_k)
    weights = np.exp(scores - scores.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True))
    weights /= weights.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    return weights @ V

# Step 2: test it against the library implementation on the same input.
# Step 3: apply it to a problem you own, where you already know the baseline.
# A method you have not applied to your own data is not yet knowledge.
```

Finally, contribute. Writing up a method for others, answering questions, or
maintaining a small package exposes the gaps in your understanding faster than
any amount of reading, because a vague explanation survives private study and
does not survive publication.

> Key Takeaways
> - Layer your learning by depreciation rate: foundations repay depth, tools
>   are learned on demand.
> - Strong foundations make new tools cheap to learn; the reverse does not
>   hold.
> - Filter for signal density and let new methods age a few weeks before
>   evaluating them.
> - Evaluate anything new against a specific problem you have.
> - Reproduce and apply rather than only read; teach or write to find the gaps
>   in your understanding.

> 🧪 Practice
> 1. Classify your last ten hours of learning by layer and check the balance
>    against the depreciation rates above.
> 2. Implement one mechanism you currently use only through a library, from
>    the paper description, and test it against the library version.
> 3. Write a short explanation of a technique you believe you understand and
>    give it to someone who does not. Note every question you cannot answer.
> 4. Interview: How do you decide whether to adopt a new technique?
>    (Hint: a good answer names a problem you had first, and the technique
>    second.)
